27099-reminiscences-of-queensland-1862-1:
W. H. Corfield's Reminiscences of Queensland, 1862-1899, published at Brisbane in 1921, recalls a West Country Englishman seeking fortune in Australia. An uncle from Australia, H. C. Corfield, owner of pastoral country in the Burnett district, painted bush life in glowing terms.

On a cold, foggy February morning in 1862, Corfield sailed from Plymouth Sound with schoolmate George Custard aboard the City of Brisbane, 1,100 tons, bound for a land of promise. Later memories run from trail-blazing in the north and west to the Murdering Lagoons, dedicated to the men and women who blazed the trail.
4196-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-71-jan:
January 1668 to 1669 opens, like the full year, with Captain Beckford's noble silver warming pan, which Pepys doubts whether to take. With Hewer he goes to the New Exchange, then to cabinet shops, agreeing on a cabinet to give his wife for a New Year's gift.

The two-month volume follows that gift-hunting start through office, shops, and company. Pepys's New Year begins in presents and doubts, a fitting overture to his final diary year. Readers who want the last winter in short form will find this volume brisk and bittersweet.
4197-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-72-feb:
February 1668 to 1669 sends Pepys by water from the Tower to Whitehall. It is the first time in two or three months he has gone that way by water, since he kept a coach. He calls the coach a great convenience and prays God send it propitious to him.

He goes to a Tangier committee that does not sit, a small frustration in a late diary month. The volume follows the diary toward its close, with coaches, committees, and river trips. Readers meet Pepys in his final year, still working, still noting every convenience and cost.
4198-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-73-apr:
April 1669 sends Pepys with Colonel Middleton, at Rear-Admiral Kempthorne's desire, to a court martial aboard a yacht in the river. The court tries the purser's complaints, Baker against Trevanion, his commander of the Dartmouth, in a naval quarrel of accounts and authority.

But Lord, Pepys begins, as the hearing opens its tangles, in one of the diary's last working months. The volume follows Pepys to his final entries, still attending courts and committees. Readers get the diary's closing spring, with a clerk's duty outlasting his eyesight. A court martial aboard a yacht closes the working diary.
agrippa-vanitie-and-uncertaintie-1569:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's attack on the arts and sciences appeared in English in 1569, translated by James Sandford. The Latin original, De Vanitate, had shocked readers decades earlier. Agrippa, himself a famed scholar and occult writer, turned on the very learning he practiced.

Chapter by chapter, Agrippa mocked the claims of grammar, poetry, history, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself. He showed experts disagreeing, frauds thriving, and each art failing to give sure truth. Only faith, he argued, stood firm. The book is a great skeptical performance, half serious and half sly. It influenced later doubters and shows how deep distrust of experts ran even at the height of Renaissance learning.
arnold-culture-anarchy-1869:
Matthew Arnold published Culture and Anarchy in 1869, a set of essays on English society. Arnold defines culture as the pursuit of perfection through knowledge of the best that has been thought and said. Against culture he sets anarchy: each person doing as he likes without shared standards. He sorts England into Barbarians, Philistines, and Populace by class.

Sweetness and light is his shorthand for beauty and intelligence joined. The book became the founding text of modern cultural criticism in English. Arnold's urbane wit softens a serious call for public standards. Debates about culture and education still start from his terms. It is his most famous prose work.
arxiv-2412-00269:
Henry Crumley examines what happens to a quantum system when its energy slowly loses coherence, a process called energy decoherence. The paper, from twenty twenty-four, opens with a teaching review of the classic experiments that forced the creation of quantum mechanics, including the ultraviolet problem in heat radiation and the double-slit experiment. It then explains how decoherence is usually handled and turns to a version that arises on its own inside a closed system, with no outside environment involved.

The test system couples a vibrating oscillator with spins. Using both hand calculation and computer work, Crumley tracks how the energy decoherence changes the quantum behavior, and compares runs with and without the effect. Links to thermodynamics are drawn at the end. The paper suits readers who want both an introduction to quantum theory and a worked study of one subtle effect.
arxiv-2412-03169:
Max van Horssen and Philip Schlösser constructed shift functions for Askey-Wilson math rules in a 2024 paper. These math rules sit at the top of a famous hierarchy of orthogonal groups. Shift functions step their settings up or down, revealing form and norms. The even family's shift functions are classified first, giving a firm base to build on.

Non-even versions, which drop the evenness condition, are assembled from even pieces in two unlike ways, yielding difference-reflection functions that act as shifts. The authors track when those functions restrict back to even shifts, then use them to work out the non-even norms. A limiting case lands on shift functions for Heckman-Opdam math rules recently found by others, tying two theories jointly.
arxiv-2412-18469:
Zhan Wang and colleagues proposed an origin story for superconductivity in a nickel compound in a 2024 theory paper. The layered material, a lanthanum nickel oxide, recently joined the high-temperature superconductor family, and its double-layer structure offers a fresh test bed for how strong electron interactions create the effect. Starting from a two-layer Hubbard model, the authors find a molecular Mott insulator: electrons lock into a bonding band, frozen by repulsion and strong coupling between the layers.

Weaken that coupling and electrons spill into the antibonding band, doping the insulator from within, much as chemical doping awakens cuprate superconductors. Two nickel orbitals shape the state, and an atomic coupling's effects check out under exact small-system calculations.
arxiv-2501-08969:
Takashi Moriya and a large team of co-authors report properties of six Type II supernovae found at high redshift by the JADES transient survey, in a two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. The James Webb Space Telescope survey caught these explosions at redshifts from below one to above three.

Modeling the light curves gives explosion energies and progenitor clues. Two events show high energies around three times ten to the fifty-one ergs, while four look typical of the local universe. Dense confined circumstellar matter improves fits for two events, suggesting it is common at high redshift too. Progenitor masses remain hard to pin down with sparse data, and two supernovae sit behind heavy host-galaxy dust.
arxiv-2501-15369:
Chuanyang Zheng showed iFormer in 2025, a group of vision networks built to run fast on phones. Convolutional networks read local detail quickly, while transformer focus captures global form efficiently; a good mobile model needs both without the usual memory cost. Zheng rebuilt the local part by slimming down a modern convolutional design, and replaced standard multi-head focus with a mobile modulation focus that drops the memory-heavy operations while keeping dynamic global modeling.

On the standard ImageNet benchmark the network reached just over eighty percent top-one accuracy. Its latency was near one millisecond on a recent iPhone. It beat a leading mobile rival under similar speed limits. The same design boosted results on object finding, instance splitting, and semantic splitting benchmarks, evidence that the hybrid travels well beyond classification.
arxiv-2501-15969:
Shaheer Ahmad Khan and co-workers built a plain watch system that flags chronic disease risk a year ahead in a 2025 paper. Most predictive tools lean on laboratory results, but this system works from what routine practice already records: medical history. Vital signs, diagnoses, and medications, drawn from electronic health records across multiple United States practices on the CureMD platform. For each chronic disease, three random forest models forecast risk at three, six, and twelve months before a possible diagnosis.

Internal validation used standard discrimination and F-scores, and a panel of physicians judged the models' thinking for health sense. Explanations combine Shapley values and surrogate models with a new rule-engineering setup. The authors describe rollout inside the live medical record system, aiming at decision support a health worker can interrogate rather than obey blindly.
arxiv-2502-10269:
Vasco Goncalves, Maria Nocchi, and Xinan Zhou compute a six-point correlation function for gravitons in a curved spacetime in a 2025 theoretical physics study. Their arena pairs a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space with a five-sphere, the classic holographic setting. Bootstrap methods fix such functions from symmetry and consistency alone, without grinding through the full theory.

A new ingredient joins the toolkit: operator expansions taken in the lightcone limit, combined with a chiral algebra constraint. Those tools separate the correlator into pieces that can be fixed one at a time. The authors also learn which bootstrap constraints carry the real power.
arxiv-2503-01769:
Andrew Konya, Luke Thorburn, and colleagues use AI-assisted dialogue to find shared ground between Israeli and Palestinian peacebuilders in a 2025 case study. Earlier lab work showed language models and social choice methods can surface consensus inside divided groups. The open question was whether those tools help in a real conflict setting, in the period after the October attacks that reshaped the region.

Collective dialogues gathered statements from working peacebuilders, and the methods distilled points of agreement. Even partial common ground, documented carefully, gives negotiators and funders something firmer than impressions to build on.
arxiv-2503-05969:
Beyza Kalkanlı and colleagues proposed a correction to a standard estimation method in 2025, aimed at active learning. Active learning builds a labeled training set by repeatedly choosing which examples are worth paying to label. Because each choice depends on earlier ones, the collected examples are not independent, yet the usual maximum likelihood estimation treats them as if they were, which can bias the fitted model.

Their dependency-aware version adjusts the estimation step to account for those dependencies, keeping it consistent with how the data were actually gathered. Across several benchmark datasets the corrected method reached higher accuracy earlier in the labeling process than the conventional approach. The gains were largest in the earliest rounds, after roughly the first hundred labeled samples.
arxiv-2503-07469:
A 2025 study asked whether the heat of the quantum vacuum leaves a fingerprint on the oldest light in the universe. Finite-temperature quantum field theory corrects the cosmological constant, and inside the standard cosmological model those corrections appear as two extra density parameters. Because the corrections are computed rather than freely fitted, the framework predicts in advance that both parameters should be small, which makes any measured preference for them meaningful.

The authors implemented the modified model in a standard cosmology solver and compared its cosmic microwave background power spectrum against the Planck satellite's 2018 measurements. Scanning parameters by brute force and refining the search with machine learning regression, they found the extra terms improve the fit to the fine structure of the observed spectrum. The paper presents this as evidence that quantum loop effects deserve a place in precision cosmology.
arxiv-2503-09669:
Sangwon Jang and four colleagues demonstrate a quiet way to poison text-to-image models, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Diffusion models train on public data, which attackers can seed with doctored examples. The authors' Silent Branding Attack makes a model insert brand logos into its images.

No trigger words are needed. When certain visual patterns repeat often enough in training data, the model starts reproducing them on its own. An automated algorithm slips logos into ordinary images so they blend in naturally. Models trained on the poisoned data then generate logos unprompted. Image quality and prompt alignment stayed intact in tests. Experiments on large photo datasets and style personalization data reached high success rates.
arxiv-2503-13769:
Kartik Thakral and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 on removing concepts from image generators. Text-to-image models sometimes produce unwanted or protected content. Retraining a huge model from scratch is impractical. The authors introduce continual unlearning: deleting concepts one after another, on demand.

Their method, called DUGE, uses three training goals together. One goal steers attention away from images containing the target concept. A second protects knowledge about related, allowed concepts. A third guards the model's general ability from wearing away. Experiments showed targeted concepts disappearing from generated images. Overall quality and unrelated concepts stayed largely intact. The approach may lower copyright and misuse risks.
arxiv-2503-20069:
Allyson Bieryla leads a large team reporting TOI-2005b, a warm Jupiter whose orbit is both highly stretched and unusually well aligned with its star's spin. The planet circles a bright, fast-rotating F star every seventeen days or so. It was first flagged by the TESS space telescope.

Ground-based photometry, spectroscopy, and sharp imaging confirmed the planet. Transit spectroscopy showed the orbit nearly aligned, even though its eccentricity is high at roughly zero point six. Few planets combine low obliquity with such an eccentric path, hinting at gentle coplanar migration rather than violent scattering. Near its closest approach, the planet heats to temperatures rivaling some hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2504-11969: Tania Robens surveys the state of the art for particle physics models that extend the scalar sector beyond the single standard Higgs field. The short review gives examples of investigations into such models. Its emphasis falls on processes at lepton colliders, where clean collisions suit hunting for extra scalar particles and measuring their properties.
arxiv-2504-17569:
Huajie Wu and seven co-authors build a full system that lets small flying drones weave through crowded, moving spaces with the aid of laser ranging. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Fast or sudden blocks are the hard case for such craft. The system senses and plans fast enough to run on board, with low lag. A past tool from the team spots moving things of varied size, color, and type. A plan-and-control frame then uses forecasts of where those things will go, so the drone can dodge in time. The team proves the setup in both fake runs and real flights.
arxiv-2504-17669:
Subash Neupane, Sudip Mittal, and Shahram Rahimi design an agentic health AI that respects United States privacy law in a 2025 study. Language model agents can draft reports and summarize cases on their own, working directly on protected health information. The health privacy law sets strict rules for such data, so autonomy must be fenced by anonymization, access control, and policy checks.

The authors present their design as a work in progress toward a compliant system. Getting compliance right early matters: a summarizing agent that leaks patient details would end adoption of far safer tools along with it.
arxiv-2505-02169:
Kravchenko gives a sum form for wave spread work on the Zakharov-Shabat set. The set drives both the straight and the back spread tasks. His sums stand for the Jost waves in a changed range mark. In that mark, the sums stay sound in the unit disk. Each sum term comes from a plain loop of add-up steps. The straight task thus drops to two jobs: find the terms, then find the zeros.

Zeros of a smooth task in the disk hold the key facts. The back task drops to a set of straight sums for the terms. The sought field then reads off the first term found. Tests with worked sums show the path is plain and fast. Both tasks share the same core steps in the frame.
arxiv-2505-03269:
Leon Oostrum, Bram Veenboer, and colleagues release a fast beamforming library that runs on graphics processor tensor cores in a 2025 computing study. Beamforming combines signals from many sensors into one focused stream, serving radio astronomy, medical ultrasound, and radar alike. Tensor cores, built for neural network math, offer huge speed if the signal math can be reshaped to fit them.

The library hides that reshaping from users and supports both sixteen-bit and one-bit precision. Benchmarks on two vendors' hardware measure the gains. A shared, fast beamformer saves each field from writing its own accelerator code.
arxiv-2505-08169: Morales-Amaya, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, proves that touch facts can pin down the shape of an oval, known as an ellipsoid. The work sits in the math of convex forms. Take two such ovals, one scaled from the other, with the small one inside the large. Touch cones drawn from twin points on the large oval meet in a flat slice of a third oval of the same line. The author proves a like fact for convex forms forces them to be ellipsoids.
arxiv-2505-09869:
G. Nicolaou and colleagues examine how the coarse settings of spacecraft plasma instruments distort measurements of the solar wind. Instruments of a common design sort charged particles by energy and direction in discrete steps, which blurs the true spread of particle speeds. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team built a forward model of such an analyzer, fed it a standard bell-shaped speed distribution, and pushed the simulated readings through the usual conversion steps. They then compared the recovered density, speed, and temperature with the true values used to make the data.

Limited resolution thinned the core of the distribution and fattened its tails. As a result, recovered density came out too low and temperature too high. Errors grew for cold, fast streams of protons. The authors supply a formula that predicts the size of the bias from plasma and instrument traits, to help teams judge real observations.
arxiv-2505-12469:
E. Cortés García and co-workers stated a first direct sighting in 2025 of beam trapping inside resonance islands at a modern synchrotron. Synchrotrons circulate charged tiny bits to produce bright X-ray light for tests. Curved resonances can carve the beam's motion space into islands that trap tiny bits. Even when the machine is tuned far from the resonance itself, a subtle effect that had not been watched straight in a fourth-making source.

The team examined the trapped beam's motion and traits in detail. Trapping may explain stray tiny bits that spoil beam purity and create halos around the main bunch. It could also open new test tricks for photon science. The effect doubles as a probe of the machine's curved optics.
arxiv-2505-15569:
Rinat Kashaev and Vladimir Mangazeev find that a familiar algebra from geometry secretly carries a whole family of braided quantum structures. The exterior algebra of a vector space, built from wedge products, can be viewed as a Nichols algebra, and through that lens it gains a one-parameter family of braided Hopf algebra structures. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors compute the structure constants explicitly against a natural basis built from subsets. A matching one-parameter family of diagonal symmetries then produces solutions of the constant Yang-Baxter equation, the consistency condition at the heart of integrable systems and knot theory.

The authors conjecture that these solutions generate the two-variable Links-Gould polynomial invariants of links, which are tied to a super-quantum group. Small cases were checked by direct computation and matched. The exterior algebra case requires the space to have dimension at least two.
arxiv-2505-19169:
Ryosei Hara and colleagues rebuild a user's hand as a three-dimensional mesh from an event camera worn on the head. Ordinary cameras fail here in the dark and blur during fast motion. Event cameras report brightness changes with extreme speed and range, but they also fire on moving backgrounds and camera shake. Earlier event methods assumed still rooms and fixed cameras. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's method first segments the hand region from the event stream. That module strips away dynamic background events before reconstruction begins.

On a standard egocentric hand data set, the approach cut the joint position error by well over two fifths against prior methods, the authors report. The gain is credited to the segmentation front end. Head-worn hand tracking matters for augmented and virtual reality, where hands are the controllers.
arxiv-2505-20269:
Levi Cordeiro Carvalho, Saulo A. F. Oliveira, and Thiago Alves Rocha published a computer science paper in 2025 on explaining neural network decisions. Logic-based explanations can carry correctness guarantees. Turning a network into logical rules is the slow, hard step. Different encodings of the same network may change that cost.

The authors compared two ways of encoding networks as constraints. One encoding was already used for explanations in earlier work. The other was adapted here and needs fewer variables. Building the logical form ran notably faster with the adapted encoding. Overall explanation time also improved by a clear margin. Run times for single explanations were otherwise similar. Leaner encodings may help explanations scale to bigger networks.
arxiv-2506-18269:
Min Yin, Haoyu Liu, Boyi Lian, and Chunlei Chai introduce Co-Persona for building user personas from social media. Their twenty twenty-five study joins language models with expert checks. A Chinese maker of bedside lamps serves as the case study. The goal is scale without losing a real sense of users.

The team processed tens of millions of posts from Xiaohongshu. Language processing sorted posts, and experts validated the results. Five personas emerged from bedtime behavior patterns. The groups ranged from health-focused users to parents and heavy workers. Each group showed distinct pre-sleep habits and product wishes. The authors argue the method can guide marketing and product choices.
arxiv-2506-20769:
Katalin Ferenc and colleagues published a software paper in 2025 introducing a tool called inMOTIFin. The tool simulates DNA regulatory sequences for bioinformatics research. Testing methods that read gene control patterns needs artificial data with known answers. Existing simulators were often rigid or hard to plug into pipelines.

inMOTIFin is a lightweight Python package built for flexibility. Users can create sequences and place motif instances with exact positions and spacing. They can also edit real sequences directly. The authors show three uses for the tool. It can benchmark motif discovery, test how factors cooperate, and support explanations of deep learning models. The package is public on the Python package index.
arxiv-2507-03069:
Yuxuan Zhang, writing alone in twenty twenty-five, argues that human feedback for language models should be read as rich text, not just yes-or-no tags. Tags cost a lot to get and hide how users truly vary. Zhang notes that happy and unhappy replies show steady word patterns across users, so free-form notes hold more signal than tags keep.

The new method, called ARF, turns free notes into smooth score paths over time. A new search rule, TraceBias, then trains the model to chase those paths. Tests across models and topic fields beat two top past methods. Gains in fit with human wants reached a clear margin in the best cases.
arxiv-2507-04369:
Wang and co-authors build a fusion system that helps self-driving sensors spot objects in 3D. Camera and LiDAR data each miss part of the scene. Joining them well needs speed, long-range context, and full detail at once. Past methods traded one of those for the others. The team uses Mamba blocks, a fast sequence model, to fuse the streams densely. Their tests showed naive use of such fast methods can hurt results.

The team traced the loss to height data dropped when the streams were aligned. Their fix encodes LiDAR height faithfully before fusion. With that, a pure Mamba design reached top detection scores while staying efficient. The work shows detail care matters as much as model choice.
arxiv-2507-04869:
Philipp Weder extended a foundational study result in 2025 from flat domains to curved ones. Part-based Sobolev spaces measure functions with a part-based degree of smoothness. And a domain is an extension domain when every such function on it can be prolonged to the whole space without losing smoothness or blowing up in size. Lipschitz domains in Euclidean space have long been known to qualify; many real problems, though, live on surfaces.

Weder proves that Lipschitz subsets of compact Lipschitz submanifolds are extension domains too, adapting the classic building through local coordinate charts that flatten the manifold piece by piece. Every estimate tracks clearly how the constants depend on the size of the region being extended. A detail the paper stresses because numeric study, above all geometry simplification for computation, needs exactly that dependence to certify its errors.
arxiv-2507-08469:
Melissa Pesce-Rollins, Alexander MacKinnon, and colleagues report energetic ion production during a solar flare in a 2025 space physics study. The flare, rated in the middle class of flare strength, erupted from a flux rope in a region with several magnetic null points. Instruments recorded gamma rays at high energies alongside hard X-rays and microwaves with a fast rise and slower decay.

The high-energy emission during the main phase showed two peaks. The second peak was about three times stronger than the first, which had followed the X-ray and microwave peak. Such timing clues reveal how and where the flare accelerated ions so efficiently.
arxiv-2507-09169:
Anirban Chatterjee and Yungui Gong analyze a cosmology where dark energy and dark matter exchange energy, with the exchange rate modulated by the curvature of spacetime itself. The dark energy is a quintessence field rolling down an exponential slope, and the coupling grows with the field's speed and the matter density, then bends with the Ricci curvature term. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair recast the cosmic equations as an autonomous dynamical system and map its stable resting points, hunting for non-phantom accelerating states the universe could settle into. The curvature knob proves powerful: turning it up flips some attractors into repellers.

Perturbation analysis tracks how matter clumps grow, and the computed expansion history and distance measures agree well with observations. The field's tracking behavior addresses the coincidence puzzle of why dark energy matters now. For moderate settings, structure keeps growing into the future.
arxiv-2507-16569:
Rahul Khorana builds optimal transport tools for data living on cell complexes, structures richer than graphs that include faces and volumes. Machine learning on such CW complexes lacks suitable methods. He derives an explicit expression for the Wasserstein distance between signal distributions on a cell complex in terms of a Hodge-Laplacian matrix.

That formula gives a structurally meaningful way to compare complexes and defines the optimal transport map between distributions. He extends the fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which mixes feature and structure information, to cell complexes. Finally he introduces new kernels over probability measures on complexes, based on the dual formulation of optimal transport, enabling kernel methods for this data type.
arxiv-2507-19569:
Leuchs and Sánchez-Soto trace the history of a puzzle at the heart of quantum electrodynamics: the vacuum is not empty. Evidence points to zero-point fluctuations and a sea of virtual pairs. The vacuum even carries Maxwell's displacement current. Yet the theory, for all its success, works by approximation. Its math breeds singularities and runaway values. A direct calculation of the fine-structure constant blows up to infinity.

What can be pinned down is how that constant changes with energy. That running is a triumph of the theory despite its gaps. The article reviews past efforts to outgrow the limits and looks at current attempts. A simple vacuum model anchors the tale.
arxiv-2508-10869:
Sushant Gautam and four colleagues describe Medico 2025, a research challenge on visual question answering for gastrointestinal imaging, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The challenge belongs to the MediaEval task series. Systems must answer clinical questions about endoscopy images and explain their reasoning in ways doctors can judge.

The benchmark is the Kvasir-VQA-x1 dataset, built from 6,500 images and 159,549 complex question-answer pairs. One subtask covers answering varied visual questions. The other asks models to generate multimodal explanations that support clinical decisions. Scoring mixes quantitative metrics with expert review of explainability. The organizers aim to push medical image AI toward answers clinicians can actually trust.
arxiv-2508-17369:
Sebastian Andres, Martin Slowik, and Anna-Lisa Sokol proved in 2025 that a random discrete field settles into a smooth universal limit, even in a messy environment. They study the discrete Gaussian free field on random subgraphs of the integer lattice, including percolation clusters, where each edge carries a random conductance. Those conductances may be unbounded, subject only to a moment condition, and the underlying graph itself is irregular.

Their main result shows that for almost every environment, the rescaled field converges in law to the continuum Gaussian free field. They also prove a scaling limit for the field's covariances. The covariance result rests on a quenched local limit theorem for the Green's function of the associated random walk, with boundary conditions imposed. Such theorems reassure physicists that continuum models honestly describe large random discrete systems.
arxiv-2509-00269:
Maria Parelli, Michael Oechsle, Michael Niemeyer, Federico Tombari, and Andreas Geiger present 3D-LATTE in 2025, a training-free method to edit 3D assets from text instructions. Making 3D assets with diffusion models has leapt ahead, but editing them by instruction lags far behind. Prior methods lean on 2D priors, which give edit signals that clash across views.

Their method works inside the latent space of a native 3D diffusion model, so geometry is manipulated directly. Attention maps from generation are blended with the source object to guide the edit. Geometry-aware guidance, a spectral tweak in the frequency domain, and a refinement step add precision. Tests show high-fidelity edits across many shapes and edit types.
arxiv-2509-00369:
I. V. Solovyev, working alone, shows in 2025 that some antiferromagnets with a center of symmetry can be cast as simple ferromagnets. A ferromagnet breaks time-reversal symmetry, the symmetry that flips the arrow of time. That break yields effects such as the anomalous Hall effect and orbital magnetism. Some antiferromagnets, whose spins cancel out as a whole, break the same symmetry while they keep spatial inversion.

The question is whether such a state can be written in the simplest ferromagnetic form, in a cell with just one magnetic site. Solovyev shows it can. A special form of the spin-orbit interaction in an antipolar lattice makes the rewrite work, since inversion symmetry constrains that interaction into the needed shape. The result reframes how such magnets might be modeled and probed. The point matters for labs that hunt these states in real materials.
arxiv-2509-01069:
White dwarfs are the dense remains left when most stars die, and some form when two stars merge instead. Huahui Yan, with seventeen co-authors, reports a magnetic white dwarf found in a young star cluster called RSG 5. The cluster is only about thirty-five million years old, which sets a tight limit on how fast the dwarf formed.

The dwarf weighs less than expected for a star born alone, and it spins in about six and a half minutes. Its surface magnetic field is very strong, at least two hundred million gauss. Yan and the team read these traits as signs of a binary merger, where two stars joined. The find shows mergers can make magnetic dwarfs very early.
arxiv-2509-01269:
Regional climate records are less studied than global ones, especially in developing countries, yet local warming shapes daily life. Mairembam Kelvin Singh, with three co-authors, models seventy-three years of maximum temperature data for Imphal, the capital of Manipur in northeast India. Their data come from public climate records.

The team builds a hybrid model that joins dynamic methods, such as spectral analysis and Fourier decomposition, with stochastic noise terms and nonlinear feedback. Noise diagnostics help separate real patterns from random swings. The analysis finds a positive rise in temperature for the region over the period studied. Singh and the co-authors present the framework as a way to read local climate variability more clearly, linking broad warming concerns to one city's long record.
arxiv-2509-01369:
How long an excited nucleus stays in a state before emitting a gamma ray reveals the strength of its internal motions. D. Kumar, with six co-authors, directly measures lifetimes for two low-lying states of xenon-130, a nucleus with seventy-six neutrons. The states were populated through the beta decay of iodine-130, made in a uranium reaction with alpha particles.

A fast timing method with gamma-gamma coincidences, using an array of eight fast detectors, gave the lifetimes. From them the team derived reduced transition probabilities, numbers that state how likely each decay is. Those values were compared with two theories: a large basis shell model calculation and an interacting boson approximation. The comparison tests how well current nuclear models capture the structure of this xenon isotope, a check that feeds back into wider nuclear theory.
arxiv-2509-01569:
Phones and wearables can track stress over months, but people report their feelings at irregular times, leaving gaps that break standard models. Louis Simon and Mohamed Chetouani study time embeddings, numeric codes for when each report arrives, as a way to model those sequences. They introduce Ema2Vec, a time embedding built for ecological momentary assessments, brief in-the-moment questionnaires sent during daily life.

The method is tested on a new task, predicting stress over time from those irregular self-reports. It beat standard baselines that slice time into fixed daily windows, and models trained on raw sequences without time-aware codes. Simon and Chetouani conclude that how timing is represented matters as much as the reports themselves when modeling human states from messy, real-world sampling.
arxiv-2509-01669:
Stefano Ciabattini, Stefania Salvadori, and Leonardo Testi ask whether small dwarf galaxies near the Milky Way could shelter planets for billions of years. Such dwarf spheroidal galaxies hold old stars and few violent events. The authors build a model from the stars' chemical makeup and birth histories. They check whether stars gained enough heavy elements to form planets and then stayed safe from blasts.

Two outcomes depend on how little metal a new planet can start with. If planets form at low metal levels, even the faintest dwarfs may have hosted safe worlds long ago. If more metal is needed, only larger dwarfs qualify, and far fewer stars host safe planets. A middle size range looks safest in both cases.
arxiv-2509-01869:
Yu Lu leads four co-authors on smarter scan paths for fly-scan X-ray microscopy. In fly-scan mode, the probe moves without stopping, cutting scan time versus step by step grids. Not all image regions matter equally, yet standard fly-scans treat them alike. The team instead steers the scan toward regions of interest and fills the rest by image completion.

Each round scores the current image to place anchor points near promising regions. An objective then tunes those points, and the shortest path links them for the next scan. Fresh data update the picture before the next round begins. The loop shortens scans and may lower X-ray dose while keeping key detail sharp. It also drops the need for large training sets.
arxiv-2509-01969:
Zain Khan leads seven co-authors on mediation analysis when sample selection biases the data, applied to liver transplant listing. Mediation splits a total effect into direct and indirect paths through a middle factor. Here the focus is how social position shapes listing chances, partly through mediators. Listing calls are seen only for patients who finish evaluation, not all who were referred.

That selection can bias effect estimates if only the selected group is studied. Using referred group data allows an analytic correction under stated causal links. Directed graphs spell out when a reweighted mediation formula recovers the target effects. The case study lets selection depend on race, gender, age, and other social factors. Direct, indirect, and path specific effects are all identified.
arxiv-2509-02069:
Srinivas Anumasa, Barath Chandran C, Tingting Chen, and Dianbo Liu add data dependent smoothing to diffusion based protein generation. Diffusion models create samples by reversing a noising process step by step. Protein data are sparse and uneven, with a few dense clusters and vast thin regions. Standard methods ignore that unevenness when picking noise scales.

Their walk-jump framework first estimates density around each data point to set its own noise scale. A score model then trains with those per point scales baked in. Local geometry thus shapes the denoising process directly. Evaluations show consistent gains across multiple metrics over uniform smoothing. The lesson is that data aware noise prediction matters for sparse, high dimensional generation.
arxiv-2509-02169:
Luis J Goicoechea and Vyacheslav N Shalyapin report strong microlensing driven color change in a doubly imaged quasar. Gravitational lensing splits the quasar light into two images with a time delay of about four months. Microlensing by stars in the lens galaxy can tint one image as it crosses caustics. Long term spectro-photometric monitoring was designed to catch exactly such events reliably.

Delay corrected spectral ratios in the latest epoch show a dramatic changing look versus prior years. The ongoing event spans several years of monitoring data. Follow-up in coming years promises rich returns while the event lasts. Such rare catches can reveal the structure of the innermost accretion flow around the central black hole. Test and auxiliary data support the robustness of the detection.
arxiv-2509-02569:
Emily Dodwell wrote a 2025 solo algebraic geometry paper on tropical geometry inside torus bundles. Tropicalisation turns algebraic curves into weighted graphs, and a balancing condition at each vertex normally constrains those weights.

Dodwell shows the usual condition breaks when the bundle is twisted rather than trivial. The failure is measured exactly by first Chern classes, numerical invariants of the line bundles that build the space. A geometric view treats the weights as coming from intersection theory, where relations among divisors force the corrected balance law. The result extends tropical methods to a wider family of spaces.
arxiv-2509-02669:
Marc Riembau and Minho Son wrote a 2025 particle physics paper on the energy density created by a vector current in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. A single parameter describes that density, and unitarity confines it between two extreme values reached by free theories.

Confinement, the process that binds quarks into ordinary matter, changes fermionic matter into scalar-like behaviour. The authors reconstruct how the correlator flows between its extremes as that change happens. Two tools cover different regimes: perturbative calculations for weak coupling and chiral perturbation theory for low energies. The observable can be extracted from data already available, which makes the theoretical flow testable. The paper links an abstract bound to a concrete, measurable quantity.
arxiv-2509-03369:
A. V. Bednyakov, A. S. Fedoruk, and D. I. Kazakov analyzed renormalization-group methods for the Standard Model in 2025. Renormalization-group equations track how the model's coupling strengths change with energy, a key tool for high-energy behavior. The authors review the classic one-loop equations and then compare state-of-the-art results across loop orders.

Most comparisons count loops diagonally, treating all coupling families at the same order. The authors also study non-diagonal countings inspired by Weyl consistency conditions, a set of cross-checks among the equations. They examine how starting values are matched from experiment and split uncertainties into parametric parts, from input precision, and theoretical parts, from missing higher orders. As an application they estimate how likely the electroweak vacuum is to decay, and trace how those uncertainties affect the estimate. Non-diagonal schemes, they argue, inflate theoretical uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-04669:
Local detail and global context pull vision models in opposite directions. Mustafa Munir, lead author with two co-authors, try to combine both in VCMamba, a 2025 computer vision backbone. Convolutional networks capture fine local features well, while Mamba state space models handle long sequences with linear cost.

VCMamba starts with a convolutional stem and early convolutional blocks for local features. Later stages use multi-directional Mamba blocks to model long-range links across the image. Tests on ImageNet classification and ADE20K segmentation show strong accuracy while keeping cost linear in image resolution, offering an efficient hybrid design.
arxiv-2509-04769:
Collisions between dark solitons in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate can create long-lived breathing waves. Yixiu Bai, lead author with two co-authors, study ferrodark soliton and anti-soliton collisions in a 2025 paper. The system is the easy-plane phase of a spin-1 condensate, a quantum fluid with internal spin states.

At low speed, one pair type annihilates and forms an extremely long-lived breather that slowly loses energy. Above a critical speed, a separated pair is reproduced instead. Another pair type only reflects. In mixed collisions, magnetic structure reflects while density profiles pass through each other, separating spin and mass behaviour.
arxiv-2509-04969:
Hospital triage notes hold rich detail about injuries, but privacy rules and limited hardware block easy analysis. Midhun Shyam, lead author with six co-authors, present a pipeline for classifying kinetic-related injury in triage data in a 2025 paper. Natural language processing must run on site, and expert labelling is slow and costly.

Their pipeline fine-tunes a pretrained language model first on a small open dataset using a graphics processor. It then fine-tunes further on a smaller hospital-specific dataset using only a central processor. Careful dataset curation lets the approach classify triage records successfully with limited compute, offering a template for other hospitals.
arxiv-2509-05069:
Perfect codes in Cayley sum graphs ask whether a subgroup can tile a group perfectly by adjacency. Ankan Shaw, lead author with two co-authors, study that question for symmetric and alternating groups in a 2025 algebra paper. A perfect code is a set of vertices no two adjacent, with every other vertex adjacent to exactly one code vertex.

The authors prove no proper subgroup of the symmetric group forms such a perfect code. Using that result, they give a complete characterisation of subgroup perfect codes for the alternating group. The work settles which subgroups can serve as perfect codes in this graph family.
arxiv-2509-05269:
Eccentric black hole pairs, spiralling on stretched oval orbits, fill a new public waveform catalog from J. Trenado and three co-authors in a 2025 relativity paper. The release is the first such catalog from the Institute of Cosmos Sciences at the University of Barcelona.

The set holds well over a hundred simulations of equal-mass pairs with strong ovalness, some swinging past each other up to three times before merging. Spins are aligned and range from negative to positive values. For each run the catalog gives wave modes extracted far away, strain modes derived from them, plus the settings files needed to rerun the work with an open-source code. A Python tool helps users reach the data.
arxiv-2509-05769:
Event logs for process mining can be mined from raw machine sensors instead, Edyta Brzychczy and four co-authors show in a 2025 paper. Mines and factories record sensor streams, but the structured event logs that process analysis needs are usually missing, and raw data carry no activity labels.

Their IoT Miner pipeline cleans the data, clusters it without supervision, asks a language model to label clusters from their statistics with domain-aware prompts, and builds the event log. A new scoring metric weighs label accuracy by similarity. Tested on a load-haul-dump mining machine, richer prompts produced more accurate and consistent labels. The method makes process mining possible where only sensors exist.
arxiv-2509-06269:
Personal advice with its reasons showing is the promise of REMI, a 2025 architecture from Vishal Raman and two co-authors. Generic assistants ignore a user's tangled personal data and causal history, so their lifestyle tips lack explanation. REMI stores life events and habits in a personal causal knowledge graph and plans through reusable schemas.

A causal reasoning engine walks that graph toward the user's goal, enriched with outside knowledge and hypothetical what-if steps, then retrieves adaptable plan templates. A language model orchestrates the parts and answers with transparent causal explanations. The authors propose new metrics for personalization and causal accuracy, and report more context-aware, user-aligned recommendations than baseline language-model agents across fashion, wellness, and planning.
arxiv-2509-06369:
Rickard's derived Morita theory, a turning point in representation theory, is surveyed in a 2025 paper by Gustavo Jasso and two co-authors. Jeremy Rickard's papers on Morita theory for derived categories and derived equivalences recast when two algebras have the same representation theory at the derived level. They later catalyzed Keller's algebraic theory and Schwede and Shipley's topological one for triangulated categories.

The survey covers the main results and their descendants. Rickard's notion of splendid equivalence gets special attention for its role in Broué's abelian defect group conjecture, a central problem about modular representations. The authors also indicate an alternative proof of parts of the derived Morita theorem using completions of triangulated categories.
arxiv-2509-06669:
What a scattering experiment reveals about the forces inside a nucleon is sharpened by Víctor Martínez-Fernández and three co-authors in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Deeply virtual Compton scattering probes the energy-momentum tensor, which encodes how momentum, pressure, and spin are distributed. Standard analysis keeps only the leading-power terms.

The authors work out the next corrections, at twist four, and connect them to energy-momentum form factors beyond the familiar pressure distribution, namely those for momentum and total angular momentum. In the nucleon these corrections are not small at energies experiments can reach. The scattering subtraction constant then becomes a measurable constraint on all three distributions at once. Using continuum and lattice QCD results, they predict its size and find momentum distributions supply roughly a third of the expected signal.
arxiv-2509-06769:
Transducers, machines that read input and produce output, are lifted into category theory by Fosco Loregian in a solo 2025 math paper. Loregian defines a bicategory whose arrows give a higher-level version of transducers, extending finite-state automata with output. Objects are categories, and each arrow carries its states plus a profunctor encoding how they change.

Extending that data in the standard way, each input word yields an endoprofunctor over those states, enriched over presheaves on output words. Several other descriptions of the arrows are given, along with a Kleisli-like universal property. Links to other bicategories of computing models, including Walters' bicategory of circuits, are explored. The bicategory is treated as the loose part of a double category, whose completeness, companions, and monads are studied.
arxiv-2509-06969:
Exercise in later life, and when in the day it happens, is linked to brain health in a 2025 population study led by Wasif Khan, with five co-authors. The data come from the UK Biobank: nearly forty-six thousand participants aged sixty and over with wrist accelerometer records, cognitive tests, and brain MRI scans. Moderate-to-vigorous activity was measured in minutes per week and against the World Health Organization guideline threshold.

More activity was associated with better reasoning, memory, executive function, and processing speed, and the associations survived full adjustment for demographic, social, and health factors. Meeting the guideline level was linked to still better results. Greater activity also tracked larger volumes in several deep brain regions and in gray matter areas for emotion, working memory, and perception. Activity at any time of day helped, especially midday to evening, with dose-response patterns across subgroups.
arxiv-2509-07569:
Zakeria Sharif Ali, writing alone in 2025, presents uGMM-NN, a neural network whose neurons carry probability curves. A standard neuron computes a weighted sum and applies a fixed curve, giving one number and no sense of doubt. In uGMM-NN, each node sets its output as a univariate Gaussian mixture. That is a blend of bell curves with learnable centers, widths, and mixing weights.

This design lets single neurons show several plausible output regimes at once. It also lets them express uncertainty in a direct way. The network still scales like an ordinary feed-forward network, the author reports. It reaches performance on par with standard multilayer perceptrons on classification tasks. Its outputs also carry a probabilistic reading that standard networks lack. The framework is offered as a base for uncertainty-aware parts in both classification and generative modeling.
arxiv-2509-08069:
Shiping Ma and 2 co-authors add honest doubt to laser-based robot tracking in a 2025 robotics paper. The standard method aligns one laser scan with the next to track motion. It gives a pose, but no sense of how wrong that pose may be. Fusion systems need that doubt. Bare halls and tunnels make laser data weak, and doubt grows there.

Their method is called SVN-ICP. It treats the pose as a spread of options, not a single point. A set of samples stands in for the full spread. Noise levels are learned from the data, not set by hand. Tests plug the method into a Kalman filter, the standard tool for merging sensors. The aim is a pose that other sensors can trust at the right weight.
arxiv-2509-08369:
Weather models that learn from data are usually trained to minimize root-mean-square error, a habit Kieran M. R. Hunt argues is wrong for rain. In a 2025 research paper written alone, Hunt shows precipitation breaks that loss function's assumptions. Rainfall is zero most of the time, never negative, and occasionally extreme. A Gaussian-style target tolerates impossible negative predictions and underweights the heaviest events.

Hunt proposes the Tweedie deviance instead, a likelihood-based loss matching rainfall's actual distribution. It places a point mass at zero and a smooth tail above it. Tests in two settings, downscaling over Beijing and nowcasting over Kolkata, showed consistent skill gains. Rare heavy rain was recalled better, and nowcast errors shrank. The loss adapts smoothly across time scales, giving forecasters a statistically honest training target.
arxiv-2509-08969:
Nima Karimian Kakolaki compares identifier schemes for distributed systems in a 2025 paper. Systems spread across many nodes need unique IDs that index well. Auto-increment keys, UUID versions, and ULIDs are the main options studied.

Math for collision risk is combined with experiments on generation speed and network overhead in a simulated setup. ULIDs, which are time ordered and sortable, perform best in these tests. The author reports large gains in speed and lower overhead versus UUID forms, with very low collision risk. All code, data, and scripts are shared in a public repository for checking and extension.
arxiv-2509-09469:
Freedmore Sidume and 12 co-authors built a glioma segmentation tool in 2025 aimed at hospitals with limited computing and scarce labelled scans. Gliomas are the most common primary brain tumours, and outlining them on MRI guides diagnosis, planning, and follow-up. Sub-Saharan African sites hold little high-quality annotated data, which blocks many advanced models from clinical use there.

Their compact system pairs a 3D attention U-Net with residual blocks and transfer learning from BraTS 2021 weights. On 95 African cases it scored well across tumour regions despite limited data quality. The model file is about ninety megabytes, and each volume takes under a minute on consumer hardware.
arxiv-2509-09769:
Rutav Shah and 7 co-authors teach a humanoid robot new chores from videos of people playing in a 2025 robotics paper. Showing a robot a few examples at test time is an efficient way to adapt, yet gathering robot demonstrations by remote control is slow and limits scale. Human play footage, long and unlabelled recordings of people handling their surroundings freely, offers a far larger well to draw from.

Their system, MimicDroid, pairs up stretches of play with similar manipulation behaviour and trains the policy to predict one stretch's actions from the other. Human wrist poses are first retargeted onto the robot's body, and random patches are masked during training so the policy stops leaning on human-looking cues. New objects and rooms can then be handled from a handful of examples.
arxiv-2509-09969:
Zhitian Hou and 4 co-authors survey how large language models are reshaping legal artificial intelligence in a 2025 review paper. Legal work rewards precision and punishes loose language, making it a stern test for general models that now draft, search, and summarise at speed. The authors organise a fast-scattering field so newcomers can enter it without drowning.

Their census covers sixteen families of legal language models and forty-seven frameworks that apply such models to legal tasks. Fifteen benchmarks and twenty-nine data sets for testing legal skill are gathered alongside. A closing analysis weighs the open challenges, from reliability to professional limits, and maps directions the authors expect the field to take next. Shared resources accompany the survey online.
arxiv-2509-10069:
Christian Ikenmeyer and 2 co-authors build a bridge between two symmetry spaces in a 2025 paper. The bridge works over any field. It links a space of invariant tensors to a plethysm space. It respects the action of the special linear group in two dimensions. Such a map was known only in characteristic zero. Even there it was known only through character counts.

Their map is written down in full. It needs no assumption on the field at all. It joins a small web of such maps. Hermite reciprocity and Hodge duality sit in that web. The Wronskian map completes the set. The authors add a short proof about one older map. Over the standard basis, that map is triangular. Its diagonal holds only ones. Matching coefficient patterns sit behind the new bridge.
arxiv-2509-10569:
Watermarking the output of image-generating models needs shared tools. Leyi Pan and eleven co-authors provide them in this 2025 paper. They introduce MarkDiffusion, an open-source Python toolkit. It targets generative watermarking for latent diffusion models. That family stands behind most current image generators.

Three parts make up the kit. A unified framework gives watermarking algorithms a common home. Its interfaces are meant to be friendly. A visualization suite shows the patterns being embedded and extracted. It aims to help the public grasp what watermarking does. An evaluation module rounds out the kit. It standardizes twenty-four tools across detectability, robustness, and output quality. Eight automated testing pipelines come with it. The authors hope shared infrastructure helps researchers compare methods honestly. It could also build public consensus around watermarking practice.
arxiv-2509-11069:
Diego Jaure and Christopher Maulen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper. It studies a special kind of solution to differential equations. These are remotely almost periodic solutions. Their pattern nearly repeats when viewed far out along the time line.

The authors treat nonlinear systems with a stable linear part. Small disturbances are added to that part. They give conditions that guarantee exactly one such solution. The proof leans on an exponential splitting of the linear system. It also uses a matching property of the system's Green's function. The team then applies the result to the Brusselator. That is a classic model of chemical reactions. They obtain the special solutions for a version with time-varying coefficients.
arxiv-2509-11469:
Chinonso Onah and Kristel Michielsen ask when quantum computers could help route delivery vans. This 2025 quantum computing paper takes on the capacitated vehicle routing problem. It is a classic hard task. Claims of early quantum edge need a fair, open test.

Their frame counts resources in closed form. Any encoding and any hardware profile can be fed in. Three go-or-no-go figures sum up the verdict on one diagram. A direct mapping needs vast qubit counts. A compact higher-order encoding needs far fewer. On a standard benchmark, the gap ran to thousands against hundreds of thousands. Even the best case looks out of reach for today's noisy devices. Clever problem splitting may matter more than hardware gains.
arxiv-2509-11769:
Huaxin He and four co-authors twist the trap holding a quantum gas. This 2025 physics paper treats a binary Bose-Einstein condensate. Two superfluid components interpenetrate. The trap is a two-dimensional harmonic one, spin-twisted. Detuning varies with position, polarizing the edges.

The ground state falls into three phases. They are separated, polarized, and mixed. The Rabi coupling between components governs the split. The ratio of inter- to intra-component interactions matters too. Twisting matters as well. In the mixed phase, the condensate shows a finite spin-scissors response. The local density approximation describes it well. Dynamics in the mixed phase beat in a stable period. Stronger interactions route the system through damped stages first. A waiting time appears, unlike one-dimensional spin-dipole motion.
arxiv-2509-12369:
Hyperkähler manifolds are rare, rigid shapes that sit at the crossroads of geometry and physics, and many come fibered by tori over a base space. Ljudmila Kamenova and one co-author study that fibration in 2025, focusing on the smooth part where the fibers stay intact.

Away from a thin exceptional set in the base, they show the smooth part carries the structure of a torsor over a bundle of abelian groups. The construction mirrors the classical Néron model from arithmetic geometry, rebuilt here with complex analysis. Their route gives an independent proof of a result first obtained by Y.-J. Kim.
arxiv-2509-12469:
Quantum gravity may smooth out the singularity at a black hole's heart. Alfio Bonanno and three co-authors derive such regular black holes in 2025. Their route is a proper-time flow in asymptotically safe gravity. Then they ask what an observer would notice.

Far away, the holes look like ordinary Schwarzschild holes. But their ringing tones deviate clearly from the classical values. Those tones are the quasinormal modes. Hawking radiation comes out strongly suppressed. So these holes evaporate slowly. That loosens limits on primordial black holes as dark matter. Their shadows still fit current observations. So do their innermost stable orbits. The authors stress that the results survive changes of scheme.
arxiv-2509-12869:
Jason Evans, Nan Li and Junyuan Lyu compute in 2025 new shifts to electric dipole moments, the tiny charge splits in particles, caused by a background of axion-like dark matter. Such shifts test whether nature treats matter and mirror matter the same.

They add one-loop and two-loop paths where the axion-like particles link to light, leptons, and nucleons with mirror-breaking links. The new shifts are large, so null results now bound those links when the particle mass is very small. The work sharpens how dipole searches can hunt for dark matter that breaks mirror balance.
arxiv-2509-13269:
Ramesh Bhandari, writing alone in a 2025 paper, explores redundancy in a modular quantum processor. Quantum operations can be disrupted by failure of a critical element, for example from a catastrophic cosmic ray event. A recently new superconducting modular architecture uses a star-like configuration, with a router at the center enabling qubit contacts across modules.

Regarding that router as a vital element, Bhandari offers a double-star configuration in which the loss of one router is backed by a second. He also examines the usefulness of the design under normal settings, when hardware has been made safe against cosmic rays by shielding or underground placement. In that case, simultaneous two-qubit-pair interactions and multiqubit gates are easily facilitated. Redundancy thus serves both resilience and skill.
arxiv-2509-13369:
Rashid Mushkani, writing alone in a 2025 paper, formalizes a right to override critical urban control systems. Machines now steer building heating and cooling, electricity grids, and traffic signals. When such a system hurts inclusion, safety, or access, the people affected can rarely stop it. Residents have almost no authority to pause it, or to push it in another direction.

The proposed Right-to-Override names who may step in. It sets the evidence a person must show before stepping in. And it defines safe fallback states, checked for each domain, that a system drops into when it is overridden. A deliberative audit method adds ready-made playbooks. The author tests the ideas in simulation. The cases are load shedding on a smart grid, climate control in buildings where occupancy is uncertain, and traffic signals run by many agents. Harm fell, he reports, while efficiency losses stayed small.
arxiv-2509-13469:
Jonathan Z. Sun and 4 co-authors review two chip-scale ways to make true random numbers in a 2025 paper. True random bits are a must for codes and secure computing, and small, low-power sources fit best on chips. Both ways use a magnetic tunnel junction, a tiny part whose resistance flips with its magnetic state.

One way lets heat noise flip a free magnetic layer on its own, and reads the stream at high speed with low power. The other uses a stable layer and fires write pulses that flip it about half the time. That also yields a fast random stream and fits standard chip flows used for magnetic memory. Both passed the standard national test suites for randomness. Both also take up a tiny area and use far less energy than older sources.
arxiv-2509-13569:
John Mendonça and 6 co-authors report on a shared task about judging dialog systems at DSTC 12 in a 2025 paper. As chatbots built on large AI models spread, judging them well has grown both more urgent and more hard. Old scores miss much of what counts, and safety checks are often narrow or shaped by one culture's norms.

The task had two parts. One asked for auto scores of whole dialogs across ten traits. The other asked for safety checks that work across languages and cultures. On the first part, the best baseline score still tracked human grades weakly, which shows how much room is left. On safety, teams beat the baseline by a wide margin on the multi-language set, yet the baseline won on the culture set, a sign that culture-aware checks need much more work.
arxiv-2509-13969:
Jonathan Stensberg and thirteen co-authors report a restless superconducting state in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The iron-based material Fe(Te,Se) has a sparse, patchy superfluid. That raises a basic question. Below its transition point, is that state truly settled and coherent? Or is it still fluctuating, as in many unusual materials?

Using terahertz spectroscopy, the team find fluctuations that persist undiminished far below the transition. They do not freeze out as textbook theory expects. Above the transition, the precursor state's losses converge on the Planckian limit. That limit is a proposed universal ceiling on scattering. Their conclusion is pointed. In emerging new superconductors, assumed phase coherence must be checked, not presumed. Extended quantum swings can dominate both sides of the transition.
arxiv-2509-14269:
Jianbin Zhang and five co-authors build SparseDoctor in 2025, a medical chat model designed to cost less to train than a full large language model. Full fine tuning updates billions of values, which takes time and money. Clinics still need models that answer medical questions well.

SparseDoctor uses a mixture of experts design, where only some expert blocks run for each input, paired with low rank adaptation, a cheap tuning method that updates small matrices. A routing step sends each case to suitable experts, and contrastive learning, which pulls like cases together, sharpens the tuning. The design aims to keep medical skill high while cutting the trainable size sharply. Tests in the study compare the model with standard fine tuned medical systems.
arxiv-2509-14469:
Seungmin Seo, Oleg Aulov and P. Jonathon Phillips measure soft biometric leakage in speaker anonymisation in 2025. Systems that hide who spoke should also hide traits such as age range, dialect, sex and speaking style. Most evaluations check identity recovery only.

Their Soft Biometric Leakage Score combines three checks into one number. Pre trained classifiers try to infer traits directly from anonymised speech. Mutual information analysis tests whether traits can be linked across samples. Subgroup checks test robustness where traits intersect. Applied with public classifiers to five de identification systems, the score found leakage in every system tested. Voice privacy tools thus need trait level audits, not just name hiding checks.
arxiv-2509-14769:
Marija Brkic and four co-authors benchmark small vision language models on video in 2025, controlling how frames are sampled before the model sees them. Video question answering performance mixes model vision skill with frame choice. Different sampling strategies across studies create a suspected bias in published comparisons.

Their frame accurate benchmark evaluates leading small models under controlled sampling strategies on the same tasks. Results confirm the bias: rankings move when sampling changes. Behaviours split by data type and task type under different samplers. Fair video benchmarking must therefore report and fix the sampling recipe, or a win may belong to the sampler rather than the model. Small models matter most here, since they are the ones deployed on device.
arxiv-2509-14869:
Arnab Roy, Michael A. Schmidt, and German Valencia compare two ways of hunting invisible scalar dark matter in a 2025 particle physics paper. One way watches for a single jet recoiling against missing energy at the Large Hadron Collider, the monojet signal. The other listens underground for dark matter particles striking atomic nuclei directly.

Direct detection usually gives the stronger limits, but the authors find regions where collider searches add real complementary power. They work both with an effective field theory, where scalar pairs couple to ordinary matter through operators up to dimension six, and with a concrete model containing vector-like quarks. In that model the quarks can decay only into a jet plus an invisible scalar. Recasting current ATLAS monojet data constrains the model, and comparing the two descriptions clarifies how much trust effective theories deserve.
arxiv-2509-14969:
Jean-François Aujol, Jérémie Bigot, and Camille Castera design step sizes for stochastic gradient descent that need no tuning and no line search, in a 2025 optimization paper. Gradient descent without descent is an adaptive method that reads local geometry from gradient information alone. Bringing that idea to noisy, stochastic gradients is the paper's goal, since most machine learning training uses noisy estimates.

Their strategy uses only a first-order stochastic oracle, the standard noisy gradient source, and adapts the step size from the local shape of the objective. Convergence proofs are given under several sets of assumptions for convex problems. In experiments, the untuned method competes with baselines whose step sizes were carefully tuned by hand. Removing the tuning burden matters because hyperparameter searches often cost more than the final training run.
arxiv-2509-15769:
A. S. Serdyuk and I. V. Sokolenko bound the error of Fourier sums on a class of smooth periodic functions. A Fourier sum rebuilds a function from waves, and the error is the gap between the partial sum and the true curve. Their class, named for Weyl and Nagy, holds functions whose special derivatives stay within a unit ball in an integrable sense.

For that class they establish exact top bounds on the worst error of the partial sums. Those bounds let them write clean limit formulas for the largest gap as the number of waves and the smoothness grow. The formulas hold for any relation between those two parameters. The paper is a technical result in approximation theory.
arxiv-2509-15869:
E. Ruiz-Velasco leads a team, with the H.E.S.S. Collaboration, that sums up fifteen years of chasing gamma ray bursts at the highest energies. H.E.S.S. is an array of telescopes that watches faint flashes from particle showers in the air. From 2004 to 2019 it rushed to follow bursts spotted by other means.

Most chases found nothing, and the team turn those misses into the widest set of upper limits yet for this energy band. Comparing bursts seen and unseen at these energies, they find the seen ones are not a separate breed. They pair with bright X ray afterglows and small distances. The team also model a few bursts in full. Next tools should catch fainter, farther bursts.
arxiv-2509-16169:
When a symmetry group splits into two linked parts, the math of its action on phase spaces can spawn extra terms called cocycles. Viacheslav Goncharov studies such terms for actions where one part of the group is first reduced away, leaving an action of the other part. The work grows out of the study of surface shapes that carry a large symmetry algebra.

A general setup for the problem is given first. Then an easier route is offered to reach a classic family of cocycles for actions on those surface spaces. A simpler path to these terms helps others who work on such spaces.
arxiv-2509-16569:
Shota Maehara, working alone, studies line arrangements in a 2025 math paper. The topic is how flat lines can cross in a plane, and what counts, called exponents, say about their form. Past work by Wakefield and Yuzvinsky gave a matrix method for these counts. Maehara takes that line of work further for small cases.

He brings in a new class of two-dimensional arrangements. For these, the exponents sit as close as they can for most weight choices. He also pushes ahead with sorting the counts for a key small case. Some known results get fresh proofs along the way. The paper sharpens a niche but active corner of arrangement theory.
arxiv-2509-16769:
Prasanth K K and Shubham Sharma build a fast, clear classifier in a 2025 paper. Many real classes form several clumps rather than one blob. A single flat split handles clumps poorly. Heavy models fit clumps but are hard to read and tune. Their model gives each class a mix of flat splits instead.

The mix keeps the model open to inspection. A tuning step after training sharpens its probability scores. Tests show a good balance of accuracy, speed, and clarity. It beats plain linear models while staying lighter than kernel or deep rivals. Clear models help in fields that must explain each call.
arxiv-2509-16969:
M. S. Al Ghafri, Y. Estaremi, and M. Z. Gashti characterize special operators on a Hilbert space in a 2025 math paper. The operators combine a weight with a composition, and act on square-integrable functions. The team study forms that preserve lengths in a generalized sense, called m-isometries and their quasi variants.

They find that normal versions of these operators have only finitely many spectral values. For a key case, higher-order isometry collapses to the second-order form. Examples illustrate each result. Such characterizations help analysts predict how measurement and dynamics operators behave over repeated use, a concern in quantum and signal models.
arxiv-2509-17269:
Hadley Black and Christopher Ye study testing with polluted data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Sometimes a tester cannot sample the target distribution directly. Instead the samples come mixed with a flood of junk, and only a tiny share is relevant. The authors add a tool: a verification query that asks whether a given sample came from the target or from the junk source.

In general, samples and queries can always carry out any task that clean samples could. The paper asks whether clever tasks can slash the number of queries. For the classic problems of uniformity, identity, and closeness testing, they prove matching upper and lower bounds. The bounds reveal smooth trade-offs: spend more samples and you need fewer queries, and the reverse. The results set a clean price list for testing under heavy noise.
arxiv-2509-17369:
Guang-Xing Li and Mengke Zhao present a tool that rebuilds the depth of molecular clouds from flat sky maps. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles a classic limit: telescopes record column density on a two-dimensional map, while the true cloud spreads through three dimensions. Star formation depends on that hidden volume density.

Their algorithm, the Volume Density Mapper, uses constrained diffusion to stretch the flat map back into a volume. It splits the column density into parts at several scales and rebuilds a field that keeps the mean, peak, and spread along each sight line. Tests against FLASH and ENZO simulations show tight accuracy for the mean density. The same code runs on systems from a nearby galaxy to protostellar disks. Outputs give cloud thickness and density distributions that feed star formation studies, and the code is public.
arxiv-2509-17469:
Matteo Cancellieri leads a team of thirteen co-authors on a 2025 arXiv overview of the LongEval lab at CLEF 2025. The lab tests search systems over time, with documents, queries, and relevance judgments all changing. That temporal view matters, since a search engine that shines today may fade as its corpus drifts.

This third edition ran two tasks: ad hoc web retrieval and scientific article retrieval. Each came with a data set that captures an evolving search scenario. Nineteen teams submitted systems, which the organizers scored with nDCG and a set of measures for how effectiveness shifts over time. The overview lays out the tasks, the data, and the entries. It serves as the reference record for the edition, and as a guide for teams that want to build search tools that age well.
arxiv-2509-17569:
Daniel Quinn, Lorenzo Buffoni, Stefano Gherardini, and Gabriele De Chiara extend a generative quantum model so one network can serve many targets. Their 2025 arXiv paper works with quantum denoising diffusion models, a new frame for generative quantum machine learning. Such models learn to build quantum states from noise, but a fresh model per target state is wasteful.

Their conditioning mechanism feeds the model a label for the class of state wanted. Parameters are shared across classes, so a single model draws states from several target distributions. Simulations cover single-qubit states, entangled states, and many-body ground states. Conditioning cut the error of targeted generation by more than a factor of ten. A side study maps how key hyperparameters move the score. The result makes diffusion-style generation more practical for labs that need many kinds of states.
arxiv-2509-18069:
Siraj T M and 4 co-authors track how Indian researchers who move abroad fare, and how many come back. Their 2025 study uses a large open database of scholar records over time. Moves abroad can grow a career and spread skill, but a home country can lose talent for good.

Close to a third of the tracked scholars moved at least once, most often to the US or Europe. More than seven in ten of those who left never came back. Movers gained in citation impact and in foreign co-work, and folk who did return kept strong world links. Most movers came from top Indian schools.
arxiv-2509-18469:
Brain data often curl around curved shapes rather than lying flat in a grid. Han-Lin Hsieh and Maryam M. Shanechi present a new way to shrink such data while honoring its curve. Their 2025 paper extends a classic tool, probabilistic principal component analysis, to data spread around a known nonlinear surface. The new method is called PGPCA, with G for geometric.

First, a surface is fit to the data. The method then builds two coordinate sets: one flat, and one tied to the surface that tracks distance from it and noise. A data-driven learning routine finds the model settings. In simulations and real brain data, PGPCA modeled curved spreads better than the flat version. It can also test whether the curved view truly fits better. The tool reduces size while keeping the geometry that matters for neural analysis.
arxiv-2509-19069:
Young stars are wrapped in dust and gas, and their shapes in telescope images change as they age. David Hernandez and seven co-authors set out to link how young stellar objects look with how far along they are. Age classes today rest mostly on the spread of a star's light across wavelengths, yet shape itself carries age clues too. The work sits inside the NEMESIS project, which revisits star formation with machine learning.

The team gathered survey images for about ten thousand candidate young stars in the Orion star-forming region. A self-organizing map, an unsupervised learning method, sorted the images into a grid of typical shapes, using near- and mid-infrared views. They then estimated which shapes best match each age class.
