The shape grids, built from data alone, show that appearance does track stage, with limits, laying groundwork for a future combined shape-and-light classification.
arxiv-2509-19269:
Conceptual spaces describe things by meaningful dimensions, like sweetness for foods, and cognitive science uses them to model how minds organize ideas. Nitesh Kumar and two co-authors extract such spaces from large language models. Models seem to encode perceptual features well, but turning that knowledge into an explicit dimensional map has been missing. Their trick is to represent each feature by the embedding of a prototype description, like a very sweet food for the sweetness axis.

Fine-tuning aligns those prototype embeddings with the true dimension directions. Tests find the approach highly effective at recovering conceptual dimensions. The authors frame the method as a step toward explainable AI grounded in human-like concepts. Instead of opaque vectors, a model's knowledge could be read along named, graded axes. That would let users inspect why a model groups things as it does.
arxiv-2509-19469:
Rohan Surana and six co-authors built MusiCRS, a test set for chat-based music advice. Most past tests judge picks from text alone. Music picks, though, depend on how a song sounds. The team linked real Reddit chats to the songs named in them. The set holds 477 chats across styles such as classical, hip-hop, jazz, metal, and pop.

Each chat can be tested three ways: sound only, words only, or both together. The team ran audio models, search models, and older methods on the set. Systems often did worse when sound and words were mixed than when they used one alone. That gap shows how hard it is for models to tie talk about music to the sound itself. The data and code are shared in public.
arxiv-2509-19969:
Squeezing a layered crystal can flip its structure, and morphology decides how cleanly the flip happens. Shiyu Feng and six co-authors press few-layer indium selenide inside a diamond anvil cell to sixty gigapascals. Raman spectroscopy tracks the lattice vibrations under load. Atomic force microscopy and Raman together gauge each flake's thickness.

The thin flakes follow the same structural sequence as bulk powder. One transition, though, fires abruptly in flakes where the bulk smears it across a wide pressure range. The authors blame specimen form: single crystal versus powder. Their method for high-pressure Raman work on tiny flakes is part of the contribution. Phase-change materials serve memory and switching devices, so knowing which form flips sharply matters.
arxiv-2509-20069:
Roads flex under rolling wheels, and simulating that flex fast enough for a digital twin demands shortcuts. Atul Anantheswar and five co-authors merge two: a moving-frame formulation that follows the load, and model order reduction that shrinks the system. Their combined MORALE method handles both elastic and viscoelastic materials. Pavement structures under moving loads are the test case.

Speed and efficiency gains are significant, the authors report. A digital twin must answer what-if questions while the real road is in service. Full simulations cannot keep that pace. Reduced models that respect the moving load's physics can. The work targets roadway infrastructure, where twins could schedule maintenance before failures surface. The formulation is the contribution; pavements are its proving ground.
arxiv-2509-20369:
Workforce training in data science is the setting for VITA, a teaching platform described by Fadjimata Anaroua and three co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Its chatbot tutor, BotCaptain, gives dialogic help inside an adaptive learning system. The design aims at reflective reasoning rather than quick answers. Integrity-aware assessment patterns guard the value of the exercises.

Chat logs are converted into standard experience statements that feed instructor dashboards. Those dashboards flag outliers so teachers can step in at the right moment. An adaptive engine routes each learner among progression, reinforcement, and remedial material. The paper compares the design with rival tutoring architectures, weighing grounding, interoperability, and deployment effort. It closes with lessons from implementation and a roadmap toward retrieval support, hallucination control, and broader course trials.
arxiv-2509-20569:
A brief seed of polarized light can plant a lasting memory in a polariton cloud. D. Novokreschenov, A. Kudlis, and A. V. Kavokin model that memory in a 2025 arXiv paper. Polaritons are part-light, part-matter states inside a chip cavity. When loose excitons scatter into one mode, the cloud condenses, and its polarization takes the hue of the tiny seed that set it off.

In their model, the cloud locks its Stokes vector, the arrow that marks its polarization, to the seed's arrow. It holds that lock far longer than any one polariton lives. The seed can be as faint as a single photon, treated as a weak first nudge. A plain score tracks how well the lock holds over time. With real-world settings, the memory lasts on a nanosecond scale. The scheme points to both plain and single-photon memory devices.
arxiv-2509-20669:
Four-dimensional shapes that shrink under Ricci flow arise in geometry and in models of gravity. Xiaodong Cao, Ernani Ribeiro, and Hosea Wondo study a special class of them in a 2025 paper set to appear in Advances in Mathematics. These are gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with positive modified sectional curvature.

The authors prove that under a sharp pinching condition on curvature, such a soliton must locally be a Kahler metric. The condition ties the self-dual Weyl tensor to the scalar curvature. They also prove a characterization result and a weighted integral gap result for compact cases. A Hitchin-Thorpe type inequality adds new limits on which topologies these spaces can have.
arxiv-2509-20769:
Tracing where an ancient object came from takes expert judgment across texts, images, and style. Tuo Zhang, Yuechun Sun, and Ruiliang Liu built a support tool for that work in a 2025 paper on archaeological provenance. Their system combines multimodal retrieval with a large vision-language model.

The system builds a knowledge base from reference texts and images. It searches by raw appearance, by edge-enhanced views, and by meaning, looking for stylistically similar objects. The vision-language model then combines the retrieved candidates into structured inferences. These cover date, place, and culture, with reasons spelled out. The authors test the system on Eastern Eurasian Bronze Age artifacts from the British Museum, and experts judge the outputs meaningful and interpretable.
arxiv-2509-21169:
Hermite processes extend fractional Brownian motion into non-Gaussian ground, and basic facts about them remain open. Laurent Loosveldt and three co-authors settle one such fact in a 2025 probability paper. They ask whether the joint laws of these processes have densities.

For the Gaussian case, order one, the answer has long been known. For higher orders it was unsettled. The authors adapt the classic three-step proof: split the determinant into conditional terms, prove strong local nondeterminism, and show non-degeneracy. Malliavin calculus carries these steps into the Hermite setting, with a new determinant identity for the Malliavin matrix. The Bouleau-Hirsch criterion then gives absolute continuity. Densities matter because they justify statistical methods that assume smooth laws.
arxiv-2509-21369:
Servicing a hundred charging stations across Istanbul is a routing problem shaped by traffic and density. Its authors are Onur Yenigun and 2 co-authors. Charge point operators must service large station networks in mega cities. Poor planning of field staff wastes time and raises costs. Istanbul adds dense population, heavy traffic, and limited resources. The study presents an integrated method to optimize maintenance planning.

Charging stations are grouped by geographic proximity with K-means clustering. A genetic algorithm then finds short routes between clusters. The method was built in Python. It was applied to a data set of one hundred charging stations in Istanbul. The aim is sustainable management of charging infrastructure as electric vehicle use grows rapidly in large cities.
arxiv-2509-21569:
Multi photon correlations from quantum emitters in vibrating environments exceed standard theory. Mateusz Salamon and 3 co-authors build a Markovian framework for them in a 2025 paper. The quantum regression theorem cannot handle these correlations. Their target is frequency resolved correlation functions for any photon number. A driven semiconductor quantum dot serves as the test system.

The framework gives a tractable description of phonon effects on fluorescence beyond the single photon spectrum. It captures the phonon sideband, which conventional treatments miss. Rich phonon induced structure appears in the filtered two photon spectrum. Photons emitted through the sideband inherit second order coherence properties of the Mollow triplet. The result extends photon correlation theory for solid state emitters.
arxiv-2509-21769:
Bo Feng and four co-authors present a new way to simplify Feynman integrals in this 2025 paper. Such integrals sit at the heart of particle physics calculations, and the multi-loop ones are notoriously hard. The standard approach builds huge systems of relations that grow explosively with the size of the problem. Their method aims to cut every integral down to a small set of master integrals.

The key tool is a generating function, a single object that packages many integrals at once. Equations for that function yield step-by-step rules for reducing the integrals one by one. The team turns those rules into an efficient algorithm. It avoids the blow-up of the older relation-based approach. That makes it possible to reduce high-rank, multi-loop integrals that modern precision calculations in quantum field theory depend on.
arxiv-2509-21869: Hong Wang and Shukun Wu work in harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory. Their 2025 paper proves two-ends Furstenberg estimates in the plane. The estimates concern a Katz-Tao set of lines, a family of lines whose overlap is controlled at every scale, with a general dimension parameter. Furstenberg-type estimates bound how much a set of lines can concentrate, and the two-ends condition is a strengthening used in modern work on projection and incidence problems.
arxiv-2509-21969:
Lang Yu and Nanjing Huang present a faster algorithm for recovering sparse signals in this 2025 mathematics paper. Sparse recovery rebuilds a signal with few nonzero parts from limited measurements, and it works better when the penalty term is nonconvex and ratio-shaped rather than plain. The authors study one such penalty, built from a ratio of two norms, which is scale-invariant and hard to optimize directly.

Within a standard framework called the null space property, they first pin down when exact and stable recovery is possible. For the practical, unconstrained version of the problem, they design a solver based on the alternating direction method of multipliers, with a splitting strategy. They prove it converges globally and at a linear rate under stated assumptions. Tests across noise levels and measurement setups beat existing methods. Trials on pruning neural networks also improved prediction accuracy while making the networks sparser.
arxiv-2509-22169:
Kirsten Odendaal, Neela Kaushik, and Spencer Halverson combine three known tools to make image generators easier to steer. StyleGAN produces images with a well-organized inner space of controls. DragGAN lets a user drag points on an image and have the picture follow. Principal component analysis squeezes data down to its main directions. Their 2025 paper, DragGANSpace, weaves the three together and tests the blend on a data set of high-quality animal faces.

Adding the squeezed representation inside DragGAN's working layers cut the total editing time while keeping visual quality high. In shallower layer settings, the similarity of the edited images to their targets even improved. The team also aligned images from two StyleGAN models trained on sibling domains, dogs and cats. The authors present the result as a route to faster, more interpretable control of generated images for editing work.
arxiv-2509-22669:
Paramahansa Pramanik, Joel Graff, and Mike Decaro dissect a usage-based pricing scheme for a medical portal. The portal is the Intelligent Medical Objects ProblemIT service used by eClinicalWorks clients. Their framework first sets a stable monthly unit price per request. That price is the median from semi-parametric Bayesian smoothing spline analyses over a period spanning late 2015 to late 2016.

Clients then fall into eight volume-based tiers. Each client's charge is the unit price times its total request count. The data hold anomalies: hundreds of accounts with one or two registered users show disproportionately high request volumes. The proposed model builds in adjustments for those outlier accounts.
arxiv-2509-22969:
Some data arrive as curves, not points, and each case holds several curves at once. Samuel Singh, Shirley Coyle, and Mimi Zhang cluster such multi-dimensional functional data by shape. Their framework, FAEclust, uses a deep functional autoencoder. It squeezes each curve set into a code and rebuilds it, even on curved spaces. New penalty tricks steady the training.

A clustering loss joins the training goal, so codes form with grouping in mind. The shape-informed part makes clusters resist shifts in curve timing. The team prove their decoder can approximate any target map. Wide tests check how well the method works in practice.
arxiv-2509-23069: Markov chains can show a cutoff, a sudden drop from far-from-random to nearly random. Lucas Teyssier asks which cutoff shapes can occur at all. He introduces fruit-inosculated-tree Markov chains as a flexible source of examples. Their parameters are easy to tune. With them, he proves a sweeping claim. Every cutoff profile is possible, at any cutoff time and with any window size.
arxiv-2509-23369:
A binary code for algebra basis elements ties a wide family of algebras to one simple operation. Derek Courchesne and Sébastien Tremblay build that link for multicomplex and Clifford algebras. Multiplier and index functions form the framework. The componentwise XOR operation mirrors the algebra structure in binary form. The result holds in any dimension for both algebra families.

Necessary conditions for a diagonal basis drop straight out of the link. In the commutative case, an algorithm-like route finds the change-of-coordinates matrix. The same frame defines an algebra of conjugate operations. Its properties get studied as a second payoff.
arxiv-2509-24169:
Task vectors are compact codes that capture a task from a few prompt examples. Haolin Yang and 3 co-authors argue such vectors should be learned, not extracted. Past work pulled them from hidden states with awkward methods and left their inner role unclear. Learned task vectors beat extracted ones on accuracy and can act at any layer or position.

The team then traces how these vectors steer the model. A small set of key attention heads does most of the steering through their output circuits. Early vectors rotate toward task-relevant directions, while later ones mostly grow in size. The picture stays largely linear despite the model's nonlinear parts.
arxiv-2509-24269:
A small slip early in a chain of thought can snowball into a harmful answer or a needless refusal. Zihao Zhu and 5 co-authors name that failure mode in safety training for reasoning models. Models trained to copy flawless scripts never learn to recover from their own drift. AdvChain instead teaches dynamic self-correction through adversarial tuning.

Its training set pairs temptation with correction and hesitation with correction, so models practice steering back from both harmful drift and excess caution. Tests show stronger resistance to jailbreaks and thought hijacking, with far less over-refusal on benign prompts. Reasoning skill stayed intact, giving a better safety-utility balance.
arxiv-2509-24369:
Maps that turn satellite views into street-level scenes must keep geography consistent across a huge change in viewpoint. Khawlah Bajbaa and 5 co-authors built a hybrid framework that joins Stable Diffusion with a conditional adversarial network. Diffusion alone struggled with consistency, while adversarial models alone had their own limits.

A multi-stage training plan runs diffusion as the core inside a two-branch design, with the adversarial part producing panoramic street views. A fusion step blends the strengths of both. On the standard cross-view benchmark, the hybrid beat diffusion-only methods across measures and rivaled leading adversarial systems. Fine details such as street markings, side roads, and clouds survived the transfer.
arxiv-2509-24569:
Josep Lumbreras studies, in thesis form, how to learn properties of an unknown quantum state online, round by round. Each round the learner picks an observable from a set of actions, aiming to maximize its expected value for the streaming state. Past results refine the picks to minimize regret, the running gap to the best possible reward.

He derives information-theoretic lower bounds and matching optimal strategies, with regret that typically grows as the square root of rounds. Applications include quantum state tomography that disturbs the state as little as possible, quantum recommender systems, and work extraction. The last shows an exponential edge over tomography-based protocols in wasted work.
arxiv-2510-00069:
Jiancong Xie and seven colleagues published this 2025 paper presenting OIG-Bench, a test of how AI models read one-image guides. Such guides pack text, pictures, and symbols into a single page that sums up a topic for human readers. The team wanted to know whether large image-and-text models grasp these dense pages as people do. They also needed a cheaper way to label test data.

The team built a labeling pipeline where several AI agents draft captions and humans then fix them. With that help they scored 29 leading models on guide reading. Qwen2.5-VL-72B did best, reaching about seventy-seven percent correct overall. Even so, every model showed weak spots in meaning and in step-by-step logic. The agent pipeline beat all the models at writing captions, which makes it useful for building future test sets.
arxiv-2510-00369:
Andrew Lundeen and three colleagues wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on producing scalar mesons with an electron beam. Their stage is a simplified scalar field model in three space dimensions plus time. Earlier work in one space dimension could not address beam spin asymmetry at all. The fuller model lets them compute that asymmetry for scattering off a scalar target.

The asymmetry turns out detectable in a middle band of momentum transfer, then shrinks where distribution factorization should hold. They derive analytic forms for the leading-twist generalized parton distribution in both of its kinematic regions. A sum rule over the two regions holds for every current component, they verify. But the neat split into valence and non-valence parts survives only for one special current component. The results give background for interpreting future measurements at Jefferson Lab and the Electron-Ion Collider.
arxiv-2510-00469:
Omid Armantalab, Jason Hawkins, and Wissam Kontar published this 2025 study of how city movement patterns change during long emergencies. Travelers split into returners, who revisit a few places, and explorers, who range widely. The team tracked those types over fifteen days in a dense metro region using a large public mobility dataset. Fine-grained data exposed shifts that coarse maps would hide.

Behavioral change took at least two weeks of data to detect reliably. During prolonged emergencies, trips back to non-essential places resumed more slowly than normal. Explorers cut their long-distance travel sharply, while weekends always looked returner-like and short-range. Residents of neighborhoods poor in points of interest traveled toward richer areas, exposing a spatial gap. The authors link the findings to the fifteen-minute city idea: stronger local access could steady life in a crisis.
arxiv-2510-01069:
Perrier proposes a formal way to check whether a language model's chain of thought is faithful, in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretability. Chain-of-thought prompting improves reasoning scores, but a rationale may not reflect the computation that produced the answer. The Curry-Howard correspondence, which equates proofs with programs, supplies the lens. Under that view, a faithful reasoning trace should behave like a well-typed program, with each step a typed inference.

Perrier maps natural-language steps into a formal typed proof structure, so a successful conversion certifies computational faithfulness. Experiments on the GSM8K mathematics benchmark gave the idea empirical support. Only forty to sixty percent of correct answers reached the strictest certification level, yet those runs achieved precision above ninety percent. Weaker partial structure was common among rejected runs and correlated with correctness. Faithfulness, the paper argues, is a gradient that typed structure can measure.
arxiv-2510-01269:
Thorat, Singh, and Nayek make reinforcement learning safe enough to practice vibration control on a real structure. Shaking damages buildings and endangers occupants, yet learned controllers must train somewhere. Training on the physical system is the honest route, but a naive learner pushes randomly at first.

A classical regulator chaperones the learner during this dangerous apprenticeship. Even an imperfect model-based guide kept exploratory forces within safe bounds. The learner still ends up model-free, having absorbed the guide's caution through experience. Code for the controller is published openly for replication. Model identification, the tedious step avoided, normally eats engineering weeks. Guidance during training, not deployment, is the safety contribution. Response history and reward weights were tuned in simulation first. Occupant safety and maintenance costs motivate the whole control problem. A chaperoned learner can practice on the real thing.
arxiv-2510-01669:
Cao and five co-authors introduce UniVerse in this 2025 computer vision paper. Their problem is rebuilding a three-dimensional scene from photos that clash with each other. Lighting may shift between shots, or objects may move. Earlier methods modeled each flaw inside the scene model itself, and they needed many dense views to work well.

UniVerse splits the job into restoration first and reconstruction second. It turns the clashing photos into short videos, then a video diffusion model cleans them into consistent images. A radiance field is then built from those repaired views. Tests on synthetic and real data gave strong results and good generalization. The system can even restyle a scene by swapping its reference image.
arxiv-2510-02169:
Safronov, McCaigue, Allott, and Martin extend software bills of materials to AI systems in this 2025 paper. SBOMs brought openness to software supply chains by listing every component. AI systems break that model with dynamic, data-driven behavior and loose links among datasets, models, and code. Their framework, TAIBOM, rebuilds the bill of materials around those AI specifics.

TAIBOM contributes three pieces to the assurance puzzle. First, a structured dependency model describes AI parts and their links. Second, integrity statements travel across mixed pipelines, so a claim about data follows the model it trained. Third, a trust attestation process verifies where parts came from. Together they support security, compliance, and assurance reviews across AI workflows. The authors argue current frameworks cannot deliver that accountability alone. Split governance makes a common, AI-native inventory format urgent. TAIBOM offers one concrete blueprint for it.
arxiv-2510-02369:
Cai and co-authors teach language model agents to learn the facts of one world. Their 2025 artificial intelligence paper names a missing kind of context. Agents usually get manuals with global rules. They also get guidance tied to each task. Neither tells them where objects sit in this place. Recipes, local rules, and locations decide success in complex tasks. The team calls these reusable facts instance-level context. Their method, AutoContext, explores to gather facts. A TODO forest steers the search under tight budgets. Found facts get validated and formatted for later use.

The gains in the TextWorld test setting were dramatic. A simple ReAct agent jumped from thirty seven percent success to ninety five. A top exploration method also improved when paired with AutoContext. Facts about one world transfer across many tasks there. Agents stop failing for knowable, checkable reasons. The approach needs no changes to the agent itself.
arxiv-2510-02469:
Park and co-authors edit real driving scenes with plain language commands. Their 2025 computer vision paper presents an editor called SIMSplat. Teams testing self-driving cars need fresh scenarios cheaply. Rebuilding sensor scenes by hand is slow and limited. SIMSplat reconstructs scenes with 4D Gaussian splatting. Language alignment ties words to the objects in the scene. Users can query road objects directly by description. They can add objects or rewrite vehicle and pedestrian paths. A motion prediction module refines every path afterward. Other agents in the scene react to each edit realistically.

Experiments used the public Waymo driving dataset. The editor reached the highest task completion rate and precision there. Its range of edits beat rival frameworks clearly. An agent built around a language model runs the system. Scenario libraries for safety testing can grow fast this way. Rare dangerous cases become easy to stage.
arxiv-2510-02669:
Ma and co-authors search automatically for the best team shape behind a language model service. Their 2025 paper presents a framework called AutoMaAS. Multi-agent systems shine across many task domains. Hand built designs freeze one shape for every query. Simple and hard questions then cost the same resources. AutoMaAS treats agent structure as a searchable architecture. Operators get created, fused, or dropped by performance and cost. Settings adjust in real time as feedback arrives. Decision traces keep the search itself interpretable. The system evolves its design while it runs.

Six benchmarks tested the framework against known methods. Accuracy improved by one to seven percent across them. Cost fell well below a plain chain-of-thought baseline. On three headline benchmarks it topped the accuracy table. Math and coding tasks gained the most visibly. Self-designing agent teams cut wasted compute. The search traces also help engineers debug failures.
arxiv-2510-02769:
Kashyap and co-authors control robot-like systems on a deadline while respecting state and input limits. Their 2025 control theory paper studies Euler-Lagrange systems. Such systems cover robots, vehicles, and mechanical plants. Tracking must finish within a prescribed time bound. Disturbances push against the plan the whole way. Their controller uses an adaptive barrier design. No function approximation is needed anywhere. Updates fire only at periodic checks of a trigger rule. A time varying threshold trims triggers during transients. A proven bound on the monitoring period guards performance.

Stability analysis certifies all errors reach the bound on time. Zeno behavior, the infinite trigger pileup, is excluded. Communication bandwidth for control signals drops with event firing. Simulations and experiments showed superior tracking performance. Monitoring frequency itself trades against accuracy visibly. Factories want guarantees with less chatter on the wire. This design delivers both in one package.
arxiv-2510-02869:
Rusnak asks what it means for a machine to recognize beauty. Beauty feels personal and cultural, yet it guides art across ages. Deep learning systems now seem to model taste with skill. Rusnak draws on studies of how models represent the world. Different models, trained on different data, often converge on like internal maps. He asks whether beauty drives a stronger version of that merging.

His answer is yes for beautiful images. Pretty images produced more aligned internal maps across models. Plain images did not show that extra alignment. That hints that beauty has a real structure, not just social habit. Rusnak roots that structure in both matter and culture. Humans sense it first, then shape it through creative acts. Machines can survey it at vast scale. He casts beauty as a shared attractor for human and machine work. Co-creation, on this view, is the natural path for art.
arxiv-2510-03169:
Li and co-authors plan smooth drone routes that cover every inspection point in cluttered airspace. Power grid checks increasingly rely on quadrotor drones. A good route must visit all points of interest once. It must also stay smooth, quick, and clear of obstacles. Their algorithm works in two stages. A genetic algorithm first orders the points efficiently. That ordering solves a traveling salesman problem over the sites.

A back-end stage then polishes the route itself. It bends the path into a smooth B-spline curve. Smoothness, flight time, and obstacle clearance enter one cost. A nonlinear least squares solver balances those three aims. Simulations flew the full cycle in cluttered scenes. The drone never swung into sharp angular maneuvers. Attitude changes stayed under twenty degrees throughout. Velocity profiles ran smooth with no sudden steps. Gentle motion protects both the airframe and the camera shots.
arxiv-2510-04069:
Deng and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on rebuilding CT images from very few X-ray views at low dose. Sparse scanning cuts radiation exposure, but reconstruction from a handful of projections is severely ill-posed. Details vanish, artifacts grow, and purely learned models can invent anatomy that is not there. The authors combine a generative diffusion prior with regularizers inside one iterative scheme.

Their method, TV-LoRA, couples the diffusion prior with anisotropic total variation and a low-rank nuclear norm penalty. An ADMM framework alternates between data consistency and these constraints. A slice-based strategy with fast Fourier acceleration and tensor parallelism speeds the heavy computation. On three CT datasets, with as few as two projection views, it beat seven competing baselines. It led on similarity scores, texture recovery, edge clarity, and artifact suppression. The result points toward safer low-dose scanning without diagnostic quality loss.
arxiv-2510-04769:
Michele Caprio, Siu Lun Chau, and Krikamol Muandet wrote this 2025 paper on when uncertain beliefs settle down under repeated updates. Many learning methods revise their state, from variational inference to multi agent training. When beliefs are imprecise, they are kept as credal sets: whole families of probability distributions at once. Updating a family repeatedly raises a basic question. Does the process stop moving, and under what rules?

The authors give the first analysis of that question. They prove fixed point results that say when stable resting states exist for credal updates. They also show when the updates can actually reach those states. A concrete test case comes from credal Bayesian deep learning, where networks carry sets of distributions. Adding imprecision, they argue, does more than enrich the uncertainty picture. It exposes structure that explains when learning stays stable. The results guide anyone building iterative systems on imprecise beliefs.
arxiv-2510-04869:
Abrahão and the Double Chooz Collaboration wrote this 2025 physics paper on the neutrino glow of used nuclear fuel. Reactors pour out antineutrinos while running, revealing power and fuel state in time. After shutdown, long lived fission leftovers keep decaying and emitting a flux. That signal had never been measured in quantity. The team used a detector at a French power plant, four hundred meters from the cores.

They gathered days of data with the reactors off. In the energy band where the signal peaks, they counted about one hundred six candidate events. Simulations of the decaying fuel predicted about eighty eight events. The match is close, and the signal stands at six standard deviations of confidence. Cooling pools of spent fuel near the cores add the glow. The measurement proves residual neutrinos can be counted, not just modeled. Reactor monitoring gains a tool that works when the reactor sleeps.
arxiv-2510-04969:
Satrio Pambudi and Filippo Menolascina aim to match patients to the right medical scans in this 2025 arXiv paper. Doctors follow the ACR Appropriateness Criteria, a huge guideline library for imaging choices. In practice, those guidelines are underused because patient stories arrive as free text. Mapping a story to the right guideline entry is slow, manual work.

Their multi-agent system reads a clinical narrative and retrieves matching guidelines automatically. A fine-tuned retriever, trained on 8,840 synthetic scenario pairs, found the right entries with a top-10 recall of about 94 percent in their tests. Language-model agents then pick and justify a final recommendation. The full system matched the guideline's exact procedure set in 81 percent of test cases. That beat a strong GPT-4.1 baseline by 67 points.
arxiv-2510-05069:
Dachuan Shi and six co-authors make AI reasoning both sharper and cheaper in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models can reason in written steps or silently in latent space. Silent reasoning explores more paths at once but often fails to settle on one answer. Both styles can also overthink, burning tokens on easy problems.

Their framework, SwiReasoning, switches between the two modes without any retraining. A controller watches entropy trends to judge the model's confidence block by block. Falling uncertainty triggers a switch to explicit steps; rising uncertainty reopens latent exploration. A cap on switches curbs overthinking. On math and STEM benchmarks, accuracy rose by up to 2.8 percentage points. Under tight budgets, token efficiency improved by as much as 79 percent.
arxiv-2510-05169:
Guangyu Shen and six co-authors teach poisoned AI models to confess their own backdoors in this 2025 arXiv paper. A backdoor attack implants a secret trigger in a model. When the trigger appears, the model performs a forbidden action. Safety training rarely finds these hidden triggers, because nobody knows what they look like.

The team's framework uses reinforcement learning to reward introspection about the model's own behavior. The model learns to reverse-engineer the trigger behind its misaligned outputs. Surprisingly, this self-awareness emerged abruptly, like a phase transition, within a short training window. The aware model can then name its implanted trigger even when the trigger is absent. Two defense strategies built on that ability beat six baseline methods across five attacks.
arxiv-2510-05469:
Schindl compares two frameworks for a delicate corner of analysis. Ultradifferentiable functions are smooth functions whose growth is tamed by a chosen weight. One classic framework measures growth through the Fourier transform of test functions. A newer framework controls growth through derivatives, in the style of weight sequences.

The two frameworks agree only when the weight function meets a convexity condition. That condition has quietly become a standard assumption in the field. Schindl characterizes exactly when one class of functions sits inside another in both settings. He works inside a general weight matrix framework to make the comparison precise. He also builds a counterexample weight that breaks convexity and shows the frameworks diverging. The study was funded in part by the Austrian Science Fund. It restates older results in one shared language. The paper clarifies what the standard assumption really buys.
arxiv-2510-05769:
Shen and colleagues make abstractive summaries carry more real information. Summaries often stay fluent while dropping the most informative content. Cross-attention learns relevance to the source, but focal facts in reference summaries get missed. Their 2025 InforME approach steers learning toward salience.

An optimal transport method builds informative attention over the source text. It teaches the model to focus on what reference summaries actually use. A second method reduces joint entropy over named entities accumulatively. That pressure raises the salience of the entities summaries keep. ROUGE scores beat prior work on CNN/Daily Mail. Results stay competitive on the very different XSum benchmark. Factuality improves alongside informativeness in their analysis. Human judges also rated the summaries more informative than a strong baseline. The study stays limited to English news, with other genres left for later.
arxiv-2510-06169:
Lustig-Yaeger and twenty-six co-authors extract hot Jupiter WASP-17b's nightside emission spectrum in a 2025 exoplanet study. The work tests the planetary infrared excess technique, which promises to characterize thermal emission from many planets. The technique lacked validation, so the team ran it as a controlled test within the JWST DREAMS survey.

They combined NIRSpec transit and eclipse observations taken half an orbit apart. The stellar spectrum measured during eclipse removed any need for ultra-precise star models. The result is JWST's first nightside emission spectrum built only from transit and eclipse data. The nightside temperature lands near one thousand kelvin, far cooler than the dayside. That contrast supports inefficient day-to-night heat transport plus a sizable bond albedo. The spectrum also hints at nightside sulfur dioxide absorption. If confirmed, that gas would be the first direct evidence of transport-driven chemistry on a giant exoplanet.
arxiv-2510-06869:
Tim Harris and Harvey Meyer refine an ingredient of lattice QCD calculations. Their 2025 paper updates correction factors for the non-singlet vector current. Lattice QCD simulates quarks and gluons on a discrete grid. The grid spacing creates errors that correction factors, called improvement coefficients, are designed to remove.

Their earlier work had fixed two such coefficients for a used fermion setup. A new estimate then appeared for a related axial coefficient that their method relied on. The update matters because the calculation chain shifts with it. Harris and Meyer redo the analysis with the new input. They also add simulation ensembles that follow a different path through parameter space. The new estimate improved consistency between the two paths. It also agreed better with a previous determination made another way. Results are validated at two values of the bare coupling. Careful updates keep precision flavor physics on firm ground.
arxiv-2510-07069:
Hongbo Hu, Yisong Wang, Yi Huang, and Kewen Wang teach machines to learn logic programs that carry degrees of possibility. Their 2025 paper opens inductive learning for possibilistic logic programs under stable models. Answer set programming reasons with rules and stable models. Possibilistic programs add graded certainty to that reasoning, a variant in the field.

Induction means extracting a program from background knowledge plus positive and negative examples. Nobody had formalized that task for this program family before. The authors define induction tasks precisely and study their properties. Two algorithms compute solutions, one of them hunting minimal programs. Both algorithms are proven sound and complete. A prototype of the minimal version was implemented and tested. On randomly generated data with ordinary logic programs, it beat an inductive system. The work extends learning of rules to settings where facts carry weights of belief. Such settings suit diagnosis and other uncertain domains.
arxiv-2510-07369:
Danhaive and Tacchella release geko, a Python tool that extracts galaxy motion from a new kind of telescope data. Their 2025 paper supports the James Webb telescope's slitless spectroscopy mode. That mode spreads every object's light without a slit, surveying many galaxies at once. The catch is that a galaxy's shape and its rotation blur together along the spread direction. geko forward-models the whole observation to untangle the two. It combines standard galaxy brightness profiles with a smooth rotation curve model.

Instrument blur from both optics and disperser is folded into the model. Gradient-based sampling in a modern probabilistic framework keeps fits fast, around twenty minutes per galaxy on graphics hardware. Mock data tests map exactly where shape-motion confusion limits recovery. Real observations demonstrate the tool end to end. Outputs include galaxy size, random gas motion, rotation speed, and dynamical mass.
arxiv-2510-07469:
Goyal and Rosso classify the finite-dimensional representations of a quantum mirabolic group. Their 2025 paper works in quantum algebra. The mirabolic setting, classical and quantum alike, tracks a group together with a distinguished vector, enriching the usual symmetry story. The authors first show the mirabolic quantum group forms a comodule algebra over the quantized enveloping algebra of the special linear Lie algebra. That structural fact organizes everything that follows. With it, they give a complete classification of the finite-dimensional representations of the mirabolic quantum group, an explicit list rather than an existence claim.

A correspondence then matches those representations with the ones of the mirabolic Hecke algebra. The bridge is mirabolic quantum Schur-Weyl duality, the quantum descendant of the classical duality between general linear groups and symmetric groups. Explicit correspondences let representation theorists transport problems to whichever side is easier.
arxiv-2510-07569:
Singh and co-authors present LOTUS, a recommender that picks machine learning pipelines for unlabeled data. Their paper tackles unsupervised automated machine learning, a neglected corner of the field. Supervised AutoML can validate candidates against labels; clustering and outlier detection offer no such ground truth, so pipeline choice is usually folklore. LOTUS bets that a pipeline succeeding on one dataset will succeed on another with a similar underlying distribution. It measures dataset similarity with optimal transport distances that compare structure without labels.

Experiments against strong baselines favor the approach. Statistical comparison gives LOTUS a high probability of improvement over existing methods on both tasks. The authors frame it as a first step toward unified model selection across unsupervised problems.
arxiv-2510-07669:
Benhamou and Weltsch wrote this 2025 set theory paper on supercompact measures and the Galvin property. Set theorists study huge infinite cardinals through objects called ultrafilters and measures. Galvin's theorem guarantees an intersection property for normal filters on a single cardinal. The authors ask whether that property survives in the two-cardinal setting of supercompactness. There, measures live on collections of small subsets of a larger cardinal.

They prove the Galvin property fails for normal fine ultrafilters in this setting. That negative answer settles a question raised by Benhamou and Goldberg. The authors then draw consequences for ultrafilters on successor cardinals. They generalize a result about ground model sets in supercompact Prikry extensions. They also define adjusted versions of the Galvin property suited to the two-cardinal world. With those versions, they extend a theorem on filter games to this setting, answering a second open question.
arxiv-2510-08069:
Gorai, Saberi, Khouri, and Danilovich wrote this 2025 astronomy paper probing sulfur chemistry around five aging oxygen-rich giant stars. Sulfur isotope ratios trace how stars forge elements. The team used ALMA data in three bands toward o Ceti, R Dor, W Hya, R Leo, and EP Aqr. They detected sulfur dioxide and sulfur monoxide, plus their sulfur-34 forms, measuring temperatures and isotope ratios.

Sulfur dioxide temperatures ran a few hundred degrees, in gas tens to hundreds of astronomical units from each star. High-excitation lines hugged the hot inner envelope, while low-excitation lines traced wider structures. The sulfur isotope ratio came out near the solar value for R Dor and W Hya. It ran higher for o Ceti and lower for EP Aqr and R Leo. Those differences record each star's history. The survey shows sulfur species probe the envelopes' middle zones, a region few tracers reach.
arxiv-2510-08369:
Viacheslav Meshchaninov and co-authors rework how masked diffusion models generate text and code, in a 2025 arXiv paper. These models build outputs by unmasking hidden tokens step by step. Standard sampling makes each choice final, so early errors cannot be fixed. Quality also drops when only a few generation steps are allowed.

Their sampling algorithm reshapes generation around a star-shaped scheme that allows error correction. A learnable re-masking scheduler spots likely errors and hides those tokens again for revision. The method works with pre-trained models after fine-tuning just one layer, a light touch. Quality gains were largest when sampling steps were few, the costly regime for fast generation. In broad tests on text and code generation, the sampler beat or matched existing methods. Ablation studies checked which parts of the design drive the gains.
arxiv-2510-08569:
Qin Liu and co-authors evolve benchmarks automatically so leaked test questions stop inflating model scores, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Language model benchmarks guide development, yet pretraining corpora often contain the test items themselves. Models then match memorized answers instead of generalizing, distorting comparisons. Their framework, ArenaBencher, updates test cases while preserving what each case measures.

Given a benchmark and a diverse pool of models, ArenaBencher infers each test case's core ability. It generates candidate question-answer pairs with the same objective, then has a language model judge verify correctness and intent. Feedback from multiple models selects candidates that expose shared weaknesses across the pool. Iteration with in-context demonstrations steers generation toward harder, more diagnostic cases. Applied to math, commonsense, and safety domains, it produced verified, diverse updates. Difficulty rose while objective alignment and model separability improved.
arxiv-2510-08769:
Chakraborty and co-authors address admission control for 5G network slices in this 2025 arXiv paper. Slicing lets one physical network host separate virtual networks for very different jobs. Some carry broadband traffic, while others carry urgent signals that cannot wait. A provider must decide which slice requests to accept, sharing limited capacity while still earning a profit.

The team builds DePSAC, a controller that learns its decisions through trial and error, a method called deep reinforcement learning. Its reward counts both profit and delay, with penalties that push urgent slices to the front of the line. A smoother style of random exploration helps the controller settle on a stable policy faster. In tests on a simulated 5G core network, DePSAC beat the rival DSARA method on total profit. It also cut delays for urgent slices, accepted more requests, and used capacity better.
arxiv-2510-08869:
Mesana, Caporossi, and Gambs expose a hidden cost in paying people for the data that trains AI, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Valuation methods score each person's data by how much it helps a model. Used as a pay formula, they would give nothing to contributors whose data adds little on its own. Yet all data must first be collected and assessed, a cost the formula ignores.

The authors model the situation as a game between a member-run data union and a company that wants the data. The union pools its members' data and releases it gradually, blurred with noise that protects privacy. Strategies draw on valuation scores plus a bandit method that balances trying new options against using the best known. Simulations on predicting helpful reviews showed the acquisition cost is real. The union's release policy also changed how that cost fell across members.
arxiv-2510-09469:
Bharath Muppasani, Ritirupa Dey, Biplav Srivastava, and Vignesh Narayanan tackle multi-agent path finding in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many robots or vehicles must cross a shared space without colliding. Central planners with full information find high-quality routes but scale poorly, while local learning methods scale better yet often produce weaker routes. Sharing everything also costs bandwidth, hardware, energy, and privacy.

Their hybrid framework, IO-MAPF, lets each agent plan independently with reinforcement learning while a lightweight central coordinator sends only small, targeted signals. The signals flag conflict cells or short conflict paths and change as the situation evolves. The authors define an Information Units metric to count how much information the system uses. Their alert-driven design cut that usage by between twofold and twenty-threefold compared with fuller sharing, while keeping solutions feasible.
arxiv-2510-09569:
F Poidevin and a large team of co-authors, among them Jesper Sollerman, investigate an exotic supernova in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large sky surveys such as the Zwicky Transient Facility now catch rare explosions whose origins are unclear. Their target, SN 2021lwz, sits in a faint dwarf galaxy at redshift zero point zero six five and shone near the lower edge of the superluminous supernova range.

The team followed it with spectroscopy, photometry, and polarimetry across several campaigns. Its light curve rose in about seven days to a peak near five times ten to the forty-third ergs per second, placing it among rapidly evolving transients. Spectra looked more like a normal stripped-envelope Type Ic supernova than a superluminous one. A radioactive nickel power source could not explain the light curve, while a magnetar engine fit better, suggesting a low ejecta mass explosion in a low-mass setting.
arxiv-2510-09669:
Jacopo Lenti, Lorenzo Costantini, Ariadna Fosch, Anna Monticelli, David Scala, and Marco Pangallo make fake populations with real maps in a 2025 arXiv paper. Planners need fake residents whose statistics match real ones, for tasks from flood response to disease spread. Giving each fake home true map coordinates is hard, since latitude and longitude bunch up in clumps with big empty gaps, unlike most data fields.

Their method first sends the coordinates through normalising flows, which warp them into a smoother latent space. A variational autoencoder then joins the warped coordinates with other traits of each home, learning how place and traits link. The team built fake homes matching real ones in one hundred twenty-one datasets from varied parts of the world. Their checks test spatial accuracy, day-to-day utility, and privacy at once. The design beat common benchmarks, such as copula methods and uniform placement inside fixed areas.
arxiv-2510-09869:
Hamilton, Matthew Wilkens, and Andrew Piper present NarraBench in this 2025 arXiv paper on how AI systems understand stories. NarraBench is a framework that sorts narrative understanding tasks into a taxonomy, a structured map of what story comprehension involves. It also surveys how current tests measure those skills.

The team reviewed 78 existing benchmarks for narrative understanding. They find a clear need for new tests, because many parts of story understanding are either skipped by current work or scored with metrics that fit them poorly. NarraBench ties its task map to narratology, the scholarly study of narrative form. The goal is a shared yardstick for judging whether models truly follow plot, character, and story structure.
arxiv-2510-09969:
Namiq computes graded Betti numbers for skeletons of simplicial complexes in this 2025 arXiv paper in commutative algebra. Betti numbers count the generators and relations in a minimal free resolution, a standard way to measure an ideal's complexity. The skeleton of a complex keeps only its low-dimensional faces.

The author studies a class of squarefree monomial ideals defined by a dimension condition on the quotient ring. The ideals in this class arise from skeletons, so their algebra reflects the shape of the underlying complex. For this class, the paper works out the graded Betti numbers, which split the counts by degree. Those numbers let algebraists read structural facts about the complex from its ideal.
arxiv-2510-10069:
Ling, Xiaodong Gu, Jiangnan Tang, and Changqing Zou introduce SyncLipMAE in this 2025 arXiv paper on talking-face video. The framework pretrains on unlabeled audio-visual streams to learn facial dynamics that sync with speech. Such representations transfer to tasks like lip reading and dubbing checks.

SyncLipMAE couples masked visual modeling, hiding parts of frames and rebuilding them, with cross-modal contrastive alignment between sound and image. Three per-frame prompt tokens encode the factors of each frame: identity, vocal motion tied to speech, and ambient motion such as blinks and head turns. Splitting those factors helps the model learn transferable structure. The authors aim for pretraining that captures synchronization itself, not just appearance.
arxiv-2510-10369:
Hoque and Sanjukta Bhanja design domain wall memories with a magnetic topological insulator in this 2025 arXiv paper on spintronic devices. Domain wall memory stores bits as magnetic boundaries that shift along a nanowire for reading and writing. Making the pinning sites as notches in the wire deforms it, so pinning strength varies and shift errors follow.

The authors use a magnetic topological insulator to control the domain walls without topographic notches. Uniform pinning should cut the faults that plague shift operations. The design targets faster, more reliable shift, read, and write steps. Racetrack-style memories promise dense, nonvolatile storage if their walls can be moved with precision, which this material approach addresses.
arxiv-2510-10569:
Qunqiang Feng, Michael Fuchs, and Tsan-Cheng Yu study a graph statistic on random recursive trees, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Zagreb index sums the squares of node degrees in a tree. The generalized version replaces squares with higher powers. Earlier work used martingale techniques for the plain index on random recursive trees, but those methods do not adapt easily to higher powers. The authors instead use a moment transfer approach.

They obtain the first order asymptotics of the moments of the generalized index. They also prove limit laws for its properly normalized distribution. For random non-plane recursive trees, the limit law is normal for every higher power. For plane recursive trees, they show that for cubes and fourth powers the limit law is not normal. The contrast is neat: a small change in how trees grow reshapes the distribution of a global statistic.
arxiv-2510-10869:
Nataly Brukhim, Ariel Bruner, and Orit E Raz study a classic geometry problem transplanted into finite fields, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Erdős distinct distances problem asks how few distinct distances a set of points can determine. Their version uses Hamming distance, the count of coordinates where two strings differ, for sets inside a finite field space. They prove a lower bound on the number of distinct distances: it grows at least like the logarithm of the set size, divided by a log factor in the dimension.

This bound is tight for sets of polynomial size. They then study rainbow sets, subsets whose pairwise distances are all distinct. In contrast to the Euclidean setting, a set with many distinct distances need not contain a large rainbow set, and they give an explicit construction proving it. Nevertheless, large rainbow sets exist, and every large set contains a nontrivial rainbow subset.
arxiv-2510-11169:
Average loss is a crude way to judge a learning model when some subgroups in the data matter far more than others, or when the data distribution may shift. Hind Atbir, Farah Cherfaoui, Guillaume Metzler, Emilie Morvant, and Paul Viallard introduce a family of risk measures for that problem in this 2025 arXiv machine learning theory paper. Their constrained f-entropic risk measures use f-divergences to control distributional shifts and subgroup imbalances.

The family includes Conditional Value at Risk as a special case. The authors derive both classical and disintegrated PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for these risks, the first disintegrated guarantees of this framework beyond standard risks. Building on the theory, they design a self-bounding algorithm that minimizes the bounds directly, yielding models with guarantees at the subgroup level rather than only on average. They close with experiments demonstrating the usefulness of the approach.
arxiv-2510-11369:
Image quality assessment models that reason generalize well, but they are far larger and slower than older scorers. Shijie Zhao and co-authors investigate why the reasoning helps in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Through extensive experiments, they hold that reinforcement learning teaches the model to convert redundant visual information into compact text representations that align across domains. That conversion is the source of the generalization.

Building on that insight, their algorithm RALI uses contrastive learning to align images directly with the generalizable text representations that reinforcement learning produces. The resulting scorer needs no reasoning and does not load a language model. For scoring it matched the generalization of reasoning-based models while using less than 5 percent of their parameters and inference time. The work reframes reasoning as a route to better representations rather than a feature that must run at deployment.
arxiv-2510-11469:
At the future High-Luminosity LHC, the ATLAS detector's liquid-argon calorimeters must reconstruct particle energies from signals buried under many overlapping collisions, within strict hardware limits. Georges Aad and co-authors study neural networks for that reconstruction in this 2025 arXiv instrumentation paper. The networks must run on FPGA readout boards, so they have to be small and fast while still measuring energy precisely under pile-up.

The team optimized dense, recurrent, and convolutional architectures with a Bayesian procedure balancing energy resolution against network size. The dense, convolutional, and hybrid networks reached a transverse energy resolution of about 80 MeV, outperforming the optimal filtering method now in use and recurrent networks. They reproduced the energy scale across the full dynamic range, where the older methods underestimate it. A deep evidential regression variant produced per-event uncertainty estimates consistent with the actual errors, at minimal extra size.
arxiv-2510-11569:
Holographic dark energy ties the universe's accelerating expansion to entropy bounds, so changing the entropy formula changes the cosmology. A. Sheykhi, A. Asvar, and E. Ebrahimi revisit the Kaniadakis version of that idea in this 2025 arXiv cosmology paper. Here Kaniadakis entropy is built into the Friedmann equations, with the Hubble radius as the infrared cutoff.

In a dark-energy-dominated universe the model mimics a cosmological constant, with equation of state parameter equal to minus one, suggesting the constant might have a theoretical origin in this framework. Unlike standard holographic dark energy, it explains current acceleration without any dark sector interaction. With interaction switched on, the total equation of state can cross the phantom line today. They also find a negative squared sound speed for the interacting case, and statefinder diagnostics distinguish the model from the standard one.
arxiv-2510-11769:
Ruida Wang and four colleagues speed up how AI learns to prove math theorems. Formal provers work in languages like Lean, where every proof can be checked by computer. Training them usually needs a fixed set of problems, which wastes effort on problems that are too easy or too hard. The team's 2025 arXiv paper proposes GAR, short for Generative Adversarial Reinforcement Learning.

GAR trains two models together in a loop. A composer invents problems while a solver learns to prove them, and the composer keeps the difficulty near the solver's growing edge. This creates an automatic curriculum, a ladder of tasks matched to current skill. With GAR training, two leading provers improved their pass rates on the MiniF2F test set by about four percent on average. On the harder ProofNet test set, one prover's success rate rose from about twenty-three percent to about twenty-six percent.
arxiv-2510-11869:
Lael Edwards-Costa studies a little-explored cousin of the classic billiard problem. In ordinary billiards a point bounces inside a table; in outer billiards it hops around the outside. Each system also has a variational form, where paths are chosen to extremize a quantity such as length or area. Edwards-Costa's 2025 arXiv paper takes the newest combination, outer billiards with length, and restricts the table to a polygon.

The paper describes how orbits behave far away from the table, where intuition from the classical systems runs thin. For the special case of a square table, Edwards-Costa poses conjectures about an escaping orbit, a path that wanders off and never returns. The work complements a companion study of smooth tables with positive curvature. Together the two papers begin a map of a dynamical system whose basic questions, including which starting points escape, remain open.
arxiv-2510-12069:
Sandeep Mishra, Oindrila Saha, and Alan C. Bovik edit videos by transplanting motion onto new subjects. Creators often want a different object performing the original action, with structure and meaning both free to change. Existing diffusion editors either freeze structure too tightly or let identity drift and timing wobble. Their 2025 arXiv paper, VidMP3, steers by pose and position priors instead of dense pixel guidance.

A module called MotionGuide learns a general motion representation from the source video's correspondence and depth maps. Its features are injected into the temporal attention of a text-to-video model, so generation follows the learned motion while inventing fresh appearance. The method handles cross-domain swaps, where the new subject means something entirely different, and heavy structure edits that reshape the object. It also adapts to personalized editing tasks. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations rate VidMP3 above existing methods.
arxiv-2510-12169:
Akshay Naik, William R. Norris, Dustin Nottage, and Ahmet Soylemezoglu plan off-road routes that respect both soil and steering. Autonomous ground vehicles must find curvature-feasible paths through terrain whose strength varies meter by meter, in real time. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a hybrid planner around a continuous terrain cost metric.

The metric fuses a Bekker pressure-sinkage soil model with slope and attitude penalties from elevation, staying analytic, bounded, and stable under sensor noise. Exact steering primitives, Dubins and Reeds-Shepp curves plus bicycle-model arcs, serve both skid-steer and Ackermann vehicles. A vehicle-dynamics RRT-star explores globally, while a vehicle-dynamics D-star Lite repairs the plan locally, replanning in milliseconds without heuristic smoothing.  Hardware trials on an off-road platform crossed soft soil and slope transitions in real time.
arxiv-2510-12469:
Rezabek and colleagues close a trust gap in confidential cloud computing with a design called Proof of Cloud, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Confidential machines run inside hardware isolated environments that shield data in use. Yet those trusted execution environments exclude attackers with physical access. Tenants must trust that the provider's hardware is genuinely protected, and standard remote attestation cannot verify it.

Their Data Center Execution Assurance design binds a confidential machine to its physical platform using measurements anchored in a virtual trusted module. This ensures launch evidence and platform quotes refer to the same physical chassis, using the fact that data centers are identifiable through these hardware modules. The design covers provider controlled stacks and single tenant bare metal machines. It enables remote verification of a machine's platform origin and integrity, and blunts replay and attestation proxying attacks. A test implementation on Google Cloud with Intel tech is included.
arxiv-2510-12669:
He, Drineas, and Khanna show that randomly sampling graph edges uniformly, the simplest possible strategy, can preserve spectral grouping quality when the graph clusters well, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Spectral clustering partitions a graph using special vectors, which is expensive on massive graphs. Classical sparsification samples edges by their effective resistances, an importance measure costly to estimate.

Their main result concerns graphs admitting a well separated grouping, quantified by a large structure ratio. For such graphs, sampling a modest number of edges at random yields a sparsifier. The count scales with the number of vertices and a logarithmic factor. Its key eigenspace stays nearly at right angles to the cluster markers, keeping the spectral embedding faithful. The analysis introduces new resistance bounds for edges inside clusters. It adds a matrix concentration bound adapted to the main eigenspace. Under strong clusterability even uniform sampling stays structure aware, bypassing importance sampling entirely.
arxiv-2510-12869:
Nishiura, Kamijima, and Ioka unify three wave scattering processes in this 2025 arXiv paper on plasma physics. In magnetized electron-positron plasma, the plasma made of matter and antimatter in equal parts, electromagnetic waves can scatter through induced Compton, Brillouin, and Raman processes. These instabilities matter for extreme settings such as magnetar magnetospheres, the regions around ultra-magnetic neutron stars. The work is purely theoretical.

Starting from kinetic theory, the authors solve dispersion relations that include the ponderomotive force from beating waves. They derive growth rates for ordinary, neutral, and charged fluctuation modes. They clarify which scattering type wins under given temperature, resonance, and density settings. Strong magnetic fields usually suppress scattering of perpendicular waves, though by varied powers. Raman scattering, forbidden without a field, becomes possible in the charged mode.
arxiv-2510-13269:
Ma, Xiong, and Zhang prove potential estimates for mixed local and nonlocal equations in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. They combine a classical p-Laplace operator, for local diffusion, with a fractional operator for long jumps, and their right-hand sides are general measures rather than functions. Such mixed problems arise from processes that combine random walks with Lévy flights.

The authors prove pointwise estimates bounding the solution and its gradient through Riesz and Wolff potentials, standard tools that convert measure data into pointwise control. Their key device is a new fractional maximal function that captures local and nonlocal features at once, with matching pointwise bounds for the maximal operators. The estimates hold for both superquadratic and subquadratic cases. They need only low regularity on the local coefficient and mere measurability on the nonlocal kernel. They identify the borderline case that governs solution size.
arxiv-2510-13469:
Katre and Krishnamurthi ask when matrices over certain noncommutative rings split into sums of squares and cubes. Their 2025 arXiv paper works over maximal orders in cyclic division algebras over the rationals. These algebras generalize quaternions, the number system where multiplication order matters. Earlier work by Wadikar and Katre covered the quaternion case for matrices of size at least two.

The authors extend the question to algebras of odd prime degree. Under stated conditions, they show every matrix of size at least two over these rings is a sum of squares. The same matrices are also sums of cubes under those conditions. The problem belongs to Waring's problem, the classic study of writing numbers as sums of powers. Here the numbers are replaced by matrices over a noncommutative ring. A discriminant condition on the algebra governs when such decompositions hold.
arxiv-2510-13669:
Li and Zhang fix two flaws of masked autoregressive video generation with a trick they call a canvas. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies models that build videos token by token in random order. Early sampling lacks any global structure, so generation starts slowly and incoherently. Errors then pile up across space and time as frames proceed.

Their model, CanvasMAR, first predicts a blurred sketch of the whole next frame. That canvas seeds the masked generation, giving global structure from the first step. A compositional guidance scheme strengthens both the canvas signal and the pull of past frames. Random noise added to the canvas during training hardens the model against its own mistakes. On the BAIR and Kinetics-600 benchmarks, CanvasMAR made high-quality videos in fewer steps. It led autoregressive models on Kinetics-600 and rivalled diffusion methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-13769:
Olivo models how graphene quantum dots take in and give off visible light by fusing two kinds of theory. His 2025 arXiv paper studies tiny graphene flakes whose edges are capped with hydrogen atoms. Such dots act like large aromatic molecules, with coronene as the working case. Their glow can be tuned, suiting them for photonics and solar uses.

Density functional theory, a standard way to compute electron states, supplies the dot's energy levels first. A quantum electrodynamics model of a dot then adds how those levels change over time. Merging the two gives the light tied to each jump between levels, and how strong each jump is. How long each state lasts also falls out of the model. The model's spectrum matches lab results closely, the author reports. That match supports the fused method for real two-dimensional nanomaterials. Uses range from solar energy to room-temperature single-photon sources.
arxiv-2510-13869:
Ali, Rossi, and Bertozzi teach GANs new image tasks from a few examples without forgetting old ones, using tiny low-rank adapters. Their 2025 arXiv paper, CoLoR-GAN, joins continual learning with few-shot learning for generative models. Leading methods bolt on many new weights at every task, ballooning over time. Data from past tasks is usually gone, so forgetting lurks constantly.

Low-rank adaptation updates only small matrices layered onto frozen weights. Even a plain LoRA setup already performed well in their early tests. Their LoRA-in-LoRA trick shrinks convolutional adapters further still. A hyperparameter study maps how to pick ranks and scales without blind search. Benchmarks across continual and few-shot tasks show state-of-the-art generation quality. The resource cost, though, is enormously lower than competing approaches. Source code is public for replication and extension.
arxiv-2510-13969:
Bhubanjyoti Bhattacharya and co-authors revisit how symmetry assumptions shape the analysis of B meson decays, in this 2025 arXiv paper. B mesons are particles containing a bottom quark, and their decays into pairs of light mesons carry information about CP violation, the difference between matter and antimatter behavior. Analysts relate decay amplitudes using flavor symmetry, but a puzzle in one decay family may hinge on using the wrong symmetry.

Relations derived in 1998 connect electroweak penguin processes, rare loop-level effects, to simpler tree processes, assuming the full three-flavor symmetry. The authors show relations follow from isospin symmetry alone, the smaller symmetry relating up and down quarks. For one class of decays the relations barely change, but for the puzzle's class they differ sharply. Using the correct isospin relations, the discrepancy with the Standard Model grows to four or five standard deviations, much larger than previously reported.
arxiv-2510-14169:
Praphul Singh and co-authors present JEDA, a system that retrieves clinical orders from doctors' conversations without first rewriting them into queries, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clinical talk mixes explicit commands, such as ordering a chest X-ray, with ambient reasoning, such as noting a worsening cough and suspecting pneumonia. Many systems insert a language model to translate talk into structured queries, adding delay and opacity.

JEDA uses a bi-encoder, initialized from the biomedical PubMedBERT model and fine-tuned with a duplicate-safe contrastive objective, to match talk to canonical orders in an embedding space. In query-free mode it encodes a rolling window of dialogue, making it resilient to disfluencies and speech-recognition errors. Training records pair each order with command-only, context-only, and combined formulations. The authors report gains in retrieval accuracy and latency over rewriting-based pipelines and strong results against open embedding models.
arxiv-2510-14469:
Ricardo Ferreira, David Marsh, and Eike Ravensburg re-derive the limits on axion-like particles from supernovae, focusing on their couplings to electrons and muons, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Axion-like particles produced inside a collapsing star would carry energy away, and astronomers constrain them through anomalous cooling, energy deposition, photon signals, and a gamma-ray line.

The authors identify and calculate six production channels, including two loop-level processes involving photons that treatments missed or approximated, and they improve the treatment of production and absorption. Applying the constraints, they obtain robust bounds on the electron and muon coupling spaces. They also quantify how much the answer depends on the supernova model itself. They run three state-of-the-art models from two simulation codes. The constraints vary by factors of a few up to ten, a sobering measure of the astrophysical uncertainty behind particle limits.
arxiv-2510-14569:
Borovik and Yalçınkaya explain, in a 2025 arXiv note, how to implement a set of maps between matrix groups on a computer. The maps connect three objects. One is the group of two-by-two matrices with determinant one over a prime field. The second is the same group over a so-called black box field. The third is a black box group encrypting the first group. Black box means the group is given only through operations on encoded elements, not explicit entries.

The note implements the authors' earlier algorithm in GAP, a system for computational group theory, with worked examples. The code is public on GitHub. It targets prime fields, assuming at least thirteen elements to keep the coding simple. Their main interest is black box groups over very large fields, where direct matrix methods fail and such maps become essential.
arxiv-2510-14669:
Altamirano, Vreeken, and Ghebreab review, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how well Dutch public health research handles bias in machine learning. These models promise better surveillance, risk prediction, and resource allocation. Used carelessly, though, they can deepen the very health disparities they should reduce. The authors set out to measure how often researchers even look for such bias.

They built an assessment tool, RABAT, by combining elements of established bias and responsible-AI frameworks, and applied it to thirty-five peer-reviewed studies from 2021 to 2025. Sampling and missing data were usually documented well. But most studies skipped explicit fairness framing, subgroup analyses, and open discussion of possible harms. In response, the authors propose a four-stage framework, ACAR, covering awareness, conceptualization, application, and reporting. It comes with guiding questions meant to carry fairness through the whole life of a model.
arxiv-2510-14969:
Wang and a UCLA-Harvard team propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, letting language models manufacture the practice data that digital agents train on. Agents that operate websites and apps need numbers of task trajectories, and collecting them from real interfaces costs heavily in annotation, infrastructure, and engineering. Their system, UI-Simulator, has a language model simulate the digital world, generating interface states and transitions.

Guided rollouts explore this simulated world coherently, and a trajectory wrapper packages the results into training data. A growth variant, UI-Simulator-Grow, scales efficiently by prioritizing high-impact tasks and synthesizing variants of them. On the WebArena and AndroidWorld benchmarks, agents trained on synthetic data rivaled or surpassed agents trained on real interfaces, with better robustness, despite weaker teacher models. The growth variant matched a seventy-billion-parameter model's performance while using an eight-billion-parameter base, evidence that targeted synthesis can substitute for scale.
arxiv-2510-15069:
Zhu surveys, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how machine learning is changing the study of nonlinear waves, and is candid that the tour is subjective. Nonlinear waves, from solitons in optical fibers to ocean swells, are governed by equations whose solutions and structures are hard to extract by hand. Data-driven methods have become part of the hunt, and the article maps the landscape rather than reporting a result.

The review introduces pillars of machine learning, operator learning, deep learning, and data-driven equation discovery among them, then showcases each in wave problems. Applications range from learning lattice models and reduced descriptions of dynamics to discovering conservation laws from data. They also probe whether a system is integrable, exactly solvable in disguise. The author's message is integration. These methods complement the community's existing tools. Joining the two toolkits expands what can be discovered in the age of data.
arxiv-2510-15469:
J. O. Button examines which groups built from a single relation behave like rank-one lattices, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. The groups in question are 1-relator groups, defined by one defining relation, and groups whose presentations have deficiency at least one, meaning more generators than relations. Such groups are common, but their deeper properties vary widely.

Button studies second bounded cohomology and mod-p homology inside finite-index subgroups to tell the cases apart. Those tools detect quasimorphisms and related rigidity features that separate rank-one behavior from higher-rank behavior. The payoff is an exact determination of which 1-relator groups are boundedly generated, a strong finiteness property from Lie theory. The same classification is obtained for deficiency-one groups, up to a class of groups conjectured not to exist. The paper imports a Lie-group distinction into everyday finitely presented groups.
arxiv-2510-15769:
Allen Daniel Sunny reports an early experiment in a 2025 paper. The question was whether explaining an AI system builds trust. The test used a web-based loan approval simulation.
