Participants saw different styles of explanation. Some saw simple lists of key factors. Others got interactive what-if tools. Those tools let users change inputs and watch the outcome flip.

Interactivity raised both engagement and confidence in the system. Clear, relevant explanations mattered more than having any explanation at all. The author presents this as early measured evidence. It supports human-centred explanation design. The stakes are high in fields like lending, law, and healthcare.
arxiv-2510-15869:
Jie-Ying Lee leads eight co-authors in building city scenes in three dimensions from satellite pictures alone. Large, exact city models serve immersive and embodied uses. Yet real three-dimensional scans at that scale are scarce and costly. Their framework, Skyfall-GS, takes a new supply route for the raw material.

Satellite work supplies realistic coarse shape. Open diffusion models then add fine, close-up looks. A stepwise loop refines the scene in stages. Shape gets more complete and texture more photo-like at each stage. No costly three-dimensional labels are needed. The result supports real-time immersive exploration at city-block scale. In tests, Skyfall-GS gives shape that agrees better across views than leading prior methods. Its textures also look more real, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16569:
Hadi Abbaszadehpeivasti, Etienne de Klerk, and Adrien Taylor rate a boosted solver in a 2025 paper. The Difference-of-Convex Algorithm, or DCA, solves tasks whose cost splits as a gap of two dome-shaped parts. Each step solves a dome-shaped sub-task, then moves on. Boosting adds one extra step along the same line. Past number tests praised the boost, but no proof said why.

The trio prove the boost is strictly better in the worst case, for set classes. Their proof leans on performance estimation with matrix tools. Those tools turn worst-case bounds into a solvable matrix task. The result backs wide reports that boosted runs beat plain runs. It also shows which cost splits gain most from a boost.
arxiv-2510-16769:
Shuo Han and five co-authors present GraphVista, a framework that helps vision-language models understand the structure of very large graphs. Graphs encode networks of nodes and links. Language models read them poorly at scale because long inputs overflow token limits, and text and image views of a graph are hard to combine.

GraphVista stores graph facts in a light retrieval base and pulls only the text and high-detail subgraphs a task needs. A planning agent then routes each sub-task to text or image, whichever fits best. Experiments show the system handles graphs far larger than older benchmarks and beats text-only, image-only, and fusion methods. The design targets tasks where both global facts and local shape matter.
arxiv-2510-16969:
Kimiya Jozani leads four co-authors in joining epidemic forecasts with vaccine logistics in a 2025 paper. During epidemics, fast decisions prevent infections and deaths. Most older models forecast disease spread separately from supply planning. That split weakens responses tailored to each region.

Their framework models disease and a multi-level vaccine supply chain together. Infection rates vary across place and time with local behavior. Two versions balance fairness and vulnerability in different ways. One uses an inequality measure, the other a knapsack-style ranking. Scalable solution methods keep the large model computable. Validation used United States COVID-19 data. A forecasting method checked the model despite limited data. The authors aim at proactive control of future epidemics.
arxiv-2510-17169:
Roland Croft and three co-authors test attacks on face match systems in this 2025 paper. Small tweaks to a face photo can fool match models or shield a user's face. Real systems first clean and crop faces before they match them. That first step is often skipped in attack tests done in the dark.

The team finds the face finder choice can cut attack wins a lot. In some cases the drop reached over three quarters of wins. Down-scale style had far less effect on attack strength. A fix that varies inputs lifted attack transfer by over one quarter. The work urges full-pipe tests when face safety is judged.
arxiv-2510-17269:
Luis Wiedmann and eight co-authors release a huge open image-text set for vision-language models in this 2025 paper. Past public sets clash in form and repeat test items by leak. Such flaws stall fair growth of models that read and see. The team built one clean corpus from more than two hundred sources.

The corpus holds twenty-four million samples in one hundred eighty-five subsets. A half-auto pipe with human checks maps, dedupes, and cleans each source. It also strips leaks against sixty-six public test sets. Agent tasks with a shared action set join the mix. Models trained on the set beat those trained on past open mixes.
arxiv-2510-17369:
Soft robots bend and flex, which makes them safer around people, but the newest language guided robot controllers were built for stiff arms. Haochen Su and five co-authors test whether those vision language action models can run a soft continuum arm instead. Such models take camera views and spoken or written instructions and turn them into robot actions.

Straight out of the box, both models Su and his co-authors tried failed on the soft arm because its body differs so much from a rigid one. After targeted fine tuning through their deployment pipeline, the soft robot matched the rigid version on the test tasks. The results argue that careful retraining, not new models, bridges the body gap.
arxiv-2510-17469:
Language models based on the transformer design can reason in steps about new sequences they never saw in training, and Jing Liu, writing alone, asks what inside the model makes that possible. Liu uses a tidy test bed called the Random Hierarchy Model, where sequences are built by recursive rules much like a grammar. Models are trained on only part of the possible sequences and then tested under four conditions, from plain memorisation to transfer across rule layers.

Scores rose steadily with task difficulty handled and with more examples given in context, though unfamiliar rule use needed far more examples. Inside the model, Liu finds that separate layers gradually specialise during training, forming ordered, hierarchical representations. That inner specialisation tracks the outer reasoning gains closely.
arxiv-2510-17669:
Bartosz Bieganowski, with Pietro d'Avenia and two co-authors, proves a solution exists for a gravity equation in a 2025 arXiv paper. The equation is the Lichnerowicz equation, used when building starting data for Einstein's field equations. Their setting couples gravity with a scalar field on a closed manifold, meaning a finite space with no edge. The mean curvature of the space is not constant, which is the non-CMC case.

Non constant mean curvature adds terms that grow faster than standard ones. Singular terms, which blow up at some points, appear as well. The team uses a recent fixed point argument built on sub and super solutions. They prove a positive, essentially bounded solution exists. They also give conditions on the coefficients under which no positive classical solution can exist.
arxiv-2510-17769:
Michael Nestor and three co-authors design grid controls for a power system full of inverters. Inverters turn solar and battery power into grid-ready alternating current. Many arrive as black boxes, with hidden internal models. That secrecy strains older frequency control methods, which kept grid cycles steady.

Their approach lets inverters talk peer to peer, with no central controller. A design framework trades network communication needs against control performance. The controller then follows the chosen communication layout. It also carries a proof that the closed loop stays stable. Tests on a standard thirty-nine-bus system confirmed the trade-off worked.
arxiv-2510-17869:
Gerard Asbert, with four co-authors, generates fake handwritten music symbols to help teach computers to read old scores. Real labeled examples of handwritten historic music are scarce, which limits optical music reading. The team trains a generative network at the level of single symbols, then builds full scores with engraving software.

Judged by eye, the made-up symbols look close to real handwriting. That realism marks progress toward synthetic scores that training sets can use. Readers interested in music archives get a route to more training data without years of hand labeling by experts.
arxiv-2510-18669:
Djalil Chafaï, with David García-Zelada and Yuan Yuan Xu, studies a random matrix built as the ratio of two simpler random matrices. Each ingredient matrix has independent entries with mean zero and unit variance, but dividing one by the other creates entries that depend on each other and include occasional huge values. The authors ask how far the ratio's spectrum, its set of eigenvalues, reaches as the matrix grows.

Their main message is that the farthest eigenvalue, properly scaled, settles into a single universal heavy-tailed distribution as the dimension grows without bound. The proof leans on a symmetric Gaussian special case, whose spectrum can be pictured as charged particles on a sphere, plus tools from random matrix theory and determinantal processes. Curiously, they note, the ratio case proved more tractable than the same question for a single random matrix.
arxiv-2510-18769:
David Jewitt and Jane Luu report on an interstellar comet, 3I/ATLAS. They watched it approach the Sun from July to September 2025 with the Nordic Optical Telescope. Brightness was tracked as the Sun distance shrank. It followed a clean power law. Dust production seemed driven by a highly volatile material. Separate findings point to carbon dioxide as that driver.

Such behavior is normal beside solar system comets. The authors find no basis to call the visitor ancient or pristine. Its look changed over the months. An early fan of dust faced the Sun, and a tail pointing away took over later. The delay is blamed on the dust itself. The grains are large, about a tenth of a millimeter across. They leave slowly, at roughly five meters per second, so sunlight's push moves them only sluggishly. Tiny grains seem scarce, possibly because they stick together.
arxiv-2510-18869:
Juan José Gálvez-Viruet and his four co-authors bring quantum computing to fragmentation functions. Those functions describe how a fast quark turns into a specific hadron. No one has computed them from first principles in general. Their approach uses light-front chromodynamics. It is a form of the strong force theory set on light-like coordinates. The theory is discretized and trimmed down. It fits a particle-register encoding built for quantum simulation.

A proof of concept runs on a classical simulator. It computes a charm quark fragmenting into a J/psi particle. That particle binds a charm quark and an antiquark. A known perturbative evaluation from 1993 exists for comparison. The work shows the full pipeline running end to end. It is a first step toward quantum computation of hadronization. That is the process turning quarks into particles detectors see.
arxiv-2510-18969:
Tushar Gupta and three co-authors test a two-source idea for dark matter. Light Higgsinos could freeze out in the early universe. Right-handed sneutrinos could slowly freeze in. The model adds right-handed neutrinos to a supersymmetric frame. Its seesaw scale is very low. Both sources are tracked in one frame.

The heavier source would decay into the lighter one, but with a delay. The authors rule out the whole setup. Sterile neutrinos from a second route live too long. They would outlast the universe and add too much dark matter.
arxiv-2510-19169:
Thomas Wang and Haowen Li present OpenGuardrails, an open-source platform that guards large language models in real applications. As these models spread, builders need protection against harmful content, attacks that manipulate the model, and leaks of private or sensitive data, all in one deployable system.

OpenGuardrails unifies detection by large safety models with defense against prompt injection, jailbreaks, and code abuse, plus checks for data leakage. Its configurable policy adaptation lets operators tune rules to their setting instead of accepting fixed ones. Being fully open, the platform can be inspected and extended by the teams that rely on it.
arxiv-2510-19369:
Jorge Vallejo Bustamante and seven co-authors map how the twist angle between graphene and boron nitride layers changes the electronic zones of the stack. When graphene aligns with one boron nitride layer, a moiré pattern forms with extra Dirac peaks; aligning a second layer creates two patterns that can interfere in periodic or irregular ways.

Using rotatable layered structures, the team turns the top layer in place while the bottom stays fixed, and tracks charge transport across angles. The maps identify the special zones that appear in this double-moiré system, guiding future devices built from twisted layers.
arxiv-2510-19569:
Miguel Barroso Varela and Álvaro de la Cruz-Dombriz work out the complete equations for how cosmic structure grows in f(R) theories of gravity, which modify Einstein's theory by changing how curvature enters. They check the full scale-dependent perturbation equations against the common quasistatic shortcut and show the two agree for viable models. The test case is the Hu-Sawicki model, a popular f(R) proposal.

Applying recent data on the late-time growth of structure, they find the model's key parameter must be extremely small, around a millionth or less. At that size the model adds nothing beyond an effective cosmological constant. It therefore cannot ease the standing tension between early- and late-universe measurements of how clumpy matter is.
arxiv-2510-19769:
Ameya Nambisan and fifteen co-authors report that a vortex in a granular superconducting film can act as a quantum two-level system, not just as a dissipative defect. In plain superconductors, Abrikosov vortices have normal cores. They are treated as classical objects that limit uses from power wires to quantum devices. Granularity on the scale of the coherence length changes that picture.

Using circuit quantum electrodynamics tools on granular aluminum resonators, the team steered vortex states and read them out without destroying them. A vortex kept quantum coherence for microseconds. Its energy relaxation times reached fractions of a millisecond. The findings support modeling granular superconductors as networks of tunnel junctions with gapped vortices. They also suggest uses in quantum information, materials testing, and sensing.
arxiv-2510-20169:
Tongkai Lu, Shuai Ma, and Chongyang Tao propose HyperNS, a neighborhood search method guided by a hyper tour for large traveling salesman problems. Neural methods for this classic hard problem struggle to scale, because global heatmaps and access matrices use too much memory and starting tours are often weak. Their approach follows a clustering first, route second strategy.

A sparse heatmap graph first divides the instance into clusters, which are treated as supernodes joined in a hyper tour. That tour guides both the starting solution and the later local search, narrowing attention to the most relevant edges. On synthetic and real-world data, HyperNS beats existing neural methods and closes more of the gap to the optimal tour, especially at large scale.
arxiv-2510-20269:
Ismail Emir Yuksel and seven co-authors experimentally show that ordinary commercial memory chips can generate true random numbers by activating several rows at once. Random numbers are vital for security, and DRAM chips already inside computers are an attractive source. The team characterized ninety-six DDR4 chips, varying the number of rows activated together, data patterns, temperature, and chip location.

All of their designs pass the standard NIST statistical tests for randomness. Several row-count designs beat the leading earlier DRAM-based generator on throughput, and entropy generally rises as more rows are activated together. Operating conditions matter a lot: higher temperature lowers entropy noticeably, while moving from two rows to thirty-two rows more than doubles it on most modules tested.
arxiv-2510-20369:
Zhenghao Xu and eleven co-authors propose routing hard cases from a fast reward model to a strong language model judge during reinforcement learning from human feedback. Reward models trained on human preferences can be hacked and generalize poorly to new inputs, while strong judges generalize better but cost far more to run. Their framework uses uncertainty to decide which judge scores each preference pair.

By framing advantage estimation as pairwise preference classification, they obtain principled uncertainty scores for the routing decision. Confident pairs stay with the cheap reward model and uncertain pairs go to the strong judge. On reward benchmarks the routing beats random judge calling at the same cost, and downstream alignment experiments show gains for online training.
arxiv-2510-20569:
Feilong Zhang and five co-authors pair fluid antenna sets with fixed sets to send facts and power in one wave. Fluid antenna sets lift link rates by a shift of place. The pair task, called SWIPT, sends one wave from the base to both a fact taker and a power taker. Their aim is to top the power that lands at the power taker.

The plan tunes send and catch fluid spots and the send spread grid as one task. A floor on wave grade at the fact taker must hold. Sim marks show fluid sets lift the power take by a clear span next to fixed sets. Place turns into a new design knob next to wave craft.
arxiv-2510-21069:
Pranav Saxena and one co-author present ZING-3D, a zero shot framework that builds three dimensional scene graphs incrementally from vision language models. Scene graphs record objects plus their semantic and spatial relations, a structured memory embodied agents need.

Prior zero shot methods work from single views, cannot update as new observations arrive, and lack explicit geometric grounding. ZING-3D updates its graph as scenes unfold and anchors nodes in real three dimensional space, using foundation model knowledge without task specific fine tuning. Open vocabulary coverage lets robots describe novel rooms with concepts they were never explicitly trained to label.
arxiv-2510-21369:
Vivian S. Medeiros and five co-authors help four-legged robots cross ground that may collapse underfoot, a hazard in rescue missions and planetary exploration. Rather than adding special sensors or trusting maps alone, their system judges the ground from the robot's own joint measurements while it walks.

The framework joins four parts: probing steps that test the surface, a load-bearing check that rates how much weight a spot can hold, motion planning, and control. A predictive controller balances stability against the need to probe, while a state machine schedules the probing moves, so the robot can spot weak regions and shift its footholds in time. Trials on built collapsing platforms and rocky ground show safe crossings with stability kept throughout.
arxiv-2510-21569:
Tran Quang Hoa, Nguyen Duy Phuoc, and Tran Nguyen Thanh Son study the weak Lefschetz property for certain algebras. The property tests whether multiplication by a generic linear form behaves as fully as dimensions allow. The authors study tensor products that glue two algebras together. They focus on monomial algebras built from polynomial rings.

One case pairs two Artinian monomial algebras. Those are rings that vanish beyond a top degree. Another case uses complete quadratic monomial algebras. As a concrete use, the authors classify the property for algebras built from lollipop graphs. A lollipop graph joins a complete graph to a path. The algebras also include squares of the variables. That sorting turns a graph's shape into a verdict on the algebra's maps.
arxiv-2510-21769:
Harry Zhang and Luca Carlone teach machines the full grammar of how people use objects, without paying humans to label any of it. An affordance is more than a contact patch. People also face objects from preferred sides and occupy favored zones around them, like standing before a microwave rather than behind it. Datasets for such subtleties are costly hand-made affairs.

Their framework, H2OFlow, learns contact, orientation, and spatial occupancy together from synthetic scenes produced by 3D generative models. The representation is a dense flow over point clouds, learned by a diffusion process, from which rich three-dimensional affordances can be read off. In quantitative and qualitative tests, the system transfers to real objects and beats methods that relied on manual annotation or mesh-based representations.
arxiv-2510-21869:
E Horsdal studies energy lost to friction inside a swinging counterweight trebuchet, the medieval siege engine whose hanging weight swings as the arm throws. Builders and historians modeling these machines need honest loss figures, since a shot's range depends on how much energy survives the moving joints.

Horsdal derives the drag effects of sliding friction at the arm's bearings and at the counterweight hinge, plus air resistance on the sling. Folds them into the equations for the machine's internal motion. Solutions come from perturbation methods, a way of layering small corrections onto a simpler answer. The calculated losses are checked against shots from a small experimental engine, and the paper closes by asking how the effects scale up to full-size machines.
arxiv-2510-22269:
Miaomiao Li, Bin Pei, Yong Xu, and Xiaole Yue study systems with two clocks. A slow variable matters. A fast one mostly averages out. Their setting is a slow-fast system of rough partial differential equations. The driving signal is too jagged for classical calculus. The state spaces form a nested family of interpolation Hilbert spaces.

The averaging principle promises a simpler fate for the slow part. As the time-scale gap widens, it should follow an averaged system. The team proves strong convergence in the supremum norm. A controlled rough path framework is adapted to the nested spaces. A time discretization argument handles the fast oscillations piece by piece. Results of this kind license the reduced models that scientists actually compute with. Climate, fluid, and materials work all rely on such reductions.
arxiv-2510-22369:
Egor Kolodin, with four co-authors, presents GigaEmbeddings, a way to train text embeddings aimed at Russian. The work builds on GigaChat-3B, a decoder model made for Russian, and adds instruction tuning in stages. Embeddings turn text into numbers that computers can compare for search and sorting tasks.

Training runs in three stages, from broad contrastive learning on web text to fine tuning with hard negative examples. The design also uses two way attention, a new pooling method, and cuts about a quarter of the layers for speed. On a benchmark with twenty three tasks, the model scores highest among the systems tested.
arxiv-2510-22769:
Chaoming Song, writing alone in 2025, builds a supersymmetric geometry. Supersymmetry pairs ordinary and odd variables. His base is the Fock-Goncharov cluster ensemble. It is tied to a Lie supergroup and a marked surface. The result is a super higher-Teichmuller geometry.

Each seed in the structure carries a weight matrix. That matrix encodes Cartan weights of an odd slice. Mutations follow a column vector rule. The setup yields a flat superconnection and a volume form. Song then defines a form on a loop fibration. For one key group, its period encodes loop amplitudes. Those amplitudes come from planar super Yang-Mills theory.
arxiv-2510-22869:
Tiered memory mixes fast memory with slower, larger memory. Rohan Kadekodi leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they present Jenga, a tiered memory manager. Prior systems suffered two flaws. Hot and cold objects shared the same pages. Hotness shifts also caused thrashing, or wasteful page swaps.

Jenga allocates pages by allocation context. That separates hot from cold objects early. Its hotness measures react fast to change. Yet they avoid thrashing in tests. Ten memory heavy apps ran faster than with the best prior system. Gains were large when fast tier size matched working set. Overhead stayed under a few percent.
arxiv-2510-23069:
Laura Rinaldi, Alvise Sommariva, and Marco Vianello describe a cheap, stable way to integrate polynomials over oddly shaped elements. Their method compresses a continuous measure into a discrete signed measure that matches the same moments. It needs only an orthonormal basis and a small quadrature rule on a simple bounding set.

Unlike rival approaches, no matrix inversion is required, so conditioning problems do not arise. The authors bound the total size of the signed weights and show examples on curved planar elements with spline edges. Accurate integration on such shapes supports high-order finite element codes for complex geometry.
arxiv-2510-23169:
Marah Ghoummaid, Vladimir Tchuiev, Ofek Glick, Michal Moshkovitz, and Dotan Di Castro introduce MATCH, a way to grade AI-generated code against developer intent. AI tools now write a large share of code, yet checking intent is hard. Unit tests are costly, text similarity misses function, and some scores need reference code that may not exist.

MATCH uses contrastive learning in a task-driven, reference-free setup. It judges whether code does what was asked rather than how it looks. Reliable intent grading would help teams trust automated coding tools and catch silent mismatches before they ship.
arxiv-2510-23569:
Baoqi Pei and seven co-authors built EgoThinker, a framework that teaches AI models to reason from first-person video. In egocentric footage, the person filming stays unseen while their hands reshape the scene, so a model must infer hidden intentions and catch fine hand-object contact. Today's multimodal models handle visible events well but lack that embodied, first-person grasp.

The team first built EgoRe-5M, a question-answering dataset drawn from thirteen million varied first-person clips, with step-by-step reasoning notes and dense labels for hands and objects. They fine-tuned models on that data, then applied reinforcement fine-tuning to sharpen where and when things happen. EgoThinker beat prior methods across several first-person benchmarks and improved sharply on fine-grained localization tasks. The authors released the full code and data for others to use.
arxiv-2510-23769:
Sebastian von Hausegger and five co-authors re-examine the cosmic dipole anomaly using the clustering of 1.6 million quasars from the CatWISE2020 catalog. The anomaly is a mismatch: the dipole in the matter distribution does not match what the cosmic microwave background says our motion should produce. That tension challenges the Cosmological Principle, the assumption that the universe looks the same in every direction on large scales.

Measuring the dipole cleanly requires controlling all other large-scale structure, which can bias the fit. The team infers the large-scale multipoles directly and checks the small-scale angular power spectrum against the standard model. After correcting a known trend of quasar counts with ecliptic latitude, every other large-scale signal matches noise, and no octupole shows up. The clustering dipole's own share is marginal. The bottom line: the quasar dipole stays anomalously high, and local clustering does not explain it away.
arxiv-2510-23969:
Harshavardhana T. Gowda, Daniel C. Comstock, and Lee M. Miller present a system that turns muscle signals into speech. Sensors record electrical activity from face and mouth muscles while a person forms words without sound. Their method, called emg2speech, translates those signals directly into audio.

The team found that self-supervised speech features track muscle power closely, with a correlation of 0.85 reported. Signals for distinct mouth movements also formed clear, separate clusters in their analysis. Building on that link, they mapped muscle signals into the speech feature space to generate speech end to end. They tested the system with a participant with ALS who silently mouthed speech. The result points toward a voice option for people who cannot speak aloud.
arxiv-2510-24169:
Vikas and two co-authors, Rahul Marathe and Anjan Roy, ask how well different rules for cell division can be told apart from data. Cells may divide by a timer, by reaching a size, or by adding a set size, and these models are called Timer, Sizer, and Adder. Known tests use correlations between birth size, division time, and related measures.

The authors show other statistical traits of those same measures can also separate the models. The patterns can even distinguish linear from exponential single cell growth. Yet at the population level, distributions of age, size, and added size look the same across models, so population data alone cannot reveal the true division rule.
arxiv-2510-24669:
A Vitrier and one hundred five co-authors look ahead to what a large sky survey with the South Pole scope could teach. Its third camera is scanning about a quarter of the sky for faint heat left from the early cosmos. They ask how well that data could pin down key numbers for the cosmos.

The team checks two hot topics: early dark energy and a shift in the mass of the electron. They also test if scanning each field on its own loses facts versus one joint scan. Their mock pipe line shows the loss, if any, is small for these goals.
arxiv-2510-25069:
Gabin Taibi and Lucia Gomez build TOPol, a frame to map how word sense leans in more than one way at once. Past tools treat lean as one line, from bad to good, which misses the rich form of a tale. Their frame works with a human in the loop who sets the edge between two talk zones.

Texts are set in space by a big model, then grouped into themes by a graph split. For a set edge, shift arrows are drawn between theme hubs on each side. Those arrows form a lean field that can show fine moves when zones swap. The model then names what each arrow means by its end texts. Human picks can then be honed.
arxiv-2510-25169:
Shinji Watanabe, Tsunetomo Yamada, Hiroyuki Takakura, and Nobuhisa Fujita run Monte Carlo tests of a spin model on a quasicrystal with twenty face form. Such forms lack the plain repeat of a crystal, yet hold long range order. Their grid is the ytterbium web of a known cadmium mix, built of full twenty face blocks.

By size scale reads of the runs, they got the key brink scores for pull, response, and link span. The scores pass a known scale check and let them draw the rest. The set of scores marks a new shared class, apart from plain magnets and spin glass. Site types in the web split by how many peers each has.
arxiv-2510-25469:
D Fernandez-Martinez led four co-authors on surfactant kinetics. E J Vega, J M Montanero, and U J Gutierrez-Hernandez helped. D Fernandez Rivas closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper studies rapid interface creation experimentally. A submillimeter jet impacts a surfactant-laden liquid pool. The pool is much larger than the jet.

Cavity retraction and closure occur within a submillisecond. That speed tests dynamic surface tension reduction ability. They compare two surfactants with varied adsorption speeds. Sodium dodecyl sulfate adsorbs at moderately fast rates. Its collapse pathway looked nearly like pure water. Dynamic surface tension reduction seemed negligible there. Surfynol 465 adsorbs at ultrafast rates instead. It allowed deeper cavities that persisted longer. A harmonic oscillator model captured cavity retraction well. That held in the deep seal regime specifically. Fitted damping ratios matched dynamic surface tensions always.
arxiv-2510-25669:
Kirill Boguslavski led four co-authors on minijet thermalization. Florian Lindenbauer, Aleksas Mazeliauskas, and Adam Takacs helped. Fabian Zhou closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper applies QCD kinetic theory. High-momentum partons, called minijets, thermalize in quark-gluon plasma. Weakly coupled kinetic theory models that process. Isotropic hard thermal loop screening is incorporated.

Soft quark and gluon exchanges are modeled that way. Kinetic runs propagate minijets through thermal gluon plasma. Longitudinal and transverse quenching settings are compared. Energy loss and drag coefficients also enter comparisons. Standard definitions neglect recoiling medium particle contributions, they find. Minijet thermalization time scales remarkably with quenching setting. A phenomenological quenching time value is produced. Heavy-ion collision uses motivate the whole study.
arxiv-2510-25869:
Arnaud Marsiglietti and James Melbourne extend a classic probability puzzle to a broader family of distributions. The Littlewood Offord problem asks how concentrated a random signed sum can be at a single value. The original version used fair coin style Bernoulli variables, which take two values with set chances. The authors replace those variables with discrete log concave ones, a wider class with a regular, single peaked shape.

Marsiglietti and Melbourne prove the extension and also discuss a version for arithmetic progressions and an entropy based version. Along the way they recover and extend a known result by Madiman and Woo on the entropy power inequality for discrete uniform variables. The note links counting, probability, and information ideas in one short argument.
arxiv-2510-26069:
Leixian Shen, Yifang Wang, Huamin Qu, Xing Xie, and Haotian Li build a formal model for instructions that mix text prompts with direct screen actions. People working with generative AI usually type a prompt, but fine or pointing intent is hard to put in words. Adding actions such as brushing or clicking can sharpen what the user means, yet designers lacked a shared model of how the two channels combine.

Their Interaction Augmented Instruction model is a compact graph of entities and relations that captures how prompts and actions reinforce each other. From prior tools they distill twelve reusable interaction patterns that can be combined, and four usage scenarios show how the model helps apply, refine, and invent new patterns for future systems.
arxiv-2510-26769:
Anushka Sivakumar, Andrew Zhang, Zaber Hakim, and Chris Thomas add a light steering module to vision-language models. These models answer questions about images, but steering them toward wanted behaviour usually means retraining or hand-tuned interventions. Their module, SteerVLM, learns from paired prompts that show a target behaviour and its opposite.

Sivakumar and her three co-authors adjust the model's internal activations, dimension by dimension and layer by layer, at inference time, without touching its weights. The module's size is a small fraction of the base model's. They also introduce VNIA, a data set of visual narratives built to develop and test steering methods. On steering and hallucination benchmarks, SteerVLM beat existing intervention techniques while holding performance on off-target tasks.
arxiv-2510-27069:
Mohammad Shokouhi and Vincent Wong design beam steering for cell-free massive MIMO inside open radio networks. In this wireless design, many distributed radio units serve users jointly instead of one cell tower per area. Precoding, meaning how each unit shapes its beams toward intended users while limiting interference, can be centralized, which scales poorly, or fully distributed, which can leave heavy interference.

The pair propose distributed precoding where agents exchange limited information to curb interference while maximizing total throughput under minimum rate guarantees. A multi-timescale scheme blends multi-agent deep reinforcement learning with guidance from a classic iterative algorithm. Simulations across unit, user, and antenna counts beat distributed baselines and match centralized throughput with far less signaling overhead.
arxiv-2510-27169:
Yucheng Xing, Jinxing Yin, and Xiaodong Liu present DANCER, a diffusion framework that animates a single person dancing from a reference image and a motion sequence. Video generation must keep both quality and continuity, and human dance is especially hard due to many degrees of freedom in body motion. The system builds on a recent stable video diffusion model.

Two modules exploit the two inputs fully. An appearance enhancement module locks onto fine details of the reference image during generation, while a pose rendering module draws motion guidance from extra domains to sharpen pose control. The team also assembles a new TikTok-3K dataset from online videos for training. Extensive experiments on real datasets show performance above prior state-of-the-art methods, with data and code promised on acceptance.
arxiv-2510-27269:
Deokhyung Kang, Seonjeong Hwang, Daehui Kim, Hyounghun Kim, and Gary Lee investigate why reasoning models perform worse in low-resource languages. Reasoning language models excel at complex tasks in English yet lag elsewhere, and the cause was largely unexplored. The team shows the gap stems mainly from language understanding failures: inputs are not translated into the language dominating the model reasoning traces, usually English.

Understanding failures prove detectable to a meaningful extent, with supervised detectors performing best. Their fix, selective translation, inserts an English translation into the trace only when failure is detected. On a mid-size model it nearly matches full translation while translating only about a fifth of inputs. The results clarify the gap origin and suggest a cheap path to fairer multilingual reasoning.
arxiv-2510-27369:
Tosin Adewumi leads seven co-authors in a systematic survey of natural language processing across the whole battery life cycle. Most prior reviews cover one stage or method; this survey follows the PRISMA method across three major databases, screening hundreds of papers down to a final relevant set. The team also introduces a technical language processing framework aimed at the European Union proposed digital battery passport and general battery predictions.

Findings show new language tasks emerging in the battery domain that aid materials discovery and other life-cycle stages. Challenges remain, notably the lack of standard benchmarks. The proposed framework, incorporating agentic AI and optimized prompts, targets some of those gaps. Review artifacts are publicly provided for validation and reproducibility.
arxiv-2510-27469:
Chenyang Shao, Sijian Ren, and two other co-authors pair two kinds of language models in this 2025 paper. Standard models write one word at a time, so proposing many candidate thoughts costs a lot. Diffusion language models work the other way: they clean a noisy draft in parallel, yielding varied samples in one pass. The team uses them as thought proposers.

A diffusion model drafts candidate steps; a standard model grades them. The split keeps quality while cutting the cost of brainstorming. Word-by-word drafting scales poorly as more compute is spent at test time. Parallel drafting dodges that trap. Across several hard reasoning benchmarks, the paired setup scored strongly. The authors offer it as a path to cheaper, deeper machine reasoning.
arxiv-2510-27569:
Qi Luo and six co-authors present MARAG-R1 in 2025, a search upgrade for language models that rely on one fixed retriever. A retriever is the tool that fetches text for a model. A single tool that returns a fixed top set can miss facts spread across a large corpus, which is a full body of text.

MARAG-R1 gives the model four tools: meaning search, word search, filtering, and pooling facts. Training first copies good paths, then uses rewards so the model learns when to use each tool. The model can thus think and fetch in turns to build proof. Tests on three question sets show broader and more exact access to facts.
arxiv-2510-27669:
Xiuzhen Ye and Wentao Tang present a data-driven way to certify stability traits of unknown nonlinear systems in 2025. The trait at stake is dissipativity, an energy balance rule that covers stability, passivity, and bounded gain in one frame. Past methods fit the needed functions with fixed quadratic forms, which can miss curved behavior.

Their method places those functions in a kernel space, where curves are captured through feature maps without a set form. The learning task becomes a convex program, a well-behaved search with one best answer, built from kernel matrices. Learning theory then bounds how well the result should hold on fresh data. Model-free proof of stability traits aids safe control of complex machines.
arxiv-2511-00069:
Oleksandr Volkov and Nataliia Voinalovych — writing in Ukrainian, per the record's original language — examine a power series distribution built from a certain square-root function and mean-based by its mean. The power series growth of the function is derived with clear coefficients. A spread function is found, expressed as a cubic polynomial in the mean.

A distribution with mean mean form is then built, with chances given in closed form using binomial-like coefficients. Properties of the final family are proved. Probability readers get a new fully worked distribution family. Mean mean form is prized in general linear models because coefficients then describe effects on the mean directly.
arxiv-2511-00669:
Noah Zambrano and Karthik Duraisamy write a turbulence closure that lives in physical space rather than Fourier space. Two-point closures track how flow statistics at pairs of points evolve, but they usually need spectral transforms that fail near sharp jumps. Their approach evolves the longitudinal correlation function directly, in discrete physical form, for uniform isotropic turbulence as the proving ground.

Linear terms keep the near-exact form prized from rapid distortion theory, while nonlinear moments close along the lines of the classic EDQNM model. New features appear: a matrix exponential inside the evolution equation and triple integrals from the nonlocal pressure term. Nonlocal length-scale information enters on its own. Checks against direct simulations and classical forecasts succeed, and extensions to uneven, directional flow are sketched for flows where spectral methods falter.
arxiv-2511-00769:
Zheyuan Lai and Michael Choi study how to approximate a family of Markov chains with simpler models that split into independent parts. The cost of an approximation is measured by information loss, and they want the worst case loss over the whole family to be as small as possible.

Duality results and geometric identities turn that minimax problem into a concave maximization over a simplex, which they read as a game whose mixed strategy equilibrium always exists. A projected subgradient method solves it with guarantees. They also link the choice of split to submodular optimization and test the algorithms on Curie-Weiss and Bernoulli-Laplace chains, where the best approximations turn out to have sparse structure.
arxiv-2511-00869:
Hue Nguyen and colleagues study the k-submodular cover problem, a generalization of a classic covering problem that shows up in influence maximization, resource allocation, and sensor placement. Earlier algorithms either guarantee only weak approximation quality or need far too many evaluations of the objective function.

They propose a fast stochastic greedy algorithm that samples rather than scanning everything, sharply cutting the number of function evaluations. The method keeps a strong two sided approximation guarantee, in the bicriteria sense, while running much more cheaply than the best known alternatives. For large real world artificial intelligence tasks where each evaluation is expensive, that combination of speed and guarantee is the practical point of the work.
arxiv-2511-01569:
Matúš Dubecký proposes a cleaner way to split the correlation energy of electrons, the part of a molecule's energy that simple mean-field pictures miss. His split is based on the wavefunction's sign structure: the nodes, the surfaces where the wavefunction changes sign, which govern the hardest part of quantum Monte Carlo calculations.

Static correlation is defined as the energy penalty for one specific force. The force is making the wavefunction keep a chosen reference node instead of the exact one. The remaining symmetric part holds dynamic correlation, plus a strong but nodeless contribution. The framework is state-based and method-independent. It clarifies how the terms dynamic, nondynamic, strong, and static correlation relate. It also explains why fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo is excellent for some systems yet fails for others.
arxiv-2511-02169:
Xiao-Dong Ma, Michael Schmidt, and Weihang Zhang examine how hypothetical light particles could show up in one of the rarest processes nature might allow. The process is the decay of a nucleon in a way that violates baryon number. Such decays, involving a new light scalar particle, would carry distinctive experimental signatures and are tightly constrained by current experiments. The analysis is carried out systematically inside an effective field theory framework, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory extended by the light scalar.

Using current data, the authors place stringent bounds on the baryon-number-violating operators and predict several three-body nucleon decays that experiments could look for. They also study dinucleon transitions to dileptons inside a nucleus, which complement single-nucleon searches. Three complete ultraviolet models are supplied, each generating a distinct subset of the operators, giving experimentalists concrete targets.
arxiv-2511-02469:
Kaito Takano, Masanori Hirano, and Kei Nakagawa forecast central bank decisions by simulating the committee that makes them. Their subject is the Federal Open Market Committee, whose rate decisions are usually predicted from policy texts with static classifiers that ignore the deliberation behind the decision. The authors instead field a panel of language-model agents, each starting from its own initial belief, reading the same qualitative texts and macroeconomic indicators.

Over several rounds the agents see each other's predictions and revise their own, mimicking deliberation and consensus formation. A latent variable tracks each agent's underlying stance, hawkish or dovish. The theory shows how that stance shapes both what an agent notices in the data and how it responds to peers. The debate-based system significantly beat standard language-model baselines on prediction accuracy, and the explicit beliefs made the forecasts easier to interpret.
arxiv-2511-02569:
E. Kongkui Berinyuy and four co-authors propose a device physics trick for making quantum correlations flow one way. Nonreciprocal entanglement, which changes with direction, is a prized resource for quantum technologies. The authors seek it in a molecular optomagnonic system: a sphere of yttrium iron garnet, a magnetic material, placed inside a microwave cavity that also hosts molecules. The Barnett effect, magnetisation induced by rotation, supplies the asymmetry.

Their scheme adds squeezing to strengthen the effect, and the analysis identifies the parameter regimes where nonreciprocal entanglement and quantum discord are best produced. The correlations prove robust, surviving thermal noise up to high temperatures in the model. The authors present the setup as a new tool for engineering noise-tolerant quantum correlations and, in time, nonreciprocal quantum devices that marry magnons with molecules.
arxiv-2511-02769:
Bum Chul Kwon and nine colleagues built STAR-VAE, a model that generates new molecules under user control. Many molecular transformers lack a proper latent space, so users cannot sample variations or steer properties smoothly. Their 2025 model pairs a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder, pretrained on 79 million molecules from PubChem written in SELFIES notation.

A property signal conditions the prior, the posterior, and the decoder at once, so generation can aim at chosen traits. Light LoRA adapters allow fine-tuning on small data without touching the backbone. Under standard sampling the model produced fully valid molecules with near-perfect novelty, and it steered traits like synthetic accessibility and docking scores for several protein targets. Seed-based sampling also recovered known scaffolds for drug targets.
arxiv-2511-02869:
Amirreza Esmaeili and four colleagues test AdvFusion, a method that lets a code model borrow knowledge across programming languages before settling on a target task. AdapterFusion does something similar but leans mainly on the target language. Earlier tests of AdvFusion used smaller pretrained models and only two tasks. Their 2025 analysis moves to large code models and three new tasks.

The tasks were code generation, code translation, and commit message generation. Results split by task. In code generation, AdvFusion beat AdapterFusion but lost to other tuning methods like LoRA. In commit messages, AdapterFusion came out ahead, and rival methods did not dominate. In translation, AdvFusion trailed AdapterFusion, with the gap growing slightly as models got bigger. The lesson is that no single adapter scheme wins everywhere.
arxiv-2511-03069:
S. Isayama, S. Matsukiyo, T. Sano, and S. Chen describe a multi-stage way that strong Alfven waves can boost electrons to near light speed. The setting is a plasma threaded by a strong magnetic field, where counter-propagating waves first resonate with particles and push them across the field. Their 2025 paper follows the chain stage by stage, through instabilities the waves themselves trigger.

Growing modulations build electric fields inside the wave packet, sharpened by the wave's ponderomotive force, and a surfing resonance then accelerates electrons within a few gyroperiods. Later the parent wave traps particles for another boost, and trailing fields behind the packet add a final push to other electrons. The full chain beats the trailing-field route alone, and may help explain high-energy cosmic rays.
arxiv-2511-03269: Ville Nordstrom settles a guess by Belmans, Fu, and Krug about a homology theory for symmetric powers of a small differential graded category. Hochschild homology measures how a category acts on itself, and symmetric powers build larger categories by allowing unordered collections. Nordstrom shows those homology groups split into pieces fixed solely by the homology of the starting category. That split is valuable because it turns hard new computations into known parts. Later work can lean on it without redoing the full analysis.
arxiv-2511-03369:
Rom Himelstein and colleagues argue that safety-tuned chat models can look fair while still hiding unfair leanings inside. Standard fairness checks use plain question formats, and a model's refusal to answer often gets scored as a good, neutral outcome. The team names the hidden leanings silenced biases: preferences buried in internal patterns and masked by alignment training.

Earlier probes for such leanings relied on trick prompts or hand-built indirect questions, which scale poorly and can taint results. Their approach hunts the buried preferences more directly and broadly. The warning is sharp: refusal is not proof of fairness. Audits that count silence as virtue may certify biased systems for sensitive work where hidden leanings still steer subtle choices.
arxiv-2511-03569:
Rene Henke and colleagues create repulsive polarons in a strongly interacting quantum gas, a regime where such quasiparticles kept falling apart. A polaron is a moving impurity dressed by the medium around it. Attractive versions are well studied, but repulsive ones usually bind into molecules or decay before a dressing cloud can form.

Their medium is a superfluid of lithium dimers held in a flat trap. Promoting a few dimers to higher levels of the trap creates synthetic-spin impurities whose decay routes are blocked. Dressing can then build up even under strong repulsion. Measured traits of the new polarons open a window on impurity physics at the strong end, with echoes for electrons in solids.
arxiv-2511-03669:
Nirmal Ghorai, Partha Paul, and Nemani V Suryanarayana work out sky-sphere products for a four-dimensional gravity theory. Celestial holography rewrites scattering as a theory on the sky sphere. The team uses a bosonic part of a conformal supergravity. Their sums use a layout with helicity set to a peak case.

A lead soft graviton current acts just as in plain gravity. A sublead soft current gains extra terms, though. Its soft rule is not the same for all bulk theories. Those terms still obey the Ward identity of a chiral algebra. They do so through a changed form that can switch particle type. The checks test if the sky dual holds in higher-derivative gravity.
arxiv-2511-04269:
E Trentin is the lead author among fourteen authors reporting new spectroscopy of classical Cepheid stars. These are the period-luminosity calibrators that anchor the extragalactic distance ladder and trace young populations in the Galactic disc. Their survey installment covers one hundred thirty-six spectra of sixty stars from three high-resolution spectrographs.

More than half the stars pulse with periods above fifteen days, doubling that long-period sample. Radial velocities, atmospheric parameters, and abundances for up to thirty-three species were derived, with an updated list of trusted lines. Dysprosium abundances appear for Cepheids for the first time in their knowledge, alongside systematic erbium, lutetium, and thorium estimates, feeding a fresh galactic metallicity gradient.
arxiv-2511-04469:
Dennis Thumm and his co-author build market simulators that can answer what-if questions. Deep generative models already make realistic synthetic price data, but they lack causal reasoning. Without it, they cannot support sound counterfactual tests or risk checks.

Their model joins a variational autoencoder with a structural causal model. A directed acyclic graph inside the decoder enforces the causal order during generation. Training uses a causal version of the Wasserstein distance between data sets. On synthetic series modeled on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, the method beats rivals at counterfactual probability estimates, a step toward simulators regulators can probe.
arxiv-2511-04669:
Arjan Cornelissen leads five authors generalizing quantum search with wildcards. The original problem hides a bit string that algorithms probe by testing chosen subsets. Earlier quantum methods reached a tight cost near the square root of the length.

The new version limits which subsets may be tested, set by a chosen collection. Costs stay unit per test, whatever subset is picked from the allowed family. The team proves near-tight bounds for several natural collections, including bounded-size subsets. The results show how query limits, not just string size, set the true quantum advantage in such search games.
arxiv-2511-04769:
Phat Nguyen leads eight authors with ReGen, a generative system that builds robot simulations by inverse design. Simulation scales robot learning, but building each scene by hand is slow. ReGen starts from the robot's behavior and works backward to the world.

Given a trajectory or objective plus a text description, it infers scenarios that could cause that behavior. A language model grows a directed graph of causes, entities, and their properties. That graph becomes a symbolic program that sets up and runs the simulation. The approach can augment training worlds instead of requiring engineers to draft each one.
arxiv-2511-04969:
Hiroaki Hashida, Yuichi Kawamoto, and Nei Kato study whether rival mobile firms can share one intelligent reflecting surface in future 6G nets. Such panels bounce radio waves around blocks and stretch cover, but one panel per firm wastes money and space.

A shared panel lets firms use common gear, cuts cost, and lowers clashes between their signals. Tests in the study show the shared plan balances gains across firms while it holds down cross-firm noise. The authors frame sharing as a path to greener, cheaper 6G build-out in dense towns and cities.
arxiv-2511-05069:
P. Berk and co-authors study measures and links for affine interval exchange transformations, maps that cut an interval into parts, stretch each part, and swap their order. They focus on cases tied to standard exchanges of hyperbolic periodic type.

The team finds the Hausdorff dimension of the maps' invariant measures and of conformal measures for self-similar cases, plus ties between them. One high point is an exact formula for that dimension when a slope vector is of central-stable type. Such maps model flows on flat surfaces, so their measure traits matter broadly.
arxiv-2511-05269:
Ishan Kavathekar and co-authors introduce TAMAS, a benchmark for hostile risks in systems where many language model agents work as a team. Single-agent safety tests miss the fresh weak spots that appear when agents plan, share tools, and sway each other.

TAMAS sets tasks that probe those team-level risks in a shared way. It aims to give builders a common yardstick for attacks that spread through agent talk or shared state. As multi-agent systems spread to real work, such a test bed helps teams find flaws before attackers do in practice.
arxiv-2511-05569:
Alessandro Contini, Davide Cacciarelli, and Murat Kulahci study how to forecast jet fuel demand at Copenhagen Airport. Fuel sellers must know demand about thirty days ahead to source supply well. Too little fuel risks shortages, while too much ties up stock and money, yet few studies treat this task with machine learning.

Working with data from a major Danish fuel distributor, the team compared classic time series tools, Prophet, neural networks, and hybrid models. They tested the models on three data sets to check how stable the results were. Their case study shows where data-driven models beat expert judgment and how extra input variables change the forecasts.
arxiv-2511-05669:
Jake Miller and co-authors report four years of watching the glowing disks around eighteen active galactic nuclei. By timing how light echoes between color bands, a method called continuum reverberation mapping, astronomers can measure the size of the bright region near each black hole. That light was long blamed on the accretion disk alone.

The team gathered high-quality light curves and measured lags between bands for each galaxy. Adding their sample to older ones, they tested how lag grows with brightness. Lag rose with luminosity at close to the rate theory predicts. The result fits light coming from the disk, from the surrounding broad-line region, or from a mix of both.
arxiv-2511-06169:
Sanskar Amgain and co-authors study federated learning, where many separate clients train one shared model without pooling their data. Wrong labels on some clients can poison the shared model and hurt its accuracy for everyone. Older defenses assume enough clean clients exist to lean on, which often fails in messy real settings.

Their fix regularizes each client locally before anything is sent to the server. A rule based on similarity between nearby data points, measured in a self-supervised model's representation space, keeps local training honest. The method needs no shared architecture between the helper model and the classifier, and it beat leading federated methods on vision and medical image benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-06469: Johnathon Taylor constructs, for any given limit sketch, the universal example of a realized limit sketch built from it. Limit sketches are category-theoretic blueprints that describe mathematical structures through chosen limit cones, and a realization turns such a blueprint into an actual category. Taylor's construction organizes the classical argument through factorization systems, giving the technical steps a cleaner and more unified form. The result frames realizations of limit sketches in terms of factorization data, supplying structured groundwork for later work in categorical logic and sketch theory.
arxiv-2511-06669:
Mathieu Yahiaoui and Mario Kieburg study how to classify one-dimensional disordered quantum systems that have chiral symmetry. Their tool is a winding number, a count of how many times a certain determinant wraps around as it travels once around a circle. The determinant comes from a random matrix model of the disordered substance's off-diagonal block.

The authors compute the related partition function exactly for a broad family of two-matrix models, going beyond the standard Ginibre ensemble studied before. For very large matrices they derive how the average winding number grows, showing a leading term with universal features. They also identify a new correction term that depends on the ensemble's tails and was absent in the earlier Ginibre case.
arxiv-2511-06769:
Ridoy Chandra Shil and colleagues release a colonoscopy image dataset gathered in a resource-limited clinical setting. Finding polyps early prevents colorectal cancer, and computer-aided diagnosis needs training data that looks like real practice. Popular public sets are small, polished, or free of the artifacts that crowd everyday endoscopy suites.

The dataset holds nearly thirteen hundred polyp images from one hundred sixty-four patients, each with an expert-checked mask, plus more polyp-free images. Motion blur, glare, stool, blood, and dim frames all appear as they do in routine work. Baseline classifiers reached about ninety-one percent accuracy and the best segmentation scored moderately, trailing curated sets precisely because the images are harder.
arxiv-2511-07069:
Seçil Şentorun constructs exact solutions in a modified theory of gravity where the Einstein-Hilbert action gains a term quadratic in the curvature. The work sits at the theory's critical point, where the effective gravitational coupling vanishes and the field equations become degenerate. On product geometries combining a Lifshitz-type spacetime, which scales space and time differently, with a constant-curvature space, the author treats static, rotating, and hyperscaling-violating configurations in one system.

The theory admits broad new classes of exact Lifshitz black holes and black branes, including extremal ones, with scaling exponents and horizon structures constrained by the higher-order terms. Reflecting that degenerate point, these solutions carry almost no entropy and no net charge despite nonzero temperature. The results extend earlier Lifshitz builds in Einstein and higher-derivative gravity.
arxiv-2511-07369:
Dorje C Brody and Rishindra Melanathuru work out what happens when a quantum system is watched by measuring everything at once rather than watching one preferred observable. This universal tomographic watching is modeled in two equivalent ways: repeated positive operator-valued readings, and a continuous-time version of the Lindblad equation. The decoherence it causes is tracked through Stratonovich-Weyl quasiprobability distributions, which can dip negative for truly quantum states.

The authors show the watching step by step makes any such distribution manifestly positive, a concrete sense in which classicality emerges from being watched. More striking still, the decoherence time, the time after which every initial state's distribution is nonnegative, shrinks as the Hilbert space dimension grows. Larger quantum systems, in this model, lose their quantum nature faster than small ones.
arxiv-2511-08069:
Loris Di Cairano, Matteo Gori, Reza Karimpour, and Alexandre Tkatchenko reveal a long range interatomic force coming from many body quantum electrodynamics. Familiar emergent forces such as van der Waals and Casimir effects fade quickly with distance. Fundamental forces fall off far more slowly, so a persistent inverse distance interaction between neutral atoms would be surprising.

Modeling atoms as charged harmonic oscillators, the authors apply perturbative quantum electrodynamics in the non retarded regime. Coupling between virtual photons and molecular plasmons produces the slow decaying force, scaling with the third power of the fine structure constant. Though weaker than van der Waals forces, it may beat gravity in future microscopic tests.
arxiv-2511-08369:
Xinyu Zhou, Yu Wu, Jiayao Ma, and Wenhao Wang define text based aerial ground person retrieval, finding a person from a written description when photos come from both drones and ground cameras. Traditional text to person search uses only ground views, so viewpoint gaps between aerial and street images add a major new difficulty. The task matters for surveillance and search settings where both camera types operate together.

The team builds TAG-PEDES, a data set with automatically generated, diversified descriptions drawn from public benchmarks. Their TAG-CLIP model routes features through a mixture of experts to learn view specific and view shared traits, then decouples viewpoint information for cleaner text alignment. Results improve on the new data set and older ground only benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-08469:
Minchi Hu proposes a cluster triggered encoding that turns static images into spike trains for spiking neural networks, the event driven networks modeled loosely on brains. Common encodings such as rate coding or time to first spike ignore spatial correlations and produce inconsistent timing, hurting efficiency and interpretability. The new method first clusters the image in two dimensions, using connected components and local density to find salient foreground regions worth encoding carefully.

Extending the clustering across time gives a three dimensional spatio temporal scheme with stronger temporal coherence. On the N-MNIST data set, a simple single layer network using this encoder reaches higher accuracy than time to first spike encoding. It also uses notably fewer spikes per sample, improving efficiency without sacrificing recognition quality.
arxiv-2511-08969:
Robert Angarone, Jang Soo Kim, Jaeseong Oh, and Daniel Tamayo Farber study entrywise products of matrices that encode Schur polynomials. Jacobi-Trudi matrices build these symmetric functions from complete homogeneous pieces, and a conjecture of Sokal said their Hadamard products would stay strongly positive, building on an older theorem about Toeplitz arrays.

The authors prove that Temperley-Lieb immanants of such products are Schur positive when the skew shapes look like ribbons. That settles Sokal's conjecture for all minors coming from ribbon-like shapes. Better still, they give a positive expansion of these immanants into Schur functions for products indexed by ribbons. A representation built for the ribbon case supplies a proof from representation theory, tying the algebra to symmetry in a concrete way.
arxiv-2511-09569:
George Stamatelis and George C. Alexandropoulos filter signals from systems that jump between modes, when parts of the dynamics are unknown. Jump Markov systems switch among operating regimes. Estimating their state in real time is complicated by unknown noise statistics and transition rules. Classical filters need that knowledge and degrade without it.

Their filtering network pairs two recurrent networks. One predicts the current mode, the other filters using a mode-aware version of KalmanNet. Joint training by alternating least squares lets the networks adapt to each other without labels for the hidden modes. On target tracking, pendulum, Lorenz, and real-life data, it beats classical filters and deep baselines. The margin grows under heavy, non-stationary noise.
arxiv-2511-09769:
Aaron Miller, Sahil Kommalapati, Robert Moser, and Petros Koumoutsakos test a long-standing idea about why turbulence models so often fail. Reynolds-averaged simulations need closure terms, and Kassinos and co-workers argued in 2001 that the usual statistical description of turbulence is simply too thin. Their proposed fix was a richer set of quantities called structure tensors.

The team builds symmetry-aware closures from those tensors using equivariant neural networks, which respect the geometry of the problem by construction. They also give an algorithm that enforces the algebraic relations among tensor parts. Trained on rapid distortion theory data, the networks learned high-order tensor relationships and proved far more accurate than existing models for the rapid pressure-strain term, supporting the structure tensor hypothesis.
arxiv-2511-09969:
Juliana Nieto-Cardenas, Erin Joy Kramer, Peter Kurto, Ethan Dickey, and Andres Bejarano present Owlgorithm, a platform that uses a large language model to prompt reflection in competitive programming students. Self-regulated learning matters in such courses, and Owlgorithm generates context-aware metacognitive questions tailored to each submission using GPT-4o. Correct solutions draw prompts toward deeper insight, while partial or failed ones draw structured debugging questions.

Deployed in a second- and third-year course, the system drew mixed reviews: many students found the questions useful for reflection and debugging. Teaching assistants raised concerns about feedback accuracy and classroom usability. The authors conclude that model-driven reflection can work, provided prompt design, dynamic adaptation, and usability get careful attention, and they offer recommendations for educators.
arxiv-2511-10469:
David Hume and John M. Mackay work in geometric group theory, a field that studies the large-scale shape of spaces and groups. Their paper strengthens the link between two quantities: the conformal dimension of a compact metric space and a critical exponent drawn from the Poincaré profiles of its hyperbolic cone.

They prove the two values are equal in two settings, including spaces built as a product with an interval and cones that resemble certain Heintze manifolds. A lower bound for round trees does much of the work and also applies to random groups and Coxeter groups. For torsion-free hyperbolic groups, the results tie the exponent to how fast the separation profile grows, and they yield new obstructions to coarse embeddings.
arxiv-2511-10769:
Akram Aldroubi, Carlos Cabrelli, Ilya Krishtal, and Ursula Molter survey dynamical sampling, a family of problems where measurements are gathered over time from a signal that evolves under some dynamical system. Instead of sampling a static object once, the observer watches it change and tries to reconstruct what matters from the moving record.

The goals vary: recovering the initial state, identifying the evolution operator, or locating the sources and sinks driving the motion. The survey lays out the theoretical foundations, which lean on frame theory, operator theory, and functional analysis, then summarizes recent results. It closes with directions for future work, including open problems and conjectures, and notes applications across engineering and the sciences.
arxiv-2511-11169:
Ayush Pandey, Jai Bardhan, and their colleagues introduce AlignVQA, a debate-based system that makes visual question answering models report confidence that matches their true accuracy. Modern vision-language systems answer well but often sound sure when they are wrong, a risk when they act alone in high-stakes fields. Calibration, the match between stated confidence and real hit rate, is the gap addressed here.

Several specialist models, each prompted in a distinct style, draft answers first. Generalist agents then critique, refine, and merge those drafts in a two-stage exchange. Better calibrated specialists led to better aligned final confidence, and a new trainable loss pushes calibration further.
arxiv-2511-11269:
Yang Xiao and Yuxiao Xie extend a theory called compactified imaginary Liouville theory to surfaces with a boundary. The theory is a conformal field theory. Such theories describe systems that look the same at every scale. This one is not unitary, and it has a logarithmic twist. It is thought to capture the scaling limit of loop models. Two such models are the Potts model and the O(n) model.

The work starts from a Gaussian free field on a surface with a rim. The field obeys a Neumann condition at the rim. Curvature terms are then added, in the bulk and on the rim. So are potential terms built from a chaos construction. The authors prove the result meets the axioms of conformal field theory. The gluing axioms are among them.
arxiv-2511-11469:
J. Maxwell Riestenberg and Peter Smillie prove a test they call stability. The test tells when a rough map must lie close to a true harmonic map. The map runs from a curved space into a Hadamard space. Such spaces have nonpositive curvature and are used in geometry and group theory.

Under extra conditions, the harmonic map is also unique. The test then proves a broad form of the Schoen-Li-Wang claim on maps between rank-one spaces. The rank-one demand on the target can be dropped. This lets the authors define a universal Hitchin component for each real projective group. It is a higher analogue of universal Teichmüller space, with two natural descriptions.
arxiv-2511-11569:
Héber H. Arcolezi introduces ModularSubsetSelection, an algorithm for estimating how often each value appears in a population while giving every user local differential privacy. Each phone or device must report its value in a way that hides the true value, yet the server still needs accurate totals.

Values are encoded through a residue number system built from pairwise coprime moduli, and each user sends one random index plus a perturbed residue using an optimal subset selection step. Messages shrink to a handful of bits, far below standard methods, while server decoding stays efficient. Privacy-preserving analytics for large surveys and telemetry are the natural home for the method.
arxiv-2511-11669:
Dmytro Hospodarchuk sketches the H-Model, a neural network design whose internal structure reshapes itself in response to each input. A routing mechanism lets every layer influence how its outputs travel onward, so computation becomes iterative and adaptive rather than a fixed pipeline.

Inspiration comes loosely from thought processes, where information flow depends on both the data and the system's own state. The author is explicit that the goal is not to rival state-of-the-art language models. Instead the work is a conceptual prototype, an architectural framework meant to open a new direction for adaptive processing that later, stronger systems might build on.
arxiv-2511-11869:
Bengt Friman and Volker Koch test a standard fix in heavy-ion physics. The fix is the centrality bin width correction. It aims to remove fake fluctuations from grouping collisions of distinct sizes into one bin. Proton number cumulants are hunted as signs of a critical point in hot nuclear matter. A faulty fix could fake or erase a discovery.

An analytically tractable model is built for the test. It has realistic links between multiplicity and proton number. Resonance decays are included as a correlation source. The model shows where the fix works. It also shows where it misleads. The failure modes protect one of the field's most delicate measurements.
arxiv-2511-12669:
K. Folias and Ch. C. Moustakidis build a model of hot quarkyonic matter, a proposed state inside very dense objects such as neutron stars. What neutron stars are made of is still an open question. One leading idea is that matter there mixes traits of ordinary hadronic matter and freed quark matter, forming quarkyonic particles. The makeup chosen decides the equation of state, the rule that links pressure and density, and through it the star's size and mass.

Their model borrows from hadronic physics and lets the interaction between quarkyonic particles depend on both position and momentum. They show this choice can notably change the shape of the equation of state, especially for hot stars where temperature matters. Because the model is flexible, recent observations of neutron stars can be used to pin down its parameters. The paper offers one testable route to describing matter at extreme density and heat.
arxiv-2511-13269:
Lingfeng Zhang and 9 co-authors test whether vision-language models are ready to guide drones through real space. Such models see and reason well in many settings, but their spatial skill in flight had not been measured. Their new SpatialSky-Bench checks perception and scene grasp across thirteen sub-tasks, from boxes and color to height and landing safety.

Tests of major open and closed models showed weak results in complex flight scenes. To close the gap, the team built a dataset with one million labeled samples and trained Sky-VLM, a model tuned for drone spatial reasoning. Sky-VLM scored best on every bench task in their tests.
arxiv-2511-13669:
Sydney Erickson and 14 co-authors forecast how strongly lensed active galaxies from the coming LSST survey can constrain dark energy. A lensed galaxy whose light arrives with a time delay lets astronomers read the universe's expansion history, independent of other probes. Hundreds of such lenses must be judged jointly, so the team built a scalable hierarchical inference tool.

Their simulation emulates the full joint analysis for an assumed sample of eight hundred lenses, including image modeling, delay and velocity measures, and outside mass effects. Baseline forecasts reach a few-percent measure of the Hubble constant with a solid dark energy score. Adding many lenses with plain delay data nearly tripled that score, and richer follow-up helped further.
arxiv-2511-13969:
Erick Ross, Alexandre van Lidth, Martha Rose Wolf, and one co-author count modular forms by their Atkin-Lehner signs, a pattern of plus and minus values attached to each form. For a fixed level and even weight, they first work out the exact share of forms, in both the full space and the newspace, that carry each possible sign pattern.

They then study Hecke operators restricted to the subspaces with a given sign pattern. The eigenvalues turn out to be equidistributed under the p-adic Plancherel measure as level and weight grow. Combining exact proportions with limiting distributions gives a fine-grained picture of how these arithmetic symmetries organize the spectrum.
arxiv-2511-14069:
Zhuoqing Zheng, Tao Liu, and Xuyang Wu speed up two classic methods for equality-constrained convex optimization. Dual ascent and the method of multipliers both update through a simple linear stand-in for the dual function, and that crude approximation slows them down. The authors adapt a bundle framework that keeps a list of sharper surrogate functions.

Applying the bundle idea to both primal and dual updates yields a family of primal-dual bundle methods that contains several known algorithms as special cases. Under standard assumptions they prove convergence guarantees for the whole family. Numerical experiments show faster convergence and much better robustness to parameter choices than the methods they generalize.
arxiv-2511-15069:
Haoyong Wu and Yongmei Liu propose ProRAC, a neuro symbolic method for reasoning about actions and change. The task is tracking how a world evolves as actions happen and answering questions about the result. Their framework uses a large language model inside a structured progression process rather than asking for an answer in one shot.

ProRAC first extracts the actions and the question from a problem, then executes each action step by step to derive the final state, and finally checks the query against that state.
