Evaluations on several benchmarks show strong performance across different domains, language model backbones, and kinds of reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2511-15169:
Xin Gao, Shaohan Yu, and nine co-authors build SafeRBench, a benchmark that grades the safety of large reasoning models across their whole thought process. Reasoning models show their chain of thought, and that openness cuts both ways: steps can be used to excuse harmful acts or to hide intent. Most safety tests read only the final answer and miss risks that drift in midway.

SafeRBench probes safety at graded risk levels, beyond simple banned topics, to stress the boundary harder. A micro-thought analysis chops the reasoning trace into small chunks to pinpoint exactly where a response turns unsafe. The end-to-end view, from input to trace to answer, gives developers a way to catch failures that final-answer checks never see.
arxiv-2511-15269:
Robert Kraft, Florian Bruckner, and two co-authors release jaxFMM, a fast multipole solver for point charges that runs on graphics processors. The fast multipole method computes long-range forces, such as those from electric charges under the Laplace kernel, without checking every pair. Their version is written in the JAX framework, whose just-in-time compiler and automatic differentiation come along for free.

An adaptive scheme refines the grid only where charges cluster, and rotations are computed on the fly to keep the code strikingly short. Benchmarks show strong speed at moderate accuracy, even for highly uneven charge layouts. The immediate win is faster stray-field calculation in micromagnetics, with inverse design and machine learning uses opened by the built-in gradients.
arxiv-2511-15569:
ATLAS Collaboration reports measurements of pairs of Z bosons produced in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The Z boson is a heavy carrier of the weak force, and pair production tests the Standard Model at high energy. Data at thirteen tera-electronvolts were collected with the ATLAS detector, covering both plain pair production and production alongside two extra jets.

In the studied channel, one Z decays to charged leptons and the other to invisible neutrinos. Measured rates for both processes match Standard Model predictions well, and results are broken down across many motion variables. The data also set limits on anomalous self-interactions among gauge bosons, tested through two different theoretical frameworks.
arxiv-2511-15869:
Kaelee S. Parker, Danielle A. Berg, and twenty-six co-authors compare ways of estimating how many ionizing photons escape from nearby star-forming galaxies. That escape fraction matters because early galaxies reionized the universe, but direct measurement is impossible for distant galaxies whose light is blocked by intergalactic gas. Nearby galaxies from a Hubble legacy survey serve as a test bed where indirect methods can be compared.

Six diagnostics, based on ultraviolet absorption lines, continuum slope, hydrogen line shapes, a multivariate model, simulations, and emission line ratios, were applied to forty-five galaxies. Predictions vary, yet classifications into weak and strong leakers broadly agree. Evidence points to two escape routes: early escape driven by very young stars, and delayed escape linked to supernovae.
arxiv-2511-16069:
Junchao Zhou, Junkang Liu, and Fanhua Shang present ILoRA. ILoRA is a frame for federated learning with low-rank adapters under uneven client conditions. Federated learning trains a shared model across clients with no central data pool. Low-rank adaptation tunes small matrices instead of the full model. Uneven clients cause three problems: random starts misalign client subspaces, ranks that differ break averaging, and non-identical data drift clients apart.

ILoRA answers each problem in turn. A shared orthonormal start keeps clients in one subspace. An aggregation step joins and then decomposes updates of differing ranks, keeping information and aligning sizes. An optimizer with rank-aware control terms corrects local drift. Convergence guarantees are given, and vision and language tests show better accuracy and stability.
arxiv-2511-16169:
Zijian Wang, Xiaoyu Bao, and four co-authors present UT-OSANet, a deep learning model for event-level diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea. Sleep apnea is a common disorder tied to cardiovascular risk and higher mortality, yet existing tools classify severity only roughly or detect isolated events. Their model aims for detailed identification of apnea, hypopnea, oxygen desaturation, and arousal events across home, clinical, and research settings.

Inputs are flexible: brain wave, airflow, and oxygen saturation channels can be combined in varying subsets. Random masked modality training teaches cross-modal relationships while keeping performance steady when channels are missing. Trained and evaluated on over nine thousand sleep recordings from five independent data sets, the model reached high sensitivity and strong overall scores.
arxiv-2511-16469:
Weixuan Wang and five co-authors design state observers for networked linear systems whose dynamics split into fast and slow parts and whose measurements carry noise. In such emulation-based designs, a continuous observer is implemented over a network, and the central question is how long the gaps between transmissions may safely be.

Modeling the system as a hybrid singularly perturbed system lets the authors derive explicit bounds on the maximum allowable transmission interval for both the fast and slow channels. Under those bounds the observer's error has an exponential stability property, with the final error scaling in proportion to the noise size and the rate of change of the control input. A numerical example confirms the design works as the theory predicts.
arxiv-2511-16669:
Junhao Cheng, Liang Hou, Xin Tao, and Jing Liao propose answering questions with generated video instead of text, for the many tasks where showing beats telling, like teaching a hands-on procedure. Their task, Video-Next-Event Prediction, gives a model a video plus a procedural or predictive question and requires a video answer.

Their model, VANS, uses reinforcement learning to align a vision-language model with a video diffusion model. A shared reward, optimized by their Joint-GRPO method, pushes the language model to write captions that are accurate and easy to visualize. It also pushes the video model to render clips faithful to those captions and the input. A new dataset of a hundred thousand examples supports training, and the system leads on procedural and predictive benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-16769:
Johan Sebastián Galindez-Acosta and Juan José Giraldo-Huertas test a mechanism they call deferred trust: when people distrust human advisors, their reliance shifts to AI systems that look more neutral or competent. Fifty-five undergraduates chose guidance from AI agents, voice assistants, peers, adults, or priests across thirty factual, emotional, and moral scenarios.

Adults were picked most overall, AI second. Clustering showed AI dominating factual scenarios while humans prevailed on social and moral ones. Lower prior trust in priests, peers, and adults consistently predicted choosing AI, exactly the deferred trust pattern, and machine learning models predicted selections well from trust and demographic variables. Profiles high in AI trust combined human distrust, lower technology use, and higher socioeconomic status. The authors warn that fluency-driven over-reliance is a real risk and argue for transparency that calibrates vigilance.
arxiv-2511-17069:
Yunsung Kim, Mike Hardy, Joseph Tey, Candace Thille, and Chris Piech address a gap in machine grading of student work: scores that no one can explain. Machine scoring can handle complex student answers at scale, yet schools still lack a widely trusted way to make those scores clear. The team starts by asking what each group around a test, from students to officials, needs from an explanation.

From those needs they set four principles, covering faith to the student's work, grounding in the task, a clear trail, and parts that can be swapped. They then build a sample system, AnalyticScore, that follows the principles for written answers. In their tests it beats many opaque scoring methods, which suggests clear scoring need not mean weaker scoring.
arxiv-2511-17669:
Ashish, Aparajita Jaiswal, Sudip Vhaduri, Niveditha Nerella, and Shubham Jha present Empa, an AI mentor that teaches global teamwork skills inside computing courses. High-performance computing now runs through world-spanning teams, yet standard courses rarely train students for cross-cultural work. Empa, built on large language models and delivered as a web app, guides students through structured activities on cultural dimensions, communication styles, and settling conflicts.

The mentor is aimed at undergraduates who will join international research teams and shared computing projects. By weaving intercultural practice into technical training, the authors hope to produce graduates who can handle both the machines and the human mix around them. The paper sets out the system's design and the gap in current curricula that it is meant to close.
arxiv-2511-17869:
Subramanyam Sahoo and Jared Junkin tackle reward hacking in embodied artificial agents, where a system games its score instead of doing the real task. Their method breaks a task into clear subtasks inside a three part transformer design with planner, coordinator, and executor roles.

The design also produces visual diagnostics that show where the model attends and how signals flow. On a set of human feedback samples, breaking tasks into about twelve to twenty five steps cuts reward hacking across four failure types by about a third. The authors argue that built in decomposition beats watching behavior only after the fact.
arxiv-2511-17969:
Seokkyu An and Taisuke Ozaki build a rigorous density functional framework for core level X-ray absorption, a spectroscopy that probes an atom by lifting a deep core electron. Good simulations need absolute energy alignment without hand tuned shifts, which standard practice often lacks.

Their method rests on a constrained search for core excited states and a scheme that treats different edges consistently, including spin orbit effects. A reformulation using dipole selection rules cuts the cost of key quantities by a factor tied to system size. Benchmarks on carbon, boron, oxygen, and lithium edges in molecules and solids reproduce shapes and onsets well.
arxiv-2511-18069:
Pranav Kumar and four co-authors study how hydrogen moves inside a titanium chromium Laves phase alloy used for hydrogen storage. They cover both its cubic and hexagonal forms and a range of hydrogen content. They combine quantum calculations with machine learning potentials that make long simulations affordable.

Migration barriers are much higher for paths that break a titanium hydrogen bond than for those breaking a chromium hydrogen bond, so hydrogen travels mainly along rings of the easier paths. Diffusion varies non monotonically with concentration, follows a standard temperature law, and runs faster in simulation than in some experiments, likely because real defects trap hydrogen.
arxiv-2511-18469: G. S. Bisnovatyi-Kogan constructs an approximate analytic model, in one dimension, of the boundary layer where an accretion disk meets a neutron star whose magnetic field is too weak to affect the inflow. The model covers the high luminosity case, where radiation pressure dominates in the inner part of the disk. In that regime the layer's structure is hard to compute exactly, so a tractable analytic description helps interpret luminous accreting neutron stars.
arxiv-2511-19369:
Mohammed Almekhlafi, Antoine Lesage-Landry, and Gunes Karabulut Kurt design a hybrid satellite system to bring computing services to Canada's far north. Arctic communities suffer patchy, high-latency connectivity because low Earth orbit satellites cover them sparsely as they sweep past. The proposal pairs those fast low satellites with medium Earth orbit satellites, which linger longer over a region. It offloads computing tasks across both layers under an optimisation framework that maximises how many tasks are admitted while respecting energy and delay limits.

Satellite visibility windows and limited onboard computing shape the plan, which selects paths dynamically and allocates radio and processor resources jointly. The hard optimisation is recast into a form standard solvers can handle. Simulations show the hybrid beating single-layer designs, a step toward dependable services for remote northern regions.
arxiv-2511-19569:
Wentao Ye and nine co-authors attack a privacy risk: recovering the hidden prompt behind a language model's output. Their idea rests on an invariant latent space hypothesis. Outputs from one prompt should keep consistent meaning, and mapping output back to input should be self-consistent in a shared latent space.

The system, called Inv2A, trains only a light inverse encoder that maps outputs to a cleaned pseudo-representation, treating the model itself as the decoder. Several outputs can be merged to add information. Training mixes contrastive alignment with supervised reinforcement, and an optional local search refines results. On nine data sets it beats rivals on prompt recovery scores.
arxiv-2511-19669:
Souradip Poddar and five co-authors automate analog and mixed-signal circuit design with a reasoning agent built like a tree. Classic AI design tools lean on fixed high-quality data sets, transfer poorly between circuit types, and cannot adapt. Their framework, HeaRT, organizes design reasoning hierarchically to mimic a human designer's loop.

On a benchmark of forty flattened SPICE circuits, HeaRT beats few-shot prompting baselines by wide margins on spotting subcircuits and loops, across several language model backbones. When design goals shift, it converges at least three times faster than rivals. Both reshaping the circuit layout and resizing parts are supported.
arxiv-2511-19769:
Amit Lavon introduces Blini, a lightweight tool for searching nucleotide sequences and for dereplicating sequence collections, removing near-duplicate copies so a data set shrinks to its distinct members. Biologists assembling genomes end up with large piles of long sequences that are too big to search with online tools and too demanding for an ordinary local machine. Blini is built to do both jobs quickly on modest hardware.

Benchmarks on simulated data, the author reports, show Blini running faster than existing tools while using less memory, and holding onto search and clustering accuracy. For labs cleaning and characterising big collections of assembled fragments, a tool that runs locally without a cluster could shorten the dull first pass of almost every sequencing project.
arxiv-2511-19969:
Weizi Shao, Taolin Zhang, Zijie Zhou, Chen Chen, Chengyu Wang, and Xiaofeng He present M3Prune, a way to cut chatter in multi-agent retrieval systems. Teams of multimodal agents that fetch outside knowledge beat single models, but their messages pile up token cost and computing cost. That overhead blocks large-scale use.

M3Prune prunes the communication graph in a hierarchy. It first sparsifies links inside the text and image modes, keeping the edges that matter most for the task. Those key edges then build a dynamic topology across modes, and redundant edges are removed step by step. On general and domain-specific benchmarks, the method beats single-agent and multi-agent rivals while using far fewer tokens.
arxiv-2511-20069:
Healy, Prosdocimi, and Antoniano-Villalobos model how extreme downpours cluster over Italy's Piave Basin. Their 2025 paper studies hourly rainfall extremes in northeast Italy. Floods and landslides there trace back to intense rain bursts. Seasonal patterns shape both rainfall size and spatial spread. Dependence between sites weakens as events grow more extreme.

Hourly records came from sixty-five monitoring sites initially. Data spanned 1990 to 2023, averaging nearly twenty-eight years per site. Strict quality rules trimmed the network to forty-nine sites. Monthly maxima of hourly rain formed the analysis target. The team compared covariate-driven models for extremes. Climate variables entered at several space and time scales. A flexible max-id model handled dependence flexibly. Modeling only the margins missed real variability, they found. Seasonal change in dependence mattered just as much. Risk estimates improve when both layers vary.
arxiv-2511-20269:
Ding, Jin, Lei, Li, and Vesnin build finite-type invariants for virtual knotoids. Their 2025 paper extends Vassiliev theory to open-ended knot diagrams. A knotoid is an immersed interval with two loose ends. Virtual crossings add a modern twist to the diagrams. Invariants sort such objects up to allowed moves.

Two smoothing invariants, F and L, are introduced first. They take values in a module spanned by flat knotoids. Both prove to be Vassiliev invariants of order one. A third invariant, G, is built to be universal. Universal means it captures all order-one information. G turns out stronger than both F and L. The proof extends Turaev and Henrich's matrix invariant. Singular virtual strings become singular open strings there. One singular crossing is the test case handled. Knotoid theory began with Turaev in 2012. Finite-type methods now reach its virtual branch. Classification tools for open knots grow sharper.
arxiv-2511-20369:
Schüssele, Zumkeller, Lagunes-Rochin, and Klumpp shrink correctness proofs for concurrent programs. Their 2025 paper addresses software verification, which checks programs mathematically. Verifier tools can contain bugs that undermine their verdicts. Certificates let outsiders validate results independently and cheaply. But proofs based on thread interleavings can explode in size. The team converts such proofs into modular ones instead.

Their approach follows the Owicki-Gries proof style. Ghost variables are synthesized automatically to hold interleaving information. Those variables capture only the details that actually matter. The key concept is an empire, a compact summary of ordering facts. Evaluation showed the method is efficient in practice. Ninety percent of annotations were computed in under one second. Imperial annotations averaged about fifteen times smaller than naive ones. A naive baseline failed on 204 benchmark cases from resource exhaustion. Validation ran faster than verification in seventy-eight percent of benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-20569:
Ahmadi, Malavazi, Mazurek, Horodecki, and Barzanjeh charge quantum batteries at a spectral cliff edge. Their 2025 paper engineers exceptional points without any gain medium. At an exceptional point, two modes merge into one singular state. Systems there react hugely to tiny changes. Using that for energy storage seemed to need amplification tricks.

Their design uses a dissipative middleman between charging and storage modes. Careful reservoir engineering creates an effective complex coupling. The exceptional point appears in the equations' drift matrix directly. The setup stays fully passive and physically consistent throughout. Two regimes emerge from the engineered singularity. In the stable phase stored energy saturates under drive. In the broken phase it grows exponentially from a bounded drive. Dissipative interference boosts the energy flow between modes. No nonlinear amplification or balanced loss is required. Several physical platforms could host it. Fast, robust quantum energy storage is the target.
arxiv-2511-21069:
Andrius Burnelis and Daniel R. Phillips sharpen in 2025 the theory of how helium-3 nuclei bounce off helium-4, a reaction chain feeding the Sun's neutrino output. Their tool is halo effective field theory, which exploits the wide gap between the cluster's internal energy scales and its gentle collisions. The twist is a 7/2-minus f-wave resonance that changes the theory's power counting as energy grows. They model the truncation error at the partial-wave level, building a covariance matrix whose structure shifts with energy.

A Bayesian analysis with SONIK scattering data, beam energies from 0.7 to 5.5 MeV, then fits the range parameters and the uncertainty model together. Without f-wave interactions the fit covers data only up to 2.6 MeV; with them it reaches 5.5 MeV. The analysis confirms f-wave interactions become necessary above about 3.6 MeV in the laboratory frame. Inferred breakdown scales match earlier work, validating the error model.
arxiv-2511-21369:
Tingkai Xue and colleagues present in 2025 a hybrid physics-neural model that collapses hours of 3D simulation into under a minute. The target: scalar transport, how a pollutant spreads through a complex domain, where analysts need plane-level values like concentration at human height, 1.5 metres up. Simulating the volume to get one plane is wasteful. Their framework couples a finite-volume solver on the plane with a neural closure supplying the 3D effects.

The closure is non-Markovian, meaning it remembers the past, as Mori-Zwanzig theory requires; an LSTM network carries it. Training and physics parameters, like direction-dependent diffusivity, are learned end to end. It needed only 26 training simulations. It stayed stable over long rollouts and generalised to a moving source outside its training data, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.96 at the final time. The authors offer it as a template for fast surrogates of costly physics.
arxiv-2511-21569:
Alex Diep audits whether AI models admit they are AI when dressed in expert personas, in a 2025 behavioral study. A chatbot playing neurosurgeon or financial advisor without disclosing its simulated nature invites misplaced trust in high-stakes settings. Diep ran sixteen open-weight models, from 4 billion to 671 billion parameters, through identical conditions across 19,200 trials and measured how often each persona volunteered the truth.

Disclosure proved wildly inconsistent across domains: the Financial Advisor persona disclosed at 30.8 percent of first prompts, the Neurosurgeon persona at only 3.5 percent in the same setup. Across model families, rates ranged from under 3 to nearly 74 percent, and size did not predict honesty: one 14-billion model hit 61.4 percent while a 70-billion model managed 4.1 percent in testing. Reasoning-optimized variants disclosed up to 48.4 percent less than their base versions. Diep calls the trust spillover a Reverse Gell-Mann Amnesia risk.
arxiv-2511-21869:
Islam and colleagues describe a model-agnostic way to hunt for new physics at the Large Hadron Collider, plus a public web tool called ADFilter. Traditional searches target predicted particles and can miss unexpected ones. Anomaly detection instead trains an autoencoder, a neural network that compresses and rebuilds data, on ordinary collision events, then flags events it rebuilds badly as suspicious.

The work builds on recent ATLAS analysis that encoded each collision in a 36 by 36 rapidity-mass matrix of 1,287 values and compressed it to 200 numbers, finding no deviation from physics. ADFilter lets users run the autoencoder on their own simulated events and see how anomalous they look. The authors also compare anomaly detection with supervised methods on heavy particles decaying into Higgs pairs, arguing the agnostic approach strengthens limits because it is not tuned to one signal.
arxiv-2511-22369:
Pram and Schipper ask how to design rules for collective choices when people may not even know about some possible events. Mechanism design builds games, such as auctions, whose outcomes have desired properties. Their setting adds unawareness: agents and even the designer may lack any concept of certain contingencies, not just information about them. The authors work with private values and payments that can offset gains and losses.

They show that a dynamic version of the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism can still deliver the outcome that is efficient once everyone becomes fully aware. In their design, participants report their types and gradually reveal more as awareness rises in back-and-forth rounds. They also prove that surprise contingencies are no excuse for budget deficits. They give a reverse second-price auction for buying complex, partly unspecified projects that stays within budget while keeping participation worthwhile.
arxiv-2511-22569:
Reustlen and colleagues measure how much a widely used spintronics signal varies from device to device. The spin Hall magnetoresistance appears in bilayers of a magnetic insulator and a metal, and probes how spin currents cross the interface. Almost nothing was known about how its size fluctuates across one sample. The team patterned hundreds of nominally identical Hall bar devices into yttrium iron garnet and platinum heterostructures and recorded the amplitude statistically.

Within any single bilayer, amplitudes followed a Gaussian distribution with a narrow spread of about ten percent around the mean. Between samples, though, the mean could differ by up to thirty percent despite nominally identical fabrication. Local variations in interface quality, captured by the spin mixing conductance, are the most likely microscopic cause. The warning: spatial variation cannot be neglected when comparing heterostructures, because one device's reading may flatter or understate the material widely.
arxiv-2511-23069:
Sahasrabuddhe and Lambiotte build a measurement framework for residential segregation, the sorting of ethnic and social groups into different neighborhoods, that can say at which scales the sorting happens. A single segregation number hides whether the pattern is driven by whole regions differing from each other or by fine-grained separation street by street. And the same question applies to demographic groupings themselves.

Extending an information-based measure called the Divergence Index, their method splits total segregation into contributions from nested spatial units and from demographic levels at once. It includes segregation inside broad groups, which earlier decompositions could not isolate. They demonstrate it on the 2021 census of England and Wales. There, 5 broad ethnic groups, the White majority at 82 percent and the Asian group at 9 percent among them, split into 19 finer identities. This lets planners see which scales carry the inequality they might act on.
arxiv-2511-23169:
Yamauchi and colleagues recast topological data analysis, the study of a dataset's shape through features like loops and voids, as a physics measurement that quantum hardware can perform. They reinterpret a time series' dynamics as the eigenvalue spectrum of a supersymmetric Hamiltonian, where the zero-energy states correspond to Betti numbers, the counts of those topological features. The low-lying excited states measure how stable the features are.

They apply the idea to the chaotic Lorenz system, embedded with Takens' method and processed with a resource-efficient quantum phase estimation routine run on IBM quantum hardware. They found the spectral gap of the supersymmetric Laplacian tracks how persistent the loop structures are. The gap's minimum coincided with the onset of chaos. Its reopening marked the attractor settling into its mature shape. The quantum approach promises an exponential speedup over classical diagonalization for large complexes.
arxiv-2511-23369:
Tian and colleagues build SimScale, a simulation framework that manufactures the rare. Safety-critical driving situations real-world logs almost never contain, so self-driving planners can learn from them. Starting from recorded driving logs, the pipeline perturbs the car's trajectory, renders high-fidelity multi-view observations of the altered scene with neural rendering in a reactive environment. And automatically generates pseudo-expert trajectories to supervise what the car should have done at scale.

Co-training planners on the mix of real and simulated data improves scores by up to 6.8 points on the hard navhard benchmark and 2.9 points on navtest across regression, diffusion. And vocabulary-scoring planner families, compared with real data alone. Performance keeps improving smoothly as simulation data alone grows, with no extra real driving required. And the authors further study how pseudo-expert design and policy architecture shape those scaling gains in practice.
arxiv-2511-23469:
Jiahao Guo and colleagues ask whether vision-language models trained only to understand images secretly already know how to generate them. And propose Visual Generation Tuning to unlock that latent ability. Instead of the usual pixel-level autoencoders, whose latents are poorly aligned with autoregressive modeling. Their VGT-AE aligns the semantic encoder of any pretrained vision-language model with a lightweight pixel decoder in this work.

The tuning accelerates convergence of continuous-space autoregressive generation by a factor of 20 compared with training generative heads from scratch, and the autoencoder reconstructs images at 26.67 PSNR with a 0.50 reconstruction FID at a 28-fold compression ratio, beating specialized VAEs. On generation benchmarks the approach reaches 0.77 on GenEval and 78.73 on DPG-Bench, reported state-of-the-art results among autoregressive models, and it can directly endow other understanding-trained models with generation ability as well.
arxiv-2512-00069:
Everyday instructions leave out small steps that people take for granted, and robots often fail because of those gaps. Ohad Bachner addresses the problem in a 2025 project on cognitive robotics. His idea is to let a large language model supply the missing commonsense details that symbolic planners need.

Given a task in plain language, the language model suggests likely preconditions and smaller subgoals. A symbolic planner then works with that fuller description instead of a thin one. Writing every detail by hand is slow and often incomplete, so the method aims to make robot planning more reliable with less manual effort. The project sits where language technology meets classical planning.
arxiv-2512-00569:
Chow groups classify algebraic cycles up to rational equivalence, and filtering them reveals layers of structure. Thomas Jaklitsch defines a descending filtration on the Chow group of zero cycles in 2025. The varieties are products of an abelian variety with several smooth projective curves. Each layer of the filtration captures cycles of a restricted kind.

Filtrations like this connect Chow groups to conjectures about how cycles decompose, including the Bloch-Beilinson philosophy in arithmetic geometry. An explicit filtration gives other researchers a tool for testing those conjectures on concrete varieties. The work is pure algebraic geometry, building structure where computation alone cannot reach. Zero cycles are points with multiplicities, the atoms of the Chow group. The work is pure math at its most spare, and its worth is in the frame it builds. A way to sort point sets by depth that later work can lean on.
arxiv-2512-00669:
C Drum, J Nagy, and L Onisk wrote a 2025 paper in numerical math on solving inverse problems. Such problems work backward from noisy data to the hidden cause, and they are often unstable. Tikhonov methods calm that instability, and repeating them in steps can sharpen the answer.

The authors study a projected, repeated form of the method that works inside Krylov subspaces. Those are small, smart search spaces built step by step from the data. Their twist is to run the math in lower precision than usual double precision. Lower precision saves time and memory, so knowing whether the method still behaves well matters for large jobs.
arxiv-2512-00769:
Xingchen Zhou and nine coauthors present an AI agent for finding radio sources in sky survey data, in a 2025 paper. The next big radio telescope, the Square Kilometre Array, will flood astronomers with data. Programs like SoFiA-2 extract sources, the bright objects hidden in that data.

The catch is tuning. Each program needs the right parameter settings for each dataset, and finding them by hand is slow and tricky. The team's agent searches for good settings for SoFiA-2 on data from a major sky survey challenge. Automating that tuning could let huge surveys be processed faster and more evenly.
arxiv-2512-01069:
Euzeli dos Santos Jr and four coauthors test a solar weed control idea in a 2025 agriculture paper. In tropical semi-arid regions, prickly pear cactus is a vital forage crop because it tolerates drought and needs little water. Even light weed infestation can cut its productivity badly, since the cactus competes poorly for water, nutrients, and sun.

The team assesses Fresnel lenses, flat lenses that can focus sunlight into hot spots, for weed control in cactus fields. Their angle is spatiotemporal coverage: where the focused light lands, and when, across the field. Focused sunlight could kill weeds without chemicals if coverage is right.
arxiv-2512-01369:
Rafiul Biswas, Firoj Alam, and Wajdi Zaghouani built a tool for live social media study. The tool, MARSAD, focuses on the Arabic-speaking world. It lets users with no code skill study live or saved posts. Clear charts and reports come out with a few clicks.

The tool checks mood, feeling, and hate speech in posts. It also flags propaganda and checks claims for truth. Safe scraping with API keys pulls in public posts. Such a tool helps news staff, scholars, and groups track fast shifts in online talk across the region.
arxiv-2512-01569:
Shibu Meher, Manoj Dey, and Abhishek Kumar Singh explain bright quantum light from silicon nitride. The material is a strong base for single-photon sources on chips. Bright emissions with a high share of clean photons were seen. Their source at the atomic scale was not known.

Using hybrid density functional theory, the team pinpoints a defect center. A charged nitrogen-related center in a set shape fits the data. Knowing the source lets makers grow the centers on purpose. On-demand single photons are a key part for quantum networks and secure links.
arxiv-2512-01669:
Johannes Schneider and Heinz Pampel map dashboards that track open access growth. Open access shapes science policy more each year. Leaders need to know what share of output is open. Dashboards have sprung up to show that share for labs, lands, and the world.

Their data set catalogs those dashboards in one place. Each entry can aid research and infrastructure work. A shared map stops teams from building the same tool twice. It also shows gaps where no dashboard yet tracks open output well. Entries note scope and update pace as well, since a stale dashboard can mislead policy just as much as a missing one can.
arxiv-2512-01869:
Reaz Shafqat gives a digamma-function form for the ground-state energy of the Heisenberg XXX chain. The antiferromagnetic chain is a central exactly solvable model. Its ground energy per site for spin one-half is a famed closed value. Exact forms anchor the whole integrable systems field.

Shafqat recasts that energy via the digamma function. A new form can ease sums that the old form makes hard. It may also link the chain's energy to other special functions. Such links often seed fresh exact results in quantum spin systems. Digamma forms recur in free fermion sums, hinting the chain result may share roots with those better-known special function identities.
arxiv-2512-02069:
Smart contracts move real money on blockchains, and a single bug can drain them. Yining Yuan and five co-authors present LLMBugScanner in 2025, a system that uses large language models, fine-tuned and combined in an ensemble, to audit smart contract code for vulnerabilities.

The authors begin by identifying what makes language models hard to apply to auditing, from subtle bug patterns to noisy judgments. Fine-tuning adapts the models to contract code, and ensemble learning pools several models' verdicts for reliability. Automated auditing that catches real flaws early would strengthen a software ecosystem where fixes after deployment are nearly impossible.
arxiv-2512-02269:
M dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy, small, dim, and complicated, their atmospheres troubled by dust, convection, and magnetic patchiness. Aishwarya Iyer and four co-authors present in 2025 the second SPHINX paper, a new grid of model atmospheres and spectra for mid-to-late M dwarfs.

Standard methods often struggle with the coupled effects inside these stars, so a self-consistent grid is needed to derive their fundamental properties. Comparing observed spectra against the grid yields temperatures, compositions, and more. Since M dwarfs host many known exoplanets, reading their spectra well is a foundation for judging those planets' climates.
arxiv-2512-02369:
Image segmentation models degrade when the pictures change domain, and privacy rules may hide the model's parameters just when adaptation is needed. Qingmei Li and four co-authors present SAGE in 2025, a style-adaptive approach to semantic segmentation that generalizes across domains under privacy constraints.

Domain generalization aims to survive shifts in style and setting without seeing the target data. Doing it without access to model internals, for security and privacy reasons, rules out the usual fine-tuning tricks. SAGE adapts through style instead, a route suited to medical and surveillance imagery where models and data are both guarded.
arxiv-2512-03069:
Grouping buildings by how they use energy is the core problem here. Loup-Noé Lévy and five co-authors, writing in 2025, ask how to sort use profiles across a wide area. Checking each of thousands of buildings one by one would cost too much time, money, and skilled staff.

The authors use a math tool called pretopology to build groups step by step. Their groups aim to show shared patterns in energy use across many sites. Clear groups could help managers plan repairs, set budgets, and cut waste. The work speaks to cities and firms that run large sets of buildings.
arxiv-2512-03269:
Cold electrons fill Earth's magnetosphere but are hard to measure. Opal Issan, Vadim Roytershteyn, Gian Luca Delzanno, and Salomon Janhunen study their effects in this 2025 work. These electrons carry little energy yet often dominate the plasma density.

Spacecraft charging and stray photoelectrons blur their measurement. The authors use moment-based quasilinear theory to study how cold electrons affect whistler chorus waves. Those waves shape radiation belts that can harm satellites. Better theory helps forecast space weather around Earth. Chorus waves scatter radiation belt electrons, so cold electrons may sway space weather more than their low energy suggests.
arxiv-2512-03369:
Predicting where a wildfire will spread saves lives. Nan Zhou and co-authors build a benchmark data set for that task in this 2025 work. Fine-grained forecasts can improve emergency response and decision making.

Past research used coarse scales and low-resolution satellite data. That captures only broad fire states and limits precise local modeling. FireSentry is a multi-modal, spatio-temporal benchmark for fine-grained spread forecasting. A shared benchmark lets teams compare methods fairly and push accuracy where it matters most, near homes and crews. Shared data also reveal which fire features models miss most often in practice.
arxiv-2512-03769:
Quantum sensors can measure phase with precision beyond classical reach, and the state of light used as a probe sets the limit. Jiajie Guo and colleagues show in a 2025 quantum physics preprint that cubic phase states beat every Gaussian state at the same average photon number. These non-Gaussian states were already prized as a resource for continuous-variable quantum computing.

The team finds that only moderate initial squeezing is needed to reach the best sensitivity. The advantage also survives realistic loss and noisy detection, which often erase quantum gains. They identify which measurements extract the most information from such probes. Several preparation schemes that laboratories can already perform also pass the Gaussian limit, some approaching the ideal cubic phase performance. The results promote these states from a computing curiosity into a practical tool for quantum-enhanced measurement.
arxiv-2512-03869:
Blood vessels in the brain form a branching network whose shape may carry signatures of ageing and disease. Daniele Falcetta and colleagues present CaravelMetrics in a 2025 preprint, an automated framework that turns brain vessel scans into graphs. Skeletonised vessel centrelines become the graph's edges, and atlas-based regions divide the network into arterial territories.

From each graph the framework computes fifteen features spanning vessel shape, topology, fractal structure, and geometry, either for the whole network or region by region. Applied to hundreds of three-dimensional angiography scans from the IXI dataset, covering adults from their twenties to their eighties, the tool produced reproducible vessel graphs. The features tracked age and sex differences, and linked greater education with more complex vasculature, matching earlier literature. The authors offer the system for population-level studies of vascular health and normative modelling of ageing.
arxiv-2512-03969:
Fish swim in two broad styles: eels ripple their whole bodies, while many faster fish flex mainly near the tail. Zahra Maleksabet and colleagues study what those styles do to the water in a 2025 fluid dynamics preprint. They focus on burst-and-coast swimming, where bursts of motion alternate with glides, a pattern that can save energy but reshapes the wake.

Three-dimensional simulations follow eel-like and jack-fish-like swimmers across duty cycles from intermittent to continuous motion, at two Strouhal numbers. Both produced bow-shaped wakes whose side rows merge into a coherent trail as swimming becomes continuous. Surprisingly, intermittent motion at the higher Strouhal number created more drag, not less. The authors quantify vortex strengths around each body and trace which body sections produce the unsteady forces. Their analysis links anatomy and gait to wake physics, informing bio-inspired underwater robot design.
arxiv-2512-04069:
Vision-language models describe scenes fluently but measure them poorly, a problem when a robot must grasp at exact coordinates. Siyi Chen and a large team give such a model tools and teach it to use them, in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their SpaceTools system can call depth estimators, segmentation models, and pose estimators to ground its spatial reasoning in numbers.

Training uses Double Interactive Reinforcement Learning, a two-phase scheme. First the model learns from a single-tool specialist's demonstrations mixed with traces from a frontier model using every tool. Then it refines multi-tool coordination through further reinforcement learning. The result tops several spatial benchmarks and reliably drives a seven-axis robot arm. Gains over plain fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines were double-digit on the headline benchmark.
arxiv-2512-04269:
The data work behind artificial intelligence, moderating content and annotating training sets, has moved to the Global South, where it stays invisible. Jessica Pidoux and colleagues map that supply chain across Africa in a 2025 preprint on computers and society. Their project, run with an NGO and a union, centres the workers.

Desk research and a questionnaire tuned to unions' organising goals, answered by eighty-one respondents, underpin the map. Data labour, they find, spans forty-three of Africa's fifty-five countries, with seventeen major firms serving North American and European clients. Workers endure psychological stress and economic instability on short-term contracts. Those conditions hide the adaptability and resilience the work demands. Drawing on Honneth's idea of a struggle for recognition, the authors frame workers' demands for professional and social acknowledgement. They offer the map as a first account of the industry.
arxiv-2512-04469:
Philip Stephens and Emmanuel Salawu build a shared math language for comparing the many ways people design AI agents. Agent designs go by names like ReAct, multi-agent systems, and fixed control flows. Talk about them stays loose, which makes trade-offs hard to weigh. Their 2025 arXiv paper recasts each design as a chain of probabilities that a builder can shape and study.

In this frame, each step of an agent's work carries a chance of success. A strategy is a way of pushing those chances up or down. The authors add a notion called degrees of freedom: the set of levers a given design lets a builder tune. That notion sorts designs by what can be optimized in each. The result is a common yardstick for picking an agent plan for a task, and for seeing in advance where a plan is strong or brittle.
arxiv-2512-04969:
NaHyeon Park, Kunhee Kim, and Junsuk Choe rethink how to catch AI-generated images, finding that the best clues hide in the early layers of vision transformers. Most detectors read only the final layer of a CLIP vision model, where features are polished and abstract. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes each layer's contribution to the fake-spotting task. Earlier layers keep local, general traits that often beat the final layer's features outright.

Different layers also capture different aspects of an image, each adding its own evidence. The authors turn that insight into MoLD, a method that blends layer features through a learned gating mechanism, weighting each layer per image. Tests on both GAN-made and diffusion-made pictures show clear gains over final-layer detectors. As generators improve, detectors that read across the whole depth of a network may keep pace longer.
arxiv-2512-05269:
Weixi Chen, Mee Seong Im, Catherine Lillja, and Nicolas Rugo count some slippery objects in combinatorics by building exact matchings between families of objects. Their first correspondence pairs nilpotent matrices over a Boolean semiring — matrices whose powers eventually vanish — with directed acyclic graphs on ordered vertices, showing the two counts agree. The engine is a bijection that translates algebra into pictures.

The main construction counts pairs of maps from one finite set to another whose two compositions are eventually constant. Such a pair is matched to a spanning tree inside a complete bipartite graph, together with one chosen edge — generalizing the principle behind Joyal's celebrated proof of Cayley's tree-counting formula. The authors then lift the idea to vector spaces, matching nilpotent pairs of linear maps with balanced vectors between the spaces. The outcome is an elegant closed formula for the number of nilpotent pairs, extending work of Leinster.
arxiv-2512-05569:
Rémi Coulon, Arnaud Hilion, Camille Horbez, and Gilbert Levitt ask how the size of a group element changes under repeated maps. Their 2025 paper works with toral relatively hyperbolic groups. Such groups mix flat, torus like parts with curved, tree like parts. The team tracks two kinds of size: conjugacy length and word length.

They prove that for each element, both lengths grow in a clean pattern. Growth is part polynomial and part exponential, set by a whole number and an algebraic rate. For any one map, only a few such patterns can occur across the whole group. In the purely hyperbolic case, they describe special subgroups as well. Those subgroups capture exactly the elements whose growth stays at or below a given rate. The result gives group theory a tidy way to sort elements by how fast a map stretches them.
arxiv-2512-05669:
Talha Enes Koksal and Abdurrahman Gumus built a system that reads facial expressions from video as they unfold, in real time. Reading a face moment by moment helps computers respond to people more naturally. Their 2025 method first finds facial landmarks with MediaPipe FaceMesh, a fast tracking tool. From the landmarks it measures plain geometric features: distances and angles between points on the face.

Changes in those measures between frames reveal the life of an expression, from its onset, through its peak, to its fade. A ConvLSTM network with classifier blocks then names the expression being shown. The system was tested on four public datasets, and reached solid accuracy on each. It also handled mixed datasets, a sign it can adapt to new settings. Running at well over one hundred frames per second on ordinary hardware, it suits live uses, from personal devices to smart surveillance. The code is public.
arxiv-2512-05969:
Hokin Deng reports that video generation models have begun to reason. The testbed is a suite of visual puzzles: chess positions, mazes, Sudoku grids, mental rotation tasks, and Raven's matrices, the classic nonverbal intelligence test. A video model answers by generating the frames in which a solution unfolds. Leading models, Sora-2 among them, now reach about sixty percent success across these tasks. A system trained to make moving pictures can solve a maze on camera.

The experiments rest on a Task Pair design, Deng's methodological core: matched task presentations that keep scoring honest and comparable across models. A code framework ships with thirty nine models ready to test, and users can add models and tasks with little friction. Automated scores track human judgment closely. The obvious next step is reinforcement learning on this paradigm. If generation and reasoning are one skill, the implications reach past puzzles.
arxiv-2512-06269:
Quan Tran and Tuan Dang improve a fast way of building three dimensional scenes from photos. The method, Gaussian Splatting, fills a scene with soft blobs that render in real time and look true to life. Left to match photos alone, though, the blobs can drift into floaters and mushy shapes, so the surfaces pulled from the scene fall short.

Their method, TriaGS, adds a check on shape that spans many views at once. Points from nearby views are matched up to rebuild where a surface point should sit in space, and blobs that stray from that agreed spot are penalized during training. The penalty is built in a way the training can learn from directly. On standard test sets the method reached top scores among peers, with clean surfaces and few stray blobs. The team plans to release the code for others to test.
arxiv-2512-06469:
Siddhant Pinjarkar, Martin Hardcastle, Jonathon Pierce, and Frits Sweijen revisit a long standing claim about the most powerful galaxies in the sky. The claim says radio galaxies and radio quasars are the same kind of object, seen from different angles: quasars face us more nearly, so their radio jets should look foreshortened and smaller. Some past surveys failed to find that size gap, which cast doubt on the claim.

The authors argue the test needs a less naive model of projection. Real sources have width and varied shapes, so they model them as cylinders with a spread drawn from real data. Their simulations predict the size ratio between the two classes for varied sample sizes. A fair test, they conclude, needs fully identified samples with sizes for all targets, and more than eight hundred sources. No past sample met that bar, so the claim may never have been tested cleanly.
arxiv-2512-06569:
Sayan Bhattacharya, Rhiddha Acharjee, and Atanu Nandy study how an excitation moves, or fails to move, on a fractal corral. Their lattice is self similar, built in generations, and each cluster of sites forms a quantum prison whose size depends on the generation. On this substrate a tight binding model traps many modes in place, in a pattern that echoes the fractal's own hierarchy.

Threading a magnetic flux through each small plaquette changes the story. The flux frees the trapped modes into a band of extended states that run across the structure. The team confirms this with measures of how spread out each state is and with direct transport sums. The freed states survive a dose of disorder and uneven hopping. Where trapped and free states meet, a mobility edge appears, mapped through multifractal analysis. Interference, the authors stress, is the lever that flux uses to rewrite the motion.
arxiv-2512-06869:
Wanyang Hong and co-authors name a slow failure that hits chatbots in long conversations: as turns pile up, the model's grip on the talk decays. Early instructions get diluted, attention drifts to stray details, and answers wander off course. Their fix, called Rhea, splits the chat history into two separate stores. One holds the standing instructions with high priority, and the other holds the passing episodes of the exchange.

When the model answers, Rhea builds a clean context from both stores. Relevant episodes are pulled in by a heuristic search, while noise is held down by design, and the standing instructions always win priority. On several benchmarks for long multi-turn talk, Rhea cut the usual decay and lifted overall scores by a clear margin over strong rivals. It also kept instruction following near perfect across long exchanges, a gain the authors call a principled step for steadier chatbots.
arxiv-2512-06969:
Adrian Przybysz and co-authors compare two ways of guiding optimization, the step-by-step search for the lowest point of a cost surface. Smart methods use the surface's curvature, summed up in a matrix called the Hessian, but for neural networks that matrix is huge and costly. The classic BFGS method keeps an estimate of it through a famous updating rule. The estimate is forced to stay positive definite, which assumes the surface always curves upward.

The challenger, Online Gradient Regression, watches how gradients change as positions move and fits the curvature from that stream. An averaging scheme keeps the estimate current, and no matrix inversion is needed. Crucially, it can report downward curvature too, so it copes with non-convex surfaces that BFGS must misdescribe. On standard test problems, the regression method reached lower costs faster, with its edge largest in non-convex cases.
arxiv-2512-07169:
Xu-Fei Xue and co-authors measure how the hottest matter ever made, the quark-gluon plasma, drags on the heavy quarks passing through it. In lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, charm quarks slow, scatter, and flow with the plasma, and their fingerprints survive in the D mesons finally detected. Two transport numbers govern the story: how heavy quarks diffuse, and how strongly jets are quenched, both changing with temperature.

For the first time, both numbers are inferred together in a Bayesian analysis of the same data, the D mesons' suppression and their elliptical flow pattern. A unified transport model handles energy lost by collisions and by radiation, then the making of mesons by merging and breaking. The middle-central collisions pin the numbers down far better than head-on ones.
arxiv-2512-07269:
Mike Diessner and Yannick E Tarant build digital twins of critical infrastructure, the water and energy plants whose failure society cannot afford, without the usual laser scanners. Virtual models of such plants feed simulations that test resilience, but scanning them in three dimensions is expensive and demands specialists. Their pipeline works from ordinary color images plus depth from a stereo camera, using photogrammetry instead of laser point clouds.

Deep learning first finds and outlines the relevant objects in the images. Then user-defined rules infer how the objects relate, turning detections into a graph of the plant. On two hydraulic systems the produced graphs came close to the ground truth. Because the linking rules are written by people rather than learned opaquely, every connection in the graph can be explained, a quality the authors stress for high-stakes decisions.
arxiv-2512-07569:
Joel Ekstrand, Tor Mattsson, Zahra Taghiyarrenani, Slawomir Nowaczyk, Jens Lundström, and Mikael Lindén wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. It tackles forecasting when sudden odd events disturb a time series. Their test case is cash demand at cash machines, where sharp shifts can disrupt supply plans.

Modern deep forecasters shine on calm, normal data but stumble when patterns shift. The authors answer with a training method called Weighted Contrastive Adaptation, or WECA. It teaches the model to keep normal and anomaly-boosted views of the same series aligned. That way, odd events stay visible in the model's inner picture instead of being smoothed away. The team tests it on a nationwide record of cash machine transactions. They inject realistic anomalies shaped by domain knowledge. Forecasts on the disturbed data improve clearly over a normally trained model. Accuracy on normal data barely moves, so reliability rises without a trade-off.
arxiv-2512-07869:
Johannes Bertram, Luciano Dyballa, T. Anderson Keller, Savik Kinger, and Steven Zucker wrote this 2025 neuroscience paper. Foundation models can mimic the brain's visual system with striking success. Their inner workings, though, stay black boxes that teach little about brains.

The authors open one such model of neural activity and inspect it closely. They treat its units like neurons a physiologist would record from. Each unit is characterized by its responses to timed, parametric stimuli. Two manifold views organize what they find inside the model. Decoding manifolds show how stimuli are laid out in activity space. Encoding manifolds show how units are laid out in stimulus-response space. The model's stages turn out to differ sharply in structure. Its recurrent stage pushes apart the patterns for different time courses. Its readout stage wins biological fidelity through many specialized maps.  The study shows how to interrogate a model productively.
arxiv-2512-08669:
Krishna Menon and Emil Verkama study Ehrhart polynomials for cross polytopes and for pyramids built over them. It was known that the coefficients of those polynomials are all positive, but a clear counting reason was missing. The authors supply that reason with a combinatorial proof.

They show that a scaled form of the polynomials counts certain colored permutations, acting as a generating function for them. That link explains the positivity in concrete counting terms rather than through algebra alone. The result answers a question posed by Stanley, a leading figure in the field. Readers who work in enumerative combinatorics will find a clean new bridge between geometry of polytopes and permutation counting.
arxiv-2512-08769:
Eranga Bandara and a large team offer a practical guide for building production grade agentic artificial intelligence workflows. Agentic systems combine several specialized agents, language models, tools, and orchestration logic to reason, plan, and carry out multi step tasks. As use grows, teams struggle to make such systems reliable, observable, and safe to operate.

The guide lays out a full engineering life cycle, from breaking down a workflow and designing agent patterns to tool integration, deterministic orchestration, and deployment. Nine core practices are stressed, including tool first design, single responsibility agents, external prompt management, and keeping designs simple. A case study applies the ideas to a multimodal workflow that analyzes news and generates media. The authors aim to give builders a reference for robust, extensible systems that meet governance needs in real production use.
arxiv-2512-08869:
Anantaa Kotal and Anupam Joshi propose ContextGAN, a method to generate synthetic data that is both private and faithful to hidden domain rules. Synthetic data can reflect real patterns without exposing sensitive records, which matters under strict privacy laws in health, finance, and security. Standard generators often miss implicit rules that link fields, such as drug restrictions for certain conditions.

Their system is a differentially private generative adversarial network guided by a constraint matrix. That matrix encodes both explicit and implicit domain knowledge. A constraint aware discriminator checks synthetic records against the rules, while differential privacy protects details from the source data. Tests across healthcare, security, and finance show high quality output that respects domain rules and preserves privacy. The authors argue the approach improves realism and utility for settings where unstated constraints are as important as visible patterns in the data.
arxiv-2512-08969:
Elias Hossain and coauthors propose an confidence based contrast method to learn robust forms for detecting malicious content under noisy, uneven labels. Many real tasks have only positive and unmarked examples, which makes standard training hard. Their method is built for that positive unmarked setting.

The method joins an confidence based contrast loss with changing temperature scaling and an attention guided looping encoder. Contrastive weights adjust with sample confidence, positive anchors stabilize training, and temperature adapts to batch level variation. When applied to malicious content classification, the learned vectors let several classic models reach high accuracy and precision with near perfect recall. False negatives stay minimal and ranking scores are competitive. Visual study shows clear separation between positive and unmarked cases in the vector space. The authors present the method as a scalable solution for high stakes domains such as security and medical text mining.
arxiv-2512-09169:
Theo Cavignac and coauthors present an artificial intelligence driven workflow that expands the Alexandria database. Finding compounds close to thermodynamic stability is the key screening step for new compounds. Their multi stage workflow joins a generative model, a universal machine learning potential, and a graph neural network for energy prediction.

From a huge pool of created candidate structures, the workflow adds more than a million density functional validated compounds to the database,. Its success rate for finding near stable compounds is far above previous methods. The expanded database now holds millions of structures,. Predicted disorder rates match lab databases, unlike some recent created data sets. Study reveals patterns in symmetry, coordination, and stability networks. A large out of equilibrium data set with forces and stresses is also released for training universal force fields, under open licenses.
arxiv-2512-09269:
Yixuan Wang, Dan P. Guralnik, and Warren E. Dixon ask how much an observer can learn about where a moving agent is headed. The agent might be a robot or vehicle whose true goal is hidden. The observer sees only a noisy record of its path and must guess its intent.

The authors introduce intent inference based on a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter, a sampling method that handles part of the math exactly to work more efficiently. Their setup assumes the agent steers itself with a stabilizing controller whose form is known. Two estimators turn the filter's output into a goal distribution, one using all samples, one only the effective ones. The team bounds how much intent information can leak, using information theory, and shows the cheaper estimator performs almost as well as the full one. Experiments recover goals quickly and accurately, pointing toward controllers designed to hide intent.
arxiv-2512-09369:
Yezi Liu and colleagues present PathHD, a system for answering questions over knowledge graphs with help from a large language model. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, and good answers often follow a path through those links. Existing systems score paths with neural encoders or repeated language model calls, which is slow, costly, and hard to audit.

PathHD removes the encoder. It represents relation paths as hypervectors, a high-dimensional computing technique, using a binding operation that respects path order. A calibrated similarity search with top-K pruning retrieves candidate paths, and a single language model call then picks the answer and cites the supporting paths. On the WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA benchmarks, PathHD matched or beat strong neural baselines while using one model call per query. It also cut end-to-end delay substantially and used several times less graphics memory.
arxiv-2512-09469:
Haijian Shao and colleagues present LiePrune, a method for shrinking quantum neural networks in a single pass. Quantum neural networks and parameterized quantum circuits are key building blocks for near-term quantum machine learning. They carry too many parameters, suffer from barren plateaus where training stalls, and strain limited hardware. Pruning, removing unneeded parts, is a natural remedy if done on principle.

LiePrune represents each gate twice: once in a Lie group and algebra picture, which captures the gate's mathematical structure, and once in a quantum geometric feature space. That dual view lets it detect redundancy with mathematical grounding and compress aggressively. On quantum classification benchmarks, a generative modeling task, and a quantum chemistry calculation, LiePrune achieved more than tenfold compression with negligible or even improved performance. The authors also provide guarantees on redundancy detection, approximation quality, and computational cost.
arxiv-2512-09569:
Nicholas Rungi gives a construction linking two worlds: equiaffine immersions in flat space and maps into pseudo-Riemannian space forms, the pseudosphere and pseudohyperbolic space. Those have directions of both signs in their metric. It produces immersions into those curved spaces from equiaffine ones, and runs in reverse as well.

He describes how these immersions interact with a para-Sasaki metric built on a principal bundle over a para-Kähler manifold. When the starting object is a hyperbolic affine sphere, it yields spacelike maximal immersions meeting a transversality condition. First, for any strictly convex region in real projective space he defines a boundary set in a flag variety. He proves there exists a unique spacelike, Lagrangian, maximal submanifold with that boundary. Second, he shows that the Blaschke lift of the hyperbolic affine sphere, introduced by Labourie, is a harmonic map.
arxiv-2512-09969:
Paul Hueber and colleagues redesign top event based eye trackers as spiking neural networks for wearables. Eye tracking in glasses must be fast and sip power, yet ordinary camera pipelines suffer motion blur, heavy computation, and coarse timing. The team converts leading event based models by swapping their recurrent and attention parts for light leaky integrate and fire layers, and by using depth wise separable convolutions to shrink the model.

Their networks locate the pupil with mean error close to the best application specific neuromorphic system. At the same time, the models are far smaller and need vastly less computation than the nearest conventional variant. Projections suggest operation at a few milliwatts with millisecond latency, fast enough for a thousand updates per second. High performing eye tracking can thus be rebuilt in spiking form, fit for real time wearables.
arxiv-2512-10169:
Alexander Wan and colleagues publish the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index, the third annual scoring of how openly major AI developers disclose what they do. New indicators this year cover data acquisition, usage data, and monitoring, and companies such as Alibaba, DeepSeek, and xAI are scored for the first time. The headline is regression. The average score fell sharply from the prior year, out of one hundred points. Developers are most opaque about training data and training compute, and about how their flagship models are actually used and what impact they have after release.

One company stands far above the field, near the top of the scale, while two prominent names sit near the bottom. The big frontier labs cluster in the middle. The authors suggest those firms avoid the reputational cost of terrible scores without gaining incentives to lead.
arxiv-2512-10669:
Lingjing Kong and co-authors explain compositional generalisation, the knack of understanding new combinations of known ideas, by analogy. A person who has never seen a peacock eating rice can picture it from a chicken eating rice. The authors argue a model needs the same move: break high-level concepts into basic parts that recombine across similar settings, rather than memorising whole scenes.

They formalise the idea with causal modularity and a principle of minimal change, building a hierarchical data-generating process with levels of concepts and their interaction rules. Theory shows this richer structure supports generalisation with complex, non-additive relations between parts, going beyond earlier work that assumed simple effects. They also prove the hidden hierarchy can be recovered from observable data such as text-image pairs, and report sizeable benchmark gains from applying the framework.
arxiv-2512-10769:
Borja Pérez-Díaz and co-authors map how chemical enrichment varies across the discs of galaxies whose nuclei show LINER emission, a low-ionisation glow whose nature is still debated. Abundance gradients record how enrichment processes act at different scales, but galaxies hosting active nuclei are poorly charted, and LINER hosts worst of all. This study takes a first systematic pass.

The team selected ninety-seven MaNGA galaxies with LINER-like nuclei. They estimated oxygen and nitrogen ratios in star-forming regions across each disc and in the nucleus. The tool was the HII-CHI-Mistry code. A free-form piecewise fit found most galaxies depart from a single straight gradient, as inside-out growth would predict. Those departures tracked no property, and the elements' profile shapes rarely matched, leading the authors to propose active nucleus feedback, acting at varying scales, as the culprit.
arxiv-2512-10869:
Francisco Romero-Lara and a large team rewire a molecule's magnetism by lengthening its arms. Open-shell nanographenes host unusual magnetic states in their carbon networks. And triangulenes are prized because their radical count grows with size, though the radicals blur together and cannot be addressed one by one. The team started from an aza-triangulene carrying a single radical.

By covalently extending it with armchair anthene arms of increasing length, they coaxed the single radical to reorganise into three topologically protected spin states. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy watched the three spins form a frustrated trimer whose coupling weakens as the arms grow. Multi-reference calculations explain why: the correlated frontier orbitals progressively reshape into three edge-localised natural orbitals, leaving nearly independent edge spins. The molecule becomes an analogue of a three-qubit register, a step toward spin-based quantum devices built one molecule at a time.
arxiv-2512-11069:
Giuliano Romeo and Giulia Salvatori develop arithmetic for continued fractions in the p-adic numbers, an alternative number system used widely in number theory. Continued fractions represent numbers as nested sequences of quotients and give excellent rational approximations over the real numbers. Doing basic arithmetic directly on those representations has long been a delicate problem, and the p-adic case was largely open.

The authors give a complete method for computing the continued fraction of a Möbius transformation of a p-adic number, and of more general fractional transformations. That covers the standard arithmetic operations. Surprisingly, unlike the real case, knowing arbitrarily many terms of the inputs sometimes cannot determine even the first terms of the result. They prove, however, that such bad inputs form a set of measure zero, so the method works for almost every p-adic number.
arxiv-2512-11169:
Akhil Anand and colleagues rethink how optimisation models for sequential decisions are trained. Such problems are usually written as mixed integer linear programs and solved by branch and bound search. A model that describes the real world imperfectly can still make poor decisions, even when solved exactly.

Recent learning approaches tune these models for decision quality, but they need known optimal answers and approximate gradients. The team's CORL framework instead fine tunes the whole model with reinforcement learning on real data, judging it by operational performance. They recast the branch and bound solver as a differentiable stochastic policy that reinforcement learning can adjust end to end. A simple illustrative decision problem validates the idea as a proof of concept for data driven optimisation.
arxiv-2512-11469:
Pranav Ramanathan and colleagues stage the first systematic contest between classical optimisation and AI methods on the no three in line problem, a famous puzzle in combinatorial geometry. The task is to place as many points as possible on a square grid so that no three ever sit on one straight line. Exact solvers guarantee optimal answers but scale exponentially as grids grow.

Integer linear programming proved optimal arrangements up to moderately large grids. A transformer based learning method called PatternBoost matched the optimum on smaller grids while sharply reducing its training loss. A reinforcement learning agent solved small grids perfectly, then failed one size up, because its placements began violating the no three rule. The authors conclude classical optimisation remains essential for exactness, AI methods compete well on smaller cases, and hybrids offer the most promising path to larger grids.
arxiv-2512-11669:
Lázaro Martínez-Ortíz and co-authors find a steady clock inside turbulent hot fluid. When fluid is heated from below, a large scale circulation, a slow giant roll, forms and drives much of the motion. Textbooks treat the roll as steady, but it pulses.

Using lab tests and simulations in a cylinder cell, the team shows the pulse obeys one fixed rule. Mean speed divided by length times pulse rate stays constant. They then split the roll with a thin wall into two stacked rolls. Each kept the same clock value, even when the pair was uneven. The clock ties plume shedding to the roll shape, a neat order inside chaos.
arxiv-2512-11969:
Zarif Kader and co-authors test whether a split radio burst shows true quantum style coherence between its parts. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space. Plasma clouds can lens a burst into copies, and copies from one lens should keep a shared phase.

The burst FRB 20220413B, caught by CHIME, has a complex multi part shape that a plasma lens can mimic in form, though not in brightness. Using raw voltage data, the team hunted for phase links between parts. Excess correlation showed up in power only, not in phase. All parts share the same scattering width, pointing to one Milky Way screen. The burst looks shaped by common scattering, not coherent lensing.
arxiv-2512-12169:
Avinash Khare and Avadh Saxena revisit the plane pendulum in a 2025 paper on classical mechanics. A plane pendulum swings in one flat plane, and its exact motion is a classic problem. They link its solutions to those of hyperbolic and inverted pendulums, and to still solutions of two Gordon type equations.

Working in first and second rough forms of the motion, they find many exact periodic and hyperbolic solutions. They also define an elliptic pendulum that turns into the plane form at one limit and the hyperbolic form at another. For one special case, its period stays fixed even in a rough form, a rare trait.
arxiv-2512-12369:
Francois Fillastre, Yusen Long, and David Xu build an explicit exotic action of a Lie group in a 2025 math paper. The group PSL2(R) acts on hyperbolic space, and in infinite dimensions it admits continuous, irreducible actions that finite versions forbid when dimension tops 2. Delzant and Py first showed such actions exist.

Fillastre and co-authors construct one directly, using a hyperbolic model for convex bodies from earlier work. Their action is convex cocompact, and the quotient of its smallest invariant convex set matches a classic compactum. They also study one orbit map's geometry and compute the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set.
arxiv-2512-12669:
Jiawei Shen and eight co-authors present DynaGen for temporal knowledge graph reasoning in a 2025 paper. A knowledge graph stores facts as links between entities, and a temporal one adds time. Missing facts can be filled by interpolation, using known times, or extrapolation, predicting future events. Past methods handle the two apart, with weak context for one and bias toward surface patterns for the other.

For interpolation, DynaGen builds entity centered subgraphs on the fly and reads them with a dual branch graph network. For extrapolation, a conditional diffusion process forces the model to learn deep evolutionary rules. On six benchmarks, it beat the second best models by 2.61 points of mean reciprocal rank for interpolation and 1.45 for extrapolation.
arxiv-2512-12769:
Mohammad Jalili Torkamani and Israt Zarin present ASTA, an adaptive speech to action system for voice controlled IoT devices, in a 2025 paper. Voice control is natural, but edge devices face a trade-off. Cloud models understand language better. Yet they add delay, need connectivity, and raise privacy issues. On device models are fast and private, but weak hardware limits them.

ASTA routes each command between edge and cloud at runtime, guided by live metrics like CPU load, device temperature, and network latency. On device speech recognition and a light offline model handle some commands locally. A rule based validation and repair step fixes broken commands. On a Jetson platform with 80 spoken commands, all commands routed to execution; speech accuracy was 62.5 percent.
arxiv-2512-12869:
Yongmin Yoo, Seungwoo Kim, and Jingjiang Liu tackle the hard task of putting a value on a patent. Counts of citations, a common proxy, arrive slowly and miss much of what a patent is worth. The authors want a method that works in real time and can explain itself.

Their framework, ERA-IT, fine-tunes a large language model using patent renewal records. Paying to renew a patent shows that its owner sees real value in it, so renewals act as a market signal. The model learned from 10,000 patents at the European Patent Office. It beat standard models and plain language models on accuracy, and it gave clear reasons for each value call.
arxiv-2512-13369: Patrick Bennett, Quentin Dubroff, Alan Frieze, and Wesley Pegden discuss the expected minimum cost of rainbow structures in random graphs. A rainbow spanning tree or Hamilton cycle uses edges of all distinct colors, one per color. The graphs here are randomly edge colored, so costs and colors interact in subtle ways.
arxiv-2512-13469:
Vikram Nadig works on homological stability for maps that preserve symmetric bilinear forms. His paper studies groups linked to odd orthogonal groups, which act on spaces with a kind of dot product. Stability means that certain algebraic patterns settle into a fixed form as the size grows.

Nadig proves stability over a class of rings that includes all fields and the whole numbers. He also includes the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers in that class. Paired with Grothendieck-Witt theory, the result fixes much of the stable cohomology of these groups in low degrees. That gives mathematicians a firmer base for later work on these groups.
arxiv-2512-13869:
Wenda Li and co-authors present a diffusion-based method to train drone detectors for finding humans with synthetic data.
