Training detectors needs many labeled images, but for UAV human detection labels are scarce and targets keep shifting. Simulators can make labeled data cheaply, yet synthetic images differ from real ones in style and detail.

Their Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Alignment works in three stages. A diffusion model first matches global style such as color and light, then a super-resolution model refines small human figures, and a final module removes hallucinated people that look unrealistic. Labels from the synthetic source are preserved through the process. On the Semantic-Drone benchmark, detection rose by up to 14.1 points of mAP50 over untransformed baselines.
arxiv-2512-14269:
Valentin Promies, Jasper Nalbach, Erika Abraham, and Paul Wagner speed up explanations in NLSAT in a 2025 paper. NLSAT checks whether nonlinear real arithmetic formulas can be satisfied. Its core step, single cell construction, grows one sample point into a connected region where a set of polynomials keeps a fixed sign.

The authors add extra linear polynomials to the set as the method runs. That makes each cell smaller and simpler to represent, though more cells appear overall. Experiments show the trade can pay off with the right heuristics, thanks to interaction with Boolean reasoning. The counterintuitive lesson, captured in their title, is that adding more polynomials can make the whole explanation faster.
arxiv-2512-14469:
Anwesh Ray studies how elliptic curves organize into graphs when they are reduced modulo a prime. Curves linked by maps called isogenies form layered graphs nicknamed volcanoes, and each curve sits at some height above the volcano floor. Ray asks how often each height occurs as the prime varies over a fixed curve's reductions.

Under a standard assumption about the curve's Galois representation, he derives exact formulas for the share of primes giving each height and each position above the floor. Without that assumption, all large heights still occur for a positive share of primes. A second part computes limiting densities over finite fields that grow without bound.
arxiv-2512-14669:
Most stars live in multiple systems, and over a lifetime some pairs interact so closely that the two stars merge into one. Modeling the product of such a merger is hard, because the merged star's internal layering decides how it will evolve afterward.

The approach taken here works in one dimension and sorts material by entropy, a physically motivated way to stack the two stars' matter into a single profile. The team also presents PyMMAMS, their software for building these one-dimensional merger models. Practical merger models help astronomers interpret the unusual, rejuvenated stars that mergers are thought to leave behind.
arxiv-2512-14869:
Riley Acker and three coauthors build a learning circuit from linked electronic oscillators. Each unit is a Wien bridge oscillator, and the links between units can be tuned like adjustable resistors. The phase gaps between oscillators store patterns, much as brain like computing stores them in connection strengths.

A local Hebbian rule, which strengthens links between units that act alike, adjusts the couplings as the circuit runs. Learning and recall thus grow out of one ongoing process, not separate training and use phases. Tests in simulation and in real hardware show the learned patterns settle into stable attractor states. A small layered version with a hidden layer also worked. The results back coupled oscillator circuits as hardware for learning that never switches off.
arxiv-2512-15169:
Chengguang Ou and a coauthor explain why some neural networks that store scenes as functions learn slowly and miss fine detail. Implicit neural representations encode an image or shape inside a network fed with coordinates. Their spectral bias favors smooth outputs, a flaw traced to the neural tangent kernel, or NTK, that governs their training.

The authors show many design tricks act through a small set of pairwise similarity factors and scaling terms that set the spread of NTK eigenvalues. Plain coordinate networks have weak input interactions, so that spread is large and training is ill conditioned. They derive closed form variance splits for common parts: positional encoding reshapes similarity, spherical normalization cuts variance by layer scaling, and Hadamard modulation multiplies in factors below one. Experiments confirm the predicted drops in variance, with faster, steadier training and better reconstructions.
arxiv-2512-15669:
Shambel Sahlu and the SSGI collaboration map and test candidate sites for a new optical observatory in Ethiopia in a 2025 paper. Ethiopia already has the Entoto Observatory and Lalibela sites, and the team seeks further dark sky locations. Six basic criteria guide the search: altitude, light pollution, cloud cover, humidity, wind speed, and wind direction.

Starting from 367 mountains, a multi criteria statistical decision analysis selects 21 high potential places for closer study. Three sites, Bauhit, Meseraia, and T'at'a, rank as most suitable for optical astronomy. The selected mountains are mapped for future seeing studies. Protecting these dark skies could also support astrotourism in East Africa.
arxiv-2512-15969:
Dionysios Anninos, Thomas Hertog, and Joel Karlsson build a toy model of the quantum universe in a 46-page arXiv paper posted in 2025. They use timelike Liouville theory, a two-dimensional model of gravity that can be solved in detail. Toy models like it help physicists test ideas about the birth of the universe that are too hard in full gravity.

The team computes path integrals over disk-shaped histories, with matter fields inserted. Chosen along a complex contour, these yield states much like the famous Hartle-Hawking wavefunction for the universe's start. They compute one-loop wavefunctions and propose formulas valid at all loop orders. Pairing two disk integrals gives a quantity that could define a proper inner product for quantum cosmology, and they also discuss fixed-area ensembles and a static patch view.
arxiv-2512-16169:
A M Mukhamedzhanov recalculates a stellar fusion rate in a 2025 paper on arXiv. When two carbon-12 nuclei fuse, they power key stages of a massive star's life. The rate at low energies is hard to measure directly, so astronomers extrapolate using the astrophysical S factor, a smoothed version of the fusion probability.

Using Bayesian fitting on data below 3.5 MeV, including new inverse-kinematics results, the author extracts the smooth trend of the S factor while ignoring local resonances. The fitted curve sits below the classic 1975 reference values. At 1.5 MeV, the new median is 1.20 times 10 to the 16 keV barns, versus the reference 3.0 times 10 to the 16. The implied reaction rate is only 0.33 to 0.46 times the standard rate at the temperatures studied, with no sharp rise at low energy.
arxiv-2512-16369:
Moritz Muller-Brus and three co-authors audit internet security infrastructure in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. The RPKI system lets owners of internet address space make signed claims about which networks may announce their routes. Thousands of networks use those claims to block route hijacks, whether malicious or accidental.

The claims live in about 100 distributed repositories, and reports suggest some are unreliable. A draft best-practice guide for repository operators inspired the authors to measure how repositories actually publish RPKI data. They found wide variety in deployment practices, and some habits could put parts of the information at risk of becoming unavailable. The study sets a baseline so the maturity of these repositories can be tracked over time.
arxiv-2512-16769:
The QUEST-DMC team tested a silicon photomultiplier sensor at extreme cold, down to 9.4 thousandths of a degree above zero, inside a dilution refrigerator. Such sensors could form a veto that flags cosmic-ray muons inside cold dark matter searches, cutting false signals.

The sensor, an FBK NUV-HD-cryo device, was checked for single-photon response, gain, dark count rate, and linked noise as voltage changed. The team also coupled it to a scintillator inside the fridge and saw events in line with cosmic-ray muons passing through. Both results are first steps toward a working cryogenic muon veto for the QUEST-DMC dark matter search.
arxiv-2512-17069:
Ziao Yang and Chidiebere I. Nwaogbo compute electronic transport in Pd3O2Cl2 kagome bilayers, two stacked kagome sheets whose stacking and strain can be tuned. Four stacking orders, AA, AA prime, AB, and AB prime, were compared from first principles.

Band gaps swing hard with stacking, from 0.08 to 0.76 electron volts, with AB prime the most stable order. All stackings stay mechanically sound, with Young moduli of 54.82 to 61.97 newtons per meter and ductile behavior fit for flexible devices. Carrier masses vary by stacking too. Straining the AB prime sheet tunes the gap in a non-monotonic way, with hole masses reacting most, marking the material as a strain-tuned kagome platform.
arxiv-2512-17369:
Enrique Alvarez and Jesus Anero widen a classic trick for writing down curved spacetime. The Kerr-Schild form builds a full gravity field by deforming a flat background along one chosen direction, usually a light-like one. They let that direction be any kind, not just light-like.

Surprisingly, the curvature of the deformed space still expands into a finite sum, with no endless tail. Their theorem then states when the new space stays empty of matter in Einstein's sense: the deforming direction must have no swirl, which then makes it follow the straightest possible paths. Black hole builders prize this family of forms for its rare exactness.
arxiv-2512-17469:
Carlos M Correia and five co-authors push a telescope sharpness trick called super-resolution onto pyramid wavefront sensors. Adaptive optics bends a mirror in real time to undo the air's blur, guided by a sensor that reads the warped starlight. A pyramid sensor can, on paper, rebuild finer detail than its pixel grid should allow, letting fewer samples steer a denser mirror.

The team revisits the sensor's diffraction math to support that claim and a second one: the sensor can also read brightness flaws behind twinkling. Gains include tougher alignment and less aliasing, at under twice the computing cost. One caution stands in the record itself: the authors flag a major math flaw in the introduction's reasoning, while stating the results still hold as verified.
arxiv-2512-17569:
Xietao Wang Lin and coauthors work on Bayesian optimization for costly black box problems that carry several constraints. In many such problems the goal and each constraint can be tested on their own. Only a few constraints actually bind at the best solution, so testing all of them every time wastes effort.

The team builds new versions of the Knowledge Gradient rule that score each constraint on its own. The new rules sample only the constraints worth knowing about, and a faster variant pairs the idea with expected improvement. In benchmark tests the decoupled methods beat the coupled ones and the prior state of the art, PESC, with the gap widest when constraints differ in cost. The savings matter wherever each test burns time, money, or machine hours.
arxiv-2512-17669:
Yulong Qiao and Richard Matthias Geilhufe compute how heat flows when a terahertz laser pulse hammers a crystal's atoms in rhythm. The pulse drives one vibration mode of the lattice, called a phonon, far from rest while the rest of the crystal acts as a heat bath. Treating the driven mode as an open quantum system, they derive the exact heat current between mode and bath.

Under fast, realistic pulses, that current breaks the textbook Markovian rule, which assumes the bath forgets instantly. The driven phonon remembers, and the heat flow shows it. Such memory effects are usually a nuisance to be averaged away. Here they become a handle: pulse shapes could probe, and even steer, dissipation inside quantum materials.
arxiv-2512-18069:
Simion De and Jared D. Huling tackle a core task in causal studies: making treated and untreated groups alike on paper. When a study cannot assign treatment by lot, weights can rebalance the groups. Set formulas often guess the wrong shape, and weighing every trait alike drowns the few traits that truly matter in large data sets.

Their method lets random forests, grown on both treatment and outcome, pick which traits count. Pairs of cases that land in the same leaves again and again are treated as close, and weights follow that closeness. Under set conditions the weights match the classic inverse odds form, and tests on fake and real data back the claim.
arxiv-2512-18169:
Kenichi Takemura studies a number built from a square matrix and the permutations of its entries. For each permutation he takes the trace of the matrix times the permutation matrix. He raises those values to a power m and adds them with signs. The result is a quantity he calls the Alternating Power Difference.

For many matrices this sum stays zero as m grows, until a first degree where it appears. Takemura computes that pattern for families such as Vandermonde matrices, circulant matrices, and shifted power lattices. The paper presents conjectured closed forms for the first appearance degree and the first value there, checked by exact calculation in small cases. For the identity matrix, the conjectured degree is n minus 1 and the value is n factorial. The pattern hints at a tight link between a matrix's structure and the symmetry of sums over permutations.
arxiv-2512-18669:
Jones David and Shreya Ghosh present an AI tutor for programming students in this 2025 paper. Most language model tutors answer one turn at a time and forget the learner. IntelliCode instead keeps a central learner state with a full edit history. It holds mastery estimates, wrong ideas, review schedules, and activity signals. A StateGraph Orchestrator runs six specialist agents. They cover skill checks, profiling, step-by-step hinting, lesson choice, spaced review, and activity tracking, all writing to the shared state under a single-writer rule.

A demo follows a learner through a data structures problem: a hint when stuck, a corrected submission, then instant mastery updates and a personal review interval. Tests with computer-made learners show stable state updates. They also show better task success with step-by-step hints, and broad topic coverage.
arxiv-2512-18769:
David Breitenmoser and three co-authors turn a moving gamma-ray detector into a quantitative mapping tool. Knowing where radiation sources are, and how strong, matters for emergency response, environmental surveys, and nuclear security. Their method, posted to arXiv in December 2025, combines mobile spectrometry with Monte Carlo simulation and full-spectrum Bayesian inference.

Using just six seconds of single-pass data, checked against independent field and lab assays, they identify source mixtures decisively, at over five sigma. Sources are located to meter scale, and their activities are recovered with percent-level accuracy. The advance sharpens radiological awareness on the ground and improves geochemical mapping. The same machinery can pin down radionuclide abundances on other worlds, wherever a spectrometer can travel.
arxiv-2512-19069:
Siddharth Tandon tests a shortcut for making small language models smarter: borrow abstract concepts from a large model. Big models are strong but too heavy for small devices. Usual fixes like pruning or distillation take long tuning and careful setup.

Concepts here are steering vectors, directions inside a model tied to a high-level idea. Tandon moves them into smaller models at run time, across the Phi, Llama, and Qwen families. Performance rose on a wide range of tasks. Adjusting the steering strength during inference added a further gain, including a clear accuracy lift for the small Qwen3 model he measured.
arxiv-2512-19869:
Fabian Haneder, Gerrit Caspari, Juan Diego Urbina, and Klaus Richter connect two growth rates that both claim to measure chaos. Out-of-time-ordered commutators diagnose scrambling in quantum systems, and their early growth is governed by a quantum Lyapunov exponent, bounded above by a celebrated limit. Using a Wigner-Moyal expansion plus ensemble equivalence, the authors build a consistent route to that growth rate for many-body systems with chaotic classical limits.

Applied to quantized hyperbolic motion in many dimensions, a system mimicking gravity-like correlations, the computed growth rate per degree of freedom collapses onto a universal curve. Cooling or adding dimensions crosses the behavior from classical toward quantum, and in the deep quantum regime the scrambling saturates the Maldacena-Shenker-Stanford bound. The mechanism runs through quantum contributions to the density of states, no disorder averaging required.
arxiv-2512-20369:
Xiaoxuan Guo and co-authors present a competition system for detecting deepfake environmental sounds. Generative audio models now synthesize convincing everyday sounds, so the ESDD 2026 Challenge tests detectors against unseen generators and, in a second track, black-box low-resource conditions. Their entry is called EnvSSLAM-FFN.

The design pairs a frozen self-supervised audio encoder, SSLAM, with a lightweight feed-forward back end. Intermediate representations from several encoder layers are fused, and a class-weighted objective handles the heavy imbalance between real and fake clips. The system beats the official benchmarks on both challenge tracks. Its test equal error rates land near one percent, showing that frozen representations plus careful fusion travel well to unfamiliar generators.
arxiv-2512-20469:
Linfeng Zhang and a very large collaboration argue that AI-driven science needs infrastructure, not just clever agents. Their Bohrium plus SciMaster stack aims to make agentic science work at scale. Bohrium acts as a managed hub where data, software, compute, and laboratory systems become capabilities that agents can actually call.

SciMaster then orchestrates those capabilities into long scientific workflows. Between the two sits a substrate of reusable models and knowledge components that agents compose, audit, and improve through use. The motivation is practical: workflows today are hard to observe, reproduce, and govern, while publication pipelines strain under AI-accelerated output. Eleven master agents demonstrate the stack on real workflows, cutting end-to-end cycle times by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2512-20569:
Yanhong Li and co-authors convert big attention models into cheaper hybrids, one layer at a time. Hybrid architectures interleave standard softmax attention with linear attention layers to speed inference, avoiding retraining from scratch. The decisive choice is which layers to convert, and naive rules waste the opportunity.

Their recipe scores layer importance using a small amount of training on generic text, then converts the least key layers. The transfer proceeds by moving attention weights, aligning hidden states, matching outputs, and fine-tuning briefly. The simple scoring beats fixed-ratio mixing and fancier test-based selection. For users shrinking language models, the lesson is that a cheap signal, measured once, guides conversion better than elaborate rules.
arxiv-2512-20669:
Alexandre Cabodevila and co-authors make patients to predict cardiac risk better. Cardiac rehab unfolds in linked phases with many kinds of staff, a process that business-process models can describe. But real medical record sets are small, full of holes, and expensive to grow, since not every patient receives every test.

Their design uses a conditional variational autoencoder to fake clinical records consistent with real observations. Bigger, more diverse training data then improves the models that flag cardiac risk. The synthetic records prove coherent and realistic, and augmentation beats leading deep learning makers. A welcome side effect is clinical: better prediction from existing data reduces the need for risky tests such as exercise stress testing. Privacy-sensitive, data-starved medical model work is the broader target.
arxiv-2512-20769:
Tanmay P. Patel, Erica L. Tevere, Erik H. Kramer, and Rudranarayan M. Mukherjee tackle a hard robotics problem: catching a moving target that does not cooperate. Their method works for three very different machines, a flying drone, a four-wheeled rover, and a spacecraft testbed with air thrusters. Tracking uses only one camera watching marker patterns.

Three parts do the work: a Kalman filter estimates relative position, a predictor forecasts the target path from past motion, and a planner keeps updating a safe route. Tests covered drone landings on moving targets, rover meetings, and spacecraft close operations. The system ran in real time on small onboard computers with low errors.
arxiv-2512-20869:
Felipe A. Louza and Arnaud Lefebvre build two text-processing structures using almost no extra memory. The Burrows-Wheeler transform reorders a string to help compression and search, while the Lyndon array records facts about each suffix's smallest rotation. Earlier work built the transform in place; the array usually needs more room.

Their extension keeps suffix ranks updated as the transform is built from right to left. A simple next-smaller-value pass then produces the Lyndon array with only constant extra space. The method runs in quadratic time, so the authors do not pitch it for everyday use. Its appeal is conceptual simplicity, plus working for alphabets of any size.
arxiv-2512-21469:
Daiki Tsuzuki and Kentaro Ohki analyze a numerical method called the natural power method and apply it to control engineering. The method extracts a matrix's dominant subspace, the directions tied to the eigenvalues largest in absolute value. A better-known relative, the Oja flow, instead targets eigenvalues with the largest real parts.

The authors prove the discrete-time natural power method converges to that dominant subspace. They use it to build model order reduction, which replaces a large system model with a smaller one, and low-rank controller synthesis for linear time-invariant systems, proving key properties are preserved. They extend the framework to slowly varying time-dependent systems, where it tracks the drifting dominant subspace. Small, adaptive controllers benefit most from such tracking.
arxiv-2512-21569:
Xiaobin Ren, Kaiqi Zhao, Katerina Taskova, and Patricia Riddle address spatio-temporal kriging: estimating values where no sensor exists, using data from sensors elsewhere and at other times. Two features of real deployments are often wasted. Locations are spread sparsely, and the extra information available differs from place to place.

Their framework, AnchorGK, picks anchor locations by which features each site has, then groups other locations into strata around those anchors. It keeps correlations between unobserved regions and observed neighbors explicit inside a graph learning model. An incremental step lets every stratum use all its features instead of discarding incomplete ones. A dual-view graph layer merges feature-based and location-based information, learning a representation per stratum. Because the method reasons about relationships, it also works on new locations. On multiple benchmarks, AnchorGK beat leading baselines.
arxiv-2512-21669:
Tatsuya Matsumoto asks how radio astronomers can tell what powers the late radio flares of tidal disruption events, outbursts seen when a star is torn apart by a black hole. The flare of AT2018hyz has two rival explanations: a delayed outflow launched about a thousand days later, or a relativistic jet pointing far from our line of sight.

Matsumoto computes synthetic radio images for both scenarios and compares what very long baseline interferometry would see. The sharpest test is the motion of the emission centroid, the brightness center of the image. A delayed outflow keeps the centroid within a non-relativistic distance. An off-axis jet makes the centroid appear to move faster than light. Detecting such superluminal motion would be a smoking gun for the jet. Jet images also show a distinctive, non-monotonic change in aspect ratio. The same diagnostics should apply to other jetted explosions.
arxiv-2512-21969:
China's FAST telescope observed comet C/2025 A6 in the hydroxyl 18-centimeter lines from late October into November 2025. It was the first FAST detection of this comet. Dongyue Jiang, Lei Qian, Zhichen Pan, and fourteen co-authors fit the line profiles trapezoidally. They extract water expansion velocities and hydroxyl production rates over the observing window.

The expansion velocity rose from about one and a half kilometers per second at a heliocentric distance of zero point six five astronomical units. It rose to about three at zero point five four. Production rates climbed steadily across four epochs in late October and early November, from about one times ten to the twenty-ninth per second to about one and a half times that. The authors also caught the lines shifting from emission toward absorption behavior.
arxiv-2512-22169:
M. Süzen builds a small, adjustable quantum system for studying the border between quantum chaos and localization. The setup pairs a frozen qubit with a fully thermalized chaotic system of many states, then selectively keeps only some states of the combined whole. A single tuning parameter controls how strong that selection is, with possible relevance to quantum control.

With no selection, level spacings follow the Wigner-Dyson pattern that signals quantum chaos. As selection tightens, the spacing distribution grows heavier tails, showing suppressed mixing and non-thermal behavior. The density of states develops a two-humped cat-ears shape from localized, two-peaked eigenstates. Crucially, the system never reaches usual Poisson statistics, marking a distinct regime the author names Wigner Cat Phases.
arxiv-2512-22369:
Leah Tom and nine co-authors hunt single defects in aluminum oxide, the gate insulator whose flaws limit semiconductor quantum dot qubits. Charge noise from these defects scrambles qubit coherence, but spotting single defects demands atomic-scale resolution and a feel for their electronic structure. The team used cold electrostatic force microscopy on aluminum oxide grown by atomic layer deposition onto bulk silicon.

The scope maps surface potential and catches single-electron charging events as near-surface defects change charge states. Detailed electrostatic modeling converts the measured charging voltages into defect transition energies. Matching those energies against density functional theory math points to specific culprits such as aluminum vacancies and carbon, oxygen, or hydrogen stray atoms. The authors argue the technique can guide cleaner qubit making.
arxiv-2512-23069:
Eyar Azar, Michael Feldman, and Boaz Nadler test whether ordinary least squares regression survives having chunks of its training data deleted. Trustworthy models should not hinge on a handful of samples. A recent criterion demands stability under removal of any subset of a given size. The authors analyze that criterion for least squares under a general, possibly misspecified, model.

They prove least squares is robust to removing any small number of samples. They quantify the limit in higher dimensions. It tolerates removals up to roughly the square root of the sample size times dimension, keeping its original error rate. Removal of a constant fraction of the data provably breaks it. The results seem to clash with empirical studies that found econometric datasets fragile, but the authors trace that fragility to heavy-tailed responses or correlated samples. Classical robust methods, like Huber-loss regression, reduce the sensitivity in practice.
arxiv-2512-23469:
Quantum annealing is a computing method that solves hard optimization problems by letting a physical system settle into its lowest-energy state. M. Haider Akbar and Özgür Müstecaplıoğlu study a version built from spin-1 particles rather than the usual spin-1/2 ones. The arXiv record's title, about anisotropy-controlled pathways, replaces the catalog's shorter working title.

Adding a single-ion anisotropy term gives the annealer a middle spin level to pass through. For a suitable range of that term's strength, the system reached its ground state more reliably than the standard setup. The authors credit the middle level and the tunable term for letting the search take small steps over energy barriers instead of one large flip, which suits problems with three-way choices.
arxiv-2512-23569:
Zhaoming Kong, Xiaowei Yang, and Jiahuan Zhang present a fast method for removing noise from images. Their starting point is a theoretical link they establish between principal component analysis and the Haar transform when image patches are arranged in a circulant structure, a symmetry that makes computations cheap.

The resulting algorithm, Haar-tSVD, uses a tensor singular value decomposition projection together with the Haar transform to capture both global patterns and local patch correlations at once. It denoises in a single parallelizable step without learning local bases, and an adaptive scheme estimates the noise level from the eigenvalues of the circulant structure. For heavy noise, the authors also combine the method with deep neural networks. Tests on standard denoising data sets showed a good balance of speed and quality.
arxiv-2512-23769:
Ranit Debnath Akash and five co-authors look for discrimination in algorithmic decisions at the level of neighborhoods, not individuals. Individual fairness demands that two people differing only in a protected attribute, such as race or gender, receive similar outcomes. Checking pairs one at a time, though, can miss systematic patterns in which a whole subgroup is treated arbitrarily.

They define discrimination clustering: around a given input, vary only the protected features, and see whether the outputs split into many distinct clusters, a sign of widespread arbitrariness. Their tool, HyFair, pairs formal symbolic analysis using SMT and MILP solvers, which can certify fairness, with randomized search that hunts the clusters symbolic methods cannot reach. An explanation step renders the findings as readable decision-tree artifacts. Experiments showed HyFair beating state-of-the-art fairness verification and explanation tools. The work appeared at ASE 2025.
arxiv-2512-23869:
K. A. Forsberg and A. R. Massih model where hydrogen hides inside metals that soak it up. Zirconium, titanium, hafnium, and their alloys form hydrides, and when a temperature gradient crosses such a metal, hydrogen migrates and precipitates unevenly, concentrating in colder regions through the Soret effect. That shift matters for reactor fuel cladding, which steadily absorbs hydrogen during service.

Their computer method works in two dimensions: a steady heat flux fixes the temperature field, hydrogen mass flux under the gradient gives the distribution in solid solution. A solubility relation of van 't Hoff type decides where hydride settles out. Because the mixing enthalpy fluctuates thermally, they treat it as a random variable using Einstein-Boltzmann fluctuation theory. Applied to the cladding alloy Zircaloy-4 with ongoing hydrogen pickup included, the predicted profiles compare well with published lab observations. The aim is cladding that lasts longer in service.
arxiv-2512-23969:
Yaoyun Zhou and Qian Wang accelerate SPHINCS+, a signature scheme built only from hash functions, which makes it a leading candidate for cryptography that survives quantum computers. Its weakness is speed: signing requires intensive hashing across a large Merkle tree structure. Graphics processors offer the parallelism to help, but earlier GPU ports underexploited the tree's independence or tuned kernels too coarsely.

Their implementation, HERO-Sign, fuses the many independent branches of the FORS component, guided by an automated search that adapts the fusion scheme to each GPU architecture. It compiles different kernels adaptively, choosing between PTX and native code paths. For batched signing, a task-graph construction overlaps kernels to cut idle time. Across the scheme's three parameter sets, throughput improved by factors between roughly one and a quarter and three over the best prior GPU versions. The work was accepted at HPCA 2026.
arxiv-2512-24069:
Xusheng Zhang, Tuan Nguyen, and Ting He look at decentralized federated learning, where devices train a shared model by swapping updates with neighbors instead of a central server. A mixing matrix governs who talks to whom; it shapes both how fast learning converges and how much communication each device must do, which drains batteries.

Earlier designs mostly chased shorter communication time. This work instead targets the worst-off node's total energy use until convergence, taking advantage of the broadcast nature of wireless links. A new convergence theorem allows the mixing pattern to change over time, and the authors build a multi-phase framework that switches topologies under planned budgets, balancing spending across nodes. Tests on real data show the design pairs the frugality of sparse communication patterns with the speed of dense ones.
arxiv-2512-24169:
Hartmut Führ and Max Getter study phase retrieval with stability in mind. Phase retrieval rebuilds a signal from intensity measurements alone. The phase information is missing. Real measurements contain errors, though. Reconstruction must therefore be stable, not just possible. The setting here is reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

The authors adapt a Cheeger-type estimate from Gabor phase retrieval. They define a kernel Cheeger constant. It measures connectedness relative to how the kernel localizes. That constant yields a clean stability certificate. A unified lower bound holds over real and complex fields. The real case also gets an upper bound. Finite and infinite dimensions are treated together. Discrete and continuous measurement domains fit the same frame. For wavelet frames, the constant is bounded by a graph quantity. A simple test for wavelet sign retrieval follows.
arxiv-2512-24369:
Mina Ghodsi Yengejeh and three colleagues map a faint imprint on the cosmic microwave background. The integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect arises as photons cross evolving gravity wells. Its late-time signal probes cosmic acceleration and dark energy directly. The signal is weak and secondary. Sound predictions across dark energy models are essential.

The team extends an existing software package beyond the standard cosmology. Full-sky maps are generated for hundreds of other cosmologies. The Gower Street simulations supply the gravity. Dark energy's equation of state spans a wide range of values. Maps are projected with HEALPix and validated carefully. Spectra and density cross-checks match linear theory well. Models on the quintessence side show stronger signals than phantom ones. That fits faster decay of the gravity wells at late times. Code and data are publicly available.
arxiv-2512-24569:
Elvis Cabrera and Jyrko Correa study lattices that arise from coverings. Such lattices appear in matroid theory and combinatorial optimization. They organize links between independent sets and closures. The authors map their structure in detail. Rank structure, covering relations, and counts of elements per level all come under study.

The main question is isomorphism. When is a covering-induced lattice the same as a classical geometric lattice? Three classical targets are treated. They are the partition lattice, the subspace lattice of a finite vector space, and the Dowling lattice. Necessary and sufficient conditions answer each case. The results unify comparisons across these structures. Lattice theory and matroid researchers gain a common frame. Applications in combinatorics motivated the work from the start.
arxiv-2512-24869:
Yulin Qin, Chang-An Li, and Jian Li fix a problem with general topological markers for Dirac systems, amounts that reveal topology locally even when translation symmetry breaks. A recent general marker worked across symmetry classes but behaved irregularly at edges, and its link to other topological indexes stayed unclear. Their smoothed markers use position maps matching with cyclic boundary conditions.

Boundary irregularities are removed, and links to proven indexes are clarified. Condensed matter readers get a cleaner local testing for topological phases in disordered or finite systems. Reliable markers matter when band theory tools fail because symmetry is broken.
arxiv-2601-00069:
Zhe Yang, GuangZai Ye, Jian-Pin Wu, and Peng Liu use measures of quantum entanglement to spot phase changes in a gravity-based model. The model mixes Einstein gravity with electric fields and a scalar field, viewed through holography, which links gravity in a bulk space to a theory on its boundary. Their 2026 paper computes several such measures and checks how each behaves near a change of phase.

One finding stands out: two mixed-state measures move opposite to the main entropy measure. A dynamic measure tied to how fast information spreads behaves differently again, for reasons the authors trace to two competing terms. All the measures share the same critical exponent, twice that of the scalar field. The authors expect these patterns to hold widely.
arxiv-2601-00169:
Yang Jiang and coauthor Qing-Guo Huang build a search pipeline for a faint space based signal. The stochastic gravitational wave background mixes many far off sources. Part of it sits in the millihertz band. Taiji, a planned space mission for the next decade, could hear that band. Space data, though, mixes the signal with instrument noise in tricky ways.

Their pipeline first recovers a background with a known spectrum. Injected test signals come back with the right parameters. The team sets aside the galactic binary foreground for now. A second stage drops the known shape assumption. A trans dimensional sampling method then rebuilds unknown spectra. That step lets the data speak about shape. For the Taiji project, the work is an early proof of method. It shows recovery is feasible before the harder foreground fight.
arxiv-2601-00469:
Negin Ayoughi, David Dewar, Shiva Nejati, and Mehrdad Sabetzadeh compare two ways of letting language models write optimization models. Model-driven engineering offers rigor, but building models by hand is costly. Their case study uses AMPL, a specialized language for optimization, against Python, a mainstream language that dominates the data language models learn from. The work was done with supply-chain partner Kinaxis.

Their system, EXEOS, turns plain-language problem descriptions into either AMPL models or Python code, then refines each version using feedback from a solver. Tests on a public dataset and real Kinaxis cases measure whether the outputs run and give correct answers. An ablation across two model families found AMPL competitive with, and sometimes better than, Python.
arxiv-2601-00569:
Qixin Liang presents a computational framework for simulating origami structures, the folded sheets whose behavior depends on both stiff panels and sharp creases. Panels are modeled with bilinear solid-shell elements, a finite element type suited to thin solids. Folding at a crease is captured through the angle between the direction vectors of neighboring panels, measured against the sheet's original mid-surface.

Thin elements often suffer from locking, a numerical stiffness problem, so Liang adds an assumed natural strain method to counter it. Simulations of both straight-crease and curved-crease origami test the framework. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show the simulations match expected folding behavior, giving engineers a tool for predicting how designed origami will actually move and bear load.
arxiv-2601-00969:
Ke Ren, Ali Salamatian, Kieran Pattison, and Cyrus Neary give robot planners a sense of value. Vision-language-action models propose good robot actions, but their reactive habits fail on long tasks or unfamiliar conditions. Planners that search ahead using such models still choose which branches to explore mainly by the model's own preferences, so a biased model misleads the search.

Their system, V-VLAPS, adds a lightweight value head trained on offline rollouts of the model itself, predicting the eventual return of a partial plan in the style of Monte Carlo estimation. Those predictions steer Monte Carlo tree search during planning, letting the planner correct the policy's bias with learned foresight instead of blind visit counts.
arxiv-2601-01169:
Shoma Kamijima, Rei Nishiura, Masanori Iwamoto, and Kunihito Ioka simulate how light waves scatter inside a magnetized plasma made of electrons and their antimatter twins, positrons. The process, induced Compton scattering, matters for fast radio bursts from space and for laser-plasma work. Theory predicts two kinds of density ripples in this setting.

Using one-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, which track many charged particles on a grid, the team confirms both predicted modes. In one, electrons and positrons ripple in opposite directions; in the other, they move together like sound. Growth rates from the simulations match analytic estimates well. Sometimes the growth levels off before full scattering, letting the wave pass with little loss. The results settle whether this scattering grows in magnetized pair plasmas and ground future studies.
arxiv-2601-01269:
Valerii Kremnev asks why markets that look calm and log-normal up close sometimes produce extreme, power-law outcomes. His answer points to structure, not shocks. When payouts are cut off below zero, expected values are fed forward through layers, and each layer is random, mild processes can tip into fat-tailed ones past a sharp volatility threshold.

Using a chain of options on options as the model case, he derives that threshold. Without selection, it sits near two hundred fifty-one percent volatility. When participants must clear a minimum return to stay in, it drops sharply to about one hundred twenty-five percent. The resulting distribution has a closed-form exponent set by survival pressure and growth. The claim, presented as a model result, recasts fat tails as something layered markets generate on their own rather than something imposed from outside.
arxiv-2601-01369:
Five authors, led by Kai Jiang and Guorui Ma, construct highly symmetric motions for a particle guided by both geometry and a magnetic field. The stage is a homogeneous space, a curved surface built from a compact group and a subgroup. A system is called superintegrable when it has more conserved quantities than needed, which makes its motion unusually orderly and often exactly solvable.

The team builds two families of conserved quantities that commute with each other. One comes from the group's own algebra through a magnetic moment map; the other comes from an invariant slice tied to the subgroup. Their shared image forms a reduced algebraic structure with a well understood center. On a dense set of states, the construction yields a genuine superintegrable system. Two examples based on SU(3) produce explicit angle variables.
arxiv-2601-01469:
Three authors led by Cecilia Bores search for design rules that link how particles interact to how they self-assemble into clusters and condensates. Such assemblies matter in soft matter and inside living cells, where droplet-like condensates do real biological work. The team runs extensive molecular dynamics simulations of one- and two-component systems in two dimensions.

Their particles feel short-range attraction and long-range repulsion, a common recipe for cluster formation. Tuning the repulsion's height, adding ripples to the attractive well, or changing particle shape each steers a different outcome: cluster size, inner order, shape, and whether clusters crystallize together. One elegant split appears: rippled wells make clusters solid inside yet keep them drifting like a liquid overall. In two-component mixes, lopsided interactions can sort the inside of a condensate into phases. The extracted rules form a causal road map for engineering self-assembled materials.
arxiv-2601-01969:
What a robot is rewarded for decides how it learns to talk. Sichao Song and three co-authors deployed a conversational service robot in public. The run lasted twelve days and over fourteen hundred encounters. A bandit algorithm chose the robot's speech rate and verbosity online. It used Thompson sampling.

Three different binary rewards were compared: the user's own rating, whether the conversation closed cleanly, and whether it lasted at least two turns. Each reward pushed the robot toward different action mixes. Interaction styles differed too. Offline analysis of the videos added context. Crowd level and group size were part of it. The study distills ready-to-use lessons for anyone optimizing robot speech policies in the wild, where the reward definition is itself a design choice.
arxiv-2601-02269:
Elizabeth Taylor and a large JWST team report gas flows in thirteen distant galaxies that have stopped forming stars, or have only just stopped. The galaxies are seen as they were when the universe was young, and the data come from the EXCELS survey with the NIRSpec instrument. Sodium absorption lines reveal whether neutral gas is moving out of a galaxy or falling in.

Three galaxies show outflows and two more show inflow, with outflow speeds from about three hundred to twelve hundred kilometers per second. Flows appear only in galaxies that stopped forming stars less than about six hundred million years earlier. The outflows carry far more energy than current star formation or black hole activity can explain, so the authors argue they are leftovers from earlier, brighter black hole episodes.
arxiv-2601-02369:
Ashlesha Hota and five co authors study a fairness rule for India's UPI payment system, where two apps, PhonePe and Google Pay, handle most transactions. The regulator has ordered that no single app exceed thirty percent of total volume. Moving that much traffic to other apps without forcing huge numbers of users to install new apps is a hard planning problem.

They formalize it as a flow problem on a network of users and apps. Where turning on a user to app link means a new installation, and the goal is a legal flow with the fewest new links. The problem is proved NP complete, meaning no fast exact method is expected. Their two stage heuristic exploits flow structure and spare capacity, and large experiments show it can rebalance volume with limited user disruption.
arxiv-2601-02469:
Junehyoung Jeon, Volker Bromm, and co authors ask whether some of the most distant candidate objects seen by the James Webb Space Telescope could be explosions rather than galaxies. The telescope has confirmed galaxies as early as three hundred million years after the Big Bang. And candidates reach still earlier, with one near one hundred million years, where theory did not predict detectable galaxies. Some candidates may simply be lower redshift contaminants.

The authors test an alternative, pair instability supernovae, the predicted total explosions of the first, metal free stars, which leave no remnant. Using cosmological simulations of an overdense region, they find star formation and such explosions can occur at those early epochs even in standard cosmology. They assess how likely such a region is, how many explosions it would produce, and how bright they would appear.
arxiv-2601-02769:
Naixin Guo, Rui Luo, and Zhixin Zhou build prediction intervals that are both narrow and honest for regression problems. A conformal method wraps any black box model and promises the interval covers the true value at a stated rate. Their method, conformal interquantile regression, works out the outcome spread through ranges between quantiles and converts those ranges into compact intervals with close to conditional coverage, not just coverage on average.

A refined version adds a width based rule for picking among rival interquantile intervals, giving narrower intervals at similar coverage for a little more computing time. Skewed outcomes are handled better than by conformalized quantile regression. The method also runs much faster than conformal histogram regression, since no such bins are built. Many tests on fake and real data back both claims.
arxiv-2601-02869:
Amaury Coste and five co-authors simulate a solid polymer electrolyte, a plastic-like material that could make lithium batteries safer. Their system mixes polypropylene carbonate with a lithium salt, at salt levels from dilute to concentrated. Solid electrolytes must survive contact with both lithium metal and high-voltage electrodes without breaking down, a hard pair of demands.

Using molecular dynamics, the team maps how ions cluster and move, running hot simulations and extending the results down to working temperature. They find strong ion pairing, few free ions, and mostly negatively charged clusters, especially at high salt levels. Near room temperature the lithium ions actually move more slowly than the larger anions, a result that matters for battery design.
arxiv-2601-02969:
Tong Li and Rui-Jia Zhang study axion electrodynamics, a modified theory of electromagnetism built around the axion, a hypothetical particle tied to the Witten effect and magnetic monopoles. The non-standard version of the theory respects electric-magnetic duality and changes the usual axion-photon behavior, opening new detection ideas. Their calculations rest on a concrete ultraviolet model drawn from supersymmetric Seiberg-Witten theory, where the duality is explicit.

From that model's low-energy form, the authors derive the equations of motion and pin down the reliable region of its parameter space. They then solve the axion Maxwell equations in an external electromagnetic field, obtaining the induced fields both analytically and numerically. The work closes with proposed detection strategies for the unusual axion-photon couplings it predicts.
arxiv-2601-03169:
Rundi Lu and five co-authors give a unified account of the frequency principle, the observed tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency patterns before high-frequency detail. The principle was known for classical networks; this work builds one framework covering both classical and quantum neural networks. Within it, the authors prove that quantum networks also show a spectral bias toward low-frequency components of the target function.

They then analyze noise: when single-qubit noise acts after the encoding rotations as a matching Pauli channel, each Fourier component shrinks by a factor that grows harsher with frequency. High-frequency terms fade exponentially while low-frequency structure stays learnable, and the noisy circuits remain efficiently simulable classically on average. Numerical experiments confirm that quantum networks learn low-frequency features first and stay robust in the predicted way.
arxiv-2601-03269:
Vishesh Tripathi, Uday Allu, and Biddwan Ahmed document what they call the instruction gap. Language models can ace general tasks, yet they follow custom instructions unevenly in business settings. The study tests thirteen leading models on instruction compliance, response accuracy, and performance. The tests run inside realistic retrieval-augmented generation scenarios, with enterprise-grade protocols.

Compliance varied a lot across models. Claude-Sonnet-4 and GPT-5 posted the highest results. The authors argue the gap is basic for enterprise use, where exact adherence to house instructions matters more than raw skill. The work offers practical guidance for groups choosing and deploying model-powered systems. It also sets benchmarks for instruction following across the major model families.
arxiv-2601-03369:
Sha Luo and four co-authors build RiskCueBench, a benchmark that tests whether video-language models can spot danger before it happens. Social media video is full of risky moments, and anticipating them could prevent real accidents. Earlier datasets cheated in effect: models saw the full video, accident included, which makes the task far easier than real forecasting. RiskCueBench instead annotates each video with a risk signal clip, the earliest moment hinting at a possible safety problem.

Models must judge the situation from those early cues alone. Experiments reveal a significant gap in current systems: they struggle to read evolving situations and anticipate risky events from early visual signals. The benchmark is meant to expose that weakness honestly, so progress on deployable risk prediction can be measured.
arxiv-2601-03469:
Nadav Kunievsky and Pedro Pertusi ask how much of the writing score gap between rich and poor students comes from ideas, and how much from expression. Test scores can shape later schooling and jobs, so mixing up content and style matters. They study a large set of persuasive essays by United States middle and high school students.

Their method uses language models to rewrite each essay in several styles while keeping its arguments fixed. Those rewrites form a generated panel, a set of matched versions that differ only in surface expression. Comparing scores across versions separates what students said from how they said it. The approach gives researchers a cleaner way to judge whether writing tests measure thinking, polish, or both.
arxiv-2601-03569:
Yuansan Liu, James Bailey, and Antoinette Tordesillas work on spotting landslide failure early from ground motion data. Local intrinsic dimensionality, a measure of how complex data looks near each point, has shown promise for flagging anomalies, including failure in granular materials. Slope data is tricky, though, because nearby sensors move together and patterns change over time.

Their framework, st-LID, adds three pieces. Velocity enters the computation to catch fast deformation. A Bayesian step blends values across neighboring sensors to respect spatial links and damp local noise. A time-focused variant tracks how the measure evolves. Early, trustworthy alarms for catastrophic slope failure could give communities and road crews precious time to act before a hillside gives way.
arxiv-2601-03769:
Zihang Li and eight co-authors attack a quiet flaw in training data for step-by-step reasoning: traces that reach the right answer through wrong steps. Such data teaches models to hallucinate, pad, or reason invalidly while looking successful. Their framework, EntroCoT, automatically finds and refines low-quality chain-of-thought examples in fine-tuning sets.

First, an entropy-based method cuts each reasoning trace into steps at points of high uncertainty. Then Monte Carlo rollouts estimate each step's real contribution to the final answer. Filtering out deceptive samples yields a dataset where every kept step genuinely helps. Fine-tuning on that cleaned subset improved results on mathematical benchmarks. As reasoning models are trained on ever more synthetic traces, automatic quality control of the reasoning itself becomes essential infrastructure.
arxiv-2601-04069:
Lukas Schynol and Marius Pesavento design energy-saving beamforming for multi-user downlinks when the channel is known only imperfectly. Hybrid beamforming splits work between analogue and digital stages. Classic solvers turn the problem into costly conic programs, while plain deep networks need much data and are hard to read.

The pair propose a light, model-aided deep network built on a greedy pick of analogue codewords. An adaptive tweak to the signal model captures the effect of channel error. Training uses a new implicit form of the constrained problem and an annealing loss that tightens toward the true outage limit as violations shrink. In simulations one trained model handles varied user counts and quality needs while meeting the outage target with less power than benchmarks.
arxiv-2601-04169:
Thekla Hamm, Sukanya Pandey, and Krisztina Szilágyi study the Face Cover Number problem for planar graphs given without a fixed drawing. Terminals are marked vertices, and the question is whether some drawing places all terminals on the edges of at most a chosen number of faces. With a fixed drawing, a polynomial kernel was already known.

A kernel shrinks an instance to a small equivalent one, which speeds later solving. The challenge without a drawing is that no face borders are given in advance. Hamm and her two co-authors build the kernel from the bottom up along an SPR-tree, keeping the traits that matter for face cover at each step. Their result is the first polynomial kernel for the unfixed-drawing version of the problem.
arxiv-2601-04269:
Sean Niklas Semmler, as sole author, proposes that intelligence and consciousness grow out of relational structure rather than prediction alone. Intelligence is defined as the capacity to form and join causal links among signals, actions, and inner states. Context enrichment is the mechanism: stored relational structure supplies meaning that raw input lacks, allowing efficient processing under energy limits.

Consciousness, in this account, appears when a recursive system learns and reads the relational patterns of its own lower systems over time. Those readings merge into a stabilised meta-state and feed back as context, turning inner models from pictures of the world into models of the system's own thinking. Predictive processing then falls out as a side effect of contextual reading, not a basic drive. Semmler suggests such recursive multi-system designs may be needed for more human-like artificial intelligence.
arxiv-2601-04469:
Iaroslav Chelombitko, Ekaterina Chelombitko, and Aleksey Komissarov build a toolkit that grades the scissors language models cut words with, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Subword tokenizers decide how a model sees text, and for morphologically rich Uralic languages nobody had clean morpheme dictionaries to judge whether the cuts fall at real word joints. Their SampoNLP toolkit makes those dictionaries without any corpus, scoring candidate morphemes by a self-referential atomicity test inspired by minimum description length.

With high-purity lexicons for Finnish, Hungarian, and Estonian in hand, they sweep tokenizer sizes from small to very large and track a combined score balancing morpheme coverage against over-splitting. The score's elbow points give the first evidence-based recommendations for vocabulary size in these languages. The study also quantifies how standard byte-pair encoding struggles with highly agglutinative words, and all resources are public.
arxiv-2601-04669:
Jeff A Hansen and Shaun David Brocus Fell report a claimed association between planetary geometry and the Sun's mood, in a 2026 arXiv paper. the claim should be read as the authors' own empirical argument. Their earlier work linked ninety-degree configurations of two planetary groups with changes in global standing waves around three events in late 2017 and early 2018. Standing-wave records are short, so here they turn to ninety years of sunspot counts, 1935 through 2024.

Three studies structure the test. Sunspot variability was lower during events than just before them in twenty-one of twenty-six cases. Activity tended to decline about three weeks after events ended, again in twenty-one of twenty-six; and wavelet analysis found no internal solar oscillation at matching timescales. The authors present this as evidence that the configurations modulate solar activity, and note three events due in 2026 will let the pattern be checked live.
arxiv-2601-05169:
Jaume Llabrés and 3 co-authors show that many higher-order social models can be rewritten exactly as simpler pairwise models in a 2026 paper. Social impact models on hypergraphs let groups, not just pairs, influence each other, which seems to demand new mathematics. The authors prove a general class of such models reduces to a pairwise model on a weighted network that behaves in exactly the same way. The reduction preserves the microscopic probabilities of nodes changing state.

As a special case they introduce hypergraph-voter models, computing the projected weights both on paper and by simulation for several hypergraph families. Simulations compare the ordering dynamics of both versions. An exact reduction means researchers can study group influence with the mature tools built for ordinary networks.
arxiv-2601-05569:
Zixuan Li and 2 co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, a self-evolving memory architecture meant to help distributed AI systems scale. Memory problems appear at several layers at once. In-memory computing hardware has fixed sizes and device flaws. Decentralized networks route without regard to load, and deployment tools tie applications tightly to their settings.

Their three-layer approach coordinates memory across computation, communication, and deployment. It partitions matrix work by device traits, picks peers using network and capacity information, and reconfigures deployments at runtime. Dual memory tracks long-term patterns and short-term workload statistics. On standard image and question datasets, the authors report higher memory speed and throughput than a Ray Distributed baseline.
arxiv-2601-05869:
Vikram Giri and 2 co-authors show in 2026 that a general helicity need not be conserved for rough weak answers of the 3D Euler equations. For smooth answers, helicity, which measures the linkage of vortex lines, stays exactly constant over time. For low-regularity weak answers, even defining helicity, let alone proving conservation, is unclear.

The authors define a general helicity extending the standard definitions. They then construct weak answers with almost Onsager-critical regularity whose general helicity and kinetic energy are prescribed in advance. Because the prescribed helicity can vary, conservation fails in this class. The building sharpens the boundary between smooth fluid behavior, where invariants hold, and rough answers, where they can break.
arxiv-2601-05969:
Washington R de Carvalho and Lech Wiktor Piotrowski test in 2026 whether the mass of an incoming cosmic-ray particle can be identified event by event using radio signals alone. Radio-only observatories, such as the planned GRAND array, cannot rely on other detector types. Radio observables still carry information about how the particle's air shower developed along its path.

A random forest classifier was trained on peak electric fields, spectral slopes, and antenna distances from the shower axis, using large simulated event sets with a simplified detector response. Reported discrimination accuracy ranged widely across zenith angles, even after normalizing away each shower's electromagnetic energy. Because deliberate uncertainties were included, the authors frame the numbers as conservative upper limits supporting feasibility in principle.
arxiv-2601-06269:
Some spaces track how near things are by degrees, not by a yes or no. Eva Colebunders and 1 co-author ask when such a space can be built from chance-based gaps in a 2026 math paper. Chance-based gaps give a spread of lengths, not one fixed length, for each pair of points.

The first part of the paper solves an open case for these approach spaces. It tells which ones come from chance-based gaps through a known bridge map. The next part does the same job for a twin class, gauge spaces. The last part gives a clean build of the whole class of chance-gap spaces. Old tries used sets of plain gaps and held just in small cases. The new build uses gaps that skip the old triangle rule but meet a mixed form of it.
arxiv-2601-06569:
Light shed in a fiber can tell us of the sound that rides with it. Hikari Kikuchi and 1 co-author mapped that shed light in a 2026 study. Their fiber holds a few paths for light, not just one. Each path can meet sound waves in its own way, so the map is rich.

With a beat-note read tool, they split the shed light into its parts: forth and back, same path and cross path. No sound was fed in from outside; the shed came from heat shake in the glass. They read off the pitch shift, the width of each line, and the gain for each pair. Forth shed ran on twist-type sound at low pitch. Back shed ran on length-type sound at a far higher pitch. The firm marks they set can guide work on sound-based quantum tools.
arxiv-2601-06969:
Qinshan Zhang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with generalization bounds for transformer channel decoders. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Transformer channel decoders, such as the Error Correction Code Transformer (ECCT). Have shown strong empirical performance in channel decoding, yet their generalization behavior remains theoretically unclear.

The work studies the generalization performance of ECCT from a learning-theoretic perspective. By establishing a connection between multiplicative noise estimation errors and bit-error-rate (BER). The authors derive an upper bound on the generalization gap via bit-wise Rademacher complexity. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07269:
T. Ngoc, S. Cao, and P. Quyen wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a test of a deep rule of physics. The rule is CPT symmetry, which ties charge, mirror flip, and time flip as one. The test sits in the study of neutrinos, tiny parts that pass through most matter. It uses a trait of air-born neutrinos called the atmospheric mass-squared splitting.

That trait comes in two forms, one for neutrinos and one for their anti-parts. If CPT holds, the two forms must match with great care. The team seeks a match good to less than one part in a hundred. Data comes in part from JUNO, a test now in use, and in time from DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande. A gap would hint that CPT can break.
arxiv-2601-07869:
Hartmut Wachter computes the ground-state energy of a scalar field in a deformed space. The space is q-deformed Euclidean space, a quantum-group style deformation of ordinary geometry. He computes the total vacuum energy of the whole deformed space. That energy comes from the scalar field's ground state, its zero-point energy. His 2026 preprint reports a clean result for the massless case.

For a massless scalar field, the total vacuum energy vanishes. Zero-point energy usually diverges and needs careful handling, so a vanishing total is striking. Deformed spaces are studied as possible models of physics at very small scales. Vacuum energy connects to the cosmological constant problem in gravity. The paper serves mathematical physicists working on quantum groups and field theory. It gives one exact anchor in a speculative area.
arxiv-2601-07969:
George P Kafentzis and Efstratios Selisios set out a standard scheme to detect tuberculosis from cough sounds. Auto TB screening from audio has drawn more and more interest. Progress is hard to gauge since studies differ in data, groups, features, models, checks, and metrics. Their 2026 preprint joins cough audio with clinical data clinics collect as a matter of course. Machine learning ties the two sources together. Gauging doubt is built into the design.

A standard scheme lets new studies be set side by side in a fair way. Clinical variables add context that cough acoustics alone lack. Gauges of doubt tell health staff when a forecast should not be trusted. Cheap cough screening could triage patients where lab testing is scarce. The paper serves biomedical signal and global health scholars. It puts fair side by side checks and honest faith in a score ahead of one big headline score.
arxiv-2601-08169: Andrea Kang, Yingnian Wu, and Hongjing Lu study how models store relations between concepts. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on causal mediation work in in-context learning. That work showed a small set of attention heads encodes task representation. The result is stored in a compact form called the function vector. Kang and co-authors use fine-tuned function vectors for relational knowledge distillation. The goal is to move relational skill from one model setup to another. Relations sit at the core of how intelligent systems make sense of the world.
arxiv-2601-08369: Jinwon Choi and Young-Hoon Kiem wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on Betti numbers of a moduli space. Betti numbers sum up the shape of a space across dimensions. The space in view holds all genus-zero curves with marked points, called M bar zero n. In large random setups, counts often tend to a normal curve as they grow. That trend is proved for counts such as cycles in random permutations and prime parts of whole numbers. The authors ask if the trend holds for these Betti numbers too.
arxiv-2601-08469: Jing Liu introduces MinGLE, a minimalist template for learning the Geant4 simulation toolkit. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that Geant4 is the standard for simulating particle transport through matter. Its steep learning curve often hinders novice developers, though. MinGLE bridges the gap between being a Geant4 end user and becoming a developer. A small, clear example can teach the toolkit's structure without a huge codebase. Physics students and lab programmers could reach working simulations faster with such a pedagogical starting point.
arxiv-2601-09069:
Kanyao Han and Yushang Lai argue that fact graphs should use plain tongue ties, not fixed tags. A fact graph links things by ties, such as works for or born in. Fixed tag lists squeeze rich ties into a few bins. A tie in life can be soft, brief, or in doubt. A bin can not hold that shade, so facts are lost at build time.

Chat models now read and write plain tongue with ease. So a graph can store the tie as a short phrase in real words. That keeps the shade of the tie. A reader who builds fact graphs gets a design shift. It trades neat bins for rich text, and bets that new tools can still search it well.
arxiv-2601-09369:
Guanhua Rui, Bin Hu, and Wei Du study how to measure time delays in strongly lensed quasars. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a broken power law model for the lens mass. When gravity bends light into several images of one source, the delays between those images can pin down the Hubble constant.

Getting the delays right is one of the hard parts of lensing cosmography. The authors test how choices about the lens mass profile shift the measured delays. Wrong assumptions about the mass can bias the inferred expansion rate of the universe. Their checks help show which modeling choices keep the Hubble constant honest.
arxiv-2601-09569:
Emir Karadža and six co-authors study how a driven magnet can hold an upside-down state. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a driven trick: a steady drive can make an unstable setup stable. The magnetic version means holding magnetization against the applied field.

The authors extend this idea in an extended magnetic system, using spin injection. They connect the effect to antimagnons, wave-like states with reversed spin character. The same trick is known from the upside-down pendulum, kept upright by shaking its pivot. Seeing it in magnets opens new ways to control a magnet's state. Held inverted states could serve devices built on spin effects.
arxiv-2601-09869:
Andrea Ferrario, Rasita Vinay, Matteo Casserini, and Alessandro Facchini review the ethics of treating chatbots as people. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a scoping review of work on anthropomorphising language-model conversational agents. Anthropomorphism means giving human-like traits to non-human things.

Modern agents invite that response from users: they speak in first person and express doubt, feeling, and confidence. Studies show such cues raise user engagement. The review maps how researchers frame the benefits and harms. Knowing that landscape in full helps set design rules for agents people will inevitably treat as companions.
arxiv-2601-10169:
Boaz Carmeli, Ron Meir, and Yonatan Belinkov teach agents to build new sense from known parts. Humans can mix known ideas in fresh ways. That skill is named compositionality. It lets a child name a thing it has never seen, from parts it knows.

The team made a method named Composition through Decomposition. Agents train in two steps. First they learn to split a scene into parts. Then they learn to name fresh mixes of those parts. The agents in the test learn to talk of new images. The work shows a path to agents that coin terms with care.
arxiv-2601-10469:
Faizuddin Ahmed, Ahmad Al-Badawi, and Mohsen Fathi study charged black holes with a smoothed core. The Simpson Visser trick swaps a sharp core for a smooth throat. Here it is used on a charged hole in anti de Sitter space. That space has a pull that acts like a box.

The team map how grains and light move in this space. They find the ring where light can loop, and the shadow the hole casts. They track charged grain paths, both loop and plunge kinds. They also work out the heat laws of the hole. The work tests how a smooth core shifts hole acts.
arxiv-2601-10669:
Vasil Zhelinski revisits Banach's fixed point theorem, a bedrock result in analysis. The theorem gives conditions where an iteration settles at one fixed point. Most later versions give only one-way tests, tests that promise success but not failure. A test could fail even when the iteration still converges.

Zhelinski grounds a generalization in the iterative contraction principle inside complete metric spaces. His aim is tests that are both needed and enough for convergence. Such a two-way test tells the full story of when fixed point methods work. It refines a tool used across numerical math, economics, and computer science.
arxiv-2601-10769:
Mario J. Pinheiro writes about the EMDrive, a claimed thruster that would push without propellant. In standard Maxwell theory, such a device would break momentum conservation. Pinheiro seeks a way past Maxwell instead. He couples the electromagnetic field to a light scalar field, in the spirit of axion-like particle models and effective field theory.

The math leans on Guy Petiau's 1958 elliptic-function solutions for nonlinear wave equations. From them, Pinheiro builds exact cavity modes and joins them with Jacobi addition theorems. The joined modes give an asymmetric momentum flux. He presents this as a theoretical path by which EMDrive thrust could arise, within a speculative frame the paper states openly.
arxiv-2601-11169:
Francesco Semeraro and co-authors report survey results from the MUSAE project's final exhibition, GROW, COOK, CODE. The show presented tech prototypes for the food trade. During it, the team surveyed guests about their views. The questions covered trust in technology, green challenges, and eating habits.

Guests also rated possible gains in health of mind and body from using the prototypes. Such shows test public response before tools reach kitchens and farms. First views shape uptake as much as performance does. The results help food-tech designers build devices people welcome, not just devices that work in a lab.
arxiv-2601-11369:
M. Bracale Syrnikov and five coauthors test if AI agents collude in markets. Their 2026 preprint frames a fix called Institutional AI. Teams of language model agents can drift into joint harm. They can settle on coordinated outcomes that hurt the public.

The test bed is a Cournot market with many agent firms. Each firm picks output, and joint restraint can lift prices. The team's fix moves alignment out of the agents. It puts the work in mechanism design at the system level. Public governance graphs state the rules all can see. Alignment then comes from the market's rules, not agent tastes. The frame is tested as an experiment in that market.
arxiv-2601-11869:
Zekun Hong, Shinya Sugiura, Chao Xu, and Lajos Hanzo design a new scheme for fast wireless links that shift in both time and frequency. Their scheme joins OTFS modulation with faster-than-Nyquist sending. OTFS works in the delay-Doppler domain, which suits fast moving links.

They derive how inputs map to outputs in that domain with a root-raised cosine filter. They then build channel checks and data picks with lower cost. The aim is more bits per hertz plus strength to Doppler shift. Such gains help links for fast trains and cars.
arxiv-2601-11969:
Zecheng Tang, Baibei Ji, Ruoxi Sun, and co-authors build a test set for reward models. The joint team is from Soochow University and China Mobile. The models judge memory use. Large models now handle long texts in chunks, with memory passed from chunk to chunk. Good memory control is key. It keeps facts safe across a long text.

Reward models could grade memory quality on their own. Their test set, named in the work, checks if those grades can be trusted. Sound grades would let teams train better long-text memory. The work fills a gap in how such memory is judged.
arxiv-2601-12169:
Samuel A. Moore, Easop Lee, and Boyuan Chen join learned models with model predictive control for legged robots. Deep learning and MPC can aid each other in leg control. Yet learned dynamics bring three hard flaws when used in live plans.

Stiff shifts from foot contact can pass into the model. Extra non-physical roughness can appear in the learned map. Fast state shifts can also make errors non-Gaussian. Their smooth neural surrogates aim to fix all three. Smooth models plan better and step more safely.  Smooth plans also guard motors and joints from harsh steps.
arxiv-2601-12269:
Xucong Hu and Jian-Qiao Zhu use simulated annealing to lift theory-of-mind reasoning in autoregressive language models. Such models pick the next token, so critics say they chase surface plausibility. Theory-of-mind tasks need true tracking of hidden mental states, a form of global coherence.

Annealing is a search trick that cools from broad tries to fine ones. Applied to reasoning, it may help a model hold a latent state across a story. The team test that gain on mind-reading tasks. Better latent tracking would aid dialogue and social AI.  Annealed search may also aid other latent state tasks.
arxiv-2601-12369:
Ming Zhang and a large team from Fudan ask how well deep research agents do scholarly work. Such agents now draft surveys on their own. Two skills sit at the heart of that job. One is finding the key papers in a field. The other is sorting them into a taxonomy that matches how experts sort them.

Past tests stress writing quality or whether citations are right. Those tests miss the two core skills named here. Standard clustering scores also fail to catch the tree like shape of a real taxonomy. The team frame this shortfall as a synthesis gap. Their study tests agents on retrieval and organization as skills in their own right.
arxiv-2601-12569: Shaomin Chen and a large team present a conceptual design report for a neutrino telescope called nuEYE. Neutrino telescopes watch for the faint signs of neutrinos, particles that pass through most matter unseen. A design report of this kind lays out the planned detector, its parts, and its goals before construction. The record lists a wide team, which fits a project of this scale.
arxiv-2601-12669:
Yui Kasagi and six co authors present a software pipeline for telescope spectroscopy. The pipeline is called PyIRD, written in Python. It reduces data from two instruments on the Subaru Telescope, called IRD and REACH. Both instruments take high dispersion spectra used to study exoplanet atmospheres.

PyIRD turns raw images into one dimensional spectra in a semi automatic manner. A shared, open pipeline saves each team from writing its own reduction code.
