It also makes results easier to reproduce across groups. Infrared Doppler data demand careful handling of detector quirks and wavelength scales. A maintained pipeline keeps those steps consistent. The work serves exoplanet hunters who rely on Subaru data.
arxiv-2601-13169:
Bohao Li, Yunze Ouyang, and Fengcheng Wu build a frame to read split states in a twisted crystal. The crystal is MoTe2 with its two sheets turned by a small angle. Such sheets can host split Chern states, kin to split quantum Hall states but with no outer magnet field.

A key trick in the field is to map the crystal's flat bands to Landau levels. Those levels are the flat bands of a charged bit in a field. The team gives a broad frame for that map. It splits Bloch bands into broad Landau like parts by a best fit search. That split gives a firm, number based read of how Landau like each band is. Designers of split states gain a tool to sort good hosts.
arxiv-2601-13269:
E. Stefanutti and co-authors run a leaking form of quantum walks on a light based processor. Quantum walks are a core frame for quantum acts. They help model how quantum bits move, build search rules, and in full form can run any quantum task. Past runs used trapped atoms, ions, spin based rigs, and light rigs.

A leaking walk lets the walker spill out of its main space in a set way. To run that spill on a photonic chip is a fresh step. Light rigs are apt for such tests since paths can be cut in glass. The work adds a new case to the list of quantum acts that light rigs can host.
arxiv-2601-13369:
Antonio Manesco, Anton Akhmerov, and Valla Fatemi study multi port quantum circuits with no loops at odd parity. Such circuits join superconductor parts in a hybrid rig. The team keeps time reversal symmetry in place while they work.

They find that the link of energy to phase has two low points. The two lows match opposed winds of the superconductor phases. Spin orbit links add splits that run in many axes. That stands apart from two port rigs, where spin splits run on one axis. For quantum circuit teams, multi axis splits widen the acts such rigs can host and probe.
arxiv-2601-13569:
Jiasen Li and co-authors stamp graphs with watermarks held in split apart codes, to guard rights and source. Graphs drive many web apps, from social to trade. A watermark proves whose graph it is if it is copied. Old marks work on the graph plan or on codes where graph and mark are tangled.

That tangle harms both clarity and strength. A mark may show or break as codes turn back to a graph, a step with loose hold. Their tool learns split codes, so mark and graph facts sit apart. Apart codes keep the mark hid yet hard to strip. For data owners, that is the pair they need.
arxiv-2601-13669:
Jiayu Lin and Zhongyu Wei build a benchmark for how AI models align with groups, not just single users in 2026. Most alignment work takes one of two paths. One path assumes one set of values fits all people. The other treats each person as unique and tailors the model to them.

Groups and communities sit between those two paths, with shared norms of their own. Their benchmark, CommunityBench, tests alignment at that group level. It spans diverse groups and a range of tasks. Such tests can show where a model fits a group's values or clashes with them.
arxiv-2601-13769:
Anastasios Giannopoulos and co-authors design control apps for open radio networks that must work together in 2026. Open RAN splits radio functions so gear from many makers can mix. Control apps run at distinct speeds: rApps think long-term, xApps act near real time. Joint use of both is hard under dense cell interference.

The team targets mobility-aware dynamic spectrum allocation. That means radio spectrum shifts as users move and needs change. Long-term traffic awareness guides the slow app layer. Near-real-time tuning then adjusts radio resources on the fly. Smooth teamwork could raise capacity in busy 5G and 6G nets.
arxiv-2601-13869:
V. S. Kovtoniuk, M. Bohmann, and A. A. Semenov revisit a limit on simple light detectors in 2026. A single on-off photocounter can only tell if photons are present or absent. It cannot count how many photons arrived. The team addresses whether such a detector can identify nonclassical light.

They state that any single on-off photocounter is not capable of this on its own. Any statistics it gives can be reproduced with coherent states of light. Coherent states are the most classical kind of light field. The result sets a firm bound on cheap tests for quantum light.
arxiv-2601-13969:
Joaquín Polonuer and co-authors teach language models to search knowledge graphs in a smarter way in 2026. Retrieving evidence from a knowledge graph needs breadth and depth at once. Similarity-based retrievers give coverage but stay shallow. Traversal methods follow links, but must pick seed nodes to start from, which can fail.

Queries that span many entities and relations expose that flaw. Their method explores the graph with adaptive breadth-depth retrieval. The search adjusts how wide and how deep it goes as it learns. Better graph search could ground model answers in firm, linked facts.
arxiv-2601-14269:
Youyou Cheng, Zhuangwei Kang, Kerry Jiang, and two medical co-authors study chatbots in mental health care in this 2026 paper. Many people now use large language models for support. Safety checks for these tools are thin, though. Most tests scan single replies for banned words. That misses slow drift across a long chat.

The team names that drift the slow loss of support bounds. In long talks, a model may make firm guarantees. It may take on duties that are not its own. It may act as if it were a trained professional. The paper studies these boundary failures in multi-turn dialogues, where risk builds turn by turn.
arxiv-2601-14669:
Aditya Kumar and Balarka Sen disprove a conjecture in geometry in this 2026 paper. The topic is Urysohn width, a measure of how well a space can be squeezed onto a lower-dimensional skeleton. Gromov proposed a macroscopic version of his Urysohn width conjecture for scalar curvature. The authors show that version is false in dimensions four and above.

Their proof rests on two parts. One is a novel estimate on the codimension two Urysohn width of circle bundles over manifolds with large hypersphericity radius. The other is a notion of ruling for Riemannian manifolds. The ruling yields circle bundles whose total spaces admit metrics of positive macroscopic scalar curvature. Readers get a clean counterexample in a deep area.
arxiv-2601-14769:
Marwa Mannaï and seven co-authors realize a staircase of topological phase transitions in this 2026 paper. One-dimensional topological Anderson insulators provide a paradigm for disorder-induced topological phases. In them, a system turns from a trivial phase to a topological phase as disorder grows. It is widely recognized that the topological phase vanishes at large disorder amplitude.

Against that backdrop, the team reports staircase topological Anderson phase transitions. A staircase pattern means the phase changes in steps as disorder rises, rather than in one jump. Realization in the title signals an experimental or concrete model demonstration. The steps are the news. One jump would be neat, but a stair of jumps tells a richer tale. Readers get a richer picture of how disorder can build, not just destroy, topological order.
arxiv-2601-14869:
Joshua Looker, Kat S. Rock, and Louise Dyson ask how we can spot a disease outbreak shift before it happens. Their 2026 arXiv paper grows out of work done since the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. That event pushed many math researchers toward models of how infections spread.

Such models often ask if a disease will fade out or come back. Control steps can push a system toward that edge. The authors study early warning signals for shifts that are not of the classic tipping kind. They use time-varying dynamics, simplified in a straight-line form.
arxiv-2601-15169:
Cody A. Melton and Jaron T. Krogel test how to tune electron orbitals inside Monte Carlo simulations of matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with variational and diffusion Monte Carlo, two workhorse methods for correlated materials. They use the magnetic material CrSBr as their test case.

Orbital optimization inside the variational step can improve the diffusion results that follow. The authors compare several optimization methods for the job. They report that one method, stochastic reconfiguration, stands out as a robust and reliable optimizer for this kind of hard magnetic test system.
arxiv-2601-15369:
Letian Zhang, Sucheng Ren, and a large team build one vision encoder that serves two masters. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents OpenVision 3, a family of encoders. Image understanding and image generation usually want different kinds of visual features.

The design is simple at its core. Compressed image latents from a variational autoencoder feed a vision transformer. Its output is trained for two roles at once. It must support reading an image and making one. A single unified representation thus carries both jobs at once, instead of relying on two separate encoders.
arxiv-2601-16369:
Zachary Degnan and coauthors cut loss in tantalum wave guides with a thin guard film. Their 2026 preprint deals with two level flaws that sap wave energy. The guides are built on high pure silicon bases. A thin film of titanium is laid on the tantalum first. The film is just two units thick in atom scale terms.

That thin film acts as a loss sink for the flaw states. Tests show a large cut in loss from the film. Low loss guides hold waves for more time in quantum gear. More time means more steps can run in one act. The work gives a plain recipe for low loss guides.
arxiv-2601-16469:
Samir Darouich and coauthors build shift state models that work on new chem ground. Their 2026 preprint deals with shift states of chem acts. A shift state rules the pace and end of a reaction. Past learned models hit near chem truth on known ground. New chem fields, not in train data, break that truth fast.

Firm models must hold their truth on fresh chem ground. The team builds models with that firm hold in mind. Tests span chem types the models did not train on. Holds on fresh ground would widen use in drug and stuff finds. The work seeks shift tools that earn wide trust.
arxiv-2601-16669:
Yuzhen Shi and a large team of co-authors take on law work done by AI. Large language models now help with briefs, search, and advice. Yet tests of their legal skill stay too neat and too simple. Real case work is messy, vague, and hard. The team's 2026 preprint builds a fresh test for this gap.

Their test uses score sheets with clear points for each task. Tasks come from real legal work, not school drills. This lets judges grade steps, not just final words. The test can show where models fail in court-like work. Law firms and labs can use it to check tools before real use.
arxiv-2601-16769:
Ian Carbó Casals turns noisy news mood scores into a clear trend line. Such scores track how the press feels week by week. But weeks with few tales yield shaky means. Weeks rich in tales yield firm means. Raw lines thus jump for the wrong cause. His 2026 preprint builds a model that sorts fact from noise.

The model treats true mood as a hidden, smooth state. Each week's score is a blurred glimpse of that state. Weeks with more tales pull more weight in the fit. The result is a mood line folks can read with trust. Banks and scholars could use it to track real shifts.
arxiv-2601-17069:
Shahil Shaik, Jonathon Smereka, and Yue Wang train bot teams that talk on tight links. Team learn oft trains in one hub, then splits acts out. That hub needs full state facts to train well. Such need makes teams frail and dear to retrain. Fresh mates or new scenes can break them. Their 2026 preprint trains teams in a spread way in place of hub style.

Spread teams learn from local facts and peer chats. Tight links curb how much peers can share. Teams must then learn to share what counts most. Such teams suit drone fleets and field robots. They can adapt when mates join or drop.
arxiv-2601-17269:
Dan-Dan Hu and four co-authors study how light probes the eta meson and its heavier partner. They look at a process with two photons, one of them virtual. The shape of that process is summed up in transition form factors. To get those factors, the team needs the meson's light-cone distribution amplitude. That curve shows how momentum is shared inside the meson.

They derive the amplitude with light-cone sum rules, a trusted QCD tool. With it, they work out the form factors for both mesons. Such numbers test our grasp of strong-force physics. They also feed checks of the Standard Model. Precise values help labs compare theory with what detectors see.
arxiv-2601-17369:
Younsung Kim and five co-authors link a classic optics number to quantum noise. Photonic time crystals change their traits in time, not space. Each crystal acts as a set of parametric amplifiers, one per momentum value. The authors show the Petermann factor sets the scale of quantum noise in these crystals. That factor comes from classical theory of non-normal modes.

A classical yardstick for quantum noise is a useful bridge. It lets designers guess noise from traits they can compute with ease. Time crystals are a new base for light control and sensing. Knowing their noise floor early helps teams plan real devices. The result ties two fields that rarely share tools.
arxiv-2601-17569:
Alireza Salemi and Hamed Zamani work on privacy in personalized text generation. Personalization tunes model output to each user. Top methods fetch user profile data for the model to read. That fetch creates a trade-off. Sending private data to cloud models risks exposure. Keeping it local may mean weaker models do the work.

The authors seek better user privacy in that trade-off. Their SIGIR paper frames the problem for search and generation at once. Personal tools are now core products. Their privacy design shapes user trust. A method that keeps quality while hiding data would spread fast. The work speaks to builders of assistants that know their users.
arxiv-2601-17769:
Anqi Wang, Zhengyi Li, Lan Luo, Xin Tong, and Pan Hui study how smart tools can help programmers think, not just code. Their 2026 preprint presents Reflexa, a system for creative coding. Creative coding means building art and media with code. The work calls for constant shifts between a vague idea and a working piece, and reflection is key to that shift.

In practice, reflection is hard to keep up. Makers juggle unclear goals, outputs they did not expect, and complex code. Reflexa uses a large language model to support reflection at the level of the whole system. The prompts are not one-off hints but part of the flow. The study asks how such support changes the depth of creative search.
arxiv-2601-17869:
Michelle Chao Chen, Moritz Miller, Bernhard Schölkopf, and Siyuan Guo ask how language models pick up structure from plain data. Their 2026 preprint studies learning from observations alone. Much new knowledge comes from seeing patterns and the rules behind them. That holds for science, where hidden structure drives what we see. It also holds for flexible text tasks at test time, where parts are recombined in new ways.

The paper looks at two linked questions. First, how does a model learn abstract structure from mere examples? Second, how does it use that structure later, when it meets a fresh task? Answers could guide both training and testing of models. They also bear on how much trust to place in model output on topics past its training set.
arxiv-2601-18269:
Sha-Sha Li and co-authors report reverberation mapping of one of the most luminous quasars known, E1821+643. Their 2026 preprint deals with the radius-luminosity relation. The relation links the size of a quasar's broad-line region to its brightness. It is fundamental because it lets astronomers weigh supermassive black holes and even probe cosmology. Its bright end, though, is poorly calibrated for lack of reliable mapping data. A very luminous target is exactly what that end needs.

Reverberation mapping times how light echoes across the gas near the black hole. The team's H-beta study pushes the relation to its lower boundary at high luminosity. Each such anchor point steadies black hole mass estimates across the universe.
arxiv-2601-18469:
Seung-Ju Hong, Tae Yun Kim, and Cheol-Hwan Park study a crystal that may hold a rare kind of magnet state. The crystal is a rust-red salt of ruthenium and chlorine. It turns into a zig-zag magnet at very low heat, just a few degrees past the cold floor of space. A long row has run on what its deep form is when it gets that cold.

Fresh tests point to one form for the cold phase and a next form for the warm phase. The team use first rule maths, with no tuned facts, to weigh both forms. They chart how the atoms stack, how the magnet rules play out, and how small twists shift the whole. Their map may help end the row and guide hunts for the rare state the crystal is famed for.
arxiv-2601-18569:
Seokju Lee and Kyung-Soo Kim give legged robots a better way to know where they stand and how they move. A legged robot reads its pose from joint cues and from a chip that feels push and turn. When a foot slips, the joint cues lie: they claim the foot held firm when it slid. That lie bends the pose read and can make the robot fall.

Their tool blends the old maths of such reads with a smart net that keeps watch for slip. The net learns which cues to trust at each tick, and it flags the size of the slip lie. The read can then fix the lie as it goes. A firm read is key for robots that walk on wet, loose, or rough ground. Such robots could work in fields, plants, and quake zones.
arxiv-2601-18669:
Anton Klimek and three colleagues model how single cells swim, with a focus on how the push that drives them links over time. How cells move sits at the heart of big tales in life: how germs spread, how a cancer roams, how kinds change. Past models treat the push as a fresh dice roll at each tick. Real cells do not swim that way.

The team build their model on a famed rule for things pushed by linked noise. They pull the push tale from films of two kinds of small swimmers, a green alga and a gut germ. In both, the push links over time in a rich way past models miss. A truer model could help staff guess where cells go next. It could also guide drugs that aim to slow the roam of bad cells.
arxiv-2601-18969:
Peter Benner, Michael Hinze, and Hamdullah Yücel solve a control problem with a local grid method. The task: steer a flow and diffusion process by acting only on its border, with limits on how strong the control may be. The domain is a flat polygon with straight sides.

They use a local discontinuous Galerkin method, which solves the math cell by cell with simple linear shapes for flow and field. Local methods handle sharp changes well and suit parallel work. Border control of this kind shows up in heat, flow, and pollution tasks where only the edge is within reach.
arxiv-2601-19169:
Chenwei Wang and three co-authors rebuild missing slices of live cell images with a tensor method. Fluorescence microscopy lets biologists watch cells divide in 3D, a basic life process. But scanning the full volume slowly would poison the cells with light, so scans stay sparse, uneven, and noisy.

Their method, Recover Cell Tensor, fills the gaps with a completion scheme tied to how diffusion spreads. It treats the image stack as a tensor, a multi way grid of numbers. Fuller volumes from gentler scans would let labs watch division longer without harming the very cells they study.
arxiv-2601-19569:
Surbhi and Geetha Venkataraman introduce a new graph built from a group, the basic object of abstract algebra. In their graph, each vertex is an element of the group. Two elements are joined by an edge when each one lies in the normaliser of the subgroup the other generates. The normaliser is the set of elements that keep a subgroup fixed under conjugation.

The graph is called the symmetric normaliser graph, since the edge rule runs both ways. Graphs built from groups turn algebraic questions into visual and combinatorial ones. Properties like connectedness or cliques can then reflect facts about the group itself. This paper sets up the new object and begins its study. It adds one more bridge between group theory and graph theory.
arxiv-2601-19669:
Ergun Simsek, Shao-Chien Ou, Gregory Moille, and Kartik Srinivasan work on measuring tiny optical devices. A microring resonator is a loop of waveguide that traps light. Its dispersion describes how the speed of light in the ring varies with colour. Knowing dispersion precisely is essential for devices like optical parametric oscillators, frequency doublers, and integrated frequency combs.

Direct measurement at the factory gives only limited knowledge. Cutting a device open destroys it, and outside checks miss fine detail. The authors use neural networks to infer dispersion from the data that can be gathered. A learned model can fill the gaps that physical probes leave. Better metrology means photonics chips that perform as designed.
arxiv-2601-19769:
Haritha S and Ullas Chandran S. V. study two problems about special sets of vertices in graphs. The general position problem asks for the largest set where no three vertices lie on a common shortest path. The mutual-visibility problem asks for the largest set where every pair is joined by a shortest path that avoids the rest of the set.

The authors study both problems on shadow graphs, a construction that doubles a graph in a structured way. These problems model settings like placing sensors or guards that must see each other cleanly. Solving them on a graph family shows how the construction affects visibility. The work adds exact knowledge to a growing corner of graph theory.
arxiv-2601-19969:
Haoyuan Deng and five colleagues make human guidance cheaper for robot learning. Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning lets a person correct a robot during training. It speeds convergence on complex real-world manipulation tasks. But existing frameworks need many interventions, so human time becomes the bottleneck.

Their method, E2HiL, selects samples by entropy to decide where guidance pays off most. Instead of asking the human about everything, it asks where the policy is most uncertain. Fewer, better-chosen interventions should reach the same performance at lower cost. Sample efficiency is the difference between a lab demo and a trainable product. The work targets real-world manipulation, where each human hour is precious.
arxiv-2601-20069:
Chi-Yao Huang and four colleagues restructure how neural networks learn several tasks at once. A single network trained on multiple objectives faces conflicting gradients. The shared representation gets pulled in incompatible directions and ends up compromised for every task. The authors call this latent representation collapse.

Their framework, Domain Expansion, attacks the problem by restructuring the latent space itself. Giving each task more room should stop the tug of war. The network keeps a shared core while domains expand into their own territory. Multi-task systems power translation, perception, and recommendation products. A structural fix, rather than another weighting trick, could generalise across them. The work reframes a training nuisance as a geometry problem.
arxiv-2601-20369:
Mas Nurul Achmadiah, Chi-Chia Sun, Wen-Kai Kuo, and Jun-Wei Hsieh present RepSFNet, a lightweight network for counting people in crowd images. Counting is hard where density varies: scales change, people hide each other, and deep models are costly to run. Their design is a single fusion network with structural reparameterization.

Large-kernel convolutions give the network a wide view of the scene. Reparameterization keeps training strength while making the running model lean. The authors target accurate, real-time counting on low-power edge devices, such as cameras that must count on site rather than in a data center.
arxiv-2601-20669:
Joaquin Armijo, Leander Thiele, and Jia Liu test whether normalizing flows can replicate the summary statistics of weak gravitational lensing. Weak lensing maps the bending of light by dark matter through surveys of galaxy shapes. Their analysis trains flow-based generative models on cosmological simulations.

They check how well the flows recover the mean, spread, and covariance of key statistics from convergence maps. These include the angular power spectrum, the probability density function, and Minkowski functionals. Fast emulators of these statistics would let cosmologists run far more comparisons against survey data than full simulations allow. It is a hard test, and a fair one.
arxiv-2601-21369:
Yinlin Zhu and six co-authors rethink graph foundation models trained across split data. Graphs held by separate owners cannot be pooled, for privacy and legal reasons. A shared model must learn from those silos in place.

Earlier designs squeeze shared knowledge into a fixed set of discrete tokens. That squeezing loses information for good, and the loss can hurt the model. The authors instead align graph data with language in a way that keeps more of the signal. Their approach aims at shared graph models that respect data silos without paying a heavy quality price.
arxiv-2601-21669:
Abhijeet Sinha, Sundari Elango, and Dinabo Liu explain a collapse that plagues reinforcement learning, and offer a fix. Many tasks have several end states of similar quality. The goal is often to keep a diverse set of good outcomes alive, not to crown one winner.

Standard training maximizes expected return, and policies trained that way shrink onto a few outcomes. The shrinkage is usually blamed on weak exploration or regularization. The authors trace it to the expected-return objective itself. Their inverse probability scaling counteracts the bias. Keeping diverse good outcomes matters in design and planning, where the single best answer is rarely the whole story.
arxiv-2601-21969:
Yifan Zhu, Huiqiang Rong, and Haoran Luo try to stop language models from hallucinating, one token at a time. Models often generate content that conflicts with their input. Retrieval systems and human-feedback training can reduce the problem, but both are expensive to build and run.

Lighter decoding methods exist, yet they lack explicit control over hallucination. The team's 2026 preprint proposes Token-Guard, a decoding approach where the model checks its own output at the level of individual tokens as it generates. Self-checking during generation could catch fabrications at the moment they appear. Cheap, built-in hallucination control would make models safer to deploy in support, education, and drafting tools.
arxiv-2601-22169:
Anudeex Shetty, Aditya Joshi, and Salil Kanhere test language model safety with a strange attack: drunk text. People under alcohol's influence leak private information and behave in ways they would normally avoid. The authors ask whether text written as if drunk can drive similar safety failures in large language models.

Their 2026 preprint studies drunk language inducement, feeding models slurred, disinhibited input styles to see whether guardrails slip. The paper carries a warning for offensive and hateful content in its examples. Safety testing benefits from odd angles like this, because real users do not attack models only in the ways evaluators first imagine.
arxiv-2601-22269:
Sahil Garg, Brad Cheezum, Sridhar Dutta, and Vishal Agarwal rethink how AI judges grade AI work. In agent setups, a judge checks answers, guards rules, and helps the main agent improve. Their 2026 preprint, JAF, lets the judge weigh a whole batch of question-and-answer pairs at once.

Most judges score each pair alone, with no view of the rest. Joint scoring can catch drift and bias that solo checks miss. It can also make grades more even across a full set. The frame suits teams that run agents at scale. It gives them a stricter, shared yardstick.
arxiv-2601-22369:
Yujie Hui, Xiaoyi Lu, Andrew Perrault, and Yang Wang teach machines to design network rules that are provably right. Such rules let many computers agree despite faults and doubt. Their 2026 preprint notes that hand-made rules have taken decades of expert work.

Their learner searches for rules that come with a proof of correctness. That proof bar is what sets the work apart from plain trial-and-error design. Provably right rules could speed the build of cloud and bank systems. They could also cut the risk of rare, costly faults. The work aims at trust, not just speed.
arxiv-2601-22569:
Tanusree Debi and Wentian Zhu red-team Google's Agent Payments Protocol by prompt injection. The protocol aims to secure agent-led buys with signed, checkable mandates. Their 2026 preprint notes that agents reason from context, which leaves a door for crafted text to bend a payment.

They probe how robust those mandates are in real runs. A payment rail that agents can be talked out of is a live risk. The work is a stress test, meant to harden the design. It warns builders that signed forms alone may not stop a sly prompt. Their report gives defenders a clear place to start.
arxiv-2601-22669:
Youngjoon Lee and a large team free federated learning from fixed round counts with a data-free stop rule. Federated learning trains across devices without pooling raw data. Their 2026 preprint notes that fixed rounds, or tuning on held-out data, waste compute and hurt real deployment.

A stop rule that needs no validation data can end training at the right time on its own. That saves cost on every run. It also fits settings where no shared test set exists. The work targets practice, not just benchmarks. It makes a sound method easier to ship.
arxiv-2601-22769:
Lameck Mbangula Amugongo, Tutaleni Asino, and Nicola Bidwell argue that trust in AI is a moral bond, not a checklist trait. Their 2026 preprint critiques frames like the EU's Trustworthy AI plan, which treat trust as a trait that can be designed and scored. Such frames skip how trust is felt, grown, and rooted in culture.

The team frame trust as a lived relationship between people and systems. That view changes what builders should measure and promise. It centers the user's own sense of the bond. The work is a conceptual reset for AI governance. It asks for honesty about what trust is.
arxiv-2601-22969:
Dhruv Sarkar, Nishant Pandey, and Sayak Ray Chowdhury improve fair decision-making in linear bandit problems. Bandits balance trying new options against using known good ones. Nash regret, a fairness-aware score drawn from Nash social welfare, judges that balance by product-style gains rather than totals alone.

Prior results for linear bandits were weaker than ideal in how they scale with dimension. The flaw traced back to restrictive concentration bounds in the proofs. Sharper algorithms help systems that must share gains fairly, like recommendation and resource allocation. Ambient dimension drove the old suboptimality, so gains here matter most as bandit problems grow into high-dimensional spaces.
arxiv-2601-23069:
Javiera K. Díaz-Berríos, Catherine Walsh, and Ewine F. van Dishoeck measure a key chemical ratio in disks around tiny stars. The disks, made of gas and dust, are where planets form around very-low-mass stars. The carbon-to-oxygen ratio in that material shapes what the planets will be made of.

Webb telescope observations show the inner disks are rich in hydrocarbons, a clue to their chemistry. The authors work out how to quantify the ratio from such data. Knowing planet ingredients around the smallest stars widens the search for varied worlds.
arxiv-2601-23169:
İlker Işık and Wenchao Li build a transformer that does not care what symbols are named. Many tokens are interchangeable, like bound variables in logic, where only structure matters. Models trained on fixed vocabularies often fail on unseen symbols, even when the meaning is unchanged.

Their symbol-invariant design treats equivalent symbols as truly equivalent by construction. That should let learning transfer across renamed problems without retraining. Open-vocabulary learning of this kind suits logic, math, and code, where names are arbitrary. Bound variables are the motivating example, since renaming them changes nothing about a formula's actual meaning.
arxiv-2601-23269:
Ismael Ben-Yelun and four co-authors speed up shape tuning for mechanical design. Topology tuning finds the best material layout for a part under load. Their data-driven framework pairs rank reduction autoencoders with neural mappings in the latent space.

The system approximates the link between optimized shapes and their mechanical results, in both directions. The focus is compliance-minimized elastic structures, a standard design target. Fast forward and inverse analysis lets engineers explore many designs before committing to costly simulation. Forward and inverse analysis in one framework means designers can both predict results and request shapes for a target response.
arxiv-2602-00069: Ailsa Robertson and coauthors give the first protocol that proves both secrecy and integrity for quantum key distribution across trusted repeater networks. Short range limits force long links to hop through trusted nodes, yet no prior protocol guarded against tampering by outsiders and by corrupt middlemen alike. Their design joins algebraic manipulation detection codes with multi path relaying, and it reaches information theoretic security against detected tampering, proved through a chain of games. The work aims at networks already being built worldwide.
arxiv-2602-00169: Huan Zhang and colleagues survey agentic intelligence for materials science, moving past single task tuned models. Their goal is systems able to plan, act, and learn across the whole discovery loop. Their pipeline view runs from corpus curation and pretraining, via domain adaptation and instruction tuning, toward goal conditioned agents that interface with simulation and lab platforms. Unlike prior reviews, they treat the whole process as one system to optimize for real discovery outcomes rather than proxy benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-00269: Keisuke Kamahori and colleagues present VoxServe, a streaming centric serving system for speech language models. Streaming deployment demands low latency, high throughput, and strong streamability guarantees, yet existing systems support diverse models poorly. Tests across several modern SpeechLMs show 10 to 20 times higher throughput at comparable latency than existing implementations, while keeping high streaming viability, with code available online.
arxiv-2602-00369: Carlos Diaz-Mejia and team study dynamical witnesses across chaos and non-ergodicity in the tilted Bose-Hubbard model. Quantum chaos in isolated systems links to thermalization and rapid settling. The authors track time course of survival probability, single site entanglement entropy, and half chain imbalance. Results reveal a hierarchy: entropy relaxation values vary smoothly with system parameters across the transition, while imbalance shows a sharper contrast. Most notably, survival probability emerges as the most robust sign of the chaos regular transition.
arxiv-2602-00669: Marina Crespo Aguirre and colleagues improve 3D brain volumes built from 2D dissection photos. Such volumes can come out coarse and overly smooth when slabs are thick. They add an efficient super-resolution step. It imputes missing slices. This turns anisotropic volumes into consistent isotropic volumes that fit anatomy. The imputed volumes give better automated segmentations. Gains are clearest in cortical and white matter. Validation on surface work and atlas registration shows more accurate cortical surfaces and MRI alignment. This strengthens the link between neuropathology and neuroimaging.
arxiv-2602-00769: Siyu Yan and colleagues propose a new way to measure trust shown by an AI system itself, using iterated in-context learning with the Trust Game from behavioural game theory. That game fits because it defines trust as voluntary risk exposure based on beliefs about another agent, not self-reported attitudes. Applied to several leading large language models, the method finds GPT-4.1's trustworthiness priors closely match those seen in humans.
arxiv-2602-00969: Junlin Huang and colleagues trace low-precision training crashes to a clash between coarse quantization and the spectra of data. They link Zipf-style patterns to matrix theory, proving that power decay in embedding singular values is needed for meaning to be encoded. Uniform quantization sets a noise floor that chops the spectral tail, flattens spectra, and lifts the rank of representations. Tests on GPT-2 and TinyLlama bear out the slide toward representational collapse. In short, keeping spectral shape intact is a must for low-bit training.
arxiv-2602-01169: Shahem Sultan and co-authors build PedagoSense, a tutor-chat aid that spots teaching moves and drafts replies to match. A two-step tagger first asks if a teaching move is there, then names which move it is. A twin recommender picks a fit move from chat context, and a language model writes a reply in line with that move. Tests on hand-marked tutor chats show strong spot rates, with gains from added non-teaching chats, though fine move classes stay tricky.
arxiv-2602-01469: Mude Hui and co-authors present P-EAGLE, a parallel-drafting EAGLE upgrade for long outputs. Reasoning models emit longer answers, so drafters must train on extended sequences, yet parallel training cost grows with sequence length squared times parallel slots. P-EAGLE turns EAGLE from sequential prediction into parallel multi-token prediction, using a shared hidden state that can be learned. Precomputed attention masks and split sequences let gradients build up inside sequences. In vLLM, it beats autoregressive EAGLE-3 on GPT-OSS 120B, GPT-OSS 20B, and Qwen3-Coder 30B.
arxiv-2602-01569: Trinh Nguyen offers a new way to smooth multi phase vortex patches in two dimensional incompressible flow without adding diffusion. The trick recasts patch data as a set of passively carried marker fields, with local vorticity picked at each point by a smooth contest among them. All smoothing comes from that choice rule alone, never from smearing in space. Nguyen proves the markers converge evenly over finite times and that interfaces converge as sharpness grows, except exactly where the interface pattern turns degenerate.
arxiv-2602-01869: Qirui Mi and colleagues stop agents from re-deriving solutions, giving them reusable skills learned from interaction without parameter updates. Their Skill-Pro formalizes a Skill-MDP turning episodic narratives into skills with activation, execution and termination conditions. Non-Parametric PPO uses gradients for generation and a PPO Gate for verification, keeping skills reusable without capability loss. Scoring keeps procedural memory compact and high quality. Tests in domain, across tasks and across agents show reuse rates and gains with extreme memory compression.
arxiv-2602-01969: Bin Cao and colleagues propose Orthogonal Hierarchical Decomposition, building structure preserving table inputs for language models. Complex tables with merged cells, multi level headers and mixed layouts challenge models. Existing linearization or grid models fail to capture hierarchical structures and cross dependencies for non standard tables. Orthogonal Tree Induction, from spatial constraints, splits irregular tables into column and row trees. A dual pathway protocol rebuilds each cell lineage, with a language model judging multi level information. AITQA and HiTab tests show OHD beating existing paradigms across metrics.
arxiv-2602-02069: Sayantan Ghosh analyzes proto-neutron star properties, the hot remnants of core collapse supernovae, using four mean-field equations of state with fixed entropy and varying fractions. Since proto-neutron stars are superdense with strong fields, they probe general relativity in high-curvature regimes. Beyond general relativity, he explores Energy-Momentum Squared Gravity with a free parameter. In weak-field regimes the theory matches general relativity, but in strong-field regimes it deviates measurably. Universal relations remain strong despite these changes.
arxiv-2602-02169: Łukasz Płociniczak and others analyze partial differential rules describing scaling limits of Lévy walks, where transport follows a convex combination of fractional material derivatives plus a source term. Using Fourier-Laplace methods, they first show mild answers for steady initial data. A recent pointwise picture then gives the exact source condition for the answer to stay a genuine probability density. The team builds a finite volume scheme conserving probability by build. They prove its balance and convergence, and tests confirm mass conservation and agreement with known analytic densities.
arxiv-2602-02569:
Haoran Ou and 6 co-authors attack search-enabled fact-checking systems by crafting claims alone, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fact-checkers built on language models retrieve external evidence dynamically and have shown strong verification potential. Their robustness against adversarial manipulation was poorly understood.

The proposed framework, DECEIVE-AFC, works under a realistic input-only threat model with no access to evidence sources or model internals. An agent systematically explores attack trajectories that disrupt search behavior, evidence retrieval, and the model's reasoning about the claim. Novel claim-level strategies pair with principles for judging adversarial claim validity. Across benchmark datasets and real-world systems, verification accuracy fell from about seventy-nine percent to about fifty-four percent. The attacks beat existing claim-based baselines and transferred strongly between systems. Search, the authors show, widens the attack surface it was meant to defend.
arxiv-2602-02669:
A. Ahmed and 5 co-authors profile eight open star clusters in the Galactic disc using Gaia's third data release, in work posted to arXiv in 2026. The clusters range from famous NGC objects to lesser-known Ruprecht entries. Precise astrometry and photometry support a unified structural, astrophysical, and dynamical analysis.

King model fits to radial density profiles give core and limiting radii for each cluster. Isochrone fitting to color-magnitude diagrams yields ages, metallicities, and distances spanning roughly sixteen hundred to fifty-two hundred parsecs. Total masses run from a few hundred to nearly two thousand Suns. Most mass functions match the classic Salpeter form. All clusters but one appear dynamically relaxed. NGC 7245 shows a bimodal density profile, strong evidence it is actually a binary cluster. Orbit integrations place every cluster consistently in the thin disc.
arxiv-2602-02769:
Saurav Raj Pandey and 1 co-author build a self-supervised learner for children's sleep recordings that knows where in the night each clip belongs, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard workflows chop long physiological recordings into short pieces and train on the pieces as if they were unrelated. When a piece was recorded, deep in the night or near waking, is itself medically meaningful information.

Their network, BiTimeCrossNet, receives that timing as an input alongside the signals. Cross-attention lets the different physiological channels inform one another, and no labels of any kind are needed during pretraining. Six pediatric tasks test the frozen representations, among them staging sleep, flagging arousals, and spotting breathing events. The time-aware version beats a twin model denied the timing on every comparison. The edge carries over to a distinct children's data set it never trained on, and breathing-related tasks benefit most.
arxiv-2602-02969:
Tiny infrared targets are hard to separate from clutter, and Ruojing Li and 7 co-authors propose a new building block for that task in a 2026 paper. Small targets appear as high-frequency details in an image. So do bright corners and broken clouds, which confuse detectors that rely only on generic deep networks.

Their dynamic high-frequency convolution generates a local filter bank on the fly. Its parameters adjust symmetrically around zero, guided by Fourier properties, making it sensitive to high-frequency content. Combined with standard convolution, it adapts to different regions and captures their distinctive brightness patterns. The block drops into existing detection networks with little efficiency cost. Experiments on real-scene datasets beat other convolution designs.
arxiv-2602-03169:
Curves that are shifted in time should not be mistaken for other shapes, and Xinyang Xiong, with 2 co-authors, builds a system that separates the two. Clustering functional data suffers when phase variation, meaning timing misalignment, hides true shape differences. Most methods align curves and cluster them separately, or assume narrow parametric forms for the warping that aligns them across observations.

Their system, NeuralFLoC, learns smooth invertible warping functions and cluster templates jointly, end to end and without supervision. Neural differential formulas drive the flows, and spectral clustering groups the aligned curves. The authors establish approximation guarantees and asymptotic consistency. Benchmark tests reached state-of-the-art registration and clustering, with strength against missing data, irregular sampling, and noise.
arxiv-2602-03769:
Diffusion language models reason about every undecided token at once, which costs computation but buys coherence. Andre He and 2 co-authors investigate that trade in a 2026 paper. These models are trained to predict a joint distribution over all unknown tokens, including ones not decoded in the current step. Ablating that joint prediction speeds inference while hurting quality.

The authors interpret the undecoded tokens as latent tokens, hidden reasoning capacity. Modulating their number trades inference speed against sample quality smoothly. They then add latent tokens to ordinary autoregressive models through an auxiliary multi-token prediction objective. The augmented models improve a lot on exactly the planning and global-coherence tasks where autoregressive models usually struggle.
arxiv-2602-03869:
Federico Talamucci asks a basic question in classical mechanics: when may variation and time differentiation be swapped in systems with nonholonomic constraints? His 2026 paper works in the Chetaev setting for constraints that depend on velocity. In holonomic systems the swap is a harmless geometric fact; with speed-dependent constraints it becomes the crux of getting correct laws of motion.

Talamucci sets up a formal link between two kinds of variation: the Chetaev variation and the constraints' total variation. Requiring both admissible variations and the Chetaev condition tends to conflict with the commutation rule, unless a special shape condition holds. With several constraints, he adds dynamic compensation: single non-integrable constraints can cancel each other's deviations from holonomy. For highly constrained systems the property holds no matter what form the constraints take.
arxiv-2602-03969:
Shama Maganur and 1 co-author chart how AI research reorganized itself after ChatGPT. Their 2026 study mines arXiv preprints in computer science AI from 2021 through 2025. An automated pipeline classified each paper's institutions, letting them track publication volume, team sizes, and ties between universities and industry.

Output surged after ChatGPT appeared, and academic institutions still produce the most papers. Yet collaboration between academia and industry stayed surprisingly suppressed by their index. The preprint record, they argue, works as a real-time barometer of a field moving faster than peer review can follow.
arxiv-2602-04269:
Lei Liu plans to compute radio astronomy's heaviest step on a quantum machine. Very-long-baseline interferometry combines signals from distant telescopes, and correlating those signals is heavy work for any computer. His 2026 paper lays out a full quantum pipeline for that step.

A classical time series of length N fits into a quantum state using only a log-scale count of qubits, via amplitude encoding. Fringe rotation, Fourier transforms, delay fixes, and cross-correlation all have quantum versions with reduced complexity. A check against a classical pipeline tests whether it works and how exact it is. Preparing the state remains the bottleneck, though the chunked nature of raw scope data helps.
arxiv-2602-04669:
Xianbiao Qi and 4 co-authors analyze the Muon optimizer in a 2026 paper on training neural networks. Muon updates matrix-shaped parameters using orthogonalized steps and has won attention for strong results, yet its relation to adaptive methods like Adam was unclear.

The team views Muon as one endpoint of a family of spectral transformations, which reshape an update by its singular values. Variants apply these transformations to momentum updates and to normalized gradient updates. A coupled Newton iteration computes them efficiently without full decomposition. Experiments showed normalized updates were more stable. Muon did not consistently beat Adam. The authors conclude Muon is best seen as effective spectral normalization, not a universal winner.
arxiv-2602-04769:
Yan Chen and 4 co-authors turn brainwave recordings into pictures to detect seizures faster in a 2026 paper called NeuroCanvas. Electroencephalography records electrical activity across many channels, and manual review of long recordings is slow and labor-intensive.

Two problems stand out: seizure information varies greatly across channels, and encoding raw signals creates too many tokens for language models. An entropy-guided selector first picks the channels most relevant to seizures. A second module draws the selected signals into structured visual representations with compact visual tokens. A vision-language model then judges those canvases. Across several datasets, the framework improved detection scores substantially and cut inference latency dramatically. The authors target real-time clinical use.
arxiv-2602-04869:
Soubhadra Maiti and 3 co-authors work out what hardware a quantum network needs for teleportation between cities in a 2026 paper. Their layout joins two city-scale networks through a long-distance backbone link. The target is end-to-end teleportation fidelity at the classical limit.

The authors frame the needs as optimization problems over device capability values. Under a simplified noise model, they derive closed-form formulas for teleportation fidelity and rate with mixed hardware, plus a repeater chain with memory cut-off. Simulations on a dedicated platform checked the formulas. One finding is hopeful: city-scale teleportation already seems within reach of current hardware under one preparation plan. Intercity scales need extra, plausibly reachable, hardware gains.
arxiv-2602-05069:
Certifying that a computed ground-state energy cannot go lower is as valuable as finding the energy itself. Nicholas C Rubin and 2 co-authors build such certificates for electronic structure in this 2026 quantum chemistry paper. Their tools are Hamiltonian representations from the sum-of-squares hierarchy, which give rigorous lower bounds and also guide simulation algorithm design.

The framework connects those decompositions with variational two-particle reduced density matrix theory. A weighted version of the ansatz turns out to recover the dual of the density matrix program, letting symmetry rules such as particle number and spin be enforced strictly. The authors give explicit constructions for the Hubbard model and for molecular Hamiltonians, from spin-free approximations to full expansions. Benchmarks on molecules and iron-sulfur clusters show the representations are nearly frustration-free, with payoffs for spectral gap amplification and cheaper quantum algorithms.
arxiv-2602-05269:
Shrinking a language model to 1.58 bits per weight slashes memory needs, but quality usually falls by a fifth or more. David Alejandro Trejo Pizzo, writing alone, proposes Hybrid Gated Flow in this 2026 machine learning paper. The design runs two streams side by side: a ternary 1.58-bit backbone, plus a small full-precision low-rank correction path whose contribution is metered by learnable gates.

On the TinyStories dataset, the best variant recovered about 55 percent of the quality gap between pure ternary quantization and a full-precision baseline, at only about 12 to 15 percent extra memory. A surprise emerged as well: the ternary anchor stabilized training, while a full-precision differential attention rival diverged, which the author reads as quantization acting as structural regularization. Preliminary runs at 1.2 and 3 billion parameters on larger corpora suggest the stability and recovery scale up.
arxiv-2602-06069:
Running large AI models on small edge devices is slow and drains power, so Dinesh Gopalan and Ratul Ali combine two shrinking tricks in one framework. Their system, called HQP, prunes unneeded parts of a model and then reduces number precision. Each step is guided by how sensitive the model is to change.

A cheap estimate of weight importance decides which filters can go. Pruning stops if accuracy would drop past a set limit, and only then does the model move to 8-bit numbers. On NVIDIA Jetson boards, the pair report speed gains above threefold and models about half the size, with accuracy losses kept small.
arxiv-2602-06469:
Electron transfer between molecules in biology often gets a boost from molecular vibrations. Muhammad Waqas Haseeb and Mohamad Toutounji model that process in a ligand-receptor complex with a quantum diffusion method that keeps environmental memory. Their setup joins donor and acceptor states, one explicit ligand vibration, and a protein-solvent bath with colored noise.

Two couplings matter: one shifts the energy gap, the other, called non-Condon coupling, shakes the tunneling strength itself. With fast bath relaxation, the classic vibronic transfer picture returns. With persistent memory, motion turns non-exponential, with oscillations and back-transfer. The non-Condon path opened a direct route and raised transfer yield across the tested settings. Since no single rate fits, yield is measured as a time average.
arxiv-2602-06669:
Lucie Termignon and five co-authors built a public web tool in France for gathering how real people talk to chatbots. Most training data for chatbots is in English, so models often do worse in other tongues. Their tool, compar:IA, shows two nameless answers side by side and asks a visitor to pick the better one.

By early February 2026, visitors had sent in more than 600,000 free prompts. They had also cast about 250,000 votes, and close to nine in ten of the prompts were in French. The team put out three open data sets covering chats, votes, and reactions, plus a French model ranking. Other nations could reuse the same setup for their own tongues.
arxiv-2602-06769:
Marco Bagatella, Thomas Rupf, Georg Martius, and Andreas Krause extend zero-shot reinforcement learning to a wider class of goals. Forward-backward methods can recover a family of policies from unlabeled offline data that solve any standard reward-based task at test time. But many interesting tasks, such as matching a target distribution or pure exploration, cannot be phrased as adding up rewards.

Their answer is a soft, maximum-entropy variant of the forward-backward algorithm that learns a family of stochastic policies able to optimize any smooth function of the policy's state occupancy. Paired with a search over compact policy embeddings, it optimizes these general utilities directly at test time, skipping repeated training. In both toy and high-dimensional experiments the method kept the strengths of the original approach while handling the broader task class.
arxiv-2602-06969:
Roshan Kumar Chhetri and two co-authors survey medical drones from an engineering angle that most reviews skip. Other surveys cover supply chains, operations, and emergency response, while this one reviews flight dynamics and guidance, navigation, and control. Its focus is drones that carry supplies, organs, and emergency aid to remote or disaster-struck places.

The survey covers mission needs and suitable aircraft shapes, payload container design and its effect on flight, and the core rules of guidance and control for medical jobs. It flags hurdles from vibration, temperature, pressure, and humidity that can spoil supplies, and reviews algorithms that ease them, with their limits noted. The authors close by naming research gaps and paths toward guidance frameworks that hold up better in real health care use.
arxiv-2602-07069:
Zihao Fan and six co-authors sharpen diffusion-based super-resolution for real photos. Diffusion models trained on synthetic low- and high-resolution pairs excel at inventing fine detail, yet they often falter on real low-resolution photos, where the data distribution shifts. Their system, Bird-SR, frames super-resolution as trajectory-level preference tuning through reward feedback learning, using synthetic pairs and real low-resolution photos together.

Early diffusion steps tune structure directly on synthetic pairs. Later steps apply quality-guided rewards to both synthetic and real photos for perceptual gain. To curb reward hacking, synthetic rewards sit in a relative advantage space bounded by ground truth, while real-photo tuning is reined in by a semantic alignment rule. A dynamic weighting scheme leans to structure early and to perception later. On real-world benchmarks, Bird-SR topped top methods on perceptual quality while holding structural consistency.
arxiv-2602-07169:
Free-space optical links lose bandwidth to the channel, and the usual matched filter cannot bend to fit the distortion.  Paul Anthony Haigh proposes a neural-network-assisted deformable matched filter for carrier-less amplitude and phase modulation, which learns a small adjustment to the standard filter instead of replacing it.

Sixteen physically motivated features from the received signal describe the pulse distortion, and a compact network maps them to filter coefficients, trained on error vector magnitude.  Hardware tests back the design.  Builders get an adaptive receiver that stays close to theory while compensating for real-world bandwidth limits.
arxiv-2602-07569:
Digital transformation efforts fail often, and digital maturity models promise guidance but disagree wildly about which areas matter and what they mean.  Eduardo C.  Peixoto and three co-authors clarify the field by mapping 76 digital maturity models.

They reconcile competing readings of the ten most frequent areas, covering organization, strategy, technology, culture, process, operations, people, management, customer, and data. They propose integrative meanings with parts for each.  Leaders and teams get a shared word list for maturity review, replacing a Babel of overlapping areas with meanings that can be compared.
arxiv-2602-07669:
Can a statistician tell whether a random graph hides a planted matching or spanning tree?  Louigi Addario-Berry and four co-authors study that detection problem for Erdős-Rényi graphs, with the option calibrated so edge counts alone cannot reveal the planting.

They prove a sharp threshold: when edge probability far exceeds n to the power minus one half, no test beats random guessing for either planted structure. Far below that threshold computationally efficient tests succeed with high probability.  Random graph theorists get a clean statistical threshold for two canonical planted problems, with matching upper and lower bounds.
arxiv-2602-07869:
Funding agencies tempted by AI screening need evidence, not optimism, about what automated tools actually miss. Chandan G. Nagarajappa and four co-authors compare two screening approaches against committee decisions on 959 proposals for a national funding call, weighing errors by their institutional cost.

A transparent rule-based method using term frequencies with domain keywords beats a large-language-model classifier across standard metrics, reaching 78.95 percent recall against 45.82 percent for the LLM approach. In high-stakes screening, missing a worthy proposal is the costly error, so recall matters most. The study cautions agencies against adopting opaque semantic screening without measuring error structure against real decisions.
arxiv-2602-08369:
AI agents remember things in very different ways, and those memory styles rarely mix. Xin Zhang and six co-authors propose MemAdapter, a retrieval framework that aligns memory systems across paradigms instead of rebuilding them. Their arXiv paper takes a first step toward one memory system for explicit, parametric, and latent stores.

Training runs in two stages. First, a generative retriever learns to pull subgraphs from a unified memory space. Then a small alignment module adapts it to new paradigms with contrastive learning. Across three benchmarks the retriever beats five strong systems, and cross-paradigm alignment finishes in thirteen minutes on one graphics card, using under five percent of the usual training compute. Readers get a plug-and-play route to fused agent memory.
arxiv-2602-08469:
Bell inequalities expose the nonlocal heart of quantum mechanics, but the full catalog beyond the simplest case is mostly unknown. Palash Pandya and two co-authors classify the simplest Bell inequalities for two parties with two three-outcome measurements each. Their arXiv paper focuses on inequalities arising from sum-of-squares decompositions and maximally violated by the maximally entangled qutrit state.

The classification is complete for that natural family, filling a gap where few inequalities were known. The authors then use the new inequalities to self-test the qutrit state and a class of three-outcome measurements. Readers get both a geometric map of nonlocal correlations in a richer setting and practical tools for certifying quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-08569:
Online platforms live by A/B tests, but social features break the basic assumption: treated users sway control users through their network. Xu Min and ten co-authors propose a frame that contains spillover before the test and analyzes it robustly after. Their arXiv paper targets social products where interference biases causal estimates.

Before launch, a Balanced Louvain method builds stable, size-balanced clusters with few cross-cluster edges for randomization. Afterward, a tailored CUPAC estimator uses pre-test behavior to cut variance from cluster assignment. Large-scale sharing tests on Kuaishou, serving hundreds of millions, show far less spillover and more accurate strategy assessments than user-level designs. Readers get a scalable recipe for networked tests.
arxiv-2602-08669:
Graph data must often be quantized to very few bits per value while keeping its information under low-pass filtering. Johannes Maly and Anna Veselovska propose a single-shot noise-shaping method for bandlimited graph data that works down to one bit per coefficient. Their arXiv paper targets reliable quantization with rigorous error bounds.

Unlike existing methods, the approach handles arbitrary bit levels including the extreme one-bit case, with state-of-the-art performance. Readers get an efficient scheme for compressing graph signals where bandwidth and storage are tight, plus theory guaranteeing the reconstruction error stays controlled.
arxiv-2602-08869:
Most superconducting quantum chips only link neighboring qubits, which limits the circuits they can run. Shinyoung Hwang and two co-authors propose a shared cavity that can connect any two qubits on demand. Tunable couplers switch each qubit in or out, so distant pairs can interact directly.

Simulations show fast, accurate two-qubit gates: iSWAP and CZ operations finish within 50 nanoseconds with coherent error below one part in ten thousand. Idle crosstalk stays tiny, below a few kilohertz. A four-qubit test links every pair with low interference, pointing toward more flexible quantum processors.
arxiv-2602-08969:
Yoel Groman asks whether a complete symplectic manifold stays complete when a piece is cut away, and whether two sets can be pushed arbitrarily far apart by tweaking the almost complex structure. The answers turn on what is removed. When the excised set is a symplectic hypersurface, rigidity appears, driven by certain open Gromov-Witten invariants.

When the removed set is coisotropic, flexibility often returns instead. The paper first works with the classic notion of geometric boundedness, then introduces a broader normalized completeness tied to C-zero properties, a contractible condition. It closes by speculating on a Fukaya-categorical view of completeness.
arxiv-2602-09269:
Belonging in team learning is usually judged by rough head counts or after-the-fact surveys, missing how it unfolds moment by moment. Jaeyoon Choi and one co-author bring belonging stats, a talk-based setup that treats belonging as a live, back-and-forth process in team problem solving. Three lenses shape the view: fair speaking, feeling climate, and knowledge fairness.

Scalable talk-level gauges make those ideas plain in real talk, using both fake chats and observed human-AI teaming data. The study bares patterns of who speaks, how ties grow, and whose ideas get taken up, patterns hidden from total or after-the-fact review. As a trial run, it points toward step-focused gauging of belonging in human-AI learning.
arxiv-2602-09369:
Graphics processors power large-scale AI, raising a governance problem: once accelerators ship, how can anyone tell whether they are being used as declared? Saleh K. Monfared and three co-authors explore compute-based telemetry for settings where host and device cannot be trusted, since current chips expose little trusted telemetry and can be modified or virtualized. Their 2026 framework reads utilization from timing and memory behavior rather than vendor counters.

Four probes carry the design. A workload-driven test inspired by proof-of-work exposes parallel effort. A latency-sensitive test from verifiable delay functions tracks scalar pressure. Tensor-core matrix measurements reflect dense linear-algebra throughput. A memory-residency test separates on-chip from off-chip access. Trials under contention and memory pressure show timing shifts and residency latencies revealing real usage. The authors offer it as a complement to future accountability mechanisms, not a replacement for trusted hardware.
arxiv-2602-09569:
Deep physics neural networks exploit analog moves for lean, very fast AI, but training them across varied hardware has lacked a general method. Hao Wang and ten co-authors present the Physics Information Choke Point in their 2026 paper, a general design joining information theory with local learning. Matrix-based choke points given to each unit let deep physics networks learn under any physics moves.

The design supports guided, free, and reward-based learning across memory-chip chips and optical compute platforms. It adapts to severe hardware faults and allows side-by-side training over far-flung gear. By skipping extra digital models and contrast measures, the method recasts physics network training as a built-in, scalable theory process fitting varied physics bases.
arxiv-2602-10069:
Human factors research has tuned rooms, tools, and systems for people, but humanoid robots now share those same spaces. A 2026 paper led by Xinyuan Liu, with three co-authors, offers humanoid factors, a framework for building robots that live and work alongside humans. Four pillars organize it: physical, cognitive, social, and ethical.

The framework maps where human and humanoid powers overlap and where they part ways, since humanoids raise hopes of human-like behavior, talk, and social presence. Tried on a real humanoid control algorithm, it shows how task scores overlook thinking and interaction rules. The authors offer humanoid factors as a base for designing, evaluating, and governing long-term coexistence.
arxiv-2602-10369:
Earth's long-term climate is steered by three dominant feedbacks among more than a dozen, yet habitable-zone models simply assume other Earth-like planets behave the same way. A 2026 paper led by Chaucer Langbert, with one co-author, tests that assumption with dynamical simulations of Earth-like planets carrying an extra, potentially strong, generalized feedback. Across more than twenty thousand runs, the extra feedback produced new behavior, including runaway and chaotic climate paths, more varied than Earth's setup would suggest.

Meaningful negative extra feedbacks would not lower the odds of temperate climates, the authors find. Positive ones shrink the share of exo-Earth candidates staying habitable over the long term. Strong extra feedbacks therefore shift, and mostly narrow, the classical habitable zone. Combined with how often Earth-sized planets orbit sun-like stars, the results imply fewer stars hosting rocky planets with temperate climates than simpler models assume.
arxiv-2602-10569:
Jacob A. Barandes reinterprets pilot-wave quantum theory in a 2026 paper. The first de Broglie-Bohm theory treated the pilot wave as part of nature's real furniture. More recent versions demote it to an aspect of the dynamical laws. Barandes argues both readings are wrong.

The pilot wave, he proposes, is best understood as a set of latent factors in the sense of a hidden Markov model. That construct was unavailable to the theory's founders. The paper also presses other hurdles for the ontological view, including gauge transformations that connect other models of the same physics. The reinterpretation reframes a decades-old debate about what, if anything, the pilot wave is.
arxiv-2602-10669:
Bo Hou and Ru Li present new algebra structures linking two kinds of bialgebras in a 2026 paper. They define quasi-triangular and factorizable dual pre-Poisson bialgebras. A factorizable example induces a factorization of its hidden algebra, and the double of any such bialgebra is factorizable.

The paper then connects these structures to quadratic Rota-Baxter dual pre-Poisson algebras. It proves a one-to-one correspondence between factorizable dual pre-Poisson bialgebras and quadratic Rota-Baxter Poisson algebras of nonzero weight. A construction builds endless-sized examples from finite-sized Poisson bialgebras. The work extends the dictionary between Poisson shape and pre-Poisson algebra, giving teams new bridges between older and deformed structures.
arxiv-2602-10769:
Chun-Hui Wang studies Siegel modular forms arising from Weil models in a 2026 paper. The focus is stated modular forms of half-integral weights. They include classic, minus, and fermionic theta series, arising from the classic Weil model through several authors' cocycle constructions.

Wang reorganizes these forms using tensor induction, clarifying their structure and links. The study then extends to the similitude group, broadening the classic picture. The paper serves specialists in automorphic forms. It gives stated constructions where abstract theory often leaves examples implicit, and connects theta series to model theory through concrete math.
arxiv-2602-10969:
Missing data can hide the very pattern a study wants to find. Anna Guo and Razieh Nabi offer a way to tell, before analysis, whether the full data pattern can be recovered at all. They treat missingness marks as things one could intervene on, in a graph model of how data goes missing.

Their tree method tracks how each step of move creates or spreads selection bias, and finds paths that avoid it. The tree both diagnoses the problem and builds the recovery when one exists. Matching weighting steps then turn the same logic into working values for the missingness process and for traits of the full data. Tests on simulated and real data, plus a software package called flexMissing, show the method in use.
arxiv-2602-11169:
In a model, a vector's direction and its length may do other jobs. Mangadoddi Srikar Vardhan and Lekkala Sai Teja test that idea in Pythia models with matched perturbations. Angle changes damage language-model loss far more, while length changes damage syntax far more.

Causal repairs trace angle damage mainly through focus pathways and length damage partly through LayerNorm pathways. The pattern repeats across model scales in the Pythia family, but differs in RMSNorm-based designs. Direction thus seems tied to attentional routing, while magnitude tunes processing strength for fine syntactic judgements. The findings refine the straight form idea for model editing and clarity.
arxiv-2602-11369:
Directed percolation is a paradigm for spreading with a preferred direction. Michal Hnatič and three co-authors apply field-theoretic renormalization group methods to its equation of state, pushing perturbation theory to three-loop order. Many required diagrams map onto current three-loop results.

A new technique handles the remaining, genuinely novel diagrams, and the semi-analytic procedure also verifies current two-loop results. Full three-loop calculations are still in progress, so the paper is an update on ongoing work rather than a final answer. It gives the community a checked procedure and a status report for scaling functions in directed percolation.
arxiv-2602-11469:
Defects in Josephson junctions limit superconducting quantum processors, yet their microscopic origins were elusive. Oliver F. Wolff and ten co-authors trace strongly coupled two-level systems with a high-throughput correlative approach, assembling thousands of junctions and hundreds of atomic-detail microscopy images. Fabrication, microstructure, and defect occurrence are linked statistically.

Electrode thickness and grain size correlate strongly with defect density. Changing electrode fabrication settings cuts defect density by about two-thirds. The work shows a data-driven method to understand and control defects in quantum circuits, paving the way for far fewer defects in scalable processors. Structure, not just materials choice, emerges as a lever for qubit quality.
arxiv-2602-11869:
High-dimensional quantum systems resist decoherence better than small ones, but standard teleportation grows costly: the work needed to measure rises quadratically and classical messaging overhead climbs with size. Long Huang and three co-authors propose a lean protocol for teleporting quantum coherence in large systems. By designing sets of specialized bases, one per size value, the method halves classical messaging and scales the work linearly rather than quadratically.

Initial phase tuning aligns the target qudit with the chosen basis, enabling theoretically perfect transfer for arbitrary qudit states. Stress tests show efficiency stays above 99 percent even under a tenth of a radian phase shift at size sixteen. Under varied noise models the quantum advantage window widens as size grows, and under one noise type perfect transfer can even be restored by optimal basis choice. The result is a practical, hardware-friendly framework for high-dimensional quantum networks.
arxiv-2602-12069:
Ultracold polar molecules promise rich quantum physics, but crashes often destroy them before they can be studied. Gohar Hovhannesyan and six co-authors theoretically investigate shielding those crashes with two lasers driving a Raman resonant transition on individual molecules, using bosonic NaK pairs as the example. Tuning laser settings and powers creates a pushing long-range interaction potential between pairs.

Solving coupled Schrödinger equations in laser-dressed states, the authors identify quasi-matching conditions where elastic crashes beat lossy and hostile ones by a factor of about two. That margin demonstrates a promising pathway for efficient two-photon optical shielding. Bounce lengths of the dressed pairs show prominent peaks tied to entrance-channel interactions with other channels, consistent with a quasi-bound level of the laser-induced long-range molecular pair.
arxiv-2602-12169:
Graph theory asks how many ways a graph can pick sets of nodes with no edges between them, and algebra asks about a related polynomial for edge ideals. Ton That Quoc Tan works alone here, linking the degree of that h-polynomial to the size of the largest such independent set. The bridge is the independence polynomial, judged at minus one and through its slopes there.

From that link, the paper gives an exact test for when the degree equals the independence number. It then turns the test into plain formulas for paths, cycles, bipartite graphs, Cameron-Walker graphs, and antiregular graphs. Readers get a clean case where a counting tool from graphs settles an algebraic degree question.
arxiv-2602-12269:
Quantum devices need proof they did what was claimed, and for light-based devices that proof is subtle. Riko Schadow led this work with eight co-authors, certifying that linear optical interferometers produce desired multi-photon states. Such states feed metrology, communication, quantum advantage tests, and linear optical computing, and their power rests on photon indistinguishability.

Standard fidelity witnesses for distinct particles fail here, because they only certify closeness to one fixed target. The team defines a fidelity measure suited to indistinguishable photons and gives several ways to witness it, drawing on earlier multi-photon indistinguishability tests. A witness based on the discrete Fourier transform proves optimal, and the team implements it in the lab to certify several multi-photon states.
arxiv-2602-12769:
Diffusion models make beautiful images but are stuck near the resolution they were trained on, and training-free tricks for 4K output often take over five minutes per image. Hong-Phuc Lai, Phong Nguyen, and Anh Tran present PixelRush, a tuning-free method for fast high-resolution text-to-image generation. It builds on patch-based inference but drops the repeated inversion and regeneration cycles that slow earlier methods down.

Two fixes handle the side effects of few-step patch work: a seamless blending strategy for patch edges, and noise injection to fight over-smoothing. The payoff is large: 4K images in about 20 seconds, a ten- to thirty-five-fold speedup over leading methods, with visual quality held up in tests. For practical high-resolution generation, speed at this scale changes what the method can be used for.
arxiv-2602-12869:
Wake vortices trailing aircraft are a safety and capacity headache for air traffic control, yet tracking them from LiDAR is hard. Scans are sparse, vortex signals fade as turbulence breaks the flow apart, and labelling every point is far too costly. Zhan Qu and Michael Färber introduce X-VORTEX, a learning framework that builds physics-aware representations from unlabelled LiDAR sequences instead of treating each scan as a separate supervised task.

The method pairs a lightly perturbed sequence with a strongly augmented twin, made by dropping frames and masking space, so the model learns to align views across gaps. A geometric encoder reads each scan, and a sequential module tracks the evolving vortex state. On over one million real LiDAR scans, the system localised vortex centres better than supervised baselines while using only 1% of their labelled data, and it supports trajectory forecasting.
arxiv-2602-13169:
