Finite-state mean-field games model large populations of interacting agents through a coupled forward-backward system: a Kolmogorov-Fokker-Planck formula for the population and a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman formula for values. Solving each system is costly, and each depends on the initial spread and terminal cost. William Hofgard and two co-authors propose operator learning for whole parametric groups, generalising to new distributions and costs without retraining.

Theory guarantees cover approximation error, parametric complexity, and generalisation, resting on a new regularity result for the flow map of a mean-field game system. Empirically, the system approximates accurately on two representative cases: a cybersecurity setting and a high-D quadratic benchmark common in mean-field game numerics. For practitioners, the payoff is a solver that learns the family once and answers new instances fast.
arxiv-2602-13269:
In internet-of-things networks, data arrives in many forms, from video to sensor readings, and stale data can stall tasks or mislead choices in time-critical services. Old freshness measures treat all data alike, missing what makes each form distinct. This paper proposes Modality-Tailored Age of Information, a single measure that blends the age of an update with how much its content matters for each modality.

The authors derive a closed form for its average, then pose a problem of choosing sampling gaps and offload choices under energy limits. Their joint sampling and offloading method cuts the average score well below rival methods in simulations for edge computing systems. Ying Liu leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13769:
Automating heuristic design in lab-driven domains needs more than step-by-step mutation of solution algorithms. Current language-model evolution methods rely on random mutation loops without long-term planning or learning from past failures, causing inefficient search and redundant trials. OR-Agent organizes heuristic search as a tree-based workflow modeling branching hypothesis generation and steady backtracking, within a multi-agent research framework for tuning problems with rich lab environments.

A layered, tuning-inspired review system adds adaptive learning: short-term reviews act as verbal gradients, long-term reviews as verbal momentum, and memory compression as semantic weight decay, together steering research work. Experiments on classic combo problems such as traveling salesman, vehicle routing, and bin packing, plus simulated team driving, show OR-Agent beating strong evolution search rivals. Qi Liu leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13869:
Josiah Dykstra and one co-author ask in a 2026 arXiv paper whether cyber defense can borrow the playbook of public health. Since 1900, systematic data gathering, proven interventions, and coordinated response lifted U.S. life expectancy by over 30 years. Cyber defense, by contrast, still lacks shared measures and coordinated testing.

Both fields, they argue, are public goods: one firm's security helps others, so markets underinvest in it. The paper proposes a national Cyber Public Health System for standard data, outcome measures, and joint response. It assigns government a necessary role in setting standards, funding research, coordinating response, and fixing information gaps that markets alone cannot close.
arxiv-2602-14169:
Yiran Guo and seven co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv problem in training language models with reinforcement learning. Good exploration means finding rare correct paths within a tight sampling budget, but standard GRPO samples only from the root, saturating likely paths. Tree methods spread budget too thin across trivial or hopeless states.

Their strategy, Deep Dense Exploration, focuses on pivots: deep, recoverable states inside failed trajectories. The DEEP-GRPO version picks pivots with a data-driven utility that balances recoverability and depth, resamples densely at each pivot, and adds a dual-stream design. The aim is to surface rare correct suffixes without destabilizing local baselines, a common failure of dispersed sampling.
arxiv-2602-14569:
Vladimir N. Potapov and one co-author offers a 2026 arXiv method for combo designs tied to bent functions. Folding on finite abelian groups is read as times by a multi-size matrix, while designs turn into perfect paints of subspace hyper-graphs of binary vector spaces. A match links eigen-modes of folding matrices to perfect paints of subspace hyper-graphs.

Perfect paints allow a mark in terms of folding, and two-valued eigen-modes match perfect paints. Uses show partial difference sets, bent and plateaued Boolean functions, spreads, and strong bent splits of binary spaces as eigen-modes and perfect paints alike. The paper also finds some eigen-values of folding matrices over binary and ternary fields, tying algebra, counting, and design views together.
arxiv-2602-14869:
Matthew Kowal and others fix a hard task in model craft: giving credit for what a big language model does, most of all when it acts in ways no one sought. Old credit tools cost much and lean on lone test cases, which tilt credit toward like wording more than like sense.

Concept credit instead traces acts to sense lines in the model, such as line probes or sparse auto-code marks found while the model runs. That shift lifts both speed and truth of credit, the team reports. Model craft thus gains a cheap, sense-first way to ask: whose training made it act this way?
arxiv-2602-15169:
Moynihan shows that machine learning can on its own rebuild flagship analytic patterns in scattering amplitudes from numerical on-shell data. Using symbolic regression on colour-ordered Yang-Mills data with Mandelstam invariants as inputs, he rediscovers the Kawai-Lewellen-Tye relations. Column-pivoted QR factorisation for feature selection at once recovers the Kleiss-Kuijf and Bern-Carrasco-Johansson rules, finding a minimal basis of partial pieces with no group theory input.

Tree-level KLT rules are found with high accuracy up to five external legs, using only minimal theory priors. He notes obstacles to lifting the method to higher multiplicity. The results establish that method as a handy tool for exploring hidden structure in that landscape and suggest a general data-driven strategy for uncovering hidden rules in other fields. A recent neural-network method serves as a benchmark for contrast.
arxiv-2602-15269:
Andam and Doulabi study pooling recovery beds across fields in random surgery room plans. Uncertainty comes mainly from surgery times and lengths of stay. They develop a two-stage random coding model. Stage one sets non-shared ICU and ward beds per field and assigns surgeries to surgery rooms.

Stage two sets shared ICU and ward beds per field each day, plus surge room and extra hours. The model cuts total cost: waiting, delays, extra hours, fixed surgery room, and surge room costs. They run it in a sample-average method, with a custom routine that quickly solves stage two for any stage-one solution. Tests evaluate pooling rules and the routine's speed, plus cost and setting response. Full sharing among fields in recovery units lifts how the system works by about 19 and a half percent. Random solutions beat fixed ones by about 17 and a half percent on the whole.
arxiv-2602-15669:
Feng and colleagues give large language models steerable personalities without retraining. Current control leans on fixed prompts or costly fine-tuning, missing the dynamic, combinable nature of human traits. Their PERSONA frame works training-free by manipulating personality vectors in activation space, on the insight that traits appear as extractable, near-orthogonal directions that support algebra.

Three stages organise the method. Persona-Base extracts orthogonal trait vectors by contrastive activation analysis. Persona-Algebra controls traits by vector arithmetic: scaling sets intensity, adding composes traits, and subtracting suppresses them. Persona-Flow composes vectors on the fly during inference for context-aware adaptation. On PersonalityBench the method scores 9.60 on average, near the fine-tuning ceiling of 9.61 with no gradient updates, and on the new Persona-Evolve benchmark it wins up to 91 percent of comparisons across model families.
arxiv-2602-15769:
Alqurnawi and colleagues test whether multimodal large language models can show their work on tables. Such models answer questions on tables in Markdown, JSON, and image form, but users also need to know where answers come from. The paper studies structured data attribution, the ability to point to specific rows and columns supporting an answer, evaluating several models across table formats and prompting strategies.

Results reveal a clear gap between answering and attributing. Question answering accuracy stays moderate, but attribution accuracy runs much lower, near random for JSON inputs across all models. Models cite rows more reliably than columns and struggle more with textual formats than images, with notable differences across model families. Overall, current models prove unreliable at fine-grained, trustworthy attribution for structured data, limiting their use where transparency and traceability matter.
arxiv-2602-15969:
Ferro studies what happens to fragile symmetry breaking states in one dimensional quantum systems when interactions enter the picture. Adding energy above the ground state is expected to restore a broken symmetry, and local nudges can then produce large scale correlation patterns, a loss of clustering, and even macroscopic superpositions.

He works with an interacting model whose domain wall number is conserved and whose ferromagnetic ground state breaks a two fold symmetry. A local quench amplifies quantum interference into a broad magnetization profile that mirrors the scattering phase. Two asymmetry measures then confirm macroscopic quantum coherence across the whole perturbed region, and a new inequality links them for mixed states, extending a result previously known only for pure states.
arxiv-2602-16069:
Ravi Raju leads a team of five researchers testing whether large language models can truly reason over very long code contexts when fixing bugs. Longer context windows have fed an assumption that models can work across whole codebases, and agentic workflows already score well on software benchmarks. Using SWE-bench Verified with an agentic harness, the team finds strong results, yet successful runs typically stay under thirty thousand tokens, with longer contexts linked to lower success.

To test long context directly, they inflate input length while keeping retrieval perfect, then ask for single-shot patches at sixty-four thousand tokens. Performance falls sharply, with one open model solving only a small share and another solving none. Failures include invented diffs, wrong file targets, and malformed patch headers. The paper argues that nominal context length far exceeds usable capacity, and current benchmarks may not measure long-context reasoning at all.
arxiv-2602-16169:
Yunshu Wu leads a team of seven authors introducing a new framework for non-autoregressive generation of discrete strings. Continuous diffusion is natural for such work but has lagged behind masked discrete models. The authors argue the bottleneck is not continuity itself. It is a code where denoising depends on timestep-indexed noise regimes. Their framework, Discrete Stochastic Localization, uses continuous states with unit-sphere token embeddings. Its Bayes-optimal denoiser stays fixed despite the nominal signal-to-noise ratio.

One trained network then supports a whole family of per-token signal-to-noise routes. Fine-tuning a pretrained masked checkpoint with the new framework greatly improves distributional faithfulness on OpenWebText across step budgets. The same checkpoint supports random-order autoregressive sampling. It also supports a hybrid continuous-then-discrete sampler using very few total steps, all without distillation or retraining.
arxiv-2602-16269:
Shun'ya Mizoguchi and Takumi Oikawa study error correcting codes that construct Narain lattices of heterotic strings as code lattices. In both E8 by E8 and Spin(32) over Z2 heterotic strings, they identify a binary code plus a set of metric, B field, and background gauge field. The lattice built from the binary code by Construction A coincides with the Narain lattice. They also construct heterotic Narain lattices using codes over finite fields of three and five elements by two further Construction A variants.

As a by-product, they clarify the relationship between codes that construct Euclidean even self-dual lattices and NSR fermions. The paper thus bridges coding theory and string theory, showing how discrete code data plus background fields can reproduce the continuous lattices that heterotic strings require. For readers in either field, it gives explicit constructions and a clarified link between code lattices and fermionic structures.
arxiv-2602-16469:
Jenny Kunz, writing alone, studies how translationese dialects shape language model learning. Translated data is widely used in multilingual processing, especially where native text is scarce. Such text differs systematically from native text, a phenomenon called translationese, reflecting traces of the source language and characteristic traits of translation itself.

Kunz examines how training on translated data affects small English models, focusing on how translationese from different sources shapes linguistic acceptability judgments across domains. Models are trained on English text from twenty-four typologically and resource-diverse source languages, allowing analysis of how source language and corpus properties influence what models learn. Results show the source language clearly affects model behavior. General perplexity follows the lexical diversity of that corpus more strongly, while grammatical scores track typological similarity to English closely when training data is available. Even translation quality predicts language modeling results.
arxiv-2602-16569:
Nicolò Di Domenico and co-authors propose Arc2Morph, a face morphing technique built on Arc2Face. Arc2Face is an identity-conditioned model that renders photorealistic faces from compact identity codes. Morphing attacks threaten passport enrollment where the photo is supplied without supervised live capture. A morphed image can blend two people and fool recognition systems. The new method aims to preserve identity information through the morph.

Tests use two large sequestered attack-detection datasets. Two new morphed sets derived from FEI and ONOT data are used too. The method's attack potential matches that of landmark-based techniques. Those have long been seen as the hardest to beat. Biometric researchers get a strong new attack to defend against. They also get fresh evidence that deep morphs now rival classic ones.
arxiv-2602-16769:
Cory Padgett and Jeffrey Fung ask how eccentric planet-perturbed protoplanetary disks truly become. Disks can turn eccentric when planets carve deep gaps, and the paper answers the question with two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of planet-disk interaction. Steady outer-disk eccentricity emerges as a balance between excitation by a key eccentric resonance and damping by gas pressure.

A scaling law ties eccentricity to planet-to-star mass ratio, disk aspect ratio, gap edge position, and the power-law slopes of surface density and temperature. A semi-analytic eccentricity profile derived from that balance matches simulations within thirty percent. The result offers a first quantitative tool for reading observed eccentric disks such as MWC 758, HD 142527, IRS 48, and CI Tau.
arxiv-2602-16869:
Jéferson Fortunato, Surajit Kalita, and Amanda Weltman test the Etherington cosmic distance-duality law with localized fast radio bursts. No cosmological model is assumed. Type Ia supernova luminosity distances from the Pantheon+ set are set beside angular-diameter distances rebuilt from localized bursts. The core method is a data-driven rebuild using artificial neural networks.

A smooth mean extragalactic dispersion-measure curve is inferred. Its redshift derivative recovers the expansion rate and hence angular-diameter distance. No parametric form for expansion history is assumed. Deviations from duality are tested through three one-parameter models, with two complementary likelihoods. Anchoring the mean dispersion measure at zero redshift yields a data-driven constraint on the average host share. Results test whether the standard duality law holds.
arxiv-2602-16969:
Laasya Koduru and co-authors present BQT+, a robust and flexible frame for gauging broadband plans. Independent, street address-level broadband data is essential for judging internet network spending, such as the large Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program. Evaluating that spending requires long-run visibility into availability, quality, and cost, including pre-disbursement baselines and changes in firms' advertised plans.

Existing systems fail to meet all three. The gap is clear. BQT+ replaces monolithic workflows with declarative state-action specs. Querying intent is modeled as an interaction state space formalized as an abstract nondeterministic finite automaton. Execution paths are selected at runtime to accommodate alternative flows and localized interface changes. BQT+ sustains long-run monitoring of dozens of firms, supporting querying for over one hundred firms.
arxiv-2602-17269:
Dezheng Meng led a large team on a single transitional type Ia supernova, SN 2024aedt, caught by the Wide Field Survey Telescope within a day of explosion. Its light curve places it in the transition zone between normal and subluminous type Ia supernovae on the standard decline-rate versus peak-brightness diagram. Early color evolution and host galaxy environment confirm the transitional character, sharing traits with both normal and 91bg-like events.

Light-curve modeling yields a synthesized nickel mass and a total ejecta mass, and comparison with theory suggests both delayed-detonation and double-detonation scenarios can broadly explain the evolution. Possible early-excess emission from double detonation could not be confirmed given sparse detections right after explosion. Spectra match other transitional events overall, but early blue-end features vary more, converging later, underscoring the value of early observations.
arxiv-2602-17569:
Raphaël Menu and a coauthor wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on noise, entanglement, and simulation in the Grover algorithm. The qubits face single-qubit amplitude-damping or phase-flip noise. The authors set quantum trajectories against full density-matrix simulations, tracking trajectory entanglement and operator entanglement in each representation. Neither is a genuine entanglement measure, but both govern how well matrix product state simulations run.

As in many quantum algorithms, entanglement falls near the end of the Grover circuit as the system nears its target product state. Operator entanglement captures that fall well, while quantum trajectories rarely follow suit. Tuned schemes lower trajectory entanglement slightly, but deep in the circuit operator entanglement runs smaller. That implies matrix product density operator runs can beat quantum trajectories. The paper also studies success probability scaling with noise rate under both noise types.
arxiv-2602-17869:
Yuxiao Chen and team introduce a compact video code schema for lean long-form video understanding in large multimodal models. Long-form videos spanning tens of minutes are now feasible to analyze. Yet video repeat-heavy nature challenges current models in two ways: fitting more frames within memory limits, and extracting telling information from vast input volumes.

The proposed end-to-end schema pairs an information-density-based tuning video sampler with an autoencoder-based space-time video squeezer, joined with a multi-input large language model. It tunes captures of essential information from clips of varying lengths and achieves high compression rates while keeping crucial telling information. Tests show good scores across benchmarks, shining in both long-form and standard video understanding tasks. The approach proves versatile and effective for long clips, where redundancy otherwise overwhelms models.
arxiv-2602-18069:
F Matković and colleagues model sunspot brightness temperature from three tenths to ten millimeters with ALMA single-dish measurements. They start from the one-dimensional semi-empirical ATLCW sunspot model. The original model takes a constant density and temperature factor over all heights, and a least-square fit in both quantities yields an improved model.

Sunspots look darker than the quiet Sun below two millimeters and brighter beyond, while the ATLCW fit implies darker values throughout. Best-fitted profiles put sunspot density three point six to four times below the original model, or one point four to one point eight times the quiet Sun density. Temperature runs about one point two times higher than original ATLCW predictions, or one point two times lower than quiet Sun temperature. Even with improved parameters, the remaining model-observation gap shows the ATLCW model and its assumptions still need further improvement.
arxiv-2602-18169:
Juan Carlos Acosta Matos and two co-authors model a Rydberg electron circling a tiny liquid droplet. Their 2026 paper builds a self-consistent potential for an electron whose ionic core is a polarizable medium, as realized in superfluid droplets. The electron's motion still splits cleanly in spherical coordinates, but the droplet's pull breaks the usual tie between angular momentum states.

The resulting spectrum shifts with droplet size and electron excitation in striking ways. Small departures from a smooth spherical medium can be added as a small correction on top of the new dynamics. The team works through superfluid helium as a model case and suggests probing droplet traits, even a possible frozen fraction, through driven jumps of the Rydberg electron. The paper gives experimenters a concrete handle on droplets too small to see directly.
arxiv-2602-18269:
Arthur Rotari and one co-author study light from three tiny emitters arranged as a triangle. Their 2026 paper treats three dipole-coupled two-level emitters pinned at the corners of an equilateral triangle, bathed in a thermal environment. The team solves for the populations of the joint three-atom states and for second- and third-order spatial photon correlations.

The incoherently driven system spontaneously emits streams of single photons with sub-Poissonian statistics, quieter than random light. At small spacings one might blame dipole blockade, but the team shows the quantum features instead come from how the symmetric emitters interact with the heat bath. At larger spacings, high-order spatial interference takes over. Sub-wavelength fringe patterns can be read from higher-order correlation measurements.
arxiv-2602-18669:
Finding a virtual object in a busy mixed reality scene is harder than it looks, and practice may help in ways users never notice. Lefan Lai, with three co-authors, reports a 2026 CHI study of visual search in mixed reality, testing how scene clutter, a second task, virtual depth, and layout shape both speed and memory.

A second listening task raised how hard people felt the work was, but did not by itself slow their searching. Cluttered scenes and varied depths did slow search, though not felt effort. Most striking, people searched repeated layouts faster even though they said they had not spotted the repeats, a sign of silent memory for spatial regularity.
arxiv-2602-18769:
Finding which genes drive which diseases still leans heavily on manual curation, which cannot scale to today's biomedical data. Osman Onur Kuzucu, with one co-author, presents GLaDiGAtor in 2026, a graph learning framework that predicts disease-gene associations from a heterogeneous biological graph.

The graph joins gene-gene, disease-disease, and gene-disease links from curated databases, and each node is enriched with language-model features, ProtT5 for protein sequences and BioBERT for disease text. An encoder-decoder graph network then learns from that enriched structure. It outperforms fourteen existing methods, and literature-backed case studies support its high-confidence new predictions, pointing toward candidate disease genes that could aid drug discovery.
arxiv-2602-18969: Paweł Borówka, with one co-author, characterises the moduli space of étale Klein coverings of hyperelliptic curves of genus 3 in 2026. An étale Klein covering is Galois with deck group of order four, built from two independent twofold symmetries. The work proves the Prym map is injective on each component. As an application, the Prym map for étale Klein coverings of genus-three curves is shown to be generically finite.
arxiv-2602-19069:
Hard reasoning tasks may need stepping stones first. Hengyuan Hu, with five co-authors, studies that idea in 2026. A stepping stone is a simplification, a reframe, or a subproblem. It prepares a model to solve a task it cannot crack in one shot. Modern reasoning models still get little help building such stones.

The authors introduce ARQ, a frame adding a question generator to the reasoning pipeline. Good stepping-stone questions exist and transfer across models. They substantially help models of varied capability on target tasks. Stepping-stone generation is then treated as a post-training task. Fine-tuning by supervised learning and reinforcement learning on synthetic data yields more useful questions. Asking the right questions thus becomes a trainable skill, not just a prompting trick.
arxiv-2602-19169:
Frozen transformers can still adapt at test time. Saba Kublashvili, writing alone in 2026, introduces Virtual Parameter Sharpening, a test-time technique. It augments frozen linear layers with dynamic, signal-based low-rank perturbations. Unlike LoRA modules, which stay static after training, these perturbations form on the fly from batch signal numbers and optional gradient signals. No persistent weight updates are needed.

Selector matrices arise from sparse signal-guided selection or Sylvester-coupled fitting. Eigen properties are analysed in theory. An adaptive policy modulates shift size from signal energy and token-level entropy. Multi-objective checks with stepwise refinement serve labelled tasks. The full algorithmic frame, its mathematical foundations, and its thought mechanisms are presented. Signal-based computation thus offers a new lever on model thought.
arxiv-2602-19369:
Susovan Pal constructs a closed hyperbolic covering surface whose nth eigenvalue is smaller than any prescribed positive number. Given any small positive epsilon, any natural number n, and any closed hyperbolic surface M, the paper builds a covering surface with that property. The construction answers a natural question about how small a prescribed eigenvalue can be made while keeping the surface closed and hyperbolic.

The main result follows techniques from a 1974 paper by B. Randol, but the author gives a new and geometric proof. An application of the result is also discussed. Readers get a concise construction in spectral geometry, with a proof that favors geometric intuition over the original route.
arxiv-2602-19469:
Robert Griffiths and Shuhei Mano construct Gaussian fields on a discrete torus-like grid from reversible long-range random walks. The covariance function comes from the Green function of a walk with killing at each transition, a construction drawn from an earlier paper. A decomposition then splits the field into a sum of independent Gaussian variables, making its structure tractable.

Letting the grid parameter grow without bound turns the field into one defined from an infinite-dimensional walk on a torus. The walk model also extends to infinite dimensions through a de Finetti random walk with exchangeable increments. A limit field on Euclidean space arises by a central limit theorem approach, and its transform, again a Gaussian field, has a covariance matrix simpler than the original's.
arxiv-2602-19969:
Attention-based re-ranking scores documents from attention weights, offering an efficient, readable alternative to text-generating ranking. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yuxing Tian and four co-authors shows two flaws in that approach and proposes a fix called ReAttn.

First, attention concentrates on a few tokens in a few documents, leaving others hard to tell apart. Second, attention overweights phrases that merely resemble the query, so word-level lookalikes that are irrelevant rank too highly. ReAttn first weights attention by cross-document inverse frequency, lowering the weight on query-overlapping tokens that recur across candidates and easing word-level bias. It then applies entropy-based smoothing to spread attention more evenly across informative tokens. Both adjustments act on existing weights with no extra training, and experiments confirm the method works.
arxiv-2602-20369:
Giorgio Del Castello introduces LANTERN, an optical calibration system for low-threshold cryogenic detectors. Such devices, including cryogenic calorimeters, have advanced rare-event searches for dark matter and neutrinos. Their region of interest runs from tens to about a thousand electronvolts. Standard radioactive sources overshoot that range and can saturate or distort signals. A source present during runs can spoil a low-background measurement.

LANTERN instead uses the photostatistics of monochromatic UV-Vis photons from LEDs absorbed in the device, reading the response curve without knowing the total energy deposited. A fast-switching LED matrix, faster than device response, can characterize sixty-four units independently. Validation included calibrating a BULLKID-DM detector to about two percent energy-reconstruction error, and checking a CALDER thin device against a commercial LED driver, with matching results. The system thus offers a practical route for segmented units.
arxiv-2602-20469:
The numerical range of a non-normal matrix captures non-normal effects that spectra alone miss. Sung-Soo Byun and Joo Young Park study non-Hermitian random matrix ensembles that interpolate between Hermitian and non-Hermitian regimes, focusing on the elliptic Ginibre ensemble, its chiral counterpart, and non-Hermitian Wishart matrices. For each model they characterize the geometry of the numerical range in the large-system limit.

For the elliptic Ginibre ensemble and its chiral version, the limiting numerical range is an ellipse, while for the non-Hermitian Wishart ensemble it follows a non-elliptic envelope. The authors also determine the range for products of n independent elliptic Ginibre matrices. At n equals one this recovers the elliptic Ginibre result, and at n equals two the Wishart result at maximal non-Hermiticity.
arxiv-2602-20769:
Gianmarco Del Sarto and three co-authors build a general method for data assimilation, the task of steering a model with partial observations toward the true state. They work with semilinear parabolic equations, a broad class that covers heat-like flows, and use a nudged model that is gently pushed by the observed data.

Under natural assumptions they prove both the true system and the nudged system are well posed. The nudged solution then closes in on the true one at an exponential rate, when the data are fine enough and the nudge is tuned right. The same method covers the Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, Sellers energy-balance, and bidomain systems for the first time.
arxiv-2602-21069:
Top quarks made at the Large Hadron Collider carry spin facts that quantum coherence can sum up. Saeed Haddadi, Majid Azizi, Artur Czerwinski, and Hamid Arian Zad probe that trait in this 2026 arXiv paper, applying a standard coherence gauge to rebuilt spin grids. They join Standard Model calls with recent CMS readings of spin-link numbers.

Coherence runs large near the making threshold and in boosted central events, while a middle-mass zone shows weaker overlap and more touchy response to radiation effects. That uneven pattern traces to how helicity overlap shapes the making process. Recast CMS values broadly match Standard Model calls, setting up coherence as a within-reach probe of top-quark spin motion.
arxiv-2602-21469:
Meet Hemant Parikh and two co-authors propose D-Flow SGLD, a source-space method for scientific inverse problems under flow-matching priors. Such problems rebuild large physical states from sparse, noisy observations. Ideally, samples of likely states stay true to learned priors and governing physics. Methods that condition diffusion models are mature, but flow-matching versions lag, above all on science benchmarks.

The authors sort strategies by where new data enters. One family uses guided transport dynamics. The other infers the source distribution. Building on the latter, D-Flow SGLD adds SGLD steps to smooth source inference. It explores likely source states for new setups without retraining the prior or changing learned motion. Tests span toy cases, chaotic wave paths, and wall-bounded turbulent flow rebuilding, where it proves a practical sampler.
arxiv-2602-21669:
Duc Trung Vu and five co-authors introduce DWA-KD, dual-space weighting and time-warped alignment for cross-tokenizer distillation. Knowledge distillation compresses large language models, but cross-tokenizer methods stay limited by weak sequence and vocabulary alignment.

DWA-KD enhances token distillation through dual-space entropy-based weighting and achieves precise sequence-level alignment using lexical and semantic data. At token level, DWA-KD maps teacher representations into student space and vice versa, performing dual-space distillation via KL. Dual-space weights favor tokens where the student is unsure and the teacher is confident, focusing learning on informative tokens. At sequence level, DWA-KD applies Soft-DTW to embedding and hidden-state layers, enabling robust alignment of lexical and contextual semantics between teacher and student. Tests across NLP benchmarks show DWA-KD beating baselines, with ablations confirming complementary roles of entropy-based token weighting and Soft-DTW alignment.
arxiv-2602-22269:
Federated learning trains models jointly without sharing raw data, but the shared updates themselves can leak or be poisoned. Arnab Nath and Harsh Kasyap examine quantum secure aggregation, which hides client updates in the global phase of entangled states. Existing protocols rely on one giant entangled state shared by all clients, and that design has two fatal weaknesses.

Large entangled states lose fidelity fast as clients multiply, and global aggregation cannot spot Byzantine clients misbehaving. The authors propose Clustered Quantum Secure Aggregation, a modular framework that reconciles those physical constraints with the need to catch bad actors. Federated systems gain a quantum aggregation design that scales and polices itself.
arxiv-2602-22569:
Chao Yang and 23 co-authors map the flaws of the Wide Field Survey Telescope, a wide-field survey instrument whose star positions must be exact. Using Zernike polynomials, the team built a global distortion model from gaps between WFST r-band star positions and the Gaia DR3 catalog, with a typical error below 10 milliarcseconds for single shots.

The pattern shows coma, an optical flaw built into the design, dominating the distortion, while fast changes likely come from the corrector that fixes air dispersion. Across 82 shots from one night, the telescope's detectors held steady within 0.1 pixel in shift and 1.8 arcseconds in rotation. The corrected WFST sky positions now sit on the Gaia DR3 frame, with fine tuning promised in later work.
arxiv-2602-22769:
Yujie Zhao and eleven co-authors test whether AI agents remember across long tasks. Agent memory is not chat history: it is a stream of states, actions, observations, and tool outputs over extended interaction. Existing benchmarks, mostly dialogue-based, miss that reality.

AMA-Bench fills the gap with real agent trajectories plus expert-written questions, and synthetic trajectories that stretch to any length with rule-based questions. Current memory systems lag because they miss causal and goal information and lean on lossy similarity retrieval. The team's AMA-Agent, built on causality graphs plus tool-augmented retrieval, scored about fifty-seven percent, beating the strongest baseline by about eleven points.
arxiv-2602-23069:
Yiding Sun and six co-authors rethink parameter-efficient transfer learning for 4D perception with Align then Adapt. Point cloud video understanding matters for robotics, but 4D datasets are far scarcer than 3D ones, limiting self-supervised 4D models. Transferring 3D pretrained models to 4D tasks is promising, yet careful analysis reveals two limits: overfitting and the modality gap.

The PointATA paradigm splits transfer into two stages. Optimal-transport theory quantifies the gap between 3D and 4D datasets, letting a point align embedder train in stage one to ease the modality gap. A point-video adapter and spatial-context encoder then join the frozen 3D backbone in stage two for temporal modelling. Results match or beat full fine-tuning models. Accuracy runs about ninety-seven percent on 3D action recognition, with nearly nine points gained on 4D action segmentation and about eighty-four percent on 4D semantic segmentation.
arxiv-2602-23269:
Ashley Babjac and one co-author present HATTER, a human-in-the-loop active learning toolkit for enzyme function guessing. Protein data from nature is growing fast, while lab-checked function data grows slowly, and that mismatch increasingly limits broad function guessing. Active learning, which picks the most telling proteins for lab labeling, offers a lean way forward that remains largely untried for this task.

HATTER mixes several active learning tactics with human-in-the-loop lab labeling to tune function guessing models with less waste. Set against standard training across diverse protein test sets, active learning matches scores while needing fewer model updates, handling less data, and cutting compute cost a lot. The toolkit shows how careful picking of what to label can stretch scarce lab labels much further.
arxiv-2602-23369:
Xuanming Cui and 12 co-authors extend mixed-media retrieval with TTE-v2, a layered design that scales scores through thinking tokens, not model size. Standard systems rely on bi-encoder designs whose scores track vector size. Think-Then-Embed showed that mixed-media thinking before vector-making can elicit extra telling tokens and improve search.

TTE-v2 augments initial mixed-media retrieval with extra thinking steps for re-ranking, for richer query-match links at test time. The re-ranking stage also supplies fine-grained guidance for hard bad-example mining and false-miss weeding, creating a feedback loop that strengthens the upstream searcher. On the MMEB-V2 benchmark, TTE-v2-7B sets a new state-of-the-art score of 75.7 percent, while TTE-v2-2B matches or beats leading 7B models trained with far larger outside data. Token-wise scaling thus emerges as a hopeful other scaling model.
arxiv-2602-23469:
Lixi Zhou and seven co-authors present CactusDB, a database system for queries that mix SQL with AI and ML model inference. Running such queries inside the database avoids reshaping and moving data, eases management, and helps privacy, but no existing system supports all joint-tuning methods at once.

The authors sort those methods into four groups: relational algebra tuning treating models as black-box functions, factorized inference, tensor-relational transformation, and general cross-tuning. CactusDB, built atop Meta's Velox engine, unifies them with a three-level middle-layer format covering relational operators, expression operators, and ML functions. A novel Monte-Carlo tree search planner then explores the large search space for efficient execution plans.
arxiv-2602-23969:
Haoyuan Shi and seven co-authors introduce MSVBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-shot video generation at a human level. The 2026 paper argues that current benchmarks, anchored to single shots, lack the story assets and cross-shot metrics needed to judge long-form coherence and appeal in multi-shot narratives.

MSVBench supplies hierarchical scripts and reference images for multi-shot generation, plus a hybrid evaluation. That evaluation joins high-level semantic reasoning from large multimodal models with fine-grained perceptual checks from expert models. Evaluating many video generation methods, the authors find that current models, despite strong visual fidelity, behave more like visual interpolators than true world models. The benchmark correlates very strongly with human judgments, and fine-tuning on its reasoning traces yields human-aligned performance comparable to leading commercial models.
arxiv-2602-24069:
Ryan DeWolfe presents COVE, an explainable high-dimensional node embedding built from nonlinear dimension reduction and random-walk co-occurrence. The 2026 solo paper removes the usual low-dimension constraint from node embedding. COVE starts high-dimensional, inspired by neural methods that treat co-occurrence on a random walk as similarity. It relates closely to a diffusion process.

When reduced to low dimension with a standard manifold method, COVE slightly improves clustering and link prediction. Extending recent community detection benchmarks, the author finds that a pipeline combining COVE with manifold reduction and density clustering performs similarly to the popular Louvain algorithm. The work offers an interpretable alternative for network analysis. In short, the walk counts stay clear at each step. A reader can see why two nodes land close. That read-out is the point of COVE. That clarity is the whole point.
arxiv-2602-24269:
William C. Tegge and Alex K. Jones propose a DRAM subarray design that enables in-DRAM bit-shifting . The 2026 paper addresses processing-in-memory, where computation inside DRAM helps combat the memory wall. Bit-shifting is a fundamental operation behind shift-and-add multiplication, carry-propagation adders, and Galois field arithmetic used in cryptography and error correction.

Existing in-DRAM shifting needs dedicated shifter circuits beneath sense amplifiers or vertical data layouts that turn shifts into row copies. The new design builds on migration cells previously introduced for row migration in asymmetric subarrays. It repurposes them by adding a row of migration cells at the top and bottom of each subarray to enable bidirectional shifting within any row. The design keeps compatibility with standard DRAM operations, works on horizontally stored data, and avoids extra complex logic. Timing, energy, circuit, and layout evaluations validate the shift operation.
arxiv-2603-00269: Ng, Zhu, Zhang and Reid compare ways to estimate the degrees of freedom in Student's t regression, where heavy tails blunt the pull of outliers. They test frequentist and Bayesian estimators, plus fixed degrees of freedom and Huber-loss robust regression, on synthetic and real data. Estimating the degrees of freedom by adjusted profile log-likelihood gives highly accurate coefficients, matching maximum likelihood with the true value fixed. Their key point: calibrating the degrees of freedom matters as much as choosing the robust distribution itself.
arxiv-2603-00469: Khan gives satellite planners explanations drawn straight from the scheduling optimizer, so every answer traces to the model itself rather than a post hoc story. Rejections cite minimal infeasible subsets, selections cite tight constraints and trade offs, and what if questions get inverse solves. On a test instance the certificates check out perfectly on cited constraints, counterfactual validity, and stability across seeds, while a post hoc baseline misattributes causes and misses joint causes. Scaling tests to two hundred orders and thirty satellites show practical extraction times.
arxiv-2603-00569: Qi and three colleagues build TopoEdge, a framework for generating and repairing network settings at the edge, grounded in topology. Each target shape becomes a router graph embedded by a contrastively trained graph neural network, retrieving a verified reference setup with an executable test driver. Target, reference, and driver feed a retrieval loop where planning, generation, and checking agents iterate repair cycles. The design answers brittle settings under topology change plus strict latency, privacy, and on site limits.
arxiv-2603-00669: He and twelve colleagues build SSKG Hub, an expert guided platform turning sustainability disclosure standards into auditable knowledge graphs. Standards such as GRI, SASB, TCFD, and IFRS S2 are long, terminology dense, and highly cross referential. A language model pipeline identifies standards, chunks text, prompts per standard, parses triples, and stores them with provenance in Neo4j. Draft graphs pass expert review and meta expert adjudication to become Certified graphs, under role based governance from guest reading to admin oversight.
arxiv-2603-00769: Song and three colleagues solve constrained parabolic control problems with an inexact alternating direction method of multipliers. Splitting control limits and rough goals from the main problem leaves a parabolic state equation subproblem whose exact solution costs too much to compute at every iteration. Their inexact plan solves that subproblem roughly, under mild flexible parameter rules proving global convergence at a linear rate. The method stays easy to build with nested loops.
arxiv-2603-01069: Ghanta, Nathwani, and Chaurasiya build SHIELD8-UAV, a sequential 8-bit hardware accelerator for drone sound detection at the edge under tight power limits. Layer-wise execution on one shared datapath plus structured pruning cuts the dense-layer size by three quarters, while a layer-sensitivity scheme spans four numeric precisions. It reaches about 90 percent detection accuracy, runs at under one watt with 116-millisecond latency on an FPGA, and beats parallel designs on logic use.
arxiv-2603-01169: Kim and five colleagues summarize long videos with TripleSumm, which weights sight, text, and sound frame by frame instead of fusing them in a fixed or modality-blind way. Frame-dependent salience matters because each modality's value shifts as a video plays. They also release MoSu, the first large benchmark supplying all three modalities, and TripleSumm leads existing methods by a clear margin on four benchmarks including MoSu.
arxiv-2603-01669:
M. P. Thejitha and S. N. Fathima extend a counting idea in number theory in this 2026 work. Partitions split a whole number into parts, and colored partitions let each part carry one of several colors. A recent function counts such splits where even and odd parts draw from different color sets.

The pair carry that counting function over to overpartitions, a broader class of partitions with extra marking freedom. Their tools, named in the study keywords, are generating functions and congruence checks. Generating functions pack a whole count sequence into one formula that can be studied at once. Congruence checks test when counts share exact divisibility patterns. The extension opens the parity-and-color count to a wider family of partition problems.
arxiv-2603-01869:
Antonio Branco, Luis Gomes, Rodrigo Santos, and colleagues argue that governments can run their own AI public services. Their 2026 work pushes back on the pull of a few global firms that supply most AI services. As AI ties into geopolitics, reliance on outside providers can threaten access and cultural fit.

Through hands-on experiments, the team shows on-premises services can work with modest compute and cost. Smaller language models, run locally, serve citizen-facing support around the clock in their trials. The setup keeps data and control inside the agency, which guards digital and cultural autonomy. Findings suggest general-purpose commercial systems are not the best choice for every public task. Deployment lessons aim to guide national agencies that want sovereign services of their own.
arxiv-2603-02069:
Jihwan Kim, Dogyoon Song, and Chulhee Yun derive scaling laws for a sign-based trainer in this 2026 paper. SignSGD updates each weight by the sign of its gradient, not its size. The team studies it on linear models with random features that decay in a power-law pattern. Both feature strength and target strength fade at set rates in their model.

They write test error as a function of model size, steps, and learning rate. Two effects set signSGD apart: one rescales drift, the other reshapes noise. When noise dominates, the reshaping can make signSGD scale better than plain SGD. Best learning rates yield clean compute-optimal laws for both methods. A common warmup-stable-decay schedule cuts noise further and sharpens the slope.
arxiv-2603-02469:
Theodore Gossett, Zilin Jiang, Adam Teets, and Zoe Wellner classify equiangular line systems in this 2026 mathematics paper. Equiangular lines all meet each other at the same fixed angle. For one specific angle, set by a square root formula, they ask how many lines can fit per dimension. That maximum count is what they determine, for every dimension.

Counts are listed exactly for dimensions two through fourteen. Beyond that, a formula takes over, with a floor of twenty-four lines. The formula grows linearly with dimension, at one and a half lines per step. The authors say this is the first full determination for a nontrivial fixed angle since 1973. That earlier landmark covered a different angle, one third, by Lemmens and Seidel.
arxiv-2603-02569:
Zheyuan Kuang, Weiwei Jiang, Nicholas Koemel, and colleagues present a toolkit for labeling emotion data in this 2026 paper. Emotion recognition needs fine-grained labels grounded in evidence across video, audio, and body signals. Cues shift over time and misalign across modalities, making annotation slow to scale. Their toolkit makes the whole process inspectable and event-centered.

Recordings are aligned and shown on one interactive timeline. Structured signals render as video tracks for cross-modal consistency checks. Candidate events are detected and packaged with keyframes and time windows. Each packet keeps pointers back to the source data for tracing. A language model with modality-specific tools drafts structured labels. Analysts then verify and edit those drafts. The workflow is demonstrated on multimodal VR emotion recordings.
arxiv-2603-02669:
Xiangyu Su, Juzhan Xu, Oliver van Kaick, and colleagues use large language models to run teams of factory robots. Their 2026 framework, IMR-LLM, faces stricter ordering rules and task links than home robot jobs. A language model alone can juggle simple chores, but factory work punishes loose sequencing.

The system has the model help build a graph of task conflicts, then lets exact solvers produce a workable high-level plan. A process tree then guides the model to write low-level programs the robots can run. The team also built IMR-Bench, a graded test set for multi-robot factory tasks. In their trials the method beat earlier approaches on every measure they reported.
arxiv-2603-02869:
Luigi Romano models a rolling tire as a stretched string with friction woven through its whole contact patch. His 2026 paper introduces string tyre models where the carcass and tread deform like strings, rather than as separate stick and slip zones. The result is a set of partial differential equations tracking the tire's state as it rolls.

Stability and passivity proofs, built on an energy-based Lyapunov method, show the states stay bounded and energy drains during contact. The energy function reads naturally as the tire's stored elastic energy, linking storage to frictional loss. Numerical and lab tests reproduce the nonlinear relaxation seen after sudden slip changes. The model offers a clear, well-posed base for vehicle dynamics work.
arxiv-2603-02969:
Yenan Wang, Carla Fabiana Chiasserini, and Elad Michael Schiller alternate real and synthetic data to make private group learning cheaper. Federated learning trains a shared model across devices without pooling raw data, and homomorphic encryption can protect the updates. Full encryption, though, is expensive and can drag down accuracy.

Their system, Alt-FL, rotates between rounds trained on real data, sent encrypted, and rounds trained on synthetic data, sent in plain form. The synthetic rounds enrich the training mix, while the rotation caps encryption work. Tests against a strong data-leakage attack showed privacy held firm. Accuracy rose by over thirteen percent against a selective-encryption rival, and encryption costs fell by up to about half.
arxiv-2603-03069:
S. Srivastav, S. J. Smartt, T. Moore, and a large team catalog every bright stellar explosion in the nearby universe over nearly six years. Their 2026 paper introduces ATLAS100, a volume-limited sample of over seventeen hundred supernovae and related transients within about one hundred megaparsecs. Volume limits make the sample fair: nothing is included just for being bright.

The team built the host galaxy list from all available redshift catalogs and matched transients near those galaxies. Spectroscopic classifications cover most of the sample, and many doubtful cases were reclassified using light curves and spectra together. Cleaned light curves, peak brightnesses, and timescales are released with the catalog. This first paper sets up a series measuring true explosion rates nearby.
arxiv-2603-03369:
Joud Khoury and five others build a way to test hidden messaging systems in an honest way. Such systems bury covert messages inside ordinary network traffic, hiding not just content but the very fact of contact. Claims about how undetectable they are usually rest on ad hoc statistics and unstated assumptions about the watcher. Their 2026 approach, Maude-HCS, makes every assumption direct and executable.

Undetectability is defined precisely: the observable traces of a system carrying hidden traffic must be impossible to tell apart from a plain baseline. Designers specify protocol conduct, what an adversary can observe, and ambient settings, then sample trace distributions by simulation. Those samples audit real claims and bound detectability against results. A tunneling test case matched readings from a physical testbed closely for passive observers.
arxiv-2603-03569:
Sepideh Mosaferi and Shonosuke Sugasawa fix a quiet flaw in how big surveys report their own uncertainty. Fine stratification samples just one or two units per group, which makes point estimates unbiased but variance nearly impossible to estimate honestly. The standard rescue merges groups into fake pairs, inflating the variance estimate and widening intervals beyond need. Their 2026 paper replaces the rescue with a Bayesian estimator that never merges anything.

Penalized splines smooth the mean and the variance together, nonparametrically, letting nearby groups share strength without being collapsed. Comparisons include the best-known earlier kernel approach. Multiple simulation studies favor the new method, and an illustration on the National Survey of Family Growth, a real United States health survey, shows it working on genuine data. The payoff is tighter, better-calibrated confidence intervals for finely stratified designs.
arxiv-2603-03769:
Youngmin Kim and seven colleagues upgrade cheap MRI scans into expensive-looking ones without paired examples. Ultra-low-field brain scanners cost far less to run but produce weaker images than standard three-tesla machines. Matched pairs of scans from both are scarce, ruling out ordinary supervised translation. Their 2026 framework learns the translation unpaired, built on a neural Schrödinger bridge with multi-step refinement.

Two additions guard the translation. A distribution-matching term, guided by a frozen diffusion model trained on high-field scans, pulls the output toward realistic high-field appearance. An anatomical preservation regularizer, paired with a patch-level contrastive loss, enforces foreground-background consistency and boundary awareness so anatomy cannot drift. On two disjoint cohorts the method improves the realism-structure trade-off on both fronts: more realistic on unpaired tests, more faithful on paired ones.
arxiv-2603-04069: Wilhelm and others monitor emergent reward hacking during output via internal activations. Fine-tuned language models can reward-hack through emergent misalignment, hard to detect from final outputs, and prior work studied completed replies only. Their method fits sparse autoencoders to residual stream activations with lightweight linear classifiers for token-level figures. Across model families and mixtures, internal patterns reliably separate reward hacking from benign conduct and extend to unseen mixed-policy adapters. Reward-hacking signals often emerge early, persist through thought, and grow with test-time compute.
arxiv-2603-04269: La Posta and colleagues map two cosmic quantities together from galaxy and microwave background data. Their joint model handles the thermal Sunyaev Zeldovich signal and the cosmic infrared background in one fit. Separating the two signals frees each measurement from galaxy clustering assumptions and from cross contamination. Applied to public data, the method traces average electron pressure and star formation density, both bias weighted, back to redshift near one. Both histories broadly match the FLAMINGO simulation, except that gas pressure runs lower at recent times.
arxiv-2603-04369: Schutte and colleagues pin down when Fisher information turns singular for sine-skewed torus models. Sine skewing, the only skewing mechanism on the hyper-torus, adds asymmetry to torus distributions. Some models suffer singular Fisher matrices near symmetry, harming inference. It was open which models show the flaw. The paper gives a general characterization of the singular class in full d-dimensional settings.
arxiv-2603-04469: Cai and colleagues detect agentic attacks by rebuilding cross layer semantic flows. Agent tool calls become process, file, and network activity downstream, where malice may first appear. Input guardrails miss such effects, and delegation adds paths. AScope links agent semantics with kernel audit events into causal trajectories, flagging data, control, and intent violations with a supervisor model. On AgentDojo traces and ten multi-agent scenarios, detection stays strong, reaching 85.3 percent node level F1 with lower path scores.
arxiv-2603-04669: Cirigliano and colleagues model strongly clustered random graphs via triadic closure. Real networks show strong linking, degree links, and odd grouping spectra. Such features resist tractable modeling, blocking theory grasp. The model closes each triad of a random network backbone with a certain probability. Despite intricate loopy local structure, the paper gives exact formulas for the grouping spectrum and degree links. It finds positive degree mixing with high linking and odd grouping spectrum structure. Exact long-run results for tree-like backbones pair with number study of finite-size effects.
arxiv-2603-04969: Minxing Zhang and team present MPCEval, a testing suite for evaluating multi-party conversation making with task-aware metrics. Multi-party settings add turn-taking hardness, role-dependent actions, long-range structure, and many valid continuations. MPCEval splits quality into speaker building, content quality, and sameness between speaker and content, separating local next-turn guess from global making. Its novel, quantitative, reference-free metrics scale across data sets and models. Applied to varied data sets, it reveals dimension-given traits in participation balance, content progression, novelty, and speaker-content sameness.
arxiv-2603-05169: Saurabh Vaishampayan and Maryam Kamgarpour model how strategic prosumers in spread grids form groups for collective self-use under uncertainty. Their cooperative game method weighs grid-operator interests next to prosumer ones, taking in grid constraints, variable load and making, and links between nearby local markets. With fixed load and making, the largest group is the optimal stable partition, while heavy crowding makes individual self-use optimal. For stochastic prosumption with moderate congestion, they give an algorithm that finds the optimal stable split, checked on benchmark and real grids.
arxiv-2603-05269: Yaobin Chen and colleagues prove that in pseudorandom graphs, Hamilton-cycle hitting time coincides with minimum-degree-2 hitting time. The random subgraph process adds base-graph edges in uniform random order to an empty graph on the same vertices. For (n,d,λ)-graphs with d/λ at least a constant, the coincidence holds with high probability, resolving 2019 Alon-Krivelevich and 2002 Frieze-Krivelevich questions. They thus determine the sharp threshold for such graphs at large d, and extend the result to k edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles versus minimum degree 2k.
arxiv-2603-05369: Tianhao Chen and team offer Progressive Residual Warmup for language model early training. Transformers back most large language models, so early training balance and settling speed matter. ProRes multiplies each residual with a scalar warming from 0 to 1, with deeper layers warming longer. Deeper layers wait until early layers settle. Tests across scales and schemes show ProRes effectiveness. ProRes stabilizes early training with a distinctive tuning path, leading to faster settling and better downstream scores.
arxiv-2603-05469: Groom and Zhou present a Galerkin time-domain boundary element scheme for acoustic scattering by vehicle surfaces, including propellers and rotors. The time-domain approach handles short-lived, rotating, and broadband sources with ease, while the Galerkin form stays robust and unconditionally stable with no settings to tune. A decomposition-based quadrature sorts out the hard double space-time integration, and three test cases with exact answers check the method. Applied to a trailing edge-mounted propeller, the forecast matches what was measured for scattering and shielding well.
arxiv-2603-05569: Nguyen and team offer CBR-to-SQL, a case-based reasoning framework splitting retrieval-boosted text-to-SQL making into two clear stages. Standard single-step retrieval struggles to tune logical structure and named items at once, often relying on near-exact matches. One stage finds examples that fit by structure, while the other aligns items with the target database schema. On two clinic benchmarks, the framework matches fine-tuned methods for rightness with much better use of samples and toughness, above all under data shortage and retrieval noise.
arxiv-2603-05769: Chen and team propose LayerBind for area and hiding control. Layout control is handy, yet training methods inherit bias, while tricks struggle with hiding. It models area making as layers. Layout and hiding are set early in cleaning. Single start creates branches watching their own regions while tying to background. At an early step, branches fuse by layer order into a latent. Meaning nursing boosts details and keeps hiding order. A layered focus path runs beside the global path. It is training-free and plug-and-play.
arxiv-2603-06469: Upadhyay and team present a Bayesian method for peculiar velocities of Type Ia supernova host galaxies, using the background cosmological model alone. Unlike Hubble tools, their method assumes neither local straightness of the magnitude-redshift relation nor a fixed cosmology. It stays fair even for large odd speeds and avoids bias from a wrong model. Tests on simulated data, plus match with the linearized estimator, shows lower bias and steadiness for larger velocity ratios. A Bayes proof extends the linear tool to include star blast magnitude link.
arxiv-2603-06869: Baig and Gillani introduce SymLang, symmetry-constrained language-led equation search for finding laws from noisy data. Search fails when readings are noisy, key state factors are hidden, or multiple symbol forms explain the data equally within doubt. First, typed symmetry-constrained grammars encode unit checks, group invariance, and parity constraints as laws, cutting trees before fitting. Second, language-led synthesis uses a fine-tuned guide fed clear data labels. Third, MDL-regularized Bayesian choice with block-bootstrap stability checks measures structure doubt rather than picking one answer.
arxiv-2603-07269: Su, Xiong and Zhong compare classes tied to two kinds of geometric spaces: open projected Richardson varieties and affine Schubert cells. For Grassmannians, where the spaces are known as positroid varieties, they give a direct counting formula for the classes. Both results rest on one step-by-step rule built from Demazure-Lusztig operators, which also ties local forms of the classes to twisted Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials.
arxiv-2603-07369: Liu and colleagues track neural populations in macaque visual cortex as monkeys learn visual discrimination tasks. Two rival ideas compete: learning trims redundancy for efficiency, or learning spreads information wider, raising redundancy. The recordings back the second idea, with redundancy rising across weeks of training and inside single trials too. Extra redundancy did not cost information; single neurons carried more of it. The authors read this as evidence for generative rather than discriminative inference in sensory cortex.
arxiv-2603-07669: Kim and Farrell extend SSD to shallow-water magnetic turbulence to study coherent structure formation. Zonal jets emerge on their own from turbulence in planetary and stellar atmospheres, yet how they are born stays open. Their small-change and nonlinear states reveal zonal jet-toroidal field structures with fixed-point and swinging behavior. The results bear on steady solar super-rotation and time-dependent events like the solar cycle.
arxiv-2603-07869: Dospinescu and colleagues prove a de Rham and Hyodo-Kato flip-flop result for dual towers of rigid analytic spaces, including those from dual basic local Shimura varieties. Their main tools are comparison theorems. These recast both cohomologies as pro-étale cohomology of matching period sheaves, which by design meet pro-étale descent. As an application, they show the de Rham and Hyodo-Kato cohomologies of finite-level covers of Drinfeld space are admissible as representations of the relevant general linear group.
arxiv-2603-08069: Wang and colleagues address a data-scarcity problem in power line insulator inspection, where drone imagery is plentiful but defect examples are rare and inspection sets are often small or closed. Training accurate defect-type classifiers on such thin data is difficult. They use an off-the-shelf multimodal large language model as a training-free image generator, synthesizing defect images from visual references and text prompts. Two-reference conditioning widens variety, light human checks plus prompt tweaks protect label quality, and a filter cleans the synthetic pool.
arxiv-2603-08269: Sato and colleagues present SAIL, a framework that reframes robot learning as an iterative polish problem that scales with test-time compute. In-context imitation learning lets robots learn skills from demonstrations, yet one-shot trajectory generation stays fragile under environmental variation. SAIL uses Monte Carlo Tree Search, where each node is a complete path and edges correspond to path refinements. Guidance comes from a stored archive of successful paths, a vision-language-model scoring mechanism for path evaluation, and step-level feedback with path-aligned scores.
arxiv-2603-08569: Mateo Crabit Nicolau gives a fresh proof of a Gross-Zagier-style result for Shimura curves of genus zero. Daas had proved the Giampietro-Darmon guess with p-adic tools, but this proof works over the archimedean side instead, by evaluating Green's function at CM points. The plan tracks the analytic proof of Gross and Zagier, stressing where it matches and where it parts from the p-adic route.
arxiv-2603-08869: Sripad Karne asks whether sparse autoencoder features track meaning or mere spelling. Serbian, written in Latin and Cyrillic with near-perfect letter mapping but zero shared tokens, lets meaning stay fixed while script changes. Same-meaning sentences in different scripts fire highly overlapping features, far above random baselines, and script swaps disturb features less than paraphrases do, with the effect growing with model size.
arxiv-2603-09369: Ru Zhang and Rulin Shen take up Zappa's 1962 question: can a coset of a Sylow p-subgroup, if non-trivial, hold only elements whose order is a power of p? Conder gave a positive answer for p equal to 5, and any smallest example must be a non-abelian simple group. The authors prove the smallest such group cannot be an alternating group of simple type, whatever prime p is chosen. The result narrows the search space for a minimal Zappa example.
arxiv-2603-09569: Ekaterina Kubyshkina and Mattia Petrolo argue that ignorance is a hyperintensional notion, tied to content rather than truth alone. An agent may lack knowledge of one of two logically equal claims yet not the other. With topic-sensitive semantics they rework three logics for three forms of ignorance and prove each sound and complete. The frame also recasts logical omniscience: what matters is whether the agent grasps the content at stake.
arxiv-2603-09669: Leonardo Baggiani and colleagues study how decentralized exchanges compete for order flow through dynamic trading fees. They find an approximate Nash equilibrium, described by a coupled system of partial differential equations, with tractable closed-form approximations for the fees. The two-regime pattern from monopoly models persists: pools raise fees to deter arbitrage, then lower them to attract noise trading. Competition shifts the switching boundary and cuts slippage for strategic takers, while noise traders fare worse in quiet markets and better in busy ones.
arxiv-2603-09769: Philipp Heering studies largest sets of pairwise non opposite flags in a finite projective space, viewed as a Kneser graph. The flags pair a smaller subspace with a larger one that contains it. Using a matching theorem for vector spaces, he finds the biggest cocliques when the field is large enough. A stability result comes with the answer, settling a stated conjecture.
arxiv-2603-09869: Gessica Alecci and Giuseppe D'Alconzo study the linear code equivalence problem, whose hardness backs the LESS signature scheme. The question is whether two linear codes match under a monomial map, part scaling and part shuffling of positions. Using Plücker coordinates and invariant rational functions, they build an algebraic model that involves the shuffle alone. The resulting polynomials are too large for practice, but the tools are new to this problem.
arxiv-2603-10269: Giuseppe De Laurentis, Kirill Melnikov, and Matteo Tresoldi show that amplitudes for vector-boson decay to massless leptons still encode every polarization state, including the longitudinal one. Earlier helicity results for electron-positron annihilation into four QCD partons in effect fixed the transverse case, and redoing them would be costly even at one loop. Spin covariance lets the authors recast those amplitudes as a matrix with open spin indices, using mostly simple replacement rules. Any one polarization piece then suffices to rebuild the full matrix.
arxiv-2603-10569: Alexander Barzykin studies market making where an aggregator routes RFQ flow by a dealer's slowly moving win score. His two-tier control model splits quote-level competition from a routing layer gated by that score, while background flow stays ungated. Solving the problem gives a clean map from optimal win chances to optimal offsets. For steep gates, the score dynamics can show bistability and a campaign-versus-harvest pattern in quoting, with background flow keeping inventory mixing alive.
arxiv-2603-11069: Valentio Iverson proves a recently posed conjecture about the 3-adic valuation of a cubic binomial sum, a question raised by Alekseyev, Amdeberhan, Shallit, and Vukusic. The 3-adic valuation of an integer counts the exact power of 3 dividing it, so the result pins down that exponent for the sum in question. The note settles the conjecture as stated, closing a small but precise problem in elementary number theory.
arxiv-2603-11269: Hong Yang and coauthors diagnose a failure of out-of-distribution detection in single-domain models, named domain-sensitivity collapse. Supervised training crushes features into a low-rank class subspace and buries the directions carrying domain-shift signal. They prove that under this collapse, distance- and logit-based detection scores lose sensitivity to domain shift. Their remedy distills class-suppressed residual structure from a frozen multi-domain teacher into the student during training, cutting far-out-of-distribution false positives across eight benchmarks at no inference cost.
arxiv-2603-11469: Bai, Hou, and Lan study how oxygen vacancies in Josephson junctions can harm superconducting qubits. The barrier is amorphous Al2O3, and radiation easily creates such defects inside it. With first-principles work and molecular dynamics, the team maps how these defects change conductivity. Two- and three-coordinated vacancies raise conductivity more than the four-coordinated kind. More vacancies mean wilder conductivity swings, tied to critical current noise. A noise model then links higher vacancy counts to shorter coherence times.
arxiv-2603-11669: Lee and Choi present SEMamba++, a general speech restoration framework tuned to the structure of speech itself. State-space models like SEMamba lead on denoising, yet they miss traits such as spectral periodicity. Their Global, Local, and Periodic module reads frequency bins in a way that uses those traits as built-in biases. A multi-resolution block then processes time and frequency in parallel, catching varied spectral patterns. A learnable mapping adds a final lift. Across baselines, the system posts the best scores while staying light on compute.
arxiv-2603-11869: Berthelier and co-authors revisit Reversible Instance Normalization, a widely used step in time series forecasting. Normalization matters in deep learning, yet its role in forecasting stays poorly understood. The authors name three hard cases: shifts in input over time, shifts across space, and shifts in the output given the input. Through ablation studies they show several RevIN parts are redundant, and some even hurt. From those findings they draw new ideas for making RevIN sturdier and better at generalizing.
arxiv-2603-11969: Nolan and co-authors introduce AstroSplat, a physics-based Gaussian splatting method for mapping small bodies like asteroids. Missions to such bodies lean on image-based mapping for planning, steering, and science. Standard splatting paints looks with spherical harmonics but skips what the surface is made of and how light bounces off it. AstroSplat instead builds in planetary reflectance models. Tested on real imagery from NASA's Dawn mission, it renders better and rebuilds surfaces with better accuracy than the harmonic approach, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-12669: Selim Furkan Tekin and co-authors fuse several vision-language models for stronger visual reasoning. Most ensemble work routes by language alone, ignoring what each model sees. Their V3Fusion measures focal error diversity and a CKA-based gap in visual embeddings. A genetic algorithm then prunes models that add no value to the pool. The fused system can beat a wrong majority and cut hallucinations. On four benchmarks, it topped the best single model in accuracy.
arxiv-2603-12869: Andrew Qing He and Wei Cai extend a neural pushforward method to fractional Fokker-Planck equations. Here the usual diffusion operator is swapped for a fractional Laplacian. Their weak adversarial scheme writes the solution as a pushforward through a neural network. All steps use Monte Carlo sampling, with no time mesh at all. Plane-wave test functions keep operator cost the same as in the classic case. Seven benchmarks, checked against particle runs, agreed closely throughout.
arxiv-2603-12969: Marco Mattuschka and co-authors present an algorithm that finds moving contaminant sources fast from sparse sensor data. A deliberate release of toxic chemicals can be invisible, which slows response. Their method couples local CBRN sensor readings with an advection-diffusion model of the air. It detects, localizes, and quantifies a source with unknown start time and path. Spatial sparsity serves as prior information in the search. Wind tunnel calibration and a digital twin plan raise the method toward real use.
arxiv-2603-13069: Ann Dooms shows that denoising diffusion models act as partitioned iterated function systems, a fractal frame for their workings. The deterministic DDIM chain, run in reverse, fits this system form. From it, she derives three geometric quantities that need no model runs. They explain the two-regime pattern: broad context assembly at high noise, then fine detail at low noise. Self-attention appears as the natural contraction step. The frame also yields design rules that match four known tricks.
arxiv-2603-13469: Paolo Arnaudo and Benjamin Withers compute the holographic Euclidean two-point function for scalar operators in a thermal state. They work directly with the Fourier series on the thermal circle. The series converges as a distribution, not as a function, which matches QFT expectations. Their outcome is periodic by construction and fits analyticity in the set strip. Expanding in the thermal time gives all OPE coefficients, including the double-trace sector. Bouncing singularities appear as non-perturbative sectors in the transseries, with zero parameters in this case.
arxiv-2603-13969: Krnjaca, Krames, and Nahm use a statistical shape model to mass-produce labeled training data for liver landmark segmentation. Labeling medical shapes by hand is slow, so the mean shape is labeled just once. The model then stamps those labels onto thousands of new liver shapes. A network trained on 8,800 such shapes scores a mean intersection-over-union near 91 percent on unseen synthetic shapes. On real patient livers, early qualitative checks look promising.
arxiv-2603-14369: Hevapathige and co-authors propose a Theory Compiler that turns formal domain theory into neural network design. Hand-built theory-guided models work well but the translation is manual, unchecked, and stuck in one domain. Their system takes a typed, machine-readable theory and outputs an architecture bound to obey it by construction. Three open problems set the agenda: a universal theory language, a correct compilation method, and soundness tests. The authors conjecture that compiled models will match hand-built ones with far less training data.
arxiv-2603-14469: Chandra and co-authors add physics rules to reinforcement learning for robot control. Actor-critic methods learn well but need many samples and can break physics. Their PIPER framework adds a soft physics term to the policy loss. The term is a differentiable Lagrangian residual taken from the robot simulator file. It nudges updates toward motions that fit the dynamics. No simulator or core algorithm changes are needed. Tests show gains in learning speed, stability and control accuracy, the authors report.
