Peak picking is a basic preprocessing step, with each sample holding hundreds to thousands of ion images. Existing methods need careful per-dataset tuning and often fail across acquisition protocols. IonMorphNet is trained as a spatial-structure-aware representation model on 53 public datasets, using six structural classes of ion image patterns, and it then assesses new ion images with no further tuning.
arxiv-2604-19569: Lee develops a new framework for analyzing constant step-size tabular Q-learning from a switching linear system viewpoint. Q-learning is a fundamental primitive in reinforcement learning. The paper derives a stochastic switching linear system representation of the Q-learning error. It adds a finite-time error analysis through the joint spectral radius of the corresponding system model. The joint spectral radius is the exact worst-case exponential rate of the associated system.
arxiv-2604-19669: Goertzen, Alim, Min, and Azizan introduce HardNet++, a neural network design that forces outputs to satisfy nonlinear constraints exactly, even at run time. Soft methods only penalize violations during training and cannot guarantee clean outputs later, while projection methods guarantee compliance only when a tractable projection onto the allowed set exists. Many real problems lack that special structure, so HardNet++ aims to enforce general nonlinear limits without needing a tractable projection.
arxiv-2604-20069: Morris, Kennedy, and Black build a multiscale model joining individual viral load trajectories with stochastic household transmission. Full joint inference is computationally hard, so they pass information from the within-host model to the between-host model but not back. Viral load data thus inform transmission parameters such as infection times and symptom onset thresholds. On simulated household outbreaks, recovery is unbiased when sampling is frequent, while sparse sampling biases results unless external viral load data are added.
arxiv-2604-20169: Kim proposes Semantic-Fast-SAM, a semantic segmentation system that pairs fast mask generation with a labeling pipeline for real-time use. Built on FastSAM, a convolutional re-implementation of Segment Anything, it labels each mask at a fraction of the original cost and memory. On Cityscapes it reaches a mean IoU near 70.33, with about 48 on ADE20K, matching prior SAM-based accuracy. It runs about twenty times faster than SSA in closed-set tests and handles open-vocabulary labeling through CLIP-based heads.
arxiv-2604-20469: Morgulis and Malal study predator-prey systems where predators chase a cue made by prey, not the prey itself. Cue production also reacts to an outside field, so the team builds a short-wave asymptotic expansion for cross-diffusion equations. That expansion is an approximation for varying signals, in any spatial dimension with no limits on reaction kinetics. Through Kapitza theory for the inverted pendulum, they find cases where the signal suppresses prey-chasing transport. It can stabilize the species balance, destabilize it, or blur the stable-unstable line.
arxiv-2604-20569: Domanti, Mock, Agnoli, and De Angeli ask whether systems judge idea originality like humans, and whether they favor their style. They analyze Alternate Uses responses from stronger and weaker human creators and ChatGPT-4o. Two university students served as human raters, while machine raters were two tuned systems, OCSAI and CLAUS, plus ChatGPT-4o with the instructions. Results confirm a self-preference bias: automatic systems privilege artificial responses. Yet that bias disappears once analyses control for idea elaboration, the detail and development of an idea, with implications for creativity assessment.
arxiv-2604-20969: Weber and colleagues study what happens when a magnetic cavity field couples to molecules, using high-precision quantum Monte Carlo that keeps electron correlations in play. In hydrogen molecules, strong enough coupling turns the bound ground state metastable and flips the singlet-triplet gap. In ring molecules, the coupling holds symmetric shapes steady, giving open-shell rings such as H4, H8, and C4H4 exotic spin- or current-polarized antiaromatic ground states.
arxiv-2604-21069: Arun Mannodi-Kanakkithodi and three colleagues survey a decade of data-driven shortcuts for simulating point defects, the atomic flaws that shape how materials behave. Descriptor models and interatomic potentials trained on quantum calculations now predict defect energies, relaxations, and even heat-related vibrations at a fraction of the old cost. The review closes by linking these tools to experiments and sketching where the fast-moving field heads next.
arxiv-2604-21169: Yuzhe Tang and four colleagues warn that multi-round transaction simulation, the subsystem that previews blockchain transactions before blocks are built, faces a fresh denial-of-service risk. Earlier attacks hit single-round or two-round builders, but the authors examine a new exploit rooted in dependencies between transactions that show up in smart-contract state. The position paper maps the threat for builders relying on several simulation rounds.
arxiv-2604-21369: Tatsuhito Hasegawa tackles human activity recognition across varied IoT sensors, where channel counts, orders, devices, body spots, and sensing types all vary. Usual channel-fixed models fail to transfer because their inputs cling to preset channel structures. His strict channel-free system encodes each channel on its own with a shared encoder, fuses with metadata-based late fusion, and jointly trains channel-level and fused predictions. Sensor metadata like body spot, sensing type, and axis recovers structure that channel-by-channel processing alone loses.
arxiv-2604-21469: Fariz Ikhwantri and Dusica Marijan study data picking for compliance checks across rules, framed as natural language inference, where models trained on one rule often fail on others. They compare four ways to pick extra data from a larger source domain: random sampling, Moore-Lewis cross-entropy difference, importance weighting, and embedding-based retrieval, varying the picked share. Targeted picking cuts negative transfer a lot. The work offers a practical path toward scalable, reliable compliance automation across varied rules.
arxiv-2604-21669: Dober, Glazman, and Ott study the q-state Potts model on the square grid where its transition is discontinuous, for q above 4. At the transition temperature, q ordered phases and one disordered phase coexist. The paper gives the first precise geometric account of wetting in this whole regime. A disordered layer forms between two ordered phases. Its boundaries converge, under diffusive scaling, to two Brownian motions conditioned not to intersect.
arxiv-2604-21769: Jung and four colleagues argue that LLM leaderboards hide as much as they reveal, since one aggregate score reflects benchmark designers' priorities rather than users' varied goals. Analysing the LMArena dataset, they find heavy topic skew, rankings that shift across prompt slices, and preference judgments used beyond their intended scope. Their interactive interface lets users set their own priorities by selecting and weighting prompt slices, and a qualitative study finds it improves transparency.
arxiv-2604-21869: Bisset and four colleagues improve telling models apart in coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering experiments. Few events, errors, and coarse bins make telling explanations apart hard. Total rates alone can be thrown off by source normalisation and by similar totals from different models. Patterns linking baseline, recoil energy, and timing let likelihood analysis tell a 3+1 sterile framework from non-standard interactions in favourable regions. Neural networks still tell them apart with total rate removed, and the same measures pin down the sterile benchmark point in favourable regions.
arxiv-2604-22069: Urusov and three colleagues study liquidity provision in concentrated markets using trade data from WETH/USD pools on the Base chain across Uniswap, Aerodrome, PancakeSwap and SushiSwap. The authors rebuild provider gains and losses from chain events and add a gauge tracking funds over time. Using this framework, they count winning providers, sort their habits, and list 15 position kinds. Only about one in six providers dodges losses in this market.
arxiv-2604-22469: Santamaria and four colleagues propose Riemannian optimisation on unitary symmetric matrices, which model scattering of reciprocal beyond-diagonal smart panels. They give the tangent space, a simple retraction and closed-form geodesics. They develop two methods: a line-search scheme and a phase-optimisation update along geodesics. They apply the method to BD-RIS multiple-input multiple-output links, for sum-gain, rate and minimum mean-square error problems, where they beat methods. When BD-RIS parts exceed aerials, the optimal scattering matrix is low-rank, spurring low-rank forms.
arxiv-2604-22569: Jurečková and three colleagues frame malware defense and evasion as a dueling contest solved with bilevel optimization. Learning-based detectors are open to hostile cases, and one-shot training often fails against learning attackers. Their framework models both sides' strategy as an iterative contest. Tested on Mokes, Strab, and DCRat, standard models and retraining stay open, with evasion rates as high as 90 percent. The bilevel approach cuts evasion to 0 to 1.89 percent and raises the cost of evasion by up to two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2604-22669: Wu and three colleagues introduce DeepHartree, a Poisson-coupled field linking real space to LCAO. Atomic-orbital DFT is costly from Coulomb-matrix construction and self-consistent iterations. Equivariant networks predict the Hartree potential, whose Poisson gives electron density. Atom-centred fields resolve nuclear structure, with electron-count correction. Gaussian integrals and quadrature assemble the Kohn-Sham matrix; one diagonalization gives a density matrix. Density errors under a quarter percent on coarse grids, rising to over 2 percent on level-3 grids. Density-trained models transfer to larger bases.
arxiv-2604-23069: Wu and six colleagues present ContextWeaver, a memory framework that arranges an agent's exchange trace into a graph of reasoning steps linked by ties. It selects relevant context for future actions, using compact link summaries and a lightweight validation layer with execution feedback. On five software-engineering and terminal benchmarks, it improves resolve rate over a sliding-window baseline on all five, using fewer agent steps. On SWE-Bench Pro it raises resolve rate to 72.6 percent across three model backbones.
arxiv-2604-23169: Kano and Yamaguchi give a deterministic linear-time method to find an odd or even cycle through two chosen vertices of an undirected graph. They prove a wider claim for any group where every element has order at most two. For any graph labelled by that group, one can test in linear time whether two cycles with distinct labels pass through both chosen vertices or edges. When such cycles exist, the method finds them. The result turns a parity-flavoured cycle question into a fast, exact graph procedure.
arxiv-2604-23669: Feik and colleagues study games where many agents, such as electric-car chargers, face uncertain crowd behaviour. Each agent guards against the worst total outcome within a set of plausible totals around the emergent crowd behaviour. This yields a new equilibrium idea between standard Wardrop play and full security play. They prove such an equilibrium exists for convex aggregative games. They also show robustness can even lower everyone's costs.
arxiv-2604-23769: Moore and seven colleagues present an additive-manufacturing method for pixelated plastic scintillator arrays used in neutron imaging. A custom automated machine and photo-curable resin first produce one-dimensional layered arrays autonomously, then cutting and stacking forms two-dimensional pixel arrays. One-dimensional arrays run at about four layers per hour, two-dimensional arrays reach 7 by 7 pixels, and readout tests show per-pixel position resolution plus gamma-neutron separation.
arxiv-2604-24169: Reichardt, Ebert, and Wasenmüller present PointTransformerX, a fully PyTorch-native vision transformer for 3D point clouds with no custom CUDA operators. It encodes 3D spatial relations in attention with a rotary embedding that needs no neighborhood construction, and it swaps sparse convolutional patch embedding for a linear projection. On ScanNet it reaches 98.7 percent of PointTransformer V3 accuracy, with far fewer parameters and much faster execution in only 253 MB of memory. It runs natively on NVIDIA, AMD, and CPU hardware, giving a portable base for point cloud perception.
arxiv-2604-24269: Cai and colleagues describe onboard data processing for the SVOM Visible Telescope. It matters for rapid identification of burst counterparts, especially high-redshift candidates. To fit the VHF downlink while keeping data live, they built the VT Onboard Data Processing Pipeline on an FPGA and a CPU. The pipeline assesses image quality, corrects dark and flat fields, and stacks images against cosmic rays and background. It also emits catalogs and compressed 1-bit images for downlink, with VHF data for 78 percent of slewed bursts and counterparts found for 56 percent, within 18 minutes.
arxiv-2604-24369: Wang and four colleagues study beam scheduling for cross-layer joint sensing and communication systems. Sharing resources must balance communication and sensing needs under tangled traffic and queues in multi-user settings. They propose a deep reinforcement learning method that cuts feedback overhead by using sensing observations instead of channel state data. Simulations show the method weighs buffer status, adapts to wireless conditions, and lifts throughput with only modest delay growth. Beam management also lands near a genie-aided benchmark with perfect departure-angle knowledge for both communication and sensing.
arxiv-2604-24569: Lapp and Tvalavadze introduce the Limiter, an enlarged number system that gives a canonical limit to every real sequence, even divergent ones. The idea draws on Borel summation and Ramanujan-style assignments. It respects ordinary limits, depends only on a sequence's cluster points, and shifts continuously when that cluster set moves slightly. The paper sets out the extension and its basic properties.
arxiv-2604-24769: Reclik and five colleagues present SPARSE, an open-source Python tool for scanning electron microscopy of rare tiny features over large areas at high resolution. A fast scan first finds regions of interest, which are then rescanned with settings suited to quantitative analysis. Scanning, detection and rescanning run in separate processes that talk only through queues, so work does not extend scan time. It reaches 99 percent detection for damage in dual-phase DP800 steel, at about 58 percent of usual scan time.
arxiv-2604-24869: Chou and Cao evaluate post-quantum certificate chains and time to first byte. Post-quantum handshakes grow from 5 times to over 20 times classical sizes. Time to first byte jumps as chains exceed flight limits. Comparing ECDSA and ML-DSA schemes with similar chains, they test mitigations. Session resumption, size optimizations and geography reduce penalties. Merkle Tree Certificates allow a 2 to 3 times increase in supportable chain size. CDN optimizations support up to about 1.6 times increase.
arxiv-2604-25069: Wilson, Tian and Kamali propose Shaperd, an easily adopted real-time traffic shaper for encrypted protocols. Encrypted protocol tools help circumvent censorship in restrictive regions and are valued for speed and security. Censors block them via passive traffic analysis and active probing. Shaperd operates on packet contents in real time. A novel constraint system lets users generate traffic flows with desired features. Early results show Shaperd adds minimal overhead to system throughput. The abstract presents Shaperd as a practical aid making censorship tools harder to detect.
arxiv-2604-25169: Mizoguchi and three colleagues identify two properties of the Gor'kov Green's function of finite topological superconductors. At low frequency, the normal and anomalous Green's functions, for single-particle and Cooper-pair correlations, match up to a phase factor. End-to-end correlations grow exponentially with system length. Local ones vanish at zero frequency. These features mark nonlocal Cooper pairs tied to a mode of Majorana end modes, linked to fermion parity and transport.
arxiv-2604-25569: Yamada investigates a scenario in which a higher-dimensional universe becomes four-dimensional in effect before inflation, through curvature-assisted modulus trapping. Bulk quantum fields supply the late-time Casimir term that stabilises the radion and early-time thermal terms that shape cosmic growth. Negative curvature sustains tracker radion evolution, letting it settle in a compactified vacuum before later inflation dilutes its remnant. Though it uses a five-dimensional toy model, it shows a broader mechanism for such change before inflation.
arxiv-2604-25669: Li proves that finite-energy weak solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations stay regular up to the boundary of a smooth three-dimensional domain. This holds provided the solution stays small in a certain space-time norm. The result answers a question raised by Albritton, Barker, and Prange. The proof uses a new layering method near the boundary. It controls the solution layer by layer. It sharpens understanding of when weak solutions to these fluid equations remain smooth at the edge of their domain.
arxiv-2604-26169: Pillai proposes budget-constrained causal bandits for ad spending with little historical data, where offline uplift models fail or mislead. The method learns individual treatment effects, explores uncertain users, and paces spending over time. Each decision follows from the optimality condition of a relaxed budgeted allocation problem. On an uplift dataset, a data-efficiency crossover appears near seventy-five hundred observations: below it offline methods falter while the online method works from the first user. It beats four online baselines at every budget tested, with lower run-to-run variance.
arxiv-2604-26369: Borodzik and three colleagues extended Carter and Saito's work on links that stay fixed under a half-turn in three-space. Such links are called involutive, and the team built a matching equivariant version of the theory of cobordisms between them. They found 39 equivariant movie moves that suffice to link any two movie views of the same equivariant cobordism pair. They also proved the equivariant Reidemeister theorem by studying singular points, and traced loops of equivariant moves using embedded Morse theory.
arxiv-2604-26869: Pintér and seven colleagues present KAYRA, a microservice system for karyotyping, the laboratory task of sorting and examining chromosomes. Its pipeline segments chromosome images, detects individual chromosomes, and classifies them, narrowing its focus step by step to chromosome-bearing regions. The same container images run in the cloud or on site, suiting clinics that cannot let patient data leave. In a pilot test on 459 chromosomes, segmentation reached about 99 percent, beating both commercial reference systems, and expert review stays in the loop.
arxiv-2604-26969: Wu and nine colleagues present AgenticRecTune, an agentic framework for tuning system-level configurations in large recommendation pipelines. Traditional work tunes single models, but final scores blend outputs from pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking stages, so each model change demands fresh system settings. Five specialized agents, Actor, Critic, Insight, Skill, and Online, manage the end-to-end workflow, with the Actor proposing candidates and the Critic filtering weak ones. Large-model reasoning drives the search over configuration spaces.
arxiv-2604-27169: Kozlowski and Boutyline show that geometric links between meaning features in large language models mirror human psychological associations. They build feature vectors for 360 words and project them onto 32 meaning axes, such as beautiful-ugly and soft-hard. The projections track human ratings closely. Links between the axes themselves predict links between survey scales, and much of the variation sits in a low-dimensional space.
arxiv-2604-27269: Vittor and seven colleagues present OptimusKG, a multi-mode medical labeled property graph. It is built from structured and semi-structured resources to preserve factual, type-specific labels across molecular, body, clinical, and outside-world domains. Many medical knowledge graphs derive from unstructured documents and lack schema-level constraints. Structured graphs prove hard to unify. OptimusKG holds 190,939 nodes across 10 entity types and 21,818,752 edges across 27 edge types. It draws from 18 word lists and controlled word lists, with a top-level schema.
arxiv-2604-27369: Hasan, Soumik, and Shahid attack clickbait detection from the other side, generating clickbait that uses emotion to slip past classifiers. Their framework models feeling in valence-arousal-dominance space and pairs headlines with similar social media posts, then rewrites them in several styles with large language models. A curiosity-gap function measures how headline variation stirs curiosity and dodges existing systems. In tests, emotion-aware styling degraded top classifiers badly, pushing misclassification as high as about 31 percent on the base system.
arxiv-2604-27669: Pedro de Carvalho and three colleagues review fairness notions and metrics for distribution network planning and operation. Fairness costs efficiency, a loss called the price of fairness, paid for social cohesion through fair outcomes. Locational disparity drives schemes to level the playing field, from egalitarian to merit-based criteria, with math ranging from linear to non-linear programming. The study compiles these notions and metrics, reviews their effects on stakeholders and resource allocation, and aims to support consistent, transparent planning and decisions.
arxiv-2604-27969: Yang and colleagues expose a flaw in vision-to-code generation for circuits, where models score well even when the diagram is blank. They show models lean on names in the module header to recall standard code templates instead of reading the diagram, a hidden defect they call Mirage. Their anonymised training method, VeriGround, restores genuine visual grounding and rivals a much larger frontier model while refusing blank diagrams.
arxiv-2604-28069: Akıskalıoğlu and colleagues plan wireless charging for electric cars driving over powered road strips. Their control setup uses edge computing and car messages to favour cars with low batteries, tested in a modelled Istanbul scene. Sharing power with no plan wastes energy at full load and strands empty cars when demand tops supply. Their plan rebalances road strips and puts empty batteries first, which lifts fairness.
arxiv-2604-28169: Narayanan's team gives video generation physics control through PhyCo, tackling drift, flat crashes and wrong matter. They build a large dataset of simulated videos varying friction, rebound, bending and force, fine-tune a diffusion model with physics-tuned control, and add vision-language reward feedback on physics queries. The result makes motion that stays true to physics and users can steer, without a sim at run time. It lifts realism on a physics benchmark and in human studies.
arxiv-2605-00069:
Christopher Holder and Anthony Bagnall introduce Soft-MSM, a differentiable version of an elastic distance for time series. Elastic distances compare sequences that are locally out of step in time. Soft-DTW smoothed the classic warping distance into a usable gradient loss, but the trick does not extend to distances whose step costs depend on the local alignment context. The move-split-merge distance is one of those, with its split and merge penalties.

Soft-MSM supplies a smooth gated stand-in for that piecewise cost, so gradients flow through both the dynamic programming recursion and the local transition structure. The authors derive the forward and backward recursions, the soft alignment, and a closed-form gradient. On more than one hundred standard datasets, Soft-MSM lowers barycentre loss against earlier methods and clusters and classifies better than Soft-DTW rivals. The implementation ships in the open-source aeon toolkit.
arxiv-2605-00269:
Hamidreza Saghir studies a trap in out-of-distribution detection for language models: features that separate two groups of texts may still rank odd cases badly. Detectors are meant to flag inputs that deserve closer inspection. Saghir tests this gap on model trajectories while controlling for text length and fixing the scoring direction.

On spam data, one detector's score fell from strong to near chance once text length was matched. The same features served a labeled linear classifier far better than a distance-based score fitted on normal data. The pattern repeated on hate speech, toxic chat, and frozen test sets beyond toxicity. Odd groups sat farther from the center but clustered more tightly, and a fix that equalized spread helped some tasks while harming others.
arxiv-2605-00469:
K. N. Raghavan, Krishanu Roy, and S. Viswanath study pi-systems inside symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebras, a vast generalization of the Lie algebras behind much of modern algebra and physics. A pi-system is a set of real roots no two of which differ by another root. Such sets serve as simple roots of regular subalgebras, studied classically by Dynkin, Morita, and Naito.

The authors show that a binary relation introduced by Morita defines a partial order on these systems when the algebra is of finite, untwisted affine, or hyperbolic type. They also formulate principles for building pi-systems, and for ruling out diagrams that can never appear for a given algebra. As an application, they determine the maximal hyperbolic diagrams in ranks three through ten relative to Morita's order. The work orders a landscape that was previously explored case by case.
arxiv-2605-00769:
Amir Norouzi and Michael Morel examine voltage ride-through for very large electrical loads, such as artificial intelligence data centers. Ride-through means a load stays connected and stable when grid voltage dips briefly. If large loads drop off together, the wider power system can suffer. The authors test the usual fix, which relies on reactive power alone.

Their analysis shows reactive power hits hard limits set by the load's own wiring and by grid constraints. They propose a dual approach that uses both active and reactive power from non-grid resources with fast control. Worked examples also show that at extreme dips, keeping load voltage acceptable may become impossible and disconnection may follow.
arxiv-2605-00969:
Harshit Rajgarhia and six co-authors present MedMosaic, a large benchmark for medical audio question answering under realistic clinical constraints. Medical audio is hard to collect because of privacy rules and costly expert annotation, so existing benchmarks underrepresent complex cases. MedMosaic includes condition-related physiological sounds, synthetic voices designed to mimic speech artifacts, and real short and long clinical conversations.

The dataset holds tens of thousands of question-answer pairs in multiple-choice, multi-turn, and open-ended forms, enabling tests of multi-hop reasoning and answer generation. Benchmarking thirteen audio and multimodal models shows reasoning remains hard for all systems, with wide spread by question type. Even a leading model reaches only about two thirds accuracy, underscoring the need for stronger domain-specific models.
arxiv-2605-01369:
Ahmed Y Radwan and Hina Tabassum use Wi-Fi signals to sense human activity for several users at once, with no cameras and low cost. Deep models read the fine channel data well, but they falter in new rooms, and users acting at once tangle the signals.

Their framework, MU-SHOT-Fi, adapts a trained model to a new setting using unlabeled data from that setting, since labeled source data may be private. Training matches predicted activity sets without caring about order. Adaptation freezes the classifier and tunes the feature layers. A weighted rule pushes for varied guesses on slots likely to hold a person. A rotation-guessing task teaches room-proof features on top. A single-user variant swaps in other self-training tricks. On two public data sets, across shifts in room, frequency, and facing, the method restores multi-user accuracy and keeps head counts right.
arxiv-2605-01669:
Xihang Shan and Da Zhou learn how much trust to place in prior beliefs while discovering causal structure from data. A prior graph can speed the search, but priors vary wildly in worth: physics is solid, a language model's suggested arrows are guesses, and blind trust or blind refusal both lose.

PRCD-MAP assigns trust edge by edge. A soft layer turns trust into weighted penalties inside a Bayesian objective. It calibrates the trust by an empirical Bayes estimate and spreads it along the prior graph with a small network. Confirmed neighborhoods earn trust, and contradicted ones lose it. Theory gives a safety bound, and when the prior carries no signal trust provably sinks to its floor and the method becomes the no-prior baseline. On real causal time series it beats strong rivals, exploits good language-model priors, and mutes itself on a stress test built to punish trust.
arxiv-2605-01769:
Jia Li, Zhuangbin Chen, Yuxin Su, and Michael R Lyu teach a language model to patch security holes the way an expert would. They give it the expert's pattern book. Automated repair tools based on language models are promising, yet the structured knowledge in weakness catalogs and vulnerability databases usually enters as a bare ID in the prompt, which buys almost nothing.

VulKey distills that knowledge into three stacked levels: the weakness type, the syntactic actions a fix takes, and the semantic key elements that must appear. A first stage matches a flaw to its repair pattern, and a second, pattern-guided fine-tuned model writes the patch. On a real-world C and C++ benchmark it repairs about a third of cases, clear of the best baseline and of a flagship general model. It also leads on a Java benchmark, showing the patterns travel across languages and models.
arxiv-2605-02069:
Hallac and Ogul turn pairwise comparisons into absolute essay scores. Many scoring tasks need a definite number, yet judging which of two essays is better is often easier than scoring one essay cold. Their framework, Pair2Score, first trains a ranking model on pairs of essays drawn from known trait scores. It then transfers what it learned into a model that predicts absolute scores for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax. The transfer uses a parameter-efficient adaptation of the LLaMA language model.

Tested under a five-fold protocol that rotates held-out data and random seeds, the best transfer variant beat an absolute-only baseline on all three traits. The agreement measure was quadratic weighted kappa. Not every setup helped, though: one epoch of pairwise training transferred more reliably than longer training. The lesson is that how the pairwise stage is configured matters as much as including one at all.
arxiv-2605-02369:
Zhida Qin and colleagues present BST-CDSR, a recommender that moves user behaviour and meaning across domains while respecting time. Cross-domain sequential methods fight sparsity by modelling a user's actions in several domains at once. Past work misses two issues. Domains differ in how often users act and how fast interest decays. Semantic taste also changes over time during transfer.

Their behaviour part splits long-term interests from short-term aims. It models taste over continuous time with a neural differential equation, updated by events. A semantic generator, aided by temporal counterfactuals, captures time-aware semantic taste. Together, the parts aim to transfer what a user likes now, not a timeless average of past taste.
arxiv-2605-02469:
Yao Shu and four co-authors clarify when offline fine-tuning can match an online reinforcement learning target for language models. In learning with verifiable rewards, the ideal updated policy tilts a reference policy toward high-reward answers. Offline methods that train on stored rollouts look simpler, but their result depends on how samples were drawn and weighted, not on rewards alone.

The paper identifies the weighted objective whose induced policy equals that ideal target. Matching forces a specific density-ratio weight, tied to how much more likely each answer is under the tilted policy. Their procedure, BOLT, estimates this projection from stored samples. A finite-sample analysis splits the error into parts from stored support, estimation, generalization, optimization, and approximation, giving readers a map of where one-shot methods lose ground.
arxiv-2605-02769:
Darío González Picos and five co-authors measure the atmosphere of a brown dwarf companion with the James Webb Space Telescope, while correcting for starlight that leaks into the spectrum. The companion, HD 19467 B, sits close to its bright star, so leftover speckles can bias what gases seem present and in what amounts. The team compares it with a free-floating brown dwarf of similar type.

Medium-resolution spectra cover the near to mid infrared. Bayesian retrievals, run with a standard atmosphere code and nested sampling, fit a flexible temperature profile and free gas amounts. A linear speckle model is fitted alongside the atmosphere for the companion. Water, methane, carbon oxides, and ammonia were detected in both objects, and carbon isotope ratios were measured from carbon monoxide lines. Speckle effects concentrate in one wavelength band.
arxiv-2605-02869:
Vasiliki A. Mitsou reviews the long search for magnetic monopoles, isolated north or south magnetic poles that have never been observed. Every known magnet has both poles joined, yet strong theoretical arguments say single poles should exist. The tension between theory's confidence and experiment's silence has driven searches for decades, across cosmic and laboratory settings.

The review first sets out the theoretical foundations briefly, from Dirac's early argument onward. A historical survey of attempts to observe monopoles follows, with stress on the current state of the art. Cosmic searches and collider experiments both feature, with particular attention to the Large Hadron Collider at CERN and its dedicated efforts. The article serves as a map of a hunt that remains open.
arxiv-2605-03069:
Zahir Alsulaimawi and Huaping Liu present a privacy tool for releasing data from scattered devices without exposing sensitive traits. Keeping raw data local helps, but gradients and released features can still leak private attributes.

Their Gaussian Privacy Protector learns a random encoder that maps raw input to a small cleaned output. Training limits what the output reveals about a chosen sensitive trait while keeping a chosen useful trait. In the federated version, sensitive labels never leave each device. Tests on images and activity data kept utility near baseline while attacker success fell to near guessing.
arxiv-2605-03169:
King and twenty-seven colleagues release a Python package that unifies brain data and AI models. Neuroscience and AI increasingly meet, but the software is fragmented: tools are split by recording type, from brain scans to electrode spikes, and built for small in-memory jobs. NeuralSet splits experimental metadata from lazy, memory-saving data extraction, so it can handle massive natural datasets spanning brain recordings and stimuli like text, audio, and video. One PyTorch-ready interface then covers local tests through cluster runs.

Standard preprocessing steps are harmonized with pretrained deep learning embeddings, and full provenance removes manual data wrangling. The package is built by a large team across Meta, Paris universities, and research institutes, reflecting how broad the neuro-AI community has become. By making diverse recordings and stimuli speak one language, NeuralSet aims to give the next generation of brain-AI research a shared, scalable base.
arxiv-2605-03269:
Dongyoung Kim and sixty-seven co-authors report RLDX-1, a general robot policy for skilled hand work. It builds on vision, language, and action models. Such models gain broad scene sense from vision-language training. But they still falter on tasks that need motion sense, long memory, and touch.

RLDX-1 uses a multi-stream transformer. It fuses separate modality streams with joint attention. Synthetic data covers rare cases, and fast inference aids real-time use. In simulation and real tasks, it beat recent frontier policies. On a humanoid robot with many joints, its success rate was far higher than its rivals.
arxiv-2605-03769:
Jinghui Yuan and four co-authors propose Nora, a matrix-based optimizer for training large language models. A good optimizer needs three things at once: Muon-like preconditioning for speed of learning, strict respect for the scale invariance of neural networks, and low computing cost. Existing methods tend to give up one of these, either costing too much or allowing radial jitter that harms stability.

Nora steadies weight norms and angular velocities by projecting row-wise momentum onto the orthogonal complement of the weights. Using the block-diagonal dominance of the Transformer Hessian, it approximates structured preconditioning at optimal complexity in the matrix dimensions. The authors prove Nora is a scalable optimizer and establish its scaling behavior, aiming to unify efficiency, stability, and speed.
arxiv-2605-03869:
Hassan Dbouk, Nidham Gazagnadou, Matthias Reisser, and Christos Louizos investigate adaptive zeroth-order optimization for memory-constrained fine-tuning of large language models. Zeroth-order methods estimate gradients from function values alone, saving memory, and adaptive versions such as ZO-Adam were claimed to converge better. The authors show those claims do not hold against well-tuned plain ZO-SGD.

Their analysis reveals that in high dimensions zeroth-order gradients lack coordinate-wise heterogeneity, so per-coordinate adaptation wastes memory. They propose MEAZO, which tracks only a single scalar for global step-size adaptation, supported by convergence guarantees under standard assumptions. Across several model families and tasks, MEAZO matched ZO-Adam's performance with ZO-SGD's memory footprint, and proved more robust to step-size choices in block-structured settings.
arxiv-2605-03969:
Mohamed Mady, Johannes Reschke, and Björn Schuller study how well supervised detectors can tell AI-generated text from human writing when test data shift across domains and generators. They train transformer-based detectors on the HC3 PLUS dataset. They set a single decision threshold, chosen for best balanced accuracy on held-out validation. That threshold is then kept fixed for all downstream test distributions. The fixed threshold reveals domain- and generator-dependent error gaps under shift.

Base models reached near-ceiling in-domain performance. But performance under shift was brittle and strongly model-dependent. Feature augmentation via attention-based language feature fusion improved transfer. The best model reached about eighty-six percent balanced accuracy on the M4 benchmark. It beat strong zero-shot baselines by up to seven points. Multi-seed experiments confirmed high stability. Category-level breakdowns showed that readability and vocabulary features contribute most to robust transfer.
arxiv-2605-04069:
Gregory Magarshak introduces LAWS, a self-certifying inference caching architecture that learns from actual workloads symbolically. LAWS builds a growing library of certified expert functions from deployment observations. Each expert covers a region of input space defined by a node in the base model's Probabilistic Language Trie. Each carries a formal error bound holding uniformly over its region. The central result is a self-certification theorem bounding approximation error by checkable quantities.

Magarshak proves LAWS generalizes both mixture-of-experts models and key-value prefix caching as special cases. It is strictly more expressive than any fixed-size mixture or finite cache. Further results cover a monotone hit-rate theorem. They also cover expert library growth tied to workload entropy, a fleet learning convergence speedup, and an over-the-air update bandwidth bound. The results are aimed at neural inference, robotics, and edge deployment.
arxiv-2605-04169:
Vincenzo Marco De Luca, Antonio Longa, Giovanna Varni, and Andrea Passerini model surgical team dynamics in real time, using graphs that expand over time. Surgical performance comes from craft plus non-technical skills such as talking and coordinating. Yet surgical AI mostly models visual workflow signals. In their setup, team members become time-indexed nodes. Messages between them become directed edges.

The expansion over time lets them model the interactions as they unfold. It still allows fast inference with a static graph neural network. The model predicts how far a procedure runs from its expected duration. Beyond prediction, a what-if analysis finds the smallest changes in how the team talks. It also finds plain behavioral variables tied to better predicted outcomes. Tests on recorded procedures show earlier flags for prolonged interventions. They also give coherent, actionable explanations.
arxiv-2605-04269:
Sharan Sahu and three co-authors analyse Adam, a widely used training optimizer, when the objective keeps changing over time, as in shifting data or moving targets. In that nonstationary setting, the optimizer must track a moving solution rather than settle on a fixed one.

Their bounds split the tracking error into clear parts: starting point, drift of the objective, and errors tied to Adam's two averaging parameters. They also give a high-probability guarantee for a projected stationarity measure under distribution shift. The results expose a trade-off: averaging and adaptive scaling help when noise dominates, but stale averages hurt when drift dominates.
arxiv-2605-05269:
Loay Abdelrazek, Leyli Karacay, and Marin Orlic propose a dynamic authorisation framework for software agents sharing knowledge bases in future 6G networks. As these networks decentralise into multi-agent systems, shared semantic knowledge needs finer protection than role-based access control gives. Roles alone cannot express what an autonomous agent should see for one specific task in its life cycle.

Their hybrid design combines roles with first-order logic predicates to enforce zero-trust checks at the level of single knowledge-graph triples. Permission inheritance is removed, so each subject-predicate-object fact is authorised on its own. Agents then receive only the metadata their current function requires, tightening access across the shared knowledge base.
arxiv-2605-05369:
Mohadeseh Azari and five co-authors ask how many raw entangled pairs a quantum data centre network needs to deliver high-quality entanglement over long multi-hop paths. Each swapping step along a path degrades the shared state, and purification can restore quality only if enough raw copies arrive. Extra copies from topology and repeated attempts do not by themselves answer that resource question.

Their topology-independent model treats each link as a Werner state and computes how ideal swapping compounds the loss with path length. They compare a classic recursive purification scheme with newer many-to-one protocols, computing success chances exactly by dynamic programming. The resulting resource landscapes show a threshold structure set by the basic entanglement condition on each path.
arxiv-2605-05469:
Simulating charged particles in a plasma takes serious computing power. Sonali Mayani, Paul Fischill, Sriramkrishnan Muralikrishnan, and Andreas Adelmann compare particle-in-cell schemes built in the IPPL library. The schemes differ in how they solve for the electric field, and all must run well on very different supercomputers.

They benchmarked the methods on Landau damping, a standard plasma test, at two large grid sizes. A Fourier solver was fastest in raw time but limited in where it applies. The other solvers cost about ten times more yet scaled just as well, and a Fourier-particle scheme offered a high-fidelity option.
arxiv-2605-05569:
Optimal transport asks the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. Anton Selitskiy and David Millard study the stability of the Monge map, the optimal reshaping itself, in the semi-dual form of the problem. They show that form has a degenerate saddle-point structure, and solving it amounts to a constrained optimization problem.

They derive exact conditions for when the transport maps converge, without demanding that the dual potential be optimal. The result explains a familiar annoyance: numerical solvers often need more iterations to settle the map than to settle the potential.
arxiv-2605-05769:
Fine-tuning large models across private devices with LoRA adapters runs into a structural annoyance: the adapter's two factors multiply, so averaging them across devices injects error, and privacy noise amplifies it. Myoungjun Kim, Sangwoo Park, Yoseob Han, and Jin-Hyun Ahn propose choosing, per layer and per round, which component to update. Their AS-LoRA framework adapts along three axes at once.

Layers independently select their active component; selections evolve over communication rounds; and a curvature-aware rule guides the choices. The design respects the asymmetry between the two factors instead of imposing one update mode everywhere.
arxiv-2605-06069:
U. Jena and three co-authors review topological spin freezing in frustrated quantum materials. In such materials, competing interactions, band topology, and quantum fluctuations combine to produce exotic group behavior. Glassy dynamics, first studied in amorphous solids and biology, now draw fresh study for the light they cast on spins and odd textures in these systems.

The review gathers evidence from heat measures, nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin probes, and neutron scattering. Together these reveal unusual spin dynamics, short range correlations, and low energy excitations that mark topological spin glass states. The authors also discuss fluid like spin modes and spin jam states in frustrated lattices. Their survey aims to link scattered observations with theory and guide the design of new quantum materials.
arxiv-2605-06169:
Pengqi Lu identifies a silent collapse mode that threatens very deep diffusion transformers. As these networks grow to hundreds of layers, token representations can homogenize while training still looks stable on the surface. Lu names the trigger event Mean Mode Screaming, a mean coherent backward shock that opens deep residual branches and pushes the network into a mean dominated state.

An exact split of the gradients into mean coherent and centered parts explains the collapse. Attention logit gradients also fade once values homogenize, compounding the problem. Lu's fix, Mean-Variance Split Residuals, gives the centered update its own gain and replaces the trunk mean with a leaky version. On a 400 layer model it prevented the crash that killed the baseline, and a 1,000 layer run stayed trainable.
arxiv-2605-06269:
Prince Mathew and Saina Sunny prove that the edit distance between finite-valued transducers is computable. Transducers generalize automata by producing output words for each input word, defining a relation between strings. A transducer is finite valued when every input yields at most a fixed number of outputs. It is functional when that number is one, the special case where edit distance was already known to be computable.

For transducers in general, the same question is uncomputable, so the boundary of what can be decided matters for formal language theory. Finite valued transducers are strictly more expressive than functional ones, which makes the extension substantive rather than cosmetic. The authors show the minimal number of edits needed to turn every output of one such transducer into an output of the other can always be computed.
arxiv-2605-06769:
Lucie Scharré and twelve co-authors ask why young galaxies show such extreme emission-line ratios compared with nearby ones. Galaxies at redshifts three to eight display oxygen line ratios pointing to harsher ionization and gas conditions. Their Lumen framework models nebular emission from many distributed star-forming regions inside a cosmological simulation, and is validated against low-redshift data before testing rival explanations.

No single mechanism suffices: alpha-element enhancement alone fails, while moderate offsets arise from combining it with a higher stellar mass cutoff and active nucleus contributions. The most extreme ratios need very massive star clusters driving high ionization, plus enhanced nitrogen for the highest nitrogen ratios. Dense gas helps some ratios but conflicts with sulfur observations.
arxiv-2605-06869:
Roger Creus Castanyer, Pablo Samuel Castro, and Glen Berseth present Agentick, a unified benchmark where reinforcement learning agents, language model agents, hybrids, and humans face the same sequential decision tasks. Agent research lacked common ground across these paradigms. Agentick offers thirty-seven randomly generated tasks across six skill groups, four hardness levels, and five input formats, all behind one standard interface.

The package includes reference oracle policies, fine-tuning datasets, a modular harness, and a live ranking board. In tests of twenty-seven setups over ninety thousand runs, no approach dominates. A small paid model leads overall, while a classic RL method wins planning and multi-agent tasks. A reasoning harness lifts language model scores several-fold. ASCII inputs beat natural language ones.
arxiv-2605-06969:
Yuchen Guo and five co-authors tackle how to judge fused infrared and visible images. Fusion combines heat information with visible detail, but common scoring methods can reward the wrong qualities. Human ratings help, yet reducing them to one averaged score loses disagreement between viewers.

Their system, FuScore, uses a multimodal language model to give a continuous quality score, closer to how people perceive images. Training labels reflect how much raters agreed on each image, and extra losses preserve ordering between methods and scenes. In experiments, FuScore matches human preferences better than earlier approaches, reaching leading results on the measures reported.
arxiv-2605-07269:
Al Muhit Muhtadi and Mostafa Rifat Tazwar defend retrieval-based language systems against indirect prompt injection in more than one language. Attacks hide instructions inside retrieved content, and multilingual settings make them harder to characterize. Their MIPIAD framework combines a fine-tuned sequence classifier with classic word-frequency features and tuned ensemble methods.

Testing used a synthetic benchmark of well over a million samples across email, table, question answering, abstract, and code tasks, in English and Bangla. Lexical features alone were already strong, and the hybrid ensemble reached the best overall detection score. Ensembles consistently shrank the performance gap between the two languages.
arxiv-2605-07469:
Francesco Giordano studies which game outcomes can be achieved when players see only coarse stats of an unsure process, not its full shape. Players know the means of a few random values and fill in beliefs by maximum entropy. He asks what a designer can achieve by sharing such partial information.

With open message spaces, workable outcomes coincide exactly with a class he calls jointly coherent ones, widening the usual linked balance points. For standard schemes, the test reduces to one cross-entropy check involving a linked balance point through the target. Cases across several game classes show how far it reaches.
arxiv-2605-07669:
Zhiqiang Wan and two co-authors study the initial value problem for the improved Boussinesq equation, a wave equation with a mixed time-space derivative term, when the starting data are quasi-periodic in space. Quasi-periodic means the data are built from several incommensurate frequencies at once, a harder setting than plain periodicity.

For a non-resonant frequency vector, they prove local existence and uniqueness of classical solutions that keep the same frequency vector. Two Fourier-side classes are covered: with exponentially decaying initial coefficients the solution keeps that decay on an explicit time interval, and with polynomially decaying coefficients it preserves the same decay rate. The results extend to a stronger power nonlinearity as well.
arxiv-2605-07769:
Thibaud Gloaguen and four co-authors show that autonomous coding agents often fail at doing nothing. Deployed agents will meet bug reports for issues already fixed, where the right move is to abstain; patching anyway piles up technical debt. They built FixedBench, two hundred human-verified tasks where no code change is required, to measure exactly this.

Across five recent models and four agent harnesses, even the best systems proposed unwanted changes in a large share of cases. Telling agents to reproduce the issue first helped, but created a new failure: on partly fixed issues they abstained when a patch was still needed. The authors name an action bias in current models and argue inaction must be framed as a route to success.
arxiv-2605-07969:
Ahmad Aghapour and Erhan Bayraktar explain why diffusion samplers stay efficient in high dimensions when theory said they should not. Many convergence guarantees charge the discretization error to the ambient dimension, which would make image models need far more steps than they use. Improved results assumed intrinsic geometric structure; this paper offers an information-theoretic alternative.

For Gaussian mixture targets, they prove the discretization error is controlled by the Shannon entropy of the latent mixture component, not by the ambient dimension. Step counts therefore scale with that entropy and only logarithmically with the data's second moment. The analysis extends to discrete targets, where the target's own entropy is the governing quantity. Compact latent structure, widely believed to underlie natural images, is what makes diffusion cheap.
arxiv-2605-08669:
Yizhe Huang, Bin Ling, Song-Chun Zhu, and Xue Feng model cooperation through will: a drive that holds a goal steady instead of recalculating profit at every step. Standard rational models blame failed cooperation on weak incentives, but constant maximizing can itself destabilize groups. Willed agents are cast as minimizers of a potential, set apart from cumulative utility chasers.

In endless population analysis, willed agents narrow the reachable state space and speed convergence in classic dilemmas. In spatial stag hunt simulations, they act as catalysts that push groups past risky thresholds where pure maximizers stall. Mixed will strengths help most, suggesting cooperation needs the capacity to pause calculation on purpose.
arxiv-2605-08769:
Chengdong Xu and six coauthors build multi agent workflows while a task runs, rather than freezing the design before execution starts. Long tasks shift subgoals and information needs stage by stage, so one shot workflow design fits poorly. EvoMAS treats workflow building as a sequence of decisions along one trajectory, constructing an explicit task state at each stage through planning, evaluation, and updating steps.

A learned adapter then assembles a stage specific layered workflow from a fixed agent pool, trained mainly on final verifiable success. Across research and question answering benchmarks, EvoMAS beats single agents and recent automatic design methods. Coordination that adapts as evidence arrives proves stronger than coordination fixed in advance.
arxiv-2605-08869:
Zeyu Li and five coauthors set the sub fields of AI side by side, and trace them through time. They use the paper stock itself as data. One block view of AI hides how its parts drift apart. Vision, learning, language, and web search each go their own way. Their count frame rests on talks with field pros and a sift of signs. It tracks twelve signs of reach, team work, and who writes, in more than one hundred thousand papers from 2000 to 2024.

All sub fields now spread fast through open, cross field webs. Yet their forms split. Vision leads in reach. Machine learning's firm ties shrink. Web work stays firm led. Language work stays calm. AI as one field has grown into a set of unlike fields.
arxiv-2605-09069:
Dong-Hui Yang and Bao-Zhu Guo study a class of wave-like equations in which a key term fades out inside the region, making the equations degenerate. Their 2026 paper works in higher dimensions, a setting the authors say had not yet been treated for this kind of problem. The central question is whether such hard equations have solutions, and whether those solutions can be steered as control theory requires.

First the pair prove that solutions exist. Then they approach the degenerate equations through a sequence of smoother, evenly wave-like equations that are easier to handle. That limit argument carries over into control results for the original equations. The work gives later researchers a route into a class of problems that had stayed largely open.
arxiv-2605-09169:
Ankit Hemant Lade, Sai Krishna Jasti, Indar Kumar, and Aman Chadha test a striking claim about causal discovery. The claim held that a Mamba model trained only to predict the next step could reveal which variables cause which, using a simple readout of its weights. Their 2026 paper packages the tests used to check that claim into a reusable benchmark meant to falsify weak claims.

Walking the claim through five stages, the team finds it does not survive. Simple linear methods match or beat the model, and tuned older tools lead on the clearest real benchmark. Much of the reported gain from added data turns out to reflect sample size, not method. A narrow result survives, but the benchmark itself is the lasting product.
arxiv-2605-09569:
Knight and Chhor pinned down the exact difficulty of spotting a planted submatrix hidden in noise. Given a noisy matrix, the task is to tell a pure-noise matrix from one carrying a small block of raised entries. Earlier work needed restrictive assumptions on the matrix and block sizes, leaving gaps in the theory.

The authors proved a minimax lower bound, the smallest signal strength that can possibly be detected, then built tests that achieve it. Extensions adapt to unknown block sizes without losing optimality. Their upper and lower bounds match for every configuration of sizes, closing the problem in non-asymptotic form. Biclustering in genomics and community detection in networks are the motivating uses.
arxiv-2605-09769:
Galat and Rizoiu built a system that classifies psychological defense mechanisms in emotional support dialogues. It placed second among 64 teams at the PsyDefDetect task with an F1 score of 0.406. Defense mechanisms are defined by absence: missing affect, blocked thought, denied reality. The team encoded that insight as an affect-cognition spectrum in prompt-level clinical rules, worth the largest single gain of 11.4 points.

Their core engine is a deliberative council of Gemini 2.5 agents, where class advocates rate evidence strength rather than voting, reaching 0.382 with no fine-tuning. The council proved confidently wrong on minority classes, with 59 to 80 percent of stable minority calls incorrect, pulled toward the majority class by an L7 attractor. A targeted override ensemble from three fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models added 2.4 points through just 16 overrides.
arxiv-2605-09969:
Wang, Isola and Cheung ask a basic methods question: when a language model generates tokens one by one, how should its hidden states be combined into one representation of what it knows? Tokens are produced under causal masking, so later tokens cannot see the future, yet averaging hidden states across generated tokens beats any single token. The paper measures this with kernel alignment to reference spaces.

The averaging gain holds across language, vision and protein domains, which fits information being spread across generated tokens rather than parked in one spot. Representations from generated tokens also beat those from prompt tokens alone. Tracking alignment across generation further reveals interpretable dynamics in model behaviour, suggesting generated text carries a richer internal record than the prompt does.
arxiv-2605-10069:
Tomo, Tamano and Yoneoka propose a rule-based way to average epidemic models into one shared trajectory. SEIR-type group models split a population into at-risk, exposed, infectious and removed groups. Different setting choices give different curves, and planners need a single summary that still respects the inner workings. Their method computes a constrained power Fréchet mean, a broad average, over a function space.

Exposed and infectious pairs are treated as objects in a Hilbert space, with equation and population limits baked into the optimisation so the average keeps some machine-like meaning. Full dynamics, including susceptible and removed groups, are then recovered from the estimated curves and parameters. A block-optimisation method makes the computation fast, and the method is illustrated with mock and literature-derived COVID-19 parameters from the early 2020 phase, with promise for model averaging and ensemble prediction.
arxiv-2605-10169:
Chatterjee and four colleagues solve infinite-state polynomial reachability games. These are two-player graph games where one player aims to reach a target set and the other aims to stay away. Such games matter for artificial intelligence and reactive synthesis, and many applications yield infinite-state versions. The paper asks whether the reaching player can win from a given start and how to compute a strategy.

Their first contribution is ranking certificates, a sound and complete proof rule showing the reaching player wins from a given start. Second, for polynomial games, where transitions and objectives are polynomial constraints over real variables, they give a fully automated algorithm. It computes a winning strategy plus a correctness witness. The algorithm is sound, semi-complete and sub-exponential in time. It solves literature examples beyond prior methods, including an optimal strategy for the classic Cinderella-Stepmother game at arbitrary precision.
arxiv-2605-10469:
Konstantinos Bampouras and Adrián Llinares compute an exact operator norm that had resisted calculation. The backward shift operator on Hardy spaces removes the constant term of a function and divides by the variable. It is a classical object in operator theory. Only three p values had known norms: 2 trivially, infinity at 2, and 1 sharply at 2 over root 3. Their 2026 paper adds p equals 4.

The authors prove that the backward shift on H4 has norm equal to the fourth root of phi, the golden ratio, one plus root 5 over 2. They also characterize all extremal functions: precisely the functions of the form mu times an inner function minus the square root of one over twice phi. Here mu is any complex number, and the inner function takes the value root of phi over 2 at zero. Readers get a sharp constant plus a full description of the functions attaining it.
arxiv-2605-10569:
Adam Gould and Francesca Toni make deep learning clear through argument. Deep learning dominates high-power modeling across diverse data types. But models tightly link feature mining with task goals and often lack clear reasoning steps, making it hard for humans to understand how predictions arise. Their 2026 paper introduces Deep Arguing.

Deep Arguing is an approach pairing deep learning with symbols, argument building, and reasoning for clear sorting across data types. Deep neural networks build an argument structure where data points back their assigned label and attack different ones. With smooth argument rules for reasoning, the model trains end-to-end to jointly learn feature patterns and argument links. The resulting structures give faithful case-based reasons for predictions. Structure constraints over the argument graph guide learning, improving both clarity and results. Tests on tabular and imaging datasets show performance matching standard baselines while offering clear argument reasoning.
arxiv-2605-10769: Wang and four colleagues propose MPerS, a system for segmenting remote-sensing scenes that lets multimodal language models perceive them from several expert viewpoints. Prompts generate high-quality captions, DINOv3 extracts dense visual features of land cover, and a Dynamic MixExperts module blends the most useful text semantics. Linguistic Query Guided Attention then steers visual features, giving superior results on three public segmentation datasets.
arxiv-2605-11069:
Alexey Ermakov and Alessandro Principi show that valley tilt controls the viscosity of two-dimensional Dirac fluids, motivated by twisted bilayer graphene tests. Moving the two low-energy Dirac cones against each other gives a direct handle on electron-fluid flow.

As cone splitting grows, the system passes through valley drain, charge-neutrality crossing, and electron-hole scattering start, producing a pronounced up-and-down response. By contrast, single-layer graphene's flow resistance falls smoothly as temperature rises because its inertial mass density depends strongly on warming, while a two-dimensional electron gas differs again. Dirac teams get valley control as a tuning route for fluid-like transport.
arxiv-2605-12269: Raluca Balan and Jaime Garza construct an Itô integral for a two-sided Lévy process with finite variance and no Gaussian part. Using Rosenthal's inequality for discrete-time martingales, they estimate the p-th moment of the integral for every even integer p at least 2. Through Poisson-Malliavin calculus, they show the integral extends the Hitsuda-Skorohod integral for the compensated Poisson random measure tied to the Lévy process.
arxiv-2605-13069: Zhao argues that Chinese computer science and engineering needs two words where it now uses one. Safety and security both translate as anquan, a compression that muddles standards interpretation, risk analysis and academic writing. While established legal and standards titles should stay, Zhao proposes scholarly and engineering writing translate security as anbao and reserve anquan mainly for safety. The article surveys the safety-security boundary in standards, tests the idea against AI assurance cases, and proposes a staged dual-track writing practice.
arxiv-2605-13169: Wang and seven co-authors study how multimodal models handle a 360-degree panorama as a whole, viewer-centred space, instead of splitting it into flat views. They define key skills including meaning anchors, spherical localisation, frame shifts and depth-aware 3D sense, and build a setup turning mixed-source shots into geometry-aware training. Their PanoWorld model injects spherical geometry into the visual stream via Spherical Spatial Cross-Attention. A new test benchmark, PanoSpace-Bench, shows PanoWorld clearly beats closed and open-source rivals.
arxiv-2605-13369: Song and colleagues present QueST, test time self training that adapts a language model to each query. Fixed models cannot fix their own misconceptions, and generic test time objectives lack query specific alignment. QueST builds structurally related problem solution pairs from the query itself and fine tunes efficiently on them before answering. Across seven math reasoning benchmarks plus a science benchmark, it beats strong test time baselines without any outside data.
arxiv-2605-13469: Emma Elley and three colleagues simulate radio-loud galactic nucleus jets to study how magnetisation and flickering shape their form. The physics that sets jet form is not fully understood. Using relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations with the PLUTO code, they cover steady and variable jets at two magnetisation levels. Steady high-magnetisation jets can produce lopsided cocoons, while a variable high-magnetisation jet can show a broken form. The interplay of magnetisation and variability can also produce kink instabilities along the beam, and both factors matter alongside power and environment.
arxiv-2605-13769: Abdalrahman Wael studies dense and mixture-of-experts transformers in a small-scale pretraining regime under one shared LLaMA-style decoder recipe. The sparse model swaps dense feed-forward blocks for Mixtral-style routed experts. In a three-seed full-data test, the dense active-match model reaches 1.6545 validation loss, MoE reaches 1.5788, and the dense total-match model reaches 1.5608. MoE thus lifts validation loss with active-parameter matching but does not beat dense training at equal total stored capacity.
arxiv-2605-13869: Alberto Ancilotto and three colleagues introduce the Elastic Spiking shifter, a runtime-flexing design bringing stretch into the spiking field. Current designs are rigid static networks with fixed setting counts and compute graphs. Spurred by doll-style coding learning, it embeds nested stretch in the Feature puller, Spiking Self-focus and Feed-Forward blocks. One Elastic Spiking shifter spans a broad range of tangle-hits swaps on CIFAR10/100, CIFAR10-DVS and the EHWGesture clinic gesture data.
arxiv-2605-13969: Duha and Bilitewski test if a spin-squeeze phase flip in bilayer spin models holds across the board. They swap grid shapes: square, triangle and honeycomb two-dimensional bilayers, plus one-dimensional ladders. They also rescale the links between layers against links inside layers. Bogoliubov instability checks plus truncated Wigner runs show the flip lasts in all four grids and over a wide rescale range, with critical exponents that match within error.
arxiv-2605-14069: Rezaei, Balaji and Krishnan offer SurF, a generative model for irregular multivariate event streams. Token-based methods break down when gaps between events span orders of magnitude. SurF leans on the Time Rescaling Theorem as a learnable bijection between event sequences and unit-rate exponential noise, letting one model train across mixed event-stream datasets. Three efficient parameterizations of cumulative intensity scale to long sequences, and a Transformer encoder supports multi-dataset pretraining. On six real benchmarks it leads on time error for three datasets.
arxiv-2605-14469: Jyothis and Martinez-Granado study geodesic currents, measures on the geodesics of a surface, whose dual distance is strongly hyperbolic, a coarse form of negative curvature stronger than Gromov hyperbolicity. They prove such currents are dense among all geodesic currents, using finite covers and boundary data. Currents from non-positively curved metrics are shown not to be dense, yielding infinitely many strongly hyperbolic metrics that are not CAT(0).
arxiv-2605-14569: Wei, Ma, Gao, Wang, Zhang, Gong, Tan, Yuan and Shan rebuild moving scenes from brain scans. Their CineNeuron framework first maps noisy fMRI signals onto rich embeddings covering words, images, actions and object types. A Mixture-of-Memories stage then picks relevant memories from earlier data and fuses them with the brain embedding to sharpen the video. The system is claimed to beat current methods on two fMRI-to-video benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-14869: Cermenati and team extend self-trapping of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays to mixed nuclei in cosmic threads. Escaping cosmic rays stir magnetic turmoil delaying release from magnetised sources, causing a hard spectrum. A leaky-box model with escape, photodisintegration, and secondary output is tested against Auger data, plus neutrino and gamma-ray output. Self-made turmoil suppresses escaping flux below the exa-electronvolt scale for plausible source brightness and field coherence spans, while heavy nuclei break into secondary protons below the ankle.
arxiv-2605-15269: Florian Ecker and four others construct rotating black holes in Carroll gravity by two routes. One dresses the Carroll-Schwarzschild solution with a spin charge using freedom in the Carroll-compatible connection. It yields a solution with no Lorentzian analogue. The other extends magnetic Carroll gravity from general relativity through an odd-power series in the speed of light. It gives a Carroll twin of Kerr, dubbed the Kerroll black hole, whose rotation is a by-nature odd-power effect. Conserved charges are worked out for both.
arxiv-2605-15569: Penghui Li, Hong Yau Chong, Yinzhi Cao, and Junfeng Yang present Neo, an agentic program-analysis framework for finding privilege-escalation flaws in microservices written in many languages. A language-model agent plans analyses, adapts code search, and checks semantics, supported by search primitives that scale across services. Tested on 25 open-source applications spanning seven languages and 6.2 million lines, Neo found 24 previously unknown privilege-escalation flaws with 81.0 percent precision and 85.0 percent recall, plus 18 more flaws in other domains.
arxiv-2605-16069: Honoré and Xiao introduce ITGPT, an attention-based model for mixed-type time series sampled at irregular intervals with missing values. Such gaps are common in health care and predictive maintenance. Trained with self-taught and generative goals, it reached top results on a health-monitoring task and a maintenance task. It needed no resampling, feature fusion, or explicit imputation.
arxiv-2605-16169: Ugwuanyi and three colleagues present LeanBET, a runnable and formally checked BET surface-area pipeline in the Lean 4 prover. Real-world BET code runs many steps whose correctness is rarely spelled out. Their checked version covers window listing, monotonicity checks, knee choice, and linear regression, with floating-point runs and proofs over the reals. Against the BETSI reference, LeanBET matches to machine precision on 18 of 19 isotherms, missing by only 0.03 percent on UiO-66.
arxiv-2605-16269: Yarlagadda and ten colleagues propose a Train-the-Trainers framework for peer-based mental health support in battlefield settings. Soldiers face sustained psychological stress, yet trained professionals are scarce in forward-deployed areas, so early distress often means evacuation and delayed care. In their model, soldiers who completed therapy and returned to duty train as peer facilitators, aided by specialized AI agents for triage, guided support, and documentation. A prototype built with the McDonald Army Health Center works in air-gapped and low-connectivity settings under human oversight.
arxiv-2605-16369: Magnot closes with the claims first: the total spherical space is smoothly contractible for any diffeological group. D-numerable principal bundles over them admit a classifying theorem with no regularity assumed. That comparison pits the product-subset diffeology on the Magnot-Watts Milnor join against the locally finite final diffeology carried by a signed spherical model. Squaring is smooth in the canonical map, while its positive square-root section is generally not. A separate smooth injection built on the locally finite simplicial model has a non-smooth inverse.
arxiv-2605-16469: Nützel, Dombrowski, and Kainz propose an offline plan for medical image boosting adding useful priors for tail classes. Rare diseases are scarce in hospital data sets, causing models to fail where detection matters most. Coarse labels lump diverse kinds into multi-modal settings biasing makers toward top submodes. The method partitions each coarse label into coherent groups via Gaussian mixture modeling, then learns subclass-conditioned source distributions per group. On long-tailed chest X-ray and CT benchmarks it improves tail-class fidelity and diversity and downstream balanced accuracy.
arxiv-2605-16569: Stefanescu surveys spectral bounds for Schrödinger operators with complex potentials, both deterministic and random. The survey covers both flat space and compact manifolds. It gathers existing results on eigenvalue bounds. It adds a new theorem stretching the compact-manifold bounds to fractional Laplacians, using methods of Cuenin and Sogge. The bounds are expressed through norms of their potentials. Together they give a single reference point for this corner of non-self-adjoint spectral theory.
arxiv-2605-16669: Peterson builds a framework that brings deformation and rigidity methods into continuous model theory for type II1 factors. He settles several open problems with it: the group von Neumann algebras of SL3(Z) and the free group on two generators are not elementarily equivalent, and the latter is not pseudomatricial. A Bass-Serre type rigidity result yields infinitely many pairwise non-equivalent full factors, each inside an ultraproduct of the hyperfinite factor. Building on Boutonnet, Chifan and Ioana, he also gives a continuum of such factors as group algebras.
arxiv-2605-17169: Hu and colleagues argue that responsible agentic AI needs explicit provenance. That means a traceable record across an agent system's whole life, so blame can be assigned when harm comes from combinations no single party designed. They formalize what such provenance must encode and show it can be estimated and acted on during operation. A concrete incident then shows who answers for what.
arxiv-2605-17369: Zhao and colleagues build a dual-branch deep-learning model that fuses magnetograms with magnetic parameters to predict solar flares a day ahead. Cross-attention merges the two streams. Cross-scale interaction then enriches multi-scale features. The model handles both binary prediction of C-class-or-stronger flares and multi-class sorting into C, M and X classes. Careful grouped cross-validation gives strong skill scores, best on intense X-class flares, with a low false-alarm rate.
arxiv-2605-17469: Dash and Kumar explain the magnetization plateaus of rare-earth tetraborides through partial Kondo screening. Hybrid and semiclassical Monte Carlo runs of the Kondo lattice model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice yield robust plateaus at fractions from one-sixth to three-quarters of saturation. Most plateau states are partially screened, born from competition among kinetic energy, Kondo coupling and magnetic frustration. The mechanism also simply explains anomalous magneto-transport in erbium and thulium tetraborides.
arxiv-2605-17569: Mokhtar Adda-Bedia and Rica argue helicity self-focusing drives finite-time singularities in inviscid flows. A self-similar flow field inspired by the Leray ansatz splits variables. That reduces Euler equations to a solvable nonlinear ODE system with a continuum of cases parametrized by exponent nu. Conservation laws then select singular ones. It focuses inside a shrinking tubular region separated by a sharp edge from an outer zero-helicity zone. Singularities may be point-like or line-like, and point-like cases recover Leray scaling.
arxiv-2605-17669: Zhang and colleagues propose a multimodal approach for extending heritage graphs. They introduce WJoconde, a new French heritage knowledge graph joining text and images, plus three versions for downstream research, with a benchmark for completion methods.
