They also propose a framework for growing cultural graphs with large language and vision-language models, combining automated extraction with a validation pipeline. Results show joining text and image information well enhances graphs with high trust. All code, benchmark datasets and original data with a live access point are open-sourced.
arxiv-2605-17869: Sivakumar K. S. and two colleagues defend classical SIFT against claims that learned descriptors have replaced it. Across an eight-configuration ablation on four benchmarks, SIFT with DSP multi-scale pooling beats neural replacements on metric while running 2 to 18 times faster. Learned matchers complement rather than replace classical features. The team presents PySIFT, the first GPU-resident SIFT, with zero-copy handoff to downstream frameworks. On an RTX 3050 it beats OpenCV SIFT on HPatches, runs faster on MegaDepth pairs, and gives bitwise deterministic output across runs and architectures.
arxiv-2605-18469: Federico Moretti and Andrés Rojas study, in a 2026 paper, positivity of twisted rank-g Picard bundles. They work on the g-fold symmetric product of a smooth projective curve. As an application they bound the degree of irrationality of any genus g Jacobian above by 2 to the g. They also bound the degree of irrationality of any (g-1)-dimensional Prym variety above by 2 to the 2g-3.
arxiv-2605-18569: Jiaji Zhang and two co-authors extend, in a 2026 paper, the reinforcement learning eigensolver RL-CQE. It now covers electronic excited states and real-time dynamics. A deep Q-network agent picks two-body operators on the fly each round, yielding compact ansätze robust to key hyperparameters. A compact state picture based on ACSE residuals grows with the one-particle basis but not with the number of targeted states. Tests on chemical systems hit chemical accuracy with few operators across bond lengths.
arxiv-2605-18869: Jan Büssing and four colleagues optimize prompts for performance and inference cost together, instead of chasing accuracy alone. Existing multi-objective methods lean on generic NSGA-II search and ignore efficiency. Their MO-CAPO algorithm adds budget allocation and a cost measure covering the full compute profile of inference. Across four tasks and three models it finds varied Pareto fronts of prompts trading accuracy against cost. It beats the NSGA-II baseline in eight of twelve noisy comparisons at far lower budgets.
arxiv-2605-19069: Sajjad Abdoli and four colleagues benchmark five commercial speech-recognition systems on speech that switches between languages mid-sentence, covering Egyptian and Saudi Arabic with English, Persian with English, and German with English. Their set holds 300 samples per language pair, chosen with a two-stage filter that cut language-model scoring costs by about 91 percent. Word-error and meaning-based scores agree on system rankings, though word error inflates the gaps roughly threefold by punishing correct transliterations. ElevenLabs Scribe v2 leads on both measures, and the dataset is public.
arxiv-2605-19369: Ravishka Rathnasuriya and Wei Yang tackle code-model answers that swing between bold errors and timid correct calls. Deployment needs three skills at once: gauging how likely an answer is right, holding back when unsure, and routing held-back cases to checks or repairs. Existing tuning tools, built for plain language, often fix score alignment without improving which answers rank as most likely right. Their unified design joins uncertainty scores, tuning, and tool-based handling, supporting risk-aware use across code sorting and generation tasks.
arxiv-2605-19469: Vignola and team propose SBSRL, a model-based reinforcement method that keeps learning safe by using constraints across a finite set of dynamics samples. That scheme approximates worst-case optimization over unknown dynamics and supports practical safety guarantees in continuous domains. Exploration instead limits epistemic uncertainty, removing the need for explicit exploration bonuses. Under mild conditions the authors prove high-probability safety in learning and a finite-time sample bound for near-optimal policies. Simulation and real-robot tests confirm safe, efficient exploration that extends to deep-ensemble control.
arxiv-2605-19669: Cao studies basic precision limits for gauging several parameters with a quantum probe at thermal equilibrium. He first shows the Heisenberg limit in probe number can be reached, with the bound matching the known single-parameter bound when only one parameter is estimated. The low-temperature limit then differs sharply from the finite-temperature case. An example shows the main results, and the paper gives rules under which the sensitivity bound can be reached plus the optimal readings giving it.
arxiv-2605-19769: Wei, Ma, Zhao, Zhou, Ni, Gan and Cohan build OpenComputer, a testbed for computer-use agents. It checks work against real software states instead of an AI judge. Four parts combine: state verifiers for apps, a self-improving verification layer, a pipeline that invents checkable desktop tasks, and a harness recording full runs with partial credit. Covering thirty-three apps and one thousand tasks, it matches human judges better than judge models. Leading agents still fail whole tasks, and open models fall sharply from their OSWorld scores.
arxiv-2605-19869: Sriram, Mokaria and Singh present a passive end-of-shift safety monitor for construction sites, the deadliest US industry sector. Video from body worn and wall mounted cameras passes three stages. YOLO11 covers protective equipment and hazard detection, SAM 3 covers segmentation and deduplication, and Qwen3-VL with a persona scaffolded adversarial protocol covers compliance checks. Persona backstories in the stage three prompt lift precision over single pass prompting, most on hallucination prone violations. The system maps violations to OSHA standards, scores ergonomic risk from pose keypoints, and issues reports.
arxiv-2605-19969: Biswas and nine co-workers build Argus, a 2026 defence for decentralised learning against hidden backdoor triggers. Honest nodes inspect model updates they receive, share suspected triggers with neighbours, and use a structural similarity test to separate true backdoors from false alarms caused by varied local data. Updates that fail the shared test are rejected, and repeat offenders are evicted. The authors also prove convergence guarantees, and tests on three datasets cut attack success by up to ninety points while keeping model quality close to an oracle.
arxiv-2605-20069: Alexander Goldberg, Giulia Fanti and Nihar Shah design partial lotteries that stay stable when scores shift. Lottery designs let a small change in one candidate's score cause large swings in selection probability, undermining the goal of softening fine distinctions near the cutoff. They formalise smoothness as a Lipschitz condition mapping scores to selection probabilities. Their Clipped Linear Lottery scales probability linearly with estimated quality between always-accept and always-reject thresholds. It matches the best regret for smooth rules up to a factor, and beats alternatives on peer-review data.
arxiv-2605-20569: Xu Han and seven colleagues improve hyperspectral object tracking by treating material separation and target location as one joint problem. Hyperspectral images carry rich material clues, but most trackers adapt colour trackers and ignore them. Their method couples the two tasks through a weighted loss that aligns material maps with location accuracy. It adds a decomposition module with adaptive frequency splitting for deep spectral unmixing.
arxiv-2605-20969: Indrajith VS and Disha Verma explore ergotropy and work output in quantum heat engines via quantum channels. Their engines use qubit and qutrit working media coupled to thermal baths through broad amplitude damping channels. They study how quantum channels model heat absorption, dissipation, and work output in open quantum thermal systems, giving conditions for positive work output. Effects of quantum links, emission probability, population shifts, and system-bath interactions are studied across operational regimes, with multilevel systems showing enhanced output and robustness.
arxiv-2605-21069: Philipp Bartmann and Matthias Keller study the boundary operator on simplicial complexes. They study the rule that applying the operator twice gives zero, on a weighted, infinite, and maybe non-locally finite complex. They characterize that rule in l-squared space via recurrence of the links of simplices. That rule ensures Hodge Laplacians act as delta-operator plus operator-delta and split into a direct sum of maps on k-forms, enabling relative cohomology classes.
arxiv-2605-21169: Artem Agafonov and co-authors propose a decentralized inexact cubic Newton method with a consensus step. Each agent holds a local goal and talks only to neighbors in a connected network, and consensus steps roughly average local iterates, gradients, and Hessians. Their method assumes L-one-smooth gradients and L-two-Lipschitz Hessians, with theory tracking errors from consensus and local disagreement. It matches exact cubic Newton iteration complexity with only polylogarithmic extra rounds of talk. An accelerated variant for strongly convex goals is also developed.
arxiv-2605-21569: Vivienne Bihe Chi and co-authors study when support escalates distress in language-model responses to venting and advice-seeking. People more and more turn to language models for emotional support. Yet tests rewarding replies that feel helpful may miss harmful acts. They add a method splitting feeling-support replies into Soothe, feeling comfort, Reframe, mind view shift, and Endorse, accord with a user's causal or moral framing. Friend- and therapist-style roles both raised Soothe but moved Reframe and Endorse in opposite ways.
arxiv-2605-21869: Dinithi Dissanayake and coauthors present a two-stage multimodal framework for emotion mimicry intensity prediction, entered in the Hume-ABAW10 challenge. The task predicts six continuous emotion intensities from in-the-wild clips. Modality-specific encoders train independently, then fuse through a regressor with modality dropout and encoder adaptation. The best validation system, fusing text, audio, vision, and motion under a four-to-one split, reaches an average Pearson correlation of zero point four seven two two. Placed third, with test correlation zero point five seven.
arxiv-2605-22469: Bartkowiak and colleagues introduce MaSC, a masked metric for text-to-image concept generation. Existing metrics judge the whole image, not subject versus background, and match human views poorly. MaSC uses foreground masks to split evaluation into concept preservation and prompt following. Concept preservation is scored by masked matching of foreground patches. Prompt following compares background and subject-stripped prompt embeddings. On DreamBench++ ratings, MaSC reaches Krippendorff alpha of 0.471, beating non-LLM baselines and GPT-4V. On ORIDa, it reaches AUC of 0.992, separating same from cross-subject pairs.
arxiv-2605-22669: Souza proves a strong local global conjecture on subnormalizers and character correspondences for p solvable groups with p odd. The result holds when the subnormalizer subset forms a subgroup, and also in general when the p length of the group equals 1. Along the way, Souza derives fresh properties tied to the Glauberman correspondence, extending a family of conjectures recently proposed by Moretó. The paper thus settles the strongest subnormalizer conjecture across a wide class of finite groups.
arxiv-2605-23769: Yang and colleagues show Hubbard correlations can split the spectral flow of a Thouless pump. DMRG calculations identify at filling two-thirds a pump with Chern number two, or two charge units per cycle. A model gives the same response through edge flow in two spin channels. In the Hubbard model, the bulk pump works differently at an open boundary: edge flow separates into two events, and the intervening state is a neutral triplet excitation. Thus charge transport remains integer, but correlations reorganize boundary form into charged and neutral sectors.
arxiv-2605-23869: Christophe Eloy offers a unified theory for how soft bodies move and deform in slow viscous flow. The problem spans swimming microbes to soft microrobots. Applying virtual power and a reciprocal theorem to a hyperelastic body yields one configuration dependent differential equation for its generalized coordinates. That equation extends rigid body mobility theory with deformation dependent tensors. Tests on spring linked sphere assemblies validate the approach. A differentiable JAX implementation enables inverse design. It recovers a three sphere swimmer optimum and designs a soft surfer that outclimbs its rigid twin.
arxiv-2605-24269: Karim and eight co-authors push star-quake detection for cool dwarfs using TESS light curves. Solar-like tremors, stirred by near-surface boiling, are well listed in evolved stars but rarely confirmed in main-line dwarfs, whose signals run faint. A conv autoencoder trained on TESS two-minute light curves spots tremor features with near-perfect test scores and strong hits and recall. From the Asteroseismic Target List it flags 3463 tremor-star hopefuls, cutting to 24, several in color-brightness zones needing pricey spectra, widening the TESS frontier.
arxiv-2605-24569: Roblex Nana Tchakoute and Claude Tadonki survey energy-efficient computing across the cloud-edge-HPC continuum, from microcontrollers to multi-megawatt data centers. Energy use has become a systemic bottleneck as large-scale AI workloads grow, driven by climate, carbon, and energy-supply constraints. The authors organize a taxonomy spanning hardware and software, measurement, and scheduling. It also covers voltage scaling, workload consolidation, federated learning, and cooling. Large-scale AI gets emphasis for its heavy resource demands, and the 2026 survey closes with a forward-looking roadmap for sustainable computing.
arxiv-2605-24669: Md Sharif Hossen and others map how altitude reshapes 5G service for drones. Downward-tilted antennas serve and jam flying users through sidelobes. That regime differs sharply from ground users. The authors build a standards-compliant model with multi-site tri-sector layouts, realistic antenna patterns, and line-of-sight odds. They track received power, received quality, and signal-to-interference ratio. Higher flight shifts users from coverage-limited to interference-limited service. Power fades gradually, but interference grows fast, while wider site spacing improves quality despite lower power.
arxiv-2605-25069: Enrico Lampetti and Michele Pernice prove that a class of geometric objects called perverse character varieties always has an algebraic structure known as quasi-affineness. Their argument stays entirely inside stack theory, a framework for handling spaces with symmetries. It works by producing enough sections of the structure sheaf, the object that tracks functions on the space. The result settles the shape question for these varieties in one short, self-contained proof.
arxiv-2605-25169: JungHo Lee, Johnna Sundberg, Pim Welle, and Bryan Wilder design trials that learn treatment effects while still serving highest-need people first. They are randomized into priority queues by risk score, then served by queue and arrival order as budget allows. With exogenous arrivals, treatments are conditionally randomized and standard effects can be read off. With endogenous arrivals, queue randomization instead acts as an instrument, yielding local effects induced by queuing. Optimized queue plans trade statistical efficiency against prioritizing higher-need applicants, shown with housing allocation data.
arxiv-2605-25469: Kai Yi, Vignesh Vivekraja, Harshit Khaitan, and Steven Li train low-precision models without the straight-through estimator. That estimator forces gradients through quantizers by fiat, making training brittle near bin edges and misaligned with low-precision behavior. Their JacQuant framework learns a lightweight surrogate of local effects, cheap in diagonal form and compatible with common quantizers. It proves convergence for non-convex goals with linear rates under a PL condition. At most 2 bits it beats straight-through training at negligible added cost.
arxiv-2605-25569: Yufeng Yang and colleagues give users a dial for brightening dark photos instead of a single fixed result. Earlier enhancers train on narrow sets with one target, limiting control and generalization. ControlLight trains on a large set of real degraded images labeled with continuous illumination strength, and a misalignment-aware flow-matching loss keeps structure steady as the dial moves. Users can therefore tune strength freely while outputs stay consistent and realistic, and tests report state-of-the-art quality with strong generalization.
arxiv-2605-25969: Lin and four colleagues merge two fixes for slow, costly text generation: linear-time recurrent models and diffusion models that fill in many tokens at once. The clash is that diffusion needs two-way attention while recurrent models read one way only. Their B3D-RWKV design resolves it with a triplet-block layout, keeping linear-time inference while generating in parallel. A 7.2-billion-parameter version matches rival models on an eight-task suite and decodes about 1.6 times faster on average.
arxiv-2605-26069: Saha, Jangid, Sharma and Sadhu study how slow bonds change current fluctuations in a classic particle model. The symmetric simple exclusion process hops particles on a lattice, one per site, out of equilibrium. Exact large-deviation results for current exist widely, but localised slow bonds alter them. Three geometries are treated: a finite line between unequal reservoirs, a semi-infinite line with a boundary reservoir, and an infinite line with slow bonds near the origin. For each, exact large-deviation functions are derived and checked by rare-event simulation.
arxiv-2605-26169: Pierre Dantas, Lucas Cordeiro, and Waldir Junior survey ESBMC, a checker that proves software free of certain errors by testing logical rules. It began in 2009 as a tool for embedded C code. The 2026 survey follows its growth into a platform with nine language front ends, industrial solvers, and recent links to language models and autonomous agents. It records dozens of competition wins, major awards, public funding, a spin-off, and a defense deployment, then maps open problems.
arxiv-2605-26269: Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay's 2026 benchmark, AgentSecBench, tests security for language-model agents that treat prompts, fetched records, and tool observations as one shared channel. That sharing lets untrusted strings sway secret answers or action proposals without any fixed policy. Their framework defines three games, for instruction integrity, retrieval confidentiality, and capability integrity, with noninterference from intent to execution and permitted leakage. Tests of six defense classes on two small Qwen models show when risk falls with channel closure and when visible adversarial capability stays exploitable.
arxiv-2605-26469: Yu Liu, Yu-Zhe Liu, and Panyue Zhou study quotients of extriangulated categories. Motivated by hereditary algebras, they define a hereditary-type subcategory W inside a category E. They prove the quotient E/W is quasi-abelian: additive, with kernels and cokernels where kernels survive pushouts and cokernels survive pullbacks. They further show E/W is abelian exactly when W forms a cluster tilting subcategory under a suitable relative structure. Examples recover known abelian hearts and yield fresh abelian or quasi-abelian quotients outside classical settings.
arxiv-2605-26569: Daniel Schweizer and five colleagues present Distribution-aware Conformal Prediction, or DCP, a unified framework for time-series intervals. DCP mixes Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, and quantile fits with conformal tuning. Numerical inversion builds bounds, taking any pairings. Benchmarks on made-up and real series show adaptive tuning under shifting uncertainty. Modular design supports tests of predictor-score pairings, backed by a new Winkler score for truth and speed. DCP extends Conformalized Quantile Regression and Conformalized Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2605-26969: Zhu and six colleagues build Recon, a method that scores reasoning traces for user modeling by their power to predict actions. Older methods condition traces on both context and action, guaranteeing justification but not true causal reasoning. Recon instead asks a reconstruction model to predict the action from context plus candidate reasoning, and fidelity sets trace quality. Recon wins 54.7 percent of comparisons against Backward Synthesis and up to 70 percent downstream, and its traces transfer across models.
arxiv-2605-27569: Georgina Cosma and Axel Finke introduce RULER, a representation-level check for machine unlearning. Output tests can pass while forgotten records linger in middle layers, so one metric compares forget-set positions against a retrained model, and another reads traces from internal similarity alone. Four approximate methods pass output tests yet show clear traces in 10 of 12 conditions.
arxiv-2605-27669: Pedro Barbassa, Gabriel Barbosa, and Mauricio Correa study stacky shapes and logarithmic topology of transversely affine foliations. To each foliation they attach a holonomy group and quotient stack, the base shape for the multiplicative developing map, with reparametrizations as stack maps. On the log side, the Kato-Nakayama space gives edge traits that rule edge-torus motion and a log lift of the same map.
arxiv-2605-28169: Liu and colleagues automate chip hardening against soft errors, which grow likelier as transistors shrink. FT-Pilot first uses a graph network to spot vulnerable circuit assets at RTL level, then lets a language-model engine rewrite the code for fault tolerance with retrieval help and auto-repair. The hardened designs check out as correct and synthesizable while cutting output error rates sharply.
arxiv-2605-28469: Francesco Ancilotto studies wetting between self-bound quantum fluids in a three-component mixture of sodium and potassium atoms. Tuning one interspecies scattering length varies the softer liquid's surface tension, driving a shift from partial to complete wetting of the stiffer liquid. In the complete-wetting regime, the softer liquid wraps a spherical droplet, forming a free-standing core-shell droplet with a hollow, shell-like density profile. Such shell droplets can also sustain quantized vortices, opening a route to study capillarity, topology, and superfluidity.
arxiv-2605-28669: Jan Christian Blaise Cruz and Alham Fikri Aji introduce ACROS, which induces a sense pathway into a frozen pretrained decoder model. Sense representations, meaning decompositions, aid disambiguation, steering, and cross-lingual alignment, but require pretraining with sense structure in place. ACROS adds a gated residual addition, preserving model quality while supporting zero-shot word-sense disambiguation, low-KL steering, and cross-lingual adaptation. On SmolLM2-360M it reaches competitive disambiguation scores, recovers about ninety percent of positive steering shifts with a proxy, and adapts to four languages.
arxiv-2605-28769: Kevin Y. Li, Asher Trockman, Ananda Theertha Suresh, and Ziteng Sun propose Oryx, a hybrid model switching between mixers across a token sequence. Softmax attention costs linear memory and quadratic compute, while linear recurrent models lag on long-context retrieval and in-context tasks. Oryx ties at least 90 percent of parameters across mixers, letting attention and recurrent modes share representations. With Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet variants up to 1.4B, Oryx matches or beats single-mixer baselines under fixed token budgets, and at 1.4B every instance beats its counterpart.
arxiv-2605-28969: Aarik Gulaya introduces representational accuracy: how well a system captures a person's reading, via a Behavioral Specification. The build compresses personal data tightly into reading patterns served as context to a language model. Tested on 14 memoirs with a five-judge panel, the Specification lifts accuracy and nearly ends hedging. It recovers most of the raw corpus value at about 25 times less context cost. Gains are largest where scores start lowest and on reading questions, while on recall questions the layer can get in the way.
arxiv-2605-29169: Ahmad Tashfeen and Qi Cheng strengthen sieving for the shortest vector problem, the backbone of modern quantum-safe cryptography. Older cryptography rests on integer factorization and discrete logs, both open to attack by a fully working quantum computer, threatening even data stored today. The authors enhance Laarhoven's genetic view of Ajtai and coauthors' sieving with field-aware vector codes and crossover. Their approach extends from integral lattices to module lattices, giving quantum-safe schemes a sharper tool against future decryption.
arxiv-2605-29669: Collin Cranston, Zhichao Wang, Todd Kemp, and Michael W. Mahoney ask whether linear stand-ins for nonlinear matrices still mean anything for nonlinearly separable classification. They study the conjugate kernel of a one-layer net on XOR, tracking outlier eigenvalues and whether their vectors line up with labels. A sturdy quadratic stand-in for the kernel matrix traces informative spikes as sample size, signal-to-noise ratio, activation choice, and pretrained features vary. They find regimes where these knobs push past the linear stand-in and spark label-aligned spaces.
arxiv-2605-29769: Lihong Feng, Ali Hassan, and Shuwen Sun build surrogates for convection-heavy parametric problems, where slow width decay defeats linear reduction. Their hybrid pairs a projection-based reduced model with a net that learns leftovers, keeping the model small. Net and model parts are built offline, then coupled online for predictions. Where solver internals hidden, a non-intrusive variant drops the need for operators, with a lighter net than deep-learning surrogates. On one- and two-dimensional Burgers tests, both variants beat rivals on accuracy at lower prediction time.
arxiv-2605-29869: João Paulo Biazotto, Daniel Feitosa, Paris Avgeriou, and Elisa Yumi Nakagawa present TagDebt, a GitHub bot for technical debt management. Technical debt names suboptimal choices harming maintainability, and tracking it matters though taking it on is not bad. TagDebt labels issues as self-admitted debt or not, making debt visible in workflows. A design study built it, and sixteen practitioner interviews found it useful for organizing issues and cutting manual work, with clear documentation. Team and codebase size shaped adoption; users suggested code checking and updating.
arxiv-2605-30069: Simon B. Porter and eight colleagues publish a revised shape model for Arrokoth, the Kuiper Belt object visited by New Horizons in 2019, built from every resolved LORRI image. A faster GPU-aided fitting method pins down shape and spin pole better than the first post-flyby model. The contact binary turns out thicker and larger, with small lobe Weeyo near-spherical and larger lobe Wenu flattened, at a volume ratio near two to one. Wenu's squashed shape would dim average brightness at some viewing angles, affecting counts of contact binaries.
arxiv-2605-30269: Zhongling Wang, Raymond Zhou, Shahrukh Athar, Wenbo Yang and Zhou Wang propose a general framework for unsupervised image quality score fusion using deep Maximum a Posteriori estimation. Individual quality models are often biased toward certain image content or distortions, depending on design. Their model estimates uncertainty at the score level to increase accuracy and reduce uncertainty in fused predictions. Tests show superiority over individual models and other fusion methods, plus an ability to reject bad models during fusion.
arxiv-2605-30669: Dalbah and colleagues sharpen covariant density functional theory by tuning the harmonic-oscillator basis. Building on earlier work on point-coupling functionals and excited states, they set the oscillator frequency against infinite or extrapolated benchmarks. They produce globally tuned scaling factors and basis sizes for set accuracy. Tuned bases also sharpen potential energy curves, fission barriers, and fission isomers in actinides and heavy nuclei. Bound single-particle energies improve too, except weakly bound neutron states with low orbital momenta. Halo densities come out well with very large bases.
arxiv-2605-30869: Bellingeri, Gassiat, and Nouaille prove Young shifts fill the rough-path space densely. Starting from one geometric rough path, smooth-path shifts can bring it as near as wanted to any other, measured in rough-path topology. From this they draw full-support tests for paths coming from random series and Gaussian processes, non-centered fractional Brownian cases included. Put simply, shifting alone reaches every corner of the space.
arxiv-2605-31369: Caucheteux, Bonet, and Korba unify a family of generative models that tune one distribution toward another. Wasserstein gradient flows give a continuous-time recipe for this tuning, approximated by implicit steps known as the JKO scheme. The authors show many existing methods fall out as instances of parametric JKO schemes. They push the frame past f-divergences to integral probability metrics and squared mean discrepancy. From there they derive fresh JKO-based generative algorithms.
arxiv-2605-31469: Gedeon and colleagues expand the Hungarian dialogue speech corpus BEA-Dialogue into BEA-Dialogue+. They ease its strict speaker split, so 200 hours of transcribed natural talk become usable, up from 85. Primary speakers still never cross the train and test sets. That setup lets researchers study how speaker overlap trades off against data size. Tests with Whisper- and FastConformer-based models show the larger set is harder raw, but fine-tuning with serialized output training improves all four error scores.
arxiv-2605-31569: Yanakieva and team present a logic-based system in Datalog for CRDTs, covering conflict-free replicated data types. Local-first collaboration lets many users update shared data at once without global coordination, which demands careful design for concurrent use. The system models CRDTs as live logic programs over operation contexts, making concurrency plain and open to auto checks. Property-based testing compares implementations, and a graph editing case study assesses correctness and scalability as operations and replicas grow.
arxiv-2606-00069:
Turacan and co-authors make LiDAR perception honest about its own uncertainty in this 2026 arXiv paper on Invascal. Self-driving systems use LiDAR, laser ranging that maps the surroundings in 3D, to segment scenes into objects and surfaces. Knowing when a segmentation is unreliable matters for safety, yet standard confidence scores are overconfident, while trustworthy ensemble methods cost too much computation for real-time driving. Their adapter head splits the job: one part ranks classes, another estimates how much evidence supports the prediction.

The strength signal is trained with a new self-calibration objective that trains uncertainty quality while preventing runaway evidence growth, a failure mode of earlier evidential methods. Across several LiDAR datasets and backbone networks, calibration improved over deterministic training with minimal added cost. Accuracy stayed competitive, whereas prior evidential approaches usually sacrificed accuracy for theirs. The authors release their code publicly for the intelligent transport community.
arxiv-2606-00169:
Saif and co-authors weigh old and new tools for spotting clients set to leave a shop. Firms lose when buyers switch to rivals with ease. Sound forecasts of churn help aim ads and keep buyers. The team frames churn calls as a yes-or-no task on time-based data.

They test three classic tools: random forests, XGBoost, and support vector tools. These face a fresh joint model built for time-based tasks. That model can track rich time links and ties between inputs. Still, the classic tools win on most counts. They score higher, need less data, and cost less to train and run. The edge holds across data sets and ways of marking churn.
arxiv-2606-00369:
Saakyan, Rastogi, and Aroyo gauge how much land and lore shape AI safety marks. Safe world use of AI needs fit with values that shift by place. Judge pools in safety sets still hail from few lands. Demos like age and sex may not catch the true split.

The team first scan past safety sets for land-based facts. Most sets log no such facts, and no shared way joins them with demo traits. They then model marks with world lore zones from Inglehart and Welzel. Zone ties add clear spread past plain demo traits in six sets. Near a tenth of items prove lore-touchy in their scan. Chat models fail as stand-in judges but can flag such items for folk.
arxiv-2606-00469:
Álvarez and co-authors view neural ODE learning through the lens of control math. Such models let a net's state flow by a law that shifts with time. Fit and broad skill for them lacked crisp bounds in the past. The team study a class with fixed weights and clear time ties.

They prove this class can fit set data in an exact way. A stronger trait lets its flows send split cells to tiny target balls at will. That trait turns fit skill into broad skill by a plain route. Risk bounds match those of bin and near-kin tools when width scales with draws. Time ties prove key: two-layer time-free forms can fit but lack the strong trait.
arxiv-2606-00569:
Sahu and co-authors refute a claimed find of a rare sulfur form in a star-birth zone. The form, dithioformic acid, bears on the case of the lost sulfur. Space holds less of it in sight than tales say it should. A past claim placed the form in the IRAS 4A2 zone.

The team re-read the same ALMA data with full line and chem models. No clean line in the data is the form's alone. All claimed lines match known, rich forms in the zone. Firm caps are set on how much of the form can hide there. Chem models put those caps in a sane frame. The null fits what rare twin-sulfur forms would lead one to hope.
arxiv-2606-00769:
Vranas and co-authors report a surprise in a layered oxide film in this 2026 paper. The material is La1/3Sr2/3FeO3, a perovskite oxide where spin, charge, and lattice effects couple tight. It is known for a joint shift near 190 K, where it turns antiferromagnetic and orders its charge at once. Its life below 100 K in thin films was less well known.

The team probes the film with X-ray scattering and spectroscopy down to low heat levels. Resonant X-ray scattering shows the known magnetic and charge order fades out in full below about 25 K. More tests trace the electron structure and how domains move in this new cold phase. The authors suggest the fade may stem from small domain size in thin films. The find adds to the study of rival forces in strongly coupled materials. Such materials can host linked orders that fight or help each other.
arxiv-2606-00869:
Li and co-authors teach language models to doubt themselves well in this 2026 paper. Reward-based training sharpens reasoning, but its outcome-only rewards breed bold answers on shaky grounds. Past fixes teach refusal at the reply level. That can drill in surface habits of saying no, not real judgment.

Their method, Cognitive Pairwise Training, is a mid-training stage. The model compares pairs of reasoning traces and learns to tell sound ones from flawed ones. That contrast builds an inner boundary for reasoning quality. The signal can then be reused, not spent on one reply style. Across five model sizes and three families, the trade-off improves, they report. At 14 billion parameters, their pipeline beats the standard one by 2.2 math points and 5.6 abstention points. Trace quality rises too, and the gains hold across settings.
arxiv-2606-01069:
Chakraborty and co-authors read emotions from faces in live video in this 2026 paper. A face can pass through many states in one clip. Those states vary a lot from person to person. Expression change is smooth, not a set of hard jumps, which makes it hard to model. A tool that tracks the drift could aid counselors as they work.

Their system is a deep network built at many scales. Supervised contrastive learning shapes its features, so like expressions pull close and unlike ones part. The design targets real time use on standard video. Training runs on a standard dataset for this task. The authors report very satisfactory outcomes from the system. They present it as a support for psychological counseling, where a second read on a subject's state has value. The paper adds to work on affect aware computing, with stress on change over time.
arxiv-2606-01169:
Pavanello, De Veld, and Armellin find the last safe moment to dodge in orbit in this 2026 paper. Low thrust satellites facing a collision must know more than a good maneuver. They must know how late it can start and still work. Their method works backward from the danger point.

The greedy sweep starts at the nominal closest approach time. It propagates the maneuver backward step by step. At each step it picks the thrust direction that locally lowers the chosen danger metric. Differential algebra carries state sensitivities along, so the closest approach time updates online. Tests run on a large set of real conjunctions. Two safety metrics are used: miss distance and collision probability. Accuracy is high, with only a small loss against an optimal control benchmark. Run times fit on board use. The tool suits operators who must decide, fast, when a dodge can no longer wait.
arxiv-2606-01269:
Singh asks if transformers learn a mental number line from pairs. People infer that A is below C from A below B and B below C. They do so with an inner line, not logic chains. Far pairs feel easier than near pairs. Singh trains small models on adjacent pairs only. A hidden total order sits behind those pairs. He then tests them on far pairs they never saw.

The models generalize to the unseen pairs. Their embeddings collapse onto a one-dimensional curve. Its main axis tracks the hidden rank near perfectly. Confidence and spacing grow with rank distance, like in humans. A large pretrained model shows the same shape. Lines fit sizes and digits, while cycles fit months.
arxiv-2606-01469:
Bakhtiyarzadeh, Tekanlou, and Razmara extract terms from Italian waste data. Automatic term extraction powers most search engines today. Accurate labels are hard for this task, though. Few annotated documents exist for training. Multi-word terms also shift meaning across domains. Their method, Peacemaker, was built for the ATE shared task. It fine-tunes an encoder model for extraction. The setup runs on small compute by design.

Scores cover type-level and micro-level views of performance. Precision, recall, and F1 all get reported. Results stay consistent and balanced against other teams. The technique is straightforward, but that is a strength. It offers a good start for low-resource models. Interpretability holds as models scale up later.
arxiv-2606-01669:
Chen, Harhay, and Li bound causal effects when a key premise may fail. Principal stratification handles intermediate variables in causal work. Point estimates of its effects need the principal ignorability premise. That premise cannot be tested in practice. Their frame is a sensitivity analysis for when it fails. A margin-free factor captures the size of the failure. It is built from relative risks tied to an unmeasured confounder.

Sharp bounds for each causal effect follow from that factor. The bounds sit inside worst-case bounds, with or without monotonicity. Cornfield-type rules say how strong confounding must be to nullify an effect. E-values state that same threshold in one number. The method extends to broader causal effects and pairwise estimands over a product space.
arxiv-2606-01869:
Lu and co-authors build a test for code that creates 3D worlds. Chat models now write interactive worlds, not just static pages. Browser 3D worlds rest on tools like Three.js. Such worlds must obey space and physics rules. Controls must stay in sync with hidden state.

Past tests watch only pixels or page nodes. The canvas hides the world's true mechanics. Their WorldCoder-Bench holds 2,026 expert-made tasks. Tasks span simulation, rendering, and app scenarios. A probe tool runs each program in a sandbox. It checks hidden contracts on states and shifts. The checks are hardened against simple mutation tricks. Scores also track return on automation and time saved.
arxiv-2606-01969:
Heander and co-authors study how developers review AI-written code changes. Chat-model agents now produce multi-file changes for review. No validated workflow exists for that review scenario. IDE tooling for it is also undesigned so far. Trust calibration emerged as the central challenge.

The study uses a participatory design process with JetBrains. Seventeen industry practitioners joined the discover phase. Seven returned for the develop phase of the study. A conceptual design came out of the deliver phase. A high-fidelity prototype was built from that design. A follow-up survey tested it with 43 practitioners. Two research questions guide the whole study. Findings shape workflows for reviewing generated changes.
arxiv-2606-02069:
Lian interprets light and heavy scalar hints in an extended Higgs model. A scalar near 95 GeV has been hinted at twice. LEP saw it in the bottom quark channel. LHC diphoton searches point the same way. Heavier scalar searches have grown more restrictive lately. A recent CMS analysis of four bottom quarks tightened them.

The model is the mu-term extended NMSSM. A singlet-like scalar can sit near 95 GeV there. Heavier doublet states fall in the CMS probed range. Higgs data and flavor limits constrain the study. Electroweak precision tests and SUSY searches also bind it. Viable regions fit both the diphoton and bottom rates. The work weighs the excesses against cascade limits.
arxiv-2606-02269:
Woo builds a cohesive infinity-topos that carries a quantum modality. The model is a functor topos over finite dimensional C-star algebras. Maps in that base are centre preserving star homomorphisms. The codomain is the smooth cohesive infinity-topos. Cohesion is lifted pointwise from that smooth base.

A quantum comonad is defined by precomposition with the centre functor. It is idempotent and product preserving by construction. A right adjoint accompanies it in the structure. Beck-Chevalley compatibility ties it to the cohesive structure. That structure has the usual cohesion operators. Day convolution gives the topos a monoidal structure. The work joins higher topos theory with quantum algebra. Category theorists are the main audience for the result.
arxiv-2606-02969:
Popik, Yang, and Bisheban compare three ways to model a flexible-link robotic arm with two degrees of freedom. Rigid-body models miss the unmodeled dynamics of flexible links. The team tests two physics-informed models that pair rigid-body dynamics with a Gaussian mixture model for residual errors and flexibility. A kinematics-based regression model serves as a purely data-driven baseline.

Using an open-source dataset, the team first estimates torque predictions with ridge regression on kinematic features. Ordinary least squares then re-estimates the same parameter set from the data itself. Physics-based parameters gave the poorest accuracy. Regularized and least-squares estimators matched measured torques more closely. Residual analysis showed the limits of purely parametric models for flexible links. The authors conclude that regularization and data-driven identification matter, and they support semi-parametric residual learning as a next step.
arxiv-2606-03769:
Cauvin and Mertikopoulos study stochastic mirror descent under heavy-tailed noise. Gradient noise with infinite variance can break standard convergence proofs. The question is whether mirror descent keeps its guarantees in that regime. A continuous-time model frames the answer. Mirror descent becomes a stochastic differential equation driven by Lévy noise. Finite moments of order p, between one and two, are assumed.

The scaling limit is named the Lévy mirror flow. Its paths can jump by any size when p is below two. Despite that wild behavior, near-optimality arrives in a set time bound. The convex case and the strongly convex case each get explicit rates. Matching discrete-time guarantees follow for several mirror descent variants. The results show exactly how frequent long jumps slow convergence. Optimization readers get a robust map of a noisy frontier.
arxiv-2606-03869:
Bacsó and co-authors resolve charge and spin textures in a gallium-doped europium magnet. The compound is Eu(Al,Ga)4 with ten percent gallium. Resonant X-ray diffraction separates the two textures. A charge density wave appears below about 75 kelvin. Its order grows steadily on cooling, then drops sharply near 15 kelvin.

Magnetic satellites mark two distinct domains below about 14.8 kelvin. That ordering point matches the charge wave's sudden drop exactly. Strong coupling between charge and spin orders is the natural reading. Azimuthal scans reveal helical spin patterns. One domain is a plain helix with an elliptical envelope. The other tilts into a helicoidal form. Intensity ratios in two light polarizations stay fixed with temperature. A single magnetic phase holds below the transition, unlike the undoped material's staged order. Substitution effects on the ground state await theory.
arxiv-2606-04069:
Sinan Yıldırım and Megha Khosla propose in 2026 a new way to measure privacy leakage in graph neural networks, models that learn from connected data such as social or citation networks. The privacy question is whether a specific person's node was inside the training graph.

Older measures borrow assumptions from non-graph settings and miss how sampling a training graph changes each node's prior odds of inclusion. Their Bayesian Membership Privacy framework treats the attack as a hypothesis test and reports the attacker's updated belief for each node. They also give a practical auditing procedure to estimate it. On benchmark graphs, the measure exposed fine-grained differences in leakage between nodes that a single global attack accuracy number completely hid.
arxiv-2606-04269:
Yilong Wang, Cheng Qian, and Edward Johns present Instant-Fold in 2026, a robot learning framework that teaches cloth-like object manipulation from a single human demonstration. Folding and similar tasks are hard because soft objects have huge state spaces and many valid ways to succeed.

Instant-Fold first learns deformation-aware visual features through temporal contrastive pretraining, teaching it what changes when fabric moves. A flow-matching transformer then conditions on the demonstration itself to infer and execute the intended folding mode, including variations in order and placement, with no further training at test time. The system was trained entirely in simulation. It generalized across diverse folding modes and transferred to a real robot with no extra data or fine-tuning, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-04469:
Brown and Russell improve the trustworthiness of facial recognition scores, in a 2026 arXiv paper on calibration. Face systems compare embeddings and report a cosine similarity. A raw score is therefore not an honest probability. Their method, Adaptive Calibration, maps similarity to calibrated probabilities. It uses local context to correct the mismatch region by region. It does not rely on one global curve.

Across pretrained models and standard benchmarks, Adaptive Calibration beat existing methods on accuracy and fairness metrics. It needs no demographic metadata. Fairness methods usually require such group labels. Deployments often cannot collect them. Its continuous, region-specific calibration avoids leveling down. Leveling down is when fairness gains come from degrading some groups' results. Here calibration raises overall performance while making scores fairer at the same time.
arxiv-2606-04669:
Shakya and coauthors presented an organised review of post quantum cryptography in software in 2026 on arXiv. That field builds protective methods meant to stay safe even against powerful future quantum computers. New standard methods now exist, yet many teams still struggle to install them in real programs. The review asks why that move is hard beyond the maths itself.

They sorted past studies by people, by organizations, and by technology, then compared the balance across those groups. Technology studies dominated the field, while work on staff skills and workplace readiness stayed thin. Problems also crossed the three groups at once, so fixing code alone could not finish the move. They propose a combined model linking all three groups to guide planning for a safer software shift. Their advice treats the change as a whole workplace shift, not just a swap of one method.
arxiv-2606-05069:
Rasika Muralidharan, Yong-Yeol Ahn, and Bao Tran Truong study how community rules scale with the size of Mastodon instances in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mastodon is a decentralized social network of independently run servers, each governing itself with mostly volunteer moderation. As communities grow they face new problems, yet there is little formal guidance on how their rules should evolve.

The authors categorized the written rules of servers of varying sizes to find governance priorities. Those priorities proved remarkably consistent at every scale: rules against problematic content such as harassment, hate speech, and illegal content dominate everywhere. Smaller communities cover narrower topics, while larger servers spread coverage more evenly. Community size strongly predicted rule development, with rules growing longer and more diverse but less readable as instances grew, while federation links to other servers played only a limited role. The pattern resembles earlier findings on Reddit.
arxiv-2606-05169:
Jason Z Wang develops a stereological theory of benchmark coverage for large language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stereology studies what slices or projections can reveal about a higher-dimensional object. Wang treats each benchmark score as a one-dimensional projection of a model's capability profile. The question is how much of that profile a leaderboard can actually see.

He bounds how far apart two profiles consistent with identical scores can be, with a matching lower bound. Three independent suites all showed an effective dimensionality between 2.86 and 4.80 on their competitive frontier, so the blind spot exceeds the runner-up score gap by two orders of magnitude. Simulated splits swapped the top-ranked model in 92 percent of trials. A greedy submodular algorithm found a stable core of four benchmarks, with seven of twelve giving 90 percent coverage. The paper also resolves a 1995 problem of Gardner in geometric tomography.
arxiv-2606-05269:
Harry Allan and colleagues model the resolution of X-ray beam-tracking microscopy in this 2026 arXiv paper. Beam-tracking is a phase-contrast imaging technique that retrieves transmission, phase, and dark-field images at once by structuring the beam into beamlets. Its resolution is widely assumed to be driven by aperture size, but no full model existed, and the dark-field channel had shown anomalously high sharpness.

The authors derive an optical transfer function model for each channel, using the Fokker-Planck equation for near-field imaging. Validation experiments at a synchrotron and a laboratory setup used circular apertures of 15 micrometers and rectangular ones of 10 micrometers. They revealed a limiting resolution of at least 3 micrometers, much finer than the apertures themselves. Together, model and experiments give a full description of resolution in this technique. They confirm the dark-field channel genuinely resolves finer detail, opening new options in system design.
arxiv-2606-05469:
Vadim Guzey and colleagues calculate diffractive open-charm production in ultraperipheral collisions at the Large Hadron Collider in this 2026 arXiv paper. In these events, two heavy nuclei pass at distances too large for hadronic contact, so one nucleus's field acts as a photon beam on the other.

They use the GγA-FONLL framework, with photon-lead diffraction modeled by parton distributions from the leading-twist shadowing approach, plus photon-flux corrections for nuclear dissociation. The team measures how much production the neutron-tagged event selection rejected. That selection was used in the first measurement of this process in lead-lead collisions, and it demanded neutron emission from one nucleus. They also extend it to proton-lead collisions, where a photon from the lead ion hits the proton. They present predictions for both kinds of production there, using proton profiles from HERA electron-proton data.
arxiv-2606-05769:
Tianxiang Jiang and colleagues let video models imagine the future in pictures, not words, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Predicting unseen events from partial video is the task. Models usually spell their guesses out in text first. Fine motion and layout cues die in that translation, and fluent nonsense follows. Future-L1 alternates language tokens with silent visual spans during generation. The spans carry future hints without rendering full frames.

Training data came from cases where visual hints provably help prediction. Latent states were aligned to embeddings of real future frames. A reinforcement step then tuned whole latent paths with outcome and variety rewards. On FutureBench the model lifted a strong baseline from about sixty-one to about eighty-five points. It beat the prior best system by over ten points. A second benchmark showed the same pattern. Keeping future semantics visual, the authors argue, beats narrating them.
arxiv-2606-06169:
Roberto Alessi and co-authors offer a new way to give fracture simulations custom strength rules in this 2026 arXiv paper on materials modeling. Phase-field models represent a crack as a smooth damage field rather than a sharp cut, which makes crack birth and branching easier to compute. The weakness is telling the model when intact material should start to fail under combined stresses. Earlier fixes either split the stored energy in special ways or broke the variational structure keeping the model consistent.

Their strategy lets the dissipation potential, the part governing energy lost as damage grows, depend on the material's current state. Stored energy still controls stiffness loss, while strength is set separately in the dissipation term. Examples pair full or partial stiffness loss with double-ellipse, Drucker-Prager, and Huber-type strength rules. Biaxial disk tests show the setup reproduces distinct mixed-mode crack nucleation behaviors.
arxiv-2606-06369:
Maëlic Neau and co-authors add common sense as a referee for image understanding in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scene graph generation labels the objects in a picture and the relations between them, such as a person riding a horse. Neural models ace frequent relations but stumble on rare ones, where training annotations are sparse. They also propose relations that any human would call impossible.

The framework mines commonsense constraints straight from training data, covering spatial, functional, and qualitative regularities, with no hand written rules. A declarative reasoning stage, implemented in answer set programming, then corrects the model's ranked predictions at inference time. Impossible relations get pruned, and missing ones can be inferred. A verifier keeps only corrections that empirically help. Across three standard benchmarks, the method improved strong baselines consistently, and it transfers across datasets and model architectures without retraining.
arxiv-2606-06469:
Overfitted models that match every training example can still predict new cases well, a puzzle at the heart of modern machine learning. Chen and El Alaoui ask a sharper question in this 2026 arXiv paper: if you pick a perfect fitting classifier purely at random, how good is it likely to be? Their classifiers are simple linear rules that label every training point correctly, possibly by only a thin margin.

Using large deviation theory, the mathematics of rare events, the authors show that nearly all such interpolators share almost exactly the same accuracy on new data. The shared value is pinned down by a single rate function they compute for two natural data models. Strikingly, rules found by gradient descent and a simple linear program beat that typical value when parameters far outnumber data. Standard training finds needles better than almost the whole haystack.
arxiv-2606-06669:
Some sets of waves behave almost independently, even when they are added together. Lewko studies such sets, called Sidon sets, in this 2026 arXiv paper on harmonic analysis, the study of how signals split into simple waves. A Sidon set has the special property that the peak size of a combined wave stays comparable to the sum of its separate parts.

Mathematicians have long known that Sidon sets break into finitely many quasi independent sets, sets where no signed sum of distinct members cancels to zero. That result was proved first for prime exponents and later for squarefree ones. Lewko settles the remaining case, where the dual group has bounded torsion, meaning its elements repeat after a bounded number of steps. The outcome is a clean two way test: in this setting a set is Sidon exactly when it is a finite union of quasi independent sets.
arxiv-2606-06769:
Modern statistics increasingly tests hypotheses as data arrive, letting researchers peek repeatedly without cheating. Clerico characterizes the tools for that job in this 2026 arXiv paper, working with e-processes, running evidence scores whose average stays at most one when the claim being tested is true. Large scores count as evidence against the claim, and the rules stay valid at any stopping time.

The hypotheses here are conditional ones, defined by finitely many constraints on what should hold given past data. Clerico proves a complete class theorem: every valid e-process is beaten, point by point, by a simple product of one step scores, each an affine function chosen with knowledge of the past. So nothing is lost by restricting attention to those product forms, called test supermartingales. The result extends earlier one step results to a broad conditional setting left open before.
arxiv-2606-07169:
A popular recipe for tuning Bayesian inference turns out to be blind in the cleanest possible test case. Le proves the blindness exactly in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generalised Bayesian inference tempers the likelihood by a learning rate, softening a misspecified model's confidence. One proposed selector picks that rate using a posterior predictive check, a p-value comparing model predictions to data.

On the Gaussian linear model the check cannot see the rate at all. With known variance, the p-value is identical for every learning rate. With unknown variance, it depends only on sample size and dimension, never on the observed data. The selector's answer is fixed before data arrive. It typically collapses to the smallest grid value, over tempering the model. The failure is special to Gaussian models with a reference prior. Informative priors break the degeneracy, and the paper maps that boundary precisely.
arxiv-2606-07869:
Shahmurov claims a full proof of global regularity for swirling axisymmetric flow, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations for flows symmetric around an axis, with arbitrary swirl, the rotational component usually blamed for blow-up. A companion paper reduced the general finite-energy problem to this class, so a proof here would be a major step.

The argument is organised around three quantities: the circulation, the azimuthal vorticity over radius, and circulation gradients adapted to the axis. The hardest obstacle is a source term near the axis in the vorticity-ratio equation. A key identity rewrites that source as a product of the circulation and one gradient component, in a form energy-like measures can absorb. Hardy-type inequalities near the axis then control it. The author reports all remaining channels close, yielding global smoothness for smooth finite-energy solutions with any swirl.
arxiv-2606-07969:
Imani Finkley, Yuanxi Li, and Melanie Walsh test what happens when AI storytellers are steered toward gender neutrality, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They asked language models to write stories about seven kinds of animal characters whose gender was never specified. Across four settings and randomness levels they collected about twenty-three thousand eight hundred stories.

The models often stayed neutral: in about nineteen percent of stories the animal was never gendered, and gender-neutral wording appeared in about thirty-eight percent. But when gender was assigned, it was overwhelmingly masculine. Feminine animal characters appeared in barely two percent of stories, against about forty-one percent featuring masculine ones. Neutrality, the authors argue, bites back: systems tuned to avoid bias default to male whenever they commit, erasing feminine perspectives. They recommend strategies that spread social possibilities more equally across imagined characters.
arxiv-2606-08069:
María V. Ferrer, Salvador Hernández-Muñoz, and Luis Javier Hernández-Paricio build the theory of a weakened kind of group extension, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An extension packages one topological Abelian group by another into a larger group. A weak-split extension asks only that the projection back down has a continuous section. That forces the big group to look like a direct product topologically, though not necessarily algebraically.

The set of all such extensions, modulo isomorphism, forms an Abelian group itself. They give two descriptions of it. Geometrically, it is the group of all continuous group laws on the product space keeping the first factor as a subgroup and the second as a quotient. Algebraically, it is a quotient of cocycles by coboundaries, maps encoding the twisting of the product law. Comparisons with ordinary extension groups locate the new invariant.
arxiv-2606-08369:
Wanqiao Xu, Zhu, and Van Roy give a precise definition of open-ended learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Many hope for systems that continually expand their capabilities in an open-ended environment. Yet there was no coherent definition of open-endedness, and no theory of how an agent ought to explore. The authors introduce an information-theoretic definition built on a new concept, the bit-equivalent. It quantifies the information required to attain each level of expected reward.

An environment counts as open-ended when an agent can attain linear growth in the bit-equivalent. They establish that classical bandit environments, where an agent repeatedly chooses among options with unknown payoffs, are not open-ended in this sense. They then formulate a bandit environment that is open-ended and give an algorithm that achieves open-ended learning inside it.
arxiv-2606-08669:
Anh-Tuan Dao, Matrouf, Rouvier, and Evans benchmark the components of voice spoofing detectors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Voice biometric systems face growing threats from spoofing attacks, synthetic or converted speech that impersonates a target speaker. Yet evaluation of detection models remains inconsistent across datasets. The authors compare four self-supervised learning feature extractors, which turn raw audio into representations without labels, paired with four back-end classifiers.

Multi-corpus training across three scenarios and six datasets yields two critical findings. First, they expose a domain bias within a major public spoofing benchmark, showing that naive data scaling actively degrades performance. Second, their cross-linguistic analysis reveals that fine-tuning with just eight hours of target-language data substantially enhances detection robustness for that language in the experiments reported here.
arxiv-2606-08969:
Bedi and colleagues wrap medical summarizers in a safety layer that flags sentences with statistical guarantees, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models draft summaries, but they omit facts and invent unsupported claims. Existing detectors give uncalibrated scores, leaving error rates unknown. CARE, short for Conformal Assessment for Risk Evaluation, is a post-hoc layer that works with any model without retraining. It uses conformal risk control, a calibration method with finite-sample guarantees, through two controllers: one bounds unflagged hallucinations, the other missed omissions.

Omissions are subtle: a gap matters only if missing content mattered and was uncovered. Tuning one dimension can break the guarantee. By tuning both jointly, CARE held its bounds while flagging up to 5 times fewer sentences than other methods. Across 5 medical summary tasks it met its risk target using about 100 labeled documents per domain. In a clinician study, the flags improved omission detection by 28.6 percentage points.
arxiv-2606-09669:
Hongcheng Gao and a large team release a benchmark that tests AI agents on active spatial work in this 2026 arXiv paper. Past tests mostly show a still scene and ask a question. Real spatial skill is live: an agent sees only part of a place and must move to learn more. SpatialWorld unites eight simulators under one shared protocol.

The set holds seven hundred sixty human-checked tasks, from home routines to travel and group work. Agents see only their own camera view and act through a plain text interface. Each task ships with a checked start state, a model path, and a tool that verifies the end state. Fifteen strong agents were tried. The best, GPT-5, passed just seventeen point four percent of tasks. The top open model reached fourteen point one percent. Mixed tasks that join travel with object handling proved hardest, at near four percent mean success.
arxiv-2606-09769:
Maria Nocchi and her co-authors extend a flat-space string recipe into curved anti-de Sitter space for any count of particles in this 2026 arXiv paper. String scattering at tree level is read from integrals over the shapes of punctured surfaces. Open strings live on a disc, closed ones on a sphere. In flat space, those integrals obey neat rules: monodromy links and a KLT split of closed into open parts.

The team dresses the flat integrals with many-variable polylog functions, and their single-valued twins for the sphere. From those blocks, they derive monodromy rules for the open-string side. The closed-string side then splits by a KLT factor rule. The move lifts a known non-commutative uplift from low point counts to full general counts.
arxiv-2606-09969:
Benakli asks whether two worlds on neighboring branes could talk using gravity alone, in a 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. Branes are surfaces inside a higher-dimensional space called the bulk, and in his setup ordinary matter stays on our brane while gravity travels through the bulk. The carriers would be Kaluza-Klein modes, a tower of massive gravity states from the extra dimensions. He studies the link.

Starting from the brane-to-brane graviton propagator, he derives the transfer kernel and maps when modes fade out or propagate freely. Below the first Kaluza-Klein threshold, only the massless graviton carries signals, so the channel behaves four-dimensionally. Above threshold, massive modes open as extra subchannels, letting information ride in occupation patterns, phases, and arrival times. He applies capacity bounds and water-filling from information theory, while stressing that building such a link is not assumed feasible.
arxiv-2606-10369:
Peng and colleagues distill a large dense model into a sparse mixture-of-experts student that learns its own routing, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning efficiency. Their framework, PADD, organizes distillation into four stages across two phases: initialization builds diverse expert functionality through teacher neuron clustering and expert warmup.

The training phase then integrates online adaptive distillation, path-refined policy optimization, and reward-augmented load balancing in a single pipeline, so routing quality develops alongside knowledge transfer. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show substantial gains over strong baselines at the same inference cost, with the mixture-of-experts student matching or surpassing its dense teacher. The results also demonstrate stable routing behavior, a common failure point where routers collapse onto few experts. The authors present path-aligned decompression as a reusable recipe for converting dense models into efficient sparse ones.
arxiv-2606-10669:
Espinosa Zarlenga defends a supposed flaw of explainable models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Concept-based models predict through human concepts, such as round or striped, so users can inspect and intervene. Their concept vectors leak, encoding extra information beyond the assigned concepts. The standard reaction treats leakage as a threat and tries to eradicate it. This paper argues the reaction is ill-posed, since evidence that leakage breaks interpretability is inconclusive, and counterproductive, since real concept lists are almost never complete.

When concepts are incomplete, some leakage lets a model stay accurate while remaining open to intervention. The author calls this benign leakage and shows a reframed objective, minimising task loss under full intervention, yields leakage that is localised and sufficient. Models once dismissed as unintervenable then stay accurate and intervenable. The closing call: control leakage, do not abolish it, and test models under realistic incompleteness.
arxiv-2606-10769:
Zuan Gu, Gao, and Langxu Zhao present a training-free pipeline for aerial image analysis in this 2026 arXiv paper on remote sensing. Satellite and drone imagery is hard: huge images, rotated objects, extreme scale variation, and crowded ports and airfields. ZODS-RS detects and segments without any task training. It chains frozen DINOv3 features and SAM-style proposals through three closed-form stages: prototype purification with robust covariance, rotation-scale equivariant matching with global assignment, and uncertainty-aware pixel merging.

The results are competitive with trained and open-vocabulary baselines. It scores mean average precision 13.06 on the FAIR1M benchmark and 16.69 on xView under the standard protocol. It reaches mask overlap 31.10 on the authors' drone data, with small-object accuracy ahead of Grounded-SAM by 30.70 points in the same tests. Ablations credit each stage, and gains hold under cross-domain shifts, where per-task training usually starts over.
arxiv-2606-10869:
Binucci and Banelli ask how to quantize a compressed representation without wasting its content in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Information Bottleneck squeezes data into a compact code that keeps what matters for a target task, and its Gaussian case has a closed-form answer. Real systems, though, must store that code in finitely many bits.

The authors analyze scalar and vector quantization of the Gaussian solution, then redesign the optimization under a finite-rate limit so the quantizer targets mutual information directly. On regression tests the task-oriented designs beat quantizing the standard solution after the fact by a clear margin. The idea extends to non-Gaussian data through bottleneck-style autoencoders.
arxiv-2606-10969:
Moindjié proposes a leaner way to analyze images in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pixel grids make images huge and costly for statistics. The framework treats an image's contour and texture as continuous random functions instead. The outline is a closed curve, and the interior's color variation is mapped to a square, provided the object's interior is star-shaped.

The payoff is a sparse, frugal representation that keeps only the shape and the color variation of interest, unlike pixel arrays that carry everything. A supervised classification test on real data shows the approach working. The star-shaped assumption is the main limit; several objects at once remain future work.
arxiv-2606-11069:
Ding and four co-authors work on Ruzsa numbers in a 2026 arXiv paper in additive number theory, the study of sums in finite systems. Fix the residues modulo m, the remainders after division by m. The Ruzsa number is the smallest cap r with this property. Some subset must write every residue as a sum of two of its elements, in at least one way and at most r ways. Bounding these numbers uniformly has been open work since Ruzsa's first construction.

Motivated by a 2024 conjecture of Ding and Zhao, the team proves neighboring Ruzsa numbers stay close: values at m plus one and at m differ by at most one hundred forty-four. They also give nontrivial bounds on the size of the extremal subsets achieving the cap. Finally, they compute exact Ruzsa numbers for every m up to one hundred, extending the 2017 table of Sándor and Yang.
arxiv-2606-11169:
Frisella and seven co-authors present Piper in a 2026 arXiv paper, a programmable system for training large models on many accelerators. Training now mixes parallelism strategies, data, pipeline, and expert parallelism, which split work in different ways, plus memory savers like ZeRO. Deployed systems usually need experts to hand-design a strategy and hand-code its execution, while flexible frameworks still hardwire a few common strategies.

Piper decouples strategy from runtime. Users declare a full strategy through a small set of model annotations and scheduling directives. Each directive transforms Piper's intermediate representation, a global training graph of all computation and communication. From it, Piper compiles per-device plans and runs them with a strategy-agnostic runtime. The system matches standard systems on common strategies such as ZeRO. It also unlocks extra gains by jointly scheduling compute and communication in composed strategies, including DeepSeek-V3's DualPipe scheme.
arxiv-2606-11669:
Shravika Mittal, Su Lin Blodgett and Q Vera Liao ran a field experiment on learning with chatbots in this 2026 arXiv paper. Participants pursued informal learning goals for eight days, half seeking information through ChatGPT and half through Google Search. Daily diaries captured how they searched and chose, in a design where each person used only one tool.

The ChatGPT group handed much of the selection work to the AI and reported a diminished sense of agency, or control over their own seeking. That loss raised their metacognitive load, the mental effort of monitoring their own learning. Two distortions appeared: the chatbot favoured ready-made solution artefacts over principled knowledge, and its conversational style narrowed exploration of the wider knowledge space. On average the ChatGPT group learned worse than the Google group, especially on higher-order critical learning. The authors frame a tension between offloading search and learning meaningfully.
arxiv-2606-11769:
Maximilian Poretschkin and Tabea Naeven tackle a legal puzzle in this 2026 arXiv paper on AI regulation. Europe's AI Act ties its strictest duties to systems with a capability to infer, but never defines inference clearly. Statistical tools such as credit scoring sit in a grey area: they are explicitly listed as high-risk, yet it is unclear whether they count as AI at all.

Drawing on statistical learning theory, the authors grade inference into five levels. The scale runs from fixed mappings with no inference, through fitted parametric models and selection among preset structures, up to models that learn their own features. They map which levels plausibly meet the Act's threshold and where regulators still owe clarity. Two realistic credit scoring workflows illustrate the framework. The whole processing pipeline matters, not just the model, and human experts shaping a system during development can significantly change its level of inference.
arxiv-2606-11969:
Xu Zhang and four colleagues correct drifting video generation in the frequency domain in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-video models built on flow matching sample a path through a differential equation, and small velocity and discretisation errors accumulate along it. The result is videos with physical artifacts and incoherent motion.

Their method, SpecLoR, is a plug-and-play inference add-on needing no retraining. Early in sampling it looks ahead to estimate the clean video latent, then computes its three-dimensional spatiotemporal spectrum. Natural videos obey known statistical patterns in frequency space, so the method rescales the amplitude spectrum toward those priors while leaving the phase, which encodes geometry, untouched. The corrected state is then re-noised and sampling resumes. Tested on the Wan2.2 model, SpecLoR significantly reduces physical artifacts and improves motion coherence across benchmarks. The overhead is minimal: only four extra function evaluations for the whole correction.
arxiv-2606-12069:
Hong Li leads an eleven-author team teaching machines to align touch with sight in this 2026 arXiv paper. Touch signals are inherently local: a fingertip feels one contact patch, not a whole object. Existing tactile learning mostly aligns whole images, leaving the local-to-global matching problem open.

The team built a collection system gathering over twenty thousand tactile contacts from five hundred five real-world objects. On it they define a holographic matching benchmark testing whether a local touch patch can be matched to its place on the whole object. Their learning methods align vision and touch at patch level rather than image level. Experiments show patch alignment beats methods without it, and fused vision-touch representations label difficult cases more accurately. Early fusion of the two senses outperforms late fusion in retrieval. Simple contrastive alignment, the authors conclude, enforces stricter correspondence than elaborate losses.
arxiv-2606-12169:
Baghbanzadeh and co-authors build a training corpus that teaches medical AI to show its reasoning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large vision-language models read images and answer in words, which suits medical scans and charts. Clinical use demands reasoning grounded in what the image shows, not just a correct final answer. Their corpus, OpenMedReason, holds about 450,000 image-question-answer cases. Its reasoning traces come mainly from curated human-written articles, not machine-invented chains.

A companion benchmark grades models on perception, medical knowledge, and rationale quality separately. Training on it lifted question answering accuracy by 20 percent on average over the base model. The trained model lands within 4.2 percent of the strongest comparable medical systems. Gains appear jointly across all three graded axes, not in one alone. Human judges preferred the model's reasoning traces over the base model's in 86.1 percent of comparisons. The dataset and code are released openly.
arxiv-2606-12269:
Yabunaka and Delamotte examine a fixed point that breaks the rules of phase transitions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A renormalization group fixed point is a scale where a system's behavior stops changing as you zoom out. Textbook wisdom links such points to massless particles and infinite correlation length.
