The tricritical O(N) model, with N field components, has a line of fixed points found by Bardeen, Moshe, and Bander, whose endpoint generates mass anyway.

Using the functional renormalization group, which tracks how the effective potential evolves with scale, the authors trace the mechanism. The generated mass is nonuniversal, not a constant of nature. It springs from a nonanalytic kink in the effective potential that forms along the flow. The correlation-length exponent, which equals 1/2 along the regular line, jumps to 1/3 at the singular endpoint. The endpoint thus separates two regimes, and scale invariance can coexist with mass generation there.
arxiv-2606-12469:
Pereira and co-authors map which design choices leave retrieval-augmented AI open to poisoned documents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RAG systems answer questions by fetching documents into the model's context. An attacker who plants hostile documents can hijack both what gets retrieved and what gets said. The team runs a full factorial study: 432 setups varying dataset, retriever type, retrieval depth, database composition, chunking, and generator model.

Retriever type, dataset, and depth dominate poisoning exposure early on. Dense and graph-based retrievers resist better than classic keyword search. Deeper retrieval, fetching more passages, raises the chance of pulling poisoned ones in. Downstream attack success depends most on the model and database mix. Copying poisoned content into several databases amplifies its influence. Adding clean sources dilutes it back. The flaw, the authors conclude, is a system property emerging from the whole pipeline, not a defect in any single component.
arxiv-2606-12569:
Labruna and co-authors release four million Italian emergency-room notes as fuel for medical AI, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clinical notes hold rich patient information, but privacy and language scarcity starve model development, especially outside English. Their eCream-MedCorpus collects notes from Italian emergency departments, fully anonymized on site, spanning the phases of a patient's stay. It is the largest free clinical-note dataset for Italian.

About six thousand notes carry expert annotation: clinicians filled a case report form of one hundred thirty-two items for two conditions, breathlessness and loss of consciousness. Items range over numbers like blood saturation, categories, and yes-no flags. The team proposes form-filling itself as a benchmark for structured information extraction. Zero-shot baselines from two large Gemma models show the task is hard; a cautious-prompting variant gains a small edge when items are queried one by one.
arxiv-2606-13369:
Neraki and colleagues ask whether machine learning can tell what a compact star is made of in this 2026 arXiv paper. Compact stars include neutron stars, built from neutrons and protons, and quark stars made of deconfined quark matter. Hybrid stars mix both, and ingredients such as hyperons or dark matter may also hide inside. Gravitational waves from mergers have sharpened interest in these objects, yet observations cannot reveal their interiors. The authors test whether measured properties can classify the possibilities.

They train neural network models on the properties of compact objects, such as mass and radius. The models learn the patterns that composition imprints on those observables. Successful classification would let astronomers sort measured stars into composition families without solving the structure problem each time. The study frames a route from gravitational-wave and X-ray measurements toward constraints on matter at unreachable densities.
arxiv-2606-13469: An arXiv research paper from 2026, this manuscript presents new work. The subject on the cover page is Simulations of 3-Dimensional Recoil Response to. The context is science and technology (careful study of how the natural and built world works). The research reported here is now part of the open record.
arxiv-2606-13769:
Seungjae Lee and colleagues present a world model that predicts three-dimensional interaction traces in this 2026 arXiv paper. World models that capture how actions change the world enable robot learning without robot-specific action labels. Pixel-space video models provide broad visual priors but spend capacity reconstructing appearance. Direct action models need labels tied to each robot body, blocking scale. The authors' model instead forecasts three-dimensional trajectories for key interaction points: objects, tools, hands, and contact regions. That trace representation is compact and independent of any robot's joints.

Training from video requires supervision that human annotators cannot supply at scale, so their extraction system builds it. It selects keypoints, constructs aligned traces, and associates them with the interactions shown. Learning to predict how contact points move through space is close to learning the physics of manipulation itself. A scalable motion interface could let one world model serve many robots.
arxiv-2606-13969:
Fava and colleagues simulate airflow over a wind turbine blade section to pin down how orderly flow turns turbulent. The FFA-W3 airfoil matches a section of the DTU ten-megawatt reference turbine. Their 2026 arXiv paper runs wall-resolved large eddy simulations with two codes, Nek5000 and EllipSys, at chord Reynolds number one hundred thousand and attack angles near three degrees. A domain only ten percent of chord wide proved enough.

EllipSys matched Nek5000 closely on mean flow and the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode in the laminar separation bubble, though it underpredicted Tollmien-Schlichting waves through extra dissipation. Transition is driven by that Kelvin-Helmholtz instability of the separated shear layer. Long runs revealed slow oscillations of normal force, amplitude ten point five percent, period forty-eight flow-through times. On the real turbine that equals seven point seven blade rotations. Periodic stalling and recovery may trigger them.
arxiv-2606-14669:
Abbaneo and the SND@LHC Collaboration measure how often muon neutrinos interact in tungsten in a 2026 arXiv paper. SND@LHC is a detector at the Large Hadron Collider. It was built to catch neutrinos from proton collisions. The team studied charged-current interactions. In these, a muon neutrino converts into a muon. They used the experiment's electronic detectors.

The data come from Run 3 collisions in twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three. The center-of-mass energy was thirteen point six teraelectronvolts. Thirty-one candidate events were selected. The expected background was about five events. The predicted signal was near twenty-four events, so the counts match. The team determined the combined neutrino and antineutrino cross section on tungsten. Its median energy was two hundred twenty-eight gigaelectronvolts. The analysis adds a calorimetric measure of hadronic energies, calibrated with test-beam data.
arxiv-2606-14869:
Yang and co-authors publish a shape catalog for about seven hundred eighty thousand galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxies come from the COSMOS-Web survey, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope. Morphology means a galaxy's shape and structure. The team measured shapes in four infrared bands. They used both fitted profiles and model-free statistics.

Fitted Sérsic profiles show structure tracking star formation out to redshift about four. Massive galaxies grew more concentrated over time. Their median Sérsic index rose from about one at redshift six to about two point five at redshift two. Low-mass galaxies stayed near one point two at all epochs. Bulge share followed the same mass-dependent pattern. Model-free measures like the Gini coefficient agreed with the fitted classes. The catalog is the largest JWST shape set so far. It supports studies of bulge growth and galaxy change.
arxiv-2606-15269:
Han and coauthors revisit axion-like particle limits from the brightest gamma-ray burst ever recorded, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Axion-like particles could mix with photons inside magnetic fields, altering how gamma rays travel. The burst GRB 221009A sent energetic photons across distances to the LHAASO observatory. Which limits follow depends on the magnetic fields along the line of sight. The authors model the host galaxy, intergalactic, and Milky Way fields.

Swapping host-galaxy or Galactic field models changed the exclusion limits mildly. Varying the intergalactic magnetic field changed them dramatically instead. Its strength, coherence scale, and structure all imprint on the exclusion contours. In an intermediate mass range, the contours develop wavy features. At low masses the intergalactic field strengthens the limits beyond background-light-only results. The intergalactic field is the dominant uncertainty in this probe. Future gamma-ray axion searches need propagation modeling above all.
arxiv-2606-15569:
Wakayama analyses test-time training in 2026, updating a pretrained model on each test prompt under distribution shift. The trick improves accuracy but is unstable, with results sensitive to the step count and which parameters to touch. Wakayama treats the procedure as implicit Bayesian inference in the kernel regime and tests it against a Gaussian process benchmark.

Updates cut prediction error when spectrally matched to the prompt's signal-to-noise ratio and aligned with query-relevant directions. Fixed step counts and fixed subspaces provably fail under some shifts, which explains the observed fragility. Selecting the step count by prompt evidence carries a PAC-Bayes guarantee against overfitting. He characterizes the Bayes-optimal update subspace under a correction model, yielding a scoring rule for which transformer blocks and heads to adapt. Small experiments back the theory: query-aware directions beat random choices, while adapting the wrong directions reliably hurts.
arxiv-2606-15669:
Goo and colleagues propose Z-Plane Neural Networks in 2026, replacing the two standard stabilizers of deep learning, ReLU activations and LayerNorm, with one geometric operation. ReLU kills negative signals and creates dead neurons, while LayerNorm imposes a global scale that destroys feature direction. Inspired by phase-modulated signals in biological axons, the design maps hidden states into two-dimensional phasor bundles on a hypersphere.

Its activation, Radial Bounding, caps each vector's magnitude at one while preserving its direction exactly. The authors prove the operation is 1-Lipschitz and keeps tangential gradients alive, so gradients neither explode nor vanish. A one-hundred-layer perceptron built only from these layers, with no ReLU and no LayerNorm anywhere, trains stably on MNIST. It reaches over ninety-eight percent accuracy with complete numerical stability. Bounded geometry alone, the result suggests, can do the stabilizing work that deep networks currently outsource to ad-hoc fixes.
arxiv-2606-16069:
Krome and colleagues tackle missing heating data in a 2026 energy paper. Switching homes from gas to electric heat needs detailed thermal load profiles, records of how heating demand varies over time. High-resolution gas metering is rare, because utilities seldom need it. Gas data are scarce, irregular, and low in frequency, which starves standard machine learning methods.

Their framework, Generalized Proxy-Guided Load and Temporal Disaggregation, rebuilds fine-grained gas profiles from billing data. Hourly electricity use, weather-normalized to isolate behavior, serves as a proxy for occupancy. Four stages extract the proxy, pool segments, and split totals over time. On 11 multi-unit buildings tracked for 18 months, rebuilt total gas use reaches a mean squared percentage error of 6.37 percent in validation. The proxy also tracks non-heating gas far more closely than raw electricity. Better profiles could guide retrofit planning where meters are thin.
arxiv-2606-16169:
Priour develops in 2026 a geometrically exact way to find when flow through the voids of a porous material stops. Fluid and charge move through the gaps between impermeable grains packed at random. Past a critical grain density, the void network breaks up and flow ceases at large scales. Irregular void shapes make that threshold hard to compute exactly.

Priour's method identifies the shape and size of contiguous voids exactly, at cost growing only linearly with system volume. Large Monte Carlo calculations then give thresholds for both grain cluster percolation and void percolation. Grain shapes cover the Platonic solids and truncated icosahedra, in aligned and randomly oriented packings. Void threshold accuracy improves significantly over earlier results, enough to resolve differences between aligned and random orientations. For cube grains cut by random slicing planes, mimicking fragmented natural grains, the critical porosity converges to 5 percent in the many-fracture limit.
arxiv-2606-16969:
Alex Gichamba and Moise Busogi probe why neural audio codecs degrade at low frame rates in a 2026 speech technology paper. A codec turns sound into tokens, and fewer per second means cheaper speech generation. Earlier work hit a quality cliff at a low rate and blamed the rate itself.

Through a controlled frame-rate study, the authors test two suspect mechanisms: phonemic collisions, where distinct sounds are forced to share tokens, and codebook saturation. Neither shows evidence of a hard barrier. The cliff instead traces to a training setup flaw: fixed clip length leaves too few tokens per training example at low rates, starving the decoder of context between tokens. Fixing the sequence length in training makes word error degrade smoothly with sound load, all the way down to very low rates and tiny bitrates. Low-rate codecs, it turns out, are more usable than the field assumed.
arxiv-2606-17269:
Sanoja presents a 2026 arXiv paper on model predictive control for factories where certified worker skill is the binding limit. Tomorrow's qualified capacity depends on training choices made today, since certifications decay unless maintained and training consumes scarce worker hours. The controller replans each shift, solving a finite-horizon mixed-integer program over production, inventory, backlog, and training, then applying only the first step before replanning again.

Tests ran on synthetic SkillChain-Gym scenarios with announced and surprise skill shocks, demand shocks, and absenteeism, under a locked configuration with paired statistics. No policy class dominated overall, echoing the benchmark's regime-dependent lesson in the author's companion work. Predictive control paid off when bottlenecks could be forecast early enough for training to finish in time. Lean static insurance plans stayed hard to beat under surprise shocks and near the demand-capacity boundary.
arxiv-2606-17569:
Brade and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on hunting for new particles whose mass changes with time, a signal that standard collider searches would wash out. Normal resonance hunts pool all events regardless of when they arrived, so a peak that wanders in mass over the run leaves only a smear. The authors build a two-dimensional likelihood over invariant mass and time together, letting a signal trace a moving path instead of sitting still for the analysis.

Their benchmark case is a Z prime boson from a baryon-minus-lepton extension of the Standard Model, with its mass modulated periodically. Dimuon events from CMS open data, taken at thirteen teraelectronvolts, supply the test sample for the method. Upper limits on the coupling are derived across masses and modulation sizes. Adding time information sharpened sensitivity where signal counts were sufficient.
arxiv-2606-17869:
Meyer and colleagues propose a better way to score sports video quality in a 2026 paper. Standard quality metrics treat every part of a frame as equally important, but viewers fixate on the action, so smart encoders give key regions more bits and starve the background. Judging such unevenly encoded video needs a metric that knows where people actually look.

Their metric, PW-VQM, weights structural similarity maps by region importance. Salient foreground areas are found by combining open-vocabulary object detection with optical flow tracking, and they count more in the final score. On sports content the metric tracked human judgments more closely than SSIM, VMAF, and other established tools, reaching a rank correlation above ninety-five hundredths in their tests. A part-by-part study confirmed that each piece of the weighting scheme helps.
arxiv-2606-18069:
Williamson and Mitra offer a way to fit smooth surfaces to shapes without a neural network in sight, in a 2026 graphics paper. Geometry tools want surface representations that are compact, explicit, smooth everywhere, and easy to differentiate, with honest normals and energies. Neural fields usually trade one of those away, and map-based methods show seams where local charts meet.

Their Blended Chart Surfaces start from a coarse proxy mesh carrying the intended topology. A polynomial map is optimized at each proxy vertex to fit a target shape given implicitly, with no input parametrization required. A one-ring coordinate blending scheme then fuses neighboring maps into one surface that is smooth by construction, even across the proxy's sharp edges. Topology lives in the proxy, fine detail in the patches, and every quantity an optimizer needs stays available in closed form.
arxiv-2606-18269:
Maiti and Ramachandran model an earthquake precursor that a student satellite hopes to catch from orbit, in a 2026 space physics paper. Hours before some quakes, low-frequency electromagnetic waves appear near the ionosphere. Traveling up along geomagnetic field lines as Alfvén waves, they can resonate with energetic protons trapped in the inner Van Allen belt. The shaking knocks some loose, producing particle bursts a satellite could detect. The IIT Madras satellite IITMSAT is built around that hypothesis.

The authors build a kinetic model of the trapped protons that reproduces the observed density profile, then simulate the wave-particle interaction with a finite-difference time-domain method. Their analysis shows pitch-angle scattering acts within seconds to a minute, far faster than the hours-long lead time reported before quakes. That gap, they argue, reflects stress building underground, and it shapes what the mission should expect.
arxiv-2606-18469:
Nath and colleagues propose a reinforcement learning framework whose state representations are shaped by ideas from neuroscience, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Brains appear to encode behavior on ordered, low-dimensional manifolds and to fuse information sources through adaptive gating. Standard reinforcement learning often squeezes dynamics and reward into one representation tuned mainly to near-term payoff.

Their method keeps two feature streams apart. Locally linear embedding pulls out features tuned to dynamics that respect the local shape of how states evolve, mirroring smooth neural population activity. The usual learning objective supplies features tuned to reward. An attention mechanism, likened to cortical gating, then fuses the two streams separately for each state. On benchmark tasks, the design improved learning speed and overall performance over standard approaches. Attention maps also revealed how the balance between feature types shifts during an episode, offering a window into the agent's choices.
arxiv-2606-18569:
Eppstein extends a classic theorem about point sets whose pairwise distances are all whole numbers, in a 2026 geometry paper. The Erdős-Anning theorem says such a set in Euclidean space, of any dimension, must be either finite or lie on a single line.

He proves the same statement in hyperbolic space of any dimension. He also gives the first quantitative version for higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. If a set of integer-distance points contains a modest subset in general position with a given diameter, the whole set's size is bounded by a function of dimension and diameter. The engine is a lemma about systems of tangent spheres, showing that a certain tangency pattern forces the spheres' centers onto one hyperplane. As a side benefit, the lemma shows that in position-finding from distance differences, a handful of landmarks always narrows a location to at most two possibilities.
arxiv-2606-18669:
Hao and the team propose a dynamical way to destroy the domain walls that plague spontaneous CP violation, without permanently breaking CP, in a 2026 cosmology paper. Spontaneous CP violation elegantly solves the strong CP problem. But if breaking happens after inflation, the universe fills with walls between degenerate CP vacua. Those walls would dominate its energy density, forcing the reheating temperature below the breaking scale.

Their mechanism adds a new scalar field. It sits at a large value with a nontrivial phase. Through a higher-dimensional interaction, it induces a temporary bias between the vacua. The pressure then collapses the wall network. As the scalar rolls toward the origin, the bias disappears. The low-energy CP structure is left intact. The authors derive the conditions for successful decay, and map the viable parameter space. The same field's coherent oscillations naturally survive as dark matter, linking the two problems.
arxiv-2606-18769:
Santonen and the team show the broad spectral lines of silicon oxide on silicon come from a continuous smear of atomic settings, not a few discrete chemical states. It is a 2026 surface science paper. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy is the standard tool for the ultrathin oxide films used in electronics and solar cells. The textbook reading of its silicon spectra assigns one shifted peak per oxidation state, implying neat stacked layers of intermediate oxides.

With measurements plus statistical simulations spanning compositions from pure silicon to silicon dioxide, the authors show the broadening is a statistical spread of core-level binding energies. It reaches five electron volts for the monoxide composition. It matches layer-by-layer spectra rebuilt from argon sputtering data. Because the spread blurs the fingerprints of single structural motifs, the conventional chemical-state assignment can mislead claims about oxide films.
arxiv-2606-18969:
Ouali and colleagues tackle causal inference on time series in 2026, where hidden traits sway who gets a treatment and when. Treatments often start at unlike times for unlike people or units. That makes a simple average of paths across treated cases ill-defined. The authors thus first gauge the effect for each unit, then combine those gauges into the mean effect for the treated group.

Their neural method, Balanced Twins, learns compact codes for each time series and treatment chance scores at the same time. A flexible match step then builds the missing counterfactual path for each unit. It drops the strict shape limits used in classic synthetic control work. Tests use real power-use data from demand-response schemes, plus care-unit data with built-in ground truth. The method copes with staggered starts and shifting dynamics, and it sharpens counterfactual gauges where hidden bias is at play.
arxiv-2606-19169:
Wasalathilaka and colleagues present RespGeomLib in 2026, a reproducible engine for generating human airway lumen geometry. CT-derived airway models aid lung measurement and airflow simulation, but distal scan resolution is limited and cleanup near branch points is heavy. Rule-based models are reproducible, yet many stitch tubes together, leaving rough junctions and poor open boundaries.

RespGeomLib builds airway surfaces from compact YAML specifications instead. Port-based assembly joins pieces, and smooth-min blending in an implicit form makes junctions seamless. Analytic segments plus local extraction near branch points avoid costly full-tree voxelization. The engine yields cleaner junctions than a Boolean stitch baseline and runs far faster with less memory than global implicit extraction. It also demos measurement-guided tree generation, controlled synthetic variants, and export ready for airflow simulation. Medical teams gain reproducible airway geometry on demand.
arxiv-2606-19569:
Sam Goring, Tom Kuipers, Nicola Paoletti, and David Watson propose QUEST in 2026, a new way to measure uncertainty in machine learning. Uncertainty quantification guides high-stakes choices in safety-critical settings. Standard scalar scores judge uncertainty by pointwise prediction risk, which can mislead when the target statistic is not the average.

QUEST instead measures the volume of the most probable region of a distribution. A robustness parameter sets how much probability mass that region must hold. Links emerge to classical statistics from information theory and economics. Unlike scoring-rule rivals, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty meet adapted axioms. They rise under distributional spread and stay fixed under location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks favour QUEST over variance and differential entropy. The frame suits regression tasks where the shape of doubt matters more than one risk number.
arxiv-2606-20269:
Avi Vajpeyi, Giorgio Mentasti, Quentin Baghi, Ollie Burke, and Lorenzo Speri give gravitational-wave analysts a complete, modern implementation of the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency transform. Their 2026 paper notes that the WDM transform is widely used, yet lacks a self-contained, explicit reference for practitioners, especially those working in Python and JAX pipelines. Their open-source package, wdm_transform, fills that gap and documents the transform's foundations and practical use.

The package provides NumPy and JAX backends. Forward and inverse transforms are validated to floating-point precision, and the JAX version runs million-point streams on GPUs in tens of milliseconds. As a worked example, the WDM-domain likelihood reproduces frequency-domain posteriors for a resolved LISA galactic binary under a shared noise model. The work sets up systematic optimization of WDM tilings for future detectors, where noisy, gappy data will demand time-frequency methods.
arxiv-2606-20469:
Md Sakir Ahmed, Kumaresh Sarmah, and Hemen Dutta rebuild the flat-minima story of SGD on Fisher geometry. Their 2026 paper targets a foundational crack: Euclidean sharpness measures, like the Hessian trace, change under reparametrizations that leave the network's function untouched. A flatness notion that depends on coordinates cannot explain generalization.

Grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the Fisher information manifold, the authors define Riemannian sharpness and prove it invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations. That answers the classic critique of Dinh and coauthors head-on. Gradient noise in mini-batch SGD is formalized with covariance tied to the Fisher matrix, linking the geometry to where SGD actually settles. Flat minima can now be discussed in terms that survive a change of variables.
arxiv-2606-20569:
Philip Waggoner clarifies what co-adaptive neural interface experiments can and cannot identify about user adaptation. His 2026 paper builds on recent work by Madduri and coauthors, where a human user and a machine decoder adapt jointly in closed loop, studied through game theory and EMG control.

Waggoner shows that the fitting procedure recovers joint closed-loop behavior, but separating the user's adaptation from the decoder's is another matter. Decoder learning rates and penalties shape observed user behavior, so naive readings credit the human for the machine's learning. The clarification tells experimenters which claims their designs actually license. Co-adaptive interface science gets a firmer footing.
arxiv-2606-20769:
Prabhjot Singh and three colleagues introduce FirstPass in 2026, a dataset and model grounded in real editorial outcomes for scientific peer review. Many AI review systems train only on computer science venues. They ignore the dialogue across review rounds. They also judge style rather than editorial judgment. FirstPass addresses all three limits using transparent peer review at Nature Communications.

The dataset holds 3,668 complete multi-round review dialogues across five domains: biology, chemistry, neuroscience, physics, and earth science. Content integrity is checked by automated audit. A Qwen model is fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation on three tasks. These are review generation, reviewer updating, and revision-cycle prediction. Response-only loss masking proves essential. Without it, accuracy is 62.0 percent. With it, outcome prediction reaches 80.5 percent. Grounding review models in real decisions could make them more useful and less imitative.
arxiv-2606-20869:
Selin Yildirim, Yingbing Huang, and Deming Chen present A3C3 in 2026, a methodology that designs AI algorithms and their hardware accelerators together. Traditional design treats model and hardware as separate stages. A model is built for accuracy first. Only later is it adapted to latency, energy, or resource limits. That separation yields suboptimal systems, especially for varied, memory-heavy workloads.

A3C3 parameterizes both design spaces and searches them jointly. It can generate model and accelerator pairs that balance accuracy, speed, throughput, energy, and hardware use. Differentiable co-search turns design choices into continuous variables for gradient methods. Hardware cost models enter the search directly. The chapter also extends the ideas to large language models. Inference there is limited by decoding and memory movement. Joint design matters because the cheapest accurate model on paper may be the most expensive one to run.
arxiv-2606-21269:
Basak and a large team of collaborators report new spectroscopy in 2026 on samarium-152, a nucleus near a shape-phase transition, where the nucleus shifts between spherical and deformed forms. Using gamma-ray spectroscopy after an alpha-induced reaction on neodymium-150, they extended several collective bands built on excited zero-plus states. Directional correlation and polarization measurements fixed spin and parity for the new levels.

Transition strengths drawn from branching ratios and known lifetimes show strong collectivity in the excited bands, not just in the ground state. The energies and strengths match the X(5) critical-point picture, which describes nuclei caught midway in the transition. Finding X(5)-like patterns in higher bands, beyond the known low-lying ones, tightens tests of critical-point behavior in finite nuclei and in the neutron-rich N=90 region.
arxiv-2606-21369:
Mate Farkas, Piotr Mironowicz, and Remigiusz Augusiak prove a best-possible result in 2026 for device-independent random number generation, the most secure way to make private random numbers with quantum devices. Security there rests only on observed measurement statistics, with no need to trust or characterize the hardware. Entangled systems are costly, though, so squeezing the most randomness from each one matters.

Using projective measurements, the easiest kind to implement, they certify two times log base two of d random bits from a pair of systems of dimension d. That holds for every d of at least two. That rate is the theoretical maximum. Their explicit protocols rest on mutually unbiased bases, and numerical bounds for imperfect devices show the schemes tolerate realistic experimental noise.
arxiv-2606-21669:
Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Yuze Du, and Guoquan Huang build a legged-robot odometry system in 2026 that teaches itself online and shrugs off sensor failure. Classic multi-sensor fusion needs meticulous calibration and platform-specific kinematic models. Their plug-and-play design instead uses packaged camera or LiDAR motion pipelines as a continuous teacher, training a velocity network on the robot's own proprioceptive signals: joint sensors and inertial data.

An invariant extended Kalman filter fuses the learned velocity with inertial measurements. When the outside-looking sensors degrade, in darkness or featureless scenes, the system falls back seamlessly on the learned proprioceptive model. Shown on different quadruped robots, the odometry stays robust in hard cases and adapts to new hardware without the usual calibration burden.
arxiv-2606-22269:
Adjovi and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, large language models translating English into Hausa and Fongbe, two typologically distinct West African languages. They test four models on five hundred to ten thousand sentences, scoring output with standard automatic metrics validated against native-speaker judgement. A recurring question is whether those metrics can be trusted for low-resource languages.

Translation quality differs sharply by language. Hausa reaches acceptable quality, with human scores of 4.0 to 4.5 out of five, while Fongbe stays poor at 1.0 to 2.2, with a consistent threefold BLEU gap. Rankings also flip by language: Gemini leads for Fongbe, GPT-4o for Hausa. Metric reliability flips too, with perfect rank correlation for Fongbe but weak correlation for Hausa. There, humans preferred GPT-4o although every automatic metric ranked Claude first. Neural metrics like BERTScore also show embedding collapse.
arxiv-2606-22369:
Rouvier and Bousquet present Kiwano in 2026, an open-source toolkit for speaker verification research. The task decides whether a voice sample matches a claimed identity, using compact speaker embeddings scored by similarity back-ends. Progress in the field depends on comparable experiments, yet toolkits often prioritize breadth over reproducibility.

Kiwano is a lightweight, extensible framework built on PyTorch. It offers standard recipes, pretrained models, and integrations of several widely used architectures. Clear training pipelines, unified scoring protocols, and ready-to-use baselines span multiple corpora. The toolkit also includes benchmarking, experiment tracking, and rapid prototyping support. It is distributed under the Apache 2.0 license, with full documentation and reproducible experiments. The authors aim to lower entry barriers and standardize scoring for both academic and applied work.
arxiv-2606-22569:
Siyuan Zhang and nine colleagues turn a material quirk into a light source in this 2026 photonics paper. Structured light carrying orbital angular momentum offers many channels for communication and imaging. Existing emitters encode each channel into gratings or waveguides, tying capacity to structural complexity.

The team instead use the anisotropy of thin-film lithium niobate, whose optical response depends on direction. In an X-cut microring, a circulating whispering-gallery mode samples a periodically varying refractive index, which modulates its phase. Each mode then emits not one vortex charge but a lattice of sideband charges with Bessel-weighted strengths. Tests resolved charges from minus thirteen to plus thirteen. Other devices showed scalable addressing, and the beams focused into annular perfect-vortex fields and healed after obstruction. A model reproduced the lattices. All of this comes from the material itself, with no separate grating for each channel.
arxiv-2606-22669:
Itai Kreisler, Yair Carmon, and Oliver Hinder tackle a barrier in adaptive optimization in this 2026 paper. Adaptive methods for stochastic convex optimization face a price of adaptivity. Under standard assumptions they cannot efficiently adapt to large uncertainty in both the starting distance to the optimum and the Lipschitz constant, which measures how fast the objective can change.

The authors circumvent the barrier by assuming some extra structure common in learning. The objective splits into a model and a loss, letting the algorithm intervene on the model's output before the loss sees it. Their method clips the learned model's output in tail events, whenever it deviates too far from a fixed reference output. With that one intervention, it matches the optimal bounds of the fully informed setting. It does so up to logarithmic factors, adapting efficiently to large uncertainty in each unknown parameter.
arxiv-2606-22769:
Shreyash Rawat argues discarded data predicts new occupations in this 2026 paper. Standard pipelines for clustering job postings discard the ten to fifteen percent density-based methods label as noise. Rawat's Emergence-Density Inversion hypothesis says the opposite: in fast-moving fields, sparse clusters signal novelty, not incoherence.

He tests this on 84,988 postings across eight quarters, late 2022 to 2024, scoring outlier groups with an Emerging Occupation Score. High-scoring groups became stable clusters in one and a half quarters, versus four for low scorers, though it failed in a fifth of cases. Extending the score with temporal velocity and cross-platform convergence lifted two-quarter prediction accuracy above four baselines. Looking backward, the score flagged MLOps Engineer, DevOps, and Data Engineer two to three quarters before they formed clusters. Its emerging picks for late 2024 were Prompt Engineer, AI Safety Researcher, Foundation Model Engineer, and Agent Systems Engineer.
arxiv-2606-22869:
Mohammed Alshahrani proposes a new algorithm for variational inequalities and equilibrium problems in this 2026 paper. These problems ask for a point in a closed convex set where a gap function, measuring distance from a solution, reaches zero. His method mixes a scaled projection step, whose size adapts through a variable metric, with a modified non-monotone line search.

The key is a structural identity: the projection step is exactly the maximizer that defines the Fukushima regularized gap. So the search direction is at once the step the algorithm takes and the direction the gap is built from. For strongly monotone, Lipschitz operators, Alshahrani proves global convergence at an R-linear rate, with the metric fixed or changed in a controlled way. For equilibrium problems he proves global convergence and a gap error bound. Tests on controlled problems confirmed the predicted rate and compared well with standard methods.
arxiv-2606-22969:
Georg Trede and colleagues ask whether models of dynamical systems can predict beyond their training regime in a 2026 paper. A dynamical system is any process whose state evolves over time by fixed rules. Models trained on many systems can recover hidden control settings from data. Yet they usually fail in new regimes, such as past a tipping point where behavior changes sharply. Retraining on fresh data is the usual fix, which defeats the point of a general model.

Trede and colleagues trace the failure to three mismatches between model assumptions and real physical systems. Their main remedy splits latent features so regime information stays separate from state information. They also derive a formula bounding how far out reliable prediction can reach. In tests, the repaired models predicted accurately into unseen regimes with no extra training, including across tipping points.
arxiv-2606-23069:
KunHo Heo and colleagues rethink prototype-based learning for few-shot object detection in a 2026 computer vision paper. Few-shot detection finds objects from new categories given only a handful of labeled examples. Prototype methods compare image features against a stored class prototype, needing no extra training. Two flaws limit them. Classes that look alike get confused because the score gap between classes collapses. The scores also say little about where the object sits, so box placement stays imprecise.

Heo and colleagues anchor the comparison in class text features, which highlight channels carrying true class signal and mute style-driven noise. The wider score gap cuts class confusion. Their second component turns box placement into a staged process, refining boxes step by step. Deep vision features guide the rough early placement, while shallow features rich in edges polish the final fit.
arxiv-2606-23469:
Tuan Tran and Zixiang Xu overturn a long-believed bound in extremal combinatorics in a 2026 paper. The Erdős-Frankl-Pach problem concerns uniform families of sets with bounded VC-dimension, a measure of complexity. Erdős, Frankl, and Pach conjectured in the 1980s that the largest such family is a star, all sets sharing one element. Ahlswede and Khachatrian disproved that in 1997 with a slightly larger construction. Their value was widely believed optimal, and Mubayi and Zhao conjectured exactly that in 2007. A recent proof for the smallest case added support to the belief.

Tran and Xu show that the Mubayi-Zhao conjecture fails for every dimension parameter from three upward. They construct families strictly larger than the Ahlswede-Khachatrian bound. The constructions suggest the true answer depends delicately on both the ground set size and the dimension parameter, reopening a problem many considered settled.
arxiv-2606-23569:
Eibert and colleagues speed up precise antenna measurements without giving up low noise, in a 2026 radio engineering paper. Antenna tests need a high signal-to-noise ratio, a clean signal well above background noise. Reaching it normally means long receiver integration times at every frequency and position. With thousands of samples, a full near-field scan can take extremely long.

Their approach collects every sample quickly, then cleans the data afterward. A Fourier transform converts the samples, a narrow bandpass filter keeps only the wanted signal, and an inverse transform returns clean samples. The trick works for plain single tones and for modulated carriers with several tones. The team demonstrates it on drone-based near-field data from two navigation aids, a DVOR beacon and an instrument landing system localizer. Converting the cleaned data to the far field yields useful diagnostic information about the antennas.
arxiv-2606-23769:
Das, Ghosh, and Puri revisit limits on hypothetical light particles using the famous supernova of 1987, in a 2026 paper on particle astrophysics. Supernova 1987A's neutrino burst lasted about ten seconds, matching standard theory. Any new particle produced in the core would carry energy away, cooling it faster and shortening that burst. Such cooling arguments bound many proposed particles, including the Z prime considered here, an extra force carrier tied to a muon minus tau symmetry.

Earlier bounds assumed the boson's polarization states mix freely inside the core. Das and colleagues argue this mixing is suppressed when the coupling is weak. Treating the polarizations as transporting energy independently then changes the limits substantially, reshaping the excluded parameter space.
arxiv-2606-23869:
Yu and colleagues report one of the faintest galaxies ever seen from the universe's first few hundred million years. A foreground cluster's gravity stretches it into an arc, in their 2026 paper on early galaxies. Strong gravitational lensing magnifies distant sources, letting telescopes study galaxies far below normal detection limits. In deep Webb images of the Abell S1063 cluster field, the team finds GAR10, a dropout galaxy at redshift about ten. Lensing magnifies it roughly forty three fold, making it among the faintest sources known at that era once corrected.

The galaxy's ultraviolet continuum is unusually blue, and one filter band shows a significant excess over its neighbors. Two explanations fit. The galaxy may be an extremely metal poor, nearly pristine stellar population. Or it may be one to three million years old, with the excess produced by intense emission lines from ionized gas. Only future spectroscopy can decide.
arxiv-2606-24069:
Du and colleagues examine a strange binary star system built around PSR J1932+2121, the slowest-spinning spider pulsar known in our galaxy. Spider pulsars are fast-spinning neutron stars whose wind slowly strips a low-mass companion. This one's radio signal vanishes for part of each orbit, as material blocks the beam. Observations from the FAST telescope in China anchor the team's 2026 modelling of that eclipse.

Fitting how the signal's delay and brightness change across the eclipse pins the orbit to a nearly edge-on tilt. It also points to a weak wind from the companion. Synchrotron absorption, where energetic electrons soak up radio waves, can reproduce the observed fading. Du's group also predicts X-ray light from the shock where the winds collide. That glow should rise and fall twice per orbit. It may be detectable by current X-ray telescopes, guiding future observations.
arxiv-2606-24669:
Liu, Huang, and Wu let a language model whisper guidance to a reinforcement learner instead of ordering it around. Language models plan well but make unreliable direct controllers, since their actions must be generated precisely. LaGO instead uses a pretrained model as a latent action prior, softly steering online policy optimisation while the reinforcement learner keeps final control of every action.

On a discrete robot benchmark and a continuous-control suite, LaGO consistently improves both reward and success rate over vanilla proximal policy optimisation, the standard baseline. Success rates multiply severalfold on the continuous benchmark and nearly double on the discrete one. Stronger pretrained language models provide more effective guidance, suggesting the benefit is genuine transferred knowledge rather than noise. Liu's 2026 design occupies a middle ground between trusting the language model outright and ignoring it: its knowledge shapes the search, while interaction with the environment still arbitrates what survives.
arxiv-2606-24769:
Matteo Raviola and Benjamin Peherstorfer add inertia to Dirac Frenkel dynamics, a method for evolving solutions written in nonlinear parameters. Such parametrisations, seen in neural networks and mixture models, can be redundant. The plain dynamics may then give parameter motion that is not unique or is badly conditioned. Inertia lets useful velocity information persist from the recent past in directions the current data barely inform. Well informed directions keep following the standard dynamics as before.

The inertial version provably yields well posed parameter dynamics, the authors show. They also derive error bounds that can be checked after the fact. After time discretisation, each step solves the same kind of regularised least squares problem as the standard method. The previous velocity simply enters as an anchor. Numerical experiments then demonstrate the payoff. Robustness improves clearly when inertia is switched on. The method targets evolution problems with learned parametrisations.
arxiv-2606-24969:
Klaus Schertler and four colleagues rebuild reservoir computing inside the frequency domain. Echo state networks train easily: recurrent weights stay fixed, so no backpropagation through time is needed and training has a closed form solution. Their weakness is scale. Expressive tasks demand large reservoirs, and updating a dense reservoir state costs quadratically in its size. The FRESCO architecture moves the whole computation into the frequency domain. A packed frequency domain readout, a dimensional zero padding input embedding, and a nonlinearity applied natively in that domain do the heavy lifting.

The result is linear complexity for dense nonlinear recurrent updates, with no domain shift overheads. Training and inference costs drop sharply. Performance does not suffer for the savings. FRESCO matches the state of the art on memory benchmarks, on sequence classification, and on multi series long horizon forecasting. Schertler and colleagues offer a scalable path for dense recurrent architectures.
arxiv-2606-25069:
Nathan Kaib and Sean Raymond argue a passing star, not just the tide, shaped today's comets. Long period comets fall inward from the Oort cloud, driven mainly by the Milky Way's tidal field. That tide should imprint an anisotropy on the perihelion directions of fresh comets. Simulations of tide driven production tell a different story: observed fresh comets look more isotropic than the tide predicts, while returning comets match well. Something extra seems to have stirred the cloud.

If the star HD 7977 passed within six to ten thousand astronomical units of the Sun two and a half million years ago, both comet distributions are reproduced. The solar system would be in the tail of that comet shower. The comet flux would run about twice the long term rate, and the Oort cloud's population should be halved. Kaib and Raymond note the Gaia release can test this.
arxiv-2606-25169:
Sampling from a complicated probability distribution often runs a noise process backwards, which needs the score, the gradient of the log density, at every noise level. Alois Duston and Tan Bui-Thanh study in 2026 how to blend two unbiased score estimators in the best possible way. Simple weighted averages use one number for the blend, but their approach allows a full matrix gate that can treat each direction differently. The optimal gate turns out to have a closed form they call the Laplace Fisher gate identity.

Because the two estimators disagree only by noise with zero mean, the gate cuts variance without biasing the result. The team proves the estimated gate stays consistent and stable with finite reference samples. On a benchmark inverse problem governed by a partial differential equation, their surrogate density improved calibration and evidence estimates over rival estimator classes.
arxiv-2606-25569:
Suspensions of soft vesicles, stand ins for red blood cells, are painfully slow to simulate because every membrane interacts with every other through the fluid. S Zhong, G Kabacaoğlu, and G Biros introduce VesNet in 2026, a hybrid solver that neuralises only the expensive local pieces. Networks approximate each vesicle's self interaction, its coupling to the background flow, and the lubrication forces that spike when two vesicles nearly touch. Classical modules still handle membrane reparameterisation and far field interactions.

The graphics processor version ran over a hundred times faster than a leading boundary integral solver on a multicore processor. It also ran about five times faster than the same solver on a graphics processor. Accuracy checks recovered single vesicle shape diagrams, pair dynamics, and thousand vesicle flows in two standard settings. Modest hardware can now run studies that once needed clusters.
arxiv-2606-25869:
Arindam Das, working with Wei Liu and Supriya Senapati, studies how the Large Hadron Collider could reveal heavy Majorana neutrinos. These hypothetical particles sit behind the tiny masses of ordinary neutrinos in the type-I seesaw picture, a leading explanation for why neutrino masses are so small. The team's focus is a matter-antimatter imbalance in lepton events, called leptonic CP asymmetry, and how that imbalance connects with collider searches.

Simulated detector-level events in same-sign and opposite-sign dilepton channels let Das and colleagues map sensitivity against the ratio of those two event classes. For heavy neutrino masses near sixty to eighty gigaelectronvolts, the projected limits beat current bounds by about a factor of ten, and the high-luminosity upgrade should add another factor of ten. Reach falls sharply when the same-sign share drops, which ties collider prospects closely to the size of the CP asymmetry.
arxiv-2606-26069:
C. Ruth Le Sueur, James Croft, and Jeremy Hutson improve the hunt for bound states in coupled-channel calculations. Such calculations model molecules and weakly bound complexes by propagating one coordinate numerically and expanding the rest in basis sets. Bound states hide at special energies. At those energies, one eigenvalue of a matching matrix passes through zero. Old methods for tracking the right eigenvalue demanded fiddly programming.

Simpler tracking is the contribution here. The algorithm follows the needed eigenvalue across its full energy range. Programming effort drops sharply as a result. The matching distance gets equal care. Coupled-channel methods run fastest when that distance sits in the classically allowed region for every channel of interest. It should also avoid nodes in the wavefunction. The guidance suits van der Waals complexes and other weakly bound systems, where these methods earn their keep.
arxiv-2606-26269:
Álvaro Adrián Carrasco Álvarez and Samuel Poncé settle a long argument about chromium oxide, a transparent conducting oxide. Textbooks label the material p-type, meaning holes carry its current. Doubts about its true character never fully died. Their verdict comes from first principles: phonon-limited mobilities for electrons and holes, computed with the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation. Electrons win across a wide temperature range.

Scattering is not the culprit. Phonons buffet electrons and holes about equally. The asymmetry lives in the electronic structure: the valence band is heavier and split across multiple valleys, which slows holes down. Intrinsic behaviour is therefore n-type, with electrons as the natural carriers. Moderate hole mobility still allows bipolar transport, a useful bonus. The familiar p-type readings must come from defects, the authors argue, matching earlier defect studies. Transparent electronics and magneto-optoelectronic designs gain a corrected foundation for this material.
arxiv-2606-26669:
Zhongxin Guo, Danrui Qi, Hanwen Gu, Peng Cheng, and Yongqiang Xiong present Skill-DisCo, a framework that turns agent experience into reusable skills. AI agents often solve near-identical tasks from scratch, wasting reasoning effort. Earlier work reused workflows, but which scenarios admit reusable procedures was unclear. The authors study settings defined by finite-state machines, where successful runs are paths through a transition graph.

A procedural skill becomes a reusable piece of control flow with adjustable parameters. Skill-DisCo distils such pieces from successful traces. It then compiles them into skills that can be called, executed, and verified like programs. Tests ran on ALFWorld, a household-task world, and WebArena, a web-task benchmark. Success rates rose and the number of agent turns fell across benchmarks and model sizes.
arxiv-2606-26769:
Qicheng Zhao, Yu Li, Qi Sun, and Zheyu Yan present ResilPhase, a method to speed up diffusion image models without wrecking quality. Such models generate images through many slow steps. Cache-then-forecast schemes skip steps by extrapolating, but quality collapses at high speed-ups. The authors trace the failure to forecasting on features misaligned with the model's true trajectory.

They recast the task as extrapolating the whole trajectory at once, in the space of the underlying flow equation. Even then, high-order derivatives of that trajectory are noisy and unstable. A derivative-free extrapolator based on Lagrange interpolation sidesteps the problem. A bounded phase mapping further steadies the forecast across noise levels. The design is plug-and-play with existing models. The authors report strong speed-ups with quality largely preserved.
arxiv-2606-26969:
Munachiso Samuel Nwadike and four colleagues propose Einstein World Models, a blueprint for language models that think in pictures. Some reasoning may need more than words: imagining how a scene unfolds could complement text. Their systems insert short visual rollouts into the reasoning trace. A world-module generates the rollout, a little film of the scenario under discussion.

The rollout is not treated as the answer. It returns as an inspectable hypothesis the model can criticise and build on. Tool calling, already used for search and code, is thus extended to visual thought experiments. The name honours Einstein's famous imagined rides alongside light beams. The authors argue such visualisation could support kinds of complex thought that language alone captures poorly. The work is a design proposal with its architecture laid out.
arxiv-2606-27069:
Sójka, Steffek, and Grabmair ask how much of a court outcome comes from case facts and how much from which judge decides. Their test bed is a set of nearly fourteen thousand United Kingdom Employment Tribunal decisions. A fine-grained outcome taxonomy, meaning detailed labels beyond win or lose, supervises their model. On top sits a gated multi-task design that can lean on judge identity only where discretion plausibly rules.

Rivals that simply fine-tune a large Gemma language model with judge facts pasted into prompts do far worse. The two context signals barely combine through that single text channel. By contrast, the gated design, built on a smaller adapted encoder, sets a new best score with far fewer trainable weights. Gains cluster on the rarest and most ambiguous outcome classes. Learned judge profiles also show exactly where adjudicative context drives a prediction.
arxiv-2606-27169:
Mainik offers a new proof of Wantzel's theorem, the result that settled which regular polygons can be drawn with compass and straightedge. Gauss showed in 1796 how to build the seventeen-sided polygon and mapped the general pattern. He knew only polygons built from Fermat primes could work, but never proved the impossibility side. Wantzel completed that proof in 1837. Mainik revisits the theorem with fresh arguments, in a paper published in 2026.

Part of the proof is carried out through two different approaches, echoing Gauss's remark that truths deserve multiple routes. Constructible side counts must combine powers of two with distinct Fermat primes. Every other regular polygon is impossible with the two classical tools alone. The new route clarifies why the boundary sits exactly there. Historical notes trace how Klein's later proof eclipsed Wantzel's priority. Students of constructibility gain a modern, self-contained path to the classic result.
arxiv-2606-27269:
Gibson and colleagues introduce Ribbon, a fast shortcut for honest uncertainty estimates around fitted models. Bayesian and bootstrap methods measure prediction doubt well but demand costly posterior sampling or repeated refits. Ribbon replaces refits with an influence-function linearisation around one fitted model. That keeps the first-order reweighting structure of the Bayesian bootstrap while needing only post-hoc linear algebra. In the 2026 statistics paper, a tunable concentration setting lets users calibrate the doubt scale on validation data.

Under a correct likelihood, Ribbon matches a flat-prior Laplace approximation as data grow. Under misspecification, it recovers the robust sandwich covariance instead. Synthetic regression, image classification, and housing benchmarks supply the tests. Ribbon stays competitive on forecasts while improving calibration in several settings. No repeated retraining is needed at any point. Large modern models, where refits are prohibitive, are the natural beneficiaries of the shortcut.
arxiv-2606-27469:
Doron Arad, Gal, and Naor repair the benchmark for online dominating set problems, where vertices arrive one by one and must be covered as they come. Comparing an online algorithm against an all-knowing offline optimum is hopeless: even a star graph forces a huge competitive ratio. Their incremental model constrains the benchmark itself to the same one-by-one choices the algorithm faces. First results cover vertex-weighted graphs and randomised algorithms, in an algorithms paper published in 2026.

A deterministic algorithm achieves a competitive ratio linear in the maximum degree, and a randomised one brings it down to a squared logarithm of the degree in the reported bounds. The results extend to connected dominating sets through a linear-programming formulation with local connectivity constraints. When each arriving vertex's neighbourhood is known in advance, deterministic algorithms match the polylogarithmic ratios. Matching lower bounds certify optimality up to constant factors.
arxiv-2606-27569:
Foucher, Delisle, and Jaouadi study coupled wave equations. These equations describe systems with several components at once. Examples include multi-part Bose–Einstein condensates, ultracold gases acting as one quantum fluid, and vector light pulses in optical fibres. Their 2026 paper develops a vector version of the Hirota bilinear method. The test case is the Manakov system, a classic fully solvable set of coupled equations.

Older methods split the system into separate components. Their method keeps the whole vector intact instead. That choice makes the coupling between components explicit. It also keeps the geometric structure visible throughout. With it they build exact soliton solutions. A soliton is a solitary wave that holds its shape. They cover bright, dark, and mixed forms. The solutions include one, two, and three solitons at a time. The work frames this approach as groundwork for rogue waves and periodic waves.
arxiv-2606-27669:
Search agents answer complex questions by retrieving and reasoning in steps. Real user requests are often vague or partly wrong, though. Ambiguity can send a long search chain down the wrong path. Yiling Tao and five colleagues built DiscoBench in 2026 to test how agents handle that. The benchmark checks whether agents notice ambiguity and ask for clarification.

DiscoBench holds 211 samples with 463 ambiguity instances. They span eleven real-world domains and four ambiguity types. A user simulator supports multi-turn interaction during tests. Scoring covers task utility, ambiguity detection, interaction strategy, and cost efficiency. Experiments on representative large language models reveal a split. Detecting ambiguity and clarifying it well are distinct capabilities. Repeated searching instead of asking often did worse than direct guessing. Proactive clarification proved far more effective in the reported comparisons. Retrieval skill alone does not make an interactive search agent.
arxiv-2606-27769:
Two frameworks dominate high-dimensional signal recovery. Approximate message passing gives fast iterative algorithms. The Convex Gaussian Min–Max Theorem gives asymptotic descriptions of convex estimators. Both often produce the same state-evolution equations. Their link has usually been indirect. Vikrant Malik and Babak Hassibi make the link direct in 2026, for regularised linear regression.

The bridge uses the theorem's two optimisations, called primary and auxiliary. When both yield the same primal-dual solution, the static framework recovers the dynamic one. The message-passing fixed-point equations come out, including the Onsager correction. The auxiliary problem's Gaussian vectors match the perturbations in its primal and residual channels. The same viewpoint handles regularised M-estimation. It recovers the fixed point of scalar-variance max-sum generalised message passing. A general payoff is suggested: new message-passing-like algorithms may be derived wherever the min–max theorem applies, where standard derivations are missing.
arxiv-2606-27969:
Meteorites preserve isotopic inhomogeneity in the solar system's oldest solids. Calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions show the effect. It may originate in the parent molecular cloud. Yoshiaki Misugi and three colleagues test that idea in 2026 with smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations. Cores form by fragmentation of a filament. The simulations track how isotopic ratios vary along the filament.

Geometry matters. Variation along the filament's minor axes has a smaller effect than variation along its length. Inhomogeneities survive into the resulting cores. Their size drops by a factor of about a hundred over the one-parsec initial filament. That is one to ten percent of the maximum ratio a core could acquire. The shells' inhomogeneity traces to turbulent velocity fields. Different centres of mass for different shells are the cause. The inhomogeneity could survive even into the circumstellar disk. The cloud-to-core inheritance route is therefore viable.
arxiv-2606-28369:
Yuanyuan Tian, Wenwen Li, Xiao Chen, Michael Brook, Michael Brubaker, Anna Liljedahl, and Chitta Baral search for similar environmental events across space and time. Community observers report odd happenings, a beached whale, a sudden fish kill, and linking related reports helps reveal patterns of environmental change that single reports cannot show.

Tian and colleagues combine foundation models in two strategies. CAMERA fuses text and images into richer event descriptions than text alone gives. ASTRA then re-ranks candidates using scale-aware spatial and temporal relevance beside semantic similarity. Tested on reports from the Local Environmental Observer Network, their vision-enhanced methods beat text-only language-model approaches at ranking similar events. Automatic linking, they argue, serves both curators and the public watching local environments change.
arxiv-2606-28469:
Thomas Vitry and eight colleagues ask when a robot should speak up. In group work, a proactive robot can offer help at the right moment, or can interrupt, split attention, and wreck turn-taking. A reactive robot protects human control but may watch a team struggle past chances to assist.

Vitry's team placed pairs of participants in a collaborative escape room with a humanoid robot, either reactive, answering only when addressed, or proactive, listening continuously and re-initiating on its own. The proactive robot multiplied interaction frequency, yet the reactive groups finished with a descriptively higher success rate, about ninety-three percent against seventy-one. Prior experience mattered: participants seasoned with language models solved early puzzles faster with the reactive robot, and robot experience and introversion reshaped how each style was judged.
arxiv-2606-28569:
B. Herrmann, K. Cao, C. A. Gonzalez, S. L. Brunton, and B. J. McKeon bring physical insight back into data-driven turbulence analysis. Resolvent analysis reveals which flow structures matter and why, but it demands specialized codes and heavy computation. Dynamic mode decomposition runs on plain simulation data, yet its structures carry no direct physical mechanism.

Their nonlinearity-subtracted variant uses snapshots of the perturbation equations' nonlinear terms to strip the nonlinear forcing out of the learned operator. What remains approximates the dynamics linearized around the mean flow, exactly what resolvent analysis studies. The team demonstrates data-driven resolvent analysis on direct and large-eddy simulations. The cases run from a minimal channel flow up to flow over a full aircraft model. It works as a post-processing step usable with any standard simulation code.
arxiv-2606-28969:
Negron and Luque introduce Democapsid, a software tool for building and picturing viral capsids, the protein shells that protect a virus's genetic material. Most capsids are icosahedral, with twenty-fold symmetry. Many are near-spherical, but elongated ones have been understudied, even though separating width from length gives extra control over packaging capacity, a trait of interest for evolution studies and virus-based technology.

A bottleneck has been the lack of tools for analysing and designing elongated capsids. Democapsid generates coordinates for spherical, stretched and shrunk capsids, plus custom graphics and journal-ready figures. Its algorithm builds on the generalised geometrical theory of viral capsids, assembling elements under folding constraints. Settings control the protein tiling, the stretch axis, roundness and body length. The tool ships as a browser application, a Python package with plugins for ChimeraX and Blender, and an R package, all under an MIT licence on GitHub.
arxiv-2606-29369:
Fowler proves an effective form of a case of the André-Oort conjecture, a statement about special points on algebraic curves. His setting is a curve in the complex plane where two coordinate functions have different degrees. The points of interest have both coordinates equal to CM j-invariants, values tied to elliptic curves with extra symmetry, called complex multiplication. Earlier effective results depended badly on the height, a measure of a curve's arithmetic size.

Fowler shows that an effectively computable constant bounds the height of every such point on the curve. Crucially, that constant depends only linearly on the height of the curve itself. Linear dependence is much better than what previous methods gave. The result is an instance of what he calls weakly bounded height. It sharpens number theory tools for finding all special points on a given curve, and it does so with explicit, usable bounds.
arxiv-2606-29569:
Silva leads a large team examining a quiet source of error in high-resolution spectroscopy: interpolation, the step that resamples spectra onto a common wavelength grid. Radial velocity measurements, which track a star's motion and can reveal orbiting planets, depend on template-based extraction. The team asks what systematic biases interpolation injects into that process.

Synthetic spectra built from Gaussian profiles let them vary the sampling location of spectral lines, as barycentric motion and instrument drift do in practice. Applying the s-BART pipeline shows biases whose peak-to-peak size reaches about twenty metres per second at low signal-to-noise, shrinking as signal quality rises. Noise-free data still show a tiny bias, far below current instrument precision. Real ESPRESSO observations of four stars confirm that high-cadence nights with small barycentric shifts are the most affected. Observations spread over a wider barycentric window show much smaller scatter.
arxiv-2606-29869:
Liu and five colleagues improve knowledge distillation for text generation, where a small student model learns to copy a large teacher. Standard distillation uses one KL divergence objective, a measure of how two probability distributions differ.

The authors show that forward and reverse KL divergence play complementary roles: one fits the main bulk of the teacher's distribution, the other covers its long tail of rare choices. Their framework, ARKD, uses reinforcement learning, where a policy network learns by reward, to set the weights of the two objectives on the fly from the teacher-student match. In experiments the method improves Rouge-L and BertScore, two text quality metrics, beating fixed greedy weighting by 0.4 to 0.6 points across benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-30069:
Yasmine Beji, Heger Arfaoui, and Slimane BenMiled map when complex contagion survives on random networks. In complex contagion, adoption needs reinforcement from several neighbors at once. Their model adds SIS-style recovery, so adopters can lapse and adopt again. The phase boundary between extinction and persistence was unmapped for this case. They reconstruct it across three parameters at once.

The parameters are spread rate, take-up threshold, and how long nodes stay infectious. The team ran over one hundred eighty thousand Monte Carlo trials. Adaptive Delaunay sampling and weighted logistic regression shape the boundary estimate. A six-parameter model with interaction terms describes the boundary well. Its structure stays the same on both network types tested. Those types are Erdős–Rényi and Barabási–Albert random networks. The changeover itself is sharp, spanning a tiny threshold band. The threshold dominates, with rate and duration playing smaller, uneven roles.
arxiv-2606-30169:
Valentin Emberger and nine colleagues bombard flight-grade X-ray sensors to predict their end-of-life behavior in orbit. The sensors serve the Wide Field Imager on ESA's NewAthena observatory. Their depleted p-channel transistor design promises very low readout noise. Radiation damage in space could erode that quality steadily. The team measures how noise components evolve under dose.

One module was irradiated with energetic protons at an Austrian accelerator. It stayed biased and cold, running as in flight, throughout the exposure. The dose equals a standard mission equivalent for these sensors. A second module received a similar dose much faster, probing annealing. Ionizing dose effects were tested in a separate run with molybdenum X-rays. Readout noise, dark current, and threshold voltage all shifted measurably. Results are compared with an earlier pre-flight sensor campaign. Required operating temperature and end-of-life state are reassessed accordingly.
arxiv-2606-30269:
Timothee Salamon, Robin Debuysschère, Adam Chafaï, Benoit Scheid, and Francois Gallaire study when a suddenly widening channel stops flowing symmetrically. Fluid enters a wider section and can hug one wall instead. Lateral inflow from the sides modifies that classic instability. The team varies the lateral-to-central flow rate ratio systematically. Experiments, stability analysis, theory, and simulations all contribute.

Three distinct flow regimes emerge from the combined evidence. Outside an intermediate ratio band, symmetry breaks above a critical Reynolds number. The central jet deflects toward one side wall in that regime. Weakly nonlinear analysis shows the bifurcation is usually supercritical. Inside the intermediate band, no critical Reynolds number exists at all. Simulations there blame residual asymmetry on geometric imperfections of the apparatus. Experimental fluctuations inside the band remain unexplained, the authors admit.
arxiv-2606-30369:
Théo Chasle Cauchy and four colleagues build a tool that judges synthetic musical sounds in words musicians actually use. Standard scores like Fréchet Audio Distance rank synthesizers but explain little. A global number cannot say which quality of a sound is off. Their 2026 predictor rates twenty timbre traits instead. Traits include words like woody, percussive, and rumbling.

A frozen CLAP audio embedding feeds a small trainable network. Training uses the RWC instrument database plus human judgments. Human raters scored thirty-one instruments on all twenty traits. The model's ratings match average human ratings strongly. Applied to the TokenSynth synthesizer, the tool proves doubly useful. Error scores over generated sounds reproduce the standard ranking. Per-sound trait profiles also flag which sounds need fixing. They show exactly which timbral traits need adjustment.
arxiv-2606-30469:
Dimitri Goutaudier speeds up simulations of elastic guided waves used to find hidden damage. Guided waves reveal corrosion and delamination early. Full simulations are costly in many-query settings. Reduced order models cut that cost by projecting onto small spaces. Guided waves are transport-dominated and dispersive, defeating static subspaces. Their Hamiltonian structure also demands care to conserve energy.

Dynamical low-rank approximation lets the reduced basis move with the solution. Goutaudier builds a parametric framework on that idea. An offline stage constructs a time-dependent symplectic reduced basis. For a simplified parameter class, the basis evolution has a closed form. That yields an energy-preserving reduced propagator with no online integration. Tests use a two-dimensional elasticity problem with damage. Compression reaches ranks of only ten to thirty. Reconstruction errors stay between a thousandth and a hundredth. Speedups run to two or three orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-30669:
Fu Xingcheng, Chen Xianjun and Li Zhihao describe the Local Pheromone Network, a small prototype that learns without backpropagation. Standard networks train all parameters together through global error signals, so new tasks can overwrite old associations. Their network is sparse and local instead. Each output unit reads only a neighbourhood of inputs, chosen by geometric distance and molecular-tag compatibility, like smells matching receptors.

Each synapse stores a weight plus short-term and long-term pheromone traces, chemical-style markers that fade or persist. Training uses pheromone-weighted Hebbian-style updates on a budgeted subset of synapses picked by local error. The budget adapts: it shrinks when loss improves and grows toward active neighbourhoods when loss worsens. Optional pieces add structural plasticity, replay and consolidation. In tests the prototype learned local linear rules, kept split memories separate through tags and masks, and forgot less under consolidation and replay.
arxiv-2606-30869:
Yohan Poirier-Ginter, Jean-François Lalonde and George Drettakis present GRay, a ray tracer for 3D Gaussians that runs almost as fast as splatting. Scenes built from 3D Gaussians are usually rasterised, projected onto the screen at high speed. Ray tracing them is more flexible but has lagged far behind, with the earlier 3DGRT system taking nearly ten times longer to optimise. GRay exploits a basic difference: a ray only touches the Gaussians it actually hits, so cost can grow logarithmically rather than linearly with scene size.

Dense starting points, which create many tiny Gaussians, slow rasterisation down but speed ray tracing up, and GRay leans into that effect. It renders nearly 4× faster and optimises nearly 10× faster than 3DGRT at similar quality. Against splatting itself it is speed-competitive, at somewhat lower quality.
arxiv-2606-30969:
Mohammad Reza Alipour, Saeed Noori Gashti and Mohammad Ali S. Afshar follow repeated extraction from a spinning, charged black hole. In the Penrose process, a particle splits inside the ergoregion; one fragment falls in with negative energy and the other escapes with more energy than it brought in. Repeating the trick changes the hole, so the team built a framework that updates the hole's mass, spin, charge and irreducible mass after every event. A triple turning-point condition yields analytic solutions of the conservation laws.

Two couplings steer the story. One governs whether particles can keep reaching the ergoregion, and so when the process stops. The other sets how deep the negative-energy states run, and so the efficiency. With an attractive coupling, the hole's spin can rise briefly even as angular momentum falls. Unlike the non-spinning case, the hole can pass through neutrality and flip its charge.
arxiv-2606-31169:
Li and three colleagues build S-OBI, a benchmark for sentence-level understanding of oracle bone inscriptions. These texts, carved on turtle shells and animal bones in the late Shang dynasty, are among China's earliest writing. AI work on them has mostly targeted single characters. A full inscription, though, is a structured divination record with a date, a diviner, and a charge. Reading it takes context, not just glyph matching.

S-OBI starts from 95 expert-verified rubbings with translations. Characters in each rubbing are swapped for clean glyph samples, keeping the layout and meaning intact. That removes rubbing noise, so tests focus on understanding rather than damage. The benchmark holds 695 question-answer pairs across semantic matching, slot extraction, and contextual reasoning tasks. Today's multimodal models performed poorly. Errors in unmasked regions spread through the reasoning chain and corrupted predictions for masked characters.
arxiv-2606-31369:
Dumas gives a constant-factor approximation for the maximum distance-2 independent set problem in graphs of bounded merge-width. A distance-2 independent set picks vertices far apart. Their closed neighbourhoods must never touch. Merge-width is a newer graph width measure, and the radius-2 case is the sweet spot here.

The algorithm rests on linear programming. So does the matching result for minimum dominating set drawn from earlier work. Together they show one key ratio stays bounded. That is the ratio of the domination number to the 2-independence number, when radius-2 merge-width is bounded. The result is tight.
