The review works through native, modified, and bottled forms and asks what the differences mean for trials and for patients receiving infusions.
europmc-pmc3622569:
Carol Pierannunzi, Shaohua Sean Hu, and Lina Balluz audited the trustworthiness of a giant American health survey in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2013. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System polls adults by telephone about smoking, drinking, weight, and disease, guiding policy nationwide. Falling response rates and new cell-phone sampling forced method changes, raising fair questions about whether its numbers still hold. Their review gathered every reliability and validity study of the system published from 2004 to 2011.

Judged against a scoring rubric that favored repeated test-retest designs and comparisons with physical measurements, the literature mostly reassured. The survey's prevalence rates stood close to those of other national surveys built on self-report, with specific gaps noted category by category. Against surveys using examinations and instruments, agreement weakened, as expected when people describe themselves. The authors conclude the system remains a usable national gauge while its methods evolve.
europmc-pmc3643869:
Two scores for rater agreement are put to the test in a 2013 BMC Medical Research Methodology study by Wongpakaran, Wongpakaran, Wedding and Gwet. Doctors who rate the same patient should land on the same call, and Cohen's Kappa is the standard score for that check. Yet Kappa is known to sag when a trait is rare or very common, which can mislead a study.

The test used 67 patients checked for personality disorders by nine raters in two rounds of talks, weeks apart. Gwet's AC1 score beat Kappa on every trait, with values from .752 to 1.000 while Kappa ran from 0 to 1.00. Kappa swung with how common a trait was; AC1 stayed close to the plain share of agreed calls. The authors urge AC1 as the steadier score for such checks.
europmc-pmc3695369:
Antal and Paulus review transcranial alternating current stimulation, a method that passes a weak oscillating current through the skull to interact with the brain's own rhythms. Unlike steady stimulation, the alternating current can in principle pull cortical oscillations into step with its frequency, or disrupt them, and long sessions may leave lasting plastic changes.

Early results suggest frequency matters: theta-range stimulation may aid thinking when timed in phase, alpha may help movement, beta intrusion may hinder it, and gamma may affect attention. Some frequencies light up the retina or alter motor cortex excitability. The authors present tACS as a young technique with specific, testable promises rather than settled therapy.
europmc-pmc3695769:
Schulz-Menger and colleagues present consensus standards for interpreting and post-processing cardiovascular magnetic resonance scans, issued by a task force of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance. These scans produce a wide range of measured values. Without agreed standards, reports vary between operators and centres.

The document sets requirements for how images should be evaluated, both by eye and by measurement, and discusses common pitfalls in analysis. The task force is candid that evidence behind many recommendations is limited, so the guidance represents expert consensus built on the best available evidence. The goal is consistent quality and repeatable reports wherever the scans are read.
europmc-pmc3792069:
Shenghua Gu and eight co-authors reported a mapping study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on bacterial communities along the mouse gut. Most gut microbe research uses feces alone, so how communities vary by gut region was little known. The team sampled seven sites, from stomach to colon plus feces, in C57BL/6 laboratory mice and sequenced a bacterial marker gene.

 From over 283,000 valid sequences, stomach, duodenum, large intestine, and fecal samples showed richer diversity than the jejunum and ileum. Small intestine and stomach communities differed clearly from large intestine and fecal ones. Lactobacillus relatives dominated the stomach and small intestine, while oxygen-shunning families ruled the large intestine and feces. Differences between individual mice were smaller in large intestine and fecal samples than in the upper gut.
europmc-pmc3871669:
Cristian Del Fabbro, Simone Scalabrin, Michele Morgante, and Federico M. Giorgi test read trimming tools in PLoS One in 2013. Next generation sequencing gives raw reads with ragged, low-grade ends. Trimming cuts those ends before analysis, yet few had checked how much the choice of trimmer matters.

The team ran nine trimming tools across four data sets and three common tasks: gene activity counts, variant hunting, and genome assembly. Trimming lifted result quality and trust in all three tasks. It also cut run time and computer load, since junk bases no longer clog the math. Gains varied by tool and task, so the study guides users to a fit choice. Their verdict is blunt: trimming should be a standard first step, not an option.
europmc-pmc3940169:
Douglas W. Fadrosh and colleagues improve a way to sequence many microbe samples at once. Their paper appeared in Microbiome in 2014. The platform is the Illumina MiSeq. Surveys read one marker gene, the 16S gene, from dozens of samples per run. Each sample wears a barcode tag on both ends. Such low-variety libraries read badly on this machine. The reads come out at poor quality.

Their fix adds a spacer before the tag. The spacer runs from zero to seven bases long. With it, samples fall out of step with each other. The machine then sees a more varied signal. The method gave high-quality data for the gene's V3-V4 zone. It worked under both the 250-base and 300-base paired protocols. The authors offer it as a cheap, flexible standard for clinical samples.
europmc-pmc4034769:
Sergey Ovchinnikov, Hetunandan Kamisetty, David Baker, and Benoit Roux predict which protein parts touch across joined proteins, in eLife in 2014. Proteins often work in teams, docking face to face. Contact points that sit close in the docked form tend to change in step over evolution, as a shift in one partner is offset by a shift in the other.

A stats method that reads such paired change had worked well inside single proteins. The team now aims it across the join. On close to thirty bacterial complexes of known shape, predicted contact pairs proved almost always true contacts, as long as the sequence set was deep enough. They then predicted contacts for dozens more complexes of unknown shape. Full models followed for four of them, among them two transport systems. It opens a route to team shapes from sequence data alone.
europmc-pmc4035669:
The 3,000 Rice Genomes Project reports a mass re-reading of rice DNA, in GigaScience in 2014. Rice feeds half the world. Output must rise by at least a quarter by 2030 to match demand, while climate change and lost farmland press the other way.

An international team re-sequenced a core set of three thousand rice strains from eighty-nine countries. Each genome was read to sound depth, covering nearly the whole genome. Aligned to a reference strain, the data yielded close to nineteen million single-letter variants. Family trees built from those variants split the rice pool into five known groups, from indica to the two japonica forms. The set gives breeders a deep store of variants for hunting useful traits. The team releases the data openly and calls for a shared global rice database built on it.
europmc-pmc4035769:
Guangshun Wang surveys the germ-fighting peptides and proteins of the human body, in Pharmaceuticals in 2014. More than a hundred such defenders have been found on skin, eyes, mouth, gut, and other surfaces. They form a first wall of innate immunity and also aid wound healing and immune tuning.

The chosen set shows a wide spread of size, charge, and shape. Their kills differ just as widely. One defensin weaves nets that trap bacteria on the surface. Two others jam cell wall building by gripping a key brick. A classic enzyme cuts wall sugars. One long peptide breaks curved bacterial skins. Others slip inside cells or form channels in the wall. The catalogue is a seed bank for new drugs against resistant germs.
europmc-pmc4036769:
Van-Mai Cao-Lormeau and seven colleagues report the first recognised Zika virus outbreak in French Polynesia, in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2014. The virus, a mosquito-borne flavivirus first isolated in Uganda in 1947, had caused only scattered human cases in Africa and Asia for decades. A 2007 outbreak on Yap Island was the first outside those regions.

In October 2013 a household cluster of mild dengue-like illness in French Polynesia tested negative for dengue. A PCR test for Zika, kept ready by the local lab, came back positive. The three patients had low fever, aching joints, headache, and rash. Dengue types one and three were spreading at the same time, complicating the picture. The report warns of a new arbovirus threat in the Pacific and calls for tighter watch.
europmc-pmc4076869:
Anil M. Narasimha and colleagues challenged the standard model of how the Rb tumour suppressor is switched off early in the cell cycle. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. The accepted view held that cyclin D with its partner enzymes gradually adds many phosphate tags to Rb, freeing growth factors in steps.

Instead, the team found Rb carries exactly one phosphate tag in early G1, in fourteen distinct versions, each with its own binding preferences for E2F factors. Full switch-off comes later, when cyclin E adds a burst of tags at the restriction point. DNA damage and cell differentiation use different Rb forms again. Mono-phosphorylated Rb, they conclude, is the only form present in early G1 and is active, not idle.
europmc-pmc4079069:
Vicent Ribas, Carmen García-Ruiz, and José C. Fernández-Checa reviewed glutathione inside mitochondria, the cell's energy centres. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Glutathione is the cell's main non-protein thiol, a sulphur compound that powers antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes.

Glutathione is made only outside mitochondria, yet its level inside them matches the rest of the cell, so special carriers must import it despite its negative charge. Inside, it defends against reactive oxygen species from breathing and neutralises fat breakdown products and other reactive chemicals. Its loss can sensitise cells to death signals. The authors link mitochondrial glutathione to cancer, fatty liver disease, and Alzheimer's disease, and to how cell death is triggered.
europmc-pmc4081569:
Rebecca M. Voorhees, Israel S. Fernández, Sjors H. W. Scheres, and Ramanujan S. Hegde produced detailed structures of a mammalian ribosome joined to the Sec61 channel. Their study appeared in Cell in 2014. As the ribosome builds secreted and membrane proteins, the new chain passes through or into the cell membrane via this channel.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, they captured the joined complex both idle and actively translating, at near-atomic sharpness. The maps allowed a near-complete atomic model of the mammalian ribosome and showed transfer RNAs in hybrid states plus a young protein chain inside the exit tunnel. Unprecedented chemical detail emerged for how the channel grips the ribosome and changes shape. Comparisons suggest how those shifts help a secreted chain cross the membrane.
europmc-pmc4082369:
Carlo Pirazzi, Stefano Romeo, and a large team tested whether the PNPLA3 protein handles vitamin A storage in human liver stellate cells. Their study appeared in Human Molecular Genetics in 2014. These star-shaped liver cells store retinoids and drive scarring in chronic liver disease, but the enzyme releasing their stores was unknown.

PNPLA3 turned out to be strongly expressed in the cells, with levels shaped by retinol supply and insulin. Raising it shrank lipid droplets and pushed retinol out of the cells after insulin. In pure form, the normal protein split retinyl palmitate into retinol and palmitic acid. A common variant linked to fatty liver disease did this far more weakly. The work ties a known disease gene to liver vitamin A handling.
europmc-pmc4086069:
José Ramón López-Blanco, José I. Aliaga, Enrique S. Quintana-Ortí, and Pablo Chacón launched iMODS, a web server for exploring how large biological molecules flex and move. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The method, normal mode analysis, predicts the collective motions a protein or similar molecule naturally makes.

Working in internal coordinates, the angles between bonds, keeps the molecule's chemistry intact while speeding the maths. Users can run vibration analysis, watch motion animations, and build plausible transition paths between two related structures, even for very large molecules. Detail can be tuned from coarse to atomic. Non-specialists get quick answers, while advanced users can adjust models and feed the moving structures into further modelling. The server is free with no login.
europmc-pmc4237769:
Shichun Tu, Huaxi Xu, and two co-authors reviewed how amyloid clusters break synapses in Molecular Neurodegeneration in 2014. Alzheimer's disease erases memory by destroying synapses, the junctions where neurons talk. Soluble clusters of amyloid-beta peptide, called oligomers, are prime suspects for that early damage.

The review follows the clusters' many attacks. They stir calcium signals out of range, switch on enzymes such as calcineurin, Gsk-3 beta, and Cdk5, and pull the receptors for the messenger glutamate inside the cell, silencing the junction. A scaffolding protein, PSD-95, that holds those receptors in place is also disrupted. Drugs that block the overexcited glutamate receptor, such as memantine, partly blunt the harm in models. The authors present synaptic rescue as a treatment goal in its own right.
europmc-pmc4267669:
Eva K Brinkman, Tao Chen, Mario Amendola, and Bas van Steensel present TIDE, a cheap way to measure how well genome editing worked in a pool of cells. Their method paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Editing tools such as CRISPR cut DNA, but the share of cells changed, and the mix of changes, can vary a lot by target site.

TIDE needs just two standard sequencing runs on DNA from the cell pool. Software then breaks the mixed trace apart at the cut site and reports the main changes and how often each one occurs. The free web tool gives far more detail than older enzyme tests and helps labs tune their editing plans fast.
europmc-pmc4283469:
Luc J Bourhis, Oleg V Dolomanov, Richard J Gildea, Judith A K Howard, and Horst Puschmann take apart the refinement engine inside the Olex2 program for crystal structures. Their paper appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section A in 2015. Refinement is the step where a rough atomic model is adjusted until it matches the measured X-ray data well.

The engine, olex2.refine, handles constraints that fix parts of a model and restraints that guide them softly, all within a least squares fit. The authors explain design choices meant for modern computers and complex structures. The account serves both users who want to know what the program does and programmers building similar tools.
europmc-pmc4367969:
Barbara Neumann, Athanasios Vafeidis, Juliane Zimmermann, and Robert Nicholls assessed future flood exposure on coasts worldwide, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Coastal zones face sea-level rise and flooding, and they already hold denser populations that grow faster than inland areas. Starting from population estimates for the year 2000, the team projected who will live in low coastal zones by 2030 and 2060, under four sea-level and social scenarios.

Asia holds the most people in low coastal zones and the most people exposed to rare, severe storm floods, now and in the projections. China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Viet Nam top the exposure list, and that ranking barely changes. Africa, though, is set for the fastest coastal population growth and urban spread. The study skips forced moves away from risk, which it flags as a limit.
europmc-pmc4373269:
Lotte Caarls, Corné Pieterse, and Saskia Van Wees reviewed how one plant hormone overrules another, in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Salicylic acid and jasmonic acid are the two main hormone signals in plant defense, and each switches on its own gene set. When both fire, salicylic acid often takes control of the genes jasmonic acid would induce. The review gathers the known routes by which that takeover happens in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana.

Salicylic acid can alter defense regulators through chemical changes driven by redox shifts inside the cell. It can park jasmonate-responsive factors in the cell fluid or lock them in repressor complexes in the nucleus. It can trigger breakdown of activators, raise repressor proteins that block target genes, and change DNA packaging at those genes. Together these routes let the plant fine-tune defense against different attackers.
europmc-pmc4380069:
Rebecca Richmond and co-authors tracked how a mother's smoking in pregnancy marks her child's DNA over life, using a British cohort in Human Molecular Genetics in 2015. Smoking in pregnancy was already tied to altered DNA methylation, chemical marks on DNA, in newborns. The team asked how dose and duration matter, and whether marks fade or persist. They studied about 800 mother-child pairs in the Avon study, with blood samples at birth and at ages 7 and 17.

In cord blood, marks at 15 sites in seven gene regions tracked with maternal smoking, rising with how long and how heavily she smoked. Some sites returned toward normal by later ages, while sites in four gene regions stayed altered through age 17. Home smoke exposure after birth explained little of the lasting pattern. The prenatal period thus leaves a long molecular trace.
europmc-pmc4392469:
Helena Chia and Benjamin Wu reviewed five years of progress in 3D printing of biomaterials, in the Journal of Biological Engineering in 2015. Printing builds devices layer by layer from a computer design, and medicine can feed it a patient's own anatomy. Early uses were surgical rehearsal models and molds. The field has moved toward one-of-a-kind implants, tissue scaffolds, diagnostic platforms, and drug delivery systems, with public access to cheap printers renewing interest.

The review walks through each major printing family, from fused deposition and laser sintering to stereolithography and direct bioprinting with cells, and gives examples in tissue engineering for each. Combining stem cells with custom scaffolds points toward personalized regenerative medicine. The authors flag the limits that remain before complex tissues like bone, cartilage, and vessels, or full organs, can be printed routinely, and set out what research must solve.
europmc-pmc4405269:
Heejung Shim and co-authors ran a genome-wide study of cholesterol particle subtypes, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Standard cholesterol tests lump particles together, but LDL and IDL come in subfractions that may carry different risk. The team measured ten subfractions by gel separation in 1,868 people of European ancestry, and also measured how those fractions responded to statin drugs. Their analysis handled all fractions jointly, which can reveal patterns single-trait tests miss.

Four known loci, SORT1, APOE, LPA, and CETP, showed very strong links to subfractions. Three of them likely hold several independent signals each. Curiously, two CETP variants hit LDL subfractions hard yet showed no link to total LDL, proving finer measures expose hidden genetics. Signals for statin response were much weaker, though APOE and LPA variants stood out there too.
europmc-pmc4483169:
Pin Wu, Dang Wu, Lijun Li, Ying Chai, Jian Huang, and Mohammed Soutto pooled studies of PD-L1 and cancer survival in PLoS ONE in 2015. PD-L1 is a protein tumors use to damp the immune attack on them, and drugs blocking it were in fast development. Whether tumors rich in PD-L1 mean a worse outlook for patients, though, was disputed across studies.

Searching the literature, the team combined dozens of studies covering thousands of patients with solid tumors. Tumors overexpressing PD-L1 were tied to worse survival at both three and five years overall. The link held for several specific cancers, including esophageal, stomach, liver, and bladder cancers at three years. The authors conclude PD-L1 carries real prognostic weight in solid tumors, while noting that its value for choosing checkpoint drug treatment is a separate question their survival data cannot answer.
europmc-pmc4489269:
Timothy Bailey, James Johnson, Charles Grant, and William Noble described the MEME Suite in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The suite is a set of web tools for finding motifs, short patterns conserved by evolution in DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. A motif may mark a protein binding site on DNA. It may mark the active site of an enzyme, or a piece needed for a protein to fold. So motif analysis underlies many studies of gene regulation and molecular interaction.

Since the suite's previous description in 2009, six new tools had been added. The article explains what every tool does, advises on their best use, and works through case studies showing how to combine results from several tools into one successful analysis. The suite is free for academic use online, and its source code can be downloaded for local installation, making motif analysis a standard utility rather than a specialist craft.
europmc-pmc4553469:
Almudena Ortiz-Urquiza and Nemat O. Keyhani review how insect-killing fungi breach their hosts' armor, in Insects in 2013. These fungi infect by landing on the insect's cuticle and drilling straight through, one of the classic cases that built germ theory. The first touch between spore and surface often decides the infection.

To stick and enter, fungi deploy enzymes that dissolve fats, proteins, and chitin, build pressured entry structures, and release metabolites that ease the way. Insects fight back with antimicrobial lipids in the cuticle, by shedding the cuticle as they grow, and by behaviors such as grooming and burrowing. The review traces this surface arms race step by step.
europmc-pmc4571569:
William F. Martin, Sriram Garg, and Verena Zimorski survey theories of how complex cells began, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2015. For over a century, endosymbiotic theory has held that eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, arose when one cell took up lasting residence inside another, becoming the mitochondrion. Over 20 versions of the idea have been published.

Most versions ignore eukaryotes that live without oxygen, a gap the authors press on. Energy is their central lens: only cells with mitochondria had the power budget for eukaryotic complexity, which is why no true halfway forms survive. Current versions cast the host as an archaeon, a member of the archaea. The survey contrasts each theory's predictions against observations.
europmc-pmc4693469:
Meaghan J. Jones, Sarah J. Goodman, and Michael S. Kobor reviewed DNA methylation and healthy aging in Aging Cell in 2015. Methylation means small chemical tags placed on DNA, often near gene switches, that track with gene activity. These patterns shift across a lifetime. Early work showed overall tag levels rising in childhood and falling late in life. Newer tools let researchers watch single sites instead.

Two patterns emerged. Some sites drift apart with age, varying more and more between people. Other sites change so steadily that a small set can predict a donor's age, a finding called the epigenetic clock. The review weighs how genes, surroundings, and these tags interact to set the pace of aging. It also notes cautions for studies that use epigenetic age as a health measure. The field, the authors show, is young but moving fast.
europmc-pmc4726569:
David Hardy, Aurore Besnard, Mathilde Latil, and nine colleagues compared mouse muscle injury models in PLoS ONE in 2016. Regenerative medicine studies how muscle rebuilds after damage, using several standard ways to injure it. The models were widely used but poorly compared. The team applied the four commonest injuries to mice engineered so stem cells and vessels glow. Repair was then tracked for a month with imaging, stains, and immune measurements.

Freeze injury was the harshest, wiping out up to ninety-six percent of muscle stem cells and their surroundings. All four models rebuilt muscle by twenty-eight days with little scarring, freeze injury excepted. But immune cells stayed elevated in two models, and stem cells kept cycling for months in three. Looks deceive: tissue can appear healed while molecular traces of injury persist. The authors urge choosing the model to fit the question.
europmc-pmc4759269:
Christian J. H. von Wintersdorff and seven co-authors review how drug resistance spreads between bacteria, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Resistance genes do not stay in the germs that first gained them. They sit in a shared pool, the resistome, held by harmless gut and soil bacteria, moving parts of DNA, and viruses that infect bacteria.

The review explains the three routes genes use to jump between cells. Direct cell contact is judged the biggest driver, but uptake of loose DNA and virus carriage may count for more than once thought. Case examples trace real resistance genes from farm and gut bacteria into disease strains. Knowing the size of the pool and how genes move from it, the authors argue, is key to slowing the spread.
europmc-pmc4769169:
Martin Steger leads a wide author team in eLife in 2016 hunting the true targets of LRRK2, a protein whose faults are the most common gene cause of Parkinson's disease. Drug makers want to block LRRK2, but the field lacked firm proof of which proteins it acts on. Without that proof, trials rest on sand.

Using mass protein scans, genetics, and drug tests, the team pinned down a set of Rab proteins as direct targets. LRRK2 tags them at one shared spot, in dish and in living cells. Faulty LRRK2 variants tag them harder, and the tag loosens the Rabs' grip on their handler proteins. The find ties LRRK2 to a known control system for cell traffic and gives drug tests a firm readout to aim at.
europmc-pmc4777569:
Setor K. Kunutsor and four co-authors pool the evidence on joint replacement infection in PLoS ONE in 2016. Infection around an artificial joint is among the worst outcomes of hip and knee replacement, and patient traits may raise or lower the odds. Single studies disagreed on which traits matter, so the team combined the record.

They drew 66 long-term studies with over half a million patients. Men and smokers faced clearly higher infection risk. Risk also rose steeply with body weight, more than tripling at the highest weight band. Past diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, depression, steroid use, and earlier joint surgery each added risk. Age and heavy drinking showed no clear link. The authors urge surgical teams to flag high-risk patients early and, where possible, fix the risks that can be fixed.
europmc-pmc4818469:
Tom R. Gaunt leads a large author team in Genome Biology in 2016 cataloguing how genes steer DNA methylation across a whole life. Methylation marks vary between people, and gene variants explain part of that spread. Whether the genetic grip holds steady from birth to middle age, or loosens as life accumulates, was unknown.

Using a long-running family cohort, the team mapped gene effects on methylation at five life stages, from newborns to their mothers in middle age. The genetic component proved strikingly stable; what grew with age was the environmental and random share. Nearby gene effects were mapped in depth, while distant effects looked scattered across many small influences. The catalogue, now public, feeds studies of whether methylation sits on the causal path to common diseases.
europmc-pmc4821869:
Helmut H. Popper, writing alone in Cancer Metastasis Reviews in 2016, dissects how lung cancer spreads. Most lung cancers are already at the metastatic stage when found, and spread travels by lymph and blood to favored sites: brain, bone, and the adrenal glands among them. The review takes the journey apart step by step, while noting the steps overlap in life.

A spreading cell must loosen its moorings and reshape itself, slip through tissue toward oxygen, enter the blood, and survive trapping by clotting and the shear of narrow vessels. Landing is not the end: it must then bargain with foreign tissue, win a blood supply, and teach local immunity to leave it alone. Each step, Popper argues, is a place where the process might be interrupted.
europmc-pmc4899869:
Megan K. Ruhland and co-authors showed in Nature Communications in 2016 that aged support cells in tissue can drive tumor growth by muting immunity. Age is a top cancer risk factor, but the steps were murky. A mouse model that copies aged skin showed senescent stromal cells, the tissue's support cells, suffice to raise local tumor promotion.

The aged cells drew in suppressive myeloid immune cells, which damped anti-tumor defense. One signal from the aged cells, interleukin-6, ran the recruitment. Clearing or quieting senescent support cells could thus cut age-linked cancer risk. The work ties a basic aging trait, worn-out cells, to a concrete cancer pathway.
europmc-pmc4917669:
Yang Y and ten co-authors review Toll-like receptor 4, or TLR4, and its role in heart muscle inflammation. Their review appeared in Cell Death and Disease in 2016. TLR4 is a sensor protein that switches on genes linked to inflammation. The authors set out the basic biology of the gene and the paths it uses to send signals inside cells.

Inside, the review covers TLR4 in myocarditis, heart attack, injury after blood flow returns, and heart failure. It explains how TLR4 turns on genes for cytokines, which are small proteins that drive inflammation, through a route that needs the MyD88 protein. The authors argue that blocking TLR4 signals could protect heart muscle, and they list open questions about how the process works and how it might guide care.
europmc-pmc4937469:
Stephen P. Bell and Karim Labib review how yeast copies its chromosomes, a model for all complex cells. Their review appeared in Genetics in 2016. DNA copying must be exact and complete, once per cell cycle. The machines that do it, called replisomes, are built in stages. Helicase enzymes load onto DNA start sites in the G1 phase. They switch on in S phase and join polymerases that build the new strands.

The review follows the whole run. Checkpoint proteins guard stalled machines and block new starts when copying is blocked. The replisome also strips and rebuilds the protein spools DNA wraps on, and links sister copies together. When two machines meet, they are taken apart. Work in budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, led most of these findings. The authors present that yeast work as the base on which cell cycle control of replication is now understood.
europmc-pmc4967469:
Francesco Iorio leads a large team mapping how cancer gene changes predict drug response. Their study appeared in Cell in 2016. Tumor sequencing reveals each cancer's mutations, but turning that into a drug choice is hard. The team gathered alterations from more than eleven thousand tumors across many tissues. They mapped them onto one thousand and one human cancer cell lines, then tested those lines against hundreds of drugs.

Cell lines faithfully echoed the driver changes seen in real tumors. Many changes tracked with sensitivity or resistance to specific drugs. Tissue of origin also shaped response, sometimes as much as mutation did. Logic models found alteration pairs that sensitize cells, and machine learning ranked which data types predict response best. The authors offer the datasets as a public resource for matching tumor subtypes to treatments.
europmc-pmc5002269:
Rune Busk Damgaard leads a ten-author team reporting in Cell in 2016 on OTULIN, an enzyme that trims one kind of ubiquitin chain inside cells. These chains help switch on NF-kB, a key driver of immune responses. The team studied a faulty human OTULIN gene and four mouse models that lack the enzyme in immune cells.

A weakened OTULIN gene in people caused a severe whole-body swelling illness the team names OTULIN-related autoinflammatory syndrome. In mice, missing OTULIN let the chains build up, fired NF-kB without a trigger, and raised levels of swelling signals in some cell types. In other cells, a partner complex broke down instead. Drugs that block TNF, one such signal, eased the illness in both patients and mice. The study shows why a single chain-trimming enzyme is vital for keeping immune responses in check.
europmc-pmc5021969:
Kirti V. Sawant and six co-authors study how a signal protein calls neutrophils to a fight, in Scientific Reports in 2016. CXCL1 is a chemokine, a chemical beacon that guides neutrophils, the first-responder white cells, into infected tissue. CXCL1 works as single units and as pairs, and it must grip both its cell receptor and sugar chains called glycosaminoglycans on tissue surfaces. The team built locked single and paired forms plus a panel of altered versions.

Both forms drew neutrophils into the mouse body cavity, but the natural form, which can switch between the two, worked best. Altering grip points in either of two regions weakened both sugar binding and cell recruitment. The change that hit both sugar grip and receptor action cut recruitment most. The results show that sugar binding is not a side detail but a tuned part of how the beacon guides cells.
europmc-pmc5105169:
Timothy P. Lillicrap, Daniel Cownden, Douglas B. Tweed, and Colin J. Akerman challenged a basic assumption about learning in Nature Communications in 2016. Deep networks, in brains and machines, must assign blame for errors to the right connections. Machine learning does this with backpropagation, which needs the backward path to mirror the forward one exactly, a pattern thought impossible in real brains.

The team showed that the mirror is not needed. Passing error signals back through fixed random connections still taught multi-layer networks about as well as true backpropagation on several tasks. The trick works because the forward connections gradually align themselves with the random backward ones. Their result reopens the question of how the brain might send teaching signals across layers.
europmc-pmc5168169:
A. Whitmore and C. S. Krishnaswami described a new infectious disease in Rangoon in The Indian Medical Gazette in July 1912. Their account begins with cases of human glanders found among the town's pony drivers, a search that opened their eyes to a different infection hiding among Rangoon's poorest residents.

The first case they detail, from an autopsy in April 1911, was a man admitted with fever whose lungs held a peculiar cheesy consolidation unlike pneumonia or tuberculosis. Smears swarmed with bacilli resembling the glanders germ, yet the man had no contact with horses, and cultures grew the organism fast and freely, unlike glanders. Whitmore and Krishnaswami present the illness, later known as Whitmore's disease, as a distinct entity that mimics glanders but is easily told apart once recognized.
europmc-pmc5191969:
Juan P. Arab, Saul J. Karpen, Paul A. Dawson, Marco Arrese, and Michael Trauner review bile acids as drug targets in fatty liver disease. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is spreading worldwide, and its aggressive form, steatohepatitis, can advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and cancer. Bile acids, once treated as simple detergents, now look like signaling molecules. They act in the liver and beyond to regulate fat and sugar metabolism and energy balance.

The review focuses on the receptors FXR and TGR5 and on the ileal bile acid transporter ASBT. Adjusting these pathways affects insulin sensitivity and several steps in disease progression. The authors judge bile-acid-based therapies among the more promising routes to new treatments. They are frank that clinical proof is still developing, and they map which approaches stand closest to patient use.
europmc-pmc5197969:
F. D'Herelle and R. H. Malone report early results from the Cholera Bacteriophage Enquiry in India. From April 27 to June 20, 1927, they followed 23 cholera cases in detail at the Campbell Hospital in Calcutta, with about 50 more observed less fully. They cultured bacteriophage from patients' intestines and tracked its strength against the cholera vibrio. The pattern was consistent. Patients whose intestines lacked phage on arrival died within hours.

When a strong phage was present in the first stool, recovery was strikingly fast, with discharge in two or three days. In 13 of the 23 cases the phage began weak, grew potent within 24 to 48 hours, and the patients recovered as it peaked. Where the phage faded, patients died. The authors present the correlation cautiously, as a preliminary report, but it shaped early hopes that phage activity decided who survived cholera.
europmc-pmc5215069:
The Japanese Gastric Cancer Association issued its gastric cancer treatment guidelines, 2014 version 4, in the journal Gastric Cancer in 2017. The document sets out the standard treatments Japanese clinicians should offer in daily practice for stomach cancer, arranged as a treatment algorithm by disease stage. It also flags promising approaches that remain investigational and should be tested in formal studies with patient consent.

Surgery is defined in careful detail. A standard gastrectomy removes at least two-thirds of the stomach with a full D2 lymph node clearance. Modified operations reduce the extent for earlier disease, and extended operations add nearby organs or wider clearance. Sections also cover non-curative surgery for bleeding or blockage, endoscopic removal under expanded criteria as a study treatment, and drug options such as neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy.
europmc-pmc522869:
Bradley E. Bernstein, Chih Long Liu, Emily L. Humphrey, Ethan O. Perlstein, and Stuart L. Schreiber mapped nucleosome occupancy across the yeast genome in Genome Biology in 2004. Nucleosomes are the spools of protein around which DNA winds, and where they sit helps decide which genes can be read. A gene-by-gene picture of that layout was missing.

Using chromatin capture paired with DNA microarrays, the team measured nucleosome levels at nearly all yeast promoters, the control regions before genes. Promoters of active genes tended to be cleared of nucleosomes. The same held for promoters carrying several conserved sequence motifs and for those that recruit the regulator Rap1. Real-time tests backed the array results. The map gave researchers a global view of how packaging of DNA relates to gene activity, a step toward linking chromatin state with the wider control networks of the cell.
europmc-pmc526369:
Pauline Ward, Leila Equinet, Jeremy Packer, and Christian Doerig catalogued the protein kinases of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum in BMC Genomics in 2004. Kinases are enzymes that switch proteins on and off by adding phosphate tags, and they control most cell processes, which makes them tempting drug targets. The parasite's genome had just been sequenced, opening a hunt for its full kinase set, or kinome. Searching the genome database with several tools found 65 kinase sequences.

Placing them on a family tree against the seven known kinase groups showed how distant this parasite is. Many of its kinases fell outside every known group, and none matched the tyrosine kinase or STE groups. The cell-cycle control group was the largest. A brand-new family of twenty, named FIKK after a shared sequence motif, appears only in this parasite's wider phylum, mostly in this species alone.
europmc-pmc5294069:
David M. Greig delivered the fourth Sir John Struthers lecture in Edinburgh on 1 February 1924, proposing the name hypertelorism, published in the Edinburgh Medical Journal. The deformity he describes, a congenital cranio-facial condition not previously set apart, has one constant feature: great breadth between the eyes. Greig builds the word from Greek parts meaning too much, apart, and to separate, and adds 'ocular' to fix the point.

He is careful to separate the condition from look-alikes: a broad nasal bridge alone is not it, nor are eyes pushed apart by a frontal meningocele or a facial cleft. Closing the lecture, he reasons about origins along the lines where face, skull, and brain develop and meet. The soft parts he clears of blame, finding no scars, no failed unions, and normal muscle action; the cause must lie deeper, in bone or in the contents of the skull.
europmc-pmc5310969:
Adrian R. Martineau led a large team in a study of vitamin D and chest infections in The BMJ in 2017. Colds, flu, and lung infections strike often and can turn grave. Past trials of vitamin D gave mixed results. The team pooled raw data from each person in past trials, which gives a sharper test than study level sums.

They found twenty-five sound trials with more than eleven thousand people, from infants to the very old. Raw data came in for nearly all of them. Across the whole group, vitamin D pills cut the risk of a chest infection. The pooled effect was modest but clear. The authors call this a major new use for the vitamin. The work also set out to find which groups gain the most, by age, body weight, and lung health.
europmc-pmc5316769:
T. Shennan, a professor of pathology at the University of Aberdeen, wrote on a rare chest condition in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1925. A spontaneous arterio-venous aneurysm is a swollen link that joins an artery and a vein inside the chest without injury. Shennan starts with the layout of the great veins and the aorta, to show where such a swelling can press.

He then works through a set of cases, weighing how the swelling grew from a diseased artery wall. Signs near death could be stark: hard breathing, delirium, fits, or coma. In some cases the body signs on exam told more than the patient's own complaints. The paper maps where the aorta sits against the vena cava, case by case, and draws lessons for spotting this rare and grave fault before death.
europmc-pmc5316869:
Hyeran Kim, Sang-Tae Kim, Jahee Ryu, Beum-Chang Kang, Jin-Soo Kim, and Sang-Gyu Kim reported DNA-free plant editing in Nature Communications in 2017. Their tool is Cpf1, a CRISPR cutter that needs a T-rich marker next to its target and makes staggered cuts. Most plant editing sends in DNA that codes for the tool. That extra DNA can end up in the plant, which many growers want to avoid.

The team instead slipped ready-made Cpf1 protein and guide RNA into plant cells taken from soybean and wild tobacco. Deep reading of the target sites showed clean edits in the aimed genes. Cpf1 mostly cut out small chunks of DNA at the target. No clear edits showed at near-match sites in the soybean genome. The result gives plant breeders an editing route that leaves no foreign DNA behind.
europmc-pmc5346569:
Lisa D. Nickerson, Stephen M. Smith, Döst Öngür, and Christian F. Beckmann studied a scan analysis method in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2017. Resting brain scans can be split into networks that pulse together. A method called ICA finds those networks with no set model in advance. Dual regression then maps group networks back onto each person's scan to test for group gaps.

Their check shows a catch. Network maps blend two facts: the shape of the network, and the strength of its pulse. Dropping the strength term can warp group claims. Head motion can fake a strength gap, which spreads false calls across the map. With the strength term kept and motion held down, shape gaps map cleanly. The paper works through fake and real data to show where blind use of the method can mislead a study.
europmc-pmc5374269:
Markus Ploner, Christian Sorg, and Joachim Gross reviewed brain rhythms in pain in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2017. Pain is not a bare sense. It is built on the fly from body signals mixed with thought, feeling, and drive. In the brain, pain comes with waves of nerve cell firing that pulse and sync at set speeds. No shared frame yet told what those waves do for pain.

Fresh theory casts waves as the brain's traffic guides. Fast waves may carry signals up the chain, slow waves may carry forecasts back down, and clashes between forecast and fact may flag news. Mapped onto pain, that frame could show how sense and context merge into one felt hurt. It may also show what goes wrong in lasting pain, where the merge sticks. The team sets out tests that could prove or break the frame.
europmc-pmc5379069:
Jinshui Lin and co-authors found a fresh iron path in a hospital germ in Nature Communications in 2017. Hosts guard their iron with binding proteins, since germs need iron to grow and to harm. The germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa was known to run three iron-grab systems. A strain stripped of all three still grew in iron-poor broth, which hinted at a fourth path in hiding.

The team screened mutant germs that failed in low iron and landed on a gene beside a needle-like secretion system. Its product, renamed TseF, is shot out by that system and rides in membrane bubbles the germ sheds. There it grips a signal stuff that holds iron. The loaded bubbles dock at two known cell doors, which pass the iron in. The find links three cell systems long thought apart.
europmc-pmc5383669:
José de la Fuente leads a large author group in a 2017 review in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology on how ticks and the germs they carry affect each other. Ticks spread bacteria, viruses, and protozoa to people and animals. Whether a tick can pass on a given germ depends in part on genes and traits inside the tick itself.

The review pulls together what is known about these links for many germ types, and it also covers the role of the tick's own gut germs. Many germs use like tricks, such as quieting the tick's defenses, to live and spread. The authors argue that blocking such shared steps could cut tick numbers and lower disease across more than one illness at once.
europmc-pmc5384769:
Zhu-Hong You and his co-authors present a computer model named PBMDA in a 2017 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. The model predicts links between microRNAs, tiny bits of RNA that help control genes, and human diseases. Finding such links by lab work alone is slow and costly, so a good model can point lab teams to the best leads first.

The model joins known links with measures of how alike two microRNAs or two diseases are, then searches paths through that web. Tests gave strong scores, and most of its top picks for three cancers were already backed by past reports. The authors offer the model as a tool to speed the search for disease-linked microRNAs.
europmc-pmc5387169:
Melissa Christine Kander, Yuqi Cui, and Zhenguo Liu review sex differences in oxidative stress and heart disease in a 2017 paper in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine. Oxidative stress means harm from reactive oxygen forms that the body fails to clear. Men tend to have heart attacks earlier than women, and a woman's risk rises after menopause, which hints that estrogen guards the heart.

Hormone treatment after menopause did not cut risk, so other paths must matter. Women seem less prone to this stress under normal states, perhaps due to estrogen's guarding action or to sex differences in a key enzyme that makes reactive oxygen. The authors sort the proof by disease and weigh the likely causes.
europmc-pmc5408169:
Katyayani Tatiparti and four co-authors review ways to deliver siRNA drugs in a 2017 paper in Nanomaterials. siRNA is a short piece of RNA that can switch off a chosen gene. That makes it a strong candidate drug for viral infections, cancer, gene disorders, and joint disease, since it can mute harmful genes with fine aim. But bare siRNA breaks down fast in blood, slips poorly into cells, and can stir the immune system.

The cure rides on the carrier. The review covers the design of tiny particle systems that shield siRNA, carry it to the right tissue, and release it inside cells. It sorts recent carrier types by their build and their strengths and flaws. The authors say delivery, more than the drug idea itself, now decides how fast such drugs reach patients.
europmc-pmc5431369:
Cappello and co-authors map fine structural damage in the lower motor system of Krabbe disease mice. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Krabbe disease stems from a missing lysosomal enzyme. A toxic lipid, psychosine, then builds up widely. Myelin-making cells die, and movement fails early. The team used the Twitcher mouse model. Electron microscopy probed three levels of the motor path. Two ages were compared: day 15 and day 30.

Motor neuron cell bodies showed mild change. Sciatic nerves showed severe damage by day 30. Nerve terminals and neuromuscular junctions fared worst. Peripheral damage was already visible at day 15. That age is nearly free of symptoms. The calf muscle wasted on its own. Its changes did not depend on denervation. The pattern fits a dying-back process. Axons fail first, far from the cell body. The authors say demyelination alone cannot explain progression.
europmc-pmc5454369:
Delaneau and co-authors present QTLtools, a full software set for finding molecular QTLs. A QTL is a stretch of DNA tied to a trait. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications. Large studies now pair gene data with traits such as gene activity in hundreds of people. The tests needed run into the millions.

QTLtools checks raw read data and matches it to the right samples. It then measures gene activity and hunts for near and far QTLs. It can fold those hits in with trait scans and genome notes. The team shows it off on 358 samples with known gene data. The program is free and open source.
europmc-pmc5472269:
Feng and co-authors present a systematic review in PLoS ONE on frailty in older adults. Frailty raises the risk of hospital stays, care homes, and death. What pushes people toward frailty was poorly mapped. The team gathered longitudinal studies of adults aged 60 and over living at home. Twenty-three studies met their quality checks.

Factors fell into five broad groups in their synthesis. Social factors included age, ethnic background, and neighborhood. Physical factors included obesity and trouble with daily tasks. Blood uric acid stood out among biological markers. Better diet quality and more fruit and vegetables protected against decline. Depressive symptoms raised the risk as well.
europmc-pmc5514969:
Bayat Mokhtari and co-authors present a systematic review in Oncotarget on combination cancer therapy. Pairing two or more drugs beats single-drug care for many cancers. Pairs can strike key growth pathways together. They may also slow drug resistance and shrink stem cell pools. Lower doses of each drug can cut side effects.

Survival for spread cancers stays low despite new drugs, they note. Building a new drug takes about 15 years and huge sums. Reusing approved drugs for new cancer roles speeds things up. One known drug in a pair lowers cost and risk. The review surveys targeted pathways and popular repurposed agents since 2012.
europmc-pmc553969:
Slater and Birney present a method for building fast sequence-alignment tools in BMC Bioinformatics. Full alignment methods are exact but slow. Shortcut methods like BLAST run fast but are hard to build. Their bridge is bounded sparse dynamic programming.

Instead of writing each shortcut by hand, users describe the alignment model itself. The system then generates an efficient shortcut version on its own. Tests showed speed and accuracy that compare well with existing tools. Worked cases come from genome annotation. The method ships inside the free alignment program exonerate. It can serve a broad range of sequence comparison tasks. Readers see a way to get near-exact answers at shortcut speed.
europmc-pmc5557969:
Garneau and co-authors present a software article in Scientific Reports. Their tool, PhageTerm, works on bacteriophages, the viruses that infect bacteria. It finds where a phage genome ends and how that DNA is packed into the virus shell. That knowledge helps explain a phage's life cycle.

The method uses data from standard DNA sequencing runs. Natural genome ends leave a bias in read counts, and the tool detects that bias. The authors tested it on phages with known packing styles, from Lambda to T4. It also set the ends for nine Clostridium difficile phages. PhageTerm is free to use. Readers get a faster way to read meaning from phage sequence data.
europmc-pmc5573769:
The GBD 2015 Chronic Respiratory Disease Collaborators report a systematic analysis in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. They estimate the global burden of two lung diseases, COPD and asthma. Figures cover deaths, prevalence, and disability across 188 countries. The years run from 1990 to 2015.

In 2015, about 3.2 million people died from COPD. Asthma deaths were near 0.4 million. Both diseases grew more common as populations grew and aged. Age-adjusted rates fell for both, though. Smoking and air pollution were the main risks for COPD. Asthma was the most prevalent chronic lung disease, with twice the cases of COPD. Readers get the standard global account of two major diseases.
europmc-pmc5635569:
Masnoon and co-authors present a systematic review in BMC Geriatrics. They ask a simple question: what does polypharmacy mean? The term covers use of many medicines at once. It is common among older people with several conditions. The team searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane sources. They also checked grey literature in English. Eligible work spanned January 2000 to May 2016.

The search found 1,156 articles, and 110 qualified. Those articles held 138 definitions in total. Most definitions, 80.4 percent, were purely numerical. The most common threshold was five or more medicines daily. Counts ranged from two or more to eleven or more. Few articles separated fitting use from harmful use. The authors warn that counts alone ignore patient conditions.
europmc-pmc5646769:
Hallmann and co-authors report a long-term study in PLoS ONE. It measures flying insect biomass in German protected areas. Malaise traps followed a standard protocol for 27 years. Sampling covered 63 nature protection areas. The dataset held 96 location-year combinations. Seasons ran from March through October each year.

The authors estimate a seasonal decline of 76 percent. Mid-summer decline reached 82 percent. The drop appeared across all habitat types. Weather, land use, and habitat traits could not explain it. Such loss threatens food webs that rely on insects. Birds and other animals eat them, and plants need their pollination. The authors urge that biomass loss enter conservation planning.
europmc-pmc5668469:
Wan and co-authors present a review in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. It gives a general account of muscle fatigue and its treatment. Muscle fatigue means an exercise-driven drop in force output. It can start in the brain or in the muscle itself. Those two forms are called central and peripheral fatigue. The review traces the sequence of events in force production.

Factors include nerve signals, ion shifts, and blood flow. Metabolic products like lactate and phosphate also build up. Heat and reactive oxygen species play roles as well. The authors cover ways to locate the fatigue site in living people. Diagnostic markers get reviewed too. Treatments discussed are non-specific but effective in practice.
europmc-pmc5765169:
Ding and co-authors build gas separation membranes from stacked MXene sheets. Membranes promise low energy gas sorting, but speed and selectivity trade off. Two-dimensional sheets form tangled channels when stacked at random. The team aimed for aligned, even channels under one nanometer wide.

Their lamellar membranes let hydrogen through at over 2,200 Barrer, they report. Hydrogen over carbon dioxide selectivity passed 160. Both figures beat the best membranes known at the time. Computer simulations backed the test results. Surface groups on the MXene sheets help hold the even spacing. The work shows a route to precise molecular sieving.
europmc-pmc5777969:
Tsuchikama and An review antibody-drug conjugates, cancer drugs that link an antibody to a toxic payload. The antibody guides the payload to cancer cells. That targeting promises stronger effect with less harm to the rest of the body. Two such drugs had won approval, and dozens more were in trials.

The review walks through each part: antibody, payload, and linker. Its main focus is the chemistry that joins them. Old and new conjugation methods are compared. Site specific methods that yield uniform products stand out as a key path. Better chemistry should yield safer, more effective cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc5803269:
Olah and co-authors build a gene atlas of aged human microglia. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. Gene studies tie them to Alzheimer's and other late-life diseases. Yet their aged state in humans was poorly known.

The team isolated microglia from donated older brains. Sequencing revealed a gene set they call HuMi_Aged. Protein checks in brain tissue confirmed the pattern. The set grows stronger with age at death. It holds risk genes for Alzheimer's and multiple sclerosis. A protective APOE form lowered the signature. Readers get a reference profile for the aging brain's immune cells.
europmc-pmc5818369:
Anderson and co-authors review the TCA cycle as a cancer target. The TCA cycle is the cell's central energy hub. Old dogma said cancer cells skip it and burn sugar instead. New proof shows many tumors lean on the cycle hard.

Tumors with faulty oncogenes and suppressors feed the cycle varied fuels. Mutations also warp the cycle's own enzymes. Those changes aid energy output and building-block supply. Small drugs that jam the boosted cycle are emerging. The authors sort fuels, gene effects, and drug chances. Readers get a fresh look at a long-overlooked hub of tumor growth.
europmc-pmc5824569:
Oh and co-authors review child health effects tied to childhood adversity. Hard early experiences can echo through the body for years. Spotting those effects early could guide care. The team gathers long-term studies on physical outcomes before age 20.

From nearly 16,000 records, 35 studies qualified. Adversity linked to slower thinking growth, asthma, and infections. Sleep troubles and bodily complaints also appeared. Maltreatment tied to weight shifts in the teen years. Stress hormone patterns and immune changes showed as well. Telomeres, the chromosome caps, wore down faster. Readers get a body-wide case for asking about early hardship in child care.
europmc-pmc5860169:
Meier-Kolthoff and co-authors present VICTOR, a tool for classifying prokaryotic viruses. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. These viruses infect bacteria and archaea across the planet. How best to classify them from genome data was unclear. VICTOR builds family trees from whole genome sequences. It follows the rules of phylogenetic systematics for its groups.

The team tested the tool on officially classified viruses. The trees agreed well with the accepted classification. Most groups held together as single branches, they report. Family-level detail was weaker than other levels. A wider test on over 4,000 genomes suggested many new taxa. VICTOR runs as a free web service for researchers.
europmc-pmc5905069:
Miles addressed the treatment of cancer of the rectum and pelvic colon. The paper was read in Glasgow in December 1911. It appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1912. Miles drew on twelve years of study of rectal tumours. He argued surgery was then the only real hope. X-rays and radium had shown him no benefit in rectal cancer.

The paper compares two schools of operation. One favoured perineal removal, the other a combined approach. Miles urged that spread patterns should guide the choice. He reviewed how rectal cancers infiltrate and seed distant sites. Tumour types differ in malignancy, he notes. The piece records early surgical reasoning on this cancer.
europmc-pmc5933869:
Rosenberg and co-authors track reported vectorborne disease cases across the United States and its territories. Their Vital Signs report covers the years 2004 to 2016. It draws on the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System. Sixteen notifiable diseases spread by ticks or mosquitoes are included. Lyme disease, West Nile virus, and dengue are among them.

In all, 642,602 cases were reported over the period. Annual reports of tickborne bacterial and protozoan diseases more than doubled. Lyme disease made up 82 percent of tickborne reports. Mosquito-borne disease was marked by virus epidemics, the authors report. They call for stronger surveillance, diagnostics, reporting, and vector control.
europmc-pmc5964069:
Vera-Ramirez and co-authors show that autophagy keeps dormant breast cancer cells alive and feeds later recurrence. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Breast cancer often returns years after treatment. The relapse grows from dormant tumour cells that spread early. How those cells survive their long quiet phase was largely unknown. The team tested autophagy in mouse and human dormancy models.

Blocking autophagy cut dormant cell survival sharply, they report. Metastatic burden fell as well in their models. The gene ATG7 proved essential for switching autophagy on. Blocking the flow left damaged mitochondria to pile up. Reactive oxygen species then rose and drove cell death.
europmc-pmc5966769:
Lindsey and co-authors give guidelines for measuring cardiac physiology in mice. Their guidelines review appeared in the American Journal of Physiology, Heart and Circulatory Physiology. Mouse models give key insights into heart ageing and disease. Sound measurement of heart function is vital to that work. Calls for rigor and reproducibility are growing across labs. The authors set out best practice for such measures.

Sections cover echocardiography, magnetic resonance imaging, and hemodynamics. They clarify what to measure in different heart conditions. Consistent parameters help labs compare results with each other. The paper pairs with a companion guide on ischemia models. It aims to raise the standard of mouse heart studies.
europmc-pmc6102569:
Ramírez and Caballero test whether docking's top score can be trusted as the best pose. Their study appeared in Molecules. Molecular docking predicts how a ligand sits in a receptor. Programs rank poses by an energy score. Users usually take the top-ranked pose as truth.

The pair ran self-docking and cross-docking tests. Self-docking returns a ligand to its own crystal receptor. Cross-docking uses a receptor holding another ligand. Scores often found poses near the crystal answer. But the top score was not always that pose. The failure turned critical in cross-docking. The authors urge adding structural clues from similar ligands. Readers get a caution for virtual screening work.
europmc-pmc6235969:
Shkoporov and co-authors isolated a virus that infects gut bacteria. The virus family is called CrAssphage. These viruses are the most abundant in the human gut. They had never been grown in culture before. The study appeared in Nature Communications.

The team isolated the virus from human faecal material. It infects Bacteroides intestinalis, a common gut symbiont. That host matched earlier computer predictions. The virus genome is circular and about 102 kilobases long. Electron microscopy showed a podovirus-like shape. The virus lacks clear lysogeny genes. Yet it copies itself without halting host growth. It persisted in host culture for several weeks. The work opens this huge virus family to lab study.
europmc-pmc6285469:
Betsch and co-authors built a survey scale for the mental drivers of vaccination. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE. Older surveys mostly measured confidence in vaccines. Five drivers, called the 5Cs, shape whether people vaccinate. They are confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility. Each needed a place in one tested scale.

Three studies shaped and checked the scale. The first used about 1,400 German participants to build it. The second used a representative German sample of about one thousand people. The third compared it with six older measures in an American sample. Both a fifteen item and a five item form proved sound. Subscales matched related traits such as deliberation style and communal outlook. The scale lets health teams track why uptake lags. Trends can then guide targeted campaigns.
europmc-pmc6298569:
Michlewski and Cáceres review how cells control the making of microRNAs after transcription. Their review appeared in the journal RNA. MicroRNAs are small molecules that bind target messages and repress gene activity. Two enzymes, DROSHA and DICER, trim precursor molecules into mature forms. Those mature forms then join a silencing complex.

The authors focus on controls that act during this trimming path. Signals built into the precursor shape its handling. RNA-binding proteins also attach and speed or slow the cuts. Such controls matter in growth, cell change, and disease. The review shows a dense extra layer of tuning. It explains why microRNA levels vary so much between cell types.
europmc-pmc6407669:
Canarini and co-authors review root exudation in Frontiers in Plant Science. Plant roots leak sugars, amino acids, and organic acids into the soil. Soil microbes feed on these leaks, and the leaks can free nutrients for the plant.

How plants control this loss is still not settled, the authors say. Most accounts treat the leaks as passive waste. Their review builds a new frame in which plants tune exudation to need. Stress and nutrient shortage change what roots release. The frame may help design crops that feed soil life with more purpose.
europmc-pmc6411769:
Lapuschkin and co-authors probe what learning machines really learn, in Nature Communications. Top scores can hide lazy tricks, much like the horse Clever Hans seemed to count. The team used methods that explain a model's choices on vision and game tasks.

Some models used sound clues, while others leaned on shortcuts in the data. Standard accuracy scores could not tell these apart, they show. Their Spectral Relevance Analysis helps sort real strategy from trick. Such checks matter before models are trusted in medicine or transport. The work is a warning against reading accuracy as understanding.
europmc-pmc6536969:
Xiang and co-authors review traditional Chinese medicine as a cancer treatment, writing in Cancer Medicine. Used for thousands of years, these herbal therapies are now widely taken alongside standard care. The authors use modern cell and gene science to ask how they might work.

They focus on plant chemicals such as curcumin, resveratrol and berberine. Reported actions include switching cancer genes on or off, altering DNA methylation and histone marks, and tuning noncoding RNAs. Other studies show effects on the tumor's surrounding tissue and on cancer stem cells, the hardy cells blamed for relapse. The review gathers these threads as a base for sharper future tests of these therapies.
europmc-pmc6538669:
Kirchdoerfer and Ward solve the structure of the SARS coronavirus's RNA-copying machine, writing in Nature Communications. Coronaviruses build a multi-part protein complex to copy their genome. Its core engine is the nsp12 polymerase, boosted by the helper proteins nsp7 and nsp8. Until now, that engine had never been seen in high detail.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the authors map the complex at 3.1 ångström detail. nsp12 shows the cupped right-hand shape shared by viral polymerases, plus a large extra front section with a kinase-like fold. Two nsp8 units bind it, one of them paired with nsp7. The map explains how the core machine assembles and works, and gives drug designers a template for blocking it.
europmc-pmc6582769:
Farahani, Karwowski and Lighthall systematically review graph theory as a lens on the human brain's wiring, writing in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Treating brain regions as nodes and their coordination as edges lets researchers measure hubs, modules and small-world structure in fMRI data. The authors searched eight databases across three decades of work.

They find the field took off after 2009, riding the Human Connectome Project. Most studies map resting-state functional connectivity — correlations between regions — rather than causal influence. The review explains how networks get built under both approaches, weighs each method's strengths and traps, and surveys applications from cognition to epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, autism and ADHD. It closes with guidance on turning graph numbers into sound claims about the brain.
europmc-pmc6756069:
Yuan and co-authors review how the TERT gene switches on in human cancer. TERT makes telomerase, the enzyme that maintains chromosome ends. Most adult cells keep it silent, so their ends erode until growth stops. Cancers need it back on to keep dividing. TERT activity shows in up to 90% of human primary cancers.

The review gathers two decades of work on the switch. Known actors include the c-MYC protein, which binds the TERT promoter and turns it up. When leukemia cells mature, a rival protein takes that seat and shuts TERT down. New players keep emerging. Beyond lengthening ends, TERT aids cancer in other ways too.
europmc-pmc6774269:
Shakya and co-authors review advances and challenges in metatranscriptomic analysis. Microbiome studies long asked only who is present, using marker genes or shotgun DNA sequencing. Those methods cannot say which microbes are active. Metatranscriptomics reads the RNA of a whole community, revealing who is doing what, and how that changes over time.

The review covers the computational side of the field. It compares the method's strengths and limits against other microbiome approaches. Available tools and workflows are listed. Read-based classifiers work only when close relatives sit in reference databases, one of several limits discussed. Use cases show what the method adds. The authors expect the field to keep growing fast.
europmc-pmc6784869:
Ling and co-authors report the genome sequence of Triticum urartu, the wild progenitor of wheat's A subgenome. Modern bread wheat blends three subgenomes. This diploid species donated one of them. A high-quality sequence helps explain how polyploid wheat genomes formed and evolved. The team combined several sequencing methods to build it.

They assembled seven chromosome-scale pieces and identified the protein-coding genes. Comparisons with other grasses showed gene losses and booms in mobile DNA elements. A survey of 147 accessions from the Fertile Crescent found three groups. The groups differed by altitude and by resistance to powdery mildew disease. The genome is a resource for finding genes that could improve wheat.
europmc-pmc6786969:
Li and co-authors report the genomes of two ferns and what they reveal about land plant evolution. Ferns are the closest living relatives of seed plants, yet their genomes are famously huge and little known. The team sequenced Azolla filiculoides and Salvinia cucullata. Both are small aquatic ferns, which made the task tractable.

The genomes show bursts of whole-genome duplication in fern history. One fern gene conferring insect resistance appears to have arrived from bacteria. Azolla lives with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, and the partners' family trees match closely, proof of cospeciation. Azolla lacks genes used in other plant-microbe partnerships. Several transporter genes may serve its unique symbiosis instead. The resource should boost both biotechnology and evolution research.
europmc-pmc6835969:
Rinninella and co-authors review food and the gut microbiota in the journal Nutrients. The gut holds trillions of bacteria that shift with diet, stress, illness, and drugs. Their balance guards the gut wall and trains the immune system. Modern eating habits have disturbed that balance in many people. The fallout is tied to obesity and metabolic disease.

The review works through food components one by one, from fats and sugars to proteins and fibres. A Western diet rich in fat and refined sugar pushes the community toward harmful patterns in studies. Diets built on grains and vegetables favour other groups. The authors close with dietary strategies meant to restore a healthy mix.
europmc-pmc6853169:
Bohren and co-authors report a four-country study in The Lancet on how women are treated in childbirth. Mistreatment during facility births is reported worldwide. It ranges from shouting and neglect to exams done without consent. Until now, tools to measure it fairly were lacking. The team built and validated such tools, then put them to work.

Observers watched labours in twelve facilities across Ghana, Guinea, Myanmar, and Nigeria. Women were also surveyed later in their communities. The study recorded physical and verbal abuse, loss of privacy, and long delays. Comparing the two methods showed how much mistreatment direct counting misses. The authors call for care that respects women's dignity and choices.
europmc-pmc6868369:
Tørresen and co-authors review a hidden source of error in genome databases, in Nucleic Acids Research. Tandem repeats are stretches where a short DNA pattern repeats head to tail. They occur across the tree of life. Sequencing machines and assembly software stumble over them, since reads from inside a repeat look alike.

Errors then slip into genome and protein databases, often without any flag. A gene largely made of repeats may be dropped from annotation altogether. Users downstream treat the records as ready to use, with no easy way to judge their trust. The authors walk through each stage where repeats cause trouble. They argue the problem deserves open acknowledgement and better handling.
europmc-pmc6950569:
Leeming and co-authors ask how long dietary change must last to reshape gut microbes. Their review appeared in Nutrients. The gut holds trillions of microbes, forming an ecosystem tied to health and disease. Each person's mix is fairly stable, yet diet is a strong lever on it.

Short, sharp diet changes can shift the gut community within days. Those shifts, though, look temporary. Whether long diets can lock in lasting change is unknown, because few trials run long or follow up afterwards. Everyday eating habits may matter more than brief interventions. The authors review what short and long studies show, and which factors shape the response. More long-term work, they argue, must come before firm clinical advice.
europmc-pmc6964869:
Kosiborod and co-authors report how dapagliflozin affects daily life in heart failure patients. Their report appeared in Circulation. The DAPA-HF trial enrolled people with heart failure and weakened pumping. Earlier results showed the drug cut cardiovascular death and worsening heart failure. How patients actually felt was the open question.

Health status was measured with the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire, covering symptoms, physical limits, and quality of life. Dapagliflozin improved all three, whatever the starting level of impairment. Benefits appeared early, held over time, and grew. More patients on the drug gained small, moderate, and large improvements in health status. The authors stress a gap this fills: some heart failure drugs extend life without easing daily symptoms. This one, they show, does both.
europmc-pmc6988269:
Corman and co-authors deliver a validated lab test for the new coronavirus within weeks of its emergence. Their report appeared in Eurosurveillance. The outbreak of 2019-nCoV posed a hard problem: no virus isolates existed for test development, yet spread through travellers was already happening.

Working from the virus's closeness to SARS coronavirus, the team designed a real-time RT-PCR workflow using synthetic genetic material. The test reliably detects 2019-nCoV and tells it apart from SARS-CoV. Academic and public labs together checked it against 297 clinical specimens carrying many human respiratory viruses, confirming it reacts only to the target. Control material was shared through a European virus archive. The study, the authors note, shows the response speed that coordinated lab networks can reach.
europmc-pmc7014669:
The Eurosurveillance editorial team published this short editorial note as an e-Alert on 31 January 2020. It reports a decision made the day before. The World Health Organization had declared the new coronavirus, 2019-nCoV, a public health emergency of international concern. That was the sixth such declaration under the International Health Regulations.

The note says the decision followed a second Emergency Committee meeting. The Director-General stressed the risk to countries with weaker health systems. Readers are pointed to the journal's own coronavirus collection and to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control pages. A boxed summary of the centre's rapid risk assessment follows. It counted over 7,000 confirmed cases and 170 deaths, mostly in China. It judged the impact high, yet sustained spread within Europe very unlikely if cases were caught early.
europmc-pmc7065369:
Kamel Boulos and Geraghty survey geographic tracking of the COVID-19 epidemic in the International Journal of Health Geographics. A new coronavirus emerged in Wuhan in December 2019 and spread worldwide despite containment efforts. As with the earlier SARS epidemic and seasonal flu, geographic information systems have proved indispensable for watching an outbreak move and organising the response.

The authors describe practical online and mobile mapping tools updated in near real time as events unfold. Dashboards display case counts, while other applications map social media reactions, build predictive risk maps from travel data, and trace the movements and contacts of super-spreaders through space and time. One Chinese app described in detail, the close contact detector, uses transport booking records to warn individuals who shared a journey with a case. The paper is a snapshot of digital epidemiology in action during the pandemic's first months.
europmc-pmc7118369:
Fumagalli and co-authors show that colorectal cancer spreads mainly through cells that lack the stem cell marker Lgr5, in Cell Stem Cell. Cancer stem cells carry Lgr5 and were thought to seed metastases. Using a mouse model and human tumor grafts, the team tracked which cells actually founded distant tumors.

Most travelling cancer cells in the blood were Lgr5-negative. Yet the metastases they formed contained Lgr5-positive stem cells, meaning the negative cells regained stem-like traits on arrival. This switch needed no special signals from surrounding tissue. It was required for metastases to grow out, though not to settle. The finding reshapes how doctors may need to target spreading colorectal cancer.
europmc-pmc7136169:
Leung and co-authors deliver a consensus report on evaluating monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance, a kidney-damaging condition driven by a harmful antibody protein, in Nature Reviews Nephrology. The term was introduced in 2012 for cases where the protein injures kidneys without meeting cancer treatment criteria. The expert group met in April 2017 to refine it.

Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence testing is recommended to prove the diagnosis and identify the deposited protein.
