Blood and urine protein tests plus free light chain analysis can find the antibody and track response. Bone marrow sampling hunts the cell clone making it. The report standardises this workup; treatment itself was left for a later meeting.
europmc-pmc7158569:
Kucharski and co-authors model the early transmission dynamics of COVID-19 and the reach of control measures, in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. By 5 March 2020 the outbreak had reached 95,333 confirmed cases. They fitted a transmission model to four datasets from inside and outside Wuhan.

The datasets covered exported cases, Wuhan cases without market links, nationwide Chinese cases, and infection rates on evacuation flights. Their estimates tracked how transmission in Wuhan changed from December 2019 through February 2020. They then calculated the chance that cases introduced elsewhere would spark sustained local outbreaks. The work aimed to tell new areas how much risk imported cases carried.
europmc-pmc7243369:
Chandrashekar and co-authors ask whether recovering from SARS-CoV-2 protects monkeys against catching it again. Their study appeared in Science. The question mattered for vaccine hopes and for reopening economies. The team first infected rhesus macaques with the virus. After the animals cleared it, they were exposed a second time.

Recovered animals had built immune responses to the virus. On rechallenge, those responses protected them from a second full infection. Virus levels stayed far below those of the first round. The authors note that monkey infection differs from human disease. Still, natural immunity after recovery looked real in this model. The result supported the logic behind vaccines. It also eased fears that reinfection would be immediately common.
europmc-pmc7253669:
Hough and co-authors review airway remodeling in asthma. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Medicine. In chronic asthma, the airway walls change in lasting ways. Muscle grows, fibers build up and surface cells are lost. These changes narrow the airways and can make breathing limits permanent. Dust, chemicals and cigarette smoke can start the process.

The authors trace three linked stages. Surface cells start the response. Immune cells amplify it. Deeper wall cells carry out the structural changes. Aging of the immune system is also discussed, since it may keep inflammation going in older patients. Readers get a step-by-step account of how asthma can harden into fixed obstruction.
europmc-pmc7266869:
Al-Hanawi and co-authors survey what the public in Saudi Arabia knew, felt, and did about COVID-19 early in the pandemic. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. Answers came from an online questionnaire completed by 3,388 participants. Scores measured knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices.

Most participants were well informed. The mean knowledge score was 17.96 out of a possible range ending at 22, attitudes were optimistic, and reported practices were good. Men scored lower than women on all three measures. Older adults tended to know more and act more carefully than younger people. The authors recommend health education aimed at the groups that scored lowest, since public cooperation was central to the country's strict preventive measures.
europmc-pmc7290769:
Sardu and co-authors evaluate the claim that COVID-19 is largely a disease of the endothelium, the lining of blood vessels. Their evaluation appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Cough, fever, and breathlessness are the common symptoms. Yet patients also show high blood pressure, clots in arteries and veins, kidney failure, and diabetes-related problems, all pointing at vessel linings.

The virus enters cells through ACE2, which endothelial cells also carry. The authors weigh clinical reports and laboratory evidence together to build a mechanism for these body-wide effects: infection of the endothelium could drive inflammation, clotting, and organ damage far from the lungs. If the lining is a key target organ, treatments that protect it deserve attention alongside antiviral drugs.
europmc-pmc7332269:
Baqui and co-authors examine hospital deaths from COVID-19 in Brazil in The Lancet Global Health. Brazil's population is diverse, and its regions differ sharply in wealth and health care. The team used a national flu surveillance dataset and kept 11,321 hospitalized patients with confirmed infection and recorded ethnicity.

Patients of Pardo, or mixed, ethnicity and Black patients faced clearly higher death risk than White patients. Pardo ethnicity ranked as the second strongest risk factor after age. Northern states also showed higher risk, tied in part to a heavier burden of other illness. The authors read the pattern as two linked effects, one regional and one ethnic. Readers get hard numbers on inequality inside one country's pandemic.
europmc-pmc7335069:
Seidlitz and co-authors link gene activity maps to brain changes in neurogenetic disorders, in Nature Communications. Such disorders run in families and alter brain anatomy in region-specific patterns. The team studied six disorders caused by copy number variants, where chunks of DNA are missing or doubled.

For each disorder, the pattern of cortical change in young patients matched where the affected genes are active in healthy adult brains. They then converted gene activity data into cell-type maps. That step tied each disorder's change pattern to specific cell classes and the genes those cells express. The organizing rules they uncover could help screen candidate genes and treatments. Readers get a bridge from DNA risk to brain anatomy.
europmc-pmc7360769:
Lin and Peddada introduce a statistical method for microbiome data in Nature Communications. Comparing microbe counts between samples is tricky, because each sample captures an unknown fraction of the whole community. That unknown fraction biases standard comparisons.

Their method, ANCOM-BC, estimates each sample's fraction and corrects the bias before testing which microbes truly differ. Built on a linear model, it gives valid p-values, confidence intervals for each microbe, and control of false discoveries, while staying simple to compute. Earlier methods lacked one or more of those properties. Readers get a methods paper aimed at a common trap: mistaking uneven sampling for real biological change.
europmc-pmc7386569:
Suarez-Arnedo and co-authors present a software plugin in PLoS ONE for analyzing scratch wound assays. In these cheap, common lab tests, cells are grown in a layer, a scratch is made, and cameras watch cells migrate to close the gap. Existing analysis tools need manual tuning, which slows work and limits batches.

Their plugin for the free ImageJ program finds the wound automatically and corrects width for tilt. It reports area, wound fraction, average width, and width unevenness, for single images or stacks. It handles bright field, phase contrast, and fluorescence images and runs on common operating systems. Readers get a practical tool for measuring healing and migration, with a link to regeneration and disease research.
europmc-pmc7449469:
Islam and co-authors survey depression and anxiety among university students in Bangladesh during COVID-19. The web-based survey used a standard e-questionnaire shared through social media. In all, 476 students took part.

About 15% of students reported moderately severe depression in the survey responses gathered during the pandemic months. Severe anxiety was reported by 18.1 percent of students, a share the authors call a warning sign for campus health. Older students showed greater depression in the analysis. Students who had given private tuition before the pandemic also showed more depression. The authors urge the government and universities to act together. Fixing study delays and money problems could ease the mental strain on students.
europmc-pmc7474869:
Consiglio and co-authors study the immune profile of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children with COVID-19. Infection in children is usually mild or silent. This rare syndrome appears 4-6 weeks after infection with high fever and organ strain.

The team ran systems-level tests on blood immune cells, cytokines, and autoantibodies. Groups included healthy children, children with Kawasaki disease, infected children, and those with the syndrome. The syndrome's inflammation differed from the cytokine storm of severe adult COVID-19. It shared traits with Kawasaki disease but differed in T cell subsets and IL-17A levels. Markers of artery damage also set it apart. Autoantibody scans found several antibodies that may drive the illness. The work sharpens how doctors tell these conditions apart.
europmc-pmc7508369:
Buitrago-Garcia and co-authors run a living review of silent and pre-symptom SARS-CoV-2 infections. How often infected people never feel ill was hotly disputed. The review asks three linked questions on spread without symptoms.

The team included 94 studies in the review, with searches run to June 10, 2020. Their overall estimate was that 20% of infected people stay free of symptoms through the whole infection course. In screened groups that were followed over time, the share was higher. Contacts of silent cases caught the virus less often than contacts of ill cases. Models put much spread in the pre-symptom phase. The review updates as new studies land. Its numbers guide testing and tracing plans in outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7524869:
Masucci and co-authors review neutrophil extracellular traps in cancer. These traps are web-like strands of DNA, histones and proteins. Neutrophils release them as part of innate defense.

The review shows how traps can also help tumors grow. Cancer cells draw neutrophils into the tumor setting. Traps form in primary tumors and in spread sites. They can catch cancer cells moving in blood. They may also wake dormant cancer cells. That can lead to relapse and new spread. The authors discuss traps as a possible target for cancer therapy. It also notes links to spread and relapse risk.
europmc-pmc7532469:
Olagnier and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 suppresses the NRF2 pathway. NRF2 controls antioxidant gene expression in cells. Samples from COVID-19 patients showed this pathway turned down.

Two NRF2 activators were tested in cell work. They were 4-octyl-itaconate and dimethyl fumarate. Both set off an antiviral program in cells. That program blocked SARS-CoV-2 replication across cell lines. It also blocked herpes, vaccinia and Zika viruses. The effect did not need type I interferon. Both drugs also cut host inflammatory responses. The authors present NRF2 activation as a broad antiviral route worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc7615769:
NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) tracks underweight and obesity worldwide from 1990 to 2022 in adults and youth. Both states harm health across the life course. Combined trends show where the double burden is shifting.

Data came from 3663 population studies in total. A total of 222 million people were measured. Estimates cover 200 countries and territories in all. Combined adult prevalence rose in 162 countries for women. It rose in 140 countries for men over the span. By 2022 obesity beat underweight in most countries. That held for 177 countries for women that year. Island nations and parts of the Middle East ranked highest. School-age trends moved in a like direction overall.
europmc-pmc7617369:
James and co-authors present the Lancet Commission on prostate cancer, planning for a surge in cases. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men in 112 countries. It accounts for 15% of all male cancers.

New cases are projected to rise sharply by 2040. The annual count goes from 1.4 million in 2020 to 2.9 million. Lifestyle change alone cannot stop that surge. Four working groups covered trends, diagnosis, treatment and advanced care. Late diagnosis is common worldwide in this cancer. It is the norm in many low-income countries. Early diagnosis improves outlook and cuts costs. The Commission urges changes that can start now. Care must be fitted to local resource levels, they argue.
europmc-pmc7691969:
Nikfarjam and co-authors review vesicles shed by stem cells as a cell-free therapy. Mesenchymal stem cells are prized for repair and for calming immune responses. Much of their benefit turns out to come from what they release, not from the cells themselves. Exosomes are one such release, carrying RNA and proteins to other cells.

Using exosomes alone avoids risks of live cell treatment, such as blocked small vessels. The review covers ways to collect exosomes for clinical use. It sums up trials in heart, kidney, liver, immune, and nerve diseases, plus skin wounds. The authors see a modern, safer path to regenerative care.
europmc-pmc7875769:
Boix and co-authors present a large research resource on how gene regulation links to human disease. Most disease-linked DNA variants sit outside genes, in regions that control gene activity. The team built EpiMap to map those control regions across the body.

EpiMap brings together 10,000 epigenomic maps from 800 samples. The authors used it to define chromatin states, enhancers, and the genes those enhancers target. They then annotated 20,000 genetic loci tied to 232 traits. For each locus they predict the tissues that matter and the likely target genes. Their results show many loci act through several variants and genes at once. The resource gives researchers a way to move from a DNA signal to a testable mechanism.
europmc-pmc7896069:
Tang and co-authors present a review arguing for a shift in cancer immunotherapy targets. Checkpoint drugs have won great success, yet they are not the most used weapons against cancer. Many tumours fail to respond to them. The review blames the tumour immune microenvironment, the mix of cells around the tumour.

That local mix can shut down immune attack and let tumours hide. The authors describe the faults of current immunotherapies first. They then examine the regulators that shape the tumour's immune setting. These regulators govern how well the immune system spots and fights the tumour. Many can be reached by drugs. The authors argue that targeting them, alone or with checkpoint drugs, could help more patients. The review points therapy research toward the tumour's surroundings.
europmc-pmc7901269:
Zhou and co-authors report a laboratory study of the SARS-CoV-2 variant B.1.351 and immune escape. The variant was first seen in South Africa. It carries several changes in the spike protein, the part of the virus that antibodies target. The team tested how well blood from recovered patients and vaccine recipients could block it.

The changes let the variant grip the ACE2 receptor more tightly. They also helped it dodge many monoclonal antibodies. One change, E484K, drove much of that escape. Two other changes acted together against some antibody classes. In a number of cases, blood from past infection or vaccination gave only limited protection. The findings raised early concern about vaccine performance against new variants. They also showed which spike changes matter most.
europmc-pmc7912069:
Talapko and co-authors present a review of Candida albicans, a fungus that lives in and on healthy people. It colonises the mouth, gut, and skin as part of the normal flora. In 50% of the population it sits quietly without causing harm. Trouble starts when the balance between host and fungus breaks.

The review explains the traits that let the fungus turn from guest to invader. Shifts in gut microbes, weak immunity, or damage to the gut wall can open the way. Infections range from surface problems in the mouth to blood infection that threatens life. The authors sort the clinical forms into primary and secondary types. They also trace how the gut serves as the main store of the fungus. The review gives clinicians a clear picture of when a harmless resident becomes a danger.
europmc-pmc7996969:
Yu and co-authors present software for fast analysis of a rich kind of proteomics data. Ion mobility sorts protein fragments by shape as well as mass. Data from the timsTOF instrument are powerful but bulky, and slow to process. The team adapted their fast search engine, MSFragger, to this data type. They also built a new tool, IonQuant, to measure amounts with care.

Together the tools form a pipeline tuned to the instrument. Tests showed strong sensitivity in naming proteins and accuracy in counting them. Run times stayed short, which matters as datasets grow. The team also showed a harder trick: a half-open search that watches gas-phase breaking in early data from the instrument. The paper serves labs that run this platform and need results they can trust at speed.
europmc-pmc8045269:
Mlambo and co-authors gather how nurses say they see their own ongoing training. Such training keeps nursing skills current across a whole career. Yet nurses' own views of it sat scattered across many small studies. The team pulled the qualitative studies together in one synthesis. A total of 25 articles met the rules for the review.

Five big themes came out of the work. The culture of the workplace shapes the terms for learning. A supportive setting acts as a basic need, not a bonus. Nurses' attitudes mirror their sense of what the job demands. Blocks, from cost to time, recur across settings. The gain for daily practice stands as the core value. Nurses prize the training and link it to better patient care. The authors urge employers to fund it well and make access real.
europmc-pmc8064669:
Vasileiou and co-authors measure what the first vaccine doses did to hospital admissions in Scotland. Their national cohort study linked records for 5.4 million people, near the whole population. Vaccination, testing, GP, and hospital data sat in one database. The window ran from December 8, 2020 to February 22, 2021. In that span, 1,331,993 people got a first dose.

One dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine cut COVID-19 hospital admissions by 91% at 28 to 34 days out. The Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine reached 88% at the same point after dosing. Among people aged 80 and older, the combined effect held at 83% against hospital admission. The authors flag possible leftover confounding in the data. Even so, the roll-out's early payoff was large. Real-world protection matched the trial promise closely.
europmc-pmc8113269:
Winkler and co-authors rebuild the global record of land use change and find far more of it. They fused satellite data, historical reconstructions, and national statistics. The result, HILDA+, maps change at finer detail than before. Land use change touched almost a third of the world's land in six decades. The tally puts change at 32% of global land area between 1960 and 2019 in their reconstruction. That runs about four times the older estimates.

The map splits sharply between North and South. Northern regions show forest regrowth and cropland abandonment. Southern regions show forest clearing and farm expansion. Change sped up from about 1960 to 2005, then slowed. Global trade in farm goods explains much of that rhythm. Demand in one hemisphere plows land in the other. Climate and food policy, the authors show, must reckon with a restless map. Static land accounts understate the churn.
europmc-pmc8137869:
He and co-authors review how circular RNAs might be targeted as medicines. These looped RNAs lack free ends, so enzymes cannot chew them easily. That stability, plus tissue-specific expression, makes them tempting targets. Their misbehavior is implicated across cancers and other diseases. Turning a circle up or down is the therapeutic trick. The review sorts the available strategies by approach.

Plasmids drive gain-of-function studies by overexpressing a chosen circle. RNA interference handles the knockdown side, with known limits. Nanoparticles and exosomes promise better delivery of both. A cre-lox system can silence circles in chosen cell types. CRISPR/Cas13 tools now cut circles with high specificity. Each method carries delivery and off-target headaches still. The authors close with the field's major challenges. Early days, but the target class keeps widening. Stable circles may anchor future RNA drugs.
europmc-pmc8158969:
Goel and co-authors track antibody and memory B cell responses after mRNA vaccination against SARS-CoV-2. They followed 33 people with no prior infection and 11 who had recovered. Blood was sampled over time after each dose.

People with no prior infection needed both doses for full gains in antibodies. Neutralizing power against the B.1.351 variant rose most after the second dose. Memory B cells for the spike protein formed in all such subjects after dose two. In recovered people, one dose boosted responses strongly. Age slightly blunted the memory B cell response.
europmc-pmc8268869:
Boutilier and Elsawa review macrophage polarization states inside the tumour microenvironment. Macrophages settle into states that shape how a tumour fares. The classic split sets M1 cells against tumours and M2 cells in their favour.

Tumour-associated macrophages mostly take the M2-like side. They help build blood and lymph vessels and suppress immunity. They also foster low oxygen, tumour growth, and spread. The tumour setting recruits macrophages and steers their state. The review explains how that steering happens. Knowing it could yield therapies that flip macrophages back against the tumour. That balance helps explain many pro-tumour outcomes.
europmc-pmc8315569:
Wang, Zhang, and Chen survey drug resistance in cancer and ways to fight it. Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States. Care spans surgery, chemotherapy, targeted drugs, radiation, hormones, and immunotherapy.

Resistance defeats many of those gains. It can exist before treatment or grow during it. It drives most relapses, a major cause of cancer death. Tumours differ between patients and within one mass. Cancer cells also find new routes around each drug. The review sorts resistance routes and the counters now in study. The problem spans old and new drugs alike.
europmc-pmc8421569:
Ruiz and co-authors review the part copper plays in mitochondria and cell metabolism. Copper is vital for energy use, defense against reactive oxygen, and iron uptake. Mitochondria gather copper to build enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase.

Through these enzymes, copper shapes energy output, organelle dynamics, and cell fate. The liver keeps body copper in tight balance, yet tissue levels vary. Too much or too little copper links to blood disorders and to tumor growth. New drugs aim to raise or cut copper as cancer therapy. The review ties copper handling to regenerative medicine as well. It follows copper from food source to cell uptake.
europmc-pmc8428369:
Łukasiewicz and co-authors give an updated review of breast cancer, the most common cancer among women. About 2.3 million new cases are found worldwide each year, per the authors. Gene expression levels split the disease into molecular subtypes that guide care.

The review covers how often the disease occurs and where rates have risen. Risk factors include both habits people can change and traits they cannot. Most patients are now over 50 years old. Survival turns on stage and molecular subtype. Prognostic markers help doctors sort patients by outlook. The authors close with current treatment options matched to each subtype.
europmc-pmc8580269:
Minelli and co-authors test two-sample Mendelian randomization methods on single large data sets. Biobanks now hold genome data for many exposures and outcomes in the same people. One-sample studies grow more common as a result. But robust methods assume the two gene estimates are independent.

In one sample they come from the same people, so confounding breaks that premise. The team mimicked a typical UK Biobank study in simulations. Several standard methods held up much as they do in true two-sample work. One method, MR-Egger, bent with the direction of pleiotropy. The study maps where each method can be trusted. It helps analysts pick sound tools.
europmc-pmc8602669:
Hassani, Azapagic, and Shokri model how climate change may shift soil salt levels in drylands this century. Salt buildup harms farms and local economies. Its natural course under a warming climate was not well mapped. The team built data-driven models to project change to the year 2100.

Their maps flag parts of South America as hotspots for more salt. Southern and western Australia, Mexico, the southwest United States, and South Africa also face gains. Other drylands may see salt fall, such as parts of Eastern Europe and west Kazakhstan. The work gives planners a first global view of where soil salt risk will grow or ease.
europmc-pmc8649869:
Gao and co-authors uncover how liver cancer cells resist the drug sorafenib. This drug helps at first, but tumors almost always fight back. The team used gene silencing screens and gene activity data to find the drivers. Two related proteins, YAP and TAZ, stood out.

These proteins block a cell death path called ferroptosis. They raise levels of a transporter that guards the cell's antioxidant supply. They also keep a partner protein, ATF4, stable and active in the nucleus. ATF4 helps drive the same transporter. The authors suggest that rewiring this system could restore drug response. The work names a clear target pair for future trials.
europmc-pmc8733869:
Markmann and co-authors report a randomized trial of portable machine perfusion for donor livers before transplant. The standard method stores livers cold and without blood flow. The new method pumps warm, oxygenated blood through the organ. The trial enrolled 300 transplant recipients at many centers.

Machine perfusion cut early graft injury after transplant. It also cut bile duct problems from low blood flow. More donor livers were judged usable and transplanted. The authors conclude that portable warm perfusion improves outcomes. It may also widen the pool of usable organs. The study used the OCS Liver system for the perfusion arm.
europmc-pmc8875269:
Han, Zheng, Daines, and Sheikh pool one-year follow-up data on symptoms after COVID-19. Many survivors report problems long after infection. How many still suffer at one year was unclear. The team searched PubMed and Embase for long follow-up studies. Eighteen papers qualified. Together they covered 8,591 survivors. Random-effects meta-analysis produced pooled rates for each symptom.

Fatigue or weakness led the list at 28%. Joint and muscle pain followed at 26%. Depression sat at 23% and anxiety at 22%. Breathlessness affected 18%, and memory loss 19%. Insomnia was lowest among the leaders at 12%. Women reported more lingering symptoms than men. So did patients whose first illness was severe. The authors urge work on causes and targeted care. Long COVID, they show, is no small tail.
europmc-pmc8938269:
Sattar and co-authors pool trial data to judge the heart safety of tirzepatide, a diabetes drug. The drug activates two hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1. It is given once a week. Diabetes itself doubles cardiovascular risk, so safety proof matters. This meta-analysis was specified in advance. It gathered all seven trials of at least 26 weeks. The program was called SURPASS. In total, 4,887 people took tirzepatide and 2,328 took control treatments.

The main measure joined four major events. Heart death, heart attack, stroke, and unstable angina hospitalization counted. The hazard ratio for that bundle was 0.80. Its interval crossed one, so harm was not shown. Heart death alone gave a ratio of 0.90. No subgroup behaved differently. The authors conclude the drug did not raise major event risk. Longer outcome trials would firm that verdict.
europmc-pmc9047469:
Fan and co-authors review the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2, the most heavily mutated form seen in the pandemic. Omicron spread fast and replaced Delta in many regions. The review covers how it infects, how far it travels, and how sick it makes people. Altered cell preference seems to soften its disease while raising spread.

Omicron also resists most vaccine, recovery, and antibody defenses. The authors survey antiviral drugs and other treatments that may still work. They close with response plans for future waves and routes toward ending the pandemic. It was first reported to health authorities in November 2021.
europmc-pmc9247969:
Lazarus and co-authors revisit COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy worldwide using survey data from 23 countries in 2021. Hesitancy means delay or refusal of vaccination despite available services. Nationally representative samples of 1,000 people per country were surveyed in June 2021. The team compared results with a survey a year earlier.

Acceptance rose to 75.2% of 23,000 respondents, up from 71.5%. Hesitancy tracked with low trust in vaccine safety and science, and with doubt about efficacy. Hesitant respondents also resisted proof-of-vaccination rules for travel, work, and school. The authors say campaigns must raise confidence and widen access. Low- and middle-income countries face the steepest access gaps.
europmc-pmc9252569:
Kou and co-authors discuss extracellular vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells as a next-generation therapy tool. These stem cells can be taken from marrow, cord, and fat tissue. Their healing power rests mainly on what they secrete. Vesicles are key secreted effectors and carry signals between cells.

Because vesicles keep the parent cell's benefits with lower immune risk, they may beat cell therapy. The review explains their traits and how they regulate immunity. It stresses their role in treating fibrosis and aiding tissue repair. Molecular mechanisms are set out for several organs. Quality variation and mass production remain hard problems. The authors suggest ways to solve them for clinic use.
europmc-pmc9388369:
Subramanian and co-authors hunt for long COVID symptoms and risk factors in adults never sent to hospital. They used a UK primary care database with 486,149 confirmed infections. Nearly two million matched people without infection served as controls. Symptoms were checked beyond 12 weeks after infection, spanning 115 candidates.

Sixty-two symptoms stayed significantly linked to prior infection. Loss of smell topped the list with an adjusted hazard ratio of 6.49. Hair loss, sneezing, and reduced libido also ranked high. Risk of long COVID rose with female sex, deprivation, smoking, and obesity. Ethnic minority status and many prior conditions added risk too. Younger adults faced more risk than older ones in this group. The authors say the symptom net must be cast wide in clinics.
europmc-pmc9569569:
Chen and co-authors link lactate and lactylation to metabolic change and immune suppression in cancer. Immune evasion and metabolic rewiring are two core cancer traits. Lactate ties the two traits together in the tumor setting. It was long dismissed as a waste product.

Lactate and the acid it brings feed tumor growth steps. New vessels, invasion, and spread all gain from it. A newer find is lactylation, a protein mark made from lactate. Histone lactylation gives lactate a direct grip on gene control. The review traces lactylation in glycolysis linked cell work. Its part in macrophage polarization is also covered. Cross talk with other protein marks gets a look. The authors weigh drug targets in lactate metabolism. They propose pairing glycolysis blockade with immunotherapy as a joint plan.
europmc-pmc9697769:
Passeri and co-authors review treatment strategies for Alzheimer's disease and the limits each one faces. The disease is the most common nerve wasting illness worldwide. Decades of drug work have brought no cure at all. Current drugs ease symptoms but do not change the course.

The review sets out the disease stages and risk factors first. It splits risks into those that can change and those that cannot. Study models used in the field get a survey next. Prevention is framed as the best plan at this time. Good habits and early steps can slow the disease path. Getting drugs into the brain is the core hard problem. The blood-brain barrier blocks most compounds from entry. Soft nanoparticles draw the authors' strongest praise here. Nanoliposomes and exosomes can cross and target brain tissue. Nose based dosing is a further route they weigh.
europmc-pmc9805569:
Bouras and co-authors introduce Pharokka, a fast tool for annotating bacteriophage genomes. Phage sequences are piling up as interest in phages grows. Older annotation routes were slow or built for other microbes. Web tools also demand hand curation that breaks pipelines.

Pharokka annotates a phage genome in under five minutes. That timing holds for a typical 50-kilobase phage genome. Install and first run take just two lines of code. Outputs follow shared standards so results compare cleanly. The tool was built only for phages from the start. That focus avoids the gaps of general microbe annotators. Those tools miss many phage genes in their databases. Pharokka runs locally on standard lab computers. It scales from single genomes to hundreds at once. The authors offer it as pipeline ready infrastructure.
europmc-pmc9842669:
Yang and co-authors review microbes that live inside tumors and their links to cancer. The review covers bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other organisms found in tumor tissue. It asks how these microbes affect cancer start, growth, spread, and treatment response.

The authors describe several routes by which tumor microbes may aid cancer. These include DNA damage, chronic inflammation, and signals that help metastasis. They also set out ways microbes can aid antitumor immunity, such as STING signaling and T cell activation. Other routes can blunt immunity and help tumors grow. Readers get a map of candidate markers and treatment targets tied to tumor microbiota.
europmc-pmc9925769:
Debien and co-authors give an overview of immunotherapy in breast cancer and its prospects. Checkpoint inhibitors joined with chemotherapy worked in triple-negative breast cancer trials. Gains appeared in both advanced and early disease settings. Those results led to the first approvals of checkpoint drugs for this cancer type.

Many trials now test wider combinations across all breast cancer subtypes. Options include cancer vaccines, CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and oncolytic viruses. The review sums up key trial results and drugs in development. It also covers barriers to using immune treatment in routine care. Those barriers shape how future trials should be designed. Readers get a current map of a fast-changing treatment field.
europmc-pmc9988869:
Zhu and co-authors identify a fibroblast group that shields liver tumors from immunity. Hepatocellular carcinoma resists immunotherapy and holds many cell types. Single-cell sequencing of human and mouse tumors revealed varied cancer-associated fibroblasts. One group, marked by CD36, stood out across species.

These CD36+ fibroblasts ran high lipid metabolism and made macrophage migration inhibitory factor. Tracing showed they arose from hepatic stellate cells. CD36 drove factor output through oxidized LDL uptake and a lipid damage pathway. The factor then drew in suppressive myeloid cells. Adding these fibroblasts to tumors sped growth in living models. Blocking CD36 plus anti-PD-1 restored antitumor T cell responses. The study names a target to unlock immunotherapy in liver cancer.
finney-character-claims-of-freemasonry-1:
Charles G Finney, a leading revival preacher, published his attack on Freemasonry in 1869. Finney said he had once been a Mason himself, and he wrote as a Christian minister alarmed by the lodge. His target was not one lodge but the whole system.

Finney examined Masonic oaths, claims, and daily practice, and argued that they conflicted with Christian faith and honest public life. He warned that secret pledges could place a brother Mason above church, family, or court. The book became a key text for evangelical critics, and it shows how sharp the clash between revival faith and lodge loyalty could be.
frus-1861-d169:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1861. The dispatch is document 169 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz wrote with the flair of the journalist he had been. His Madrid reports mixed court fact with sharp judgment of men. This July letter shows the new minister finding his feet at a proud, formal court in wartime. His flair for phrase later made his memoirs a classic of the German American story. A classic memoir grew from the same pen that penned these wartime pages. The same pen later wrote a classic memoir.
frus-1861-d269:
By the date of 23 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. Congress received it as Document 269 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d69:
One of three letters dated 17 August 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 69 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The date 17 August opens a cluster of three Seward letters to London in one day. Each took up a point of its own, from notes to claims. Together they show the range of business that crossed the Secretary's desk in the war's first summer. The cluster form of 17 August shows in the printed file as three short papers in a row. Three short papers in a row show the file at its most clerk neat that summer.
frus-1862-d169:
Printed as Document 169, the third Seward dispatch of 25 October 1862 went from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Together the three letters show one day's full output from the Secretary of State's desk to his British post.

Short letters, sent often, were how a government without cables ran an embassy in wartime. Each one might carry a single order or a single piece of news. A lone dispatch like this one grows in value when read in its cluster. Set in that stream, it helped keep London and Washington in step. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d269:
On 22 April 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 269 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Paris papers under that date, the other being a Seward dispatch.

Late April brought the Union flag back over New Orleans, a loss the South felt in every European counting house. Cotton, credit, and sympathy all shifted with such news. Dayton's report from Paris that week belongs to the record of how France absorbed the blow to the Confederate cause it was tempted to aid. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d369: A translated paper dated 31 July 1862 stands as Document 369 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section after the Mercier letters. The heading marks it only as a translation, giving no author or reader. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place among the French papers of that summer.
frus-1862-d469:
George Perkins Marsh wrote from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 April 1862. His dispatch is Document 469 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Spring 1862 found Italy watching France closely, since French troops still guarded the pope in Rome and French ambition was moving in Mexico. Marsh's reports linked those Italian concerns to the American war, which shared the same French question. From Turin he could also report the new kingdom's steady sympathy for the Union. The letter is part of the volume's Italian file, where diplomacy ran on shared national hopes rather than on fear or bargaining.
frus-1862-d569:
Henry Shelton Sanford sent this report from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 September 1862. It is Document 569 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Sanford wrote four days after Lincoln's emancipation order was issued, though the news was still crossing the Atlantic. His report covered the Brussels scene as it stood: the court's connections, the press, and the war's standing in Belgian opinion. Within days he would have the emancipation news to work with, and few ministers used it more eagerly. The letter catches the Belgian file at the hinge of the autumn. The war's new moral shape had not yet reached Europe. When it did, it changed Sanford's brief for the better.
frus-1862-d669:
On 24 December 1861, Anson Burlingame wrote from China to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister there, a former congressman turned envoy. His letter is document 669 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

A Christmas Eve date on a letter from the far side of the world hints at the pace of the post. Mail from China took months to reach Washington, so envoys wrote often and covered much ground in each sheet. Burlingame's dispatch is part of that steady flow, the raw stuff from which the State Department built its view of China in the war years.
frus-1862-d69:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Charles Francis Adams, dated 22 May 1862. Congress received it as Document 69 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d169:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 24 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 169 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last of Adams's three sheets wound up the legation's work for a peak day in the file. His spring letters, read whole, are the story of the Union's cause in Britain told by its keeper. This one ends the 24 April set. It stands in the record as a working piece of the watch that kept Britain's fleet and yards from the South.
frus-1863p1-d269: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 August 1863. It is document 269 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d369:
A formal note dated 26 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 369 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d469:
A 20 April 1863 dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d569:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State received a letter dated 17 June 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d669:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d69:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 69 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening Seward's February mail in the file.

February brought no rest to the London brief. The South's agents still worked for ships and friends in Britain, and the Union's claims still needed pressing. Seward's letters kept Adams supplied with the government's views and the facts from home. This one opens a run of February sheets that runs thick in the volume, proof of how much of the war was fought with pens.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d169: A second letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 26, 1943, and it stands as Document 169 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, in the Moscow Conference section. Two presidential letters to his secretary in one day, across an ocean and a war, kept the home government's hand firm on the talks. The record names the parties and the date. The letter's text is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d269:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 25 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, take up Southeast Asia operations. Admiral Mountbatten reports his meeting of the day before with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek on the Burma campaign plan.

Chiang had insisted on the larger plan, for which the resources did not exist. It needed 535 more transport aircraft. He settled for the smaller one once the chiefs were formally asked for the planes. He also demanded a seaborne operation alongside the land advance in north Burma. On airlift over the Hump, he held out for the full 10,000 tons a month against a promised average of 8,900. Mountbatten asks for Chiang's agreement to the campaign in writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d369:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 30 November 1943 record a morning session at half past nine. The Western staffs were trying to agree a basis for that afternoon's plenary session with the Soviets. Landing craft, once again, decide nearly every question.

Brooke proposes a sequence. Italy comes first, with Eisenhower keeping his landing craft until 15 January to reach the Pisa-Rimini line. Rhodes follows only if Turkey enters the war. Then comes the south of France, with craft from Rhodes returning in time. Leahy answers that the whole knot is Overlord's date: the Russians want it fixed in May, and if that date stands, other operations must fit around it. The British doubt the returning craft can be repaired and their crews trained in time, and ask for American repair facilities.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d469:
President Roosevelt wrote to President Bishara al-Khouri of Lebanon on December 3, 1943, during the conference season at Cairo. Lebanon had just come through a crisis in November, when French authorities arrested its leaders and then released them under pressure, leaving Lebanese independence recognized in fact. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt's message reached a small new state sitting at the center of Allied supply lines and Arab politics. American interest in Lebanon mixed wartime logistics with sympathy for independence from the French mandate. For readers, the letter shows the President tending ties far beyond the Big Three table where the cameras pointed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d569:
The American consul at Colombo, Ceylon, wrote to Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius on January 9, 1945. Stettinius had succeeded Cordell Hull at the department the month before. The consul's report appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, far from the conferences themselves.

Colombo was a working port on the sea roads to Southeast Asia, and consuls there reported on shipping, local politics, and the war's edge in the Indian Ocean. A report from such a post shows how widely the conference volumes cast their net for related records. For readers, it is a reminder that the global war was also administered from small offices in distant harbors.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d69: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt dated October 29, 1943 stands as Document 69 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Splitting the day's business into two notes was the prime minister's habit when matters differed in kind. The record does not say what set this note apart from its companion. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the pause between the Moscow Conference and the November summits.
frus-1944-quebec-d169:
The President's Log for the Quebec Conference opens with a foreword by Lieutenant George Elsey. Quebec, he notes, marked the eleventh wartime meeting of Roosevelt and Churchill. The foreword looks back over the road from their first meeting at Argentia in August 1941, where the Atlantic Charter proclaimed their war aims, through Washington, Casablanca, Cairo, and Tehran.

Elsey then describes the war as the leaders gathered in September 1944. Allied armies had swept across northern France and entered Germany, Alexander was cracking the Gothic Line in Italy, and Soviet forces stood at the gates of Warsaw. Rumania and Bulgaria had fallen away from Germany, and the American Navy had just struck Mindanao. Only in China, he writes, were Allied fortunes unfavorable.
frus-1944-quebec-d269:
The combined memorandum on troop movements, forwarded September 13, 1944, examines what Operation Dracula would do to allied shipping. The buildup meant moving six British divisions, 370,000 men, from Europe to India before March 1, 1945. At its peak the movement would absorb virtually the entire British trooping lift, and a decision was needed by October 1 to beat the monsoon.

The costs elsewhere were plain. British help on the Atlantic run would fall to about 25,000 men a month, with only the two Queens sailing it. All British ocean-going troopships would leave cross-Channel work, removing 25 to 30 thousand troop spaces. Indian ports would be fully absorbed, except Calcutta for American troops.
frus-1944-quebec-d69:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on September 14, 1944, in the middle of the Second Quebec Conference. Both men were at Quebec City, and the conference was then deep in its hardest argument, over Germany's future. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Mid-conference letters carried proposals between the Citadel's sessions, where Roosevelt lodged with Churchill as his guest. September 14 fell in the days when the Morgenthau Plan was accepted, then began to unravel. For readers, a message from that moment catches the summit at its most consequential, in the leaders' own hand-to-hand written style.
frus-1945-50-intel-d169:
The meeting named in the title took place on 25 September 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. The State Department prints it as document 169 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d269: Dated 4 May 1948, "Policy Planning Staff Memorandum" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 269 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d369:
A memorandum from the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Babbitt) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 369 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d69:
Harold Smith, the budget director, set down a memorandum on his own part in the settlement on 9 January 1946. Smith rarely wrote without a purpose, and self-recording was among his habits. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Memoranda written for the file by the men who shaped events are gifts to readers, when read with care. Smith knew his bureau's plan had largely won, and his paper helps explain how. Set beside the secretaries' joint letter of the same week, it shows the two tracks of the settlement. The departments agreeing in public, the budget director noting in private how the agreement was built. The volume's balance of open and office papers is nowhere better shown.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d169:
Bulgaria is a testing ground for the three allies, this briefing book paper warns. “Principal Bulgarian Problems” was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The armistice signed at Moscow on 28 October 1944 had set Bulgaria on a wholly new course.

The United States seeks neither an equal share with Moscow in the Control Commission nor the lead. What it wants is a clearer charter for the commission, with the rights and duties of the American team made safe. Washington also reserves the right to reopen the question, once Germany is beaten, of making the body truly three-sided. One sore point is flagged: Bulgarian reparation and restitution deliveries to Greece need speeding, and Soviet foot-dragging is expected.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d269:
President Roosevelt asked for a war crimes report on 3 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It wants two things. First, the state of the work before the War Crimes Commission. Second, the American representative's stand on the charges to come.

The charges, Roosevelt directs, should include an indictment for waging aggressive and unprovoked warfare, in breach of the Kellogg Pact. Hitler and the chief Nazi war criminals are the named targets. Perhaps, he adds, that charge and others like it might be joined in a single conspiracy indictment. The short paper is an early sketch of the legal road that ended at Nuremberg.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d369:
Alger Hiss listed the room before the talk in his notes of February 7, 1945: Stettinius, Molotov, and Eden, with aides ranked behind them. Stettinius opened by offering to clear up any open points on Dumbarton Oaks. Molotov thanked him but had no new points ready. Then came the report on France.

The ministers, Hiss records, agreed that France should have a zone of occupation in Germany, held by French forces. Molotov and Stettinius wanted France's seat on the Control Commission studied by the European Advisory Commission. Eden wanted admission agreed at once. Hiss's lines catch a real split between the Western partners.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d469:
Roosevelt was to carry a piece of news to King Ibn Saud, under this draft memorandum of February 11, 1945. At the final foreign ministers' meeting, held after the President left, Eden proposed adding Saudi Arabia to the nations invited to San Francisco. Molotov and Stettinius agreed — subject, a scrawled note says, to Russian refusal being overcome.

The kingdom would qualify if it declared war by March 1. Stettinius judged the move desirable. The President should tell Ibn Saud when they met in the next few days. Colonel Eddy, the American minister traveling with the King to the cruiser Quincy, should also be informed. The draft ties Yalta to Roosevelt's desert meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d69:
Background on the unfinished business of Dumbarton Oaks fills this editorial note in the Malta and Yalta volume. Rather than write a fresh summary, the editors quote the State Department's book Postwar Foreign Policy Preparation, pages 374 and 375. The quoted passage sets up the document group that follows.

When the Dumbarton Oaks Proposals were published on 9 October 1944, six questions were still open, the voting question among them. Work on them began at once under a senior committee chaired by Acting Secretary Stettinius. By 1 November he could report the President's plan: settle the open items at a conference with Churchill and Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d169:
The British Chiefs of Staff added one item to the staff conference agenda in a memorandum dated June 25, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/1, is document 169 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It builds on their draft agenda of June 15, which had covered the Pacific war from end to end.

The new eleventh item looks past the fighting: Combined Chiefs of Staff machinery after the war with Japan. The British say they will submit a paper on the subject as a basis for discussion. The addition is a small sign that planners on both sides were already thinking ahead. They were asking what would become of the joint war machine once Japan fell. They were also asking whether the Anglo-American partnership that ran the war could outlive it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d269:
The Joint Civil Affairs Committee warned against home-grown national governments in an undated memorandum printed as document 269 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper draws a lesson from Soviet sponsorship of the Renner government in Austria and from earlier Soviet experiments with a committee of German officers.

The three powers agree that central agencies will run Germany and Austria for now, and that democratic governments may come one day. But no one has agreed that an occupying power will not recognize, on its own, a body claiming national authority. The United States should urge that no such body be recognized, nationally or in a zone, until all four governments agree and the Control Council has fixed its powers. Local cooperation in each zone would remain allowed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d369:
Grew cabled Secretary Byrnes, then at sea, on July 7, 1945, to endorse Pauley's Moscow achievement. The agreed recommendations in Pauley's cable of July 6, he writes, conform fully to Pauley's instructions. Those instructions came from the Informal Policy Committee on Germany, were cleared with the Joint Chiefs, and were approved by the President.

Winning the agreement of his Russian and British colleagues, Grew adds, was a considerable achievement for Pauley. He recommends that the Secretary send Pauley a message of concurrence and gratification. The short cable is Washington's pat on the back, sent while the Secretary sailed toward Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d469:
Premier Parri is sized up in Kirk's strictly confidential cable from Rome, sent at midnight on July 6, 1945. Kirk had talked with Parri the previous evening. The gist of the Premier's remarks was the necessity of material aid to Italy, with stress on the immediate need for coal to prevent further unrest in the north. He stressed, too, the difficulty of reconstruction under the armistice regime's restrictions.

Personal contact, Kirk writes, confirms the general impression of Parri's seriousness, simplicity, and intellectual distinction. Yet he showed none of the vitality, alertness, or assurance even Bonomi displayed, and no sign of dynamic leadership. With such a cabinet, Kirk judged, speculation about Italy's course was nearly useless.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d569:
From Caserta on June 24, 1945, Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent an urgent secret extract to Washington. It is document 569 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Kirk explains how news of the Yugoslav reservation on article 3 reached his staff late.

Kirk says General Morgan reported the signing of the Duino deal with no word of any exception. Belgrade learned of it first, since a British officer, Colonel Clarke, sat in on the talks. Morgan then held back the text until he could explain it at a meeting. Only there did he name the reservation. The extract shows the top Allied staff in Italy learning of a key flaw in their own deal from the side lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d669:
Thomas Wasson, acting chief of the African Affairs desk, recorded a talk on Tangier dated July 6, 1945. His memo is document 669 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The French embassy's counselor, Lacoste, had called on Loy Henderson in Washington.

Lacoste raised the question of Soviet delegates in the Paris talks. Henderson said the Department knew the development well. Soviet ambassador Gromyko had called on Acting Secretary Grew on the morning of July 2. Gromyko expressed surprise that Moscow had not been invited to exchange views on Tangier. He said his government was interested in the zone's future and asked that the Paris talks be put off. A Soviet expert, he said, should be arranged to take part before they went on.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d69:
Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled President Truman from San Francisco on June 16, 1945. The urgent top secret telegram is document 69 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stettinius had just heard that the State Department had sent Truman a tentative list of staff for the Big Three meeting.

Stettinius stresses that the list is only tentative. He wants to talk with Truman while both are in San Francisco about the size and make-up of the party, so the number of State Department people matches the President's own thinking. He asks for a few minutes to settle it before the list becomes final. The short cable shows the staffing of the American delegation still open a month before the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1069: George Allen sent James Dunn this memorandum extract at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It lists his understanding of the final decisions on five Near Eastern and African items meant for the closing Protocol. Only the Greece passage is printed here. Allen records that the Soviet delegation declined the American and British invitation to help supervise the coming Greek elections. Their stated ground was that such supervision would mean interference in Greece's internal affairs. The other sections of the memorandum appear in separate documents elsewhere in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1169:
General Arnold, chief of the Army Air Forces, wrote to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 20 July 1945. Arnold commanded American air power across the world. Harriman was the president's envoy to the Soviet Union and a key voice on Soviet affairs.

A letter between the air chief and the Moscow envoy links two worlds: the war in the air and the talks about the peace. Air bases, routes, and Soviet ties all touched both men's work. This message shows that wiring in use during the summit. It reminds readers that Potsdam's paper trail ran far beyond the town in Germany where the leaders sat.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1269:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 20 July 1945. It follows their paper of two days before in the volume's run. The British staff kept its own steady pace of advice as the first week closed.

Each note took up the military questions as London's chiefs saw them: forces, fronts, and the means to hold what the talks might win. This one continues that series. Together the British memoranda form a staff diary of the summit from the soldiers' side. They let readers trace how the military view held or shifted as the bargaining moved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1369:
The Soviet delegation presented another proposal at Potsdam on 22 July 1945, one of a run of Soviet papers in the volume's last section. Each proposal fixed Moscow's wording on a point under dispute. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Reading the Soviet papers in order shows a method: state a claim in full, then bargain down only as far as needed. This proposal came as the conference moved past first speeches into hard drafting. For students of the talks, the value lies in contrast. Readers can set what the Soviet side tabled beside what all three leaders signed at the end. The gap between those texts is the story of Potsdam in brief.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-69:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a private Byrnes-Molotov meeting on July 23, 1945, at 9:30 a.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Secretary had asked for the meeting out of deep concern over German reparations.

Byrnes restated the U.S. aim first. America had always favored an overall policy treating Germany as an economic whole. But Soviet positions heard at Potsdam, he said, could not be reconciled with any overall reparation plan. Handing a large part of 1937 Germany to Polish administration was one such position. Maisky's wide definition of war booty was another working against the plan. Byrnes then made the U.S. limit very plain. The United States did not intend to pay out money to finance imports to Germany, repeating the last war's pattern of American funds paying reparations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d769:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 24, 1945, as document 769. Soviet texts arrived through the conference's middle days in steady number. Each marked a position Moscow meant to defend. The proposal was printed among the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A Soviet draft mid-conference shows aims after a week of testing. The other sides had revealed their limits. Readers can judge what Moscow still pressed and where it had softened, if at all. The document keeps the three-sided shape of the talks in view. Potsdam was a triangle, and each side's paper matters.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d869: General Lucius D. Clay, deputy military governor of the American zone, wrote to the Secretary of State from Berlin on July 21, 1945. Clay explains that General Eisenhower, after meeting the President, asked him to draft a directive for the zone commanders. The draft is attached and appears next in the volume. Clay says Eisenhower believed the directive would help the commanders and the Control Council work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d969: J. Howard Marshall wrote this one-sentence memorandum at Babelsberg on July 31, 1945. Marshall was general counsel to the American delegation on the Allied Commission on Reparations. The note answers a drafting question: how should the proposed reparations plan enter the final conference agreement? His answer is simple. The most satisfactory way is to attach the plan to the Economic Principles as Annex I. Section 16 of those principles already refers to such an annex. The brevity of the note is itself the record of a settled drafting point.
frus-1964-68v06-d169:
An editorial note in the Vietnam volume reconstructs President Johnson's address of March 31, 1968, from the inside. Early that afternoon, Secretary Clifford ordered all strikes north of 20 degrees latitude halted, from seven in the evening The speech's surprise ending was finished with Horace Busby's help.

Johnson read the close to his family, then practiced before cameras. He asked for Truman's 1952 withdrawal remarks. The last pages reached the teleprompters at 7:37 that evening and the speech book at 8:55, minutes before air. The note shows a presidency's turn made in one day, on paper still wet.
galton-hereditary-genius-1869:
Francis Galton published Hereditary Genius in 1869, his first book on inherited ability. He collected the family histories of judges, statesmen, scientists, and other eminent men. Patterns in those pedigrees drive his whole argument.

Galton claims that talent clusters in families because nature outweighs training. He ranks relatives by closeness and counts how eminence fades with distance. The inquiry launched the nature-versus-nurture debate in modern form. It also launched eugenics, whose harms readers must keep in view. The statistical ambition was real; so were the blind spots. Galton later expanded its methods into the statistical study of human differences generally.
gao-gaoreports-b-295569:
Dated March 10, 2005, GAO files B-295569 and B-295569.2 record Scot, Inc., as the protester. The Navy had awarded Gentex Corporation a contract for oxygen mask, regulator, helmet, and communications test sets. Scot held the better warranty but not the lower price. GAO denied the protest. The agency fairly judged that the stronger warranty was not worth the premium charged. That judgment matched the terms of the solicitation.

Two further points back the award. The winner's past work counted as relevant though its contracts were smaller. Its pricing, though uneven across items, posed risks the agency fairly weighed.
gao-gaoreports-b-299369:
AMS Group protested terms in a Homeland Security solicitation for security guard services. The site is the Plum Island Animal Disease Center in New York. The buy was set aside for small firms. GAO ruled in B-299369 on April 12, 2007.

The firm claimed the training terms clashed with each other. It pointed to a chart that left out some training hours. Those hours were set out in the main terms. Read as a whole, GAO found, the terms held together. The chart was a brief aid, not the full rule set. The firm showed no bar to drafting its bid. Broad claims of flaws lacked proof. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299469:
Knight's Armament Company protested an Army call to cancel a solicitation. The buy covered suppressors for M4 Carbine and M16 rifles. Those parts cut a weapon's sound, flash, and blast marks. GAO decided B-299469 on April 7, 2007.

The agency scrapped the buy after bids came in. It found that no product sent in met the stated terms. It also found the terms missed its true needs. GAO weighed that twin call. Both halves rested on a sound record. An agency may cancel when no fit bid is in hand. It may also fix terms that miss the mark. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-308969:
A lump-sum floor in a services deal was charged to the wrong year in this GAO decision, B-308969, dated May 31, 2007. The Interior Department's business center hired help for a Defense unit. The 1-year deal ran from July 1, 2003 to June 30, 2004. It set a floor buy of $1 million in services. Only $45,000 was charged to fiscal year 2003 funds.

GAO held the whole floor sum belonged to fiscal year 2003. The duty to pay at least that sum arose when the deal was signed. Both departments must fix their books. The fix moves the rest of the floor sum to the right year. The ruling stresses that a set floor binds funds at once.
gao-gaoreports-b-309869:
KIC Development, LLC lost its protest. That ruling is B-309869, dated September 26, 2007. The Coast Guard sought building work on Yerba Buena Island in San Francisco. The job fixed six buildings and built a seventh. An eighth was to be torn down and rebuilt. The award went to Sergent Mechanical Systems, Inc.

KIC claimed the winner's past jobs were too small in cash terms to count as like work. GAO found no cash floor for like work in the call. It found the past-work review fair and in line with the call. GAO denied the protest. The case turns on what a call says, not what a loser wishes it said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-169:
Contract Management, GAO-05-169 of February 15, 2005, probes claims that the Air Force paid too much for radar plane parts. The Air Force has paid Boeing more than $23 million for spare parts for its AWACS fleet. Those planes have watched the skies for threats since March 1977. In March 2003, tips reached GAO that prices had jumped with no good cause.

GAO traced the price hikes part by part. It asked if the Air Force got facts strong enough to call each price fair. It asked how much true contest shaped the buys. The title gives the cure: the Air Force should buy these parts a better way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-269:
September 11, GAO-05-269 of March 30, 2005, updates the tax cost of the 2001 terror attack on New York. In 2002, city and state budget staff put tax losses at $1.6 billion for the city in 2002 and $1.4 billion in 2003. State losses were put at $1.6 billion and $4.2 billion for those years. GAO warned then that the sums may fold in the slump that was on at the time.

New state studies use fresh data to split attack harm from slump harm. GAO asks if they give a truer count. It made no count of its own. The text weighs each fresh sum and its flaws.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-369:
Smithsonian Institution, GAO-05-369 of April 25, 2005, takes stock of the halls that hold the nation's shared trove. The group runs 18 museums and art halls, 10 science hubs, and a zoo. It is the world's largest such group. Age, past neglect, and vast crowds have worn its halls down. Fix and build work from 2005 to 2013 is priced at $2.3 billion.

GAO asks how the worn state harms guest access and the goods in care. It tells what shape shifts the group has made to run its halls. It lists each build's cost, state, and cash source. The revamp strides on; the cash lags.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-469:
A Defense Department study on handing its U.S. schools to local districts is critiqued in GAO report GAO-05-469, released on April 26, 2005. The department runs 59 schools on more than a dozen bases in the continental United States. In 2002 it hired a university institute to study transfer options. GAO judged the study's logic, its cost picture, and the issues it left open.

The department had no clear policy for closing its domestic schools. GAO found it hard to trace how the study's expert panel reached many of its transfer calls. In one case it backed transfer to a costlier district whose schools mostly underperformed. Repairs to the schools could cost the department about $125 million. The department would still have to maintain them after transfer. Legal bars in some states and unclear ownership also stood in the way. GAO called for a fuller assessment first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-669:
The Army's battlefield network is at risk, GAO-05-669 warns on June 15, 2005. The $108 billion Future Combat Systems plan rides on three linked builds: vehicle radios, a tactical internet, and shared software. The lead radio program began with untested tech and shifting demands. Its set reaches 3 kilometers against 10 required and fails network security needs. In April 2005 the Pentagon halted the work and weighed killing the contract.

Pocket radios for soldiers are harder still, at about a pound against 84. The network and software builds share the same pattern: bold aims, tight dates, immature parts. First fielding in fiscal 2008 looks doubtful.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-769:
Air traffic control abroad is profiled in GAO-05-769, a report dated July 29, 2005. Many nations have moved air navigation to stand-alone firms. By March 2005, 38 nations had made that shift. GAO picked five providers, in Australia, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. It compared their traits, their results, and the lessons of the change.

GAO found shared traits across all five. Safety stays the top goal, and an outside body still checks it. Each firm funds itself through user fees. Each holds a near monopoly, with some check on prices. Data show safety held steady or improved after the shift. Each firm also cut costs and gained efficiency, in part through new technology.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-869:
Livestock grazing on federal land is counted in GAO-05-869, issued September 30, 2005. Ranchers pay a fee, usually set by formula, per animal unit month. Backers call the fee fair and the use productive. Critics call the fee too low and the damage real. GAO measured grazing in fiscal year 2004 across 10 agencies. It counted what agencies spent, what fees brought in, and how fees differ.

The 10 agencies managed over 22.6 million animal unit months on about 235 million acres. Two land agencies held over 98 percent of the grazing land. Agencies spent at least $144 million to manage grazing that year. Fees brought in about $21 million, less than one-sixth of spending. Of that, about $5.7 million went to states and counties. Fee levels and purposes vary by agency, GAO showed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-169:
The federal debt schedules are audited in GAO-06-169, a report issued on November 7, 2005. GAO must audit the government's consolidated statements each year. The debt held by the public looms large in those statements. So GAO also audits the Bureau of the Public Debt's schedules on their own. The audit tests whether the fiscal year 2005 and 2004 schedules are reliable. It tests internal controls and compliance with key debt laws too.

The bureau manages Treasury securities held by the public and by federal accounts. Those accounts, chiefly trust funds like Social Security, park their surplus cash in Treasury paper.
