GAO found the schedules fairly presented in all material respects. The bureau also kept effective internal control over the schedules. The audit is one brick in the yearly audit of the whole government's books. Clean debt figures matter because so much federal reporting rests on them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-269:
A niche Treasury borrowing tool gets a cost review in GAO-06-269, a report issued on March 30, 2006. Cash management bills are short-term notes the Treasury sells off-schedule to bridge cash dips. Their use has grown as deficits persist. Net interest is now the fastest-growing line in the budget. GAO described when and why the Treasury turns to these bills. It weighed their pluses and minuses and the steps taken to cut their cost.

The Treasury has refined its use of the bills, GAO found. Cheaper paths may still exist. Options include more use of standard bill sales, looser auction rules for the cash bills, and lessons from other nations' debt shops. Each option trades cost against risk or market strain. GAO urged the Treasury to test them and pick the mix that borrows cheapest. Small savings on vast debt add up fast for taxpayers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-369:
Unclassified papers can still be too sensitive to share freely. GAO ruled in GAO-06-369 on March 7, 2006, on how two departments guard such material. The Department of Energy marks it Official Use Only. The Department of Defense uses For Official Use Only. Both marks limit who may see the material.

GAO compared the rules, steps, and tests each department uses. It checked training and oversight as well. The question was whether staff mark and protect papers as the rules require. GAO found that policies and oversight could be improved in both departments. Readers learn how loose handling starts. They also see the controls meant to stop it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-669:
Toxic air pollutants are covered in GAO-06-669, a GAO report dated June 23, 2006. Air toxics such as benzene and asbestos can cause cancer and other serious health problems. The Environmental Protection Agency's own data indicated that 95 percent of all Americans faced a higher likelihood of cancer from breathing them. Sources range from large factories to dry cleaners and cars. The 1990 Clean Air Act set duties for the agency to cut these risks.

GAO found that the agency had made limited progress on those duties and faced hard implementation challenges. Data on the program's costs and benefits were too thin to judge its effectiveness. GAO noted that state and local programs used practices that could help the federal effort. GAO urged better management of the program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-769:
How states tax employers for jobless benefits is examined in GAO-06-769, issued on July 26, 2006. In 2006, the Unemployment Insurance program was expected to collect over $37 billion in employer taxes. It would pay $34 billion in benefits to laid-off workers. Employer taxes are experience-rated, meaning firms that lay off more workers should pay more. GAO met with officials and experts to test how fair that system is in practice.

GAO found that state financing systems limit the degree of experience rating. Minimum and maximum tax rates blunt the link between layoffs and taxes. As a result, state policies produce steady cross-subsidies among firms and industries. Low-layoff industries help pay benefits caused by high-layoff ones. GAO said steps to sharpen experience rating must be balanced against other program goals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-869:
Shortcuts in baggage screening are examined in GAO report GAO-06-869, issued on July 28, 2006. The Transportation Security Administration must screen all checked bags at United States airports for explosives. It set standard procedures built around its detection machines. It also allows alternative procedures for short-term, special cases. GAO asked how the agency ranks its screening methods. GAO also checked how much the alternatives are used and how well their use is watched.

GAO found that the agency ranked procedures by legal duties and its judgment of their strength. It had not tested the security value of the alternative procedures in real operations. The full extent of alternative use was not known. Internal controls for tracking that use could be improved. GAO urged stronger oversight of the exceptions to standard screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-969:
Farm conservation funds, and how they are split among states, are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-969, dated September 22, 2006. The Environmental Quality Incentives Program helps farmers add practices that guard water, air, and soil. The Natural Resources Conservation Service runs it, with about $1 billion a year for states.

About $650 million flows through a general formula. GAO asked if that split fits the program's aims. It also asked if outcome-based measures track how the program does. GAO urged the Department of Agriculture to improve the split process. The report links funding formulas to real gains on the land.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-169:
Hurricanes Katrina and Rita flooded the Gulf Coast and swamped the federal flood insurance program. GAO examined the aftermath in GAO-07-169, a report dated December 15, 2006. The program paid claims on a scale never seen before. GAO studied the storms' cost and where the losses fell. It also checked how the emergency agency oversaw claim adjustments. New fast-track methods had been approved to speed payments.

By May 2006, the program had paid about 162,000 Katrina claims. About 83 percent of them were in Louisiana. The average Katrina claim paid about $94,800. That was roughly three times the prior record year's average. Program debt forced its borrowing limit up from $1.5 billion to about $20.8 billion. GAO's sample of reinspections found payment errors in about 14 percent of regular claims. It urged deeper analysis of adjustment errors after future floods.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-69:
Export controls on trade secrets and design data are the subject of GAO-07-69, dated December 5, 2006. Federal rules limit exports of defense goods and the data behind them. New technology makes such data easy to send abroad. GAO asked how well the rules guard that data at firms. It spoke with officials at 46 firms that export goods or data. The Commerce and State departments run most of the control system.

Agencies check shipments of goods at set points. Data exports lack those checkpoints, so firms guard data on their own. One third of the firms GAO spoke with had no written plan to guard such data. Almost half said the rules left them unsure what steps to take. GAO urged both departments to size up the risks and give clearer guidance. Commerce agreed with the plan. State backed better guidance but not the risk review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-769:
The Small Business Administration's main loan program is graded in GAO-07-769, dated July 13, 2007. The 7(a) program backs loans to firms that cannot get bank credit on their own. In fiscal year 2006, it helped over 80,000 businesses. Its guarantees totaled nearly $14 billion. GAO read the program's legal roots and its scorecards. It weighed proof that small firms face credit blocks. It also compared cost estimates for the program's loan risks.

The program's measures count loans made, not how firms fare after borrowing. That gap makes success hard to judge. The agency works on outcome measures but has no firm date for them. Studies from the 1970s to the early 1990s hint that small firms face credit limits. They predate tools like credit scoring, though. GAO urged the agency to build measures that track real outcomes. The agency agreed with that call. It disputed one comparison on borrower credit scores.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-169:
Conflict safeguards for contractor staff are weighed in GAO report GAO-08-169, issued March 7, 2008. Many contractor employees work beside federal staff in Defense Department offices. They do much the same work on tasks that steer billions in spending. Personal financial interests could bias that work. Federal staff face strict ethics rules.

GAO counted how many such staff work in the offices and what key services they give. It mapped the safeguards that now apply to them. It also asked officials whether more are needed. GAO visited 21 offices and 23 of their firms. The title calls for added safeguards for some contractor staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-269:
Layered contract fees at the Pentagon are weighed in GAO report GAO-08-269, issued January 25, 2008. One-third of defense spending on goods and services in fiscal year 2006 went to subcontracts. Each layer can add pass-through charges while adding little value. Auditors and Congress have long worried about the waste. Congress told GAO to gauge the risk.

GAO reviewed 32 contract actions from fiscal year 2005 at 10 major buying sites. Officials judged value added with standard tools, but no set criteria exist. How hard they looked turned on contract risk. Nine private firms stressed competition as their chief guard. GAO urged risk-based checks in the final rule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-369:
Disaster mass care roles for FEMA and aid groups are examined in GAO report GAO-08-369, issued February 27, 2008. The National Response Framework, released in January 2008, moved the lead mass care role from the Red Cross to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). GAO drew lessons from the 2005 Gulf Coast hurricanes.

Both sides agreed FEMA should lead, since it can direct federal resources and the Red Cross cannot. But FEMA lacked enough specialized staff for its wider coordination role. The umbrella group National Voluntary Organizations Active in Disasters had thin staffing too, with just one employee at the time of Katrina. FEMA had also not coordinated with the National Council on Disability as a 2006 law required. GAO recommended stronger coordination on all three fronts, and officials agreed.
grettir-saga-magnusson-morris-1869:
Grettir the Strong killed a ghost, outlived a curse, and held out as an outlaw for nineteen years in Iceland. His saga, translated by Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris in 1869, tells of strength wasted by temper and fate. Grettir could beat any man or monster, yet could not master his fear of the dark.

Hauntings, wrestling matches with the undead, and lonely winters on a sea-girt rock fill the tale. Morris loved the sagas and helped give them their English shape in versions like this one. The Story of Grettir stands as the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas in outlaw form, grim and human at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-menah: Aaron ben Menahem Mendel was a Russian rabbi who flourished at the beginning of the nineteenth century. His "Seyag la-Torah," printed at Lemberg in 1810, lists the passages of the Babylonian Talmud quoted in the Tosafot. The entry notes a hard point about the book. It is a plagiarism from a similar work by Mordecai Jaffe, not an original compilation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbas-judah-b-s:
Judah ben Samuel Abbas was a Spaniard of the thirteenth century. Two works of his are named from the headings of a manuscript. One, "Minḥat Yehudah," survives as a scrap of two leaves only, and is also called "Meḳor Ḥayyim." The other, "Yair Netib," he says he wrote at the age of twenty, and it is of a moral and religious cast.

The fifteenth chapter of that work sets out a full plan of studies, laid out on sound teaching lines. A child begins with the reading and sense of the Bible. Then, in fixed order, come morals, medicine, arithmetic, logic, and physics. Metaphysics, the study of being itself, is kept for the very last place in the course.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiathar-ha-koh:
Abiathar ha-Kohen of Cairo was nagid, or chief, of the Egyptian Jews, an office he took from his ancestors. He flourished at the end of the eleventh century and died before 1112. His name is tied to the Messianic stir of the year 1096. The First Crusade was then under way, and Jews of the day read it as a sign of a new age.

The Jewish community of Nablus, in Palestine, wrote to ask him for firm word on the matter. His answer went with their letter to Constantinople, the hub of the agitation. The reply spoke for the movement, and so fanned the heat yet more among Jews in Moslem lands. Oddly, the letter itself was never handed to those it was meant for.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abu-ishak-ibrah:
Abu Isḥaḳ Ibrahim ibn Sahl was a Spanish poet of the thirteenth century. He died at sea in 1259 or 1260. Under Almohade rule he took the Mohammedan faith. Many in Spain held that he took back that step before he died. His poems were written in Arabic. Most of them deal with faith.

Three prints of his works came out at Cairo and Beirut. His editor, Ḥasan al-'Aṭṭar, added a life of the poet. That life takes up the doubt about his change of faith. The entry warns that many poems under his name may not be his. Doubt hangs over them in part because he was a Jew who had changed faith. He also ranks among the first poets to shape the muwashshaḥ song form. One such song is quoted in a small Beirut book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adar-assyrian-a: Adar is the twelfth church month and the sixth civil month of the Jewish year. It has twenty-nine days in most years. Its seventh day marks the death of Moses. Its ninth day was made a fast, tied to a clash of the schools of Hillel and Shammai. The thirteenth was once Nicanor Day, for a Syrian general's fall. It later became the Fast of Esther. Purim falls on the fourteenth day. In Shushan it ran to the fifteenth as well. Adar falls near March.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adventists-869: Adventists are a Christian sect with two chief marks. First, they hold that the Jews will be brought back to the Holy Land and turned to the faith. Texts in Romans and Ezekiel ground that hope. Some set the return after the rising of the dead. Second, they read the whole Bible in its plain sense. That takes in the Mosaic law as well. The wait for Christ's return in their own age began in England. W. Miller spread it in New England. He set the year 1843 for the coming.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahava-969: Ahava was a river, possibly a canal or a branch of the Euphrates. On its banks Ezra halted his party on the march from Babylon to Jerusalem. There they fasted and humbled themselves before the Lord. The account stands in the book of Ezra, chapter eight. From one verse, Ahava may also have been the name of a village or town. In the book called I Esdras, the place is named Theras instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albalag-isaac-1:
Isaac Albalag was a philosopher of the second half of the thirteenth century. He probably lived in northern Spain or southern France. His free views marked him as a heretic in many eyes. He read the Creation story in Genesis through Aristotle's claim that the world is eternal. Yet he also leaned toward the Cabala, while fighting its wild plays on letter values.

In 1292 he translated part of Al-Gazzali's survey of the philosophers, on logic and metaphysics. He used the work to answer a common charge: that philosophy undoes religion. Both, he held, aim at man's happiness and agree on reward, immortality, a just God, and providence. Where they cannot be reconciled, he offered a bold fix. A claim may be true for philosophy, he said, and Scripture true on a higher plane. His six days of Creation are an order of things, not a span of time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandre-edoua: Édouard Alexandre was a French organ maker and inventor. He was born in Paris on December 4, 1824, and died in 1888. He learned his trade in his father Jacob's factory at Ivry. In 1844 he received a share in the business. Father and son devised the piano-organ, the piano-Liszt, and the organ-melodium. In 1856 the firm won the medal of honor at the Paris Exhibition, for instruments that spread a taste for music across France. In 1860 he was made a chevalier of the Legion of Honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ananias-son-of-:
Ananias, son of Nebedeus, was a high priest of the Jews. Herod of Chalcis gave him the post. He served from about 47 to 59. Agrippa II then took the post from him. In 52 he was sent to Rome for a hearing. Riots between Judeans and Samaritans lay at the root. Agrippa's sway won him a full acquittal there.

Loss of post did not end his sway in the town. Wealth poured in to him day by day. He seized the tithes owed to plain priests by force. That greed drew the hate of the Sicarii bands. At the revolt his palace was burned by the mob. He and his brother were killed in that storm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anspach-philipp:
Philippe Anspach, born at Metz in 1800, rose to honorary counselor of France's Court of Cassation and officer of the Legion of Honor. He died on December 3, 1875. Trained as a lawyer, he was practicing in Paris at the July revolution of 1830.

He took part in the events of that revolution and was made a deputy procurator under Louis Philippe. Post followed post until he sat in the highest court of France. The entry stresses that he was the first Jew in France's supreme magistracy. It also records his long service on Jewish consistories and his firm interest in Jewish affairs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-approbation-or-:
Approbation is a favorable opinion given by rabbis or scholars to recommend a book in Hebrew. The entry insists the practice is not Jewish in origin, any more than censorship is. Neither Bible, Talmud, nor medieval Jewish letters know of it, one quoted scholar argues.

No prophet sought leave to speak, and no medieval author had his work approved in advance, the entry says. Each book won the standing its own worth earned. Christian clergy, anxious over ideas reaching the crowd, created both approbation and censure, with forbidden books named as early as the fourth century. The coming of printing then turned the practice into a system, and Jewish books took it up in that printed world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristobulus-ii-:
Aristobulus II, king of Judea, was born about 100 B.C. and died in 49 B.C. Youngest son of Alexander Jannaeus, he shared his father's leanings and backed the Sadducees, while his elder brother Hyrcanus II held the lawful claim to the throne. When their mother died, Aristobulus beat his brother in war, and Hyrcanus gave up the royal title after a reign of three months.

Peace failed when Hyrcanus, pushed by Antipater, brought Aretas of Arabia against him. Both brothers then courted Rome, and Pompey used the quarrel to end Jewish independence. Jerusalem fell in 63, and Aristobulus marched in Pompey's triumph at Rome in 61. He escaped in 56 and raised revolt in Judea, was recaptured, and was freed by Caesar in 49, only to be poisoned on his way against Pompey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asa-abbreviatio:
Asa, third king of Judah, was a son of Abijam and grandson of Rehoboam. He reigned from 917 to 876 B.C. The great test of his reign came from Baasha, king of Israel, who built a fortress at Ramah, four miles from Jerusalem. To break the threat, Asa bought help from Ben-hadad I of Damascus with silver from the Temple and the palace, drawing Syria into Israel's affairs for the first time.

Ben-hadad struck northern Israel, Baasha pulled back, and Asa used Ramah's materials to fortify Geba and Mizpah. He also beat off a raid by Egyptians and Ethiopians under Zerah. Kings calls him a reformer who cut down impure worship without mercy. Yet the entry finds his picture vague and doubts his reforms lasted, since no trace of them shows in later reigns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atad-2069: Atad was a place on the eastern side of the Jordan. Jacob's funeral train stopped there and mourned for him, as Genesis l. 10 and 11 tell. The entry reports the tradition found in Genesis itself. That mourning, the tradition says, changed the name of the place to Abel Mizraim, meaning mourning of Egypt. The entry adds a plainer note on the word Abel. In itself, it points out, Abel signifies meadow, not mourning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avigdor-elim-d-:
Elim d'Avigdor was an engineer and communal worker. He died in London on Feb. 9, 1895. He was the eldest son of Count Salamon Henri d'Avigdor and Rachel Goldsmid. He studied at University College, London, and the University of London. He then trained under the engineer Hawkshaw.

In 1862 d'Avigdor went to Hull, then to Rangoon in Burma, on engineering work. He oversaw railway building in Syria and Transylvania and water-works in Vienna. His railway skill and his love of Palestine led him to contract for railway work in Syria. He headed the Chovevi Zion Association from 1891 and tied it to like bodies on the Continent. He also bought a newspaper, the "Examiner," and wrote hunting tales under the name Wanderer. He served as warden of the Spanish and Portuguese synagogue and sat on the council of the Anglo-Jewish Association from 1871 until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ba-aras-ba-arah:
Ba'aras is a place in the ravine above Macherus, on the northeastern shore of the Dead Sea. Josephus places the so-called Iron Mountains there. Hot springs rise at the spot, some sweet and some bitter, mixed with cold springs. One cave is famed in the entry. From one side of its overhanging rock a very cold spring flows, and from the other a very hot one.

The mixed bath drawn from those springs was used against many sicknesses. It was held to be strong for the nerves in particular. Sulphur and alum mines lie nearby. A Midrash tale told here has Jacob fleeing Esau to these waters and escaping through the cold springs. The place also gives its name to a plant, Ba'aras, the burning one. Its flame-like color flashes at night. Exorcists used the root, says Josephus, to drive demons out of the possessed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baiersdorf-2369:
Baiersdorf is a small Bavarian city near Erlangen, once a summer home of the margraves of Kulmbach-Bayreuth. A Jewish community stood there by the fourteenth century. It served as seat of the rabbinate for all Jews of the principality of Bayreuth. Its cemetery, shared by Jews for miles around, holds stones said to reach back to the start of the fifteenth century. A Jewish hospital is named as early as 1530.

The entry centers on Samson of Baiersdorf, a court Jew and community head. In 1712 he built a stately synagogue at his own cost. His son-in-law, Moses Hameln, kept the memoirs of Glückel von Hameln alive by having them copied. Later rabbis are named in turn. By the time of writing, emigration to the United States and to larger cities had cut about 100 families in 1834 to fewer than a dozen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-jesus-son-o:
Bar Jesus, "son of Jesu or Joshua," is a Jewish magician of Acts xiii. 6-11. There he is called a sorcerer and false prophet, found with Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul of Cyprus. He bore the title Elymas, that is, sorcerer. When Paul and Barnabas came, Bar Jesus fought Paul's attempt to convert the proconsul. Paul cursed him with a blindness for a time, and a mist and darkness fell on him at once.

The proconsul, seeing this, was converted. The entry then links Bar Jesus to Simon Magus, whom Josephus places in Cyprus as a friend of Felix. Critics of the New Testament, it reports, doubt the whole story, taking the Paul tale as a counterpart to the Peter tale in Acts viii. A note on the name closes it: the Syriac text, taking offense, reads "Bar Shuma" (Son of the Name) instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-of-benev:
Baruch of Benevento taught Cabala in Naples in the first half of the sixteenth century. He taught Cardinal Ægidius of Viterbo and Johann Albrecht Widmanstadt in the Zohar and other cabalistic works. He also lectured on these subjects in the house of Samuel Abravanel.

Widmanstadt left a note from 1541 calling Baruch the best cabalist. The note says Baruch first made the books of the Zohar known to Christians through the cardinal. Some scholars took that to mean Baruch translated the Zohar into Latin. Steinschneider argued it meant only that he made the Zohar known to Christian scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bauer-george-lo:
George Lorenz Bauer was a Christian writer on Old Testament theology, born at Hippolstein, Bavaria, on Aug. 14, 1755. He taught at Altdorf from 1789 and at Heidelberg from 1805, dying on Jan. 13, 1806. He backed the rational thought of his age with great energy.

Bauer published twenty-three volumes on Old Testament subjects alone. The entry calls them sound for their time but mostly compiled, with few new ideas. His lasting claim is the first theology of the Old Testament, issued without his name in 1796. His plan followed the program laid out by his Altdorf colleague Gabler in 1787. Three later books carried the same project into Hebrew myth, Bible morals, and a short summary of results.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behar-nissim-27:
Nissim Behar was a Palestinian educator born at Jerusalem in 1848. His father taught him Talmud from age five. Hard times drove the family to Constantinople in 1863, where a patron sent him to Paris to train as a teacher.

Backed by the Alliance, Behar opened schools at Aleppo in 1869 and in Bulgaria and Constantinople after. In 1882 he opened a technical school in Jerusalem and met fierce attacks from foes of new learning there. He led that school for fifteen years. From 1899 he traveled to win support for the Alliance. By the year 1902 he was living in the city of New York, the entry reports at its close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benveniste-hebr:
Benveniste is the name of an old, rich, and learned family of Narbonne. Its branches spread across Spain and Provence and to places in the East. The name is still borne by families in Bulgaria, Servia, and Vienna, and it was also used as a first name.

The long entry then treats member after member in turn. One Abraham Benveniste stands out as statesman and court rabbi of Castile under Juan II. In 1432 he became chief judge of the Jews there. He called a synod at Valladolid that set rules for the communities on worship, study, and taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berger-samuel-3: Samuel Berger, a French professor of Protestant theology, was born at Beaucourt on May 2, 1843. A brother of Philippe Berger, he heard lectures at the Sorbonne and studied theology at Strasburg. He served as secretary and librarian of the Protestant faculty at Paris. His books all touch the Bible in some way. They treat the Bible in the sixteenth century, old glossaries, the French Bible of the Middle Ages, and the history of the Vulgate, the last printed in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bertheau-ernest: Ernest Bertheau was a Biblical and Oriental scholar. He was born in Hamburg on November 23, 1812. He died in Göttingen on May 17, 1888. From 1843 he taught at the University of Göttingen. His subjects were Oriental languages and Biblical exegesis. He also taught Hebrew archeology and history. His first book appeared in 1840. It was "Die Sieben Gruppen Mosaischer Gesetze." He wrote commentaries on many Bible books. They include Judges, Ruth, and Proverbs. They also include Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther. He edited a Syriac grammar by Bar-Hebraeus as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blessing-and-cu:
Blessing and Cursing starts from the Hebrew verbs. "Berek" means to bless, and "berakah" a blessing. "Arar" means to curse. The entry notes a curious imbalance. Curse has many synonyms in Hebrew. Bless has only one word. Both powers rested on one belief. A speaker's tie to God could help or harm others.

A spoken blessing could not be recalled. Jacob's deceit rests on that premise. Balaam's feared curse rests on it too. Oaths and treaties drew strength from curses. Cursing parents drew severe punishment. Pure monotheism later softened the conception. A causeless curse, Proverbs says, will not land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bogolyubski-and:
Andrei Bogolyubski was the first grand duke of Russia, ruling from 1169 to 1174. He took Kiev in 1169 but made Vladimir his capital. Kiev then held many Jews who ran trade between western Europe and the Far East.

Bogolyubski cut back the old freedoms of the prince's militia. He showed foreign guests his church at Vladimir to draw them to baptism. The Kiev chronicle praises his conversion of Bulgars and Jews. Two converts close to him joined the plot that killed him. A servant's lament says Jews wept for him too. The entry also blames the cruelties of his favorite, Bishop Fiodor. Those acts, it says, cast a deep shadow over the whole reign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borek-3569: Borek is a town in the district of Koschmin, in Posen, Germany. While the Church ruled the city, Jews could not settle there. A Polish owner granted that right in the middle of the eighteenth century. By 1793, when Prussia took the town, 448 Jews lived there. They kept a synagogue and a cemetery. By 1902 only 150 Jews remained out of 2,000 people. Borek was the birthplace of Elias Guttmacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brunn-3769:
Brünn, capital of Moravia, held a Jewish community as early as the twelfth century. At Capistrano's urging, King Ladislaus expelled its Jews on July 27, 1451. Among the exiles was Israel Bruna, known for a set of responsa. Jews did not try to rebuild a community until the early nineteenth century.

Small steps followed: permission for a Torah scroll in 1811, a cemetery in 1852, and a synagogue in 1853. A provisional religious community won approval in 1859. The entry also describes the Moravian general fund, handed to Jewish management in 1869 and used for schooling. An orphan asylum and a proseminary stood in the city. By 1902 Brünn counted about 8,000 Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-byelaya-tzerkov:
Byelaya Tzerkov was a town in the government of Kiev, Russia. Its Jewish settlement likely formed after 1550, when a new castle drew settlers with privileges. One account lists its community among those destroyed by Chmielnicki's hordes in 1650. Another says 600 Jewish families were slain there, which shows a large community.

From 1651 to 1793 the town passed between Cossacks and Poles, and its Jewish numbers likely stayed small. Importance returned late in the eighteenth century, with about 12,000 Jews in a town of 20,700. A Hebrew printing office opened in 1817 and issued many books. By 1898 about 9,000 Jews lived there, most of them Hasidic, with a synagogue and seven prayer houses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canon-3969: Canon is defined in this very short entry as a rule for including certain books within a set degree of sanctity. The word canonical comes from that same rule, the entry notes. No list of books is given here, and no history of how any canon formed. For the full treatment, the entry sends the reader to the article on the Bible canon. Its whole content is the definition itself, stated in one sentence, plus that cross reference.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carpi-leone-406: Leone Carpi, an Italian political economist born at Bologna in 1820, was the first deputy Ferrara sent to the Italian Parliament. After his term he split his time between Bologna and Rome, writing for Popolo Romano. His books gather firsthand facts on the social state of the newly united Italy. Works from 1871 to 1887 treat Italian emigration, colonies abroad, and social studies of Italian life. One earlier work, from Florence in 1847, spoke on the Israelites after a papal decree of interdiction.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-censer-4169:
Censer is a bowl or pan used for burning incense. The English Bible uses the word for two Hebrew terms that seem to name different objects. One term occurs only three times and points to a Temple vessel for holy service. The other, maḥtah, occurs twenty-one times. It is also rendered fire-pan and snuff-dish.

The maḥtah served chiefly to gather ashes or carry live coals, not to burn incense. Incense was offered on the golden altar. On the Day of Atonement, though, the high priest filled a censer with coals, laid incense on them, and let the smoke cover the mercy seat. Temple pans were made of bronze, silver, and gold. Some were plain and open, others had raised rims. The Mishnah shows that several forms were in use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chaussy-4269: Chaussy is a district town in the government of Mohilev, in Russia. Its Jewish community dates from the seventeenth century. A charter of Jan. 11, 1667, granted rights to its Jews, and a king confirmed that charter on March 9, 1739. In 1780 the town held 355 Jews out of 1,057 people, with one synagogue. By 1897 the town held 2,775 Jews out of about 6,000 people. Some Jewish artisans worked in tanneries and in silk and woolen factories. The wider district held 7,444 Jews that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chronegk-ludwig:
Ludwig Chronegk, a German actor and stage director, was born at Brandenburg-on-the-Havel on Nov. 3, 1837, and died at Meiningen on July 8, 1890. With little schooling, he trained in Paris and Berlin and played young roles in several cities. In 1866 he joined the Meininger troupe, becoming its stage-director in 1872.

His fame rests on how he handled crowds. Instead of moving background players like puppets, he coached each one to act as a real person. The entry says this changed German stage methods for good. Critics first attacked him, then copied him. The cost, the entry adds, was weaker lead acting. In twenty-six years he staged 2,591 plays in thirty-six cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-elias-bet:
Elias Cohen, better known as Elias Pasha, was a Turkish physician born in 1844 into a family rich in doctors. Schooled at the Camondo community school in Constantinople, he entered the imperial medical school in 1861 and graduated six years later. He then studied in Berlin under Von Graefe and Virchow, and in Vienna during the Franco-Prussian war.

Home in 1873, he taught at the military school at Haidar-Pasha and served as eye surgeon at Monastir. Jealousy forced him out, yet a cure for an imperial princess won him the Sultan's favor. He rose to general, the first Turkish Jew to reach that rank, and became the Sultan's private physician. In 1885 he used that standing to halt a threatened massacre of Jews at Kadikeuy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coronel-nahman-:
Naḥman Nathan Coronel was a Palestinian scholar of Sephardic-Ashkenazic parentage. He was born at Amsterdam in 1810 and died at Jerusalem on Aug. 6, 1890. In 1830 he emigrated to Safed, then settled in Jerusalem and studied in the Sephardic yeshibah. His passion was rabbinical manuscripts. He gathered many rare copies, sold some to European libraries, and printed others with his own notes.

His editions came out in Vienna and Warsaw between 1854 and 1872. They include a varied version of Berakot, the liturgy of Amram Gaon, and responsa of the Geonim. Rules for slaughter and a traveler's selection of regulations also appear. The entry preserves the full list of his books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crispus-4769: Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue at Corinth. He became a Christian, with all his house, through the preaching of Paul. The entry cites Acts, chapter eighteen, verse 8, for that account. In a letter to the Corinth church, Paul names Crispus among those he had baptized. A later tradition adds more: Crispus became so weighty in the early Church that he was ordained Bishop of Ægina. The entry gives that tradition on the word of the Apostolic Constitutions, and adds nothing further about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dancing-4869:
Dancing is rhythmical stepping to music, singing, or drums. Among early peoples it expressed joy and belonged to worship or to war. The entry infers the same for the ancient Hebrews. Their Bedouin kin still keep wild dances of the kind. Hebrew words for dancing often mean playing or sporting. Another verb means to leap like lambs, which shows the motion was violent, not a smooth glide.

A round dance, turning on the heels in one spot, appears in Samuel. Processions with first-fruits reached the Temple in festive joy, the Mishnah recalls. Later sections grow more somber. Post-exilic Jews, the article suggests, lost some of that open joy in worship. Wedding dances, mourning bans, and rabbinic limits on dancing fill the closing survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-moses: Moses's son David was a Russian rabbi born in 1769 who died at Novogrudok, in the government of Minsk, in 1836. He became rabbi of that town in 1794 and held the post for forty-three years, until his death. He ranked among the leading Talmudists of Russia in his time. He was noted for his keenness in pilpul, the sharp give-and-take discussion of hard rabbinical questions. His book "Galya Massekta" appeared at Wilna in 1844, in two volumes of responsa, novellae, sermons, and commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delmedigo-judah: Elijah's son Judah Delmedigo was an Italian Talmudist born in Candia. He studied at Padua under Judah Minz, then went home, where his fame as a Talmud teacher drew many pupils, Samuel Algazi among them. He spent years in sharp dispute with Elijah Capsali, the aged historian who also kept a school at Candia. Their quarrels went before the leading authorities of the day, whose responsa still mention both men. Joseph Solomon Delmedigo, the philosopher, was Judah's great-grandson, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diaspora-the-pr:
Diaspora treats the Jews in their dispersion through the Greco-Roman world. This long article studies how the scattered communities lived among Greeks and Romans. It covers where they settled, the governments over them, their legal standing, their social and economic life, and their success in winning converts, which prepared the way for Christianity.

The dispersion spread Jews along the Mediterranean shores. Its roots lay in the blows that struck Judaism in its homeland, above all the fall of Judah in 588 B.C. and the deportation to Babylonia. Afterward the race had two centers, Babylonia and Palestine. Most of the wealthy stayed in Babylonia. The poorest and most fervent returned to rebuild around the Temple at Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-durlacher-elcan: Elcan Durlacher was a Hebraist and publisher born at Karlsruhe, Germany, in 1817. He died on Dec. 21, 1889. In 1845 he went to Paris as a teacher of languages. There he founded a Hebrew publishing-house, which his son kept going after him. He compiled a Hebrew reader and an almanac, and wrote a small book, Joseph and His Brothers. His chief works are French renderings of the German Mahzor and of the daily prayer-book, the first made with L. Wogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eibenschutz-dav:
David Solomon Eibenschütz was a Russian rabbi and author. He studied under Moses Zebi Heller, writer of Geon Zebi. He held rabbinates at Buzhanow, at Soroki in Volhynia, and at Jassy. From Jassy he moved to Palestine. He died at Safed in 1812.

Many of Eibenschütz's cabalistic and Talmudic works stayed in manuscript. His Lebushe Serad comments on the Shulhan Aruk in two parts. The first, printed at Mohilev in 1818, adds Ezekiel's plan of the Temple. The second part came out in 1812. His Ne'ot Deshe gathers 138 responsa, half of them printed at Lemberg in 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elhanan-ben-sam: Elhanan ben Samuel Ashkenazi was a rabbi born in 1713. He died on Sept. 27, 1780. At the age of eighteen he became rabbi of Fordon in Prussia. In 1752 he took the post of first rabbi at Schottland, near Danzig. He wrote many notes on the Talmud and on the four Turim. Most of that work was never printed. What did appear deals with the laws of Niddah and of immersion. His son Judah Lob brought those books out at Berlin in 1783.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-rabbenu-: Elijah Tishbi was a Karaite scholar of note. He died about the year 1584. In 1579 he wrote a work called Pe'er at Constantinople. It is a super-commentary, a gloss on a gloss. Its base is the Bible commentary of Aaron ben Joseph. Only the first part of that base work is covered. His son-in-law revised the book in 1585 after his death. Copies rest in libraries at Leyden and at Oxford.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ennery-adolphe-: Adolphe d'Ennery was a French writer for the stage. He was born in Paris on June 17, 1811. He died in that city on Jan. 26, 1899. He tried clerk's work, painting, and news work in youth. In 1831 he made his start as a playwright. From then he wrote plays at a furious pace. His full count tops 280 plays in all. At one time five of them ran in Paris at once. He shaped each work to the taste of the crowd. Hit after hit made him a rich man in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-etoile-old-fren:
Etoile, in old French Estoile or Estelle, was a town in the old province of Dauphine, France. The entry warns against mixing it with Estella in Spain. In the fourteenth century, Jews living in Dijon had come from Estoile. In the sixteenth century, Jews from Estelle moved on to Carpentras.

Its scholars fill the rest of the entry. Abba Mari ben Joseph and his son Judah copied part of Alfasi's Halakot at Moras in 1333. Meiuml Kokabi wrote a Pentateuch commentary in 1313, and Samuel Kokabi wrote on the calendar about 1402. David ben Samuel of Estelle sat on the rabbinical college of Avignon in 1305. Jacob ben Moses of Bagnols wrote on ethics about 1357-61.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-felix-ludwig-60: Ludwig Felix was an Austrian economist born at Horitz, Bohemia, on February 22, 1830. He heard lectures on commerce at Vienna and turned to history and economics. His books are listed with no comment. They include The Workers and Society in 1874 and a six-volume history of property. They also include currency studies from 1890 and a critique of socialism in 1893. The entry gives no posts, teachers, or death date for him. Four titles and a birth record make up the whole notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flavia-domitill:
Flavia Domitilla was a Roman convert to Judaism and a martyr, the entry holds. She was a granddaughter of the emperor Vespasian. She married Titus Flavius Clemens, a cousin of the emperors Titus and Domitian. Clemens became consul. The couple leaned toward the faith their world called an Oriental superstition. Dion Cassius says Domitian had Clemens executed. Both had been charged with atheism, a charge laid on many who followed Jewish customs and laws.

Domitilla herself was only banished, to the island of Pandataria. Rabbinic writings seem to recall the same senator under a pictured name. It means circumcised and son of the world to come. Eusebius, though, tells of a Domitilla sent to Pontia and counts the pair as Christians. The entry suggests Eusebius must mean some other Domitilla. The Domitilla chapel in the Roman catacombs is laid out on a Jewish pattern.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franchi-gugliel: Guglielmo dei Franchi was a Jewish convert to Christianity born at Rome. He died there about 1600. On embracing Christianity he joined the monastic order of Vallombrosa. He gave himself to spreading knowledge of Hebrew among Christians. In 1596 he published a Hebrew alphabet at Rome. It gives the rules for reading Hebrew. Three years later his short Hebrew grammar came out at Bergamo. Its title means Sun of the Holy Tongue. Three short source lines close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franco-10669:
Franco is a Jewish family that took its name from a place near Navarre in Spain. Francos lived at Amsterdam, Venice, Tunis, Constantinople, and many other cities. Family tradition makes the Francos of Constantinople the seed of two Prague brothers who settled there in 1780. The entry then works through the members. David Franco Mendes of Amsterdam was a Hebrew poet of high rank. He stood next to Luzzatto and Wessely among the new Hebrew poets, it says.

David wrote a history drama in 1770 and turned a work of Metastasio into Hebrew. Moses Franco, born at Constantinople in 1864, served the Alliance as a schoolmaster in the East. He founded the Jewish schools at Safed and wrote a history of the Jews of the Ottoman empire. It was printed at Paris in 1897. Other members were a chief rabbi of Hebron and a Constantinople printer. Solomon's press there lasted nearly fifty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedland-moses:
Moses Aryeh Löb Friedland was a Russian giver of good works. He was born at Dünaburg on January 8, 1826, and died at St. Petersburg on November 21, 1899. For more than thirty years he held the army contracts of the Russian government. He was an honorary citizen of St. Petersburg and won several medals from the state. He founded an orphan home with a craft school at St. Petersburg. He also founded a home for aged Jews at Jerusalem.

His name is chiefly tied to a great Hebrew library. In 1890 he gave it to the Asiatic Museum of the Imperial Academy. It holds three hundred books in handwriting, most on skin, and more than ten thousand printed books. Together they make some 14,000 works, many of them from the dawn of printing. A list of the books was being printed at his cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gemara-niggun-6: Gemara Niggun is defined in the entry in a single sentence as the chant used by students in reading the Talmud. The hosted text gives no history of the chant. It gives no notes, examples, or account of how the chant varies by place or school. For more, the entry sends readers to the headword Cantillation. So this record fixes the term and its meaning, and leaves the fuller treatment of chant to that linked topic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldstein-eduar: Eduard Goldstein was a Russian musician. He was born at Odessa in 1851. He died at Leipsic on Aug. 8, 1887. At thirteen he already played the piano with skill. A post at Kishinef's Italian opera-house followed. In 1868 the Leipsic Conservatorium took him in. He studied under Moscheles and Reinecke and graduated with honors in 1872. Tours through Germany went well. He later led orchestras at Odessa and directed opera at Kharkof. In 1886 Anton Rubinstein made him professor at St. Petersburg. His opera "Count Essex" stayed unfinished at his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haarbleicher-mo:
Moses M. Haarbleicher, born in Hamburg on Nov. 14, 1797, was a German author who died there on Sept. 25, 1869. His father founded the Jewish School of Hamburg. Haarbleicher took an early interest in Jewish affairs and helped establish the Tempelverein. He also helped revise its prayer-book.

In 1823 Haarbleicher founded a society to promote useful trades among Jews, and he directed it until 1840. That year he became secretary of the Hamburg congregation. He knew Romance and Germanic languages deeply and wrote Hebrew with ease. Forty of his songs and poems entered the congregation's hymn-book. His history of Hamburg's German-Jewish congregation appeared in part in 1866 but stayed unfinished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanan-hanin-han:
Ḥanan was a scholar of the third amoraic generation, likely Babylonian by birth and a late pupil of Rab. In Rab's name he reports both laws and lore. He is found in Babylonia with Anan, and often in Palestine, where he debated the top scholars of his day: Ela, Hoshaiah II, and Levi.

His teachings cut deep. Whoever calls down God's payback on a neighbor suffers first, he taught, as Sarah did after asking God to judge between her and Abraham. Egypt's slavery was payback for the sale of Joseph. Ḥanan wed into the patriarch's family and waited years for a child. When a son came at last, Ḥanan died, and the funeral elegy mourned joy turned to wailing at the first caress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harris-mark-726:
Mark Harris, born March 15, 1869, was an English surveyor and soldier who worked in South Africa. His father headed the Jews' School at Manchester. Mark trained as an architect and surveyor, then served as borough surveyor at Port Elizabeth. He also rose from the ranks to become a lieutenant in a volunteer unit.

In 1896 he worked in the public works office at Port Elizabeth. The next year his column of about 1,000 men marched into Bechuanaland. Fighting ran from March into April 1897. Harris was killed in action on April 6, 1897, at the taking of Mamssepe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-elijah-i: Elijah ibn Hayyim, born about 1532, was a rabbi of Constantinople. He may have followed Elijah Mizrahi directly in that post. His answers to legal questions carry dates from 1562 to 1601. He died early in the seventeenth century, past the age of seventy. Only part of his writing survives. It includes two sets of answers and sermons on the Pentateuch. His only son Michael was a noted scholar who died at twenty. Michael added material to his father's last book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hecht-emanuel-7:
Emanuel Hecht, born in Bavaria in 1821, was a German teacher of Jewish youth. He trained at Wurzburg and taught in small towns in Lower Franconia. In 1845 David Einhorn called him to Hoppstädten as a schoolteacher. There he became the heart of a fight for equal standing.

In 1856 Hecht won state recognition for Jewish communal schools in Birkenfeld, on par with Christian schools. Jewish teachers gained the same footing as Christian colleagues. A charge that he had reviled the state religion ended in full acquittal. His many textbooks cover Bible history, Hebrew reading, and religion. He died on Feb. 25, 1862.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henriques-rober: Robert Martin Henriques, born in Copenhagen on Dec. 14, 1858, was a Danish musician, composer, and author. Trained on the violoncello, he studied at Dresden from 1877. He performed in Berlin, Leipsic, Hanover, Dresden, and Paris. His works include pieces for cello, piano, and orchestra, plus songs. His overture named for Olaf Tryggvason was played in three capitals. With Oscar Madsen he also wrote novels of local color. He worked as a music critic for Copenhagen papers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezekiah-gaon-7:
Hezekiah Gaon was principal of the academy at Pumbedita from 1038 to 1040. A member of an exilarchal family, he was chosen after Hai Gaon was murdered. He was then denounced to the government. He was jailed and tortured to death.

With Hezekiah his family ended, save for two sons who escaped to Spain. They found a home there with Joseph b. Samuel ha-Nagid. His death also ended the line of the Geonim, begun four centuries earlier, the entry says. The Academy of Pumbedita ended with it as well, closing that long era.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hisda-7769:
Ḥisda was a Babylonian amora of the third generation who died at ninety-two, the entry reports. Descended from a priestly family, he studied under Rab, his main teacher. After Rab died he learned with Huna, his peer. The two were called the pious men of Babylon.

Poor at first, Ḥisda grew rich as a brewer. A sharp question from him split his bond with Huna for forty years before they made peace. Yet he never ruled while Huna lived. He later led the Sura academy for ten years. His laws fill the Babylonian Talmud, and his moral sayings were kept for students. A legend ties his death to ceasing study for a moment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horns-of-moses-: Horns of Moses names a famous mistake in art. Old painters and sculptors often showed Moses with two horns on his forehead as he came down from Mount Sinai. The entry traces the error to one verse in Exodus. The Hebrew word there means that his face shone. Most old translations kept that sense. Aquila and the Vulgate alone read that his face had horns. Horned gods in Babylon and Egypt may have helped the wrong reading spread.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iliowizi-henry-:
Henry Iliowizi was an American rabbi and author born in the Minsk government of Russia on January 2, 1850. His father was a Hasid. He studied at home schools, at Frankfort, Berlin, Breslau, London, and Paris. At fourteen he was sent to Jassy to dodge conscription, and he left for Frankfort in 1865.

He taught for school groups tied to Anglo-Jewry and the Alliance. From 1877 to 1880 he taught at Tetuan in Morocco. In 1880 he crossed to New York. He served congregations at Minneapolis from 1880 to 1888 and at Philadelphia from 1888 to 1900. After 1900 he gave himself to writing. His books run from an epic poem and tragedies to tales of Russian Jews in the Pale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-people-o:
The People of Israel article is a long survey of the people's origins and early history. In the Bible, it says, Israel is the national name of the people known racially as Hebrews. The tale in Genesis of Jacob's name changed to Israel mirrors, in part, the real union of the tribes and their win over the Canaanites. The article calls Israel a composite people from the start.

On origins it weighs two traditions together. A Babylonian root is likely: Abram came from Ur of the Chaldees, and the Hebrews shared Babylon's oldest stories, such as Creation and the Flood. Yet the nearer tradition makes Israel Aramean at base. Emigrants from the lower Euphrates reached Charran, then spread east and west of the Jordan. The survey moves on through tribal days, the Philistine pressure, and Samuel's turn to kingship under Saul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jabez-8369:
Jabez is the eponym of a clan of the Kenite family of the Rechabites, later merged into the tribe of Judah. Chronicles speaks of families of scribes who lived at Jabez. In another passage Jabez himself is more honorable than his brothers. His name comes from his mother's word: I bore him with sorrow. His prayer asked God to bless him, widen his border, and keep grief from him, and God granted the request.

After the Exile, Jabez stood out among the Kenite clans that took up Judaism and became scribes and teachers of the Law. Rabbinical tradition makes him Othniel the Kenezite, head of the house of study after Moses died. On that reading, his prayer asked for disciples, not land. The Kenites and Rechabites, the Mekilta says, left their homes near Jericho to learn Torah from him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobi-heinrich: Heinrich Otto Jacobi was a German philologist born at Tütz, in West Prussia, in 1815, who died in Berlin in 1864. He studied at Berlin University. Königsberg gave him an honorary doctorate in 1854 for his deep knowledge of Greek. He taught at Berlin's Joachimsthal Gymnasium from 1854 to 1858, then at the Friedrich Wilhelm Gymnasium in Posen, where he became professor in 1860. He became a Protestant. His chief work is the "Index Graecitatis" to Meineke's edition of the Greek comic fragments (Berlin, 1847).
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehovah-jireh-y: Jehovah-jireh is the name Abraham gave to the place where he offered a ram in place of his son Isaac, as Genesis tells it. The brief entry gives that fact and then two notes on the name. Commentators link the name either to Abraham's words just before, in Genesis, or to the later importance of the spot, where Solomon's Temple would stand. The entry also records that the Targumim, the old Aramaic versions, do not treat Jehovah-jireh as a proper name at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-world-th:
Jewish World was the fourth Jewish newspaper printed in London. Its first number came out on Feb. 14, 1873. George Lewis Lyon owned and ran it until 1897, and Myer D. Davis was its first editor. A string of editors followed, among them Lucien Wolf. In September 1897 new owners took over and the editorship changed again.

For its first years the paper attacked Christian doctrine with a sharp pen, a course that brought it into print dealings with Gladstone. It sent a man to Russia after riots at Balta and backed the cause of Russian and Rumanian Jews. Until 1897 it stood for Orthodox Judaism, and from 1892 to 1900 it backed the Zionist idea in some form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-ben-ho:
Jonathan ben Horkinas was a Palestinian scholar of the first century and a pupil of the school of Shammai. His sharpness won him a nickname that means first-born of the adversary, a fierce debater. Though the school of Hillel set the standard in law, Jonathan won a point for Shammai's rule. He talked some rabbis into allowing a certain marriage with a brother's widow.

When wise men came to test his claim, his brother Dosa warned him by letter. Jonathan laid out his case, said to rest on three hundred arguments. His hearers could not follow it. Losing patience, he threw clods of earth at them and drove them out by three doors. He then wrote home that the visitors needed more learning than he did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-b-moses-: Joseph b. Moses Phinehas, surnamed ha-Zaddik, was a Polish rabbi born in 1726 who died at Posen in 1801. He was a man of wealth, influence, and great piety. His father-in-law was Ezekiel Landau of Prague, who often cites him in Noda bi-Yehudah. Joseph served in turn as rabbi of Yaworow, Sokoli, and Posen. He wrote Zikron Sheerit Yosef, notes on the Babylonian Talmud, printed at Kolomea in 1881. His brother Samuel followed him as rabbi of Posen and died there in 1806.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-b-ammi-89: Judah b. Ammi was a Palestinian amora of the third generation, in the fourth century. He was perhaps a son of the famed R. Ammi. His house was a meeting place for scholars. R. Ze'era, worn out by study, would sit at Judah's doorway so he could rise in honor as the rabbis passed in and out. Judah passed on a number of legal rulings in the name of Simeon b. Lakish. The entry is brief and rests on Heilprin and on Bacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kleeberg-clotil: Clotilde Kleeberg was a pianist. She was born at Paris on June 27, 1866, of German parents. She studied at the Conservatoire under Retz and Massart. At the age of eleven she won a medal and the highest honors there. The following year she made her début at the "Concerts Populaires." Tours through Denmark, Russia, Austria, and Holland followed in 1881. In 1883 she appeared in London and soon became a favorite. Her repertoire runs from Bach to Liszt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-koreff-solomon-:
Solomon Koreff, a German Talmudist born about 1700, died in Prague on May 24, 1774. For more than forty years he led a large yeshibah in Prague. His signature stands on the record naming Ezekiel Landau chief rabbi in 1754, though Koreff was said to oppose the choice.

Expulsion gives the entry its sharpest scene. When Maria Theresa ordered the Jews out of Prague on Dec. 18, 1744, Koreff spoke for the protest deputation. Rebuked for raising his voice, he answered that ten thousand souls cried from within him. After the return in 1748 he became one of four elders of the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-labatt-abraham-: Abraham Cohen Labatt, an American pioneer born at Charleston, South Carolina, in 1802, died at Galveston, Texas, on Aug. 16, 1899. He helped organize the Reform congregation in Charleston in 1825. In 1831 he moved to New Orleans and helped found the first Jewish congregation in Louisiana. Texas trips came in 1831 and 1837 on an early trading steamship. In 1849 he went to California and helped found the San Francisco synagogue. He also gained leave for the first regular Masonic lodge in California that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lauterbach-seli: Selig Lauterbach, a Galician writer born at Drohobicz on Jan. 25, 1826, works in business in his home town. His books run to two volumes dated 1882: the first treats proper names in the Old Testament, the second the Jewish settlement of the Holy Land. Notes on Talmud, Midrash, and Bible form another work. A book on magic and sorcery in Talmud and Midrash came out at Vienna in 1871. He also writes for many periodicals, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-aaron-9869:
Aaron Levy, a patriot of the Revolution, was born in Amsterdam in 1742. He died at Philadelphia on Feb. 23, 1815. He came to America young and settled in Pennsylvania. He traded with the Indians and supplied the colonial army in the war. He also dealt in land on a huge scale.

Levy lent large sums to the Continental Congress to carry on the war. The money was never fully repaid. With Robert Morris he shared many land deals. In 1779 he bought a large tract in Center county and laid out Aaronsburg on it. The entry calls it the first town in the United States planned by a Jew and named for one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-aryeh-ben-z: Aryeh ben Zachariah Löb, also called Hocher R. Löb, was a Polish rabbi born at Cracow about 1620, and he died there in 1671. As a young man he was called to serve as rabbi at Vienna for a few years. He then moved to Przemysl, Galicia. In 1665 he became rabbi in his home town and stayed there until his death. He wrote Tikkune Teshubah, a moral work in Judaeo-German, printed at Cracow in 1666.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubliner-hugo-p:
Hugo Lubliner (1846– ), who wrote under the name Hugo Bürger, was a German dramatist born at Breslau. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar profiles him. He studied at Berlin’s industrial school and managed a cotton and woolen mill. Playwriting drew him from business, first as a sideline, then full time.

The article lists dozens of his plays from 1865 to 1899, mostly comedies for German theaters. Successes include the one-act “Nur Nicht Romantisch,” which still held the stage, and “Der Frauenadvokat” of 1873, performed at all the principal German theaters. Later titles include tragedies, dramas, and two novels in a cycle on Berlin under the empire. Four volumes of his dramatic works appeared at Berlin in 1881–82. The entry works as a full play list for a popular stage writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manissa-the-anc:
Manissa, the ancient Magnesia ad Sipylum in Turkey, is given a community entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The town stands twenty-eight miles northeast of Smyrna. Of its forty thousand people, some 1,800 were Jews. The community is said to be older than Smyrna's own.

The article draws on travelers' reports and local detail. Pococke, visiting about 1733, found its Jews rich exporters and calico makers. Tournefort counted three synagogues in 1702; by 1904 there were five. Their names include Shalom, Mayorca, and Toledo, a map of the community's roots. Charities dowried brides, aided mourning families, and shod the poor. A small hospital opened in 1869. Alliance schools for boys and girls arrived in the 1890s, teaching Hebrew, French, and Turkish. The entry records a complete Ottoman Jewish community at the moment modern schooling reached it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheimer-magy:
Gustav Mannheimer, called Magyar, a Hungarian painter, gets a very short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Budapest on February 27, 1854, he trained at drawing schools in four cities. Budapest came first, then Munich, Vienna, and Rome. The entry names no teachers and gives no account of his later career.

What the article does give is a short list of his best-known canvases. On Flowery Mead and Italian Evening Landscape show his landscape work. Procession at Anacapri points to time spent painting in Italy. Young Tramps turns to figure subjects instead. The notice rests on a single source, Singer's general artists' lexicon. For a period reference, the entry still has value. It fixes a painter's training and chief works in a few lines, keeping a minor artist from vanishing altogether.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masseket-or-mas:
"Masseket," the word for a tractate of the Talmud, is defined in a short Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and S. Mendelsohn. The term literally means "a web," from a Hebrew verb for weaving, much like the Latin "textus" behind the English word text. In practice it names any gathered collection of rabbinic teaching on a subject, whether a treatise of the Mishnah alone, a set of baraitot, or Mishnah together with its Gemara.

The article then does the counting. The Mishnah holds sixty-three tractates, though ancient authorities said sixty, because they reckoned the three Babas as one tractate and Sanhedrin with Makkot as one. The Babylonian Gemara covers thirty-seven tractates and the Palestinian thirty-nine. It ends with the so-called minor tractates printed with the Babylonian Talmud, seven of which Kirchheim edited in 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-eliaki:
Meir ben Eliakim was a German liturgist who probably lived at Posen toward the end of the seventeenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His known work is “Meir Elohim,” printed without place or date. It gathers the biblical passages a worshiper should recite on entering the synagogue. It adds ethical directions for prayer, instructions on how to pray as much as what to say.

In that book Meir mentions two further collections of prayers he called “Menorot,” lamps. Steinschneider, whose catalogue is the only authority of the entry, thought a “Menorah” printed at Prague in 1696 might be one of them. The whole notice is three facts deep. Yet it fixes a name, a probable city, and a shelf of devotional books. Without it they would be anonymous.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meza-christian-:
Christian Jacob Theophilus de Meza was a Danish physician and author born in Copenhagen on November 26, 1756. Richard Gottheil and Frank Cramer profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of the physician Christian de Meza. Father and son embraced Christianity together in 1783. That same year he took his medical degree at Copenhagen.

From 1784 until his death in 1844, Meza practiced medicine at Elsinore. He published essays in the medical journals on mixed pregnancy, an epidemic fever, and a rare abnormal twin birth. One paper was reprinted in French and American journals. He also wrote a drama staged at Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1796. His son Christian Julius became a Danish general in the 1864 war with Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miracle-lit-won:
Miracle, defined as an event no ordinary natural agency can explain and therefore an act of a higher power, opens a theological Jewish Encyclopedia article by Kaufmann Kohler, published in 1906. Kohler's first move is a distinction: a miracle is not a myth. Myths personify nature's powers as gods; miracles subject all nature to one higher will working out holier designs.

Miracle is thus, for Kohler, essentially monotheistic, even where an old myth has been recast as a prophet's or saint's wonder. In the Bible the category is broad: whatever breaks the ordinary course counts as a wonder, preeminently the wonders in Egypt by which God's power was made known. He alone does wonders, the psalmists say, and nothing is too wonderful for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montpellier-heb:
Montpellier, capital of the Hérault in Languedoc, held one of southern France's most important Jewish communities from the later eleventh century, as Isidore Singer and S. Kahn write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews, trading with coreligionists worldwide, built much of the city's commerce. In Hebrew letters the town was simply Har, the Mountain.

Their second gift was medicine: Montpellier's famous medical school grew with Jewish help, and in 1180 Guillem VIII granted Jews the right to practise. Aragonese kings later required them to pass the regular examinations like everyone else — a proviso that tells how far they had risen. The article traces their standing as physicians on into the year 1300.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-cordovero:
Moses Cordovero was a physician who lived at Leghorn in the seventeenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and Meyer Kayserling, rests chiefly on the praise of Conforte. Conforte calls him a good physician and praises his scholarship and his giving.

One habit of his is singled out. Cordovero was always eager to free prisoners, working through his own influence where he could and paying ransom where he could not. He died at an advanced age. The brief notice keeps the name of a doctor remembered as much for charity as for medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosessohn-marke:
Miriam Mosessohn, born Wiersbolowsky, was a Russian Hebrew writer born at Kovno in 1841. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote her Jewish Encyclopedia entry. At thirteen she moved with her parents to Suwalki, where she kept up her Hebrew studies. She also devoted herself to German and French language and literature.

Mosessohn translated German novels into Hebrew, starting with Philippson's The Refugee from Jerusalem, which stayed in manuscript. Family troubles kept her from giving herself fully to the work. Only one book of hers reached print: Ha-Yehudim be-Angliya, printed at Warsaw in 1869. It is a Hebrew version, in pure and elegant style, of Francolm's work on the Jews and the Crusaders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagawkar-benjam:
Benjamin Shalom Nagawkar was a Beni-Israel soldier born at Bombay before 1830. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He enlisted in the Twenty-fifth Regiment of Bombay Native Light Infantry in 1848. He rose step by step to subahdar-major in 1879.

The entry is a service record, battle by battle. Nagawkar fought at Dhar, Jhansi, the Betwa, Calpee, and the capture of Gwalior, winning medal and clasp. He served through the Abyssinian campaign as well and took its service medal. He retired in 1881, a senior Indian officer of the Bombay army.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-moses-b-:
Moses b. Solomon b. Nathanael was a Provençal writer of verse for worship. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His dates and birthplace are not known. Even his homeland is given only as Provence. What survives of him is his poetry. One poem is didactic, teaching through verse.

His teaching poem is called Toze'ot Hayyim, or Results of Life. It runs to fifty-eight sections in all. Menahem di Lonzano printed it in Shete Yadot at Venice in 1618. Dukes later reprinted part of it in 1844. Moses is also thought to have written a Sabbath hymn. That hymn, Ahabah be-Ta'anugim, appears in most prayer-books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-carl-fr:
Carl Friedrich Neumann was a German scholar of the East. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Reichmansdorf on Dec. 22, 1798. His parents bore the name Bamberger. He died in Berlin on March 17, 1870.

Neumann began in business, then studied at Heidelberg and Munich. He taught at Speyer, but religious words cost him his post. He learned Armenian at Venice and Chinese in Paris and London. In China in 1830 he gathered ten thousand books. Munich made him keeper and professor of Chinese. Progressive views cost him that post in 1852. His works span Armenia, China, Russia, and America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-no-amon-11569:
No-Amon is the Bible's name for Egyptian Thebes. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name means No, city of the god Amon. Nahum and Jeremiah both use it of Thebes. Egyptian speech made it the city above all.

Thebes stood at the center of Nile traffic. Ethiopia's trade passed through it as an emporium. It first headed the fourth nome of Upper Egypt. The eleventh dynasty took its seat there early. After the Hyksos fell, it stayed the capital. Thothmes and Rameses raised Karnak and Luxor there. Assurbanipal's captures hastened its long decline afterward. By Ptolemaic days it was Egypt's great ruined city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-offenbach-jacqu:
Jacques Offenbach made French comic opera a form of its own. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Cologne on June 21, 1819. He died at Paris on October 5, 1880. His father was cantor of the Jewish flock at Cologne.

Offenbach went to Paris at the age of thirteen. He read the cello at the music school there. He then played in the band of the Opéra Comique. Tours as a solo player brought him little fame. So he turned to the stage and to song. In 1855 he opened a house of his own. It was the Bouffes Parisiennes, in the Passage Choiseul. Many of his best loved works were first sung there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orleans-or-1176:
Orleans is the chief city of Loiret, in France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish group dates from the sixth century. Church councils met in the city in that age. Those councils set harsh laws against the Jews there.

In 533 a council barred wedlock of Jews and Christians. A Christian who broke that rule faced casting out. In 538 Jews were barred from the streets at Easter time. Clerks were told not to eat with Jews at all. In 541 a new set of rules came down. A Jew who made a convert lost all his slaves. King Gontran came to Orleans in the year 585. Jews in the crowd hailed him with a Hebrew speech. He met their words with scorn, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pe-ah-corner-or:
Pe'ah is a treatise of the Mishnah about gifts to the poor. Its name means corner, the corner of the field. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The treatise stands second in the order Zera'im.

The laws rest on verses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. A farmer must leave the field's corner for the poor. The treatise runs eight chapters with many fine points. It defines which fields count as one field. It sets the time and manner of giving. It also lists good deeds that earn reward in this world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peter-of-alessa:
Peter of Alessandria was an Italian monk of the fourteenth century. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Alessandria, in Italy. His fame rests on two Latin translations. He worked daily between the Hebrew and Latin worlds.

About 1342 Pope Clement the Sixth asked for his work. Peter rendered Levi ben Gershon's treatise into Latin. The treatise described Gersonides' new star-measuring tool. That tool later bore on the finding of America. Peter also translated Gersonides' forecast on Saturn and Jupiter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinkhof-herman-:
Herman Pinkhof was a Dutch physician based in Amsterdam. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Rotterdam on May 10, 1863. He took his degree at Leyden in 1886. His practice served Amsterdam for many years.

Pinkhof wrote on medical ethics for a Dutch journal. In 1895 he founded a society for Judaism's interests. From 1898 he led the fight against Neo-Malthusian teaching. He argued that cause in many printed articles. He also served on the seminary board at Amsterdam. His learning joined medicine, ethics, and Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontremoli-esdr: Esdra Pontremoli was an Italian rabbi, poet, and teacher born at Ivrea in 1818. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Eliseo Pontremoli, rabbi of Nizza. A street in that town later bore his father's name. In 1844 Esdra became professor of Hebrew at Vercelli. For fifteen years he helped edit the Educatore Israelita. He turned a Hebrew work of Luzzatto into Italian verse. That poem came out at Padua in 1879. He died in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priority-12369:
Priority in Jewish law means whose claim on goods comes first. The Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Part of the rules deal with deeds and bonds on land. Those rules are told in another article of the set. What is left is the case of a wife's claim.

A widow or a parted wife claims her marriage sum first. Plain creditors of the husband claim the same goods too. The Talmud gives its rules in Mishnah and Gemara. The husband's marriage writ binds him to pay back her dowry. That writ is the root of the wife's strong claim. The article works out who is paid first, and why.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raba-b-joseph-b:
Raba ben Joseph ben Hama was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Mahoza in about the year 280. His father was a rich and noted scholar there. Raba died at Mahoza in the year 352.

As a youth Raba went to Sura for his learning. He heard the lectures of Hisda in that town. He kept company with Rami ben Hama as well. Years after Rami's death, Raba wed his widow. She was a daughter of Hisda, his old teacher. The entry traces his teachers and his ties of blood and marriage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-portrapa-s:
Simhah ben Gershom ha-Kohen Rapa was a Talmudic scholar born at Porto, Italy. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a younger cousin of Menahem Abraham Rapa. He later called himself Portrapa.

The article says Simhah studied at Venice in his cousin's house. His teacher was Samuel Judah Katzenellenbogen, rabbi of Venice. In 1593 he settled at Prossnitz in Moravia. He then moved to Vienna and stayed until his death. His one named work is Kol Simhah, from 1602. It is a hymn acrostic for Saturday. The entry follows a scholar across Italy and central Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reland-adrian-1:
Adrian Reland was a Dutch Christian Hebraist born on July 17, 1676. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ryp near Alkmaar. He died at Utrecht on February 5, 1718.

The article says he studied Hebrew and rabbinics at Amsterdam. In 1699 he took the chair of Oriental languages at Utrecht. His works include Analecta Rabbinica from 1702. He wrote on ancient Hebrew coins as well. His Sacred Antiquities went through five editions. His Palestine, from 1714, carried eleven maps. Both books long stood as standard authorities, they say. The entry honors a Christian scholar of Hebrew antiquity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riparian-owners:
Riparian owners are landowners along a river bank. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Holy Land had little river navigation. So the Mishnah says little about bank owners' rights.

The article finds one rule about irrigation for peace. Upper owners may draw canal water before lower owners. On the Euphrates, river traffic was heavy, they note. Men walked the shore dragging boats by long ropes. Rabbis ordered all trees cut along both banks. That cleared room for the boatmen's shoulders at the ropes. Trees fell with or without the owner's consent. No notice to the owner was even required. The entry shows public need trimming private rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-jacob:
Jacob Rosenthal was a Polish physician at Warsaw, a son of David Rosenthal. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied medicine at Berlin and at Warsaw, his home city.

In 1870 Rosenthal joined the Jewish Hospital at Warsaw as a staff physician. He gave himself to the diseases of women, then a growing field. Through his efforts a women's section opened at the hospital in 1894. He directed that department for more than a decade afterward. He also described the hospital in print and wrote a medical handbook for women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sammter-asher-1:
Asher Sammter was a German rabbi born at Derenburg on January 1, 1807. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. From 1837 to 1854 he served as rabbi and preacher in Liegnitz.

At Liegnitz Sammter introduced German preaching and the confirmation ceremony to his congregation. From 1869 he lived in Berlin, writing to the end of his life. He published the Babylonian Talmud's Baba Mezia with German translation and notes. His Mishnayyot gave all six Mishnah orders in Hebrew with German renderings.
