Using a standard line of auditory cells, the team applied the compound at several strengths and times, recording the cells' electrical state and their energy-making activity. The compound pushed the cells' resting voltage upward in a dose- and time-dependent way, a shift that can trigger ion channels and upset the cells' salt balance. Energy activity also changed with dose, though not further between one and two days, hinting that repair efforts switch on alongside damage. The authors urge implant makers to weigh corrosion products, not just device electronics.
plos-pone-0354469:
Kambiré and colleagues, in a 2026 study, purify and profile an enzyme from the gut juice of palm weevil larvae, a notorious pest of palm trees. The enzyme, beta-galactosidase, breaks down milk sugar and related compounds and is prized in food and drug making. Insect guts are a little-explored source of hardy enzymes.

Using a yellow test substrate, the team measured the enzyme's sweet spots: a warm temperature just above human body heat, by their modeling, and mildly acidic conditions. They estimated the energy the reaction needs and identified the likely acid and base players in its active site from how activity changed with acidity. Speed measures placed it in a useful working range. The authors conclude that this pest's digestion hides a capable industrial enzyme, and that insect guts deserve a place in the search for new biocatalysts.
plos-pone-0354669:
Shuang Li and co-authors built a deep learning model that predicts how strongly a cancer cell line will respond to a drug. The response measure halves cell survival, and computing it well could cut costly screening. Older models ignore either the drug's three-dimensional chemistry or the cell's biological state. Their 2026 design feeds both through separate branches.

One branch reads the drug as a molecular graph through a graph isomorphism network. The other reads fifty pathway activity scores computed from the cell line's gene expression. Training used a major public pharmacogenomics collection spanning many cancer types. Li and colleagues argue joining structure with pathway context should generalise better across data sources than either input alone.
plos-pone-0354969:
Emile Nkurunziza and Robert Kogi published this 2026 case-control study of cholera in Rumonge Health District, southern Burundi. The district suffers repeat outbreaks despite control campaigns. Comparing fifty households where someone fell ill with twice as many nearby healthy households, they asked families about water, food, and washing habits.

Taking drinking water from lakes or rivers, using it untreated at home, and eating unwashed raw fruit all raised the risk sharply. Poor handwashing after using the toilet mattered too. Nkurunziza and Kogi recommend safe water supplies and stronger hygiene teaching as the practical route to breaking the outbreak cycle.
plos-pone-0355269: Lin and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on power grids and business tech in China. They asked whether building ultra-high voltage lines, which move power over long distances, spurs firms to develop artificial intelligence. The evidence came from China's big transmission projects. If energy builds shape tech growth, planners gain one more reason to weigh where and when lines are built.
plos-pone-0355369:
Katherine Van Koevering, Yiquan Hong, and Jon Kleinberg study how Reddit organized itself around COVID-19 almost overnight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Most big discussion topics accrete communities over years; this one arrived abruptly and hundreds of forums formed within weeks. Using a nearly complete census of those communities, the authors ask what people talked about, who they talked with, and what shapes the self assembly took.

The new forums did not float free of older ones. They plugged into existing frames, political, skeptical, and geographic, and geography proved the single largest organizing theme, despite the crisis being planetary. Neighbors wanted to talk to neighbors about local rules, risks, and resources. The authors call the pattern social tectonics: under sudden pressure, online society snaps into plates along old fault lines, and any emergency communication strategy should expect local identity to dominate.
plos-pone-0355469:
Mei-Ping Zheng and co-authors mined gene data for cell-cycle markers that flag sepsis, the runaway infection response that shuts down organs. Disturbed cell cycles are increasingly blamed for sepsis immune failure. Their 2026 study overlapped genes changed in sepsis with cell-cycle genes, then let machine learning shortlist the strongest candidates.

Four genes survived screening and validation, all running more active in sepsis samples. Each separated patients from controls well on accuracy curves. Enrichment and immune profiling placed the markers inside sepsis biology, and drug prediction suggested compounds that might touch them. Single-cell data located the markers in specific immune cell types and traced their behaviour over cell development paths.
plos-pone-0355869:
Caitriona Murphy and co-authors compared a new nose-only swab against combined nose-and-throat swabs for flu and COVID testing. Good sampling decides whether a test finds the virus, and throat swabbing is unpleasant enough to deter people. Their 2026 study enrolled feverish outpatients at a Hong Kong clinic who gave both sample types for laboratory comparison.

Agreement between the two methods was very high for influenza A, influenza B, and the coronavirus alike, each around ninety-eight to ninety-nine percent. Viral signal strengths were also compared head to head. Murphy and colleagues conclude the gentler anterior nasal swab performs on par with the combined method in symptomatic patients, which could widen testing uptake.
plos-pone-0355969:
Catharina Latz and colleagues tested whether artificial intelligence can grade cataracts from eye scans without a doctor's grading. Cataracts cloud the lens, and grading guides surgery decisions. Their 2026 feasibility study trained a neural network on about eighteen hundred scan images from just over nine hundred eyes.

Human grades from a standard scale served as the reference. The system graded one cataract type, at the back of the lens, with fairly high accuracy. It graded clouding of the lens centre much less well, at about three in five correct. Most errors there landed in a neighbouring grade. Latz and colleagues call the results promising but preliminary, a base for larger and more careful validation.
plos-pone-0356269:
Oscar Emil Puntervold and seven colleagues test whether a commercial chemistry kit built for blood and other fluids can profile metabolites in dead heart tissue, in this 2026 forensic study. Forty hearts from autopsies in Denmark were sampled: donors with type 2 diabetes, with ischemic heart disease, and controls without heart pathology. The kit measures hundreds of small molecules at once using mass spectrometry.

About three quarters of the kit's targets could be quantified in heart tissue, with fat-related molecules measuring best and some other classes proving patchier. A few metabolite groups differed nominally between donor groups, but nothing survived strict statistical correction, and overall profiles did not separate the groups. The authors call the approach technically feasible and a promising standardized basis for future forensic and heart research, rather than a ready diagnostic.
plos-pone-0356469:
Karikalan Nagarajan and co-authors trained community volunteers in a remote tribal district of Manipur, India, to support tuberculosis control. Volunteers learned to spot symptoms, collect and move sputum samples, and support patients through treatment. The 2026 study measured knowledge, attitudes, and intended practice before and after the training.

More than seven hundred volunteers were trained, and about half completed the full course and both assessments. The share reaching the top knowledge band jumped from about one in ten to about two in three. Attitude scores rose only slightly, though more volunteers said they would seek care quickly for symptoms. The authors conclude that short, culturally fitting training can raise TB knowledge fast, even in hard-to-reach areas.
plos-pone-0356569:
Yujie Liu and coauthors published a 2026 evidence summary in PLOS ONE on helping family members care for a relative living with an enterostomy, a surgically created opening for waste. Family caregivers handle pouches, skin care, and daily routines, often with little training. The team systematically searched guideline networks, nursing societies, and major databases, keeping only sources that passed quality checks, then distilled the best advice.

Thirteen sources survived: clinical decision tools, guidelines, a systematic review, and expert consensuses. From them the authors drew sixteen pieces of evidence in four domains. Families need structured teaching of knowledge and hands-on skills; support through the care process; protection of the caregiver's own body and mind; and a wider support system around them. The summary is offered as a ready reference for nurses building caregiver training plans, reflecting published evidence rather than a new trial.
plos-pone-0356769:
Samuel Westaway and colleagues used the UK Renal Registry to follow 5,447 adults whose kidney transplants failed between 2012 and 2021. They asked who got what treatment in the first year. They also asked whether the answer was fair. Their 2026 cohort study tracked re-transplantation, dialysis choices, conservative care, and death. The results were broken down by age, sex, ethnicity, wealth, disease, and center.

Nearly half went onto hospital dialysis. Only about one in twenty received a new kidney within the year. Black and Asian patients were markedly less likely to be re-transplanted than white patients. Men were more likely than women. Each step of deprivation cut re-transplant chances by roughly a fifth. The registry's findings give the transplant system hard numbers on inequities to answer for.
plos-pone-0356869:
Nuray Alaca and three colleagues studied healthy aging in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They asked how two inner resources, kindness toward oneself and belief in one's own ability, relate to aging well. Their measures covered pain, health habits, posture awareness, and quality of life in older adults.

Alaca's team found links suggesting that these inner resources matter alongside physical ones. People who treat themselves with patience and trust their capacity may keep up habits that protect health. Programs for older adults often focus on exercise and diet alone. This study argues for adding mental skills training to that mix, since how people relate to themselves can shape the daily choices that add up to aging well.
plos-pone-0357369: Dingle and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a study at three Australian universities. The plan tests Tuned In Connect, a program meant to lift the success of neurodivergent students by supporting their wellbeing. The design is quasi-experimental, meaning groups are compared without full random assignment. Publishing the plan first lets other experts judge the methods before any results appear.
plos-pone-0357469:
Jordan E Hamden leads a team of eight asking whether the microbes parents carry can tune a newborn's stress hormones, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In baby mice, hormone levels inside immune organs run higher than in blood during the first two weeks of life, and gut microbes are suspected of helping set those levels. Instead of wiping microbes out, the team bred mice from two colonies whose gut communities differed modestly and measured hormones in five day old pups.

The parent colonies' microbes differed in makeup, though not in overall diversity. Pups from one line carried higher levels of corticosterone, the main mouse stress hormone, and a related hormone in blood and immune organs. The team also measured fatty acids made by gut bacteria as a possible messenger. Even gentle differences in inherited microbes, the results suggest, reach into a newborn's hormone settings.
plos-pone-0357569:
Leah Gordillo and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about desert wildlife. It studies toads in the Great Basin desert and the Mojave and their presence at artificial water sites, tanks and troughs placed in dry country. The authors test what drives that presence.

Two drivers named in the title are accessibility, how easily toads can reach and enter the water, and surface area, how large the water is. In deserts, artificial water can decide whether amphibians survive dry years. Land managers who maintain or remove these sites need to know which features toads actually use, and this study supplies that link.
plos-pone-0357969:
A Z M Fahim Siddique and six co-authors, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study, look for genes shared by two heart conditions. One is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in which the heart muscle grows too thick. The other is atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heartbeat that strikes these patients unusually often. The team wanted the genetic links that might explain that overlap.

They pooled gene lists from five public databases and compared the two conditions, finding eleven genes in common. Three stood out as central connectors, including NPPA, which makes a hormone involved in blood pressure control. Checks in separate patient datasets and in clinical samples confirmed that NPPA activity runs high in the thickened heart condition, tying it to electrical changes in the upper heart chambers.
plos-pone-0358069:
Mohamed Ahmed El Maghawry led a team of seven authors reviewing seven years of plasma therapy in Egypt, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Therapeutic plasma exchange filters harmful substances from the blood and treats a surprising range of diseases, from nerve to kidney to blood disorders. The team studied its use across organ systems at an Egyptian tertiary center.

El Maghawry's real-world cohort shows what the therapy achieves outside controlled trials, in daily hospital practice over a long span. Such records reveal which conditions the center treats most, how patients fare, and where the therapy is stretched thin. Centers in similar settings can benchmark their own programs against it. Long local records are how expensive therapies earn continued funding: by proof, not habit.
plos-pone-0358269:
Jargalmaa Amarsanaa and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE tracking loneliness in Japan through the COVID-19 years. They followed the same group of adults through five yearly online surveys, from 2020 to 2024, using a short three-question loneliness scale. Rather than taking a single snapshot, the team watched how individuals moved into or out of loneliness over time.

Loneliness peaked in 2021, eased in 2022, and then held fairly steady through 2024. Most people followed stable paths, either lonely at every wave or not lonely at any wave, while a smaller group felt lonely only during part of the pandemic. Stricter cutoffs for what counts as lonely did not change that overall picture. The authors caution that an online panel cannot give exact national rates, but the patterns show whose isolation lingered after restrictions ended.
plos-pone-0358469:
Juan Pablo Narváez-Herrera led a team of six authors measuring carbon and soil life on a Colombian cattle farm, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The dual-purpose farm, in the Amazonian foothills, raises cattle for both milk and beef across several kinds of land use. The team compared soil carbon stocks, litter breakdown, and soil animal diversity across those uses.

Narváez-Herrera's comparison shows which practices keep carbon in the ground and support soil life, and which let both slip. Cattle farming in the Amazon foothills sits at the center of climate and forest debates. Farm-level evidence like this can guide land use that keeps production while storing carbon, instead of forcing a choice between the two.
plos-pone-0358569: Teka and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a surgical training program in Ethiopia's Tigray region. The program trains non-physician surgeons to handle emergency operations where doctors are scarce. The team gathered views on how well the program fits into the wider health system. Their focus was the surgeons who are not physicians. Fit matters because a good program can still fail if the system resists it.
plos-pone-0358769:
Masaki Chujyo, Shu Liu, and Fujio Toriumi ask where a network is weakest when damage spreads outward from a single point, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such localized attacks, a fire, a flood, a failure cascading to neighbors, threaten power grids and transport webs. Standard importance scores rank nodes by connections, but the authors suspected they miss how position shapes a spreading failure. They propose an index that simulates an attack starting at each node and counts the links severed along the way.

On synthetic and real world networks, their index tracked the actual loss of robustness more closely than the classic centrality measures of degree, closeness, and betweenness. Highly connected nodes were not always the dangerous seeds; shape and neighborhood layout mattered as much. For operators hardening real infrastructure, the index offers a sharper way to decide which single points deserve protection first.
plos-pone-0358869: Susanti and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE interview study set in Java, Indonesia. They asked local stakeholders how acceptable low-intensity psychological care would likely be before it starts. Such care uses brief, guided help rather than long therapy. Views gathered early, through a theory-based frame, can reveal doubts and support that planners must address before launch.
plos-pone-0358969:
Balram Yelamasetti leads a team of seven 3D printing honeycomb sandwich panels and weighing strength against lightness, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The panels, plastic faces over a honeycomb core, promise stiff parts from little material, but four geometry choices pull the design in different directions. Eighteen configurations, varying cell size, cell wall thickness, and the two face thicknesses, were printed in PLA plastic and bent until they failed, then weighed.

Cell size and wall thickness together explained most of the variation in bending strength, and the same pair dominated the mass results in swapped order. The catch is that the geometry favoring maximum strength was not the geometry favoring minimum weight. The authors therefore blend the two analyses into a compromise setting rather than crowning a single winner. Their method suits any printed structure, from drone frames to furniture, where grams and strength must be bought together.
plos-pone-0359069:
Zihong Chen leads a team of eight hunting genetic risk markers for myasthenia gravis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease weakens muscles when the immune system attacks the junctions where nerves meet muscle. The authors focused on markers inside long noncoding RNA regions, an understudied corner of the genome. They screened candidates from large genetic datasets. Then they genotyped one hundred sixty-one patients and the same number of healthy controls.

Overall, marker frequencies looked alike in patients and controls. The signal appeared only in the generalized form of the disease, where several variants near a noncoding RNA called HCG27 were more common, including the marker named in the study's title. Laboratory work traced how that marker influences HCG27 levels in immune cells. The findings nominate a regulatory variant and its RNA partner for deeper study of disease susceptibility.
plos-pone-0359269: Callizot and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a possible new drug for Parkinson's disease. The compound, called AZP2006, was tested in lab models of the disease. The title calls it a promising protective treatment for nerve cells. Its action involves lysosomes, the cell's cleanup units, and a protein pair named progranulin and prosaposin. New ways to slow Parkinson's are badly needed.
plos-pone-0360069:
Kiran Katari and co-authors designed in 2026 a smart controller for a device that shields machines from shaking. The device is made from a rubber like material whose stiffness can be changed with a magnet. Shaking that reaches such a shield varies in speed and strength, so the control system must adapt on the fly.

Their design joins two ideas. A small neural network learns how the device behaves, while a robust control method, called sliding mode control, keeps things steady when conditions shift. Tests used shaking that changed in both frequency and amplitude. Better shields of this kind serve cars, factory gear, and fine instruments that must stay still to work well.
pmc-10655269:
Grace Kenny and colleagues published a 2023 study of long COVID symptom patterns in Ireland. Long COVID takes many forms. Grouping symptoms may reveal distinct types. The team compared early-pandemic and later-variant infections. Vaccination status was also examined. Over four hundred patients joined the cohort.

Three symptom clusters appeared in both eras. One centered on muscle and joint pain. Another centered on chest and breathing symptoms. A third group had milder overall symptoms. Variants and vaccination shifted individual symptom odds. Clusters stayed surprisingly stable across eras. Stable groupings help design targeted rehabilitation trials.
pmc-10655369:
Zhang and co-authors use gene-based methods to test whether blood metabolites cause stroke. Stroke hits middle-aged and older people hardest and brings high disability and death. Blood compounds may reveal the biology behind it.

The team took gene study data for 486 blood metabolites as exposures. Eleven stroke outcomes were tested, from any stroke to bleeding types and mini-strokes. A two-sample Mendelian randomization design used gene variants as natural experiments. Weighted methods estimated the causal push of each compound. The goal was to flag compounds that truly raise risk, not just track with it.
pmc-10687369:
Lixuan Sun, Hui Dong, and Xiaotian Zhang test problem-based learning delivered through the DingTalk platform, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. The COVID-19 pandemic forced Chinese undergraduates into remote learning. Business English vocabulary was the skill under instruction.

Fifty-eight students took part in the mixed-methods study. Vocabulary tests measured score changes, while interviews captured student experiences. Scores improved significantly under the DingTalk-based problem-based approach. Interviewees described their perceptions of learning this way at a distance. The authors frame the method as an inventive response to pandemic constraints. Digital platforms plus problem-based tasks, they conclude, can grow specialized vocabulary even when classrooms close. The sample is small, so wider trials would strengthen the claim.
pmc-10693869:
Akihiro Ikuta and six colleagues test a simple blood ratio as a prognostic sign after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Anemia and kidney failure each worsen outlook, and their ratio, hemoglobin divided by creatinine, is easy to compute the day before the procedure. The study followed 458 non-dialysis patients treated between 2015 and 2021.

Patients in the lowest ratio third died at a rate near seventeen percent within a year, versus two percent in the highest third. Heart failure hospitalizations showed the same gradient. The ratio independently predicted both outcomes, with cutoffs around ten identified for each. The authors suggest the cheap index can flag high-risk valve patients before intervention.
pmc-10703269:
Rogers and four co-authors measure isotope factors in Pacific cod for diet modeling, in work from twenty twenty-three. Stable isotope analysis traces what fish eat from chemical signatures in tissue. Models need an accurate offset value between diet and tissue, called a discrimination factor.

That offset may shift with water temperature and diet quality, both changing under climate change. The team derived the factors experimentally under varied conditions in the lab. Carbon and nitrogen isotopes were tracked separately. Climate informed factors will keep future diet models for this commercial fish honest as oceans warm.
pmc-10716169:
Taigang Zhang, Weicai Wang, Baosheng An, and Lele Wei published a hazards study in twenty twenty-three on glacial lake outburst floods. Their region was the Third Pole, the high Asian mountains centered on the Tibetan Plateau. Melting glaciers are swelling lakes that can burst without warning, and earlier risk pictures were scattered and coarse.

Combining sharp satellite images, lake-by-lake flood modeling, and detailed exposure maps, the team found proglacial lakes expanding fastest between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-two. Outburst floods have grown more frequent since nineteen eighty, especially in southeastern Tibet and near the China-Nepal border. Thousands of buildings, hydropower plants, roads, and bridges sit in potential flood paths, making regional cooperation urgent.
pmc-10745069:
Riadh Cheddadi and others looked at newborn microbiome patterns in 2023. Gut microbes shape later health deeply. New reading tools changed this field fast. Babies were once thought to start sterile. That simple view is now debated.

Birth mode shapes early germ profiles. A mother's health shapes them as well. Placenta and gut links are covered. Possible womb germ steps remain in dispute. Profiles link to obesity risk later. Brain growth links are also covered. The authors stress careful reading of profiles. Health results depend on context. Early life microbes may echo through health for years.
pmc-10745769:
Sujhey Hernandez-Bazan and colleagues tested gene therapy against resistant tuberculosis in two thousand twenty-three. Drug-resistant TB needs longer, harsher treatment. Many patients abandon therapy midway. A virus carrier delivered a protective immune signal gene. Mice carried a resistant pulmonary infection strain. Treatment came during the chronic active stage.

One dose produced complete survival in treated mice. Lung bacterial loads fell sharply as well. Tissue damage and pneumonia shrank visibly. Immune cells in damaged areas rose in number. Protective granulomas grew larger and worked better. Control virus without the gene did nothing similar. Gene therapy could someday support failing drug regimens.
pmc-10747269:
Zhaocheng Zhang and his team sift fresh gains in black phosphorus light aids that break down new foul goods in water. Their 2023 review takes in a bright non-metal stuff that light can switch on, for clean-up of foul water.

New foul goods fight break-down and put health of folk and wild life kits at risk. Black phosphorus gives a gap for charge that can be set. It takes in light in a broad way and moves charge in a top way. But the pure stuff is not firm in air. It loses its wrought-up charges too fast, which curbs how well it works. The review first looks at how the bulk stuff and thin sheets are made. It sets each way's good points next to its weak points. It then sifts built forms made to beat the weak points, a gap in past sift work.
pmc-10752569:
Noah Rubin and colleagues tested a new way in 2023 to control powered prosthetic ankles: listening to individual motor units instead of whole-muscle electrical signals. After amputation, residual muscles still fire when a person tries to move the missing ankle. Surface EMG decoders read that activity only coarsely. This study asked whether decoding the firing of single motor units could estimate ankle torque more faithfully.

Eight people without amputation and seven with amputation took part. Participants performed gentle toe-up and toe-down efforts while torque was recorded, and amputees mirrored the motion with their residual muscles. Linear decoders were compared using EMG amplitude, motor unit firing frequencies, and combinations of signals. If motor unit decoding wins, prosthesis controllers could tap a richer neural signal, giving users finer, more natural ankle control.
pmc-10753169:
Yan Cao leads a team that trials acupuncture for mild cognitive impairment. Their trial from twenty twenty-three deals with older folks with mild mind loss. Such loss can be a step toward Alzheimer's disease.

Acupuncture has gained fame as a possible help for this ill. Their method is termed Kidney Nourishment and Spirit Regulation. Folks will be split to real, sham, or blank groups for weeks. The blank group gets health teaching and later free therapy. Points across head, belly, and limbs are used in care. Mind gains and safety are the main checks.
pmc-10869269:
van Kempen, Kim, Tumescheit, and co-authors present Foldseek, a fast way to search by protein shape. Computer methods now predict millions of protein shapes, and that flood has made searching them slow. Knowing a protein's shape helps reveal what it does, so search speed matters.

Foldseek compares a query shape against huge databases by encoding how amino acids touch in three dimensions. That encoding lets it find matches far faster than older shape tools. Quick shape search helps scientists spot distant relatives of a protein and guess at roles for proteins never studied in a lab.
pmc-11537569:
Samsam Aden, Mette Munk Lauridsen, and Lea Ladegaard Gronkjaer scope the work on self-care steps for patients with cirrhosis, a grave liver scar state. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Self-care means a patient gains the facts, skills, and trust to run their own ill state day to day. The team searched four bases for such work in clinic care.

Of more than one thousand finds, just sixteen studies fit. They came from seven lands and held more than one thousand patients in all. Shapes and checks varied a lot across studies. Still, each found some gain, most of all in patient facts and life quality. The team urges fuller, set plans built to each patient's needs.
pmc-11580669:
Kotepui and four co-authors review a blood protein in malaria patients, in work from twenty twenty-four. Ceruloplasmin is a protein tied to copper and iron handling and to oxidative stress. Past studies disagreed on whether malaria raises or lowers its levels.

The registered review searched six databases up to August twenty twenty-three. Study quality was checked with standard tools for each design type. Findings were first summed in words, then pooled with a random effects model for a numeric answer. A clear pooled result could show if the protein tracks malaria severity and might serve as a helpful marker in clinics with few tests.
pmc-11589769:
Haiting Wu and colleagues reported a fast synthesis route in 2024 for decorated amides. Amides carrying silicon, germanium, boron, selenium, or sulfur appear in many active drugs. Building them has stayed difficult. The team used stable powder-like starting materials as carbene sources. Carbenes are highly reactive carbon fragments. They slip into bonds between hydrogen and those five elements. Each insertion builds the desired decorated amide directly. The method runs at high throughput in their setup.

Conditions stayed simple and mild throughout. Many starting variants worked under the same setup. Delicate chemical groups survived the process intact. The route also picked the right bond with high precision. Lab tests and computer work traced how bonds form. Five element families of products became accessible this way. All came from shelf-stable, easy precursors. The authors present insertion chemistry as a general building tool.
pmc-11594669:
Chen leads a large team analyzing a nitrogen transport gene subfamily in wheat, in work from twenty twenty-four. Amino acids are the main form in which plants move nitrogen. Transporter proteins carry them across cell membranes.

The TaATLa subfamily has eighteen members in common wheat, but their traits and roles were poorly understood, partly due to the huge wheat genome. Genomic analyses mapped chromosome positions and gene structures. Expression analyses showed where and when the genes are active. Knowing which transporters load nitrogen into grain can guide breeding and fertilizer strategies for a crop that feeds billions.
pmc-11606169:
Xiang Han and colleagues reviewed records for a small group of lung cancer patients whose tumors carried uncommon mutations in a growth receptor gene. Standard targeted pills work less predictably for these rare variants than for the common ones. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team gathered Chinese patients treated at first line with targeted therapy between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-one. The regimen paired the pill afatinib with bevacizumab, a drug that blocks blood vessel growth. Response, survival, and side effects were collected from the charts.

More than half of the patients responded to treatment. Typical time before the cancer grew again was about eleven months, and typical overall survival was close to three years. Some patients gained a resistance mutation that opens other drug options. Side effects were mild to moderate, including skin problems on hands and feet, high blood pressure, and protein in the urine.
pmc-11634469:
Zhi-Cheng Jin and a large team sort liver cancer waste states by body form paths past drug cures. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Waste can mar fate and cure take. More than four hundred folks on first-line shield plus growth drug cures had muscle and fat reads from scans at spine point three, in train.

Two paths split for each: flat and sharp fall. Sharp falls tied to short life. Three states were set by the pair: pre-waste, waste, and hard waste. Hard waste bore the worst life, march, and cure take marks, then waste. Form paths flag who needs help first.
pmc-11637769:
Ian Ross and seven co-authors published a genetic engineering study in twenty twenty-four on a reusable selection trick for editing the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. CRISPR editing needs marker genes to find the rare edited cells, and markers run out after a few rounds. Their system recycles a single marker endlessly.

The marker is the nitrate reductase gene. First, CRISPR breaks it, and edited cells survive chlorate poisoning while normal cells die. Next, CRISPR repairs the break, and only repaired cells can live on nitrate as their sole nitrogen source. Flipping the marker back and forth leaves no scar and frees it for the next edit. The authors demonstrate long chains of edits in other genes using this one gatekeeper.
pmc-11640269:
Peter Reniers and six co-authors evaluate a Dutch toolkit that helps home care teams plan around clients' pets, in a two thousand twenty-four process evaluation. Pets can complicate long-term care at home, yet they also anchor clients' quality of life.

Professional caregivers, clients, and family caregivers who had used the PET@home materials gave semi-structured interviews. Themes covered satisfaction, relevance, feasibility, and integration into daily practice. Feedback produced concrete fixes, such as clearer instructions in the client booklet. Participants judged that the toolkit improves planning and prevents pet-related problems, potentially letting clients keep their animals longer. The study shows how to refine a practical care tool with its users.
pmc-11641169:
Michał Wójcicki and co-authors pull and chart a fresh germ-kill virus that hunts drug-proof Salmonella. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. This food germ's proof strains push hunts for swap guards like such viruses. The new find was drawn gainst a proof strain and read by shape, life, and full code.

It held strong in cold to warm heat and wide sour spans, and fell with time in UV light. Its code bore no proof or tame marks, which firms its fierce kind. Class reads set it in a known tail pack. The team pitch it for food guard use.
pmc-11641369:
Yichen Wang and six colleagues engineer silkworms to spin silk containing spider egg case protein. Spider egg case silk is hard, water-resistant, and highly moisture absorbent, but spiders cannot be farmed at scale. Silkworms share a similar spinning system, making them ideal bioreactors for spider proteins.

Using a piggyBac transposon system, the team inserted the egg case silk gene from the spider Nephila clavata into the silkworm's heavy-chain expression system. The silk glands produced a new transgenic silk with significantly higher initial modulus and moisture absorption. The authors present the result as a reference for large-scale production of spider egg case proteins, with prospects for environmentally friendly fiber materials.
pmc-11643069:
Hua Xu and six co-authors build three-dimensional silk scaffolds that could host bone cells and carry osteoporosis drugs. Silk fibroin scaffolds are attractive, but how fast they biodegrade depends on stripping the cocoon's sericin coating. The team tuned that degumming step with varying salt concentrations and bath counts.

A modified gas-foaming method then expanded flat microfibers into porous three-dimensional structures, finished by freeze-drying. The strongest treatment, a double bath at the highest salt level, produced clean, smooth scaffolds. Surfaces were coated with flavonoids from semen cuscutae, a traditional remedy component, at several loadings. Cell tests showed no toxicity in vitro. The work sets up a platform for predicting anti-osteoporosis drug behavior on bone-like scaffolds.
pmc-11643269:
Maja Tomczyk reviewed omega-three fats and muscle strength in 2024. Two fats in this family act most strongly. They are known as EPA and DHA. Both support heart and brain health. Some evidence suggests muscle benefits too. Strength loss matters greatly in older age.

Studies covered healthy adults and elderly people. Some trials showed preserved strength. Others showed increased strength instead. Published work remains limited in number. Study designs also varied a lot. The review lists key research gaps. Better trials could settle the question. Clear dosing guidance is still missing.
pmc-11653969:
Gracia Sierra, Klaira Lerma, Gabriela Alvarez Perez, Anitra Beasley, and Kari White asked Texans seeking abortion care what they would trade off for care in another state in twenty twenty-four. After the state's ban, many had to travel out of state for facility care. A choice experiment put one hundred thirty-six respondents through twelve choice sets, varying wait time, distance, and cost.

Wait time mattered most, then cost, then distance. On average, people would pay two hundred forty-eight dollars more and travel nine hundred seventeen miles farther to be seen one week sooner. Willingness to pay for a faster slot was higher for those without economic hardship than for those with it. The authors say the results show how heavy the burden of delay is for people forced to travel for care.
pmc-11654369:
Hongyu Gong and five co-authors survey the career paths of Chinese pharmacy graduates in a two thousand twenty-four workforce study. China's healthcare sector is expanding fast, and pharmacy faces staffing and retention questions.

Graduates of Kunming Medical University from nineteen ninety-six to two thousand twelve answered an online survey; two hundred thirty-one responded. Just over half had never changed jobs, and a third had moved once or twice. Government institutions were the most preferred employers by far, chosen by nearly two thirds, while overseas companies attracted almost none. The analysis weighs which factors drive job changes, aiming to inform career planning and workforce stability in the profession.
pmc-11656869:
Li and coauthors build a gene score to forecast outcome in colon cancer. Colon cancer is a top cause of cancer death worldwide. Sharp risk marks can guide care tuned to each patient. Genes tied to copper-driven cell death may hold such marks.

The team used gene and clinic data from two large databases. Stepwise checks picked genes that track with survival. Those genes formed a risk score for each patient. Test curves checked how well the score sorts risk. One gene, called KIF7, got deep lab checks. The score may help split patients for closer follow-up.
pmc-11663569:
Deborah Kiervel and colleagues show that plant RNA-binding proteins interact with a virus's structural proteins and change how much virus accumulates. Their 2025 study uses Arabidopsis and turnip yellows virus, an intracellular parasite dependent on host machinery.

Screening and plant tests identified a family of nuclear adaptor proteins as partners of the virus's coat and readthrough proteins. All four family members gathered with both viral proteins in the nucleus when produced together in leaves. In genuinely infected cells, only the coat protein stayed nuclear with them. Plants lacking all four proteins accumulated significantly more virus when infected. The authors infer an unknown defence role for these proteins against the virus.
pmc-11669869:
Loro leads a large team validating a wearable heart sensor, in work from twenty twenty-four. Wearables can track body signals all day, which helps doctors set exercise doses. A new device must first prove it measures heart rate as well as a trusted standard.

Twenty healthy adults aged twenty to thirty wore the prototype and a chest strap reference. The prototype uses light based pulse sensing and a long range radio link. All did a standard shuttle walk test that ramps up effort. Heart rates from the two devices were compared step by step. Good agreement would support use in activity prescription.
pmc-11677269:
Maria Elena Cocuz and four colleagues describe COVID-19 in newborn babies treated at a Romanian hospital, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Children usually suffer mild disease, but information about neonates under one month old was scarce.

The retrospective study covered admissions from January two thousand twenty-two through December two thousand twenty-three. Babies were treated at the infectious diseases pediatric department in Brașov. Diagnosis used PCR or rapid antigen testing at admission, following national protocol. The authors analyzed epidemiological and clinical features of this youngest age group. Their aim was a clearer picture of how the virus behaves in the first weeks of life, when immunity is still immature.
pmc-11679769:
Amanda Tanner and a large team published a process evaluation in twenty twenty-four of iTransition, a mobile health program helping young people with HIV move from pediatric to adult care. Every youth in HIV care faces this handover, and gaps can break medication routines and viral control. No proven intervention existed to smooth it.

The pilot trial gathered repeated interviews with youth, providers, and clinic transition champions, plus team meeting notes. The program clearly filled a real gap for both patients and clinics. Still, busy lives, electronic record integration, clinic policies, and the pandemic all limited reach. The authors say more refinement is needed before such tools reliably protect care continuity.
pmc-11688069:
Zhengliang Sun and Xiaohong Wang tested growth factor links to oesophageal cancer in 2024. Growth factor levels might influence cancer risk. Genetic evidence for causation was missing. Mendelian randomisation used inherited variants as instruments. Public genome datasets supplied the data. Several related binding proteins were included.

No causal link emerged from analysis. Checks found no hidden bias signals. Removing single variants changed nothing important. Results stayed stable across sensitivity tests. The authors urge further validation work. Cancer development likely involves complex interplay. Growth factors alone do not explain risk. Negative results still guide future studies.
pmc-11707469:
Yumi Shiina and colleagues propose energy loss measured by advanced magnetic resonance imaging as a marker of cardiac workload in adults with congenital heart disease. Their 2024 article focuses on right ventricular problems after two-ventricle repair.

Standard imaging measures chamber size and ejection fraction, but extra information is sometimes needed. Energy loss captures energy dissipated by blood viscosity and integrates both preload and afterload burden. It can reveal overload even when chamber size looks normal. Potential uses include judging symptom severity, timing invasive treatment, and detecting burden before deterioration. The method uses velocity profiles from four-dimensional flow imaging without needing pressure-volume measurements, making it practical in living patients.
pmc-11709369:
A large team led by Sravan Gopalkrishna Shetty Sreenivasa Murthy studies a fat-cutting protein called PLD1 in mouse and human cell models of Alzheimer's disease. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Past lab work found too much PLD1 in brain tissue from people who died with the disease. This study tracks where and when PLD1 acts as harm grows.

Mice got a drug that blocks PLD1, or a virus used to change PLD1 in set brain areas. The team then ran maze and object tests for learning and memory. They also checked brain cell links with electric tests and stained tissue views. Readers get a close look at how one protein may drive loss of brain links over time.
pmc-11727669:
Anna Justyna Milewska and co-authors published a fertility laboratory study in twenty twenty-four on what freezing does to sperm shape. Freezing semen is routine before cancer treatment and in assisted reproduction, and was long assumed to damage sperm. Newer work hints the process may instead weed out weaker cells.

Samples from ninety-seven infertility clinic patients in Białystok, Poland were assessed before and after cryopreservation under high magnification. Morphology improved after thawing, with a higher share of normal-looking sperm. Viability measures accompanied the shape analysis. The authors suggest controlled freezing can raise the fraction of higher-quality sperm available for treatment. The finding reframes freezing from a necessary evil to a possible selection step.
pmc-12661769:
Marco Spada and colleagues surveyed Italy's experience in 2025 with late-onset Pompe disease in children, a treatable muscle disorder that is easy to miss. Pompe disease weakens muscle because an enzyme deficiency lets glycogen accumulate. The late-onset form can begin in childhood, but newborn screening rarely covers it, so doctors must suspect it from symptoms. Adult diagnosis is known to be tricky, while pediatric data were scarce.

The nationwide survey gathered thirty-eight Italian children and adolescents with confirmed diagnoses, all first suspected on clinical grounds. The authors traced how these patients came to attention and how long recognition took. From those patterns they propose a targeted diagnostic algorithm for pediatricians. Earlier detection matters because enzyme treatment works best before muscle damage accumulates. A checklist built from real missed cases may shorten the next child's path.
pmc-12698569:
Lihao Qiu and his team show that phenothiazine drugs help macrophages kill germs. Their study from twenty twenty-five tests care that works through the host, not the germ. Drugs that kill germs head-on face fast-rising resistance across the world. A boost to the guard cells of the body puts no such direct press on germs.

In the lab, treated macrophages showed stronger lysosome work. Cell self-eating and reactive oxygen both rose in those cells. When either path was blocked, most of the germ-killing gain was lost. One drug in the class kept sick animals safe from organ harm. Swelling from salmon gut illness also eased with the drug. Since host-led care spares gut germs, the risk of resistance stays low. Old drugs for the mind may gain a second life here.
pmc-12706969:
Anqiang Jia and colleagues mapped a little-known gene family in maize and other land plants in two thousand twenty-five. The family, named for a protein region of unknown function, helps plants grow and handle stress, yet its history was murky. The team found family members across many plants and sorted them into four subgroups.

Older subgroups kept stricter patterns, while newer ones loosened and diversified after ancient genome doublings. In maize, family genes linked to root growth and leaf stress defense, switching on in sequence under salt-like stress. Crop scientists gain an evolutionary map pointing to genes worth testing for tougher maize.
pmc-12729369:
Stephanie L Sammes and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five feeding trial on steers facing a simulated heat wave. Forty-eight Black Angus steers spent twenty-one days in climate-controlled rooms. Diets differed in extra roughage and in when that roughage was added.

One group stayed on a finisher diet the whole time. Two groups switched to a heat load diet at different points, then switched back. Researchers tracked rumen temperature and acidity, feed and water intake, and daily weight gain. The design lets readers compare diet timing as a tool for helping grain-fed cattle cope with high heat load.
pmc-12729769:
Alessandra Giuliani and co-authors review, in a set way, long-term proof on peer victimisation and later mental health in young people. Their 2025 review asks if harm from peers has effects that last past the time when it took place.

The team draws as one on twenty-four studies that tracked youth over time. They cover depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress symptoms, self-harm, and suicidality. Proof was most strong for depression and anxiety. Large cohorts in more than one land showed links that held when looked at in advance. Risk grew when the harm was done time and time again, or went on for long. Links to self-harm were raised but less firm. The review talks through paths such as rumination and hostile attributions. It also notes wide gaps in how the studies were planned and gauged.
pmc-12734469:
Nicoleta Cobîrzan and four colleagues build a phase-change composite for cooling buildings, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The base material, n-octadecane, stores heat as it melts. Pure, it conducts heat poorly and its filler can sink during melting.

Recycled aluminum chips, cheap and abundant, were mixed in as a thermal enhancer. Two chip sizes were tested at around seven percent by volume. The long-chip composite multiplied thermal conductivity roughly sixfold. Melting finished faster, though stored latent heat fell from 245 to 195 kilojoules per kilogram. Carbon dioxide savings were estimated at 150 kilograms per year for the application studied. The trade between storage capacity and conductivity is the design question.
pmc-12737469:
Ma and coauthors test a gut germ as a vaccine carrier for chickens. The germ strain, called M-11, lives well in the chicken gut. Past work showed it is safe at the right dose. A carrier must be safe and must wake immune cells well.

The team read the full gene code of the strain. They checked genes for gut life, food use, and risk. They also tested how the strain stirs key immune cells. Those cells help launch a strong vaccine response. Gene traits set this strain apart from close kin. The work backs M-11 for use in bird vaccines.
pmc-12742769:
Castañeda-Arellano and co-authors test whether blocking a sensor protein protects the brain after a brief loss of blood flow. The protein, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, helps cells respond to foreign chemicals. Newer work hints it also shapes responses in the nervous system. The team compared normal mice with mice lacking the receptor after a short block of both carotid arteries. They measured several genes and proteins in the hippocampus.

Mice without the receptor showed a different pattern of stress and defense markers. The changes pointed to less damage in the hippocampus after the insult. A drug that blocks the receptor gave similar hints of protection. The work names the receptor as a possible target for stroke care.
pmc-12751669:
Xing and coauthors build a model to flag blood need after joint surgery. Blood top-ups after hip or knee surgery vary a lot by clinic. Too many top-ups waste scarce blood stocks. Too few can harm patients who truly need blood.

They drew on records for 1,954 joint surgery patients. Records ran from mid 2019 to late 2024. Patients were split by blood use in the first three days. Seven in ten records trained the model, and the rest tested it. The model uses routine facts known right after surgery. Its aim is early, fair calls on who needs blood.
pmc-12753069:
Efat Mohamadi and others studied mosquito-borne disease drivers in Iran in 2025. Aedes insects spread several serious diseases. Ecology alone does not explain outbreaks. How people live shapes risk just as strongly. Experts and local leaders were asked in depth. Policy answers were gathered with the problems.

Disease-centred control was judged not enough here. Local involvement needs to be much stronger. Water and waste systems also need work. Health system gaps add to the risk. Sectors must work together across government lines. Ranked steps form a handy roadmap. Similar settings may reuse the lessons. Being ready, and response, both stand to gain.
pmc-12756769:
Ma and co-authors test a two-material sensor for fault gases dissolved in transformer oil. Oil-filled transformers anchor power transmission, and faults inside them release gases into the oil. Tracking those gases warns of damage before failure, through a method called dissolved gas analysis.

The sensor pairs tin selenide with germanium selenide in a heterojunction, a joined two-layer build. Using first-principles math, the team modeled how target gases stick to the surface and change its signals. Strong, selective responses mark a good fault sensor. The study screens this material pair for cheaper, faster transformer health checks.
pmc-12816669:
Kai Cui leads a fifteen-author team hunting immune therapy targets for colorectal cancer in activated helper T cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. CD4 T cells can fight or abet tumors depending on their state. Targets specific to their activation were the quarry.

The team combined transcriptome-wide Mendelian randomization with single-cell sequencing. Colocalization and multi-omics checks filtered causal claims from correlations. Twenty-eight genes tied to CD4 activation emerged as candidate targets. Two, PARP14 and ORMDL3, drew special attention. The approach uses genetic causality as a sieve before laboratory work begins. Colorectal immunotherapy has lagged other cancers; cell-state-specific targets could widen its reach beyond the minority who now respond.
pmc-12821169:
Aljohani leads a large team ranking causes of long emergency stays in Saudi Arabia, in work from twenty twenty-five. A stay over eight hours counts as prolonged there. Long stays harm outcomes and strain staff and beds, yet key causes had not been ranked locally.

Emergency doctors and nurses in Riyadh rated thirty-four possible indicators in two survey rounds. The modified Delphi method builds consensus in steps. More than a hundred twenty staff took part in each round. The top ten agreed indicators give managers a focused list for reform, rather than a vague call to work faster.
pmc-12829169:
Edwin Jeffry Palma-Díaz leads an eight-author team profiling invasive Salmonella cases at a Mexican center, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Salmonella gut infections are common across poorer countries. When the bacterium invades sterile body sites, the disease turns dangerous. Yet data from Latin America on that form are scarce.

All patients with Salmonella isolated from normally sterile sites were included. The span ran from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-five. Seventy-seven invasive cases were found in that time. Records gave demographics, comorbidities, and immune status for each case. They also gave symptoms, treatment, and outcomes in full. Laboratory archives gave the bacterial serogroups in the set. They also gave their antibiotic resistance patterns for the team. Profiles of this kind, for a region, guide empiric antibiotic choices. Those choices fail when local resistance patterns are guessed from data from other continents.
pmc-12844169:
Liu and co-authors apply a data fix called Norm-SVR to single-cell chemical scans from a ToF-SIMS tool. Stable data are vital for reading single cells this way, but handling and machine drift add noise. Old fixes lean on total signal scaling or matched sample bases.

No fix existed that was built for single-cell metabolite data from this tool. The new method borrows a regression fix used in large metabolite studies. It cut batch effects and spread in the data more than the standard scaling fix. The authors expect better quality checks for large datasets of this kind.
pmc-12846669:
Hina Jhelum, Reinhold Schäfer, Benedikt Kaufer, and Joachim Denner test whether a pig virus can infect human cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The virus, porcine cytomegalovirus, also called porcine roseolovirus, spread during pig organ transplants. It shortened survival in primate recipients and contributed to the first human pig-heart recipient's death.

Oddly, no infections appear in ordinary people despite the virus's prevalence in pigs. That suggests it is xenozoonotic, dangerous only in the transplant setting. The authors exposed human 293T cells and mouse cells with weakened antiviral defenses. The title reports the outcome: no infection occurred. The result sharpens the puzzle of how the virus harms transplant recipients specifically.
pmc-12860469:
Najmeh Tavousi and her team pool studies on links twixt chem goods in air, soil, and food that break sex gland signs and ills where the body fights safe stuff in kids. Their 2025 full review hunts more than one store for watched human studies through February twenty twenty-five.

From thousands of first files, twenty-three studies made the cut. They held more than twelve thousand folk who took part. Pooled finds showed a small link twixt chem dose and risk of such ills. That link was firm in math terms. Links that point up showed in girls and in boys on their own, though one subgroup find sat on the edge. Ills took in asthma, nose burn, skin rash, food-based ill acts, and kin states. These chem goods can break sex gland signs prior to birth, throw growth off track, and raise risk in late life.
pmc-12879469:
Klingemann and co-authors poll Polish health staff on how peers act on drink woes. Staff health steers how well sick hosts get cared for day to day. Drink strain at work links to bad ends in past proof. Yet how peers act when they spot drink woes stayed dim. Help plans for staff hinge on those peer acts to work. The poll ran in fall 2024 with talk-based screen chats.

In sum, 655 health staff took part in the poll. Half came from wards, and half from other care sites. A stress poll and a drink screen gave the trait scores. In made-up tales, 85 percent said they would act. In real tales, 72 percent had in fact stepped in. Direct words to the peer was the top act named. Boss back-up swayed acts the most in the fits.
pmc-13127169:
Catherine Spencer and seven co-authors report a rare B-cell lymphoma that spans ovary, tube, and womb in one woman. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. This low-grade lymphoma most oft grows in the gut. Just a few tube cases and one ovary case were on record before.

Their patient, a woman of seventy-eight, came in for vulvar pain, and a scan found a left tube mass. Surgery took the womb, tubes, and ovaries out. Cuts showed the same lymph growth in tube, ovary, womb layers, and a groin node. Gene tests backed the call over a kin lymphoma. Watch care was chosen, and a scan at one year was clear.
pmc-13152169:
Feng Li and four co-authors published a robotics study in twenty twenty-six on turning photographs of real rooms into the tidy grid maps that path-planning algorithms need. Hand-building such maps from laser and ultrasound surveys is slow. Their pipeline standardizes a real environment photo, then redraws every obstacle as a circle swollen by a safety margin.

An ant colony algorithm, which plans routes by simulated pheromone trails, then routes the robot across the converted map. Experiments confirmed the conversion produces workable standard grids and that planning and motion control run on them. The trick is conservative geometry: circles overestimate obstacles slightly, trading a little free space for collision safety.
pmc-13152369:
Faris Halaseh and Lindsey Spiegelman published a case report in twenty twenty-six on a sore belly that was first blamed on the wrong cause. A forty-four-year-old woman came in with pain low on the right side, sickness, vomiting, and chills. The pain was first put down to period cramps.

A CT scan told the true story: her appendix held several hard stones, and it was inflamed. Keyhole surgery found the appendix dead in part but not burst. She healed well, and the pain was gone. Stones in the appendix raise the risk of a bad course, so speed counts. The authors stress two points: keep appendix pain on the list for women with belly pain, and trust the scan to settle the call.
pmc-13158569:
Lamb and co-authors show that sulfur-bearing compounds called hydropersulfides help new blood vessels grow. These compounds act as signals in mammal cells, but their body roles were murky. Their instability made them hard to study directly. The team used donor molecules that release them in a controlled way. They also used mice lacking an enzyme that makes one such compound in cells.

The compounds switched on a growth pathway that runs through Akt and nitric oxide signals. Vessel growth rose when the compounds were supplied. Mice without the making enzyme showed weaker vessel responses. The work links the compounds to keeping vessels healthy. It names a signaling axis that future drugs might target.
pmc-13191369:
Marta Gomez-Gomez leads a 2026 chemistry study on building curved molecular chains on surfaces. Bowl-shaped aromatic molecules, shaped like tiny bowls, offer properties flat versions cannot, but joining them into chains usually gives no control over their orientation, or topology. Precise control is needed for materials with set electronic behavior.

Starting from halogen-tagged bowl molecules on a surface, the team used microscopy and computer modeling to watch the products form. Bromine-tagged starters fused into pairs and triples sharing small rings, while fluorine-tagged ones formed metal-organic chains. Chlorine sat between, needing more heat and giving messier structures. In every case only one orientation appeared, showing surface-guided selectivity, and the fused chains' electronic gap shifted as expected.
pmc-13194269:
Thomas Maskow and others reviewed in two thousand twenty-six how tracking heat from living microbes, called biocalorimetry, can steer biotech work using large natural and synthetic molecules. Microbes turning plant waste or plastic waste release heat in step with their work, even in messy solid mixtures where other sensors struggle.

Heat-based measures give sturdy numbers for how well microbes convert material, useful for running and scaling processes. The method is proven in liquid cultures but still young for composting, solid fermentation, and plastic breakdown, especially with mixed, non-sterile cultures. Industry readers gain a realistic map of promise and current limits.
pmc-13197269:
Lion R Martius and colleagues report a 2026 field study of stem water storage in Amazon trees. Trees store water in their trunks, which buffers them in dry spells. Constant measures of that store are rare in tropical forests, so the team fitted sensors through the harsh 2023 drought.

Sensors tracked stem water in two palm species and broadleaf trees growing side by side in the eastern Amazon. Palms held far more water and drew on it more each day and season. Palms kept releasing stored water at levels where broadleaf trees faltered. Below a shared soil moisture line, stem water fell fast in all trees. The method may sharpen drought science as the climate warms.
pmc-13198469:
James Charles and colleagues reviewed horse-related injuries in rural Oklahoma over ten years in a 2026 study. Horse country carries real trauma risk, yet such injuries are under-studied. Their trauma center focused on overall patterns plus urinary and genital injuries, which are often overlooked.

Records covered 259 admitted patients from 2015 to 2025. Falls from a horse led, followed by being struck by a horse. Head and face injuries were most common, then chest and spine. Urinary or genital injuries hit about nine percent overall and clustered in severe cases. Kidney injury alone hit about three percent. Four deaths occurred, all from brain injury. The authors urge helmets and safer horse contact habits.
pmc-13198669:
Joseph J Lim and colleagues review add-ons for shoulder tendon repair in a 2026 survey. Rotator cuff repair fixes torn shoulder tendons. Two helpers can support healing: bone marrow stimulation, which draws marrow cells by tiny bone holes, and patch augmentation, which lays a reinforcing sheet over the repair.

The team searched three databases for strong studies of each helper versus plain repair. Twenty studies qualified, covering more than eight hundred patients in total. No study pitted the two helpers head-to-head. Pain and function gains ran alike between helper groups, as did retear rates at latest follow-up. Methods varied a lot across studies. Direct randomized trials must settle which helper, if either, is better.
pmc-13201569:
Surgeons who use glowing dyes to find tumors get inconsistent images from handheld cameras, and a 2026 study led by Haini Zhang tests a wearable fix. The research article evaluates advanced Cancer Vision Goggles, a headset that standardizes near-infrared fluorescence imaging during cancer surgery through a dual pointer alignment system.

Zhang and colleagues benchmarked the goggles in preclinical work and then compared them with an approved surgical imaging system in patients. The goggles matched or beat the established system on tumor contrast and kept readings steady across working distances from 10 to 60 centimeters. The authors present the headset as a route to reproducible, quantitative fluorescence-guided surgery.
pmc-13201969:
An embryonic blood vessel that should have vanished before birth persisted on both sides in a 2026 illustrative case headed by Aaron Higginbotham. The article reports bilateral persistent proatlantal intersegmental arteries in a 28-year-old woman with Down syndrome who also had moyamoya syndrome, a narrowing of major brain arteries.

She arrived with sudden severe headache and unresponsiveness, and scans showed bleeding inside the brain's ventricles with fluid blockage. A drain relieved the pressure, and careful angiography mapped the rare vessels supplying the posterior circulation, with extensive collateral networks. She got better with drainage and supportive care, and the authors stress careful vessel mapping before any bypass planning.
pmc-13202169:
Support cells around a tumor can decide whether treatment works, and a 2026 study led by Zhongjian Yu maps those cells in esophageal cancer during chemoimmunotherapy. The research article blends single-cell sequencing, immune repertoire mapping, and spatial transcriptomics on samples from nine patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Responsive tumors gained particular vessel-lining cells and fibroblasts at their borders, with more killer T cells. Resistant tumors instead built a collagen-rich niche driven by a growth factor signal, pairing vessel cells with matrix-making fibroblasts that shut down immune attack. Blocking the key receptor made treatment work better in preclinical models, which points to stromal targeting as a partner plan for chemoimmunotherapy.
pmc-13205569:
An elbow tumor that broke the bone becomes the route for its own cure in a 2026 case report by Toshio Kojima. The article describes a giant cell tumor of the olecranon, an extremely rare site for this locally aggressive bone tumor, complicated by a displaced pathological fracture through the joint surface.

Surgeons worked through the fracture gap to scrape out the lesion thoroughly, then reduced the joint, grafted synthetic bone, and fixed it with a plate. Pathology confirmed the tumor type after surgery on the removed tissue. The patient was pain-free with full elbow motion at nine months and remained free of recurrence ten years later.
pmc-13205969:
Mirfat Elkashif and four colleagues test whether moral courage links a hospital's ethical climate to nurses' environmental health literacy. They surveyed 743 Egyptian nurses across government, private, and university hospitals. They measured how nurses saw the ethical climate and their moral courage, plus their self-reported knowledge of environmental health and sustainability.

The three measures were strongly linked to each other. Ethical climate explained about three quarters of the variation in environmental health literacy. Moral courage carried about a third of that link in statistical terms, though the direct path stayed larger. The authors suggest hospitals build supportive ethical climates and train moral courage together, if they want nursing practice that responds to climate issues. The study is cross-sectional and self-reported, so it shows a link rather than skill or behavior.
pmc-13206169:
Geovana Guedes Silvestre led a large team that shared a study in twenty twenty-six. It is about a bacterial natural product. The product kills drug-resistant melanoma cells. It does so by wrecking their redox balance. The product is Saquayamycin B1. It was purified from a Streptomyces strain. The team tested it on four melanoma cell lines. Its potency landed in the low micromolar range.

An antioxidant rescue experiment proved a key point. The killing runs through reactive oxygen. Cells treated in advance survived the dose. The compound drained the cells' glutathione reserves. It raised superoxide and nitric oxide too. Docking simulations pointed at two glutathione-handling enzymes as binding partners. Dynamics simulations confirmed one stable grip. The authors present oxidative sabotage as a viable angle. It is an angle on melanomas that shrug off conventional drugs.
pmc-13210369:
Trading crypto around the clock can become compulsive, and a 2026 survey study led by Dar Meshi ties that pattern to poorer mental health. The cross-sectional research article checks problematic cryptoasset trading alongside depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and social isolation in 239 adults who trade digital assets.

Regression models that accounted for demographic gaps supported the authors' hypotheses on all three outcomes. People scoring higher on problematic trading also noted stronger depression and anxiety symptoms in the survey responses. They likewise noted greater social isolation, and the authors discuss what the pattern means for future research and for clinicians who encounter trading-related harm.
pmc-13213569:
Xinghua Li, Zhongchen Bai, Qixin Chen, and Zhengping Zhang improve in 2026 a fully inorganic perovskite solar cell by treating both faces of its light-absorbing layer at once. Energy mismatches at those boundaries waste voltage and weaken performance.

One additive at the carbon contact lifted an energy level and cut wasteful recombination, raising voltage. A fluoride salt at the oxide contact improved crystal growth and boosted the fill factor, a measure of output quality. The tuned cell converted sunlight at just under ten percent efficiency with unusually high voltage for its type. A two-diode model matched the experiments and assigns each gain to its boundary, guiding future designs.
pmc-13215369:
Lesley Charles and colleagues evaluate in 2026 online training that teaches clinicians how to judge whether a patient can make their own decisions. Such capacity assessments fall to doctors, nurses, and social workers, and demand for flexible training keeps rising.

Staff in an Alberta health region worked through thirteen modules covering fifteen core concepts, answering tests before and after. Every post-test rating rose significantly, and the gains matched those from earlier face-to-face workshops, even though online learners started and ended with higher self-ratings. Self-reported knowledge is not observed skill, the design implies, yet the result supports online modules as a practical way to spread this specialised training widely.
pmc-13216169:
Philipp Lulla and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of 3D-printed stainless steel aortic stents, testing whether the material is safe against blood and living cells. Printed stents could be tailored to a patient's aorta far faster than standard stock allows.

Samples of 316L steel were printed by laser powder bed fusion, then etched, polished, heat-treated, or expanded in various combinations. Heat treatment alone raised tensile strength from about 585 to 695 megapascals. In cell and blood tests the finished material was not toxic to fibroblasts, barely damaged red blood cells, and attracted only sparse immune cells and platelets. The authors judge the printed, surface-treated steel a credible candidate for personalized stent production.
pmc-13216369:
Yin Xu and Hui Zhang report a two thousand twenty-six randomized trial on preserving jawbone after tooth extraction. The trial compared a graft made from the patient's own treated tooth dentin against a bovine bone product. Fifty patients needing one tooth removed took part.

Scans at set points tracked how much ridge width and height were lost. Bone samples at six months showed tissue-level healing. The dentin graft lost more width early at one level, but by six months the groups matched. Dental readers get a fair head-to-head test of recycling a patient's own tooth as graft material.
pmc-13218169:
Anita E. Weidmann and colleagues mine ten years of Icelandic hospital data for links between medicines, patient traits, and delirium, in a 2026 cohort study of hospital records. Delirium, a sudden state of confusion, prolongs admissions and raises the risk of death, and many prescribed drugs are suspected triggers. The National University Hospital of Iceland dataset covered admissions from 2010 to 2020.

The cohort held 55,495 patients, of whom 3,533 were diagnosed with delirium at least once. Patients with delirium were far more likely to take ten or more medicines. They were also more often prescribed proton pump inhibitors, opioids, certain antibiotics, anticoagulants, statins, and selective beta-blockers. No clear link appeared for tricyclic antidepressants or type 1 diabetes. Delirium came with longer stays, more readmissions, and higher mortality, and about a quarter of affected patients were diagnosed again in a later admission. The authors stress how many factors feed delirium, making it hard to prevent.
pmc-13221069:
Shu Hui Huang and Kerri Kobryn report a 2026 finding on how little change an enzyme needs to switch jobs entirely. They studied TelA, a bacterial enzyme that normally resolves hairpin ends on linear DNA. Earlier work needed complex edits to turn TelA into a recombinase, an enzyme that swaps DNA segments.

Changing just two aspartic acid residues proved enough to flip that activity. The simpler switch clarifies which parts of the protein lock in its normal role. It also hints that related enzymes sit close to new functions in evolutionary terms. Such minimal switches interest researchers who design enzymes and those tracing how DNA-handling proteins evolved.
pmc-13226669:
Leonardo Placidi and co-authors release a 2026 dataset called MNISQ for training machine-learning systems on quantum circuits. Today's quantum machines are noisy and small, which makes shared benchmark data valuable. The collection holds 4.95 million circuits of ten qubits, built from encoded versions of a classic handwritten-digit dataset, and ships as both quantum circuits and text descriptions.

Baseline tests classified circuits with quantum kernel methods reaching up to ninety-seven percent accuracy. Classical language-style models reading the text format also performed well, led by one architecture at seventy-seven percent, rising with data augmentation. Experiments with added noise support work on error mitigation, and the dataset is publicly posted for reuse.
pmc-13227369:
Lieying Xu, Wei Deng, Zhuoer Xu, and Hong Ren review a 2026 imaging literature on using cardiac MRI to assess heart damage from prolonged heavy drinking. Alcohol-related injury stretches the heart muscle and weakens its squeeze, sometimes ending in heart failure. Magnetic resonance scanning measures chamber sizes and function precisely while also visualising tissue changes directly.

Sequences within the scan can reveal swelling, inflammation, and scarring inside the muscle, stages that ordinary ultrasound often misses. The review weighs how those capabilities support early diagnosis, accurate staging of structural and functional abnormality, and sorting patients by likely outcome. The goal is a firmer evidence base for catching the condition early enough for timely treatment to matter.
pmc-13229369:
Brendan Boyle and co-authors test a 2026 organisational model of how authentic leadership, leaders being true to their values, encourages team members to go beyond their job descriptions. The proposed route runs through team identification: members help the team more when they feel part of it. Two recall experiments with working professionals, then a field survey of sixty healthcare teams, tested the chain and its limits.

The mediated path held only where members' professional identity was weak. In multidisciplinary teams whose members strongly identify with their own profession, authentic leadership did not raise citizenship behaviour through team belonging. That boundary condition helps explain earlier mixed findings and warns leaders that strong professional tribes can absorb or block team-level influence.
pmc-13230569:
Mohammed Asiri and colleagues describe in 2026 a magnetic catalyst that carries palladium for joining carbon-based molecules. Iron oxide particles coated with silica hold a palladium complex tied to the surface through linker groups. A full battery of lab methods checked structure, shape, magnetism, and surface area of the finished powder.

In Suzuki coupling tests, a standard way to link aromatic building blocks, the catalyst worked with high activity. A magnet could pull the particles back out of the mixture after each run. Reuse over several cycles kept performance strong, with little palladium leaking into the product. Bridging dissolved catalysts and solid catalysts this way may cut metal waste in fine chemical making.
pmc-13231169:
Azusa Maruoka and colleagues report in 2026 a man whose thyroid pattern pointed to a hidden adrenal problem. The fifty-eight-year-old had painless thyroiditis, which usually floods the blood with the storage hormone T4 ahead of its active partner T3. His tests broke that pattern, with high T3 while T4 stayed in the normal range.

Further checks found his pituitary gland failed to send the signal that drives cortisol release. Low cortisol may have sped conversion of T4 into T3, which would explain the flipped ratio. After hormone treatment raised cortisol, the ratio fell back toward normal. A high T3 share in destructive thyroiditis, the authors suggest, should prompt a search for adrenal failure.
pmc-13231269:
