Geoffrey McGregor and colleagues propose in 2026 a sampling method for probability landscapes with thin crowded ridges. pmc-13258069:

pmc-13258169:

pmc-13258669:

pmc-13258769:

pmc-13259969:

pmc-13260169:

pmc-13261369:

pmc-13261569:

pmc-13261969:

pmc-13262169:

pmc-13262269:

pmc-13262569:

pmc-13262669:

Antibodies against a protein called SEZ6L2 cause the illness, but reports were scattered. The team studied one patient in depth and reviewed all published cases to build a fuller picture.

pmc-13263569:

They note the population had lacked solid pediatric evidence until now.
pmc-13263769:

pmc-13264069:

Graphite sharply raised conductivity, so charging and release became faster. The composite stayed stable through many heating and cooling cycles, with low supercooling. The authors present it as a candidate for low-temperature logistics where steady cooling matters.
pmc-13264369:

pmc-13264769:

pmc-13264869:

pmc-13265869:

pmc-13266169:

pmc-13266369:

pmc-13266469:

pmc-13266869:

pmc-13267569:

pmc-13269169:

pmc-13270069:

pmc-13270169:

pmc-13270869:

pmc-13272169:

pmc-13272269:

pmc-13272369:

pmc-13272569:

pmc-13273169:

pmc-13273869:

pmc-13274169:

pmc-13274369:

pmc-13274969:

pmc-13275769:

pmc-13276069:

pmc-13276469:

pmc-13276569:

pmc-13276769:

pmc-13276869:

pmc-13277769:

All of them reached the standard sharp-vision line, compared with about seventy-two percent under the usual chart. Safety scores were equal, and several measures of optical distortion were lower with the new chart. The authors call it more predictable for high short-sightedness.
pmc-13278369:
Benjamin Heyman and colleagues present a 2026 real-world study of drug pairs for a blood cancer that came back or stopped responding to care. The cancer is chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The team reviewed 98 patients treated at UC San Diego from 2012 to 2024. All got venetoclax, a targeted drug, alone or with a second drug.

Paired treatment beat venetoclax alone. Full remission and no detectable leftover disease were most common when the second drug was obinutuzumab. Over a median follow-up of fifty-two months, time without disease growth was longer for paired groups: about seventy-seven months versus about fifty-nine for single-drug care. The results back paired care in daily practice, most of all for high-risk patients.
pmc-13278969:
Baskaran Chinnappan and colleagues measure two blood proteins in women with chronic fatigue syndrome in a 2026 study. ME/CFS causes disabling fatigue and thinking problems with no reliable blood test. Epstein-Barr virus has long been suspected as a trigger in some patients.

Serum from forty patients was compared with matched healthy controls for interleukin-11. A smaller set was tested for MMP-9, an enzyme that remodels tissue. Both proteins ran significantly higher in patients than in controls. Mast cells grown in the lab released large amounts of MMP-9 when exposed to a viral protein. The authors suggest this trio of mast cells and two proteins deserves study as a disease mechanism and marker source.
pmc-13279169:
Hiraku Misawa and colleagues report a 2026 case of a kidney infection found with a gentle scan method. The illness is acute focal bacterial nephritis, a germ infection in one part of the kidney. It sits between a broad kidney infection and an abscess, a pocket of pus. Their patient first had right low belly pain that looked like appendicitis, an inflamed appendix.

A first belly ultrasound scan raised doubt for the kidney illness. Contrast enhanced ultrasound, which uses tiny bubbles to boost the scan image, then proved the diagnosis. The method avoids radiation and harsh dye that can hurt kidneys. The authors present it as a safe stand in for contrast CT scans in like cases, where CT means detailed X ray scans.
pmc-13279369:
Tae Hoon Kang and colleagues report a 2026 study of neck spine fusion spacers. The surgery, ACDF, removes a worn neck disc and fuses the bones with a plate. Spacers made of bioactive glass ceramic, a bone friendly glass mix, fuse by surface bond to bone. Usual spacers hold a centre hole for bone graft, which may weaken the part.

Charts covered seventeen patients with solid spacers and seventeen with hole spacers. At one year, pain and function gains were alike in both groups. Fusion rates by motion checks were alike as well, near ninety two percent for solid and near eighty five percent for hole types. Bone bond checks leaned to the solid type. A centre hole may not be needed for this spacer class.
pmc-13279569:
Akin A. Adio and colleagues report a 2026 study of nicotine use without tobacco and collar bone surgery. Tobacco use is known to slow bone healing and raise side effects. What nicotine alone does, from vaping, patches or gum, was unclear. The surgery joins a broken clavicle, or collar bone, with plates and screws. The team used a large national health database.

Patients with non tobacco nicotine dependence were matched by score to patients with no nicotine use. They were also matched to patients with tobacco dependence. A second check split breaks by site, mid shaft or outer end. Outcomes at ninety days and one year held medical side effects, bone healing issues and opioid drug counts. The title states the core find: non tobacco nicotine dependence went with more side effects after fixation. The split from smoke matters for pre surgery advice.
pmc-13279669:
Njood Alwadei reports a 2026 case of a liver disease that first looked like a blood disease in a child. The disease is progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type three, a rare inherited liver illness. It stems from faults in the ABCB4 gene and often shows later in childhood. Cholestasis means bile flow from the liver is blocked or slowed. Their patient was a four year old girl.

She came in with anemia, a large liver and spleen, and repeat bleeding. First checks chased blood causes. Scans then showed high pressure in the liver veins with swollen veins in the food pipe. Gene tests found two copies of a harmful ABCB4 change, which proved the liver diagnosis. The case warns that long liver disease can mask as blood disease, and early liver checks can prevent grave bleeds.
pmc-13280969:
Lillie K Pennington and colleagues reviewed two decades of plant rebirth studies in a 2026 paper. In such studies, seeds saved years ago are grown beside seeds from their own offspring lines. Same soil and light let scholars split true gene change from mere bend to conditions. The team gathered sixty-one studies and ran pooled math on forty-six of them. Most used short-lived plants in North America and Europe.

More than half the cases showed fast gene change in just years or decades. The change often helped plants cope, not just drift. Short-lived plants changed more than long-lived ones. Offspring lines tended to flower sooner and grow greedier leaves. Under dry stress, both kinds flowered sooner, a dodge from drought. The authors say quick evolution is common, and dry times push it hard.
pmc-13281769:
Hongliang Gao and colleagues traced a cholesterol enzyme's role in liver cancer in a 2026 study. Liver cancer often rewires how the body handles fats. The enzyme helps package cholesterol for transport in blood. The team mined large cancer databases and checked paired patient samples. They also bred mice whose livers lacked the enzyme and exposed them to a cancer trigger. Cell tests in a dish filled out the picture.

The enzyme ran low in liver tumors, and low levels tracked with worse survival. Mice without it in the liver grew cancer more readily. A growth signal path was switched on in those livers. In dish tests, cutting the enzyme made cancer cells grow, move, and invade more. Its level also tracked with how many immune cells entered tumors. The authors say losing this enzyme helps liver cancer take hold, a clue for future drug hunts.
pmc-13281869:
Gayane von Schoen-Angerer and colleagues reviewed ten years of a liver cancer procedure in a 2026 study. The procedure threads a tube into the liver's artery to deliver chemo and block blood flow. It is standard for mid-stage liver cancer. The Swiss center treated one hundred ninety-five patients from 2013 to 2023. Most had early- or mid-stage disease. The team tracked survival and time before growth returned, split by stage.

Half the patients lived past fifty-six months, well beyond older reports. Early-stage patients went fifteen months before growth, against nine for mid-stage. Changing plan within the first month marked worse outcomes. Patients who later got cure-aimed care lived markedly longer. The authors credit a single expert center and team-based choices. They argue the procedure can serve some early patients who cannot have surgery or heat ablation.
pmc-13282169:
Nwanyieze Ngozi Jiakponnah and co-authors present a 2026 study of missed heart and metabolism disease in adults at higher risk of dementia. They looked at high blood pressure and abnormal blood sugar that tests showed but patients had never been told about. Four groups, totalling up to seven thousand adults aged forty and over, came from Nigeria, Kenya, and two United States sites.

Missed diagnoses were widespread in the African groups. High fasting blood sugar was linked to poorer thinking test scores in Kenya and in North Texas. Severe high blood pressure and diabetes were linked in North Texas to blood markers tied to Alzheimer's disease. Patterns differed by place, shaped by local care access and social factors. The authors argue that finding and treating these hidden risks could be a practical path to lowering dementia risk in these populations.
pmc-13282269:
Bibek Pramanik and co-authors describe a 2026 materials study on a hybrid coating that resists viruses on surfaces. The coating mixes a cage-like nanomaterial, shortened to POSS, with stearic acid, a common fatty acid. Single-material antiviral coatings often wear out or lose effect quickly. The hybrid's cage frame adds strength and stability, while its water-repelling surface discourages germs from sticking.

Tests used a human coronavirus and a type A flu virus, both spread through surfaces and air. The hybrid coating repelled water more strongly than either ingredient alone. Viruses attached less to coated surfaces, and their ability to infect fell sharply, suggesting the coating may also neutralise them directly. The authors present the material as a promising way to cut surface spread of respiratory viruses. Such coatings could serve hospitals, transport, and public spaces if durability holds up in real use.
pmc-13282369:
Stephanie Pitt and co-authors present a 2026 study on wholegrain intake and breast cancer risk in a large Swedish cohort of women. Findings in past research conflicted, so the team used long-term diet data. More than thirty-six thousand women, aged forty-eight to eighty-three, reported their diets at two time points. The analysis judged adherence to the 2023 Nordic nutrition recommendations for wholegrains.

Over a mean follow-up of sixteen and a half years, one thousand nine hundred seventy-nine breast cancers appeared. Women with full long-term adherence, at least ninety grams daily, had lower total breast cancer risk than long-term low adherers. The link held mainly for hormone receptor-positive cancers, a type fuelled by hormones. No single wholegrain product showed a clear link on its own.
pmc-13282469:
Elie Ghadban led a 2026 survey of Lebanese dietitians on body image worries, eating attitudes, and focused eating. Focused eating means paying close attention while eating. The study asked whether that habit weakens the link between worry about looks and poor eating attitudes in this group.

A total of 215 dietitians filled in a self-report survey with three standard scales, and the team tested for a moderating effect. Focused eating did soften the link. Worry about looks tied more strongly to poor eating attitudes when focused eating was low or average. The authors urge care in reading the results, since the design captures one point in time and the sample was mostly young women.
pmc-13282669:
Hamada and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their randomised trial of a warm-up program for adolescent golfers, published in 2025. The trial had tested whether a golf-specific low back pain prevention warm-up, called GLEP, beat a sham program in young golfers. The correction states that errors appeared in data reported in the Results and Discussion sections, and in Tables 1, 2, and 3 of the original article.

Corrected tables republish the baseline traits of the two groups, twenty-three in the warm-up group and twenty-two in the sham group. They also republish response rates for twelve weeks of self-reported records, golf activity, and how often warm-ups were actually performed. The notice fixes the record so readers use the right numbers when judging the trial. It does not, in the text shown, restate whether the trial's headline conclusion about back pain changed.
pmc-13284269:
Every large macular hole closed after a simplified flap surgery in a 2026 series by Beata Bajdik and colleagues. Macular holes blur central vision, and large ones resist standard repair. Their method flips an inner membrane flap over the hole with wider peeling.

Forty-two eyes from forty patients entered the consecutive case series. Holes split into large, extra-large, and extra-extra-large groups by width. All eyes achieved the best closure type after surgery in follow-up. Favored closure shapes grew rarer as hole size rose across groups. Vision and retinal layer defects improved over time in every group. Starting vision predicted final vision best.
pmc-13284369:
Naglaa W. Abdelbaky and co-authors test a cell-based treatment for liver scarring in rats in a 2026 animal study. The treatment used exosomes from bone marrow stem cells that had first been treated with melatonin. Rats with liver fibrosis from carbon tetrachloride got the exosomes by vein twice a week for four weeks.

Treated rats showed better liver enzyme and albumin levels, plus stronger antioxidant markers such as SOD activity and Nrf2. Harmful markers linked to swelling, cell death, and scarring fell, and tissue checks showed less collagen and less inflamed tissue. The findings suggest melatonin priming may boost the healing value of stem cell exosomes, though the work stays at the animal stage.
pmc-13284469:
Constanza Carolina Torres Montenegro and co-authors describe family and social life in a 2026 Colombian study of older adults with heart failure who take their drugs poorly. The cross-sectional study enrolled 125 adults aged 60 and older in a heart failure program in Santander between late 2025 and early 2026. Family function was scored with the APGAR tool, and outside ties were mapped across eight domains.

Median age was 73 years, and most participants lived with others and had a family caregiver, the authors report. Normal family function was found in about two thirds, while severe dysfunction was rare but linked to living alone, no caregiver, and many drugs. Strong ties centered on health, community, and faith, while work and education ties were weak.
pmc-13284569:
Yeon Ji Kim reviewed in 2026, in a Korean-language commentary, a new triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori, the stomach bacterium tied to ulcers and gastric cancer. Standard triple therapy has slipped below eighty percent success as clarithromycin resistance spreads, pushing guidelines toward four-drug bismuth regimens. The commentary examines the EVEREST-HP phase 3 trial run at forty Chinese centres.

The trial randomly assigned 700 untreated patients to fourteen days of rifasutenizol, a new drug fusing two antibacterial actions in one molecule, plus amoxicillin and rabeprazole, or to a bismuth four-drug comparator. Eradication reached 92 percent against about 88 percent, meeting the non-inferiority goal, and the new regimen looked stronger in multi-resistant infections on later analysis. Side effects were reported less often with the new pairing. Kim presents the simpler regimen as a meaningful future option.
pmc-13284869:
Yen Nguyen Le and co-authors present a 2026 case report of stomach twisting in a baby with a rare vein and organ pattern. A 13-month-old boy with right isomerism, a single heart ventricle, and no spleen came in with vomiting after feeds. Scans showed the portal vein running in front of the bowel outlet, and contrast study confirmed a twisted stomach.

Surgery untwisted the stomach, bypassed the blocked outlet ahead of the vein, and fixed the stomach in place. Recovery was smooth, and the child stayed symptom-free at nine months. The authors call this the first report of this pairing and link risk to missing stomach ligaments plus vein-related blockage.
pmc-13284969:
Birk M. Grønfeldt and co-authors give a 2026 systematic review of trial reporting for exercise therapy after total knee replacement. Early registration of a main outcome guards against selective reporting. The team searched four databases for randomized trials from 2000 to 2024 and checked registration timing, outcome clarity, and bias risk.

Ninety-four trials with 9,396 patients were included. Only thirteen were registered ahead of time, while many were registered late or not at all, and few named one clear main outcome. Effect sizes were near zero in the early-registered group but much larger in late or unregistered trials. Early-registered trials also showed lower bias risk and better reporting of dropouts and harms.
pmc-13285269:
Lucas Evangelista Marques and co-authors write a letter, published in 2026, proposing a better culture method for skin infections from nontuberculous mycobacteria. These germs often resist standard drugs and cause slow, varied skin lesions after cosmetic or surgical care. Weak culture yield delays the right diagnosis, since loads in skin are low.

The team tested a mild cleaning step with cetylpyridinium chloride on eleven biopsies from patients at a São Paulo clinic, against two standard harsh methods in partner labs. Their method grew the germs from five of eleven samples, beating both comparison labs in this small set. The authors offer the protocol as a repeatable routine to cut delays in skin diagnosis.
pmc-13286069:
Ji-Hyeon Lee and Sun-Young Jung build a scale for digital leadership among clinical nurses in a 2026 validation study. Ward nurses now guide patients and teams through records, scanners, and new apps, yet no tested tool measured that side of their work. Drawing on interviews and past research, the pair drafted items and put them through expert review and pilot checks.

The final scale holds 29 items under four heads: skill with digital tools, guarding digital safety, a teamwork mindset, and sway within the organization. Answers came from 446 nurses, and split-half checks confirmed the four-part shape held up well. Scores matched closely with two related scales for tech skill and self-leadership, which supports the tool's soundness. Nurse leaders can now gauge and grow digital strengths with a measure built for the ward.
pmc-13286269:
Lucie Khamvongsa-Charbonnier and co-authors read the fly heart's answer to rich diets in a 2026 study of diabetic heart disease. Fruit flies on heavy sugar or fat develop clogged, faltering hearts much like diabetic patients do, making them a cheap stand-in for the human condition. The team scanned heart gene activity under both diets to find which switches the organ flips to cope.

Genes for one-carbon chemistry, sugar handling, and metabolite transport all shifted, and follow-up tests marked them as real coping tools rather than noise. A satiety hormone called Fit stood out as a heart-made signal: it tunes beating from inside the heart and also reaches outward to damp feeding. The picture casts the heart as a gland of its own, both defending itself and warning the body when rich food piles up.
pmc-13286769:
Chong Wang, Lili Lv, and Rongrong Ma test a simple blood ratio as a survival predictor in older patients who cannot swallow safely and need tube feeding. The 2026 analysis reuses data from 248 patients, average age 83, collected at one center between 2014 and 2017. The ratio divides lymphocyte counts by C-reactive protein, joining immune strength and inflammation in one figure.

Higher ratios meant lower death risk. Patients in the top third of the ratio had about half the risk of those in the bottom third, and median survival lengthened across the thirds. The advantage was strongest for predicting death within a year and faded over longer horizons. The authors propose checking the ratio early to flag fragile patients.
pmc-13286869:
Hamid Bashiri and Maryam Mohebiniya report surgical handling of an outsized jaw cyst tied to an extra tooth in a 2026 case report. Dentigerous cysts grow around the crowns of teeth that never erupt, ranking second among cysts of tooth origin. Their link to supernumerary teeth, extra teeth beyond the normal set, is uncommon, and this one reached unusual size in the patient's right upper jaw.

Cone-beam scanning mapped the cyst and the buried extra tooth before surgery. The team removed the lesion and its associated tooth, and the report presents the outcome as a successful resolution. Such cases remind clinicians that a silent, slow swelling can hide a large cyst around a tooth that was never supposed to exist. Three-dimensional imaging earns its place in planning the removal.
pmc-13287069:
Nasser M. Alzain and co-authors report a 43-year-old man with bipolar I disorder who flipped from deep depression into full mania shortly after starting lurasidone, a drug approved to treat bipolar depression. The 2026 case report traces a paradoxical reaction that clinicians call a manic switch. His background mood stabilizer level was far below the therapeutic range when treatment began.

Within a week of dose increases his energy rose and sleep shrank. By week two he was euphoric, irritable, intrusive, and sleeping an hour or two nightly. Stopping lurasidone, restoring his stabilizer dose, and restarting a second antipsychotic settled him, and he left hospital stable. Close watching during the first weeks of such treatment is the lesson.
pmc-13287169:
Serena Zheng and colleagues checked in 2026 whether hormone markers measured in a breast tumour still match when cancer reaches nearby lymph nodes. They studied women with early, node-positive disease who had surgery first and gene testing on the main tumour between 2016 and 2020.

Archived node tissue was available for 73 patients. At least one marker differed in 77% of cases, most often for HER2, usually by a small amount. No node sample became strongly HER2 positive. Larger tumours and larger node deposits went with bigger HER2 shifts. The gene score itself was not clearly tied to mismatch, so node testing may still add useful information.
pmc-13287269:
R-Y Yang and colleagues compared a sensor pad placed under a mattress in 2026 with machine data from patients using airway pressure therapy at home for sleep apnoea. Seventy-five patients contributed 480 nights. Fourteen also had full home sleep testing on the same nights.

The pad recorded longer sleep than the machine's use time, at 437.4 against 395.6 minutes. It also counted far more breathing events than the machine reported as remaining. Against full sleep testing, pad counts sat much closer to the reference. The authors present pad monitoring as a fuller picture of treated sleep. It may help review during the early weeks of therapy.
pmc-13287969:
Yu-Xuan Liu and co-authors introduce HybSuite, a software pipeline for plant evolutionary studies, in a 2026 paper. Hybrid capture sequencing pulls out chosen DNA regions, but turning raw reads into family trees takes many processing steps. Each step invites errors and file confusion, especially for researchers new to bioinformatics. HybSuite wraps the whole chain into one modular Bash-based workflow.

The pipeline starts with downloading reads from a public archive and ends with species tree building. Middle steps cover trimming, assembly, and handling duplicate gene copies that can distort trees. The team tested it by rebuilding the family tree of the Elaeagnaceae plant family with a standard probe set. A second test used one hundred single-copy genes from Arabidopsis. HybSuite runs on Linux and Mac systems and is freely shared online for reuse.
pmc-13288569:
Mohamed R Asaad, Essam F El-Hashash, and Ahmed R M Ridwan field-test faba bean lines under heat in a 2026 Egyptian study. Nine genotypes grew over two years at two locations, each under normal and heat-stress conditions, while the team recorded seed and straw yields plus related traits and applied stress tolerance indices.

Heat cut seed yield and most other traits, and genotypes differed widely across years and sites. Nubaria 3, Giza 843, and Giza 429 flowered early and yielded best under stress, and several indices, including mean productivity and the stress tolerance index, picked out high yielders under both conditions. Yield traits moved together closely, so direct selection looks workable. The three leading lines could seed short-season breeding for hotter conditions.
pmc-13288769:
Faiza Yasin and colleagues study moments of deep connection between cancer doctors and patients in 2026. The authors call these sacred moments, brief encounters that leave both sides feeling truly seen. Earlier work in other fields linked them to career fulfillment and stronger trust. Their mixed-methods study was the first to examine them in medical oncology. Interviews and questionnaires were gathered at a national cancer center.

Twenty-four clinicians and ten patients took part, and every participant reported having lived such a moment. All clinicians said the moments left them fulfilled, connected, and reminded of their purpose. Patients reported full trust in their teams and a strong sense of being cared for. Interviews pointed to turning points such as diagnosis or end of life as common sparks. Learning who the patient is beyond the cancer helped create the moments.
pmc-13288869:
Vanessa da Conceicao Onofre Monteiro and colleagues study fever care in Mozambique in 2026. Their work uses focus groups and interviews. Four facilities in Maputo and Quelimane took part. Sixty people joined in all. Health staff numbered 28 of them. Community members numbered 32.

Clinicians named lung infections as top fever causes. Malaria, gut disease, and COVID-19 also featured. Usual care ran screening, malaria tests, then drugs. Antimalarial use fell after training. Community members start with home remedies. Traditional cures also come first. Late arrival stems from poor trust. Long waits, beliefs, and drug shortages count too. Non-malarial fever care stays the weak point.
pmc-13288969:
Wondossen Teklesilassie Geberemariam studies birth control right after delivery in Ethiopia. His 2026 survey covers public hospitals in Addis Ababa. It ran from February to March 2021. Staff asked 336 new mothers set questions. The method was a coil placed just after birth.

Only 42 women accepted the coil. That is 12.5 percent of the group. Job type shaped who said yes. Private staff and day laborers said yes more. Students said yes most of all. Higher monthly pay also raised the odds. The authors want clear teaching for mothers. They also want more training for health staff.
pmc-13289069:
Mohammed Abdullah Al Amad leads a 2026 heart screen of school children in Yemen. The study ran in Taiz Governorate. It used heart ultrasound in schools. Children aged 5 to 15 took part. The goal was to find rheumatic heart disease.

In all, 4,135 children were screened. Disease hit 55.9 per 1,000 children. Clear cases made up 9.9 per 1,000. Borderline cases made up the rest. Girls and rural children bore higher rates. Thin children also bore higher rates. Caregiver knowledge was low, at 36 percent. The authors urge a national control plan. School screens and penicillin access lead it.
pmc-13289369:
Chris Painter and coauthors present a 2026 cost study on bedside tests for fever without malaria in Lao PDR. In low-resource clinics, quick point-of-care tests often fill gaps left by weak labs, but use is uneven and some tests are poor or pricey. The authors modeled which tests for outpatients give best value, assuming top-quality versions.

A decision tree compared testing with clinical judgment alone, from both clinic and wider social views, including future resistance costs from antibiotic use. Tests for dengue and for rickettsia came out most cost-effective in both main and chance-based runs. Tests for typhoid and leptospirosis looked good in fixed runs but lost ground when uncertainty was modeled fully.
pmc-13289469:
Yuhang Zhang and co-authors link a RNA-reading protein to serine fuel use in thyroid cancer, in a 2026 study. Thyroid cancers that spread have few good treatments. Tumor cells often boost production of serine, an amino acid that feeds growth. The team measured the protein IGF2BP2 in tumor and normal tissue, then raised or lowered it in two thyroid cancer cell lines. A mouse model tested the pathway in living tissue.

IGF2BP2 ran high in tumors, rose with stage, and marked poorer outlooks for patients. Lowering it slowed cell growth, movement, and serine production. Adding serine back partly rescued the growth defect, tying the protein to fuel supply. The protein stabilizes the message for PHGDH, the first enzyme of serine making, through a chemical mark called m6A. Restoring PHGDH also partly rescued growth. Mouse tumors confirmed that the pair drives thyroid cancer formation.
pmc-13289769:
Hans Chinomso Chris-Uchendu and colleagues critically review a 2026 topic on lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injected HIV prevention drug that blocks the viral capsid. Trial success has been near perfect, sparking hope for reshaping prevention. The authors warn that where the drug goes in tissue, how long its tail lasts, and resistance risk deserve closer scrutiny before wide rollout.

No published human data yet measure drug levels in mucosal sites where infection starts, despite a tissue trial registered years ago. Modeling sets a protective blood level, yet the slow fade after stopping creates a window of 106 to 235 days where mutants could be selected as reported. Gaps between blood and tissue protection frame the caution.
pmc-13289869:
Constance Bwire and coauthors present a 2026 real-time survey on air pollution effects for youth in Delhi and Dhaka. Both cities rank among the world's most polluted, with fine particle levels persistently high. The study compared symptoms, well-being, and daily disruption on high-pollution days versus clean-air days, and gathered youth ideas for cleaner air management.

Digital surveys ran on set January and March dates in 2025 in both cities, reaching 814 eligible respondents aged 13 to 29 plus parents. High-pollution days brought more itchy eyes, breathing trouble, headaches, skin irritation, and stomach upset in reports. Sleep and daily routines also suffered on dirty days in the data.
pmc-13289969:
Patricia Mester and colleagues close a malignant bowel-to-vagina fistula with a heart device in a 2026 case report. A fistula is an abnormal channel between organs, and cancer is the most common cause of this type. The patient was a 44-year-old woman with advanced pseudomyxoma peritonei and many prior abdominal operations. She presented with fecal discharge through the vagina, and imaging confirmed the channel.

Given her surgical history, the team chose an endoscopic route through the vagina. A clip device could not grip the scarred tissue, and the defect was large for stitching. They cauterized the edges, passed a guidewire across, and deployed a ten-millimeter Amplatzer septal occluder, a disc device built for heart holes. No complications followed in the first day. One week later the device sat stably in healing tissue, and the discharge had fully stopped.
pmc-13290769:
AI-generated recap podcasts kept therapy clients more engaged between sessions in a 2026 feasibility study by Emily Peake and colleagues. Their tool, Talkcast, lets therapists create personalized audio episodes that reinforce what a session covered, aiming at the homework gap in psychotherapy.

Over five months on a large virtual therapy platform, 46.27% of 6,032 active providers generated at least one episode, and 12.97% of clients received one, with about half of recipients opening it. Providers rated over 90% of episodes they scored as helpful, and 76.02% of client ratings agreed, praising personal relevance. Opening an episode tracked with higher engagement on every platform metric. Users asked for sharper content and a more authentic AI voice. Peake and colleagues call the tool promising and feasible, with causality still to prove.
pmc-13290969:
Pujan Shrestha, Yijia Fan, and Jason T. George offer a 2026 modeling study on how to infer hidden tumor size from signals released into the body. Their focus is early or treated cancer, where tumor cell numbers can be tiny and hard to measure directly, so markers such as circulating tumor DNA act as noisy stand-ins.

A coupled system links tumor and immune cell dynamics with marker release driven by cell death. Two kinds of random noise cover low-count wobble near detection limits and proportional wobble at higher levels. The authors derive formulas for marker paths and for the time needed to cross a detection threshold. Their work shows how tumor mix, immune pressure, and noise shape whether a marker appears and lasts.
pmc-13291169:
Fire smoke may shape lung cancer patterns in Brazil. Saulo Brito Silva leads a 2026 area-level study in São Paulo State. Lung gland cancer has risen even as smoking fell. The team asked if biomass burning helps explain that shift.

Registry data held 51,580 lung cancer cases from 2000 to 2023. Gland cancers made up just over one third. Areas with rising gland shares also saw more wildfires. Fine smoke peaks tracked fire counts very closely. The São Paulo metro area broke the pattern, with high smoke but few fires. Such area data cannot prove cause for one person. Still, the link merits closer health watch.
pmc-13291269:
Antibiotics in infancy may raise asthma risk through fungi. Erik van Tilburg Bernardes leads a 2026 study of the infant gut. Bacteria loss after antibiotics is well known. Effects on gut fungi were barely studied before.

Babies given antibiotics showed more gut fungi. One yeast, Malassezia, grew out in their guts. Germ-free mouse pups then got that yeast plus defined bacteria. Yeast pups showed stronger gut immune responses. Their airways flared more under dust mite challenge. Virus challenge also hit them harder. A blood cell type drove part of this effect. Fungal growth may be a missed harm of early antibiotics.
pmc-13291369:
Listening to Quran recitation may ease labor for first-time mothers. Widad N. O. Al Kharusi leads a 2026 study at Khoula Hospital in Oman. Drug-free comfort aids are sought for safer births. Recitation is familiar and calming for Muslim women.

The study held 120 women in active labor. All were first-time mothers with single, full-term babies. Half listened to a recorded recitation during labor. The other half got a standard back massage. Pain, comfort, and blood pressure were scored before and after. Scores used rating scales and a comfort survey. The authors back recitation as part of whole-person maternity care. Cultural fit is central to the method’s appeal.
pmc-13291569:
Fiber in food may cut gallstone risk partly through blood fats. Wenli Jiang leads a 2026 study of United States survey data. Gallstones are common and diet plays a role. How blood lipids carry that diet effect was unclear.

Data covered 4,896 adults from national health surveys. Fiber intake and gallstone rates were modeled together. Seven lipid measures were tested as middle steps. Two carried a real share of the link. Good cholesterol and one risk index each mediated a slice. Other lipid measures showed no clear middle role. The diet-stone link is thus partly, not fully, lipid-based. More work must test cause over time.
pmc-13291669:
Stem cell and metabolism genes may forecast breast cancer course. Wanjun Li leads a 2026 study building a risk model from those genes. Cancer stem cells drive growth and spread. Metabolic rewiring feeds that drive further.

Gene data from a public set were crossed with two gene lists. Twelve genes survived as model members. The score sorted patients into high and low risk groups. Two outside data sets backed the score’s value. Tissue stains matched the gene patterns seen. Lymph spread and risk score each predicted outcome alone. Immune cell mixes split sharply by risk group. Drug response also differed between groups.
pmc-13292269:
Wenjing Wang and co-authors question a 2026 assumption about TIGIT, an immune checkpoint usually blamed on immune cells, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Their data place TIGIT on the tumor cells themselves. High tumor TIGIT tracked with shorter disease-free and overall survival in patients whose tumors could be removed.

Silencing TIGIT in cancer cells slowed their growth, migration, and invasion in the lab. Gene sequencing pointed toward cytokine-receptor and JAK-STAT signaling as likely routes for these effects. Because TIGIT seems to work both as an immune brake and as a tumor-intrinsic growth aid, the authors propose hitting both sides at once. The finding could matter in a cancer where five-year survival stays under 40 percent even after surgery.
pmc-13292569:
Öznur Adıgüzel Akman examines a 2026 modern anxiety in a stressed group: nomophobia, the fear of being cut off from one's phone, among mothers of children with ADHD. Eighty-nine mothers took part, 41 raising a child diagnosed with ADHD and 48 whose children had no psychiatric diagnosis. All completed questionnaires on phone fear, anxiety, and depression using the Beck inventories.

The ADHD mothers scored higher on all three measures, but the gaps never reached statistical significance. Within the whole sample, phone fear climbed alongside anxiety and, more strongly, depression. Depression alone predicted nomophobia in regression, explaining 35 percent of its variance in the model. Akman suggests phone fear might serve as a quick flag for hidden parental depression. She calls for larger, longitudinal, multicenter studies to firm the link up.
pmc-13292669:
Xiuwen Chi and colleagues built a nursing assessment tool in 2026 to help intensive care nurses in China prevent bloodstream infections tied to central venous catheters. Such infections lengthen hospital stays, raise costs, and add to deaths among very sick patients. The team wanted a tool grounded in proven practice that nurses could apply during line placement and daily care.

Work ran in three stages: talks with fifteen nurse experts, tool building with checks on how steady its scores were, and a trial with 183 registered nurses. The tool covers six themes, from how lines are placed and kept up to how infusion sets are changed and how the care setting is kept. Nurses scored it high as a whole, and most items lined up with current guidance. Units can use it to audit line care and spot weak points before infections start.
pmc-13293569:
Johannes Pohl and co-authors ask, in a 2026 focus group study, which digital measures of arm function clinicians in neurorehabilitation find truly meaningful. Motion sensors can track arm use in fine detail, yet clinics rarely adopt such metrics in daily care.

Three 90-minute groups at three Swiss centers gathered 11 clinicians, mostly physiotherapists and occupational therapists. They rated 17 motion metrics for a drinking task and 10 arm-use measures. Five themes emerged, led by basic movement traits like range, strength, and grasp that ground all reading of motion. Smoothness and real-world arm use also mattered when tied to visible tasks.
pmc-13293669:
Kevin C. Eddinger and co-authors present three emergency cases from 2026 in which a torn aorta starved internal organs of blood. In aortic dissection, the vessel wall splits into layers and the swollen false channel can squeeze the true channel shut, cutting flow to the gut and kidneys. Standard stent graft repair was not an option for these patients, so the team tried an extensive cutting of the dividing wall from inside the vessel.

The procedure, called endovascular septotomy, was performed along the chest and abdominal aorta in all three patients. Blood flow to the threatened organs was restored in each case, and follow-up imaging showed favorable healing of the aorta. The authors offer the technique as a rapid option when anatomy rules out stent grafting, a situation where few good choices exist.
pmc-13293769:
Mingyuan Xu and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, ultrasound-driven microbubble motors coated in neutrophil membrane to treat heart damage that follows restored blood flow. This reperfusion injury adds harm after a heart attack, and drugs struggle to cross vessel and cell walls to reach it.

The coating homes to inflamed tissue naturally. Ultrasound pushed the motors across the vessel wall into heart tissue, then bursting bubbles opened pores in cell membranes to deliver cyclosporine A inside. Enrichment and delivery at the injury site rose sharply with the combined strategy. The authors offer it as a precise route for cell-level heart therapy.
pmc-13294169:
Priscilla Gates and colleagues explore why lymphoma patients stuck with a web rehab program for thinking problems in a 2026 qualitative sub-study. Cancer and its treatment often dull memory, attention, and planning. The eReCog program was tested in a pilot trial with strong sign-up and retention, and 14 users gave in-depth interviews about their experience.

Four themes stood out: hunger for clear information, the feel of taking part, support received, and ease of use. Users valued practical strategies, feeling believed through an online peer community, and flexible access from home. Perceived mental gains plus human support, not technology alone, kept people engaged.
pmc-13294269:
Jiayan Qian leads a 2026 search for a treatment tracker in ulcerative skin tuberculosis, a hard-to-diagnose form of tuberculosis outside the lungs. No standard marker shows whether therapy works. Patient tissue from skin tuberculosis and non-tuberculosis ulcers was screened for long non-coding RNAs, and networks tied the standout signal HCP5 to partner genes, with lab knockdown and follow-up sampling for proof.

Screening found 1,994 altered long RNAs, with HCP5 clearly raised. Its partner ITGB2 fell when HCP5 was silenced in infected macrophages. Both signals dropped in tissue and blood after two weeks of anti-tuberculosis treatment. Paired tracking could give clinics an objective early readout.
pmc-13294369:
Marta Confalonieri and colleagues craft artificial cartilage from polyvinyl alcohol gel for lab testing of joint lubricants in a 2026 study. Injected hyaluronic gels aim to restore glide in worn knees, but bench tests need a stand-in that feels like real cartilage. Gels at 15%, 20%, and 25% polymer were compared for pore structure, squeeze stiffness, and friction under salt solution.

Stiffer, denser gels formed as polymer rose, and friction rose with it. The 20% gel balanced best, with stiffness near 300 kPa and friction near 0.14 in the reported values, inside the human cartilage range. Four commercial-style gels were then trialed as lubricants on the chosen stand-in.
pmc-13294969:
Jalloul Trabelsi and Mounir Esboui compute how an electric field reshapes the light-handling of a fluorinated liquid crystal molecule, in a 2026 theoretical study. Displays work by fields nudging liquid crystal molecules, so knowing how a single molecule's electronics answer a field matters for design. Using density functional theory and its time-dependent extension, the pair optimized the molecule's shape, checked its stability, and charted its excited states before applying fields along three directions.

Most low-lying excitations sat on the molecule's biphenyl core, while the brightest state, high in energy, moved charge from that core toward the saturated ring end. Fields along the long axis did the real work, shifting absorption, dipole moment, and the gap between the key orbitals. At one point the gap closed and polarizability leapt nearly tenfold, signaling wholesale charge redistribution. Sideways fields barely stirred the molecule, underlining how directional its response is.
pmc-13295169:
Yuqi Zhao and a large team engineer immune cells to repair spinal cord injury in a 2026 study. After cord damage, inflammation, cell loss, and scar disruption block natural healing. Ordinary cell therapy struggles to reach the lesion, stay active, and release help at the right times.

Macrophages primed to home toward injury signals were loaded with genetic messages for three healing proteins. The cells kept living, gathered at mouse cord lesions, and released their cargo for up to 14 days. Treated animals showed calmer inflammation, regrown fibres, restored insulation, and partial return of movement and electrical signals, supporting timed cell delivery as a repair strategy.
pmc-13295769:
Matthieu Roulleaux-Dugage and colleagues test a vessel drug against liver spread resistance in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Liver metastases blunt the benefit of chemoimmunotherapy in advanced non-squamous lung cancer. Blocking the vessel growth signal VEGF-A might reopen the tumour to immune attack.

Data from two large phase three trials covered 1,713 patients, including 236 with liver spread. Without the vessel drug, adding immune therapy to chemotherapy gave liver patients no survival gain. With bevacizumab added, both control time and survival improved clearly in that group. Gene data showed liver tumours crowded with suppressive immune cells and poor in attacking ones.
pmc-13296169:
Carol D. Ryff revisits, in 2026, personal growth as one strand of psychological wellbeing in a model she proposed over thirty-five years ago. She reviews what the idea means, how questionnaires measure it, and what decades of studies have found.

Research links growth to health, biological risk markers and thinking skills, and shows varied predictors of who keeps growing across life. Ryff then points forward. She urges tackling barriers tied to widening inequality and using arts and humanities to nurture becoming. She also wants virtue and ethics restored to the heart of a flourishing life, with historical examples offered.
pmc-13296769:
Chiagoziem Anigbogu and colleagues review the coupling between theta brain waves and rapid eye movements in a 2026 article. Theta rhythms, cycling four to eight times per second, support memory, attention, and planning. Quick eye movements, called saccades, occur at a similar pace during visual exploration.

Each saccade appears to reset the phase of theta waves, synchronising activity across the cortex, hippocampus, and eye-control networks. Theta in turn seems to time when movements start and where they aim. Broken coupling shows up in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and epilepsy, the authors note. Measuring this interplay could yield non-invasive markers and targets for brain stimulation aimed at cognition.
pmc-13297669:
Chenghao Zhang and colleagues build heat-proof capsules that break down plugging gel deep in hot oil wells on a timed delay, in a 2026 study. Crews plug cracked rock with polymer gel, then need the gel gone without harming the reservoir. Their capsule wraps an acid core in two shells, an inner cellulose layer that meters release and an outer resin that stands heat.

The capsules formed evenly, trapped most of their acid, and withstood heat up to 150 degrees Celsius. Mixed into gel, they left its strength intact in salty water and across a wide dose range. At top heat and dose, the gel broke fully within two and a half days, leaving little residue that flowed back easily. Plugging strength in cracked rock held steady for five days first.
pmc-13298569:
Marina Giannaki and others test whether boosting Notch signalling strengthens interferon responses in glioma cells, in a 2026 lab study. Earlier mouse work showed removing Notch genes weakened interferon signals and produced immune-suppressed tumours. The team switched on the active Notch fragment in a human glioma cell line using a drug-inducible system.

Activation sharply increased a key interferon signalling step after either interferon type was applied. It also raised a regulator of interferon responses and boosted production of two signals that guide T cells. In a mouse glioma model, activation drew in killer T cells and slowed tumour cell growth, suggesting a network worth exploiting.
pmc-13298869:
Sleep, time trade-offs, and heart health among Utah's minoritized women are the focus of a study protocol described by Kelly G Baron and a large community-academic team in 2026. The Sweet Dreams project builds its research around community health workers rather than treating communities as mere recruitment pools.

Focus groups draw on workers from African Immigrant, Black and African American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, and Latina communities, who act as both members and trusted leaders. The protocol lays out relationship building, joint data collection, shared analysis, and dissemination plans. The partners expect the work to surface community-specific views on sleep, set future research questions, and seed interventions against cardiometabolic disparities.
pmc-13299269:
Adam Osowski, Tomasz Antonowski, and Joanna Wojtkiewicz review protein markers in latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, in a 2026 survey. This diabetes form blends features of the autoimmune and metabolic types, which complicates early sorting. Candidate markers span inflammation, immune signalling, and metabolic measures drawn from recent papers.

Several studies place this condition's biomarker profile between the two classic types, sharing traits with each. Evidence remains uneven, dominated by small samples, one-time designs, and incomplete checking in clinics. The authors regard the markers as exploratory tools for research, not settled aids for routine labelling. Longitudinal studies with well-described patients are needed before patterns can guide identification.
pmc-13300169:
A blood marker shed from plasma cells may show within one month whether myeloma treatment is working. Laura Caponi and colleagues followed 100 people starting therapy for newly diagnosed or relapsed multiple myeloma in a 2026 prospective study. They tracked soluble BCMA alongside standard free light chain measures at baseline, one month, and six months.

All three markers fell after treatment began, yet only soluble BCMA separated patient groups at baseline and at one month. Patients whose marker dropped by less than half at one month had over five times the odds of a weaker six-month response. In combined models, soluble BCMA alone kept its link to response quality, supporting its use for early monitoring.
pmc-13300369:
Hospital stays for respiratory syncytial virus cost Switzerland tens of millions of francs each year, Maria Boesing and colleagues calculate in a 2026 nationwide analysis. Using federal hospitalization records from 2017 to 2023 plus SwissDRG cost data, they priced RSV admissions by age group and adjusted for the longer stays these patients need.

Total inpatient costs came to roughly CHF 55.1 to 76.0 million per year. Children under ten filled the most beds and drew the largest share of the bill. Adults over sixty cost nearly as much in total, because each case ran longer and more severe. The figures give prevention programs and vaccine payment decisions a firmer economic footing.
pmc-13300869:
Meng-Qian Chen and co-authors search the morel mushroom Morchella sextelata for circadian clock genes in a 2026 study. The daily clock is well mapped in the model fungus Neurospora but barely studied in edible mushrooms, whose fruiting quality may depend on day night coordination. The team hunted the morel genome for counterparts of known clock genes, then measured their activity across a day in two mating type strains and in a mixed culture.

Counterparts of seven clock related genes turned up, including the core oscillator pieces, suggesting a working clock of the familiar fungal design. All seven clock genes and four mating type genes pulsed with time of day, yet the patterns stayed consistently different between the mating backgrounds and their cross. The authors read this as a possible link between clock regulation and mating type, and they frame it as groundwork for cultivation science.
pmc-13301769:
G Giacomini and colleagues share early 2026 experience with a new catheter approach for ventricular tachycardia, a fast and dangerous rhythm arising in scarred hearts. Standard ablation burns tissue with radiofrequency energy, yet deep scar can survive and the rhythm can return. New dual-energy catheters add pulsed field energy alongside heat, aiming for deeper and more even lesions.

Fifteen men treated at one centre between April and October 2025 received one of two dual-energy catheter designs, chosen by the operator. The target rhythm could no longer be triggered after treatment in eleven patients, and no electrical storms recurred during the hospital stay. One major complication, fluid around the heart, was drained successfully. The authors call for larger prospective studies to confirm long-term benefit.
pmc-13301969:
Yeasts that look alike under the microscope scatter light in tellingly different ways, Zexi Cheng and colleagues exploit in a 2026 classification study. Their first network, FPA-YeastNet, reads light-scattering images through frequency-domain features. A second model, FGCA-YeastNet, fuses scattering with microscopy through cross-attention, letting each view correct the other.

Frequency enhancement alone lifted accuracy by an average of 6.26 percent over plain scattering models on their multimodal yeast dataset. The fused network gained 19.97 percent over single-view baselines and 7.67 percent over other fusion attempts. Faster, surer species identification could steer antifungal choice sooner, the authors argue, in clinics that now wait on culture.
pmc-13302369:
Giuseppe Alberti and colleagues review, in a 2026 narrative review, how gene science and epigenetics are reshaping understanding of hearing loss. The condition affects well over a billion people, and inherited factors explain a large share, most often through recessive patterns. Chemical marks on DNA that switch genes up or down are now drawing attention too.

Sequencing advances have sped gene discovery, with one gene, GJB2, among the best-known culprits, yet interpreting new variants remains hard. Marks such as DNA methylation appear to govern inner-ear development and the survival of sound-sensing hair cells. The authors argue that blood-based epigenetic signatures might one day flag risk early. Combining screening, population data, and molecular knowledge is presented as the route to fairer precision care.
pmc-13302769:
Years on clozapine quietly strain the heart, Ruri Okubo and colleagues warn in a 2026 cohort analysis from Japan and China. Three hundred fifteen patients with schizophrenia on clozapine alone, ninety-nine Japanese and 216 Chinese, were checked in 2025 with blood markers and echocardiography. Exposure averaged about five years in Japan and seventeen in China.

Heart failure prevalence ran well above the general population in both countries, with odds ratios of 3.2 and 6.9. Longer exposure, higher drug levels, and rising monocytes marked the silent stage-B cases, most of whom lacked metabolic problems. The pattern points to preserved-ejection heart failure, and the authors urge routine NT-proBNP monitoring.
pmc-13303369:
Genxiao Ding and co-authors report a prospective cohort study from 2026 on symptoms in people newly diagnosed with glioma. The team followed 142 adults with confirmed glioma and asked how symptoms reported at diagnosis link together and forecast burden six months later.

Fifteen symptoms were scored on 0 to 10 scales at baseline. Network models mapped links among symptoms, and a random forest model combined symptom, clinical, and mood factors to flag high burden. Speech trouble and headache sat most centrally in the network. Baseline worry, low mood, memory trouble, pain, fatigue, and age best predicted later burden. Early checks across all symptom areas may help clinics watch the most at-risk patients more closely.
pmc-13303669:
Stephanie Hempel and colleagues report a 2026 sub-study from Hannover comparing three tools women can use at home to test for high-risk HPV. Cervical screening catches disease early, yet many women skip regular checks.

Women aged 30 to 65 received either an Evalyn brush, FLOQ swabs, or a first-void urine device called Colli-Pee, after invitation by mail. About one sample in eleven came back overall, with urine and swab tools ahead of the brush. Faulty samples stayed rare, and about one returned sample in thirteen tested positive. The urine device was most liked, and two thirds of women favored home testing.
pmc-13303769:
Nasibe Aycan Yılmaz tests gallic acid as a gentler dentin conditioner for dental bonding in a 2026 laboratory study. A bleeding-control liquid with ferric sulfate can leave iron on tooth dentin and weaken later bonding.

Dentin pieces from 90 extracted molars formed 180 samples across two glues, three application methods, and clean or contaminated surfaces. Bond strength, iron left behind, and surface form were measured after heat cycling. Self-etch use gave the weakest bonds, while gallic acid matched standard acid etching on strength. Yet after contamination the gallic route kept iron deposits, so caution is advised in that setting.
pmc-13303969:
Heeyoung Hwang, Gitak Bae, and Kyeongmin Jang examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether inflammation changes the protective link between good cholesterol and clustered metabolic risks. Risk factors such as belly fat, high pressure, and poor glucose control often travel together in middle age. Korean national survey data from 2024 supplied the sample.

The analysis covered 2,283 adults aged forty to sixty-four, and about forty-six percent carried at least two risk factors. Higher HDL cholesterol meant lower odds of clustering, while higher inflammation marker levels meant higher odds. A statistical interaction suggested the cholesterol association shifts as inflammation rises. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove cause, and they avoid claiming any direct link between the two blood measures.
pmc-13304369:
Xiyao Huang and co-authors create, in a 2026 materials study, a hydrogel electrolyte that lets zinc batteries work in deep cold without growing metal spikes. Water-based zinc batteries are cheap and safe, yet water causes side reactions, dendrites short the cell, and the liquid freezes below zero. Their double-network gel guides zinc ions evenly while holding water back.

Symmetric test cells ran for four thousand hours at minus thirty degrees without failing. A full battery paired with a vanadium oxide cathode survived four thousand cycles with strong capacity retention. Flexible pouch versions kept most of their capacity after nine hundred cycles and still worked after being frozen, bent, and even pierced. The authors pitch the gel for wearable and grid storage in harsh climates.
pmc-13304469:
Seppe Driesen, Karen Leirs, and Jeroen Lammertyn review DNA origami tools for spotting single molecules in a 2026 survey. Folded DNA sheets offer hundreds of exact anchor points for arranging molecules, glow tags, and metal particles.

Design rules for working folded structures come first, covering shape switches and hotspots that boost light signals. Non-glowing readouts use scanning probes, tiny pores, and Raman light methods. Glow-based readouts use moving DNA devices and light antennas. Trends and missing pieces are mapped, pointing to what must improve before folded DNA sensors reach routine diagnostic use.
pmc-13304569:
Verónica V. Márquez-Hernández, Jessica García-González, and colleagues explore, in a 2026 interview study, how nursing students experience teaching CPR through community service-learning. Thirty students, chosen on purpose, described their training in semi-structured interviews that were coded for themes. Service-learning pairs real community teaching with coursework, a method rarely studied for CPR skills.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. Students felt the teaching deepened their own competence and gave the learning real meaning. Teaching carried an emotional charge that strengthened their sense of themselves as nurses and their social awareness. At the same time, they flagged practical difficulties in running the sessions. The authors conclude the approach builds confidence and engagement despite barriers in practice, and they commend it as an addition to classroom CPR training.
pmc-13305669:
Chitharanjan M. Shetty and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how root canal services might fit inside everyday preventive dental care. Gum and tooth pulp disease still cause much illness, yet early pulp problems are often missed in primary care settings.

Drawing on published studies and professional guidance, the review found that closer links improved continuity, earlier pulp treatment and tooth survival. Workable models joined referral pathways, shared sites, and general dentists with added endodontic skills, helped by digital tools and simpler techniques. Gaps in staffing, funding and training remain, so the authors back standard referrals, workforce growth and stronger policy support.
pmc-13305769:
Anthony Saah Tengbeh reviewed pollution evidence from Liberia in a 2026 systematic review of metals and related contaminants in work and community settings. Years of informal mining, weak waste control and fast city growth have harmed soil and water quality across the country.

From 38 candidate studies, nine met the quality and coverage rules. Reported water readings included very high cloudiness and conductivity, and iron, manganese and cadmium often passed World Health Organization limits in the cited figures. Soil samples also carried heavy loads of iron and other metals. The authors link these patterns to urgent control of mining and waste sources.
pmc-13305869:
Bryan Moreno-Chamba and colleagues examine in 2026 whether phenolic extracts from fruit waste can help friendly gut bacteria keep out harmful Escherichia coli. Extracts came from grape, cherry, and strawberry by-products, which are rich in anthocyanins. The team worked with Bifidobacterium longum in laboratory cultures and intestinal cells.

All three extracts helped the beneficial strain form biofilms and grow ahead of the pathogen, reflected in positive prebiotic activity scores. Treated bacteria also produced more lactate, acetate, and butyrate. In a cell adhesion test, the extracts reduced how much E. coli attached, most clearly during direct competition. The authors propose such extracts as food ingredients that support the gut barrier without antibiotics.
pmc-13305969:
Alex Câmpian attached bee venom peptide melittin to magnetic iron particles in a 2026 cell study against colon cancer. Free peptide can harm healthy tissue, so delivery on particles plus magnetic heating was tested as a more focused approach.

Colon cancer cells called Caco-2 and normal skin fibroblasts received free peptide, particles alone, or loaded particles with heating at set doses. Loaded particles cut cancer cell survival and energy stores while raising markers of programmed death, and heating strengthened several effects in the reported assays. Microscopy showed particle shapes and cell damage patterns that matched the lab measures.
pmc-13306269:
Claudia Campolo tested sending road hazard alerts through 5G vehicle networks in a 2026 engineering study. Connected cars must warn both nearby drivers and distant centres, yet phone networks may struggle to deliver fast enough when detection uses machine learning.

A working test platform joined on-board hazard detection with message sending toward vehicles, cloud services and road operators. Trials measured the full chain from sensing to delivery under latency limits that safety uses demand. The authors present the setup as proof that network-based alerts can reach remote users as well as local traffic.
pmc-13306669:
Yitong Lu built a light neural network that finds standout objects using colour plus depth images in a 2026 study. Heavy models score well but run slowly, while small models often lose accuracy when depth and colour disagree.

A synergy module works in the frequency domain, tuning wave height and phase parts to clear clutter and build a clean global guide. A cross-guidance module then lets each stream filter noise from the other through mutual anchoring. The combined design aims to keep strong scores while staying small enough for everyday devices.
pmc-13307069:
Claudia Steinbach measured energy band alignment in ultrathin mixed-conducting oxide layers in a 2026 study. Junctions between such oxides bend bands to balance electronic and ionic charge, but very thin layers may not behave like bulk material.

Stacks of two strontium-doped oxides were grown in both orders on strontium titanate crystals and probed at 500 °C across low oxygen pressures. Even a 0.5 nm layer of one oxide gave bulk-like bending, while the other stayed sensitive to its cover layer at that thickness. A model explains the gap through differing charge layer widths.
pmc-13307669:
Huaiyu Zhang and co-authors pilot in 2026 whether postbiotics, dead helpful bacteria or their parts, can aid fat balance and gut health in healthy adult cats. Eighteen cats ate plain food or food with one of two postbiotic types for four weeks in three small groups.

Both added diets lowered blood cholesterol and triglycerides versus the plain diet group after four weeks. One type also raised Bifidobacterium counts in droppings, and both types cut faecal smell for the cats. Small group size means the gains need proof in larger trials, yet the early signs favour postbiotics as a gentle daily feed add on for pet cats.
pmc-13307769:
Masaharu Takahashi and a nationwide team test retail pork in Japan in 2026 for hepatitis E virus RNA. More than fifteen hundred samples from eight regions were checked with a sensitive nested method calibrated against the world standard. Pigs are the main animal reservoir, and raw pork liver is a known risk, but meat data were scarce.

Fifteen samples, about one percent, tested positive, with no meaningful difference between regions or between domestic and imported meat. Quantifiable samples carried a wide range of viral loads. Genetic typing found subtype 3b most often, with smaller numbers of three other subtypes, each matching known Japanese strains closely. Whether the detected RNA means infectious virus remains unresolved, the authors caution. Even so, they present retail pork as a plausible exposure source worth food safety attention.
pmc-13308869:
Mustafa Khan and colleagues ask in 2026 whether skull suture lengths can hint at a person's height when long bones are missing, a forensic problem with incomplete remains. Two sutures, sagittal and lambdoid, correlated weakly but significantly with stature in the combined group, while the coronal suture showed nothing. Within each sex separately, no suture reached significance. Prediction equations explained under a tenth of height variation, which is far too little for standalone use. The authors therefore rate sutures as supplementary clues only. Larger validation samples would be needed before any forensic reliance. The study is exploratory by design, and its cautious conclusion matches the numbers.
pmc-13309569:
Mrinmoy Ghosh and co-authors review in 2026 the two-way relationship between muscle loss in ageing and type 2 diabetes. Countermeasures span resistance exercise, dietary optimisation, and emerging drugs aimed at the shared pathways. The authors argue for integrated treatment rather than separate diabetes and muscle clinics. Understanding the loop, they say, is the route to better quality of life for ageing patients.
pmc-13309669:
Tianqi Ren and colleagues hunt for immune-cell gene targets in arthritis using genetics in a 2026 study. Gene activity data from single regulatory T cells were joined with large Finnish genetic study results for rheumatoid arthritis, knee arthritis, and gout. A method that uses inherited variants as natural experiments tested causal links. In rheumatoid arthritis, higher activity of one gene raised risk while another gene looked protective, with differing patterns in the other arthritis types. The authors propose cell-specific targets for drug work.
pmc-13310669:
Marta Codirenzi and co-authors compare three biologic regimens for a rare vessel disease over two years in a 2026 study. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis inflames vessels alongside asthma and high eosinophil counts. Two drugs that block the IL-5 signal path are used, one at two dose levels, yet long-term real-world contrasts were scarce.

A single-center study followed 66 adults on benralizumab or mepolizumab at 300 mg or 100 mg for 24 months. Remission by 24 months reached 73.7 percent on benralizumab, 81.0 percent on the higher mepolizumab dose, and 50.0 percent on the lower dose in the reported groups, without clear statistical gaps. Steroid-free status rose over time. Statistical weighting handled the fact that sicker patients got certain regimens.
pmc-13310769:
Anaid Pérez-Ramos and colleagues use machine learning to map personal recovery in schizophrenia spectrum illness in a 2026 study. Recovery covers daily function, symptoms, and inner life, and people rate their own stage of recovery. The team asked which mix of traits marks each self rated stage in a large French care network.

Data covered 1,361 people in rehab care. A forest model sorted stages well in training data but only fairly in fresh test data, which shows how much stages overlap. Low self worth and stigma marked the earliest stage, while high wellbeing and self worth marked growth. Gains in hope and ties tracked later stages.
pmc-13310969:
Reiko Kemmochi reports a 2026 case of arm artery dissection days after aorta stent repair. A man aged 87 years had a stent graft for a wide arch aneurysm with two branch vessels rerouted. Five days later sudden chest pain, fainting, and poor arm blood flow struck.

Scans showed a tear in the brachiocephalic artery that squeezed the true channel shut. Watchful care was tried first, but repeat low pressure forced action. Two bare stents placed in a kissing pattern reopened flow to the arm and neck arteries. Later scans showed open stents and graft. Close watch after stent repair allows timely rescue.
pmc-13311169:
Anwar Kalali reports a 2026 case of a spinal blood clot that mimicked infection. A woman aged 61 years with type 1 diabetes grew weak in both legs over one week, months after severe staph lung infection. Blood tests showed strong swelling signs that pointed toward abscess, a classic trap.

Spine scans showed a front side collection at the chest to waist junction with signal traits of aging blood, plus blood spread lower down. Chest scans showed only a scarred lung cavity, and brain scans were clear. Urgent back surgery confirmed a late stage blood clot, and recovery was strong at three months.
pmc-13311269:
Irshad Ul Ala and colleagues assemble in 2026 two decades of anthrax outbreak reports to map where the disease persists and where it surprises.
