Türkiye kept livestock incident levels similar to earlier years, and six countries showed rising trends. Outbreaks also appeared in historically quiet regions, a reminder that spores sleep in soil for decades. Cattle and sheep dominated animal cases. The two reporting systems captured different slices of events, suggesting animal and human surveillance see different outbreaks. Pooling both, the authors argue, gives the honest picture needed for risk planning.
pmc-13311369:
Shani Kondo Omari, Lydia Issaria Mosses, and Hussein Hassan Mwanjali offer a 2026 perspective on body shaming as a public health harm to women's mental health. Mocking weight, shape, or looks can cut self-worth and drive low mood and anxiety.

The authors draw on world health and psychology guidance, therapy studies, and policy frames including Agenda 2063 of the African Union. Talking therapies and school programs have cut body distress in trials, and one large self-esteem project has reached millions of young people. Evidence from African settings stays thin. The piece calls for action that treats body shaming as a fairness issue, not a private worry.
pmc-13311569:
Bruno Fuchs and co-authors lay out a 2026 framework for judging health care value one episode at a time. Their Value Index scores results per cost on a 0 to 100 scale, with fairness checks built in.

The framework is set in a hospital-based sarcoma care network with hub-and-spoke paths. Two field tests are sketched: comparing care paths across a full sarcoma cycle, and using causal machine learning to aim radiotherapy at patients most likely to gain. The paper gives the index formula, how uncertainty is shown, and rules against gaming. It aims to make value talk concrete and auditable.
pmc-13311969:
Arpita Saggar and colleagues offer a 2026 study on whether ChatGPT can act out clinical exam scenarios for medical training. Real practice exams cost much time and money to stage.

Four child-health scenarios from mock exams were run with separate ChatGPT agents as patient, doctor, and examiner. The patient and doctor agents talked in writing, and the examiner agent marked the exchange. Clinicians and patients judged the dialogues. The patient agent stayed in character and showed feeling well; the doctor agent communicated clearly but slipped into jargon and repetition. The examiner agent's marks correlated well with human marks, and support for training use was moderate.
pmc-13312369:
Aine Travers and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of what drives the well-established link between armed conflict and intimate partner violence. The connection itself is documented, but the mechanisms carrying violence from the public sphere into the home were less clear. The team searched five databases for studies that explained drivers rather than merely recording the association.

Forty-nine studies qualified, split between 25 qualitative and 24 quantitative designs. Drivers clustered at individual, relational, and structural levels. The strongest support gathered behind conflict-related trauma and post-traumatic stress, the economic stress war leaves behind, and shifts in gender roles and norms after conflict. Gender and money pressures interacted across many studies. The authors urge humanitarian programs to build in partner violence prevention and call for theory that joins personal and societal levels.
pmc-13312469:
Xiaoliang Yin, Dehai Lang, and Songjie Hu recount, in a 2026 case report, a groin tumor first mistaken for a blood clot. A 56-year-old man had been treated a year earlier with anticoagulants and clot removal. His left leg had swelled, and scans had suggested femoral vein thrombosis. Returning with groin pain, he was found to have a mixed-signal mass beside the femoral vein. Surgery revealed fish-flesh-like tumor tissue encasing the artery, vein, and nerve. No clot sat inside the vein.

Frozen section suggested at least a low-grade malignancy. The team removed the vessels, nerve, and surrounding muscle with the tumor. They rebuilt the artery using the patient's saphenous vein. Pathology confirmed a high-grade leiomyosarcoma arising from the vein wall, a cancer forming roughly 2 percent of sarcomas. Despite radiotherapy and chemotherapy, scans at 20 months showed recurrence and lung spread, and the patient stopped treatment.
pmc-13312569:
Pamela N Peters and colleagues report a 2026 quality improvement project that got more gynecologic oncology patients home the same day after minimally invasive hysterectomy. The team at a large academic center set out to lift same-day discharge from a 61 percent baseline toward 90 percent within eight months, without pushing patients into emergency care.

Working under the Institute for Healthcare Improvement model, they standardized the process by dropping routine void trials and fixing consent language, taught patients what to expect, and reviewed cases at division meetings. The aim was a culture that supports early discharge. Over one year the same-day rate rose to 85 percent, and cases booked as ambulatory surgery jumped from 3.5 percent to 81 percent. Recovery room time and emergency visits within a week did not budge, which the authors read as a safe win.
pmc-13312969:
Malick Thiam and colleagues train, in a 2026 study, convolutional neural networks to identify fossil foraminifera from Senegalese sediments on the West African margin. These single-celled shells are workhorse markers for dating rock layers and reconstructing ancient oceans. Naming them by eye is slow and hard, especially in diverse assemblages or where burial has altered the shells.

Three datasets totaling 11,378 images fed models for detection, genus-level, and species-level classification across planktonic, bottom-dwelling, and agglutinated forms. Genus naming reached 72.4 percent validation accuracy, clearly beating the species model's 50.2 percent, since lumping close relatives dodges confusion from shape variation and decay. Distinctive genera classified well, while look-alike pairs tangled. The authors see genus-level automation as ready to assist biostratigraphy, with multi-view imaging and bigger libraries as the next boosts.
pmc-13313269:
Giorgia Della Polla and colleagues survey vaccine knowledge and habits among LGBTQIA+ people in Italy in work published in 2026. This group faces higher risk of infections passed through sex, yet facts on what they know and which shots they take were scarce.

An online survey ran from May to July 2025 and drew 1944 people. Only a share of 14.2 percent rightly named HPV, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and Mpox as infections passed through sex, by the figures given in the report. Knowledge ran higher among younger people, degree holders, men who have sex with men, and those told about vaccines by health staff. Only a share of 31.7 percent judged all four vaccines very useful. The gaps point to where clear, targeted outreach could lift coverage.
pmc-13313569:
Hannah Berg and colleagues map, in a 2026 brain imaging study, how two flavors of fear steer avoidance in anxiety-related disorders. Fifty-eight adults with anxiety, trauma-related, or obsessive-compulsive conditions took part, along with 77 volunteers. They answered questionnaires on anxiety sensitivity, the fear of fear itself, and intolerance of uncertainty, the fear of the unknown. They performed an avoidance task in the scanner, facing a threat cue linked to shock, safety cues, and look-alike cues in between.

Brain reactivity in the anterior insula and a prefrontal region tracked how threatening each cue was. Anxiety sensitivity tightened the link between that reactivity and harmful avoidance. Uncertainty intolerance worked elsewhere. In people scoring high on it, avoidance behavior matched motor and parietal brain patterns less during simulation. The authors conclude the traits distort avoidance through separate neural routes, which may call for aimed treatments rather than one approach.
pmc-13313869:
Akunna Perpetua Emeruwa and colleagues test, in a 2026 animal study, a vaccine adjuvant built from mushroom saponins against pneumococcal infection. The edible mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus carries immune-stimulating saponins. The team cleaned them and built them into ISCOMATRIX particles, cage-like carriers used to strengthen vaccines. Mice received the mixture through the nose, mouth, or rectum. The researchers then measured antibodies, immune cell patterns, bacteria counts, and reactions after challenge with Streptococcus pneumoniae.

All three needle-free routes raised useful antibody classes. The nasal route performed most evenly and reached the strongest result. Nasal and rectal delivery cut swelling and bacteria load, while nasal and oral dosing recruited the most neutrophils. Immune cell cultures showed both arms of the T cell response switched on. The authors present mucosal delivery of this mushroom-derived platform as a sound non-invasive option to injected vaccines, ready for more animal testing.
pmc-13314169:
Ayman Albanna and Omar A Al-Mahmood report, in a 2026 study, a molecular method for confirming the paralysis tick Ixodes holocyclus on imported cats. Ticks ferry bacterial, viral, and protozoan diseases between animals and people, and imported pets can smuggle them across borders. The team examined 100 imported domestic cats presented for checkups. They identified ticks by microscope morphology, then confirmed species with conventional and real-time PCR aimed at tick gene markers, sequencing the positives for a family tree.

Eighteen cats carried ticks matching the species morphologically. Molecular testing confirmed all, with the real-time assay returning cycle values and single-peak melt curves across two genes. The researchers report complete specificity. Sequencing sorted the eighteen isolates into four clusters, the largest hugging a known reference isolate. The authors warn that cats can carry this tick into homes and new environments, making quick confirmation at import points a health safeguard.
pmc-13314569:
Gilbert Uwizeyimana and colleagues report how leukemia patients in Rwanda answer molecular testing on treatment, in work published in 2026. Chronic myeloid leukemia became far more survivable after kinase blockers arrived in 2001, above all imatinib, but access and testing lag in poorer states.

In Rwanda only imatinib is on hand and molecular checks are scarce. The team ran a one-arm prospective study at the Kigali teaching hospital with 31 patients who had taken imatinib for at least three months, followed for 12 months, as the design states. They logged clinical traits and lab results from diagnosis onward and graded molecular response over the year. The data give Rwanda a first firm picture of how well its sole CML drug performs in real care.
pmc-13315769:
Daniel Truong and Joseph Jankovic honor, in a 2026 memorial article, Mark Hallett, a doctor who lived from 1943 to 2025 and reshaped movement disorder care. Over decades, his work moved the field from descriptive clinical practice toward a brain science discipline. Through pioneering studies of nerve science, brain firing, spasms, tremor, jerks, motor movement disorders, and brain pulses, he built frameworks that still shape research and care.

Beyond science, Hallett was a worldwide mentor and teaching ambassador whose influence reached cohorts of doctors and brain scientists worldwide. The article examines his dual legacy as transformative scientist and academic mentor. It presents a career joining scientific rigor, global teamwork, and humane mentorship. It credits his bridging of bedside observation with human nerve science for turning movement disorders into a counted branch of systems brain science.
pmc-13316169:
Bhavya Narala and colleagues prospectively studied in 2026 bedside ultrasound during in-hospital cardiac arrest and its link with survival and brain outcome. Data came from one large center between 2014 and 2025, covering 169 patients imaged by protocol during resuscitation.

Compared with true pulseless electrical activity, pseudo activity on ultrasound raised the odds of restored circulation, with an odds ratio of 3.31 in the reported analysis, and survival at six months was higher. A still heart cut the odds sharply, with an odds ratio of 0.10 in the reported analysis, and lowered survival at every time point.
pmc-13316369:
Hanman Qiu and co-authors report, in 2026, a urinary infection caused by a rare yeast in an older man with advanced bladder cancer. The 82-year-old was admitted to Jiangxi Cancer Hospital in September 2025 with urinary frequency, urgency and painful urination, plus hip pain. His cancer had spread to bone and lungs.

Urine cultures first grew a common bacterium, then a fungus that sequencing identified as Vanrija humicola. Laboratory testing showed sensitivity to voriconazole and related drugs, while echinocandin drugs performed poorly. Intravenous voriconazole plus an oral antibiotic was given with close monitoring. Urinary symptoms eased, inflammation markers normalised and the patient left hospital in October 2025. A literature review frames the case for clinicians.
pmc-13316569:
Chan-Gu Li and a team of Chinese researchers test a 2026 treatment idea for allergic airway inflammation, loading a tiny RNA that calms key allergy cells into bubbles drawn from cow's milk. The RNA, miR-146a-5p, is fragile alone and crosses cell walls poorly, so a natural carrier is needed.

Milk bubbles are cheap, plentiful, and gentle on the immune system, and the team built a production method for the loaded version. Safety tests showed no major body-wide harm in their models. The loaded bubbles strongly regulated immune activity in allergic airway disease tests. If the approach scales, milk-based carriers could offer a low-cost way to deliver RNA drugs for asthma and hay fever type illness.
pmc-13316669:
Hamza Malick and colleagues report, in 2026, the first use of tapinarof cream for a stubborn ring-shaped skin condition called erythema annulare centrifugum. The disorder produces slowly expanding red plaques with trailing scale and clear centres, often as a reaction to infections, drugs or other triggers. Steroid creams are first-line treatment but often give only brief control.

Their patient was a 61-year-old woman with a four-year itchy eruption on her arms and one leg, possibly linked to a change in her metformin formulation. A steroid cream used twice daily had failed to control it for long. Tapinarof, a nonsteroidal cream that activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, cleared the disease in this case, adding an option for steroid-resistant patients.
pmc-13316869:
Jun-Cai Lin and co-authors explored, in a 2026 United States survey study, whether the variety of microbes in the mouth links with rheumatoid arthritis. Gum disease already ties to this joint illness, and gut microbes are suspects too, but oral variety itself was under-studied.

The team analyzed 1,544 adults from the 2009 to 2012 national health survey cycles. Four measures of within-mouth variety each pointed the same way: richer oral communities went with lower odds of arthritis, in an even, dose-like pattern shaped partly by income and education factors. Whole-community makeup, though, did not split by disease status. Since the data are a snapshot, the authors call for follow-up studies to test cause and prevention.
pmc-13317069:
Tong Zhang and Liang V Tang mined UK Biobank data in a 2026 study on the CALLY index. The combined score of inflammation, nutrition, and immune strength was tested as a predictor of death in rheumatoid arthritis. Single markers each capture one slice of health; the blend might see more.

The study followed 5,626 patients for a median of 15.6 years in the tracked cohort. Higher CALLY scores went with clearly lower death risk, in a bent dose pattern with a turning point near 1.054 in the fitted curve. The index re-sorted risk better than any of its three parts alone and matched a fuller combined model. Subgroup checks held steady, backing the cheap score for long-term risk talks.
pmc-13317669:
Giulia Bernagozzi and co-authors ask, in a 2026 materials study, whether recycled polypropylene can carry a flame-retardant system as well as virgin plastic can. Fire safety additives are mandatory in many products, and proving recycled resin worthy would widen its market.

Both resins were blended with 21 percent of a swelling flame retardant mix. In cone fire tests, both cut heat release similarly, but the recycled version lit later and delayed its second heat peak, thanks to a tighter, denser char crust from finer additive spread. Both passed the strict V-0 burn rating with matched oxygen index values. Strength held up in the recycled version, with only a small loss of stretch. Recycled resin, they conclude, is ready for fire-safe uses.
pmc-13317769:
Jessie A Montgomery and co-authors test, in a 2026 bench study, how lowering eye pressure during cataract surgery affects the dangerous pressure surge when a blocked suction tip suddenly clears. The Active Sentry handpiece senses and counters such surges.

In a sealed model chamber, the team ran ten trials each at pressures of 30, 50, and 70 millimeters of mercury. Surge size and length matched at the two higher pressures, near 5.76 millimeters of mercury, but jumped at the lowest setting, roughly doubling in size and tripling in time in the recorded runs. Dropping working pressure to 50 appears safe with this handpiece, while 30 raises surge risk, a practical guide for surgeons chasing gentler settings.
pmc-13318669:
Menglong Lin, Feng Wang, and Bing Zhou offer a 2026 survey study of recreational surfers in Korea. They question the usual assumption that more participation brings steadily more flow and enjoyment. Instead, they test for curved patterns with turning points. Five measures of participation behaviour were collected.

In total, 404 surfers at major Korean coastal spots answered the survey. Flow was scored with a short standard scale, and enjoyment with a sport inventory. Flexible curve models beat straight-line models for every relationship tested. Benefits from years of surfing levelled off after about ten years. Session frequency and length showed sweet spots beyond which gains faded. Flow and enjoyment also followed a saturation curve. The authors advise care, given the one-time, single-country design.
pmc-13319369:
Lydia Reismann and co-authors map a fast growing research field in a 2026 study of health literacy linked to planet and shared human animal health. New labels for these skills have spread fast, but their meanings overlap and the field lacks a shared base. A count based map of past work was used to sort out how the labels connect.

From 1444 papers screened, 135 met the rules for a close look at shared terms. Four groups stood out, covering school training, home and work risks, joint human animal health, and food skills. Some labels acted as broad bridges across groups, while others stayed narrow. Clearer terms could help join up teaching and policy.
pmc-13319669:
Yohan Gagnard and colleagues test, in 2026, how reliably surgeons classify the shape of the acromion, the bony roof over the shoulder joint. Shape is thought to matter in shoulder impingement and rotator cuff disease. The Bigliani system sorts acromions into three types and is popular for its simplicity, yet its reliability on computed tomography was poorly studied.

Five shoulder surgeons of varied experience independently graded 420 acromions from standardised three-dimensional scan slices, giving 2,100 readings in total. Agreement with oneself over repeat readings was good, but agreement between different surgeons was poor. Type II shapes dominated. Older patients tended toward different shapes, confirming an association with age. The authors warn that research and decisions built on this classification should allow for its weak reproducibility.
pmc-13320269:
Vatsal D. Jariwala and co-authors present a software pipeline that maps shape change in brain guard cells after small injury in a 2026 study. Guard cells shift shape as they react to harm, from branchy at rest to round when alarmed, yet counting those shifts across huge image sets was slow by hand. Their tool rebuilds and measures each cell on its own from glow tagged photos.

The tool was run on 279510 guard cells from rodent brain after a probe prick injury. Shapes fell along a slope from branchy to round, sorted by span from the wound and by time since harm. Two paths split mid way, one toward short lived reactive forms and one toward rod like cells near the wound. Gene data hints the rod forms form a distinct immune tuning set.
pmc-13321369:
Jhosmer Ballena-Caicedo and co-authors review how proof on vitamin D for tuberculosis care has evolved in a 2026 umbrella review. Many systematic reviews have tested vitamin D as an add-on treatment, with mixed verdicts. The team gathered nine reviews from 2009 to 2022 and judged their quality and overlap.

The reviews covered from 300 to 2991 participants, and overlap among their trials was very high, with only 16 unique trials behind 64 appearances. Pooled results showed no clear effect on culture conversion, time to conversion, or death. One subgroup tied to a vitamin D receptor gene type hinted at benefit, but overall certainty stayed low for routine use.
pmc-13321769:
Mark Heyland and a large team study how local strain guides new bone growth during fracture healing in a 2026 clinical report. Healing is usually tracked by X-rays, and the callus, the new bone collar, signals progress. Whether callus growth truly matches local mechanical strain had not been shown firmly. The study followed 166 patients with lower limb fractures fixed by plates or nails.

Callus size and quality were measured on repeated X-rays and matched to computer models of strain for each fixation type. In thigh bone fractures, callus was largest at the back inner side, while shin bone fractures peaked on the outer side. Those peak sites matched the model sites of extreme strain, which supports strain guided healing checks.
pmc-13322969:
Seunghyeon Kim and colleagues challenge, in 2026, a textbook picture of bacterial gene expression in which copying, reading and destroying a message RNA happen as one coupled process. Working mainly in Escherichia coli, the team combined genetic, kinetic and spatial analyses to test how general that coupling really is.

Coupling required high translation activity, and nearly half of all transcripts showed signs of only partial coupling. Destruction of messages during copying was rare because the main shredding enzyme sits at the cell membrane, with an exception for messages encoding membrane proteins. Translation efficiency set how often copying stopped early, which in turn shaped destruction patterns. Two other bacterial species used different coordination strategies again. The authors argue that place inside the cell and gene features govern expression timing.
pmc-13323569:
Tatsuhisa Ozaki and colleagues ask whether diabetes changes the value of extra ablation in persistent atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 subanalysis of the SUPPRESS-AF trial. That multicentre trial randomised patients with low-voltage areas, after vein isolation, to extra low-voltage ablation or vein isolation alone.

Among 1,347 patients, 343 had low-voltage areas, split into 264 without diabetes and 77 with diabetes in this analysis, with similar scar extent across groups. The main outcome was freedom from atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia returning. The authors compare recurrence-free survival by diabetes status and treatment arm to judge whether metabolic disease blunts the added ablation benefit.
pmc-13324369:
Ye Jin Kim and team traced how dietary cholesterol drives liver scarring in metabolic dysfunction-linked steatohepatitis, and tested a drug that might interrupt it. Their 2026 study combined human liver samples, cholesterol-fed mouse models, and mechanistic work in liver cells and hepatic stellate cells. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, had emerged as a disease driver, but its upstream triggers and link to fibrosis stayed unclear.

Cholesterol-driven disease paired strong lipid damage with loss of the receptor PPAR-delta, breaking redox balance and leaving liver cells open to ferroptosis. DNA released from dying cells then activated STING signaling in stellate cells, switching on profibrotic genes. Both restoring PPAR-delta and treating with DN203316, a new selective PPAR-delta agonist, reversed these effects, and the drug eased ferroptosis, inflammation, and fibrosis without metabolic harm. The authors present DN203316 as a promising strategy against disease progression.
pmc-13324669:
Luz Bavassi and co-authors record brain signals after memory reminders in a 2026 EEG study. Recalling a memory can reopen it to change, and the outcome may depend on how strongly the reminder matches the first learning.

Volunteers received either a cue reminder or a context reminder, which differ in how easily later interference can disturb the memory. Resting brain waves after each type were then compared. Both reminders lowered high beta power in the 25 to 40 Hz band. Network analysis set the types apart, with the context reminder raising frontal betweenness centrality. The pattern hints that frontal areas steer information flow when the reminder matches learning less closely.
pmc-13325169:
Mehmet Akif Omeroglu turns corn cob waste into the sweetener xylitol with a new yeast in a 2026 study. Corn cobs are plentiful, and their xylose sugar can be fermented instead of bought as refined feed.

The yeast Pichia fermentans T12, newly isolated for this work, drank acid-treated cob liquid with no detox step. Tuning found the best run at 30 °C, starting pH 6, and 96 hours of incubation. From a feed holding 32 g per liter of xylose, the yeast made 21.6 g per liter of xylitol, a yield of 0.67 g per g. Infrared checks confirmed the product matched xylitol. The route skips costly cleanup of the feed.
pmc-13325369:
Hua Wei and colleagues explain how sulfur and iron doping each change flaw levels in indium phosphide crystals in a 2026 study. The crystal underpins fast optical and microwave devices, and dislocations spoil its quality.

Quantum calculations showed sulfur swaps at phosphorus sites shorten and strengthen local bonds, stiffening the lattice by about 15 percent. That strain pins dislocations, and grown crystals confirmed the lowest flaw counts in heavily sulfur-doped samples. Iron did the opposite, softening the crystal and forming FeP2 precipitates past its tiny solubility limit. A tuned growth process curbed the iron fallout and evened the crystals. The contrast gives growers clear doping rules.
pmc-13325469:
Amira S. A. Said and colleagues survey pharmacists in the United Arab Emirates about artificial intelligence in their work in a 2026 study. AI promises faster drug management, but adoption depends on how front-line staff judge it.

Of 400 invited pharmacists, 340 returned the questionnaire, an 85 percent response rate. Multitasking and rapid data work scored highest among benefits, at 4.1 on the five-point scale. Hopes for fewer medication errors and lower costs scored a more modest 3.3 and 3.1 on that scale. Top worries were cybersecurity at 4.2, data privacy at 4.1, and job loss at 3.9 in the same scoring. Loss of human contact also troubled many.
pmc-13327069:
Xu Wang and colleagues tested a blood pressure drug with radiation in 2026. Their target was triple-negative breast cancer. It is the most aggressive breast cancer type, with few treatment options. Radiation is a core treatment for it. Yet radiation can also quiet the immune attack inside tumors. That effect helps tumors resist later treatment. The drug, losartan, blocks a hormone system tied to that quieting.

High levels of the drug's target marked worse outlook and radiation resistance. In their tests, losartan made tumors respond better to radiation. The benefit depended on the immune system. The drug held back helper cells that suppress immune attack. It also raised the number and strength of killer T cells in tumors. Gene data showed weaker resistance signals after treatment. The authors propose pairing losartan with radiation as a strategy worth testing in patients.
pmc-13327969:
Benedetta Mignini and co-authors hunt for low blood pressure risk factors in anesthetized dogs in a 2026 record review. Pressure drops under anesthesia can harm patients, so 390 dog anesthetic records from October 2023 to April 2024 were checked. Low pressure meant a mean arterial reading at or under 60 mmHg across repeated measures.

Episodes occurred in 72 dogs, 18.5 percent of cases. Belly surgery carried the highest odds, at 5.56 times the comparison level in the main model, followed by age under twelve months at 3.12 times, and each added minute of anesthesia nudged risk up slightly. Knowing these flags helps anesthesia teams watch pressure hardest where drops are likeliest.
pmc-13328269:
Bertalan Balázs Süto and co-authors validate a Hungarian version of a spiritual wellbeing inventory in a 2026 study. Faith and spirituality tie closely to mental health, yet Hungarian tools were lacking. An online survey gathered 490 adults who completed the translated inventory plus two established spirituality scales for comparison.

The full 48-item version fit poorly in factor testing, while a shortened 18-item form fit acceptably and kept the six-factor shape, with internal consistency from 0.74 to 0.95 across its subscales. Agreement with the comparison scales supported its validity. The authors recommend the short form where brevity matters and the long form for wider coverage, with more testing planned in patient groups.
pmc-13328369:
Yue Shang and co-authors build a risk model for lasting pain after keyhole lung surgery in a 2026 prospective study. Chronic postsurgical pain follows thoracoscopic lung removal in a sizable share of patients, yet no standard forecast tool exists. Data from 744 patients at one hospital were split into 595 for building and 149 for checking the model.

Pain lasting past three months struck 284 patients, 38.1 percent overall, and five factors entered the final model: gender, early postoperative pain level, postoperative pneumonia, chest drain duration, and rescue opioid dose. A personalized score could steer pain plans toward patients likeliest to hurt for months, rather than treating everyone alike after discharge.
pmc-13328469:
Sandra B Vanegas and Sandy Magaña report outcomes of the ASPEN program in a 2026 randomized trial. ASPEN is a culturally adapted, parent-led intervention for young children with autism in low-resource households, families often left out of research. Forty-five parent-child pairs were randomized to twelve weekly coaching sessions or a lighter comparison package.

The coached parents gained confidence in using evidence-based strategies beyond the comparison group, while both groups grew in actually using those strategies. Comparison parents also felt more empowered, and their children gained social communication skills. A lighter touch may serve such families nearly as well, the authors suggest, and finding the right dose and active ingredients comes next.
pmc-13331369:
Moshanti M Ramdath and colleagues describe a 2026 case of a teenage boy whose illness began in the chest and then attacked his mouth and skin. The syndrome, reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption, is newly named and marked by severe sores of the moist linings, with little or no skin rash. It must be told apart from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, since outlook and care differ sharply.

Diagnosis rested mainly on bedside judgment and joint input from several fields, since proof arrived late. The boy received antibiotics, steroids acting through the body as a whole, and supportive care, and he made a full recovery. The report calls for wider awareness and for studies to set firm rules for diagnosis and care.
pmc-13331569:
Shiori Kawakami and nine co-authors published a cardiology study in twenty twenty-six on opening blocked heart arteries through a wrist vessel in patients revived from cardiac arrest. Distal radial access, through the hand, promises fewer vessel complications than the usual wrist route. Whether it works in the chaos of post-arrest emergencies was untested.

Forty-eight arrest patients needing emergency intervention were reviewed at one center. The distal route was attempted in forty-four and succeeded in forty-three, a ninety-eight percent success rate. Median time from door to balloon was sixty-seven minutes, and many patients also needed heart-lung support machines. Only one access complication, a limb ischemia, required attention. The authors judge the route feasible in this extreme setting.
pmc-13331769:
Hisako Katano and colleagues describe a 2026 study that built a review panel model for gene therapy in Japan. A 2024 change to the Act on the Safety of Regenerative Medicine widened the law to cover gene therapy given inside the body and related methods. The team ran an institutional study to design and test such a model in practice.

Their design adds a second, independent panel focused on gene therapy, sharing selected base functions with an existing cell therapy panel. The new panel won certification from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare in late November 2025. Its setup, membership, and workflow were checked at a first review meeting against five preset items, including structure and day-to-day feasibility. The study gives other institutions a tested template for lawful, expert review of fast-moving gene therapies.
pmc-13331969:
Yoko Taniguchi and colleagues used brain scans in a 2026 case-control study to ask which tissue losses track with executive problems in multiple system atrophy. Thinking and planning difficulties are common in this fast-moving degenerative disease, but the role of the cerebellum in them is unsettled.

They scanned 27 patients and 19 healthy controls of similar age, measuring volume both voxel by voxel and region by region, and tested executive skill with the Frontal Assessment Battery. Patients showed shrinkage in the putamen and cerebellar cortex, plus white matter loss running from the brainstem into the cerebellar peduncles. Scores on the thinking test rose modestly with volume in several rear cerebellar regions, though the links did not survive strict correction. The authors read the pattern as a hint that rear cerebellar decay contributes to executive trouble and call for larger follow-up studies.
pmc-13333369:
Rodrigo Sanchez-Bayona and colleagues review 2026 real-world evidence for tucatinib in HER2-positive advanced breast cancer. Recent years brought rapid advances in HER2-directed treatments, giving patients and clinicians many working options while making optimal ordering challenging. Tucatinib is a HER2-specific tyrosine kinase blocker that, with trastuzumab and capecitabine, showed life-extending benefits for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer already treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab-emtansine. Real-world data can add to trial knowledge, yet no full review of tucatinib studies had been done.

The literature search found studies published from January 2020 through January 2025 evaluating tucatinib effect and safety in routine practice. The summary covers response, life length, and safety outside trial settings, where patients are older, sicker, and more varied. Clinicians gain a real-world check on trial hopes for tucatinib combos. The review also maps ordering questions that trials alone have not settled.
pmc-13334069:
Yin Wang and colleagues review 2026 stem cell regulation of brain inflammation and amyloid-beta clearance as a therapy strategy for Alzheimer's disease. Dementia is a brain-wasting disorder mainly marked by thinking decline, with complex pathogenesis involving amyloid-beta deposition, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction. Stem cells have drawn much attention in dementia therapy in recent years for their multi-directional change potential and local-signal effects.

Through those properties, stem cells show remarkable protective and anti-inflammatory effects that may influence disease progression. The review sums up potential workings and effects of stem cells in dementia treatment and explores tailored plans based on stem cell tuning. Readers learn how stem cells might calm brain inflammation while aiding amyloid clearance, and where proof still falls short of clinic use. The work frames a promising but still trial-stage treatment direction.
pmc-13334869:
Abhya Niegocki and colleagues report a 2026 rebuilding of a complex shin wound using a dermal regrowth template and split-thickness skin graft. Rebuilding of the distal leg is challenging due to watershed blood supply and scarce soft-tissue bulk. While traditional guidelines rely on blood-supplied flap coverage, such interventions are higher-risk options in patients with significant other illnesses. The patient had a history of renal transplant, type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and limb vascular disease.

Chronic weak immunity induced blunt wound healing, while concurrent limb artery disease made microsurgery unreliable.
