pmc-13414869:
Abdullah Hashim Almalki and colleagues revisit a Saudi outpatient cohort to ask whether diabetes drugs of the SGLT2 class protect heart and kidney medicines from being stopped, in 2026. The cohort held 905 adults on renin-angiotensin system blockers at a Jeddah medical city, followed for a median of 28 months. Of those, 182 also took a mineralocorticoid receptor blocker.

Adding that blocker raised any high potassium finding to about 48 percent, versus about 29 percent without it. Stopping the main drug because of potassium was far more common when no SGLT2 drug was present. With SGLT2 cover, that excess risk vanished, though numbers were small. Kidney disease and age over 75 predicted high potassium most strongly.
pmc-13415269:
Charleni Crisóstomo and colleagues rank Santa Inês lambs by feed efficiency and check whether gut fermentation or methane output changes with rank, in 2026. Forty male lambs were sorted into low, medium, and high efficiency groups using residual feed intake and a combined gain measure. Methane was measured in individual chambers across two trial phases.

Intake, body weight, and methane emissions did not differ significantly among groups. High efficiency lambs still emitted about 15 percent less methane per kilogram of feed on raw numbers. Fermentation measures and protozoa counts stayed flat, which a uniform diet may explain. Efficiency rankings also shifted between life stages, limiting their stability as selection tools.
pmc-13415569:
Maryam Mahmoudi and colleagues use machine learning on plant leaf microbes to find natural defenders against a crop pathogen, in 2026. Six sets of leaf germ data came from wild Arabidopsis plants hit by Albugo laibachii, a water mold. The mold, the site, and plant genes each shaped which germs lived on the leaves.

Four models split sick from well plants by their germ mix, flagging germs tied to each state. Each short list germ, when put on plants, gave some guard gain, and germs tied to health did best. One yeast like fungus, Cystofilobasidium, worked in a made group of germs. It seemed to fight by germ on germ clash, not by waking the plant.
pmc-13416469:
Anish Karpurapu and a large team set out to connect blood protein patterns with dangerous coronary plaque features and later heart events, in 2026. Heart artery disease outcomes vary widely at the same level of blockage, and high risk plaque traits seen on CT angiography help explain why. The study combines broad protein measurement with that detailed plaque imaging in patients at low to intermediate risk.

Plaque traits of interest include low density plaque, outward remodeling, a napkin ring sign, and large noncalcified volume. Proteomics may reveal the molecular machinery behind plaque formation and rupture, which imaging alone cannot show. Pairing molecular data with artificial intelligence imaging analysis is the team's stated direction.
pmc-13416769:
Cheraghi and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the role of inflammation, meaning long-term immune activation, in heart disease. About half of heart patients lack the classic risk factors such as smoking or high cholesterol. It covers how inflammation drives atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaques in arteries, and how plaques can rupture and block blood flow.

The authors highlight C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation, as one of the best-studied signals. Higher levels of such markers go with higher rates of heart events across many studies. Inflammation also weakens the artery lining, which helps plaques form and grow. The review then surveys ways to lower inflammation tied to heart disease, from lifestyle steps to targeted drugs. The authors argue that checking inflammation could sharpen risk prediction for patients missed by classic scores.
pmc-13417269:
Sarah V Heel-Juen and colleagues watch a riboswitch RNA unfold as temperature climbs, in a 2026 biophysics study. Riboswitches are RNA segments that change shape to control genes. What RNA does after its paired structure melts was poorly known, so the team combined three methods that track shape, charge, and paired bases.

Three heat zones emerged. Mild heat melted only the upper stem, stronger heat removed all pairing, and the hottest zone produced compact folded forms unlike the native shape. Those compact forms hide some backbone charges, explaining odd charge drops. Melting, the authors show, does not always end in disorder.
pmc-13417469:
Tsuji and colleagues present a 2026 study of the rubber hand illusion, in which a person comes to feel that a fake hand is their own. Past work mostly scores it with drift measures or questionnaires. The authors instead recorded each person's own account of how the feeling changed moment by moment, paired with brain-wave recordings from the scalp.

People did not switch from no illusion to full illusion in one step. They passed through mixed states, such as feeling both hands at once or owning the fake hand only in part. Brain network maps shifted in step with those felt changes, with hubs in areas tied to body ownership such as the premotor cortex and insula. A math method for aligning unlike spaces showed the felt changes matched the brain changes in shape.
pmc-13418369:
Peng Gao and colleagues build a machine-learning model to predict mild cognitive impairment among older Chinese patients who have cerebral small vessel disease, damage to the brain's small blood vessels. Their 2026 study also tests whether blood levels of the growth factor IGF-1 relate to cognitive decline in these patients.

The team enrolled 216 patients at a Suzhou hospital neurology department, of whom 50 had mild cognitive impairment on a standard assessment. Clinical and blood measurements, including cholesterol, blood sugar, insulin, and IGF-1, fed an XGBoost model, with SHAP analysis used to explain each factor's contribution. The model performed well in validation, and decision curve analysis supported clinical usefulness. Reduced IGF-1 emerged as an important risk factor, and the authors present the approach as a tool for early detection and targeted intervention.
pmc-13419169:
The publisher issues an editorial note for a cancer study on a stress-response enzyme that helps tumor cells divide and grow. One extra figure in the paper turned out to be a copy of another extra figure, and the correct panel is supplied with the note. The publisher states regret for the error and places the fix on the public record for readers.

Later talks with the lead contact brought out a second point about method. Many blot panels in the paper came from gels run apart from each other, with counts given figure by figure. The contact states that one shared set of material fed all of the gels, with equal loads and matched handling throughout. Statements on funding and on rival interests were also wrong, and the corrected versions close the note.
pmc-13420669:
Khoi Viet Nguyen and colleagues report a 2026 case where photon-counting CT settled a high-stakes stent question in a 58-year-old man. Standard CT struggles with metal glare inside stents, yet this patient arrived with worsening chest pain despite full medical therapy after right coronary stenting.

Ultra-high-resolution photon-counting scans showed a fully blocked stent with strong collateral flow, while spectral iodine maps revealed dead transmural scar, supporting conservative care over risky revascularization. The case shows one scan answering anatomy, scar, and collaterals together for complex coronary disease and stent follow-up in daily practice.
pmc-13421269:
Duveneck and colleagues report a 2026 plant study of flowering genes in spring oilseed rape. In the model plant Arabidopsis, a gene called FLC blocks flowering until cold weather passes. Spring rape needs no cold, yet keeps nine copies of the gene. The team used gene editing to knock out each copy in a spring cultivar and watched flowering time.

Losing the copies sped flowering up clearly, so the genes do restrain flowering in spring types too, just without a cold switch. Gene activity patterns differed among the copies: some stayed active as the plant shifted to flowering, and one copy carried steady repressive marks. No cold-linked epigenetic pattern explained the timing. Knowing which copies matter lets breeders tune flowering time in a major oil crop, matching varieties to local seasons as climates shift.
pmc-13421469:
M. Rutenkröger and five colleagues investigate, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, why some patients stay dizzy long after surgery for vestibular schwannoma, a benign tumour on the balance nerve. Most patients in their group reported dizziness after the operation, and its burden on daily life varied widely.

Ninety-three patients completed questionnaires on mental health history, personality, bodily symptom focus, anxiety, depression and distress, alongside a standard dizziness handicap scale. Handicap tracked closely with vestibular symptom burden, anxiety, symptom focus and general distress. Needing more social support after surgery also accompanied worse handicap. The authors argue that psychological screening belongs in follow-up care, since distress and dizziness reinforce each other.
pmc-13421569:
Novela and colleagues explore in 2026 the lives of home-based caregivers looking after relatives with chronic mental illness in Ga-Dikgale, a rural area of South Africa's Limpopo Province. Research usually centers on patients and immediate families, leaving these caregivers in the shadows.

The qualitative study interviewed eight caregivers, six women and two men, chosen through purposive and snowball sampling, and grouped their accounts into themes. Many felt unprepared, lacking training in how to handle mental health crises. Emotional burden ran high, and support from families, government, and professionals was thin. Caregivers coped through group discussions, prayer, and leaning on friends and relatives. The authors recommend that the health department, charities, and community services work together to train and support this workforce.
pmc-13421769:
Xialing Chen and eight colleagues uncover, in a 2026 study, a tiny protein hidden on the 'wrong' strand of a silkworm virus genome. Double-stranded RNA viruses were assumed to make proteins only from their sense strand, leaving the antisense strand as a mere template for copying.

Ribosome profiling and protein analysis revealed a 78-amino-acid microprotein read from the antisense strand via an internal entry element resembling those viruses use to hijack ribosomes. The protein settles in the cell membrane and restrains viral replication. It grabs the virus's own silencer of the host's RNA interference defence. It then breaks that silencer's partnership with a key host protein, reviving the defence. The authors propose antisense microproteins as antiviral targets.
pmc-13422069:
Amir Mirhaghi argues, in a 2026 Matters Arising letter, that studies of triage reliability should report more than two agreement coefficients. He responds to a Swedish study of a modified South African Triage Scale used by ambulance crews, which found only poor agreement between raters on the overall category.

His critique starts from the study's own numbers. The coefficient it used, Krippendorff's alpha, is among the most cautious in use. That caution makes comparison with studies using other statistics treacherous. Collapsing categories into high and low acuity made agreement look worse still. Mirhaghi presses several points of method on how reliability is summed up and compared. The letter asks triage teams to check several coefficients side by side before calling a tool unreliable.
pmc-13422869:
Magdalene Yeok Yu Cheong leads a large team pairing, in a 2026 paper, a deep-learning blood-cell classifier with a second, deliberately simple model whose job is to explain the first. Microscope blood-smear reading is slow and subjective, and neural networks do it well but opaquely — a problem when clinicians must trust the answer.

Their YOLO network classifies and outlines cells; an explainer trained on its outputs uses clinically meaningful features, with importance scores flagging when the reasoning looks off. Across three datasets the classifier scored near-perfect discrimination, and its attention maps agreed with the explainer's chosen features. Nine haematology professionals concurred with nearly ninety-seven percent of predictions in a user study. The authors claim the pairing buys trust without surrendering accuracy.
pmc-13423069:
Padmasani Venkat Ramanan and Apoorva Kutar follow Indian preterm infants through their first year to see where growth falters after hospital discharge. Their prospective cohort at a South India hospital enrolled 201 babies born at or before 34 weeks. Feeding practices and body measures were recorded at six months and again near the first birthday, corrected for early birth.

Weight, length, and head size all slipped relative to age standards over the year. By 12–13 months, 21.9% of infants were underweight, 32.8% were stunted, and nearly half had small head growth. Lower gestational age and very low birth weight raised the odds of being underweight, while weak complementary feeding scores also tracked with poor growth, marking feeding support as a fixable target.
pmc-13423369:
Janssen and co-authors checked whether two advanced MRI measurements of eye tumors give the same answers when repeated at different hospitals, a requirement before scans can guide diagnosis or judge treatment response. Fifteen patients with uveal melanoma, the most common primary eye cancer in adults, each underwent two scans at two centers.

The repeat scans were separated by a mean interval of 28 days, ranging from 12 to 43 days between visits. Average absolute differences stayed small: 0.07 units on the diffusion measure, 0.11 on relative peak intensity, and 6 percentage points on outflow percentage between the two timepoints. The authors conclude that this variability is smaller than the differences clinicians rely on when distinguishing tumor types or assessing response to radiation, supporting use across centers.
pmc-13424869:
Zhenxin Rao and eleven colleagues test the lymph node ratio, the share of removed nodes containing cancer, as a prognostic and treatment-guiding measure in stage III colon cancer, alongside modern molecular markers. Records covered 361 patients who had curative surgery with thorough node clearance between 2013 and 2023 at the team's centre.

Statistical searches set the dividing lines at 0.16 for recurrence and 0.21 for survival; patients below a ratio of 0.2 lived longer and stayed freer of disease. Adjusted models kept the ratio significant for both outcomes, beside gene mutations and vessel invasion. Chemotherapy after surgery improved outcomes in the low-ratio group and showed the same tendency in the high-ratio group, keeping the ratio useful rather than merely descriptive.
pmc-13425369:
Lin and colleagues published a 2026 review on smell loss as a sign of raised death risk. Poor smell is common in older adults and ties to brain aging. The team pooled cohort studies that tracked smell and later deaths. Fourteen studies qualified, with twelve feeding the main pooled analysis.

Adults with smell loss faced about a fifth higher death risk overall. Correcting for possible publication bias softened the estimate to about nine percent higher. The link survived checks that removed one study at a time. How each study tested smell changed the strength of the link. The authors back standard smell tests in routine checks for older adults. Standard tests would also let clinics build personal risk profiles sooner.
pmc-13425869:
Huixia Hua and colleagues built machine learning models to estimate children's true glasses prescription without dilating drops in a 2026 retrospective pilot study. Cycloplegic refraction, done after drops relax focusing, is the reference standard but slows screening. Records covered 590 children aged about 2 to 15 years at a children's hospital in Zhejiang, split into training and held-out test groups by patient.

Models used ordinary clinical and eye measurement data to predict spherical power, spherical equivalent, and astigmatism components. The authors position predictions as triage for screening programs, flagging who needs full testing rather than replacing it.
pmc-13427369:
Kim and colleagues studied in 2026 how the size of clay mineral sheets changes the membranes built by stacking them. Such layered membranes, made from vermiculite, contain fine channels between sheets that let ions and molecules pass, and they are candidates for filtration and separation. Using high-resolution X-ray diffraction, the team compared membranes made from exfoliated sheets of different widths.

Sheet size clearly reshaped the membrane's internal order. It changed how the stacked crystals were aligned, a property called mosaicity, and how thick the ordered domains grew. Those shifts altered how polycrystalline, or patchwork-like, the membrane became. Since this internal structure controls how ions travel through the channels, membranes made from different sheet sizes will not perform alike. The authors say developers must control sheet size carefully and analyse structural disorder, not just chemistry, when designing these membranes.
pmc-13427569:
Moritz Thiel and co-authors report, in 2026, a small German trial of zinc tablets for children and young adults with GNAO1-related disorders. Faults in the GNAO1 gene cause movement problems, epilepsy, and delays in learning and growth. No treatment now fixes the faulty protein, though lab work shows zinc can partly restore its function. Thirteen patients aged from infancy to 25 took part for six months.

Zinc was given by mouth in doses set by age, and the main questions were safety and whether families could stick with it. Eleven of the 13 finished, and families managed the dosing on most days. Movement, motor skills, and quality of life were tracked as early signals only. A pilot this small guides design of a larger trial rather than proving zinc helps.
pmc-13427669:
Boujenah and Rozenberg wrote in 2026 to dispute a review's verdict that evidence is too weak to back universal cervix screening with vaginal progesterone to prevent preterm birth. Their charge is that the review blends two separate questions: whether screening whole populations helps, and whether the drug works in women already found to have a short cervix.

The trials behind the verdict compared screening against no screening, and fewer than three in a hundred women in them ever received the drug, which dilutes any effect toward zero. Trials that gave progesterone to women with a short cervix did show benefit. The letter also notes that screening trials used looser length cut-offs, enrolling lower-risk women. Weighing biology, pooled patient-level analyses, and the drug's low risk and cost, the authors argue for offering the strategy now.
pmc-13428169:
Oren Turgman and co-authors test, in a 2026 Dutch study, whether doctors judging the same emergency patients agree on what infection they have. Research on sepsis needs consistent labels, yet no gold standard exists for sorting infections after the fact. The team built a rulebook that adapts national surveillance definitions for emergency department use. Records came from over a thousand patients with suspected infection at four hospitals.

Two blinded doctors judged each case separately, and a third settled disagreements. Agreement on the infection diagnosis reached about 89 percent, rated very good by standard statistics. Judges also agreed closely on the likely germ and on whether sepsis was present. High agreement across four hospitals supports using the rulebook in large studies, where shaky labels would otherwise blur every result.
pmc-13430469:
Miguel Julião wrote a poem on love, loss, and parting that appeared in 2026 under a heading that pairs Dante with Cassidy. The speaker watches a loved one leave and weeps rather than prays, saying faith in gods is gone. Short lines in English mix with quoted lines in Italian and Latin drawn from older love writing.

Across the poem, sleep brings a dream filled with painful memories and the trace of a scent that cannot be held. The heart is shown as burning, broken, and eaten away from inside. Joy turns to bitter tears as the figure fades from view. The speaker stays where he was left, sunk in grief, and pleads for one more look at his heart.
pmc-13432369:
Vaeyens and team mapped which mutations in three cancer genes refuse to appear together in the same tumor. The genes are BRAF, KRAS, and EGFR. The mapping ran variant by variant. The pattern is called mutual exclusivity, and it hints the paired changes harm cancer cells. They analyzed 64,807 tumor samples, 1,570 cancer cell lines, and 2,714 Belgian clinical cases.

Co-occurrence proved rare among class I BRAF, hydrolysis-type KRAS, and classical EGFR mutations across every dataset examined. Pairwise analysis surfaced new exclusivity relationships involving atypical variants. Some overlapped pairs already known to be synthetically lethal, meaning the combination kills cells. Forcing expression of one partner in cells carrying the other confirmed the antagonism experimentally. It slowed growth in both test systems used. Survival showed no consistent penalty for co-mutant tumors, except in EGFR-KRAS co-mutant lung cancer. The authors offer the map as a precision oncology reference.
pmc-13432569:
Alexandra Hajduk and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a clinic visit in the first week or two after a heart attack lifts later health for older adults. Guides urge a visit within seven days, yet proof has split, and past work rarely weighed frailty traits that could skew who gets seen fast. A nationwide group of 1539 older patients, tied to public insurance data, gave rich detail on such traits.

More than two fifths won a visit in the first week, and a quarter more in the next week. Frailty traits ran no thicker among the early-visit crowd. Weighted math that evens out group gaps found no link between early visits and days spent out of hospital, nor with drops in life quality at six months. The authors call for care models that look past visit timing alone.
pmc-13432869:
Chen and colleagues screened in 2026 how gut bacteria affect the cholera germ, Vibrio cholerae, at strain level. The germ causes severe diarrhoea and fluid loss. Rather than whole mixed communities, the team tested liquid from single gut strains grown in the lab. They measured the cholera germ's growth, movement, biofilm building, and stress survival after exposure to each liquid.

Liquids from three strains, including Clostridium butyricum L65 and Ruminococcus bromii, strongly slowed the cholera germ's growth. Liquids from two other strains made the germ build more biofilm, the sticky layer that helps it persist. Some liquids curbed the germ's swimming, while others changed its stress defence through an enzyme called KatE. Matching the results with human cholera data singled out Ruminococcus bromii as a promising probiotic candidate.
pmc-13433769:
Thomas R Else and co-authors showed in 2026 how skin tone warps a light-and-sound scan. The scan reads blood oxygen deep in tissue. Their test group held the most mixed skin range yet gathered for such work. Forty-two sound adults spanned the full tone scale, plus people with a pale-patch state. Light tools have long skewed reads by tone, with grave care stakes.

Tone pigment drinks scan light in a hue-shifting way that rules at low pigment loads. At high loads, sound bounce off the skin's top layer rules instead. The two gears bend oxygen reads in a bent, non-step line. Fixes grow from that split: a hue fix for the light warp, plus a rebuilt sound path that dodges the bounce. Fair scans for all tones need such twin fixes, the authors argue.
pmc-13434569:
Catrin Pedder Jones and colleagues ask how England could widen free school meals in 2026. Seventeen voices from councils, national policy, universities, and schools were interviewed. Hunger at home is rising, yet cost and rollout fears slow expansion plans.

People backed plans that cut stigma first and tie meal growth to current school food rules. Sign up steps and letters to families need to be simpler and clearer. Quality checks on school food should stay firm as rolls grow. Above all, money must match the promise, the group agreed. The advice spans national, local, and school levels.
pmc-13436769:
Alimire Nabijiang and Leili Shahriyari build CellExLink, a tool that finds and standardizes cell type names in biomedical text in 2026. Cell types hide under varied names, short forms, and trait phrases. The pipeline tags each mention and links it to a Cell Ontology code.

Five test sets span full papers, excerpts, figure captions, abstracts, and anatomy text. Strict end to end scores range from 0.552 on captions to 0.725 on excerpts. Looser span scores average higher at 0.855 for relaxed matching. The tool beat shelf systems on finding, linking, and the joint task. Curators gain a faster path to linked literature data.
pmc-13437369:
Haitham Abu Khadija led a twenty-author team that built a simple score to flag stroke risk after heart bypass surgery. Stroke strikes about two percent of bypass patients and often traces to handling of the aorta during the operation, which can loose debris toward the brain. Their 2026 study gathered 6,818 adults from centers in several countries who had bypass surgery.

The new score, built only from facts already written in operation records, sorted patients into clear risk steps. Each standard rise in the score came with higher odds of stroke within thirty days, which struck 133 patients overall. Adding the score to a standard clinical model improved its sorting accuracy by a modest but real margin, and it helped where doctors actually make choices. The authors call the score a handy early warning drawn from routine data, while asking for testing in fresh groups before wider use.
pmc-13437469:
Youssuf Khanafer and colleagues revisit spleen removal for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, a rare immune defect that leaves boys with tiny, fragile platelets, eczema, and repeated infections. Removing the spleen was once the main answer to life-threatening bleeding, since it traps and destroys the faulty platelets. Their 2026 review asks what place the operation keeps now that transplants and gene therapy can cure.

The benefit fades in many patients: in the classic form, relapse strikes up to fifty-six percent within a year, while a milder related condition holds its gains better. Surgery also leaves the immune defect untouched and raises a lasting infection risk, demanding lifelong antibiotics and vaccines. The authors keep the operation for narrow roles: a bridge to transplant, a rescue where cure is out of reach. Unequal access to cures, they note, keeps this old tool relevant in poorer settings.
pmc-13438769:
Damee Choi's team measured attention in 2026 as ten drivers repeated the same public route over six days, testing whether familiarity frees or drains mental resources. Brain and eye signals were tracked, including fixation-linked brain waves, sound-evoked waves, and blink length, as indices of attention to vision and thought. Familiarity was expected to change how drivers split attention between road and mind.

Sound-evoked responses grew from early to later days, suggesting less attention to thinking tasks, while visual fixation responses fell, suggesting less attention to visual processing, as the route grew familiar. The paper gives objective support that familiar routes dull attention on two fronts. Driver safety teams get a physiological warning against assuming familiar roads are safe roads.
pmc-13438969:
Son Nguyen and colleagues report a child whose post-surgical silence lifted on a common sedative. Pediatric cerebellar mutism syndrome can follow removal of a back-of-brain tumor: the child stops speaking and swings emotionally, for reasons still guessed at. Their 2026 report concerns an eleven-year-old boy after removal of a medulloblastoma at a tertiary children's hospital.

A whiff of a related sedative during a radiation rehearsal briefly restored his speech and movement, a hint the team chased by starting daily lorazepam, which strengthens the brain's main calming signal. Within a week his functional independence score jumped forty points, and gains held. Stopping the drug brought swift regression; restarting brought recovery. The authors read this as evidence that the syndrome reflects a reversible network imbalance rather than fixed damage. They suggest gentler cousins of the drug deserve trials, aiming for the benefit without heavy sedation.
pmc-13439369:
Cong Wang and colleagues uncover a fuel pathway that helps BRCA1-deficient ovarian cancers spread, publishing in 2026. Faulty BRCA1 is best known for breaking DNA repair in hereditary ovarian cancer. Its part in spread was less clear. Profiling of cell chemistry showed that losing BRCA1 sharply raised choline handling, a nutrient route tied to membrane building. The loss freed a choline transporter, CTL4, by removing a repressive mark that BRCA1 normally helps place on its gene.

Extra transporter activity fed a choline product that steadied FAM3C, a protein that pushes cells toward a mobile state. Blocking the transporter reversed the high spread of deficient cells in tests. A compound named DT-13 curbed choline handling and suppressed spread in the models used. The authors nominate the transporter as a drug target for patients whose tumours carry BRCA1 faults.
pmc-13439569:
Asaf Madar, Tom Zemer, Ido Tavor, and Dino J Levy predict quirks of group choice from brain scans rather than listed prize features, reporting in 2026. Choices shift with the company an option keeps, a pattern called context effects. Standard models need each option described by two tidy numbers, yet people weigh hidden features too. The team first measured context effects for lotteries in a behaviour group. Two further groups then had brain scans while viewing the lotteries outside any choice.

Similarity between brain patterns for two lotteries forecast the context effects those lotteries produced. The forecasts beat classic attribute-based models on fresh data as well as on the data used to build them. Brain patterns mixed the stated features with unlisted ones that behaviour alone could not reveal. The authors offer neural similarity as a window on the full feature set behind decisions.
pmc-13440269:
Ke-Cheng Zhang's team built a real-time AI guide system in 2026 for keyhole stomach removal, where limited sense of the scene breeds errors. Videos from four top centers trained a YOLOv10 model to spot eleven tools and seven organs. Data were split by center for training, internal testing, and external validation, then deployed live in surgery rooms with workload and ease-of-use surveys.

Training accuracy ran high, internal and outside checks held up with moderate precision and recall, and live deployment proved feasible with acceptable surgeon workload and ease of use. Surgical teams get a generalizable vision aid for safer gastrectomy. Broader hospitals, rarer anatomies, and outcome trials will decide clinical value.
pmc-13440569:
Zhang and colleagues tested a small RNA, miR-15a-5p, in 2026 as a treatment for harmful blood vessel growth in the eye. The team measured the RNA in fluid from patients' eyes, then raised its levels in retinal cells and in two mouse models. They compared its effects with a standard anti-VEGF drug.

Raising it slowed vessel cell growth and blocked a change that leads to scarring. In mice it cut abnormal vessel growth, kept retinal thickness and electrical responses near normal, and reduced scarring signals. It worked by targeting VEGF and Smad2, two proteins that drive vessel growth and fibrosis, meaning scar build-up. Mice lacking the RNA developed faulty retinal vessels, showing it also guides normal growth. No harm to body or eye was seen at treatment doses.
pmc-13441269:
Shraddha Shah and colleagues catalogue interventions that might grow the heart's backup blood vessels, publishing a 2026 scoping review. Coronary collaterals are natural bridges between heart arteries that can feed starved muscle when a main vessel narrows. The team searched five databases for studies testing collateral growth in coronary artery disease. Twenty-three studies qualified, spanning drug, device, and training approaches.

Drug studies on blood pressure agents, growth factors, and statins reported improved collateral flow. Non-drug studies formed the majority and also reported gains, covering training, electrical stimulation, and external counterpulsation, a cuff-based circulation aid. Three studies paired training with heparin for benefit. Flow indexes and angiographic scores improved across intervention types, with modest effect sizes in randomised trials. The authors offer the map as scaffolding for stronger trials on whether grown collaterals change patient outcomes.
pmc-13441969:
Benjamin Fry, Kaia Slaw, and Nicholas F Polizzi design proteins from scratch that grab drug molecules tightly, using two neural networks that correct each other. Binder design must juggle protein sequence, protein shape, and drug pose at once, a triple puzzle that stalled earlier zero-shot attempts. Their loop pairs a sequence designer that reads a backbone plus docked drug with a structure predictor that folds sequence plus drug. Iterating the pair polished all three elements together and beat a physics-based loop.

Binders were built for two very different drugs, the cancer agent exatecan and the anticoagulant apixaban, succeeding in every exatecan attempt and most apixaban attempts. The tightest binders gripped at nanomolar to picomolar strength, orders beyond the next method. Network-suggested tweaks improved one binder a hundredfold with no laboratory input, and that binder shielded its drug's fragile ring from breakdown for days.
pmc-13442369:
Vaibhav Rohella and colleagues chain four vision tools into a forensic pipeline that finds weapons hidden in crime images and rebuilds their covered parts, reporting in 2026. Hands, clothing, and poor cameras hide parts of weapons in scene imagery, defeating plain detectors. Their framework pairs a transformer detector with a zero-shot segmenter for visible regions, a diffusion inpainter that reconstructs covered regions, and an edge-based sketch generator. Training used synthetically occluded images across firearm, grenade, knife, pistol, and rocket classes, plus fire as a hazard class.

Detection accuracy on occluded test data was strong by standard measures. Rebuild quality held above minimum thresholds until roughly half a weapon was covered. A demonstration app runs the chain in under a minute per image. The authors stress that reconstructions and sketches are aids for expert review and must pass independent forensic validation before any operational use.
pmc-13442769:
Ghufran Abdulal Shaheed Kemawy's team built a chitosan-based nanocarrier in 2026 delivering silver nanoparticles plus sodium butyrate to lung cancer cells. Lung cancer leads cancer deaths, and standard treatments carry heavy limits, prompting nanoparticle delivery designs. Chitosan-polycaprolactone particles about twenty to one hundred nanometers wide were characterized, then tested for drug release and killing of A549 lung cancer cells versus stem cells.

Release ran about eight times slower than free drug and three times faster at acidic pH, matching tumor conditions. The carrier killed over seventy-five percent of cancer cells at a low dose within a day while sparing stem cells relatively well. Death genes caspase-9, Bax, and p53 rose severalfold. Lung teams get a pH-sensitive carrier lead, still in cell studies.
pmc-13443169:
Zhiying Tang and colleagues release a long-span data set on nature services in China's Southern Hilly Region in a 2026 paper. The set maps five services, from water yield and soil guarding to carbon stores and habitat quality. Eight time slices run from 1990 to 2024 at a fine 30 m grid step.

One shared workflow, built on the InVEST tool set, kept methods even across years. Maps were summed to watershed and sub-watershed units, which match how land care is run. Land cover and climate feeds were paired to each model year with care. Older sets for the region were coarser or lacked the watershed frame. The authors pitch the set for long-term checks on how hills serve farms, towns, and wild life.
pmc-13445369:
Qingge Jia and colleagues trace a self-reinforcing loop of signals that helps cervical cancer resist the drug cisplatin, in a 2026 lab study. More than half of patients with advanced disease stop responding to the drug, and survival then falls sharply. The team hunted for the switches that keep resistant cells alive and stem-like.

A gene named ZIC5 ran high in resistant tumors and marked worse survival. ZIC5 switches on a receptor called CNTFR, while a partner signal through that same receptor switches ZIC5 back on, closing the loop. Blocking the receptor with an antibody broke the loop and, paired with cisplatin, shrank tumors in mouse and organoid models. The loop offers a fresh target for drug design.
pmc-13445669:
Ayşe Metin and colleagues report a 2026 survey of how perceived earthquake risk tracks sleep problems among pregnant women in Turkey's Central Black Sea Region. The team surveyed 303 pregnant women at two hospitals from October to December 2023, using scales for risk perception and pregnancy sleep problems with non-parametric analysis.

Risk perception correlated significantly, though modestly, with sleep problems, a link that matters because poor sleep in pregnancy raises risks from gestational diabetes to preterm birth and low birth weight. Most participants had never faced a major disaster, yet perceived risk still weighed on sleep. Clinicians should raise awareness and support healthier risk perceptions, the authors advise.
pmc-13445769:
Tsung-Chieh Yao and coauthors report a 2026 Taiwan claims study of whether acid-cutting drugs while expecting or in childhood raise serious illness risk in children. The team set pre-birth and childhood contact with proton pump blockers or H2 blockers against antacid contact, tracking hospital stays for illnesses with tuned hazard models.

Pre-birth contact linked to a modest overall illness rise, including sepsis, bronchitis, pneumonia, gastroenteritis, and kidney illness. Childhood contact also raised risks, with the highest risks in children exposed in both periods, including a steep sepsis signal. Doctors should weigh illness risk when giving these common drugs to mothers and young children.
pmc-13445869:
G. K. Elemuo and colleagues blend orange-fleshed sweet potato flour into cassava fufu flour and grade the mixes for nutrition, safety, and cooking behavior, in a 2026 food study. Cassava fufu is a staple with weak micronutrient content. The orange potato brings vitamin A and color that plain cassava lacks.

Four blends ran from pure cassava to thirty percent potato flour. Protein, fiber, fat, and ash rose as potato share grew, while paste behavior shifted toward steadier gels. Germ counts stayed within safe bounds in storage, and two lighter blends showed no fungal growth at thirty-five days. The thirty percent blend held the most carotene and protein, yet the twenty percent blend struck the best balance and earned the authors' pick for homes and children.
pmc-13447069:
Yanyan Xuan and colleagues test a composite blood and body index, TyHGB, as a flag for fatty liver disease in non-diabetic Japanese adults, in a 2026 study. The index blends blood fats, blood sugar handling, and weight into one number tuned to the disease's roots. The group held 13,682 adults from a community cohort.

About fifteen in a hundred adults had the liver condition. Each step up in the index raised the odds of disease, yet the link bent. Below a turning point near the top of the scale, risk climbed steeply, while above it the climb flattened out. Waist size carried near half of the link overall, and far more of it in non-obese adults than in obese ones, which recommends the index for lean people missed by weight rules.
pmc-13447169:
Jie Gao and co-authors pilot a family support programme for breast cancer in a 2026 trial with Chinese patients and their carers. Illness strains the whole household, not only the patient. The programme worked with patient and carer together over six sessions, aiming to build family resilience, meaning the shared ability to cope and adapt.

Sixty pairs were assigned at random to the programme plus usual care or to usual care alone. Family resilience scores rose much more in the programme group one week after the sessions, for patients and carers alike. Gains were still present three months later, alongside better coping and lower family burden. Recruitment, attendance and satisfaction were all high, which the authors take as a green light for a larger trial.
pmc-13447369:
Ali Robaian tests surface treatments for repairing printed dental resin in a 2026 laboratory study. Printed resins now serve for lasting fillings and crowns, yet how to make repairs stick well was poorly studied. Surface roughening and adhesive coating are standard tricks for other materials, and their value here needed direct comparison.

Sixty printed cylinders were aged by repeated heating and cooling, then split into five treatment groups. Options ranged from no treatment to roughening by bur or sandblasting, each with or without a universal adhesive. Repair material was packed on and bond strength measured, with failure patterns also recorded. Sandblasting plus adhesive gave the strongest bonds, while untreated samples were weakest and failed at the surface. Adhesive after roughening clearly helped, the author concludes.
pmc-13447469:
Nasser Alharbi, Ahmed Al-Eidan and Ghada Al-Ashaikh pilot a sibling-matched design for allergy outcomes in children with Down syndrome in a 2026 study. Wheeze, asthma, hay fever and eczema are often reported in these children, yet most earlier work compared unrelated children and ignored shared home and family factors. Matching each child with an unaffected sibling controls much of that background by design.

Thirty-four sibling pairs completed the pilot, with paired statistical tests that count only pairs where siblings differ. Wheeze and doctor-diagnosed asthma appeared somewhat more often in children with Down syndrome, though gaps fell short of clear significance. The authors stress feasibility over conclusions, since small discordant counts drive such tests. A ready framework for larger, properly powered sibling studies is the main product offered here.
pmc-13447569:
Adam El Hassouni and colleagues report Lemierre syndrome from a sinus source in a thirteen-year-old boy in a 2026 case study. The syndrome is a septic vein inflammation that usually follows throat infection and seeds clots to the lungs. Sinus origins and clots inside the skull are far less typical, raising the stakes for fast recognition.

The boy arrived with fever, neck swelling, a drooping eyelid, unequal pupils and reduced consciousness after dental pain and fever. Scans revealed sinus infection with a deep muscle abscess, vein clots in the neck and on both sides inside the skull, a small brain stroke area and septic spots in both lungs. Blood cultures stayed negative. Broad antibiotics, a blood thinner and steroids brought full clinical and scan recovery by six weeks, without drainage surgery.
pmc-13448669:
He Ren leads a team assessing mining-driven forest loss inside and around protected areas worldwide from 2001 to 2020 in a 2026 study. Protected areas anchor global forest conservation, yet rising mineral demand presses directly on their boundaries. How much mining forest loss falls inside reserves, and how far spillover reaches beyond them, needed a global accounting over two decades.

About a ninth of global mining forest loss occurred inside protected areas, and that share rose in the final five years studied. Over a quarter of mines linked to loss inside reserves stayed active throughout the whole period. Forest loss in the ten-kilometre ring around reserves ran nearly three times the inside total. Mining also reached forests with denser biomass over time, raising the carbon cost per hectare. Mitigation must work beyond reserve borders, the authors conclude.
pmc-13449069:
Lucia Ndlala and co-authors report in 2026 field trials of early- and intermediate-maturing maize hybrids bred to hold up under the multiple stresses facing Southern African farmers. Maize anchors food security in the region, yet yields lag global averages under drought, heat, and poor soils. The team grew 87 hybrids across 13 environments, mixing stressed and favorable sites, in a replicated lattice design.

Grain yield ranged widely, from 1.41 to 7.43 tonnes per hectare under stress conditions, and differences among hybrids were statistically clear. Ears per plant and ear height emerged as the secondary traits most closely tied to yield. Pulling the measurements together, the analysis singled out 20 hybrids that combined high output with stability across sites. Those selections now move forward to wider multi-environment testing for eventual release to growers.
pmc-13449469:
Haojie Ge and colleagues built a zinc-based particle that fights coronaviruses, and their work appeared in 2026. Coronaviruses harm both animals and people, and shots alone cannot give fast cover that works without the immune system. The team made a cage-like zinc material called ZIF8 and set it against plain zinc oxide.

In tests with a pig virus used as a model, ZIF8 eased harmful oxygen byproducts, kept the cell power plants working, and switched on two host defense routes, NLRP3 and STING. The particles also curbed representative beta, gamma, and delta coronaviruses in lab tests. The paper puts ZIF8 forward as a broad-acting drug lead that works through host cells rather than one viral target.
pmc-13449969:
Joanna Gemel and colleagues report in 2026 a gene mutation that produces both dangerous bleeding and dangerous clotting in the same patient. The case comes alongside atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome. The gene is THBD, which makes thrombomodulin, a protein on vessel walls that normally brakes clotting and calms the complement immune system. The team identified a variant, C256S, and studied endothelial cells grown from the patient's tissue to see what goes wrong.

Their characterization found the mutant protein is made but fails to travel properly through the cell's export pathway, so too little of it reaches the surface where it works. That trafficking defect ties the paradox together. Without surface thrombomodulin, vessels lose both their anticoagulant guard and a complement regulator. Bleeding, thrombosis, and kidney microangiopathy are left to coexist. The authors offer the case as a lesson in how one shipping failure inside cells can unsettle the clotting balance.
pmc-13450469:
Jinwon Lee and colleagues traced brown seed coats in soybean to mutations in the AGO5 gene in 2026, clarifying how seed color is silenced. Soybean seed coat color is controlled by silencing of chalcone synthase genes at the I locus, but genetic proof linking specific silencing factors to color was limited. The team studied mutants from a chemically mutagenized population.

Three independent brown-seed mutants of the normally yellow cultivar Pungsannamul all carried a single recessive trait and proved allelic, meaning they affect the same gene. Mapping narrowed the locus to a 2.83-million-base interval on chromosome eleven containing AGO5. Each mutant carried a distinct AGO5 change, including a splice-site change and two changes in the PIWI domain. Breeders gain a gene-level handle on seed coat color.
pmc-13451869:
Gur Hadar and co-authors recount in 2026 how Israel's army built a digital casualty card in two weeks during a war. Paper cards from the field had long gone missing or half filled, with full records for only a small share of the wounded in a past Gaza fight. The new system aimed to log care at the front and pass it cleanly along the rescue chain.

The team chose speed over frills, shipping a simple app with no sensor links or live hops between care levels. The write-up traces design choices, rollout under fire, and what the log showed about care in the field. The authors cast fast, plain digital records as a guard against lost facts and care errors.
pmc-13452769:
Virginia Bailey and five co-authors reflect on national trends in breast surgery that pairs tumor removal with reshaping in one operation. This oncoplastic approach grew out of proof that removing just the lump, plus radiation, matches full breast removal for survival. Their 2026 piece draws on insurance claims for more than 480,000 lumpectomy patients from 2010 to 2020.

Lumpectomies paired with reshaping rose by 249 percent across the decade, led by moving nearby tissue and by breast reduction work. Small studies tie the approach to happier patients and a better body image than plain lumpectomy or full removal. Access still lags for some groups, shaped by insurance type and other health problems. The authors frame the shift as care that now weighs looks and life quality beside cancer safety.
pmc-13454069:
Samer Mansoor Jameel studies how stroke length and stroke rate combine in elite freestyle swimming, arguing the pair interacts in a curved, not straight line, way. His 2026 study times fifty highly trained swimmers over maximal 50 metre sprints. Curved regression and a response surface map then hunt for the speed peak across the two measures.

The curved model explained 68 percent of the spread in velocity, a fifth better than the straight line model. Rather than one magic pairing, the map found a corridor of pairings where speed peaks. A stationary point test, backed by a curvature check, confirmed that zone as a true local peak. Jameel offers the framework for training plans and live coaching tools, giving coaches a range to aim at instead of a single number.
pmc-13454169:
Lawrence Merle Nelson writes a Perspective on relaxed vigilance, a state where care teams stay alert to risk without losing flexibility or trust. Chronic high vigilance, he argues in this 2026 piece, narrows attention and frays teamwork in hospitals and care systems. Humor, above all shared laughter, is his candidate signal that the balance holds.

Laughter, on his account, tells a team that risk watch persists while the social fabric needed for teamwork stays intact. He is careful to mark the link as conceptual, not proven cause and effect. Whether the state can form at all depends on hierarchy, workload, reporting culture, and how a unit talks. Nelson separates the idea from close cousins such as psychological safety and resilience. The piece aims at leaders who must hold safety and morale together over long stretches.
pmc-13454469:
Qiuhua Zhu and ten colleagues compare, in a 2026 records review, three ways to lift platelet counts in lymphoma patients after chemotherapy. Low platelets raise bleeding risk and can delay treatment. The review covered patients treated at one Guangdong hospital from April 2017 to May 2022, plus a group given no platelet-raising therapy.

One group took eltrombopag alone, one received a lab-made thrombopoietin, and one got both drugs together. Counts were similar before chemotherapy across the drug groups. By day five, the combined group already held a clear lead over each single-drug group and the untreated group. The lead persisted at day ten, when the combined group averaged well above the single-drug groups. The authors read the pairing as the stronger option for speeding platelet recovery, while noting the review design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13454669:
Ryosuke Aotani and twelve colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether the kind of home exercise matters during outpatient cardiac rehabilitation. Peak oxygen uptake, the body's top rate of oxygen use, predicts how such patients fare. Home exercise is essential between clinic visits, yet bike-based and walking-based plans had rarely been compared head to head.

The records review covered 69 patients who took exercise tests before and after rehabilitation. Patients whose home plan used a stationary bike ended with higher peak oxygen uptake than walkers, after accounting for starting level, age, and sex. Part of the edge ran through rising confidence about exercise. The share reaching a six percent gain was higher for the bike group, though not decisively. The authors credit the bike's set intensity and clear feedback, lessons walking plans could borrow.
pmc-13455269:
Jianbo Yuan and colleagues built a 2026 forecast for syphilis cases in China from public web search data. Case counts for the sexually spread infection have climbed for years in China, while routine watch systems react slowly and cannot warn ahead. The team paired monthly case reports from January 2011 to March 2025 with Baidu search volumes for linked terms, then blended the strongest terms into one search index.

A seasonal time model using that index beat the same model without it on every error measure. Mean absolute error fell from about 9,008 cases to about 5,184 cases. Mean percentage error fell from 16.0 percent to 10.0 percent in the test period. The gain matters because earlier warning could let health teams ready clinics and outreach before a rise peaks. Search data cannot replace case reports, but here it sharpened a plain forecast in a useful way.
pmc-13456869:
Roland Csorba and five colleagues report, in a 2026 case, robot-assisted removal of underdeveloped wombs in a young woman with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. In this condition, the womb and upper vagina fail to form, while the ovaries stay normal. Leftover womb remnants can ache for years and cloud daily life.

Their patient was eighteen and suffered chronic pelvic pain. Scans showed no cervix or vagina, two small womb remnants, and healthy ovaries, and gene tests confirmed a normal female chromosome set. Through robotic keyhole surgery, the team removed both remnants and the fallopian tubes. Reviews at three and six months found her free of pain and recovering well. The authors chose surgery over watchful waiting to head off future trouble. They add that mental health support remains a core part of care for these patients.
pmc-13457069:
Bing Xie, Yangsong Ou, Qiuhong Liu, and Yuan Li search, in a 2026 study, for blood markers of ischemic stroke rooted in sugar-coat molecules called glycosaminoglycans. These chains coat cells and steer inflammation after a stroke cuts brain blood flow. The team merged two public gene datasets and a hand-built list of 127 related genes, then let network and learning methods compete to find a signature.

Three genes survived every filter, all running high in stroke blood: MCEMP1, PRRG4, and VSIG4. A scoring chart built on them sorted stroke from health robustly in the data. Pathway and immune analyses tied the trio to the inflammatory wave that follows a blocked vessel. The team also checked the genes directly in blood from five stroke patients and five controls, confirming the rise. Drug databases offered candidate compounds that touch the same pathways, a starting shelf for future tests.
pmc-13457169:
Zhihui Lu and co-authors review a proposed shift in how scientists study which messenger RNAs a cell is actively turning into protein. Messenger RNA levels explain only about 40 percent of the variation in protein amounts, so translation itself needs direct measurement. Their 2026 review argues that pairing translation fractions with direct, single-molecule RNA sequencing could reveal full-length translating molecules that older methods miss.

The review walks through established tools, including polysome profiling, ribosome profiling, affinity purification of tagged ribosomes, and methods that recover intact ribosome complexes. Each approach is weighed against three shared limits. Copying steps bias and shorten reads, chemical marks and poly(A) tails get lost in preparation, and short reads cannot link distant parts of one molecule. Readers get a map of what single-molecule translatomics would need to prove before it can reshape the field.
pmc-13457269:
Haoyue Ma and colleagues show that lymph node spread worsens outlook even in stage IV bowel cancer in a 2026 Japanese study. Stage IV colorectal cancer already means distant spread, yet whether nodes matter on top of that spread stayed disputed. The team reviewed 493 surgically treated patients from 2007 to 2020 at a high-volume Japanese centre. It compared 384 with node spread plus distant spread against 109 with distant spread alone, before and after matching.

Five-year overall survival favoured distant spread alone: about 42 versus about 31 percent before matching, and about 44 versus about 27 percent after. Cancer-specific survival showed the same gap. Node spread stayed an independent risk factor in both analyses, with hazard ratios near one and a half to one point seven for overall survival. The authors argue staging subsets should reflect this split, so patients with both spread routes are not grouped with those whose spread travelled by blood alone.
pmc-13457869:
M M Mambetova and colleagues test adding nickel and magnesium to a zeolite catalyst that turns carbon dioxide into methane, in a 2026 study. Turning carbon dioxide into methane can store green energy as man-made gas, yet the support mix and metal-adding method shape gas output and purity. Lithium silicate was made from Taizhuzgen natural zeolite, then loaded with nickel alone or nickel plus magnesium by pore soaking or solution burning, and tested from 250 to 550 degrees Celsius.

The soaked nickel and magnesium mix, with evenly spread nickel and even basic sites, turned 75 to 78 percent of carbon dioxide into gas. It gave 87 to 88 percent methane share at 450 to 500 degrees. The burned mix turned all carbon dioxide into gas but gave only 20 to 50 percent methane share, favouring a side reaction, though it held off carbon build-up better. Plant teams gain a clear trade between methane share and stability.
pmc-13458169:
Sanghyeun Park and colleagues report cases where direct LDL cholesterol tests gave impossible numbers in a 2026 letter. LDL cholesterol guides heart risk and treatment, and direct automated assays are favoured because they skip triglyceride maths, yet abnormal lipoproteins can corrupt them. The team examined 16 implausible results from Asan Medical Center over December 2023 to October 2025, defined by fractions that broke arithmetic rules or by odd reaction curves.

Most patients had liver or pancreatic disease, mainly cholestasis, with markedly raised liver enzymes and bilirubin. Cobas results ran far below Beckman AU5800 results, with a mean gap of minus 304.7 mg per dL, and dilution repeats reproduced the pattern, pointing to lipoprotein interference rather than a simple inhibitor. No reference method was used, so the truer platform cannot be named, but labs gain a warning to flag and recheck impossible LDL values in cholestatic patients.
pmc-13459369:
Abraham Zormelo and co-authors surveyed adults in Ghana's Hohoe Municipality about drinking habits and what residents know about alcohol's long term harms. Municipal level data for the general adult population were missing, with earlier local work covering only students. Their 2026 study recruited 318 adults from households and alcohol selling points through stratified random sampling and face to face interviews. It defined current drinking as having at least one standard drink within the past thirty days and tested which social and behavioral factors tracked with consumption.

Of the participants, 122 people, 38.4 percent, were current drinkers, and 53.5 percent reported drinking at some point in their lives. Local gin, akpeteshie, was the most consumed drink at 47.6 percent among consumers in the survey. Knowledge lagged behind exposure: 85.6 percent acknowledged alcohol harms health generally, yet only 53.5 percent showed high knowledge of its chronic consequences. Easy accessibility was the leading reason given for drinking, at 55.3 percent.
pmc-13461169:
Kyle V. Marra and colleagues chart blood vessel twisting across the mouse oxygen-induced retina disease model in a 2026 study. Vessel twisting guides treatment in retina disease of early birth, yet its time course in the standard mouse model was undefined. Retinal flat mounts from normal-oxygen and oxygen-induced retina disease mice, after-birth days 10 to 56, were cut out by a GAN and scored with the iROP-Assist twisting index.

New vessel growth peaked at day 17 and resolved by day 23, while vessel loss regressed over a similar window. Twisting peaked with new growth at day 17 but stayed elevated through day 56, echoing medical staying power after vessel regression. Experts gain a durable, scored form for studying twisting workings and testing cures beyond new-vessel endpoints.
pmc-13461669:
Guillermo Campoy leads a 2026 memory experiment on a classic false-memory trick used with short holding times. People study lists of related words, such as sleep words, and later wrongly claim the key word appeared. The team used lists of five words, then tested memory at once or after a short gap filled with a distracting task. Gaps of 3, 9, or 27 seconds were compared.

As the gap grew, people recognized shown words less often and false words more often. The authors explain the split with two memory traces: a detailed trace that fades fast and a gist trace that lasts longer. The fading detail both supports true memory and blocks false claims, so its loss lets the trick work better. False memory appeared with no gap and when people were warned about the trap. That finding presents the effect as a feature of short-term memory, not a testing quirk.
pmc-13462069:
Lapiņa and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot study of microRNAs in chronic spontaneous urticaria, a skin disorder of recurring wheals and swelling without a clear trigger. MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that tune gene activity and circulate in blood, making them possible markers. No solid marker yet tells the disorder's clinical patterns apart.

Thirty patients were split evenly among wheals only, wheals with swelling, and swelling only, plus ten healthy controls. Plasma miRNAs were profiled across the groups with standard tools. Lapiņa found sixty-one miRNAs that differed across groups before strict correction for multiple testing was applied. After that correction no subgroup signature held up, though five candidates, including miR-204-5p, showed nominal links to clinical pattern. The authors present the candidates as leads for larger marker studies.
pmc-13462169:
L Ceriani leads a 2026 scan study on predicting first-treatment failure in a lymphoma growing as a bulky mass in the chest, called primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma. Spotting which patients will fail standard immune-chemotherapy remains a challenge. The team analyzed PET scans from 501 patients in an international trial. Scan measures captured tumor bulk, sugar use, and how uneven that use was within tumors, a trait called metabolic heterogeneity.

Image analysis in 495 patients pulled out over a hundred features, then kept those not echoing basic tumor size. One texture feature marking uneven metabolism proved the strongest risk sign. Patients with low unevenness had five-year survival without disease growth of 93 percent, against 65 percent for high unevenness. Overall survival split widely, 96 against 80 percent. Adding a sugar-use measure improved sorting further, beating standard risk scores. The authors back scan texture as an early warning tool for this lymphoma.
pmc-13462669:
Aiqin Song leads a 2026 gene study building an eight-gene outlook signature for children with acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The genes relate to tagging of RNA, through three tag types that help control how genetic messages are used. Tag genes differing between children who died and those who survived were screened, and a statistical method picked the leanest set.

The eight-gene score split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with different survival, and the split held in a validation set. The score stood as an independent risk factor, and a chart joining it with other traits predicted survival better. Low-risk patients carried more monocytes, an immune cell type, and lower tumor purity in their samples. Six tag genes tied strongly to tumor purity. The authors offer the signature as an early marker set, pending proof in larger studies of children.
pmc-13462769:
Gonzalez published a 2026 reply on tattoo ink and the immune system. The reply answers Kluger, who had questioned an earlier study from the group. That study tracked how tattoo pigment reaches lymph nodes and affects immune cells. Gonzalez defends the design while granting that care is needed in reading it.

The mouse setup, he notes, aimed for controlled doses, not beauty-parlor realism. Human cell tests in dishes echoed the key mouse findings closely. Human lymph node samples also held pigment where the model predicted. Vaccine timing in the study probed early and late swelling phases on purpose. The reply holds that the combined evidence supports real biological relevance. He closes by welcoming tests of the model in clinical settings.
pmc-13463469:
Melendez-Atao and colleagues report a 2026 study of paco, a prized Amazonian fish, farmed in ponds in Peru's central jungle. Farmers sell the fish in three weight ranges, but how harvest size affects meat recovery was unmeasured. The team compared body dimensions, gut traits, carcass yield, and edible tissue across the three commercial categories.

Most body traits grew steadily with weight, showing coordinated development. Larger fish had longer intestines and gave more edible meat per fish, while smaller fish gave a higher share of eviscerated carcass, the cleaned body before filleting.  For farmers, the results price the trade-off directly: growing fish longer yields more flesh per animal. It ties up pond time and feed, so the profitable harvest point depends on market prices per category.
pmc-13463569:
Dossybayev and a team in Kazakhstan read in 2026 the gene spread of the Auliekol, a home beef breed raised for harsh steppe life. The breed was crossed into shape last century from local and famed beef stock. The team ran a chip that reads tens of thousands of gene marks in eight herds. The reads fed counts of spread, inbreed marks, and clan maps.

The pool ran wide, a good sign for the breed's health. Herds split only weakly, and deep inbreeding did not show. Clan maps put all herds on one shared root. Marks of gene flow showed farms swap sires, which keeps the pool stirred. The authors urge leads to guard the wide pool.
pmc-13463769:
Tianzheng Sun and seven co-authors build a paired germ system in which two E. coli strains feed each other. Each strain was engineered to need a nutrient that its partner leaks. Cross-feeding like this props up cooperation in wild microbe groups, yet cooperation often breaks down.

Paired growth boosted the group, yet it also widened the spread of traits from cell to cell in both strains. Uneven sharing of leaked food across the flask explained most of that spread, through uneven gene activity. The same effect showed up in wild strain pairs from water, soil, and plant roots. Cooperation, the team concludes, trades group strength against sameness of its members.
pmc-13463969:
Peters and colleagues tested a 2026 decision algorithm for patients with endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, a precancer of the womb lining that hides real cancer in over a third of cases. The question is who needs lymph node sampling during surgery: sampling everyone over-treats many, while sampling no one can miss staging.

Fifty patients were treated by the algorithm, which sent patients to sentinel node biopsy when ultrasound showed a thick lining or pathology could not rule out cancer. Nearly half the patients proved to have cancer, and sixteen percent had high-risk cancers. Node sampling reached 92 percent of cancer patients and every high-risk case. The algorithm's sensitivity for staging cancer was 92 percent, supporting more tailored surgery.
pmc-13464069:
Zhang and colleagues uncovered in 2026 how glioblastoma recruits the immune system to protect itself. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive brain tumor. Computer analyses and lab experiments pointed to a protein called IFI30. Chemical marks on its gene's packaging switch it on. The protein is abundant in these tumors and reshapes the immune cells around them. Macrophages can make up half the tumor mass.

IFI30 pushed tumor cells to release a fatty messenger, PGE2. A two-step relay involving proteins named MAFF and PTGS2 drove the release. The messenger docked onto receptors on macrophages. It flipped internal switches that drew more macrophages in. The macrophages settled into a tumor-friendly state. Meanwhile, the share of cancer-killing CD8 T cells shrank. The chain operated in dishes and in animals. Because each link is druggable, the authors propose IFI30 as an immunotherapy target.
pmc-13464669:
Xiaoguang Yan and four co-authors build a light-based test that reads starch in corn kernels without grinding them. Old lab methods destroy the kernel and take hours. Their tool uses near-infrared imaging, which reads how light bounces off grain chemistry, across fifty-eight rainfed corn varieties.

A cleaning pipeline sharpened the light signals, and a two-stage search picked fourteen key wavelengths tied to starch bonds. Four forecasting models trained on those signals, and a neural network won out with solid accuracy on held-back grain. The chosen wavelengths carry clear chemical meaning, which helps trust the readings. Breeders gain a fast screen for high-starch lines, and mills gain a quick grade check.
pmc-13465069:
Milen Hristozov and three co-authors report two patients with rare nerve antibodies and scans hinting at tumor-linked brain disease. Paraneoplastic syndromes arise when a hidden tumor tricks the immune system into attacking nerves, often years before the tumor shows. Both patients tested positive for anti-Zic4 antibodies in blood and spinal fluid.

One patient also carried anti-NMDAR antibodies, tied to autoimmune brain inflammation. Scans in both showed focal changes matching cerebellar decay and a suspected tumor site. Follow-up imaging, though, found no tumor in either patient. The pair may mark a non-tumor cerebellar syndrome instead, the authors propose. Long watch stays vital, since a cancer could still surface later.
pmc-13465269:
Lucas Marmin, Fanny Ruby, and Patrick Philipp test nanopore DNA barcoding as a plant food fraud detector. Processed spices and teas hide swaps that microscopes and chemical reads miss. Their portable sequencing workflow scans whatever plant DNA a product holds, with no target list set in advance.

Eight single-plant reference items and five store products with mixed ingredients went through the pipeline. Undeclared mint inside oregano and outright species swaps both surfaced cleanly. Reading three gene markers together caught more than any single marker alone. Worn DNA in heavily processed goods, gaps in reference libraries, and rich species mixes still blinded some calls. Turnaround ran two to four days on minimal gear, fit for first-line screening.
pmc-13465369:
Zalak Shah and six co-authors survey patients, caregivers, and community doctors on access to T-cell redirecting therapies for multiple myeloma. The immune therapies post striking results in returned disease, yet certified centers, build delays, and cost fence them off. Awareness gaps add a quieter fence on top.

Black patients and those with less schooling knew the therapies least, though actual use ran even across racial groups among those treated. Caregivers reported heavy emotional strain and time demands from the treatment path. Doctors named patient hesitancy as the top brake on referrals to therapy centers. Better teaching, caregiver backing, and tighter care coordination top the authors' fix list.
pmc-13465569:
Ying Wu and three co-authors cast IL-33, an immune alarm signal, as a metabolic guardian of the injured liver. Beyond sounding alarms, IL-33 rewires how liver cells burn fuel. Gene data joins cell and mouse experiments to trace the effect through one enzyme, PDK4.

Raising IL-33 pushed liver cells toward oxidative phosphorylation, the high-yield fuel route in mitochondria. The shift ran through PDK4, which gates entry into that route. IL-33 thus stands as both alarm and metabolic checkpoint, the authors conclude, and a fresh target for liver protection.
pmc-13465769:
Kaszecki and colleagues study how a mixed microbial community tolerates the toxic metal cadmium in this 2026 paper. The community centers on Euglena mutabilis, a single-celled alga, living with fungi and bacteria. Cadmium poisons most life, so the team combined transcriptomics, which tracks which genes are switched on, with hormone measurements to see how the partnership responds.

Exposed to cadmium, the alga stayed alive by locking the metal away inside its chloroplasts, the green structures that capture sunlight. It also built up paramylon, a storage carbohydrate, for protection. Gene activity shifted across metal transporters, photosynthesis machinery, and hormone pathways in a coordinated way. The authors interpret this as the whole community reorganizing together to detoxify the metal rather than each member coping alone.
pmc-13465869:
Aghajani Mir and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a class of tiny RNA fragments clipped from transfer RNA, the cell's protein-building adapters. Once dismissed as debris, these fragments turn out to regulate genes during viral infection. The review covers two families: fragments made in normal processing and stress-induced halves made when cells are under attack. Their roles at the host-virus border are the focus.

The fragments fight viruses on several fronts. They silence genes, reshape the genome's control marks, and tune both the making and the reading of gene messages. Stress-induced fragments can throttle overall protein production by roughly a tenth or more. Viruses, in turn, exploit some fragments for their own ends. Because fragment patterns shift characteristically with infection, the authors see promise in them as diagnostic and prognostic markers. Personalized antiviral treatments built on them are a longer-term prospect.
pmc-13465969:
Leon A Adams and colleagues measured serious fatty liver disease in 2026 among primary care patients with metabolic risk in Victoria, Australia. Most fatty liver burden sits in primary care, yet severe disease rates there were poorly described. Records from 84 general practices flagged 110,938 people with metabolic dysfunction, with liver scores available for subsets.

At-risk MASH affected 24.3% of those with a fibrotic index, while 16.3% needed further liver checks and 4.3% already had advanced fibrosis. Male sex, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension tracked with at-risk disease, and poorer areas faced higher risk for both outcomes. The findings back risk sorting in primary care, especially for diabetes patients, plus policy action on the social roots of liver disease.
pmc-13466369:
Licznerska and co-authors review the two fronts of hormonal attack on breast cancer: blocking estrogen's receptor and stopping estrogen's manufacture. Their 2026 paper notes about seventy percent of breast cancers depend on estrogen. Receptor modulators work well until resistance develops, and they are useless in triple-negative disease, leaving the synthesis enzymes as the complementary target set.
