Sulfatase and the 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, which activate weaker estrogen forms, remain under intensive investigation as drug targets. The authors summarise recent modulators and inhibitors across both the receptor and all three enzymes, a combination few reviews attempt together. Their perspective weighs where dual targeting might overcome resistance and whether any of these routes can eventually reach the triple-negative gap.
pmc-13467169:
Zhou, Yuan, and Tan reviewed in 2026 why cloned pig embryos so often fail, and what new tools might lift the yield. Pig cloning, called SCNT, moves a body cell's core into an egg with its own core gone. Cloned pigs could serve farm breed, lab study, and organ gifts for man. Yet the embryos grow weak, are lost mid term at high rates, and yield sick young far more than bred kin.

The review lays the chief blame on half done code resets: the egg fails to wipe the body cell's marks in full. Short wear caps on the code, sick cell power plants, and harm from the hand work add to the toll. The authors sort the fixes on hand, from code mark drugs to gentler craft, and weigh what each can and cannot do. They close with pig traits that set this field apart.
pmc-13467769:
Zhamaliyeva, Brimkulov, and Mamurzhankyzy ask how common depression and anxiety are in people with a newly recognized lung pattern, in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The pattern is called PRISm, short for preserved ratio impaired spirometry. In PRISm, a standard breathing test shows reduced airflow volume. Yet the ratio between two key measures stays normal. The pattern is already tied to heart and metabolic disease.

Six studies covering 43,900 people fed the pooled analysis. Depression affected about 17 percent of people with PRISm. Anxiety affected about 15 percent in the five studies reporting it. Estimates varied widely between studies, though. The authors argue that mental health screening belongs in the routine care of this group. They also caution that only a handful of studies exist. None yet prove that the lung pattern causes the mood disorders.
pmc-13467969:
Dąbrowski and Sołek characterized in 2026 how heat treatment changes a medical titanium alloy containing niobium and zirconium, a material used where implants need strength without toxicity. They used treatment settings not tried before: dissolving at a high temperature of 1,050 degrees, water quenching, then aging at moderate temperatures.

After quenching, the alloy held a martensite structure, a hard crystal form, with low hardness but high fracture toughness, meaning it resisted cracking well. Aging broke that structure down and formed new phases, which raised hardness while lowering toughness. Microscope and fracture surface analyses confirmed the close link between internal structure and the measured properties. The authors say their parameter map expands the design knowledge for this alloy in medical use.
pmc-13468969:
Geraldine Gallen and a multinational panel present in 2026 a clinical questionnaire, named LIFESTEPS. It helps diabetes teams uncover why a person with type 1 diabetes is not using glucose technology as hoped. Pumps and sensors fail socially before they fail technically: psychosocial, behavioral, and lifestyle barriers drive uptake, continued use, and quiet abandonment. Twelve experts from eleven countries across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa built the tool from the barrier literature.

The panel grouped barriers into themes and drafted a structured questionnaire, translated into multiple languages. Two rounds of evaluation by clinicians and patients then rated clarity, comprehensibility, practicality, relevance, and freedom from bias. A barrier checklist that fits routine appointments could rescue expensive technology from being prescribed, unused, and blamed on the patient, which is the outcome the tool exists to prevent.
pmc-13469369:
Loránt Szabó, Zoltán Weltsch, and Andrea Ádámné-Major ask in 2026 when combining several warning scores actually helps self driving sensors notice unfamiliar scenes. Their pipeline merges detector scores and then calibrates them so the false alarm rate carries a mathematical guarantee. Tests covered camera images and laser radar scans from road vehicles.

Plain averaging of the scores gave little benefit and sometimes diluted the strongest single detector. One approach did help the camera data, because it paired two independently built vision models and scaled their scores before averaging. On laser scans the gain was small and sensitive to calibration choices. The authors conclude that the portable guarantee matters more than the merging itself. Shops building safety cases can reuse one certified pipeline across sensor types.
pmc-13469669:
Gordiienko and co-authors examine in this 2026 study how storage temperature changes extracellular vesicles, the tiny membrane packets that mesenchymal stromal cells release to signal other cells. Vesicles from fat tissue, umbilical cord, and dental pulp cells were kept in salt solution at refrigerator, freezer, and deep-freezer temperatures and checked at set intervals.

Particle counts and total protein stayed stable for at least 14 days under refrigeration and for at least 6 months at minus 20 degrees in a standard freezer. Samples held at minus 80 degrees kept their characteristics for at least 10 months, the longest window tested. The team also tracked a growth factor inside the vesicles to confirm that stored samples kept a biologically relevant quality, supporting their development as future cell-free therapies.
pmc-13471169:
Deng and colleagues interviewed hospital patients in China in 2026 about switching antibiotics from drip to pills, a switch stewardship programs promote to cut infections and stays. Drip antibiotics are heavily overused in China, reaching 86 to 93 percent in some hospitals. Fifteen inpatients on antibiotic therapy from five busy wards gave semi-structured interviews, structured by the Health Belief Model, which sorts decisions by perceived risks, benefits, and cues.

Willingness sorted into two themes and nine subthemes. Motivators included seeing benefits, fearing severe resistance, worrying about drip safety, and staff prompts. Barriers ran deeper: many doubted pills work as well as drips, and others felt unlikely to face resistance or rated it as not serious. A widespread label for antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs, fed the confusion, and some doubted their own ability to manage pills. The authors recommend public education that corrects the label and proves oral antibiotics' strength.
pmc-13471269:
Helena Janssen and co-authors investigate in 2026 whether women die more often than men after a brain aneurysm bursts. Women are known to develop and rupture aneurysms more readily, but reports on survival after the bleed conflict. Using the UK Biobank cohort of half a million people, the team found 990 participants who suffered this kind of hemorrhage during follow up.

About two thirds of the cases were women. Ninety days after the bleed, roughly a third of the women had died, against about twenty eight percent of the men, a modest gap confirmed by survival curves. Once age and the health differences present at the time of the bleed were accounted for, the gap shrank and lost statistical firmness. Within each sex, older age and blood pressure medication use each raised the fatality risk.
pmc-13471369:
Onder and colleagues compared two scoring systems that grade how well a broken hip is realigned during surgery, asking which one better predicts a screw cutting out of the bone afterward. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 108 patients aged 65 and older treated with the same femoral nail for unstable hip fractures.

Patients averaged 79 years of age, and 69.4% were women, with cutout occurring in 15 cases, or 13.9% of the group. The Chang criteria predicted cutout more accurately, reaching an AUC of 0.79 on a scale where higher means better prediction, versus 0.68 for the Baumgaertner criteria. The authors describe the Chang system as the more complete biomechanical tool but call for larger multi-center studies before routine adoption.
pmc-13471669:
Stoll and co-authors synthesized what pushes midwives toward quitting, organizing the evidence with the job demands–resources model. Their 2026 systematic review covered 30 quantitative studies from 17 countries published between 2010 and 2025, encompassing 17,608 midwives in total.

Intention to leave runs high everywhere. Reported rates span 40 to 53% in Europe, 25 to 67% in North America, 40 to 75% in Africa, and 43 to 52% in Australia across the included studies. The pattern the authors draw is an erosion chain: structural pressure raises workload and stress, which breeds health problems and work–life conflict, which ends in burnout. Weak pay, job insecurity, and thin organizational support independently feed the urge to exit.
pmc-13471769:
Margreet Vogelzang, Sean Dong Wei Gan, and Jamie Setch survey in 2026 whether juggling multiple languages in daily life relates to milder autistic social traits in adults. Earlier work mostly studied children in small groups and split people crudely into one language or two. Their online study enrolled 459 adults, of whom 132 carried an autism diagnosis, and measured language engagement as an entropy score capturing how evenly several languages are used.

Greater language entropy tracked with lower autistic trait scores for social interaction and overall traits, both in the full group and within the autistic subgroup. The links inside the autistic group were large by social science standards. Communication traits, by contrast, showed no relation to language use at all. The authors present multilingual engagement as reliably tied to social ease in adulthood.
pmc-13472969:
Michael Pavlides leads a 2026 study that tests blood and scan markers for fatty liver disease linked to poor metabolic health. The work ran at many centers and checked how well each test found liver inflammation and scarring. Tests covered scans that gauge liver stiffness, blood markers, and combined scores built from several measures. Results were read against a central standard for each person.

Among 357 people, scans that measure stiffness did best for late scarring and for cirrhosis, the most severe stage. One blood marker led the blood tests for finding active liver inflammation, though it fell short of the set target. Readers get a firm ranking of which noninvasive tests can replace biopsy for staging liver harm.
pmc-13473069:
Pierre Besson-Magdelain and co-authors refine a lab method in 2026 for mapping sugar forms of a human hormone called hCG. The hormone matters in pregnancy tests and in some cancer care. Older methods gave weak signals and messy spectra because the acid used to aid separation also formed extra adducts. The team tried lower acid levels and then swapped in a milder acid.

The milder acid lifted signal strength and cut adduct share from about thirty percent to about ten percent. A scanning mode that breaks apart what is left raised signals several times over. The final setup found far more sugar forms than before, with 76 forms for one hormone part and 200 for the other. Labs gain a cleaner way to profile this hormone.
pmc-13473169:
Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 that a simple blood ratio tracks low muscle mass in people with rheumatoid arthritis. The ratio, called NPAR, divides the share of neutrophils, a front-line white cell, by albumin, a blood protein tied to nutrition. Muscle loss is a common hidden burden here, driven by long inflammation and poor nutrition.

The team studied 659 hospital patients and checked the pattern in a United States survey group of 375 patients. Patients with higher ratios were more likely to have low muscle mass, and the link held after other factors were weighed. The ratio alone sorted patients with fair accuracy. Among patients with low muscle mass, a higher ratio also tracked with higher death rates. The authors propose the ratio as a cheap early warning for muscle loss.
pmc-13473669:
Ramesh Sharma and eight colleagues explored in 2026 two quaternary Heusler alloys, LiTiPtTl and LiZrPtTl, as materials for gathering energy from heat and light. Using density functional theory, plus transport theory, the team calculated electronic, elastic, optical, and heat-to-electric properties from first principles. Optical results show strong low-energy response and strong ultraviolet reflection, suggesting uses in protective coatings and solar power, while lattice heat flow stays very low at room temperature. pmc-13474069:
Cincione and colleagues review in 2026 how hormone disorders cause osteoporosis, the bone thinning that leads to fractures. Such secondary osteoporosis is often missed, especially in men, younger women, and people whose bone density looks near normal despite broken bones.

Hormone problems disturb bone remodeling, mineral balance, and sex steroid and growth signals. The authors stress bone quality, meaning the internal structure of bone, as a driver of fracture risk that standard density scans and the FRAX calculator can miss. They propose a workup that combines the hormone picture, spine imaging, a texture score for spine bone, and blood tests. Treatment should fix the hormone disorder and add bone drugs matched to fracture risk, choosing between bone-building and bone-protecting options.
pmc-13474369:
Maher Monir Akl and Amr Ahmed gather five cases in 2026 where an overactive thyroid was blamed on the wrong disease. All five people had thyroid hormone excess caused by gland damage from Hashimoto disease, a form where the immune system attacks the gland. Four cases came from past reports and one was new. Most felt tired or had racing heart feelings, while two had no clear hyper signs.

Four of five were first misread as Graves disease, often because key antibody tests were skipped. The series shows which tests prevent that error.
pmc-13474869:
Bing and colleagues measured how saddle height and pedaling power load the legs during cycling in a 2026 lab study. Overuse injuries are common in riders, and bike fit plus effort shape the forces running through muscles and joints. Twenty-five participants rode under nine combinations, three saddle heights crossed with three power outputs, while sensors tracked their motion and pedal forces for a computer model of the legs.

The model's muscle patterns matched measured muscle activity well, which supported its use for comparing the nine riding setups in the study. Higher power raised forces in the hip and knee extensor muscles and in their joints, but lowered forces around the ankle instead. Higher saddles straightened the hip and knee, cut most muscle forces, and lowered most peak joint forces. One shin muscle worked harder, though, so the authors favor moderate power with a higher saddle.
pmc-13474969:
Can and co-authors built a machine learning tool in 2026 that predicts metabolic flux ranges. The standard approach, flux variability analysis, solves many optimization problems per network and can take hours on large studies. Random forest and gradient boosting models scored best, with the lowest errors and classification results among the six model families tried. The team validated the approach on six cancer datasets, covering breast, colon, pancreatic, and prostate tumors, and says it beat the prior state-of-the-art method on both speed and accuracy.
pmc-13478169:
Lee and co-authors ran a pilot study in Seoul in 2026 comparing carried air pollution sensors against fixed city monitors for predicting lung function drops in asthmatic children. Average particle levels from all three sources, near 30 micrograms per cubic meter, ran about double the World Health Organization guideline of 15 for this pollutant. The carried sensor tracked breathing drops most closely, with a correlation of minus 0.481 against flow, well ahead of both fixed networks. pmc-13478369:
Sun and co-workers in China ran in 2026 a plan study on beam mixes for a bold radiation style aimed at the core of big belly tumors. One twin strong beam plan did both jobs worse than the top picks. The authors sort the mixes by aim: spare organs, grow the core, or strike a balance.
pmc-13479569:

The starting pool held 40,876 records flagged by the trigger-word search across the nine years of Danish prehospital data. On untouched records from 2023 and 2024, the system caught 91 percent of relevant cases and correctly filtered out 89 percent of irrelevant ones for manual review. pmc-13480169:

The team chose the newest soft septal occluder, built to flex around nearby structures, and closed the leak through a catheter. No prior report describes this device used for a baffle leak after an atrial switch. Baffle leaks affect many adults with this surgical history and can cause blue spells and stray clots. A gentler device may widen safe options where leaks sit near valves.
pmc-13480569:
Nicholas S. D. Solomon and co-authors report a 2026 effort to clock a key handoff step in nickel catalysis. Ligand choice dominated, with loose single-arm ligands running fastest, while the halogen partner mattered little and two sulfonate partners gave modest boosts. pmc-13482369:

pmc-13483569:

pmc-13487169:

About 35 percent of those screened tested positive for mild cognitive impairment on the instrument used. A boosted-tree classifier discriminated slightly better than plain logistic regression in validation, though both were modest. pmc-13487569:
Izabela Sowińska and co-workers ask what keeps life joy up for people with vitiligo, a skin disease that bleaches patches of skin. Their 2026 study surveys 215 people with the disease. Most of the group told of high disease acceptance and sound life joy. Suicidal thoughts were rare. Felt shunning was rare too. Yet long-term low mood touched 41.8 percent of the group. For a disease worn in plain sight, strong ties act like care in their own right.
pmc-13488269:

Farm waste, straw with manure, proved the most profitable feedstock tested. At full scale, the pairing's oil cost slightly less per unit. pmc-13489569:
Samsudin and co-authors run a safety check on a popular supplement paired with exercise. Their 2026 trial randomises 68 overweight or obese adults for twelve weeks. Their average age was about 29. The four groups were control, L-carnitine alone at a gram a day, exercise alone, or both combined. Exercise meant thirty minutes of brisk walking and interval training. Kidney and liver blood markers were the outcomes.

No significant changes appeared in any group for the liver enzymes, creatinine, urea, or bilirubin that signal organ stress. pmc-13490469:
Sayeed and colleagues designed a control framework for large drone swarms tracking disasters like floods or fires, where conditions shift randomly and radio links are limited. Their 2026 design bakes in risk sensitivity, planning for bad luck rather than average luck, with each drone computing its own controls from neighbor chatter alone.

Heavy planning mathematics runs offline once, leaving real-time control fully distributed across the swarm in the architecture described. Computing effort stays flat as swarm size grows, because each drone only tracks the local distribution. A worst-case robustness guarantee covers disturbances within a bounded divergence budget the authors set. Sayeed argues risk-aware mean-field control is the scalable route to dependable first-response swarms.
pmc-13491769:
Mao Nanamori and three co-authors track in 2026 the moment-to-moment chain that sparks social anxiety in daily life. Two rival models were tested against the data. The better-supported sequence began with noticing other people's gaze, which raised the sense of being evaluated, which then pulled attention inward and lifted anxiety. The margin between models was small, so the reverse order remains plausible. Even so, the authors suggest therapies that soften sensitivity to gaze and evaluation could interrupt the chain early.
pmc-13491869:
Yilin Yin and four colleagues examine in 2026 a tiny regulatory RNA that appears to restrain cervical cancer by targeting a growth-related kinase called TAOK1. pmc-13492269:
Chase and co-workers ran in 2026 a controlled leak of natural gas into dry upland soil, to see what a pulse of methane does underground. Where methane and oxygen met, they found a sharp redox edge, a zone where chemic balance flips. Soil carbon at the plume core grew heavy with a rare carbon form, and carbonate rock built up near the edge. Genes for methane eating enzymes clustered in the overlap zone, not at the core. Genome rebuilds tied the action to one bacterial group with a wide set of such enzymes. The work shows how small leaks make tight hot spots that can trap or pass gas.
pmc-13492369:
Pletzer-Zelgert, Rarey, and Kuhn present a way to predict how a drug molecule sits in its target protein by borrowing knowledge from its siblings. It keeps the shapes where sibling cores land consistently, with good contacts and low strain.

Three case studies test the idea, including rescuing a protein model from a cofolding program that had the pocket wrong. In each case the refinement exposed induced fit, the pocket reshaping itself around the ligand. It rebuilt binding modes close to the real ones, within two angstroms on the shared core. For teams stuck with a structure, that turns a dead end into a start.
pmc-13492469:

The maps showed a soft arsenic rich skin on each grain, with a less worn core inside. That flips the expected wear pattern, where the outside should be most changed. The find helps explain how such grains leak arsenic as they age.
pmc-13492869:
Shaluhiyah and colleagues tested in 2026 whether training caregivers improves health knowledge and safety skills among street adolescents in Central Java, Indonesia. Knowledge, attitudes, and risk behaviour were measured before and after.

In the programme group, knowledge scores rose by about seven points and attitude scores by about three points on average. Sexual risk behaviour fell modestly over the six months. Overall, knowledge rose by more than half and attitudes by about a fifth, while behaviour change was smaller at about a sixth. pmc-13493469:

pmc-13493969:
Conley, Townsend, and Baskin-Sommers built a virtual reality errand task to study how living around neighbourhood disorder, things like litter, abandoned buildings, and crime, affects thinking during everyday navigation. Their 2026 paradigm first taught 100 American adults a route through a virtual neighbourhood, then asked them to run errands choosing between the learned route and novel shortcuts. Disorder was dialled up with visual cues and surprise robbery events.

Adults who reported more disorder in their real neighbourhoods navigated worse, both on the practised route and when judging shortcuts. The combination mattered too: clumsy navigation strengthened the tie between perceived disorder and self-reported risky, impulsive behaviour. The authors are careful that the design cannot prove which came first, and that no calm control neighbourhood existed. They present the task as a more realistic way to study environment and cognition together.
pmc-13495269:
Shun Tsujimura and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study, a year-long program of case conferences among pharmacists at a Japanese medical center. In these meetings pharmacists discuss drug therapy cases together, which should sharpen judgment and teach, yet proof of value and of what keeps such programs alive was scarce. Forty pharmacists who joined the conferences answered a sixteen-item survey.

Analysis pulled out three strands: confidence and professional growth, sharper clinical judgment and drug therapy quality, and better communication with a safer climate for speaking up. Judgment gains scored highest. Wanting the program to continue tied most to growth and judgment strands. Pharmacists who had presented a case scored higher on growth, hinting that presenting feeds development. The authors offer the findings as groundwork for spreading pharmacist conferences to other hospitals.
pmc-13495369:
Hu and colleagues track tiny traces of leukemia left in the body around stem cell transplant. Their patients carry a FLT3-ITD change, a repeated stretch in one gene, in acute myeloid leukemia. Even in full remission, hidden traces can warn that the cancer will return.

The team used targeted gene sequencing that reads chosen genes in fine detail. Traces found before transplant linked to more relapse and worse survival. Checks repeated over time added more warning value than one test alone. Patients with traces formed a high-risk group after transplant. For them, extra FLT3 blocker drugs after transplant may help most.
pmc-13499969:
Paul Cardozo and co-authors describe in 2026 a severe lung complication of leukaemia treatment that struck despite preventive steroids. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is treated with a vitamin-derived drug that forces cancer cells to mature, yet that process can trigger differentiation syndrome, a dangerous inflammatory flooding of tissues. Their patient was a 37-year-old woman newly diagnosed with the disease. Two days after starting the drug she developed rising white cell counts, fluid retention, and severe oxygen failure with widespread lung infiltrates.

High-flow oxygen through the nose, combined with awake face-down positioning, held off a breathing machine while infection and heart causes were excluded. Oxygen measures improved over two days of support yet lung involvement persisted, so three days of high-dose steroid therapy followed, bringing clear clinical, oxygen, and imaging gains. The authors present intensified steroids plus advanced noninvasive support as an option for selected patients.
pmc-13500469:
Saeed Golshokooh, Mohammad Simjoo, and Mohammad Chahardowli introduce in 2026 a laboratory platform that manufactures porous materials with precisely chosen surface roughness. That roughness governs how fluids wet and move through rock and filters, shaping oil recovery, carbon storage, and water purification, yet natural surfaces cannot be replicated on demand. Their method sinters glass beads into thin sections and slices them with a semi-immersion technique that keeps measurements reliable.

Bead size set roughness directly in their scaling laws, moving surfaces from fine, rapid textures to broad, wavy undulations in a predictable way. That topography decided whether droplets spread flat or beaded up, and it pinned contact lines in place, producing hysteresis and trapped fluid pockets. The tunable, reproducible sections bridge random natural rock and idealised models, opening systematic study of multiphase flow engineering.
pmc-13500869:
Zhang and colleagues built a deep learning system that finds boundaries in tissue stiffness imaging, a step elastography handles poorly, in a 2026 engineering study. Optical coherence elastography sends a mechanical wave through tissue and films its propagation with light-based imaging; stiffness maps blur the edges between tissue layers. Their network, BDNet, instead reads the wave's phase patterns to localize boundaries without estimating wave speed.

Zhang evaluated the system on agar gel phantoms, models of tissue, where all tested models located single boundaries with an average error of two pixels. The new network handled the harder two-boundary phantoms with an average error over four pixels. On a human acne dataset, where stiffness signals mark disease, BDNet again performed best among the compared models with the largest absolute error reflecting the data's scale. The authors present the method as accurate and computationally efficient for dermatology and eye applications.
pmc-13501569:
Qi Chen leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 prospective study of a urine test that might flag kidney scarring in children with vesicoureteral reflux. In that condition urine flows backward from the bladder toward the kidneys. The standard check, a DMSA scan, is costly and involves radiation. Between September 2023 and December 2025 the team enrolled 81 children, isolated tiny vesicles called exosomes from their urine, and profiled the small RNA molecules inside them. Scarring was judged from the DMSA scans.

One molecule, miR-132-3p, stood out: higher levels tracked with higher reflux grade, reflux on both sides, and the presence of scarring. In adjusted analysis it predicted scarring with an odds ratio of 4.937 and an area under the curve of 0.908, a strong discrimination value. The median child was 27 months old. The authors call the marker promising but note the single-centre, exploratory design.
pmc-13501669:
Dula Dessalegn Bosho leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of poor blood sugar control in people who have both diabetes and hypertension. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, the team searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for English-language studies from January 2015 to January 2025. Ten papers covering 2,552 individuals fed the pooled estimate, computed with random-effects models. Poor control was judged by fasting glucose thresholds or by glycated haemoglobin at or above 7 percent.

The pooled prevalence of poor control was 59 percent, with a confidence interval from 49 to 69 percent on that estimate. Splitting by diagnostic criterion gave 46 percent for fasting glucose and 65 percent for glycated haemoglobin, showing how much the answer depends on the yardstick. Heterogeneity between studies was substantial, while publication bias checks showed no significant distortion. The authors offer the figure as a baseline for guideline work on this high-risk group.
pmc-13501769:
Yen Pham leads a three-author team with a 2026 qualitative study of antimicrobial resistance in Australia's Northern Territory, where up to half of some infections resist antibiotics. Framing resistance as a systems problem, the team consulted 35 people spanning human health, animal health, environment, and cross-sector work through interviews and focus groups. Thematic analysis fed a causal loop diagram, a map of reinforcing and balancing feedback loops that drive resistance up or down.

The map showed prescribing and antibiotic use in people and animals intertwined with drug residues in soil and water. Structural forces loomed large behind them: geographic isolation, thin health services, and social unfairness all shaped the patterns. Cutting antibiotic use alone, the authors argue, will not control resistance in such a setting. Extra leverage sits in culturally safe care, workforce training and retention, community awareness, and upstream basics such as working housing and essential services.
pmc-13502869:
Inoue and colleagues asked whether a grip-strength measurement reflects overall function in patients awaiting surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy. In that condition, age-related neck changes squeeze the spinal cord. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covered ninety-four patients. The condition damages walking ability and hand skill, and grip strength is an established general marker of muscle strength and frailty.

Inoue measured grip alongside leg power, pinch strength, walking speed, a hand-dexterity counting test, and a neurological score before surgery. Grip strength tracked with all of them, and patients classed as frail gripped weaker than robust patients, averaging about twenty kilograms against thirty. After adjusting for age and sex, the links with leg power, dexterity, and pinch strength stayed while the walking-speed link weakened. The authors propose grip strength as a quick complement to full preoperative assessment, pending prospective validation before it guides management.
pmc-13503869:
Lisan Yu and John M. Toole report that the Southern Ocean grew saltier over two decades, against what many models predicted, in a 2026 study. A wetter world was expected to freshen this already fresh ocean. Their data from 2004 to 2024 show the reverse across a broad band of southern latitudes.

The team blames the slow spread of vast swirling currents, the subtropical gyres, toward the pole. Those gyres carry salty water into zones where salt levels change fast with latitude. Two ocean fronts moved south at uneven rates, squeezing the zone between them. A budget of the top water layer shows sideways flow drove the trend, beating rain and melt effects by about three to one.
pmc-13504969:
Xun Ni leads a team reporting hearing loss tied to a last-resort antibiotic in a patient with kidney failure, in a 2026 case report. The drug, polymyxin B, fights germs that resist nearly all else. Its known harms hit nerves and kidneys, but hearing harm is rarely described.

The patient was a 54-year-old man on dialysis, treated in intensive care for a lung infection by a drug-resistant germ. Blood monitoring first showed mid-range drug levels; after the dose doubled, levels soared and he reported hearing loss. The dose was cut, then the drug stopped. His hearing fully returned a day later. No formal hearing test was done, a limit the authors note. They urge close drug-level checks in kidney patients.
pmc-13505069:
Zeynep Basagaoglu Demirekin and Elif Erten examine how prosthetic type relates to feeding and oral-health quality of life in completely edentulous adults. In 2026, the one-time study covers 140 patients divided among standard complete dentures, implant-held overdentures, and implant-held fixed replacements, assessed with checked quality-of-life and mini-nutritional instruments. Tooth loss impairs chewing, diet, and well-being.

Patients with implant-supported fixed prostheses scored clearly more favorably on quality of life and feeding than standard denture users. Quality-of-life tests correlated clearly with feeding status. Implant-supported healing emerges as linked to better oral-health quality of life, while feeding gaps also appear across prosthetic groups.
pmc-13505169:
Ashfaque and co-authors test whether vibrating a muscle can retrain coordination in children with cerebral palsy. Their 2026 double-blind randomised trial enrols 65 children with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, assigning them to control, 80 hertz, or 100 hertz focal muscle vibration for eight weeks. Muscle activation, fatigue, and the co-contraction between two shin muscles were measured electrically at baseline and at four, eight, and twelve weeks.

Differences centred on the tibialis anterior, the front shin muscle. The 100 hertz group activated it more strongly than controls at four and eight weeks in both legs. Fatigue told a frequency story too. The 100 hertz group sustained its signal in the dominant leg's calf muscle, suggesting better fatigue resistance. The 80 hertz group fatigued more. The authors conclude higher-frequency vibration improved activation and coordination patterns in this population.
pmc-13505369:
Dong Jin, Helin Yin, Xianghua Piao, and Yeong Hyeon Gu tackle pest recognition when only a handful of labelled photos exist for each species. Their method, MoCoProto, first learns visual features from unlabelled images using a self-supervised contrast technique. That prepared network is then plugged into a prototype-based learner that classifies new pests from one or five example shots.

Pretraining used a broad farm-image collection of more than 357,000 pictures covering sixty-five pest species and many plant diseases, with all labels stripped away. Final testing ran on the IP102 insect dataset. The method scored about forty-nine percent accuracy with a single example per class and about seventy percent with five examples, beating the rival approaches tried. The authors argue that strong unlabelled pretraining is the lever that makes few-example pest identification practical for field use.
pmc-13506569:
Anieli Cristina Maraschi leads a 2026 study of how airborne dust that settles from industry affects salt and water balance in an estuarine fish. The fish, Centropomus parallelus, sat for 96 hours in clean water or water with settleable particles at 1 gram per liter. The team then measured blood salts, enzyme activity, and metal buildup in gills and kidneys.

Exposed fish showed lower blood osmolality and lower chloride and potassium levels than controls. Gill enzyme activity rose, while kidney enzyme activity fell, a split pattern by tissue. Aluminum, iron, vanadium, and chromium built up in both organs. The shifts could weaken fish that live in polluted coastal waters.
pmc-13507269:
Zhengquan He leads a 2026 team that shows the immune signal IL-33 speeds orthodontic tooth movement in mice by steering macrophages and bone-eating cells. Braces move teeth through controlled bone remodeling, and faster movement would shorten treatment. Mechanical force raised IL-33 and its receptor ST2 in gum ligament tissue over twelve days.

Injected IL-33 quickened movement, raised the share of inflammatory M1 macrophages, and boosted a bone-cutting enzyme marker. Blocking the receptor reversed every effect. A thyroid-related factor switched on IL-33 production in ligament cells, and the signal also pushed human monocytes toward bone-eating osteoclasts. Tuning this pathway might one day shorten orthodontic timelines.
pmc-13507469:
Sönke Beier and others find a dual chemotaxis plan for germs navigating porous media. In 2026, the study studies Pseudomonas putida, a soil bacterium with run-and-turn motility, joining tests with agent-based models based on observed swimming statistics. Classic chemotaxis modulates run time by swimming direction relative to a chemical source, but porous matrices severely restrict free path length.

Beyond run-time bias, the team found turn-angle bias: upon turning, germs adjust their new direction to point more likely toward the attractant source. Directional preference arose from active motor-induced turns, while passive mechanical trapping weakened it. Models indicate turn-angle bias dominates under tight spatial constraints, broadening the picture of germ navigation in tissues, sediments, and soils.
pmc-13508269:
Guo-Qi Li and six co-authors pool trial evidence on whether resistance exercise helps older adults with sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle, in 2026 work. Muscle loss weakens grip, slows walking, and raises care costs for families and health systems. The team searched four databases for randomized trials of resistance training in this group. Thirteen trials with 546 participants qualified, split between training and control groups. Outcomes covered grip strength, walking speed, muscle mass, and a chair-rise test.

Training improved every one of those measures by a clear margin. Grip strength, walking speed, and muscle mass all rose, and chair-rise times fell. Shorter programs of twelve weeks or less, and three sessions a week, showed larger gains in walking speed for younger participants. The authors judge resistance exercise a proven way to protect strength and movement in later life, and they map which schedules work best.
pmc-13509669:
Jun Hu and seven co-authors present a way to tune computer models of blood flow in the brain to a single person, in 2026 work. Standard models use generic settings for vessel outlets, which can miss how a real person's brain adjusts flow. The new method feeds in ultrasound readings of brain artery flow plus continuous blood pressure data to set outlet resistance for that person.

The team tested the approach in one healthy volunteer at rest and during a treatment that pulses pressure on the legs to push more blood upward. The tuned model matched measured flow waves far more closely than two standard setups, in both states. It also captured uneven flow between the two sides of the brain that generic settings hid. The authors present the result as proof of concept needing wider testing.
pmc-13509969:
Federica Li Pomi and six co-authors review malondialdehyde, a compound formed when fats break down under oxidative stress, as a marker in cancer, in 2026 work. Beyond marking damage, the compound can bind proteins and DNA, forming changes that may help start or advance tumors. The review gathers findings across breast, lung, head and neck, bowel, cervical, and skin cancers.

Higher levels in blood or tissue often went with heavier tumor burden, later stage, harsher features under the microscope, and in some studies worse outcomes. Levels also rose with treatment-related injury. Many outside factors shift readings, including age, smoking, diet, metabolic disease, and lab method. The authors place the compound as a useful signal inside wider marker panels, not as a stand-alone test for diagnosis or outlook.
pmc-13510269:
Ningmei Liu and nine co-authors test whether stem cells from the placenta can help the brain recover after a stroke caused by a blocked artery, in 2026 rat work. After such a stroke, star-shaped support cells called astrocytes can turn harmful or helpful, and the helpful form aids repair. The team blocked and then reopened a brain artery in rats, and also inflamed astrocytes in dishes, to see how cell grafts shifted astrocyte behavior.

Grafted rats showed better movement scores and less tissue damage than untreated rats, with calmer inflammation and higher levels of growth-support factors. Dish tests showed the grafts pushed astrocytes toward the helpful form. A signaling chain inside the brain, centered on a growth factor and its partner proteins, quieted after grafting in the stroke model. The authors link the benefit to that chain, while noting the findings come from animal and dish models.
pmc-13510869:
Negar Taghavi Pourianazar, Narin Abdullah, and Ahmet Ilvan report in 2026 that silencing a gene called IDO1 makes stomach cancer cells far more vulnerable to the chemotherapy drug cisplatin. IDO1 normally helps tumors hide from the immune system, but its role inside cancer cells was less clear.

Working with two gastric cancer cell lines, the team used small RNA strands to switch IDO1 off, then applied cisplatin. Treated cells died more readily, built up more reactive oxygen molecules, and shifted their gene balance toward self-destruction, with death-promoting genes up and protective ones down. Activity of executioner enzymes confirmed the cells were completing programmed death. The authors suggest pairing IDO1 blockade with platinum drugs in future treatment tests.
pmc-13511269:
Adrian-Florentin Dragomir and eleven co-authors compare two memory drugs head to head in healthy rats, in 2026 work. A Y-shaped maze tested whether animals favor a new arm over a known one a day later. Five groups of eight rats received a control shot, one of two doses of donepezil, or one of two doses of tacrine before learning. Recall was tested the next day without further dosing.

Control rats showed no marked love for the new arm. Donepezil shifted behavior only slightly, and none of its changes reached statistical weight. The higher tacrine dose clearly raised time and entry ratios favoring the new arm, mainly by cutting time spent in the familiar arm rather than by adding novel-arm exploration. The authors say the broader-acting drug reshaped recall-phase choices in intact animals, while the narrower drug barely moved them under these conditions.
pmc-13512569:
Ali Abu-Nada, Russell R. Ceballos, and Lian-Ao Wu prove that hidden starting links between a quantum bit and its surroundings can be exposed by watching a single measured quantity, in 2026 theoretical work. Such starting correlations break standard models of open quantum systems, yet most tests demand full state mapping or access to the environment itself. The setting studied pairs a two-level system with its bath through an even exchange interaction.

The team derived exact bounds on one signal over time that every unlinked starting state must obey, given a one-time calibration of the starting state. If a recorded path steps outside that envelope, starting correlation is proven outright. Worked examples cover several families of linked states, and the same logic is shown to hold in a solvable model with an endless environment. Only single-axis readings are needed after calibration.
pmc-13512769:
Gigoyan and colleagues tracked mental health after wildfire exposure in 2026, following 4,346 survivors of the 2018 Camp Fire in Northern California. Survivors reported their symptoms as they recalled them at three weeks, one month, three months, and six months after the fire.

Forty-one percent reported one or more mental health symptoms three weeks after the fire. Symptoms eased over time, falling from nearly four symptoms on average to under three by six months. Among those with symptoms, severe home damage was linked with about 1.6 times as many symptoms, and prior mental health conditions and job loss also raised counts. The authors urge early mental health services after fires, aimed first at those with the heaviest losses.
pmc-13512869:
Rubén Pérez-Elvira, Daniel Cordeiro, María Agudo Juan, and Antonio Sánchez Cabaco build an age-adjusted reference model for the brain's alpha peak frequency in older adults, in 2026 work. That peak, the top speed of the alpha rhythm, marks processing pace and healthy brain aging, yet fixed frequency bands can hide age-related slowing. Resting brain recordings with eyes closed came from 81 people aged fifty-two to eighty-seven in an open database.

A spectral method that separates true rhythm peaks from background noise located each person's peak across nine back-of-head electrodes. Age tied clearly and negatively to peak frequency, with an average slide of about half a hertz per decade and age explaining a fifth of the spread. Resampling backed the link, though predictions for held-out people stayed weak. The authors offer the equation as a group-level reference only.
pmc-13514769:
Bára Frýdlová and eight colleagues describe, in a 2026 materials study, how to make a stubbornly non-stick plastic friendlier to living cells. The plastic, a fluoropolymer known as FEP, resists cell attachment, which limits its use in tissue engineering. The team copied submicron ripple patterns, grooves about five hundred nanometres wide, onto its surface and then treated some samples with argon plasma, a charged gas that remodels surface chemistry.

Plasma treatment improved cell adhesion more than the ripple pattern alone achieved. Patterning still mattered, because grooved samples responded better to the plasma step and then supported stronger cell growth than flat treated plastic. Microscopy of stained cell skeletons and nuclei, plus a metabolic activity test, backed the ranking. Frýdlová's group presents the pairing as a cheap, simple route to carriers that can steer where cells settle and how they stretch.
pmc-13514869:
Savas Gokcek and eleven colleagues compare two infusion lengths for one drug in stomach cancer chemotherapy, in a 2026 records review. The FLOT regimen, given around surgery for stomach and junction cancers, includes fluorouracil delivered as a continuous infusion lasting either twenty-four or forty-six hours. The team reviewed 300 patients and compared tumour shrinkage in the removed tissue, time without progression, and overall survival between the schedules.

The longer infusion produced a clearly higher rate of tumour response. Survival told a different story: overall survival did not differ by much between groups. The raw time without progression actually favoured the shorter infusion, a gap the adjusted analysis could not confirm as a separate effect. Gokcek's team blames the mixed picture partly on differences between the patient groups and calls for a randomised trial to settle the best infusion length.
pmc-13515169:
Obaid and Khan published a 2026 study on steering electric fields across a sitting droplet. Droplets on surfaces can shoot fine jets under electric charge, useful in printing. The field's shape depends heavily on where electrodes sit around the droplet. The team mapped that shape with two independent computer solvers.

A flat plate electrode boosted the field at the droplet's top strongly. A single pin above center cut the top field by about 40 percent. Shifting the pin sideways moved the hot spot off the top toward the pin. Two pins made twin hot spots with a dead zone at the top. Their checks agree, giving designers a menu of field shapes. A helper software search then explored design options around the maps.
pmc-13516269:
Kannan Badri Narayanan reviews, in a 2026 article, biologic medicines for autoimmune and inflammatory disease. These engineered proteins aim at single immune pathways, a sharper approach than broad immune suppression. The tour covers drugs that block T-cell activation, deplete or divert immune cells, and neutralise inflammatory messengers such as tumour necrosis factor and a string of interleukins. B-cell and IgE-directed agents complete the arsenal.

Trial and real-world evidence shows deep impact across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, lupus, bowel inflammation, asthma, and more. How tightly a drug binds its target and what it does downstream decide much of its effect. Safety watching stays essential, since immune reactions, opportunistic infections, and manufacturing variation all pose risks. Cheaper biosimilars promise wider access. Narayanan closes with the push toward biomarker-guided, precision use and next-generation antibody designs.
pmc-13517569:
Legler and colleagues described in 2026 the first clear cases of poxvirus infection in common swifts, birds that spend nearly all their lives in the air. Four young swifts that could not yet fly came to a German rescue center from three nest sites. Each bird had lumpy, crusty growths on its wings.

Tissue tests and gene-based checks confirmed an avipoxvirus, a bird pox germ spread by biting insects and contact. Damage to feather roots in two birds stopped flight feathers from growing right, so they could not be freed and were put down. The other two healed and were released after hand rearing. The cases show that even birds that rarely land can pick up vector-borne disease during the breeding season.
pmc-13518869:
Shuai Liu leads an eight-author survey in 2026 on nearsightedness among Hefei high school students after the COVID-19 period. Myopia has surged across East Asia, raising risks of retinal damage and blindness later in life. The team measured vision and refraction in over 6,400 students aged 17 to 19 across 15 schools, alongside questionnaires.

Prevalence reached 85.3 percent, higher in girls than boys. Having myopic parents more than doubled the adjusted odds, while over an hour outdoors daily cut odds sharply. Long near work, reported by most students, tracked with higher rates. School and family prevention education linked to milder myopia, yet few families used it, the authors note.
pmc-13518969:
Huangcong Tang and co-authors report in 2026 that the chloride in seawater, long treated as a poison for hydrogen-making electrodes, can instead rebuild a catalyst into a better form. Splitting seawater directly would skip costly purification, but salt usually corrodes the machinery.

Their catalyst pairs nickel sulfide particles with nickel-iron layered sheets, tuned so chloride sits near the metal sites. Chloride then guided the surface to rebuild into a dense, active layer that uses a more efficient reaction path. In alkaline seawater it needed far less extra voltage than in plain alkaline water at high current. A kilowatt-scale device ran beyond fifteen hundred hours, and a lab cell passed seven thousand hours with minimal decay.
pmc-13519269:
Rajbhandari and colleagues reported in 2026 on tuberculosis germs found in captive Asian elephants in Nepal's Chitwan valley, and on the human habits linked to infection. The disease comes from a group of bacteria that also infect people. It threatens both elephants and their handlers, called mahouts. Few studies had tied care routines to test results here.

The team tested blood from 99 elephants and spoke with 223 mahouts. About one in five elephants carried antibodies, blood proteins that show past contact with the germs. Risk was higher for elephants owned by the state or a trust, fed by hand, kept near farm animals, or whose waste went into pits. Elephants that met wild herds had lower rates. The authors call for protective gear, safer waste handling, and joint human and animal health work.
pmc-13519869:
Dzana Nuhanovic leads an eight-author count in 2026 of thyroid cancer in Tuzla Canton, Bosnia and Herzegovina, across 2020 to 2024. Thyroid cancer is the commonest hormone-system malignancy, yet local data were scarce. Records of 483 patients reviewed by a university thyroid council yielded 142 confirmed cases living in the canton.

Women made up 76 percent of cases, with a median diagnosis age of 56 years. Papillary cancer dominated at 74 percent, followed by follicular, medullary, and anaplastic types. Average annual incidence reached 6.99 per 100,000 people and rose during the period, still below global and European estimates. Both cancer deaths involved anaplastic disease. A national registry, the authors urge, would sharpen surveillance.
pmc-13520269:
Christine Atuhairwe, Hillary Muhanguzi, and Titus Ochieng survey in 2026 what shapes quality of life for Ugandans aged 50 and older living with HIV. Their tool is a composite index that blends functioning, symptoms, health perception, and living environment. Face-to-face interviews covered 439 patients at AIDS Support Organisation clinics nationwide.

The median index score sat at 0.51 on a zero-to-one scale. University education and employment each independently lifted scores, while carrying another chronic disease dragged them down strongly. Strikingly, HIV-specific measures such as viral load, treatment adherence, and years infected showed no independent link. Atuhairwe and colleagues argue care must reach beyond virus control toward income security and joined-up chronic disease management.
pmc-13522069:
Nina Kämmerling and colleagues tracked wrist replacement implants with a new high-resolution CT method over one year. Published in 2026, the study scanned nineteen patients the day after total wrist arthroplasty and again at six and twelve months, using photon-counting detector CT. Reviewers scored bone ingrowth, bone loss around the implant, and cortical thickness and density zone by zone.

Bone ingrowth rose in nearly all zones, reaching more than half the implant circumference at screw tips in roughly five sixths to nine tenths of patients by twelve months. Yet bone loss appeared in all but one patient and grew over time, starting near the joint, while cortical thickness and density fell in outer radial zones. The authors read continued ingrowth as a counterweight that may preserve stability despite bone loss. Readers get a balanced year-one picture for a complication-prone implant.
pmc-13522269:
Georgios Bouchouras, Dimitrios Doumanas and Konstantinos Kotis present in 2026 NeuroCypher ASD, a screening framework for autism in toddlers that pairs questionnaire-based prediction with a knowledge graph for exploration. Standard questionnaire scores can be hard to interpret and compare across cases.

A tabular model estimates risk from answers and demographics, while the graph organises cases for comparison, pattern browsing and plain-language querying. Leakage-aware testing compared tabular, graph and hybrid variants, finding the tabular model strongest for pure prediction. Explanation tools map model reasoning back to questionnaire items, while an anomaly module flags unusual cases for closer human review.
pmc-13522369:
Houfa Yin and colleagues tested whether giving chatbots access to medical sources sharpens their reasoning about glaucoma care. Published in 2026, the study used forty real glaucoma cases spanning early, secondary, post-surgery, and end-stage disease. Six setups were scored: three language models, each with and without retrieval-augmented generation, which pulls in guideline text before answering.

Models with retrieval beat their plain twins on accuracy, coverage, and logical completeness, with gains holding up under sensitivity checks. Yet agreement between the two masked specialist raters was limited, so scores call for consensus review and careful reading. Safety was audited apart from the main score. The authors back retrieval-backed models as supervised decision aids, not as stand-alone clinicians.
pmc-13522469:
Renuga Devi K, Sarathchandran KG, and Sreekanth Dondapati engineer a hybrid coating for magnesium alloy implants in a 2026 materials study. Magnesium implants can dissolve safely after healing, yet they corrode too fast without protection. A plasma process built a ceramic layer containing bismuth metal and bismuth oxide, with two levels of bismuth addition tested for comparison.

The bismuth-rich coating slowed corrosion sharply, from a higher rate in the plain coating to a much lower one, and kept the surrounding fluid less alkaline over twenty-eight days. Bone-like cells grown with coating extracts survived better and showed stronger bone-forming activity. The coating also blocked most growth of two common bacteria, pointing to a surface that protects the implant while supporting healing.
pmc-13523269:
Liqing Zhang and colleagues test a resting brain scan method for measuring blood vessel responsiveness in artery narrowing in a 2026 study. Forty-one patients with narrowing or blockage of one middle cerebral artery were compared with fifty matched healthy controls using resting-state functional MRI, without the usual gas challenge. Vessel responsiveness maps were derived from signal frequency bands, and network connections of altered regions were explored.

Responsiveness rose in a cerebellar region on the opposite side and fell in a sensory region on the same side as the narrowing. Connections from those regions shifted in patterns that tracked anxiety scores. Each altered region separated patients from controls with good diagnostic accuracy. The authors propose the resting measure as a potential marker of blood flow disturbance that avoids uncomfortable gas inhalation.
pmc-13523469:
Patience Fakornam Doe and colleagues review, in 2026, couple-based care before conception as a gender-responsive way to improve reproductive health. Care before pregnancy can reduce risks such as infertility, miscarriage, preterm birth, and birth anomalies, yet programs usually focus on women and leave men out. Bringing both partners in offers a more inclusive route.

Searches of four databases plus hand searching found 14 studies from 10 countries, most in high-income settings. Programs mixed medical checks, lifestyle support, psychological help, and family planning. Reported gains included better fertility treatment success, healthier habits, less distress, stronger partner communication, and greater contraceptive use. Study designs varied widely, limiting direct comparison. The authors call for stronger trials in lower-income settings and for programs fitted to local systems.
pmc-13525169:
Pe Yan and colleagues described in 2026 how a shop-bought glue stopped heavy bleeding from an eyelid growth when medical supplies were not at hand. The patient was a 23-year-old man with a tangle of abnormal blood vessels in his right upper eyelid and eye socket. He was waiting for a planned procedure to block the vessels before surgery.

Bleeding from a thin skin spot over the growth had lasted a week, and firm pressure no longer stopped it. The team spread a thin layer of ethyl cyanoacrylate glue on the bleeding surface, and the flow stopped at once with only slight oozing after. The wound healed with no infection or tissue death. The authors stress that such glue is only a short-term fix, and care aimed at the growth itself must still follow.
pmc-13527469:
Dawit Abera and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 diagnostic study, the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra test in tuberculosis cases whose sputum smears look negative under the microscope. In this group, diagnosis often stalls in southwestern Oromia, Ethiopia. Smear-negative disease accounts for a large share of Ethiopian pulmonary tuberculosis, and evidence on the newer molecular test in this group was scarce.

Against culture as the reference standard, the authors report that the Ultra test reached 90.2 percent sensitivity and 99.5 percent specificity in this hard-to-diagnose population. Those figures mean most true cases were caught while false positives stayed rare. Because culture takes weeks and demands advanced laboratories, a rapid test with this profile could speed treatment decisions. The authors argue that scaling up Ultra testing would improve early detection of active disease among smear-negative patients regionally.
pmc-13527969:
Saber SamadiAfshar and four colleagues review in 2026 why CAR-T cell therapy struggles against ovarian cancer. CAR-T cells are a patient's own immune cells, engineered to hunt cancer. The approach transformed care for blood cancers. Ovarian tumors, though, sit inside a suppressive neighborhood of cells and signals called the tumor microenvironment. Five-year survival for advanced disease is only about thirty percent.

The review maps how that environment blocks CAR-T cells from entering tumors, lasting, and killing. It then weighs new strategies: redesigned receptors, drug combinations, and tools that remodel the tumor surroundings. The authors frame the work as a roadmap. Their aim is to move CAR-T therapy from promise toward routine use in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13528069:
Alicja Okrasińska and four colleagues study a loose partnership between a fungus and a bacterium that lives inside it in a 2026 paper. The fungus Umbelopsis grows in deadwood. The bacterium Paraburkholderia sits within its threads but can also live freely. The pair is common in rotting wood. The team compared both genomes with those of free-living and tightly bound relatives.

Unlike captive symbionts, the bacterium kept a full-size genome. Its toolkit for independent life stayed intact. The fungus genome also resembled its relatives, though that family is little studied. Genes for membrane traffic and secretion, needed to host a guest, were present. The partners' wood-rotting skills may complement each other. In dishes the guest slows fungal growth. In the wild the pair may reach niches neither could alone, the authors suggest.
pmc-13528169:
Alireza Peyman and five colleagues report a fungal eye infection days after laser vision correction in a 2026 case. A healthy 21-year-old man had PRK surgery on both eyes for nearsightedness. A week later he returned with a red eye and blurred vision. Symptoms had begun three days earlier. Standard antibiotics came first.

Scrapings from the cornea hinted at fungus under the microscope. A gene test named Aspergillus as the culprit. Antifungal drugs were added promptly. Within seven days of that treatment the eye improved markedly. Fungal infection after this surgery is rare but can blind. The authors urge doctors to think beyond bacteria when early infections look odd. Quick smear and gene tests can steer treatment in time, they say.
pmc-13529069:
Gupta and colleagues followed knee surgery patients prospectively to see how recovery unfolds when a torn meniscus, the knee's shock-absorbing cartilage, is repaired during ligament reconstruction. Their 2026 single-center study enrolled 115 patients having arthroscopic surgery for a torn anterior cruciate ligament, a key stabilizing band in the knee, with meniscus repair in the same operation. Most patients were men, and inner meniscus tears were most common.

Gupta measured pain and two knee function scores before surgery and at six weeks, three months, and six months afterward. Pain fell from a moderate median level to zero by six months. Both function scores improved strongly over the same span, though one score dipped briefly at six weeks during early healing. No infections, graft failures, or re-tears occurred. Because there was no comparison group, the authors present the results as evidence that adding meniscus repair does not hinder short-term recovery.
pmc-13530169:
Dong-Ho Lee and colleagues present a 2026 way to map where electrical defects sit inside display transistors without cutting them open. The devices use an IGZO semiconductor film common in modern screens. Traps in the insulating layer create low-frequency noise, and that noise carries location clues.

Changing the drain voltage alters the effective channel length, letting the team sample defect levels section by section. Fresh devices showed fairly even defect levels, slightly higher near each end. After heavy electrical stress, defects piled up near the drain end, revealing where the insulator had degraded. The method offers a practical reliability check.
pmc-13530369:
Ping Yang and colleagues predicted giant optical effects in flat-band magnets in two thousand twenty-six. Their material is a single layer of a ruthenium compound. Its energy bands are nearly flat in both directions. Flat bands strengthen how light interacts with electrons. Calculations combined quantum methods with symmetry analysis. A record-large second-order optical effect emerged.

Light polarization rotated far more than in known materials. Absorption differed hugely by light direction as well. Those two effects peaked at different light energies. Thicker films amplified both responses further. The windows spanned the whole visible range. Device designers gain a new opto-spintronic platform. Experimental confirmation is the next step.
pmc-13530469:
Shah and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 32, a social media audit of how injectable peptides are promoted for muscle, tendon, and joint health. Online claims vastly outrun the approved evidence. Peptide drugs are a booming market, and posts about them reach millions.

The team analyzed 239 top posts across YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Reddit, and X, totaling over ten million views. BPC-157 dominated the mentions, often paired with TB-500, followed by ipamorelin, CJC-1295, and IGF1-LR3. Promised benefits most often concerned healing of soft tissue, tendon, and bone, then muscle and joint recovery, then reduced inflammation, with cognition and longevity claims trailing. Influencer accounts drove much of the content. Each post was scored for reliability with a modified DISCERN tool and against federal rules for presenting drug risks and benefits.
pmc-13531469:
Richard J Nies and co-authors report long-term real-world outcomes for tafamidis, the first drug approved to treat transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, a disease where misfolded protein stiffens the heart. Their 2026 multicentre study follows German patients who started treatment after the drug became commercially available in 2020.

The cohort held 329 patients with a median age of 80, and 80 percent received tafamidis. Over a median follow-up of 39 months, 21 percent died and 42 percent died or were hospitalised for heart failure. After matching patients on age, symptom class, disease stage, and albumin, tafamidis was linked to substantially lower mortality and fewer combined events. Among treated patients, worse outcomes were predicted by advanced disease stage, age 80 or above, and low serum albumin. The authors stress early diagnosis and timely treatment.
pmc-13531569:
Effendy and co-authors studied mental health in young adults with high blood pressure at several Indonesian centers, reporting in 2026. Their patients were aged eighteen to forty-five, younger than the groups hypertension research usually covers. The team measured anxiety, depression, and stress together with quality of life, asking how emotional strain shapes daily wellbeing early in the disease.

The study enrolled 791 patients and assessed them with the DASS-21 distress questionnaire and the WHOQOL-BREF quality of life scale. Psychological problems were common in this group. A longer time living with hypertension went with poorer quality of life, with a correlation of minus 0.45 in the analysis, and higher anxiety, depression, and stress scores each tracked with worse wellbeing too. The authors urge clinics to screen young hypertensive patients for distress.
pmc-13531769:
Pawit Somnuke leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two anesthesia styles for older adults facing major urinary surgery. Confusion and slowed thinking after surgery strike up to a third of such patients. A total of 126 patients aged 65 and over received either the liquid drug propofol or the inhaled drug desflurane.

Overall rates of confusion and delayed recovery looked similar between groups. Confusion lasted longer in the inhaled group among the few affected, a tentative signal given small numbers. A blood inflammation marker ran higher on day three in confused patients, hinting at a monitoring tool. Brain monitoring guarded depth for everyone.
pmc-13531969:
Yuxin Wang and colleagues trace in 2026 how a viral sensor inside cells summons neutrophils into COVID-19 lungs. Blood from 66 patients and 31 healthy controls was tracked for neutrophil share and a homing receptor called CXCR2. Severe patients carried more neutrophils with higher receptor levels, tied to worse outlook and higher inflammatory signals.

A viral mimic switched on the sensor RIG-I in lung and blood cells, raising receptor levels through a MAPK relay and drawing neutrophils in. Blocking the sensor, the relay, or the receptor eased lung injury in mice, nominating a drug chain.
pmc-13534469:
Peng and colleagues present a 2026 single-cell study of liver cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint drugs before surgery. The team built a gene activity atlas from 14 patients in their own trial plus 60 outside cases, then compared patients who responded to treatment with those who did not.

Non-responders carried more lipid-associated macrophages, a type of immune cell loaded with fat and marked by the genes C1QA, FABP1, and APOA1. Those cells suppressed immune attack inside the tumor. The team mapped signals between cell types and tested ways to change the fatty state of these macrophages, naming lycopene and chiglitazar as candidate options. The findings point to new drug targets for resistant liver cancer.
pmc-13536569:
Yan and colleagues tested in 2026 a nucleic acid mass spectrometry method for finding mycobacteria, the family that includes the tuberculosis bacterium. Standard tools are slow or cover only part of species naming and drug resistance. The team checked 138 clinical samples at a Beijing hospital, from sputum, lung wash fluid, and other sites. They compared the new method against bacterial culture, a rapid commercial test, and a combined clinical diagnosis standard.

Yan found the method caught nearly all true tuberculosis cases, with sensitivity close to full marks against both reference standards. Against culture alone its specificity was poor, at about a quarter, but against the combined clinical standard it rose to about three quarters, with overall accuracy above nine in ten. Its detection power matched the commercial rapid test overall. The authors present it as a sensitive option whose false alarms need care when culture is the judge.
pmc-13536769:
Sinem Cece and colleagues examine household health payments in Türkiye from 2014 to 2023 in a 2026 study using national budget survey data. Large reforms widened coverage, yet families still pay substantial sums directly for care. Models linked payment levels to social and economic traits, while payment-to-income ratios and a ten percent threshold gauged fairness and financial strain across income groups.

Direct payments rose over the decade and stayed above typical rich-country averages. Richer households spent more in absolute terms, yet poorer households carried a heavier share relative to income. After 2018, heavy burdens concentrated further among disadvantaged groups during economic turbulence. The authors argue that wider access did not bring equal financial protection, and they urge stronger safeguards plus routine tracking of who bears costs.
pmc-13536869:
Yanrong Tao, Meiyan Chen, Shanrui Tang, and Xiping Yang map a lignin-related gene family across the sugarcane genome in a 2026 analysis. Lignin stiffens cane stalks and affects how easily leftover fiber converts to fuel and products. The target enzyme helps build lignin units. Genome scans found hundreds of related genes, grouped them, and compared their control switches with activity patterns across tissues and times.

A total of 663 genes including copies spread across 77 chromosomes and fell into six groups with similar internal structures. Each group carried a distinct mix of control switches for light, hormones, and stress. Light-linked switches tracked positively with gene activity, and switch patterns matched activity patterns under cross-checks. The authors present the map as a starting point for breeding cane with friendlier fiber.
pmc-13537369:
Simon SY Lui and colleagues probe social motivation in treatment-resistant schizophrenia in a 2026 task study. Social motivation means seeking social reward and avoiding social punishment, and weakness here ties to negative symptoms. Sixty patients with resistant illness, sixty patients in remission, and sixty controls played a timed target game for happy, neutral, or unhappy face outcomes. Pleasure before and after outcomes was also rated.

Resistant patients showed flatter pleasure responses, with expected and received pleasure swayed less by social reward or punishment than in controls. Negative symptoms predicted game accuracy among patients, linking symptom load to social drive processing. The authors propose social motivation weakness as a treatment target for negative symptoms and poor social functioning in resistant illness.
pmc-13538169:
Cyryl Golański and colleagues test whether low-dose alcohol shifts judgment bias in honeybees in a 2026 experiment. Judgment bias means treating unclear cues as promising or disappointing, a pattern linked to mood-like states. Bees learned odor cues through classic conditioning, then faced mixed unclear odors after drinking a weak alcohol solution. Movement and blood alcohol levels were also measured to confirm exposure.

Alcohol levels in bee blood rose fast and stayed high through testing. Choices on unclear odors showed no detectable shift toward optimism or pessimism, and movement stayed unchanged. The authors present the work as the first drug-based judgment bias test in an invertebrate. They read the null result as evidence that bee thinking resists low natural alcohol doses.
pmc-13538669:
Hongjun Zhang and colleagues engineer a flowable stabilized soil for narrow trench backfilling in a 2026 materials study. Tight urban utility trenches resist traditional compaction, so a pumpable fill made from local loess, fly ash, and cement activated by sodium silicate was optimized through ratio tests. Microscopy and flow simulations traced hardening workings and pour behavior in confined trenches.

An even fly ash to cement split anchored the recipe, with set water, activator, and curing agent shares balancing flow against strength. The best mix spread widely yet hardened to solid strength within two weeks, meeting pumping and strength demands. Microscopy showed binding products filling pores and gluing particles. Field pours using long single runs with end slowdowns compacted well. The authors offer guidance for utility tunnel construction in the region.
pmc-13540069:
Mihirani Aththanayaka and Piyanjali de Zoysa study new mothers in Sri Lanka in 2026. They measured how often postpartum depression occurs in the Colombo district. They also asked which mothers face the greatest risk. Sri Lanka has improved maternal health a great deal. Low mood after birth is still a public concern.

Clinics recruited 401 mothers for the study. Each mother completed a Sinhala version of the Edinburgh scale. About twenty-nine percent met the depression threshold at four weeks. That share eased to eighteen percent by twenty-four weeks. Younger mothers faced higher odds. So did mothers with a past psychiatric history or a baby with health problems.
pmc-13540569:
Tumelo L Fortuin and colleagues mapped HIV killer-cell targets in southern Africa. Published in 2026, the systematic review sifted 2,103 records down to 49 studies of subtype C, the region's main HIV form. Early infection killer-cell attacks focus on Gag protein pieces that drag the virus down to a set level, yet the local map was patchy.

South Africa supplied most studies, then Botswana, Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe, and Angola, with none found in the rest of the region. The review counted 60 Gag targets, over half in the capsid protein p24, and flagged two standout targets, TL9 and TW10. Most matching immune tags were HLA-B, among them four tied to better virus control. Some targets were missing from the main HIV record set, which the authors say needs a refresh to aid vaccine design.
pmc-13540869:
David E Rebellón-Sánchez and four colleagues gather, in a 2026 systematic review, every published case they could find of cerebral tuberculoma during pregnancy or shortly after birth across fifty years. These tuberculosis lumps in the brain are rare, dangerous, and hard to manage while protecting a fetus.

Twenty-seven reports from twenty countries yielded thirty-three patients, typically in their mid-twenties. Headache, fever, and seizures led the symptoms, and diagnosis usually came late in pregnancy or after delivery. Standard four-drug therapy with steroids dominated treatment, and most women also had brain surgery for sampling or removal. Preterm delivery was common, half the newborns had complications, and a third of mothers kept lasting neurological problems.
pmc-13541869:
Takeuchi and co-authors compare brain bleed outcomes before and after a new anti-spasm drug arrived in Japan. Aneurysm rupture bleeds demand fast repair by clipping or by vessel work from inside. Delayed brain ischemia then decides much of the recovery. Vessel spasm is a chief driver of that delay. Japan long used fasudil around surgery to fight spasm. Clazosentan joined the options in 2022.

Records from several centers split patients by era and repair type. The team compared results for clipping and endovascular groups across the drug change. The study tests whether the new agent shifted real-world outcomes. Era comparisons carry bias risks the authors must weigh.
pmc-13543369:
Seyed Ali Shamsnia's team surveyed people with hypertension or type 2 diabetes in southern Iran in 2026, asking what shaped COVID-19 safety habits. Vaccines existed by then, but uptake was low. A health-belief survey was filled in by 338 patients in Kavar, and a structural model tested which beliefs tracked with habits such as masking and distancing.

The model fitted well. What people saw as barriers mattered most, and the effect ran negative: real-world and mental hurdles put people off prevention more than anything drew them to it. Feeling the disease was severe and getting cues to act both helped, while seeing clear gains helped a little. Feeling at risk oneself, and feeling able, made no clear difference after years of living with the outbreak. The authors advise clearing concrete hurdles, such as mask cost and false claims, instead of only warning people about risk.
pmc-13543469:
In 2026, Yueyao Yang and colleagues published a study using engineered bacterial vesicles to prime solid tumours for CAR-T cell therapy. CAR-T cells, immune cells fitted with a synthetic targeting receptor, excel against blood cancers but are blunted in solid tumours by a suppressive local environment.
