The team coated bacterial outer-membrane vesicles with a fragment that homes to PD-L1, a shield protein on tumours. They tested whether the vesicles could wake up local immune cells before the engineered cells arrived.

The vesicles accumulated in tumours and pushed dendritic cells to mature and stimulate T cells better, while steering macrophages toward an inflammatory, tumour-eating state. In mouse models, priming remodelled the tumour environment and let even reduced CAR-T doses control advanced tumours. Single-cell sequencing showed coordinated rewiring of immune communication. A modular priming step like this could widen where cell therapy works.
pmc-13544769:
Mohammed Alra'e and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a newborn whose blocked intestine had two causes at once: midgut malrotation and an ovarian dermoid cyst. The six-day-old girl arrived vomiting bile and passing no stool, and was first treated for suspected sepsis. At surgery through a small abdominal incision, the team found the gut had failed its embryonic rotation, with the fibrous Ladd bands that typically strangle the duodenum in that condition.

Stuck over the malrotated bowel sat an ovarian cyst, which tissue analysis confirmed as a dermoid cyst, a developmental lump containing trapped surface tissue. Either lesion alone can obstruct a newborn; together they compounded the blockage. The authors pair the case with a literature review and a practical moral: in neonatal obstruction, finding one cause should not end the search for a second.
pmc-13544969:
Albert Jiménez-Blanco presents Theseus, an algorithm for aligning a DNA sequence to a genome graph rather than a single reference sequence. Graph alignment supports pangenome analysis and multiple sequence alignment, but optimal methods are slow and memory-hungry. His 2026 paper aims to keep exactness while cutting the cost.

Theseus exploits similarities between sequences and computes only a subset of the scoring table using a sparse-data strategy, reducing memory without giving up the optimal answer. It also handles graphs with cycles. Against other optimal aligners for multiple alignment, it ran from 1.6 to 17.6 times faster than POASTA and about 7.3 times faster than SPOA on average. For pangenome read mapping it beat the standard tool by up to 16.9 times on short reads and more on synthetic cyclic graphs. The code is publicly available.
pmc-13545569:
Zhihua Li and co-authors built in 2026 a deep learning system that turns a plain CT scan of a stroke patient into a synthetic diffusion MRI image. Diffusion imaging shows stroke damage far more clearly than CT, yet it takes longer and can delay urgent treatment. Their model learned the mapping between the two scan types from paired images of 224 patients.

On a held-out test group, the synthetic images beat four rival methods on standard quality scores and on picking out the stroke core. Four radiologists rated the images near the top of a five-point scale, and each slice took only a few seconds to generate. The authors suggest such images could support fast bedside decisions where MRI is unavailable or too slow.
pmc-13547369:
Takashi Sekine and colleagues engineered in 2026 a malaria parasite line that glows red through its entire life cycle, giving researchers a window into stages that are usually hard to watch. Using gene editing, they slipped a fluorescent protein cassette into a quiet stretch of the Plasmodium falciparum genome without breaking any gene and without leaving a drug resistance marker behind. The edited line, named NF54-mCh, shines in blood stages, mosquito stages, and liver stages alike.

The parasites grew, formed sexual stages, and passed to mosquitoes normally, and their glow let the team spot infected mosquitoes without dissection. Sporozoites stayed infectious to humanized mouse livers. Similar lines worked in rodent malaria species. The authors offer the line as a parent platform for further genetic experiments.
pmc-13547569:
Yelin Song and Zuowei Li examined in 2026 how a small RNA, miR-34a-5p, can strip lung cancer stem cells of their stubborn traits, including resistance to the chemotherapy drug cisplatin. Cancer stem cells seed relapse and shrug off treatment. In patient tissue the RNA ran low while two structural proteins, KRT5 and DSP, ran high.

The RNA binds and suppresses KRT5, which drags DSP down with it. Restoring the RNA in cells shrank their stem-like behavior, lowered stemness markers, and made cisplatin work better. In mice, extra RNA slowed tumor growth. The authors present the RNA's grip on the KRT5 and DSP pair as a route to attack drug resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
pmc-13548569:
Ma. Jessica Zyra Cunanan and colleagues survey how well millennial emergency nurses work together in Philippine government hospitals, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Emergency rooms depend on smooth nurse-to-nurse cooperation, and millennials now form a large share of the workforce with distinct communication habits. The team sampled 173 nurses across five Metro Manila hospitals using a validated twenty-two-item collaboration scale.

Nurses rated collaboration favorably in every domain, covering conflict handling, shared goals, communication, and professional autonomy. Age and gender showed no connection with collaboration scores. Longer experience, surprisingly, came with slightly weaker scores for shared goals and for professionalism and autonomy. The authors offer the results as support for programs that build collaborative culture and help experienced nurses mentor newer colleagues without losing their own sense of shared purpose.
pmc-13549769:
Masanori Tsuji and colleagues measure how twisty the neck arteries are in three dimensions and relate the winding to classic risk factors, in a 2026 retrospective study. Patients with narrowed carotid arteries often have tortuous ones too, but older two-dimensional judgments disagreed about what drives the twisting. From magnetic resonance scans of ninety-six patients, the team rebuilt 168 arteries in 3D, traced their centerlines, and computed a tortuosity rate comparing the curved path with the straight-line distance.

In the common carotid segment, greater twisting came with age past sixty-five, overweight body mass, high total cholesterol, and high triglycerides. In the internal segment, overweight and high systolic pressure were the partners. The authors suggest the quantitative winding rate works as a visible summary of accumulated atherosclerotic risk.
pmc-13549969:
Kiljańczyk, Daneberga, Tooming, and many co-authors map hereditary cancer testing across Europe. Their 2026 paper surveys the ERN GENTURIS reference network. Germline testing finds inherited variants that raise cancer risk. Access and practice differ sharply between countries. Experts from twenty EU states plus Norway answered.

All twenty-one countries offer panel testing for breast and ovarian cancer risk. At least nineteen cover colorectal and prostate cancer too. Panel sizes and gene lists vary widely. Whole-exome sequencing is routine in only twelve countries. Founder-variant testing leads in a few high-prevalence populations. Every country lets clinical geneticists order germline tests. In nine countries, any physician may order them. Most countries test stored tumor tissue from deceased patients. Such tests can protect living relatives. The authors urge EU-wide shared standards and pathways. Equal access to testing is the stated goal. Finding at-risk families earlier enables prevention.
pmc-13550369:
Prathibha Selvamani and colleagues review how the lung's own slippery coating may coach a stubborn bacterium to attack, in a 2026 article on cystic fibrosis. In this genetic disease, thick mucus invites chronic Pseudomonas infection. The bacteria talk through quorum sensing, a density signal. That signal switches on toxins, biofilms, and drug tolerance. Long-running inflammation alters lung surfactant, above all its main fat, DPPC.

New evidence suggests the altered lipids are not just damage markers but signals. They may trip the bacteria's chat system early, locking in virulence and persistence. The review assembles this host and pathogen dialogue. It weighs a counter-move: drugs modeled on surfactant that jam bacterial chatter instead. Weakening bacteria without killing them could sidestep the resistance pressure that antibiotics create, the authors argue.
pmc-13550569:
Jun Zhang, with Shuli Cheng, Anyu Du, and Haixu Yang, published a 2026 computer vision study on matching the same person across different cameras without labeled training data. Unsupervised methods must invent their own labels by clustering, yet stray images and busy backgrounds make those labels noisy. The authors propose cleaning up doubtful cases while also learning richer image features.

One part grades each outlier by its distance to nearby examples and lets neighbors vote to fix the labels of low-confidence images. A second part trains global and local features together, so broad category differences and fine details support each other. Tests on standard data sets showed better clustering and cleaner labels, with steadier performance in complex scenes.
pmc-13551769:
Saya Nagata, Yu Matsumoto, Akira Iura, and Takeshi Yoshida published a 2026 retrospective report on anesthesia for open fetal surgery repairing myelomeningocele, the severest form of spina bifida, at a Japanese center. The operation is established abroad yet rare in Asia. The team reviewed ten cases from April 2021 to April 2025, describing uterine relaxation, blood pressure control, and birth outcomes with a focus on preterm birth.

Half the cases delivered preterm, mostly from early labor, with one birth before thirty weeks. Uterine relaxation used high-dose desflurane, and the preterm rate fell from the first five cases to the latter five in the reported series. A magnesium dose was lowered after blood levels ran high, and the authors advise individualized dosing while cautioning that ten cases prove little.
pmc-13551869:
Suzan Doğruya, leading four colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective series on fixing artificial lenses to the wall of the eye for Marfan syndrome patients whose natural lenses slip. Records covered nine patients and fifteen eyes treated between January 2015 and March 2023, using either sutured fixation or the sutureless Yamane technique, which tucks lens supports into the eye wall. Most eyes received the sutured approach.

Vision improved significantly on average over a mean follow-up near thirty-one months in the reported measures. Four eyes developed complications, including one retinal detachment and three lens displacements, all fixed by further surgery, while two eyes stayed limited by pre-existing lazy eye. With only two Yamane eyes, the authors treat technique comparisons as descriptive and stress long-term surveillance.
pmc-13551969:
Oliver and colleagues ran a brain stimulation trial in 2026 for social thinking problems in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. These disorders often impair social cognition, meaning skills such as reading others' minds, with few treatments available. The team targeted the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, a brain area for social processing, with magnetic stimulation. Forty-six adults finished two weeks of one of three options: standard rapid stimulation, a burst pattern, or sham treatment.

The burst pattern, called iTBS, raised connectivity inside the mentalizing network, the brain system for thinking about minds, far more than sham. Pain ratings were higher with the burst pattern, but dropout and side effect rates matched the other groups. The authors say the burst method hit its brain target and merits a larger clinical trial.
pmc-13555669:
Mai Harada, Satoshi Matsuoka, and Shigeki Ehira uncover a phosphate switch guarding the protective coat of nitrogen-fixing cells in a 2026 study. Their subject is Anabaena, a filament bacterium that builds special cells for fixing nitrogen. Those cells need a sugar coat layer to shield the oxygen-sensitive fixing machinery. A sugar-building enzyme and a phosphate-removing partner form the switch.

A version of the enzyme that cannot accept phosphate restored the coat even without its partner. Two candidate phosphate-adding enzymes were found, but deleting only one fixed the defect, naming it the true regulator. Adding phosphate switches the enzyme off; removing it switches production on. The study shows direct control of a coat-building enzyme by a partner-switching system.
pmc-13556069:
Yijun Luan and six colleagues reported in 2026 how mouth cancer cells use a protein called progranulin to quiet the immune cells around them. Macrophages inside tumours can be pushed toward a state that shelters cancer, and cholesterol handling inside those cells helps set that state. The team profiled single cells from mouth tumours, checked public datasets, then tested the pathway in cell and animal experiments.

A group of cancer cells rich in progranulin stood out. The protein pushed macrophages to export cholesterol through a chain of signals, and those macrophages released more immune-damping molecules. Blocking progranulin or its receptor reversed the effect in the dish, and silencing it in tumours shifted macrophage balance in animals. A drug that reactivated part of the pathway partly restored the quieted state, confirming the route matters.
pmc-13556969:
Yijia Huang and ten co-authors find that a common mosquito gut bacterium blocks dengue virus through its red pigment, in a two thousand twenty-six bug-science paper. Gut microbes influence whether mosquitoes transmit arboviruses, but the active molecules were obscure.

The team took Serratia marcescens strain WZ1 from field-caught Aedes albopictus in Wenzhou and traced its antiviral effect to prodigiosin. The pigment lodges in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggers stress there, and switches on autophagy, which hands virus particles to lysosomes to be destroyed. Blocking either the stress response or the autophagy gene erased the shield. That pathway names a symbiont metabolite for transmission-blocking plans.
pmc-13557569:
Omer Habis Alzoubi and twelve colleagues reviewed in 2026 the state of urease inhibitors, drugs that block an enzyme many bacteria use to neutralise acid. The enzyme lets Helicobacter pylori survive in the stomach and drive ulcer disease. Only one such drug has won approval for patients, and its side effects limit how much it can be used. The review surveys the whole field for better options.

The options under study include metal-based compounds, lab-made organic molecules, and products from nature. Peptide blockers, tiny particle carriers, and early gene-based ideas also appear. Copper compounds and a plant compound called palmatine did well in lab and animal work. Safety problems and a shortage of human trials still block the path to clinics. The authors favour mixed molecules, smarter delivery, and combined therapy, as long as strict testing in patients comes first.
pmc-13557869:
Ying-Long Peng and eight colleagues asked in 2026 whether recent antibiotic use blunts chemoimmunotherapy in widespread small cell lung cancer. Gut microbes shape how immune therapy works in other cancers, and antibiotics disturb them. The team reviewed patients treated at the Guangdong Lung Cancer Institute. Survival models compared patients by exposure to antibiotics, laxatives, and probiotics around their treatment.

Antibiotic exposure tracked with shorter time before the cancer grew again. It also tracked with shorter overall survival. The link held across several ways of adjusting the data, from models picked by fit to models built on clinical grounds. Matching methods that balance the groups agreed as well. The authors stress that the design looks backward, so antibiotics may mark sicker patients rather than cause the harm. Still, the steady signal argues for care with antibiotic use during immune therapy.
pmc-13558069:
Pärssinen and colleagues report a 2026 survey of ancient earthworks hidden under forest in southwest Amazonia. Geometric ditches and mounds there point to a monument-building society long before European contact, but most known sites sit in cleared land. The team flew canopy-penetrating LiDAR, a laser scanning method, and combined new finds with older records.

The team now counts more than 20,000 earthworks in this one cultural area, as many as earlier guesses gave for the whole Amazon basin. Working from site density, they estimate the local population between the years 100 and 300 at well over a million people, possibly near three million. Such numbers recast the region as home to a large, organized society, not scattered small groups. If other regions match, the human mark on today's forests runs far deeper than assumed.
pmc-13558769:
Peilun Shi and seven colleagues discuss intelligent medical agents for high-altitude populations. Over 81 million people live above 2,500 meters, in places such as Tibet, the Andes, and Ethiopia. These groups face harsh environments, weak health infrastructure, and thin research on their needs. Their 2026 paper argues that generalist foundation models could leapfrog current limits and deliver equitable care.

Today's medical AI tools are narrow, trained on unrepresentative data, and blind to the mix of biological, environmental, and social factors shaping health. High-altitude groups are also ethnically distinct and geographically isolated, complicating one-size-fits-all medicine. Generalist agents, the authors say, could tailor care to these unique needs. The paper frames agentic AI as a path to health equity at altitude.
pmc-13560269:
Hongbo Yu and three colleagues test whether thyroxine given after blood flow returns protects the heart by switching on mitochondrial self-cleaning. Their 2026 rat study models ischemia-reperfusion injury by tying off a coronary artery for forty minutes, then releasing it for two hours of reperfusion. Five groups of ten rats separated the hormone's effect from its proposed pathway.

Thyroxine raised the oxygen-sensing protein HIF-1α and its partner BNIP3, markers of targeted mitophagy, while easing the pileup of spent cleaning machinery. Treated hearts produced far fewer reactive oxygen species, held more energy currency, and kept healthier mitochondrial voltage. Infarct size shrank from about forty-five percent of the risk zone to about twenty in the reported estimates. Blocking HIF-1α with an inhibitor drug erased every benefit. The authors credit the HIF-1α and BNIP3 pathway for the protection.
pmc-13560569:
Róisín O'Malley and colleagues set out a protocol for an umbrella review of ways to involve hospital patients and their families in measuring and monitoring safety. Their 2026 protocol follows Joanna Briggs guidance for reviews of reviews, searching five databases for existing systematic reviews on the topic. Policy worldwide pushes patient voice, yet the full menu of approaches remains unmapped.

For each approach found, from surveys to incident reporting by patients, the team will extract evidence on feasibility, fit to context, and measurement quality. Barriers and facilitators of real-world use will be catalogued alongside. Review quality gets a CASP appraisal, and certainty will be judged with a hybrid grading approach mixing quantitative and qualitative schemes. The authors expect a practical profile of best options, reflecting the shift of patients from passive recipients to active partners in safe care.
pmc-13563769:
Wenshuai Song and five colleagues interview patients whose diabetes is nobody's main job, because they were admitted to wards that do not specialise in it. Over ninety percent of China's hospitalised diabetes patients sit in such wards, where the headline illness swallows attention. Their 2026 qualitative study spoke at length with twelve adults, six men and six women aged 30 to 81, nearly all with type 2 diabetes. Questions followed a behaviour model covering capability, opportunity, and motivation, and answers were sorted by content analysis.

Four clusters of hidden need emerged. The primary diagnosis fought the diabetes for priority; blood sugar routines confused patients; self-management met practical barriers; and the double illness piled on burdens, financial and emotional. Care paths built around single specialties routinely miss all four. The authors argue for patient-centred, integrated models that treat economic and psychological needs as part of glucose care, not as extras.
pmc-13563869:
Yutong Liu and four colleagues test a blended way of teaching breast surgery to China's elite eight-year medical students: an online platform fused with problem-based and case-based learning. Their 2026 randomised trial took fifty students interning at Nanfang Hospital and split them evenly. One half kept lectures and clinical practice; the other worked cases and problems through the online platform. Both halves sat theory exams, faced clinical assessments of skills, and filled in questionnaires.

The blended group scored higher on theory, 76.25 against 73.60, and on overall clinical competence, 7.32 against 6.92 on the workplace scale. Procedure assessments favoured the blended group across six dimensions, from judging indications to aseptic technique and talking with patients. Questionnaire dimensions showed no significant differences, only a positive tilt. The authors offer the blend as a frame for training: digital delivery carries the content, while problems and cases force the thinking that lectures cannot.
pmc-13565969:
Laura White leads a team that reviews a new drug for bowel disease. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with guselkumab. It treats both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

The drug blocks a part of a signal that drives gut swelling. It is the most new drug of its class for bowel disease. It is first in class to offer a full under skin start. Trial gains beat an older drug on many checks. The team weighs proof, safety, and where it fits. Use tips for clinic work are also given.
pmc-13567769:
Arunadevi and three co-authors build a physics-informed neural network that predicts delamination when drilling glass fiber reinforced polymer parts, in a two thousand twenty-six engineering paper. Delamination around drilled holes is a critical defect that weakens composite structures.

A full-factorial campaign ran two hundred forty-three drilling trials, varying drill angle, diameter, laminate thickness, spindle speed, and feed rate. Fracture mechanics governing thrust-force delamination was written into the network's loss function. The model fit the data closely, and sensitivity analysis ranked feed rate as the strongest driver, with higher spindle speeds reducing damage. Physics constraints improved robustness over purely data-driven models.
pmc-13569369:
Nabiha H. Saifee and Meghan Delaney compare, in a 2026 retrospective review, red blood cells stored two ways for children receiving very large transfusions during heart surgery on a bypass machine. Eighty-nine patients having a Norwood operation or heart transplant were split by whether their center's blood came in plain anticoagulant or in an additive solution, across a product switch.

Blood use, deaths, and hospital stay were similar between groups. Salt, sugar, and phosphorus ran higher right after surgery in the additive group, then normalized within a day. One acidity marker differed by operation type and age. The findings support additive-stored blood for these large pediatric transfusions.
pmc-13570469:
Ramy Awadalla and Derek Davies describe, in a 2026 surgical report, a modified forehead flap for rebuilding the nose after skin cancer removal in spots away from the midline. The classic flap reaches above the brow line, leaving visible forehead scars and brow distortion, so the new version stays below the brow and uses asymmetric side triangles to close the wound.

Twenty patients treated for basal cell or squamous cell cancers on the nose formed the test group. The authors report better cosmetic results with no brow-area complications and no deaths of the flap tip. Skin surgeons get a refinement aimed at the defects the original flap handled poorly.
pmc-13570969:
Sophia Kier-Byfield and colleagues explored what young people in Wales know about stalking and what education they want, publishing the study in 2026. Young people face the highest stalking risk in England and Wales, yet their understanding is patchy and often shaped by stereotypes of strangers, missing that stalkers are usually acquaintances. The team ran eight participatory workshops with 84 young people aged 16 to 24 across Wales.

Knowledge existed but was limited, terminology confused participants, and few had received stalking education. Young people asked for more information, delivered in ways they trust. The article sets out practice suggestions and research directions, arguing that clear, early education could help young people recognise concerning behaviour and respond before harm escalates.
pmc-13571269:
Kole Joachim and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six study predicting five-year death risk after prosthetic joint infection. The work uses health records for a large multicenter group of patients. It builds a thirty-item frailty index covering illnesses, body deficits, medicines, and daily function.

The model was trained on most of the records and checked on the rest. Both frailty score and age predicted later death on their own. Estimated risk ranged from very low in younger, nonfrail patients to about one half in older, frail ones. Clinicians get an objective tool for planning care instead of relying on judgment alone.
pmc-13571369:
Naila Badalova and colleagues describe in this 2026 case report a leak beside a reconstructed aortic valve and how they sealed it without open surgery. The patient, a sixty-two year old man, had earlier received an Ozaki procedure, which rebuilds the valve from the patient's own tissue.

He arrived with marked breathlessness, and scans showed a moderate to severe leak between two valve cusps. Because his surgical risk score was high, the team closed the gap through a leg artery using a small plug device, guided by ultrasound imaging from inside the food pipe. Only a trace of leakage remained afterward. He left the hospital stable and remained improved at six months, showing the approach can work after this type of valve repair.
pmc-13572169:
Mehri and colleagues proposed a 2026 statistical framework for poultry feeding studies, arguing that standard analysis wastes information. Trials often feed birds graded levels of an ingredient, yet analyse those levels as separate groups with ANOVA, a method for comparing group averages. Because feed levels form a continuous scale, dose patterns stay hidden.

Mehri reanalysed published broiler data where a herbal mixture powder was fed at four levels up to three grams per kilogram. Straight and curved regression models revealed rising, levelling, and bending dose responses that group comparisons had missed. Curved models also estimated the best inclusion level for each trait. Growth, fat related blood measures, antioxidant markers, and immune traits responded most, while feed intake and gut traits responded least.
pmc-13572369:
Dakota D. Witzel, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of daily stress and the sense of control over it. The question is whether feeling in control of a day's hassles softens the mood swings those hassles bring. Past work hinted at a shield effect, but tests by kind of hassle were rare.

The team used a national daily-life study with 1,263 adults, mean age near 63 years. On days when people felt more control over rows or rows they had dodged, mood swings were smaller. Control over rows at home and hassles at home also softened mood swings. The shield was clearest for same-day effects. The authors suggest that social support and active coping may help people feel more in control.
pmc-13572469:
P. Jennita Jacqueline, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 comparison of metal oxide helpers in turning plant waste into bio-oil. Heat breaks down the waste without air, in a process called pyrolysis, and helpers called catalysts can raise the oil yield. Three wastes were tested: safflower press cake, coconut press cake, and coconut shell.

Without a catalyst at 550 degrees, oil yields were 34, 29, and 26 percent for the three wastes. Titanium dioxide proved the strongest helper, above all with safflower cake. Under the best settings, that pairing yielded 71.75 percent oil, a gain of about 37.5 points over the plain run. Chemical scans of the oil found it rich in phenolic compounds and ketones. Coconut cake gave a better balance of oil quality and usable char.
pmc-13573369:
Shuyan Liu and colleagues automated the measurement of how well clear dental aligners fit teeth. Fit accuracy shapes treatment success, and micro-CT scans can map aligner-tooth gaps in three dimensions, but manual measurement is slow and varies by operator. Their pilot study built a flood-fill algorithm in Python and tested it on nine aligners from three manufacturing routes: in-house 3D printing, Invisalign, and Angelalign.

The algorithm matched manual measurement closely, with a Dice score of 0.87, and cut processing from roughly an hour to about 3.2 minutes per scan. Mean gaps were similar across groups, near 187 to 255 micrometres, with no significant overall difference. The authors present automated micro-CT as a fast, reproducible way to compare aligner manufacturing.
pmc-13573469:
Qing Hu, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 case of a rare defect cluster in one of identical twins, joined by a review of 20 past twin cases. The OEIS cluster joins four faults: a belly wall gap, an open bladder area, no anal opening, and spine defects. It strikes about one in hundreds of thousands of pregnancies.

The twins shared one placenta and one sac. Scans from week 12 onward showed the cluster in twin B, plus a single cord artery and a tailbone spine fault. At near 34 weeks, after team review, the affected twin was selectively ended by laser, and the mother delivered by caesarean. The healthy twin, just over two kilograms, grew normally to 18 months. In past cases, a lone affected twin often left a healthy survivor, while both affected spelled a poor outlook.
pmc-13574769:
T Van Grunsven, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of vitamin C and blood proteins in people with type 2 diabetes. Trials hint the vitamin helps heart and metabolic health in this group, but the protein-level story was blank. A protein-wide scan can show which body systems the vitamin actually moves.

The double-blind crossover trial gave 26 patients a gram of vitamin C a day or a dummy pill for four months each. Blood proteins were counted by a precise mass method. Fifteen proteins shifted clearly after the vitamin, twelve down and three up. The biggest drops hit a starch-cutting enzyme, a heat shock protein, a muscle protein, and an inflammation marker. Pathways for immune defence and protein folding thinned out. Some shifted proteins tracked with better blood pressure in past work.
pmc-13575169:
Francesc Ribas-Aulinas and colleagues tested whether a twisty belly aorta signals hidden vessel disease in other parts. For decades, doctors linked twisty arteries to weak vessels and to classic risks such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Their 2026 study gauged belly-aorta twist in 490 adults aged 50 and older from the Ageing Imageomics Study, factoring in neck-artery disease, stiffness, and past history.

Twist rose steeply with age and a bit with lower-number blood pressure and kidney filter scores. But diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking, vessel stiffness, and calcium deposits played no major role. The authors say the twist score does not work as an early sign of vessel disease in other parts, despite long-held hunches.
pmc-13576369:
Rui Li leads a 2026 study of chlorogenic acid, a plant compound, as a defence against skin ageing and sun-driven photoageing. Mitochondria, the energy units of cells, sit at the centre of skin ageing, and the compound was known to affect them. The team tested it on human skin cells in the lab and on a mouse photoageing model.

In skin cells the compound raised collagen production through a known growth signal route, while lowering ageing markers and the inflammatory mix that old cells release. Energy output rose by roughly 40 to 80 percent, and damaged internal structures of mitochondria were repaired. Transplanting mitochondria confirmed the ageing benefit ran through them. In mice, a gel form given for 14 days protected collagen after ultraviolet exposure and calmed ageing signals. The authors propose the compound as a candidate anti-ageing agent.
pmc-13577569:
Yu-Shuan Chen and Hsin-Yi Huang review how to design nose sprays that carry Alzheimer's drugs straight to the brain. Most Alzheimer's drugs struggle past the blood-brain barrier, a tight vessel wall that guards the brain, and current pills and infusions offer limited benefit. Nasal delivery uses smell and facial-nerve routes to bypass the bloodstream. This 2026 review takes a materials view: success depends less on the nose route itself than on what the drug is packed in.

Chitosan gels, heat-sensitive polymers, lipid carriers, surface-tuned particles, and cell-mimicking vesicles each shape how much drug reaches the brain and how reliably. Early trials of nasal insulin and cell-derived vesicles show feasibility and safety. The authors stress quantitative proof of brain uptake and reproducible recipes as the keys to moving these formulations toward patients.
pmc-13578069: Trapaga and co-authors study Sporothrix brasiliensis, a fungus that spreads from animals to people and causes skin infection. Their work identifies distinct genetic clades in the samples, showing the fungus is not one uniform strain. They also document frequent zoonotic transmission and reduced response to itraconazole, a main antifungal drug. That mix of spread and drug tolerance raises concern for clinics that treat this infection.
pmc-13578169:
Yuan Qiao and colleagues report a nationwide look back at care for advanced melanoma in China, published in 2026. Their group followed 431 patients treated with drugs that block the PD-1 protein between mid-2018 and mid-2023. Acral tumors, which grow on palms and soles, made up the largest share, followed by mucosal and skin forms.

Inside, the authors compare single-drug treatment with several paired and triple drug mixes, tracking how long the disease stayed quiet and how long patients lived. Two mixes tied to blocking blood vessel growth showed a clear gain for acral and mucosal cases. One triple mix raised the risk of severe side effects without helping survival, so the authors urge care with that option.
pmc-13578269:
Qais Al Rawahi and colleagues map the genes of the common myna across Oman in a 2026 study of a bird that has spread far from its South Asian home. Mynas push out local birds and thrive near people, yet how the Oman birds are linked was unclear. The team read thousands of gene markers in 311 birds from four regions of the country.

Birds split into two camps. One camp held the southern Dhofar birds, cut off by desert, and the other joined the capital area with two northern regions, with finer splits inside it. The northern Batinah birds formed the largest breeding pool, hinting the spread may have started there. The authors argue that Dhofar could be tackled on its own, while the linked north needs one joint plan.
pmc-13578769:
Ruoxue Cao and colleagues pin a driver role on a small protein called NOSIP in clear cell kidney cancer, the most common kidney cancer type, in a 2026 study. The protein had been tied to other cancers, yet its part here was murky. Lab work traced its contact with a second protein, SPTAN1, which acts as a cell scaffold and seems to hold tumors back.

NOSIP tags SPTAN1 for shredding, lowering its levels in cancer cells. With the scaffold gone, cells grew and moved more freely. Raising the scaffold again slowed growth and spread, while dropping it erased the benefit of silencing NOSIP. Tumors in mice grew faster when NOSIP ran high. The authors name the pair as a target lead for diagnosis and drug work.
pmc-13579069:
Marin Kalista and colleagues describe a ten week advocacy placement built into a genetic counseling master's program at the University of Pennsylvania. Counseling students pair with a patient advocacy group for a single disease and deliver real projects for that group. Patient groups have grown fast beside genomic medicine, yet few reports show how advocacy fits into counselor training.

The placement grew from a campus rare disease center's starter program into a student exchange scheme the authors lay out step by step. Four years of running it supply the reflections, drawn from students, staff, and partner groups alike. Sample projects show the range, from family guides to event support. The authors hope the blueprint helps other programs grow advocacy skills, and they flag disability teaching as the next strand to weave in.
pmc-13581669:
Di Siervi and co-authors report lattice radiation for a large leg sarcoma in an older patient. The patient was an 85-year-old woman with a tumor 20.7 by 9.8 cm. Surgery was not an option at first due to size and grade. The team used standard arc therapy plus weekly lattice boosts. Boosts of 10 gray hit four set points inside the tumor.

By week four the tumor felt softer and pain had eased. No severe skin harm occurred during the course. A scan at four months showed the same outer size but dead tissue inside. That change made later surgery possible. The authors add a short review of lattice therapy in frail patients.
pmc-13582769:
Aivija Grundmane, Caterina F Ramogida, and Valery Radchenko published a 2026 study on making targets for antimony-119. That is a radioactive form of antimony used in a type of cancer care that harms cells at very close range. Pure antimony-119 comes from shooting protons at enriched tin-119 in a medical cyclotron. That tin costs about 20,000 Canadian dollars per gram, so the used target material has to be saved and reused.

The team tested three bath mixes for coating tin onto a target by electroplating. A bath based on tin chloride worked best, laying down nearly all the tin in 72 hours and giving back most of it after later cleanup steps. Its targets were also the most even and the richest in surface tin, which should help them stand up to the beam.
pmc-13585469:
Lorenz-de Laigue and colleagues present in 2026 SNIRF2BIDS, a free tool that converts functional near-infrared spectroscopy recordings into the standard Brain Imaging Data Structure format. The recordings measure brain activity with light through the scalp. Conversion by hand is slow and error-prone.

The R package works through a graphical interface, so users click rather than code, while a Python engine underneath handles the restructuring, metadata organization, and file naming the standard demands. Everything runs locally on the user's machine after setup, with no data sent online. A step-by-step tutorial walks from raw recordings to a fully compliant dataset. The authors say the tool cuts manual work and human error, making it easier for the growing spectroscopy community to share data and reproduce each other's analyses.
pmc-13585769:
Jonathan Edwards and five co-authors ask what good supervision looks like for peer support specialists in behavioral health care. These workers use their own recovery experience to help others, and their numbers have grown past one hundred thousand in the United States. Poor supervision, often by non-peers, can blur their role.

Using participatory action research, online Delphi groups, and a national pilot survey, the team rated seventy-one supervisory tasks. One hundred specialists and supervisors judged importance, criticality, and frequency. Twenty-five top competencies emerged, favoring role clarity, active listening, and leading with empathy. The results offer a base for standard training and practice guidelines.
pmc-13586669:
Katsuya Takeuchi and eight co-authors ask whether reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome without visible vessel narrowing is another disease, in a two thousand twenty-six brain study. The syndrome of thunderclap headaches is usually confirmed by vessel imaging, but some patients' vessels look normal.

Eighty-four Japanese patients in hospital split into sixty-one with demonstrable vasoconstriction and twenty-three without. Age, sex balance, migraine history, thunderclap counts and timing, hospital course, calcium channel blocker use, imaging abnormalities, and lasting deficits all matched between groups. The authors conclude the two presentations share one clinical spectrum, while calling for larger forward-looking checks before the invisible form is diagnosed as confidently.
pmc-13586869:
Lou, Shuang, Kong, and Guo review vitamin K2 making in a dairy bacterium, in work from twenty twenty-six. Menaquinone, or vitamin K2, supports bone health and heart protection. Long chain forms are made only by bacteria and last longer in the body.

Lactococcus lactis is a key starter for dairy foods and naturally makes several long chain forms. That makes it a strong candidate for food based production. The review sums up recent gains in understanding and raising its output, by both culture tuning and genetic work. Future prospects for using this food safe microbe as a vitamin factory are discussed.
pmc-13588169:
Guangdong Zhou and colleagues report a study from twenty twenty-six on a protein-based device whose response to light can go in two directions. Most protein materials that conduct electricity change in only one direction under light. The team used silk fibroin, whose internal structure shifts when light hits it. They measured electric current under weak light and under stronger light, and they tracked how the protein chains folded in each case.

Weak light partly loosened the structure and lowered conduction, giving a current in one direction. Strong light unfolded the chains further into a form that conducts better, giving current in the opposite direction. Because the device senses and computes in one place, the authors show it tracking several moving objects at once in real time.
pmc-13589369:
Harrisson and co-authors describe a film project made with people who live with chronic pain. Pain lasting three months or more often blocks family life, work, and community roles. People with pain are also scarce in research planning and public involvement. The team set out to raise awareness and draw more of them into research. They co-produced a film that shares pain experiences and the gains of taking part.

Four public contributors with lived pain experience led the work with a filmmaker and a researcher. The project ran through five stages, from funding to sharing the film. UK standards for public involvement guided each stage. The film serves as both record and invitation.
pmc-13590669:
Eva Carlsson and five colleagues test whether a standard hospital scanner can read phosphorus signals from a healthy human kidney in its normal place. The method, phosphorus magnetic resonance spectroscopy, tracks compounds tied to cell energy and membrane building. Kidneys sit deep in the body, which makes the weak signal hard to catch. The team used a 3 Tesla scanner and a single volume method with extra signal tricks.

Clear spectra came out within a scan time clinics could accept, the team reports. Care was needed in picking the target volume, since the signal shifts with chemical type. Their healthy kidney spectra now offer a baseline. Future work can compare sick or transplanted kidneys against that healthy pattern.
pmc-13591169:
Jolie N Haun and colleagues asked how brain-harm load ties to stress signs in 105 male Special Ops vets. The men had a mean age of 42 years with mild to mid brain harm and joined a VA deep rehab course at five sites. Signs and life-partaking were scored at start, at exit, and at six months.

More brain-harm signs and more life-partaking loss each on their own foretold worse stress signs at start. Over time, though, only life-partaking shaped the path: vets with better partaking scores shed stress signs far faster. Help to get vets back into work, home, and social life may thus count as much as care for signs alone.
pmc-13594369:
Holly and co-authors size grit in farm run-off to hone rain basin builds. Top Midwest basin builds lean on soil type marks in the main. Those marks set fall pace calls from a stock code list. Yet kept fields can send fine grit that skips fall by weight. Run-off came from 13 field-edge sheds in two states. States were Wisconsin and Indiana in the work set.

Grit size tales split wide by how counts get weighed. Mass D50 sat near 30 fine marks, a coarse call in the set. Count D50 sat near 3.5, a clay-rich tale for the same flows. Mixed fits found year span and wet chem as top marks. Those beat farm acts as marks of grit size in the runs. Cold spans coarsened grit by a firm mark in fits. That hints low-mass fluff puffs size sans fall gain.
pmc-13594669:
Wong and colleagues compare four urine tests as warnings for kidney failure in rare kidney diseases. Each test scales protein lost in urine against creatinine, a waste product found in urine. Albumin-based and total-protein tests are used in different clinics, so teams need to know if they agree.

The study used records for more than four thousand patients with same-day paired tests. About one in six patients later reached kidney failure or died. All four measures foresaw that risk to a near equal degree. A worked-out albumin score from the protein test also fared just as well. No measure beat the rest in any disease subgroup or protein range.
pmc-13594769:
Lydia Serwaa Gyimah and a team of co-authors tested three finished herbal malaria products widely sold in Ghana for real anti-parasite activity and safety, since scientific checks of such products are scarce. The products, gathered through a small survey in Accra and Kumasi, were assayed against malaria parasites in the laboratory at several life stages and against a strain that resists chloroquine.

Two products strongly suppressed the growing stage of the drug-sensitive parasite, and the third was weaker; against the resistant strain the first two again performed well while the third lagged. Activity faded at the later blood stage and was modest against the sexual stage that spreads infection. Cell toxicity tests and a subacute safety study in rodents following international guidelines raised no safety flags. The authors conclude the three products genuinely act against malaria parasites and were safe in the animal model.
pmc-13596069:
Job van Essen and co-authors built transparent, 3D-printed models of small blood vessels, straight, bulged into an aneurysm, or narrowed by stenosis, and filmed tracer particles to map the flow inside. Imaging living vessels at this scale lacks resolution, so their bench platform aims to supply the missing detail for brain vessel disease research.

The printed channels went down to half a millimeter across. Under steady flow, measured speeds matched textbook predictions within a modest error band, and the setup captured local velocity fields and the friction stress on vessel walls in each geometry. The authors conclude that printed phantoms paired with particle image velocimetry give an accessible, reliable way to study how shape changes flow. The work targets diseased microvessels. It can inform how aneurysms and narrowings progress and rupture.
pmc-13598169:
João Barretto-Bittar and colleagues published a 2026 study on how brains assign credit for learning. Rewards often arrive late and vaguely. Neurons must guess which earlier activity helped. Chemical messengers called neuromodulators spread such signals. The authors model those signals as a diffusing cloud.

Their networks were spiking and sparsely connected. Error information spread locally between nearby neurons. Neurons learned from the local signal strength alone. Performance improved on three benchmark tasks. The method beat a standard comparison approach. It offers a plausible picture of learning in real brain circuits.
pmc-13604069:
Tingzhen Chen and colleagues examine what happens when a heart reprogramming factor cocktail reaches macrophages instead of its intended target cells. Their 2026 study addresses safety questions around converting scar fibroblasts directly into heart muscle cells.

The three-factor cocktail was introduced into mouse macrophages from bone marrow and a macrophage cell line. Heart-associated genes and proteins rose transiently in the mistargeted cells. A small subset even developed fibroblast-like shapes resembling reprogrammed heart cells. The team also assessed polarisation state in the cell line. In marrow macrophages, they checked markers of two cell death pathways. Unintended effects on non-target cells remain largely uncharacterised, motivating this safety-focused work.
pmc-13604169:
Yifei Wei and seven colleagues hunt the true target of sinomenine, a plant alkaloid used in osteoarthritis. Sinomenine was known to quiet the NF-κB pathway in cartilage cells, but its direct binding partner was unproven, and network methods used to guess targets rarely check their accuracy. The team intersected predictions from six resources with disease genes and cartilage expression data, then tested finalists in the lab.

The pipeline produced 96 candidates and a network of 78 nodes, with NF-κB signaling ranked first among 74 enriched pathways. Five targets led the list, and bench tests singled out IKBKB: sinomenine bound it, shifted its melting point by 4.3 degrees, and blocked it dose by dose, while two rivals showed none. Silencing IKBKB erased most of sinomenine's effect on a cartilage-degrading enzyme, and treated mice showed less cartilage damage. Benchmarking, honestly reported, found the pipeline only partly accurate once double-counting was corrected.
pmc-13605669:
Jimao Mo and four colleagues dissect how Chinese A-share stocks cluster when returns are viewed at different time scales. Analysts often split price movements into frequency bands, assuming each reveals distinct trader behavior. The team tested that assumption with wavelet decomposition and a clustering method handling positive and negative similarities separately, running 15,360 setups.

Against the Shenwan industry grouping, the reference setup scored an adjusted Rand index of 0.381, matching the strongest correlation baseline, with no orphan communities. Deeper splitting steadily hurt industry alignment, the best score falling to 0.139 at level six in every window. Stock-pair rankings agreed strongly across bands, yet band-by-band clusters differed markedly, with mean agreement of only 0.328. Stripping out market-wide and then industry effects weakened the overlap further. The overlap across frequencies is real but incomplete, the authors warn, against treating each band as a separate market.
pmc-13606569:
Zuoming Cao and six co-authors hunted for plant compounds that block an enzyme tied to high uric acid, in twenty twenty-six. The enzyme, xanthine oxidase, is a target for easing hyperuricemia. The team screened leaf extracts from four plant species and found raspberry leaf the strongest blocker. Seven extraction routes were then compared, and ultrasound-assisted extraction won out.

A response-surface method tuned the extraction to set heat, time, and solvent ratio. The extract blocked the enzyme by nearly ninety-eight percent. That was over five times the strength of a plain boiled extract. Tests showed the block is reversible and of a mixed kind. Chemical profiling found close to three thousand compounds in the leaf. Network and docking work pointed to terpenoids and coumarins, not the usual flavonoids, as the likely actives. The authors pitch the extract as a food-grade option for uric acid care.
pmc-13609469:
Abdullah Durhan and seven co-authors test if a joint blood score beats plain blood ratios at foretelling life span in colon cancer. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, reads past cases at their center.

Fire and food marks may aid the call of a cancer's course, but their best use was not set. The team read more than four hundred patients cut for colon cancer across a decade. Files gave age, kind, ill traits, and lab reads from past the cut. The joint score blends four blood marks: a red-cell count, a guard count, a serum mark, and a clot mark. It was matched to plain ratios and to care facts.
pmc-13612669:
Ayşen Toktay and Kader Mert report a 2026 study from Izmir, Turkey, on adults who had peritoneal dialysis as children and now look back on that time. Peritoneal dialysis is a home treatment for kidney failure that uses the lining of the belly to clean the blood. Eighteen adults who had at least six months of this treatment in childhood shared their memories in face-to-face interviews.

The accounts fell into four main themes, covering the mental strain of treatment and the changes it brought to daily life, school, and family routines. Most past research asks parents what dialysis is like for a child. Hearing directly from people who lived through it as children gives clinics a clearer view of the support young patients may need long after treatment ends.
pmc-13617069:
Rui Hu and six colleagues present a case report with a literature review on a rare overlap of three autoimmune conditions. Their patient, a fifty-three-year-old man, first developed limb numbness and unsteady walking, then slurred speech, swallowing trouble, double vision, and the fluctuating muscle weakness of myasthenia gravis. Testing also revealed an invasive thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland, and a paraneoplastic syndrome tied to CRMP5/CV2 antibodies.

Blood and spinal fluid tests confirmed both the myasthenia antibody and the paraneoplastic antibody, nerve studies showed widespread peripheral nerve damage, and chest imaging found the tumor. Surgeons removed the thymus, and steroids, immunoglobulin, and cyclophosphamide followed. His symptoms improved clearly and stayed stable in follow-up. The authors warn that this combination is easily misdiagnosed, and they stress antibody testing plus chest imaging for early recognition.
pmc-13617169:
Grigorios Theodosiou and Åke Svensson report a paradoxical skin reaction in a teenager treated for severe eczema. Eight months into dupilumab therapy, he developed widespread psoriasis-like dermatitis. This effect of the drug is known but uncommon, and reports in children and teens remain limited.

The clinicians switched his treatment to abrocitinib, a daily pill. The psoriasis-like lesions nearly cleared fully. The eczema underneath stayed well controlled at the same time. The authors present the switch as a sound alternative that handles both conditions at once. The case adds evidence from a young patient to a small literature. It offers a practical route for care when dupilumab triggers psoriasis.
pmc-13618069:
Mohamed H. Hekal and five colleagues synthesize a family of bromophenyl imidazolone compounds and test them as possible cancer drugs aimed at the epidermal growth factor receptor, a well-known oncology target. Starting from a brominated oxazolone building block, they reacted it with various nitrogen partners to build the series. Lab tests measured growth inhibition in liver, breast, and colon cancer cell lines alongside normal fibroblasts for safety contrast.

One derivative, a carboethoxy-substituted compound labeled 5, stood out, halting the three cancer lines at concentrations between about seven and twelve micromolar. It spared normal cells with a selectivity index around seven, markedly better than the standard drug doxorubicin on that measure. Computer models suggested most derivatives should absorb well as oral drugs, and docking placed compound 5 snugly in the receptor's kinase pocket. The authors name these imidazolones as promising anticancer leads.
pmc-13618169:
Wenqiao Hui and eighteen colleagues build a cross-species test system to ask whether the hemoglobin gene HBB drives adaptation to high-altitude thin air. They combined mesh-nanorod cell sorting, chitosan nanoparticle gene delivery, and injection into bone, then transplanted stem cells carrying HBB versions from high- or low-altitude animals into mice. The mice faced simulated and natural Qinghai-Tibet plateau hypoxia.

Gene delivery proved efficient, reaching ninety-five percent of target cells. Mice receiving high-altitude HBB switched on oxygen transport and blood-forming pathways. They performed better on behavior tests and showed protection against hypoxia-induced brain damage, unlike low-altitude HBB recipients. A second validation, using bone marrow chimeras with pika HBB in a safe-harbor gene locus, reproduced the same pattern. The authors conclude HBB is a key determinant of altitude adaptation and offer their platform as a tool for gene-function studies.
pmc-13618369:
Madeline Dow and two colleagues report a case of perioperative rhabdomyolysis, dangerous muscle breakdown, after a long kidney removal operation. Their patient was a fifty-three-year-old man with class II obesity, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension who underwent robotic laparoscopic radical nephrectomy with lymph node removal. He lay on his side for the prolonged procedure. Body weight pressing on dependent muscles during lateral positioning is a known setup for this complication.

Breakdown products such as myoglobin and potassium flood the blood in rhabdomyolysis and can injure the kidneys and disturb electrolytes. The authors' message concerns timing: in high-risk patients having prolonged surgery, measuring creatine kinase early after the operation is essential for diagnosis, before kidney damage sets in. Prompt hydration and renal monitoring are then critical to prevent acute kidney injury. They offer the case as a warning for teams planning long cases in patients with obesity.
pmc-13619069:
Juhyeon Kim and five colleagues present a modeling study of a two-species Clostridium culture grown under continuous perfusion. Their problem is that standard fermentation readings show total biomass and activity, yet they cannot reveal how many cells are active and how many have gone dormant. The work tries to recover those hidden states from data that a lab can actually measure.

Inside, a structured reconstruction first splits biomass into active and dormant parts, then a sparse method for nonlinear dynamics picks out the main reaction terms. The fitted terms cover organic acid turnover, solvent formation, and conversion of acetone to isopropanol. The authors link the patterns to acid-related state changes and stepwise exchange of products between species, and they present the approach as a clearer way to read partly observed cultures.
pmc-13620269:
Seungme Kang and six colleagues built one nanomaterial device that serves two security jobs at once: proving its own identity and generating truly random numbers. Physically unclonable functions give each chip a fingerprint from manufacturing randomness, while random number generators harvest live noise. Their platform uses mixed zinc gallate nanoclusters whose random sizes vary from spot to spot and whose electrical noise flickers over time.

The spatial variation yields device signatures through work function, capacitance, and impedance readings that differ by position. The time variation yields bitstreams that passed every reported national randomness test across twenty devices. As a demonstration, the team fed measured current traces into an image generator as a 512-part latent code, producing varied, unpredictable animal pictures. The authors present the pairing as a cheaper route to hardware security built into the material itself.
pmc-13622069:
Isabel Straw leads a systematic review of how hospital cyberattacks harm patients, a risk that has shifted from stealing data toward blocking care itself. The review gathers case studies from around the world and adds accounts posted by patients and staff on social media. Its aim is to name who gets hurt, and through which failures.

Fifty-nine studies met the rules, and together with the online accounts they yielded 316 recorded harms. Two groups stood out: patients needing minutes-fast care, such as stroke and heart attack cases, and patients who depend on digital systems yet can decline quickly, such as cancer and diabetes patients. Broken scanners, prescribing software, and network links each caused distinct injuries, including foetal deaths tied to failed monitoring. Social media revealed extra failures, from locked doors to dead ward alarms. The authors release their harm catalogue openly for emergency planners.
pmc-13623569:
Peng and co-authors tell of a vast bleed cyst in a babe of eight months. Such cysts are rare soft growths near the third brain room. Kid cysts are more rare, and vast bleed ones in babes most rare. The boy came in with one day of signs at the ward. His soft skull spot bulged, he spewed more than once, and he dulled. Brain scans showed a vast cyst mass in the mid wall zone.

That mass ran to the front third room, near 38 by 23 by 35 mm. Marks on scans showed a mild bright cyst with a clot bit. A fluid tier sat in the cyst in the scan reads. Top brain rooms swelled, with wet in the walls by them. That tale marks a sharp block of brain fluid flow. Fast cut work let off the cyst and its blood.
pmc-13626369:
Emmanuel Oloche Otukpa and colleagues look back on twenty years of co-creation at the African Population and Health Research Center, a Nairobi institute. Co-creation, people shaping research together rather than being studied, is praised across global health yet patchily done. The authors score their own practice on four dimensions, from shared agenda setting to community ownership, across six cases spanning evidence work, policy talks, training, and rights advocacy.

The honest verdict splits. Knowledge was genuinely made together, and agendas were shared in four of six cases, yet money was shared in none, and community leadership flowered only in rights work. Co-creation broke down at the hand-offs between research, policy, and advocacy, moments nobody designed or recorded. The paper closes with practical fixes for governance, funding, and those fragile transitions.
pmc-13626769:
Seunghoon Lee and co-authors unravel a one-sided lung artery blockage in a man with weakened immunity. The 62-year-old had myelodysplastic syndrome, a marrow disorder, and was on immune-suppressing therapy when his right lung clouded over with low white cell counts. Germ hunts and a small biopsy found nothing, and broad antimicrobials failed. Scans showed worsening consolidation, fluid, and rising pressure signs. A contrast scan finally exposed a filling defect within the right lung artery.

Dedicated angiography confirmed the lone obstruction, and clot-busting care did not clear it, raising fears of chronic clot disease or cancer. Surgery to strip the artery lining found an old, organizing septic clot instead. Weeks later bleeding into damaged lung forced removal of a wedge of tissue. Rare infected clots, the case warns, can mimic pneumonia for months.
pmc-13627769:
Jong-Rok Jeon and colleagues turn a plant compound into a smarter fertilizer by fusing it into soil minerals. Plants leak polyphenols under stress, and tannic acid, the test case here, glues itself to metals and loosens crystal order. The team co-precipitated tannic acid with two fertilizer minerals, calcium phosphate and struvite, cutting their crystallinity by up to nearly half and loading them with the acid itself.

The loosened minerals released nutrients faster and handed the polyphenol to the soil alongside. In pot trials, crops grew up to two and a half times the biomass, helped by richer available nutrients, a direct growth nudge from the acid, and a friendlier root microbe community. Designing minerals that plants themselves would recognize, the authors suggest, beats simply piling on more fertilizer.
pmc-13627869:
Bandar N Hamadneh leads a team stitching coffee compounds onto milk peptides with help from an apple enzyme. Chlorogenic acids dominate green coffee's phenolics, and tying such plant compounds to milk proteins could build new functional food ingredients. The team profiled coffee and apple phenolics, crowned the Braeburn apple for its strong polyphenol oxidase, the browning enzyme, and tried both enzyme-led and alkaline baths to join the parts.

Both routes bound phenolics to the two milk peptides, with the alkaline bath binding most. The enzyme route clearly converted coffee phenolics too, yet the authors flag honest limits: without a heat-killed enzyme control, the enzyme's exact share and the bond's nature stay unproven. The work sketches a natural biocatalyst route that food scientists can now tighten.
pmc-13628569:
Dominic Seißenschmidt and three colleagues designed small drug conjugates that carry a highly potent toxin to tumours displaying a marker called integrin alpha-v beta-3, published in 2026. Each conjugate joins a targeting piece modelled on the RGD peptide pattern to cryptophycin, a cell-killing compound too toxic to use on its own.

The connector between the parts is built to be cut by neutrophil elastase, an enzyme active around tumours, so the payload releases outside the target cells. The conjugates stayed stable in human plasma, kept their grip on the integrin, and once cut loose, the freed toxin killed cancer cells at extremely low concentrations. Carefully built control versions confirmed that both targeting and the correct linker geometry are essential.
pmc-13629069:
Nina Elisabeth Klevanger and three colleagues asked patients and physiotherapists in Norway about an AI advice tool. The tool supports choices in muscle and joint care. Their 2026 study drew on talks with eleven patients and ten physiotherapists who had used it. The system matches each patient to similar past successes. It then suggests treatment.

Both groups liked how the tool drew a full picture of a patient's health. Therapists said its tips often matched their own reasoning. That lent them authority. Drawbacks surfaced too. Extra health problems sometimes unsettled patients. Some tips missed the mark. The sheer volume of facts could crowd out true joint choice. The authors argue such tools reshape the therapist's role. The therapist becomes a mediator between patient and machine.
pmc-13632669:
Jiahua Zhou and colleagues built a fast alloy testing rig in 2026. Multi-metal mixes offer wide scope for tuning catalysts. Searching their mix space needs fast synthesis and testing. The rig uses a scanning flow cell. It deposits alloy samples by electricity from solution. It tests catalytic activity right after making each sample. It also watches metals dissolve during use, live. The team explored a gold, palladium, and platinum mix space. Dozens of samples mapped that three-way space.

A learning algorithm guided the search on its own. It chose later samples based on earlier results. Oxygen reaction activity changed smoothly with the mix. More gold steadily lowered that activity. Stability moved the other way, rising with gold. That trade-off shaped the best compromise mixes. The authors present the rig as autonomous materials exploration. It joins making, testing, and durability checks in one loop.
pmc-13634169:
Juliana Fong published an ecological study in twenty twenty-six on whether living near parks tracks with emergency department visits for asthma and heart attacks in Los Angeles County. Parks are promoted as health resources, yet neighborhoods with poor access often also suffer pollution and poverty. The study covered two thousand three hundred five census tracts with complete data.

Park proximity was measured as road distance from each tract's population center to its three nearest recreational spaces. Visit rates came from state environmental health data, adjusted for fine particles, ozone, and poverty. A straight-line distance version checked robustness, and spatial models tested whether patterns were just neighborhood clustering. The design isolates greenery's signal from its usual companions.
pmc-13635169:
Magnus Ross and six colleagues forecast patients' vital signs to time the switch from drip to pill antibiotics, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. To switch early shortens stays in hospital. It also cuts catheter infections in the ward. Yet one in five patients in England stays on intravenous antibiotics despite qualifying to switch.

Their system models vital sign trajectories probabilistically, with neural processes at its core. Switch readiness is judged by comparing forecasts against clinical guidelines. It is not judged by copying the habits of past doctors. Patients are ranked by review priority for the ward team. Validation used American intensive care data for the tests. It also used the records of a British hospital group. The system brought up several times more relevant candidates than baseline approaches. Guideline-based forecasting also adapts as guidelines change. It does so with no retraining of the model at all.
pmc-13635769:
Joseph Keenan wrote this methods paper on studying lived experience across time rather than in one snapshot. The approach, longitudinal interpretative phenomenological analysis, follows how people make sense of experience as months and years pass. Health researchers use it increasingly, yet the design choices are thorny. Keenan walks through five areas that demand care. They include handling the method's flexibility, weaving in creative techniques, keeping participants from dropping out, sustaining ethical practice over long projects, and tracking personal and group paths through piles of material.

The paper lays out a flexible set of analysis stages others can adapt. A worked example follows people in long-term recovery from substance use, showing how sense-making trajectories become visible only across repeated interviews. Keenan closes with a balanced account of strengths and limits. The method rewards patience with a moving picture, at the cost of heavy data and long researcher involvement.
pmc-13637069:
Irene Castellino and three colleagues published this 2026 review of small molecules that nudge the body's daily clock by blocking kinases. The circadian clock runs a near twenty-four-hour loop in almost every cell, and chemical tags added by kinases set its pace. When the clock slips, sleep, mood, metabolism, and even cancer risk can follow. Blocking the right kinase can lengthen, shorten, or reset the rhythm, which makes these enzymes tempting drug targets.

The review surveys the current crop of inhibitors, target by target. Many compounds shift the clock neatly in cell dishes. Far fewer keep working in living animals, and that gap between dish and body is the review's central complaint. The authors map which targets look most promising and where existing molecules fall short. Their guide aims future chemistry at compounds proven in whole organisms, since only those can become treatments for clock-related disorders.
pmc-13637269:
Adeolu J Alabi and Olufunmilayo I Fawole published this 2026 scoping review of period poverty among schoolgirls in rural Africa. Period poverty means lacking sanitary products, clean water, private toilets, and honest menstrual education all at once. The pair searched three databases for studies from 2015 to 2025 on girls attending school in rural communities. Twenty-one studies from six countries qualified, most of them counting surveys, with Kenya contributing the largest share.

Period poverty proved common across the settings. Girls reported body odor worries, skin burns, headaches, exhaustion, and urinary or genital symptoms. Fear, shame, and stress shadowed their school days. The reviewers also tie the deprivation to sexual exploitation risk, missed classes, weaker grades, and dropping out. They call for combined action: free or subsidized products, toilets designed with girls in mind, and menstrual education that includes boys. Anything less, they argue, leaves the health burden in place.
pmc-13644369:
Capucine Le Cam Ligier and six colleagues present a 2026 study of a dim mutant of the glowing marine bacterium Photobacterium kishitanii. Many luminous relatives control light by cell density, but this species glows regardless, hinting at other regulators.

The stable low-light mutant, named DimLum, showed sharply reduced activity of the light-producing gene cluster. Genome sequencing found a twenty-letter deletion in a gene called tfoX that shortens its protein. Restoring the healthy gene brought back both gene activity and glow. A small set of other genes also shifted. The authors identify TfoX as a supporting part of the light control network.
pmc-13645769:
Abeer Ismail, Aya Abu Aqab, and Dalal Iriqat write a perspective piece arguing that decolonizing global health must reach the knowledge systems behind it, not only its institutions. They focus on who gets to define valid knowledge, produce evidence, and set guidelines. Their examples include authorship patterns in research papers and a World Health Organization vaccine technology program in South Africa. The piece draws on decolonial theory rather than new data.

The authors contend that colonial patterns survive in how studies are credited, how guidelines are written, and how technology moves between countries. Knowledge from wealthy northern institutions is still treated as the universal standard, while local knowledge is pushed aside. They call this layer epistemic governance and argue it shapes funding and decisions throughout the field. Their closing sections outline routes toward fairer knowledge sharing, plus the obstacles such change would face.
pmc-13646069:
Alexandra Epp and seven colleagues measure how often a protein called HLA-G appears across solid tumors, since it can shut down immune attack and is a target for new cancer drugs. The team combined a protein-staining test on 252 patient tumors with gene data from early drug trials. A therapy now in testing pairs this target with a T cell activator. Rates and patterns differed sharply by cancer type.

About six in ten tumors tested positive, with the highest shares in ovarian, lung, kidney, and pancreatic cancers. Levels were mostly low to moderate and patchy within tumors. In melanoma, gene activity ran high while protein stayed undetectable, which warns that gene tests alone can mislead. Screening for the drug trial found an even higher positive rate. The authors argue that treatment selection for this target should rest on protein testing, not gene readings.
pmc-13646169:
Ihssan S Masad and three colleagues simulate a privacy-protecting learning system for connected medical devices, such as heart monitors that classify signals and watch patients around the clock. Their design trains models across devices without gathering raw data in one place. Noise is added to each device's update for privacy, and a trust layer scores devices and screens out odd updates. The work is a simulation of the learning and policy layers only.

Four setups were compared on a heart signal task: central training, plain federated learning, private federated learning, and the full zero-trust version. The zero-trust setup posted the strongest scores in the simulation. The authors are explicit about scope: the results show feasibility inside the simulation and do not prove clinical value, full privacy accounting, or security against strong attacks. The paper gives device makers a blueprint with honest limits attached.
pmc-13646669:
Ekkachai Khwanbua and colleagues grew maize under today's air and under richer carbon dioxide air to test how future climates change crop disease. They challenged the plants with six germs: a bacterium, a virus, three fungi, and a water mould.

Under richer carbon dioxide, maize grew more prone to the mosaic virus, as if its antiviral defences had weakened. The same air made plants less prone to the bacterium and to two of the fungi, while two germs showed no change. The bacterium's weaker attack paired with stronger standing immune responses in the leaves. Khwanbua warns that climate change will not shift all crop diseases one way, so each germ needs its own study.
pmc-13647569:
Yanan Li and three colleagues review a proposed chain linking oxidative stress with failing peacekeeper cells in autoimmune lung scarring. The disease group, lung disease tied to systemic autoimmune rheumatic conditions, kills through progressive fibrosis. Regulatory T cells normally suppress excess inflammation, and their master switch is sensitive to the cell's redox state. The review gathers evidence that oxidative stress bends that switch, disrupts a key growth signal, and stirs the surrounding inflammation.

Those failures may feed each other in a self-reinforcing cycle that wakes aggressive T cells, multiplies scar-building cells, and unbalances repair. The authors are frank that most mechanism evidence comes from animal models or neighboring diseases, not from these patients directly. They offer the framework as a guide for targeted studies and for therapies that might restore tolerance. The review's value is the chain itself, laid out link by link for testing.
pmc-13648269:
Rosa Kim and three colleagues test a more realistic way to judge chemical harm to plant life, using whole communities grown from soil seed banks rather than single test species. Traditional toxicity tests miss interactions between species, so the team rebuilt plant assemblages from field soil, with twenty-six species and hundreds of individual plants.

Exposed to cadmium, the communities tolerated far higher levels than conventional models predicted before diversity dropped, suggesting current safety thresholds carry a wide protective margin. Biomass fell at high doses, yet dominant species endured while sensitive ones were filtered out, and surviving plants linked together more strongly. The authors offer the approach as a platform for ecological risk assessment.
pmc-13648769:
Nasri G. Fatih and seven colleagues use the Million Women Study to measure dementia risk after clinically recognised alcohol use disorder, following more than a million British women for over twenty years. Alcohol problems are tied to dementia, but how risk varies by subtype, age, and time since diagnosis was poorly charted.

Women with a hospital record of alcohol use disorder were matched to up to five controls. Their dementia risk was nearly four times higher overall, and more than ten times higher for diagnoses before age seventy, with vascular and mixed dementia especially elevated. Risk stayed raised even fifteen years later, and self-reported drinking quantity explained far less. The authors urge priority prevention for this group.
pmc-13649469:
Feifei Chen and three colleagues studied how higher social insurance costs change hiring at Chinese listed firms. Such payments, which cover health, injury, and pension cover, form a fixed slice of labour cost. The team used firm data from 2007 to 2019 and a 2011 social insurance law as a natural test of cause.

When payments rose, firms cut staff size in a clear way. Rather than trim wages, most firms shed jobs to ease the load. Three paths drove the cuts: tighter cash flow, smaller output, and more spending on machines. The harm hit hardest at firms with weak access to funds and at firms that already employed many people.
