The authors urge balance between worker cover and stable jobs.
pmc-13649969:
Fan Bu and one colleague ask how university students turn help from generative AI into real learning gains. Their study builds a model with four linked parts. The parts are support from the learning setting, trust matched to what the tool can actually do, joint regulation of the work, and gains students feel they can carry to new tasks.

Interviews with students came first and shaped a 22-item survey, which was then given to 642 students and tested with factor analysis and structural modeling. Support in the setting predicted both well-judged trust and joint regulation, while joint regulation showed the strongest link to perceived gains. Support alone showed no direct link, so the benefit ran through trust and active regulation rather than frequent use.
pmc-13650469:
Emmanuel Ifeanyi Obeagu reviews blood transfusion care for sickle cell disease in Africa, where most of the world's cases occur and where safe blood is often scarce. Transfusion is essential for strokes, severe complications, and surgery in this inherited red-cell disorder, yet the system around it fails patients in many linked ways.

Shortages combine with infection risk, immune reactions against donor cells, almost no antigen matching, overload of iron from repeated transfusions, and scattered records. The review's central point is that available blood is not the same as compatible blood for a patient whose immune system has already reacted. Proposed fixes include steady voluntary donor recruitment, broader antigen profiling with risk-based matching, selective gene testing, lifelong transfusion records, antibody registries, and rare-donor networks. The goal is a shift from emergency, episode-by-episode supply to a durable lifelong system.
pmc-13650769:
Rebecca E Ginesi and five colleagues show that 3D printing can align the molecules inside a water-based organic electronic material, replacing energy-hungry alignment tricks that clash with water processing. Their ink blends a dye-like molecule that self-assembles into fibers with a flexible polymer, forming a hydrogel that flows through a printer nozzle.

The squeezing flow of extrusion lines the fibers up, and drying locks the alignment into a bendable film that still conducts. Bending the film to a gentle curve boosted its light-driven current response two and a half times over the flat state. After a thousand bending cycles the films kept their structure and retained half of their light response. The authors present printing itself as the alignment tool, opening a simple route to wearable sensors whose electrical behavior answers to mechanical movement.
pmc-13650969:
Shitanshu Malhotra and five colleagues survey oral health and drug use among people living homeless on the streets of Lucknow, India. In that group, poor diet, irregular hygiene, exclusion, and scarce dental care meet high substance use. The interaction between the two burdens had rarely been measured in lower-income settings.

Three hundred people were examined through outreach sampling, with tooth decay experience, plaque, and gum scores recorded and mouth lesions mapped. Over four fifths reported drug use including tobacco, and well over half reported alcohol use, much of it hazardous. Untreated decay ran higher alongside substance use, and mouth lesions were notably more common among opioid users than non-users. Tobacco tracked with gum disease, and hazardous drinking with worse plaque control, while frequent toothbrushing showed a protective gradient. The authors call the combined burden a case for integrated outreach services.
pmc-13670269:
Xing Dai and colleagues show a plant polysaccharide slows stem cell ageing in rats. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses bone marrow stem cells. Cell ageing drives osteoporosis progression in ageing skeletons. The sugar from Polygonatum, a traditional herb, may counter that ageing.

A chemical stressor aged the stem cells in dishes. The polysaccharide then treated the aged cells. Ageing stains and bone-versus-fat fate tests tracked recovery. A self-eating pathway that destroys iron stores was the mechanism. Blocking that pathway reduced iron-driven cell damage. Powerhouse function in treated cells also improved. The herb compound may protect bone-forming capacity in ageing.
pmc-13685169:
Clement Medrinal and colleagues pooled patient-level data from several intensive care cohorts to ask when breathing muscle tests are worth doing before removing a breathing tube. Such bedside tests are often proposed for everyone, yet their record at predicting failed tube removal is mixed. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team gathered adults who had been on invasive ventilation. Had at least one strength measure, such as strongest breath in, breath out, cough peak, or a limb strength sum. Failure meant reinsertion of the tube or death within two days.

About one in six patients failed. A weak breath-in score alone showed only a borderline link with failure in the whole group. Among patients ventilated more than five days, though, weak breath-in strength tracked failure clearly after adjustment. Other tests showed no clear adjusted link. The authors support targeted, not routine, testing.
pmc-4267669:
Brinkman, Chen, Amendola, and their co-authors described a simple way in 2014 to measure genome editing results. Editing methods can work well or weakly depending on the target sequence, and the mix of mutations varies too. Labs needed a quick assay to measure what an edit actually did.

Their method, called TIDE, reads the mixed signal in a normal sequence trace and breaks it into its parts. From that breakdown, users can estimate how many cells carry each induced mutation. No special equipment beyond standard sequencing is needed. A cheap, fast check like this helps labs tune editing conditions before moving to costly follow-up work.
pmc-4489269:
Bailey, Johnson, Grant, and their co-authors presented the MEME Suite in 2015. The suite gathers web tools for finding and describing motifs in proteins, DNA, and RNA. A motif is a short pattern that recurs because it carries a biological function.

Finding and describing motifs matters for understanding molecular interactions in the cell. Proteins bind DNA at motif sites, and those sites switch genes on and off. The suite lets users discover motifs in their own data and scan sequences for known ones. It has become a standard resource for labs studying gene regulation across many species.
pmc-4967469:
Iorio, Knijnenburg, Vis, and their team mapped pharmacogenomic interactions in cancer in 2016. Systematic studies of cancer genomes had given unprecedented insight into the molecular nature of cancer. Using that knowledge to guide therapy in the clinic, however, remained challenging.

The team studied how cancer-driven alterations, found across many tumor types, change a cell's response to drugs. They combined genome data with large drug screens in cancer cell lines. The resulting landscape shows which mutations make a tumor sensitive or resistant to specific compounds. Such maps help oncologists match patients to drugs and help researchers design smarter trials.
pmc-5215069:
The Japanese Gastric Cancer Association issued its gastric cancer treatment guidelines in 2014, version four of the document. Gastric cancer, cancer of the stomach, is a major cause of death in Japan, and Japanese specialists have long set standards for its care. National guidelines align surgeons and oncologists on best practice.

A treatment guideline of this kind sets out how the disease should be staged, operated on, and treated with drugs at each stage. It distills trial evidence and expert consensus into clear rules for daily practice. Version updates matter because surgery methods and drug regimens improve over time. Hospitals across Japan base stomach cancer care on this document.
pmc-5431369:
Cappello, Marchetti, Parlanti, and their colleagues characterized the lower motor system in 2016 in a mouse model of Krabbe disease. Krabbe disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by lack of a key enzyme's activity. A toxic compound then accumulates widely in neuronal, myelinating, and endothelial cells.

Twitcher mice are widely used as experimental models of this disease. The team used ultrastructural methods, imaging at very fine scale, to describe damage in the lower motor system of these mice. Motor pathways matter because weakness is a core burden of the disease. Detailed maps of cell damage help judge whether new therapies truly protect the nervous system.
pmc-5514969:
Mokhtari, Homayouni, Baluch, and their co-authors reviewed combination therapy in cancer in 2017. Combination therapy treats cancer with two or more drugs at once, and it is a cornerstone of modern care. Pairing drugs is now standard in many regimens rather than an exception.

Using drugs together works better than relying on one drug alone. Combinations target key pathways in a synergistic way, hitting the tumor at several points at once. They can also slow resistance, since a cancer must evade several drugs simultaneously. The review covers the rationale, main strategies, and challenges such as added side effects. It guides clinicians who must design regimens for hard-to-treat cancers.
pmc-553969:
Slater and Birney wrote in 2005 on faster ways to compare biological sequences. Exact alignment methods are sound but slow. Fast shortcut methods run quickly, yet they are hard to build well and their shortcuts are hard to tune by hand.

The authors present a method that bounds a sparse form of the exact calculation, so a quick run stays close to the exact answer. It also lets a program build its own shortcut rules for a given task, rather than rely on rules set by hand. Fast, close alignment is the base of genome annotation and database search. The work fed into tools that compare genes across species at genome scale.
pmc-5573769:
The GBD 2015 Chronic Respiratory Disease Collaborators reported in 2017 on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma worldwide. These two chronic respiratory diseases are common, with a heterogeneous distribution across the world. The team presents methods and estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2015 study.

They estimate deaths, prevalence, and disability measures for both diseases from 1990 to 2015. Smoking, air pollution, and occupational dust drive much of the obstructive lung disease burden. Asthma adds a large burden of years lived with disability, including in children. Comparable global figures help countries plan inhaler access, tobacco control, and clean air policy.
pmc-5635569:
Masnoon, Shakib, Kalisch-Ellett, and their team reviewed how polypharmacy is defined in 2017. Older people often live with several long-term health problems at once. That brings the use of many medicines at the same time, a state called polypharmacy.

For all its wide use, the term had no agreed definition. The team ran a systematic review to find and sum up the definitions used in past work. Some counts set a threshold number of drugs; others judge whether each drug is truly needed. A shared term would let studies of risk and benefit be compared. It is a first step to safer prescribing for older adults on long drug lists.
pmc-6988269:
Victor Corman, Olfert Landt, Marco Kaiser, and coauthors published a PCR test for the new coronavirus in early 2020. The outbreak was growing while no virus isolates were available to labs. Public health teams needed a test built from the genome sequence alone.

The authors designed and validated a real-time RT-PCR assay and shared the protocol openly. It detects the new virus while excluding close relatives like the SARS virus. Labs worldwide adopted the protocol within days. The paper became a foundation stone of the global testing response in the pandemic's first months.
pmc-7158569:
Adam Kucharski, Timothy Russell, Charlie Diamond, and coauthors modeled early COVID-19 transmission in 2020. By early March the virus had caused tens of thousands of confirmed cases. Judging control options required a clear read on how it spreads.

Combining case reports from China and international travelers, the team estimated the reproduction number and its fall as controls bit. They also weighed under-reporting and the role of travel screening. Results suggested transmission could be curbed where measures were strong. The study informed the first wave of national response plans. Sensitivity checks show the main conclusions hold under a range of plausible reporting rates.
pmc-7360769:
Huang Lin and Shyamal Das Peddada tackled a stubborn methods problem in 2020: how to compare microbe levels fairly between samples. Microbiome studies count which microbes appear in a sample, but each sample captures only a fraction of the community, and that fraction differs from sample to sample. The authors show that this uneven sampling quietly biases the usual ways of judging which microbes rise or fall.

They define the sampling fraction clearly and build a statistical method that corrects for it, so comparisons reflect biology rather than lab handling. They test the approach on data where ordinary methods give misleading answers. For a field that guides thinking on diet, disease, and treatment, a correction like this protects conclusions drawn from thousands of studies.
pmc-7615769:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration returned in 2024 with a larger pooling of studies on body weight, covering children, teenagers, and adults. This analysis combined more than thirty-six hundred representative studies with well over two hundred million participants. It tracks underweight and obesity together, and how each changed from 1990 to 2022 across the world's countries.

Reading the two conditions side by side shows the double burden many countries now face, thinness and obesity rising within the same borders. The authors report their findings country by country, so progress and setbacks are both visible. Public health teams use this kind of map to see where food policy is working and where both hunger and excess remain unaddressed.
pmc-7857469:
Gabrielle Gilmer and two colleagues test whether instability in the lumbopelvic and hip region disrupts the throwing motion in softball players. Fifty athletes from college, high school, and youth levels threw overhead from a set distance, then performed single-leg squats while an electromagnetic system recorded their movement. Players whose knee collapsed inward past a set angle during the squat counted as unstable.

Comparisons looked for differences in segmental sequencing, the order in which body parts reach peak speed, and in maximum velocities during the throw. None appeared, whether athletes were compared within their age level or pooled together. A null result still guides practice: screening with the squat, at least as used here. Does not sort throwers by how their body chain fires, so coaches should not bench or retrain players on that basis alone.
pmc-8268869:
Alyssa Boutilier and Sherine Elsawa reviewed in 2021 the shifting states of macrophages, the immune cells that patrol tissues and gather inside tumors. These cells are often described as leaning toward one of two poles. One pole attacks tumors, while the other, typical of tumor-associated macrophages, helps cancers grow, spread, and resist treatment.

The authors explain how the tumor surroundings push macrophages toward the helpful pole, and how that state can change rather than stay fixed. They also survey efforts to reprogram the cells or block the signals that corrupt them. The review usefully complicates the simple two camp picture, showing a spectrum that treatments will need to reckon with.
poems-pg1469:
Francis Thompson's Poems appear in the Burns and Oates edition of September 1909, two years after his early death. Thompson wrote in poverty and opium addiction, rescued by the editor Wilfrid Meynell and his wife Alice, to whom this book is dedicated. The contents arrange his work in three groups: love poems gathered as Love in Dian's Lap, miscellaneous poems, and poems on children.

One title outweighs the rest: the Hound of Heaven. His great ode of a soul fleeing God down the nights and down the days, only to find the pursuer is love. Other pieces include a Fallen Yew, Dream-Tryst, Daisy, and poems to his godchild. Thompson's dense, jeweled style divided readers then and now, but the Hound has never gone out of print. This edition presents the whole poet around it, as his rescuers wished him kept.
randolph-love-and-its-hidden-history-186:
Paschal Beverly Randolph wrote of love as a force of fate in Love and Its Hidden History, out in 1869. He held that love binds souls by laws as strict as those of the stars. A wrong bond can blight a life. A right one can lift both souls to health and sight.

Rules, tales, and warns fill the book. It is the hands-on mate to his later Eulis! Fans who sought his lore in full read the pair as one. The book shows his warm, grave voice at its best. Randolph wed twice and knew love's joys and griefs at first hand. That past gives his grave rules a warmth texts of law lack.
randolph-pre-adamite-man-1869:
Paschal Beverly Randolph claimed man is far more old than the Good Book says in Pre-Adamite Man, out in 1869. Bands of men, he held, lived and built on earth long ere Adam. He draws on stone tools, old bones, and tales from the East to make his bold case for deep time.

The claim was hot stuff in his day. Church men balked, while men of the dig cheered parts of it. Randolph gives the claim an occult spin all his own. The book is his word in a great row of his age. Stone finds in his day had just begun to shake old views. Randolph seized on them fast to back his claim of man's deep age.
reid-inquiry-human-mind-1769:
Thomas Reid, a Scottish professor, published An Inquiry into the Human Mind in 1764. The edition of 1769 is the text here, carrying his principles of common sense. Reid wrote against the ideal theory, the view that the mind knows only its own ideas. David Hume had drawn bleak results from that view, and Reid aimed to answer him at the root.

Reid argues that belief in an outer world, and in other minds, rests on common sense built into human nature. Perception, on his account, reaches the world itself, not a screen of images. The Inquiry founded the Scottish common-sense school of philosophy. Its plain, sturdy method still appeals to readers tired of elegant doubt.
salmon-conic-sections-1869:
George Salmon, an Irish scholar, wrote his Treatise on Conic Sections as a textbook of analytic geometry. The 1869 edition was the standard Victorian version, used by students for decades. Salmon later became a noted churchman, but math made his name.

The book studies the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola through algebra. Salmon shows how one set of equations can describe all three curves and their shared traits. Clear proofs and many worked cases made it a model textbook. Generations of students learned the geometry of cones and orbits from Salmon's orderly pages. Salmon treats both the pure curves and their use in the wider geometry course.
sargent-planchette-1869:
Epes Sargent took up arms for the faith in Planchette, his book of 1869. Its flip name calls science to scorn: The Despair of Science. The planchette was a small board on wheels that spelled words in the dark room. Sargent, a news man, holds that its words mock the cold creed that all is mere stuff and force.

He prints cases, talks with the dead, and sharp words for his foes. His aim is to show the lab has no key for these doors. The book is the faith's best fight back of its age in his land.
secrets-reveal-d-or-an-open-entrance-to-:
An English writer hiding under the name Eirenaeus Philaletha published this alchemy treatise in 1669. The title page boasts that the book holds the greatest treasure in the art of chymistry, never yet so plainly shown. The writer claims he reached the famed stone of the philosophers at age twenty-three, by inner light and by reading.

Philaletha promises an open door into the shut palace of the King, a figure for the hidden heart of the art. Readers of early science meet strong claims, veiled terms, and bold hope. The work shows how alchemy mixed craft skill, faith, and secrecy in print.
stowe-american-womans-home-1869:
Catharine Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe joined forces for The American Woman's Home in 1869. The full title calls it a guide to sound, thrifty, lovely, and Christian homes. The sisters dedicate the book to the women of America, in whose hands they say the republic's fate rests.

The introduction argues that women lack training for their duties and aims to raise home work in honor and pay. Chapters then cover house design, fresh air, cooking, cleaning, and the raising of children. Part handbook and part plea for respect, the manual treats homemaking as a skilled calling and shaped homes for years.
the-alchemists-1869:
The Alchemists, an essay of 1869 fronted by a line from Luther praising the upright art of alchemy, opens with a strange sign of old beliefs' long life. Some seventy years before, a Hermetic Society placed an advertisement in a German paper.

That notice, from 1796, called on all scattered votaries of alchemy to write in, in an age when France sat under the Directory and Bonaparte was conquering north Italy. Replies poured in from all grades of life: tailors and shoemakers, physicians, privy councillors, schoolmasters, watchmakers, apothecaries, and organists. All called themselves hands-on students of the occult science, keen for more light. Readers get a wry, rich sketch of alchemy's last believers and the art's long shadow over science.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Back Again to Paris, part of Adventures in the South in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows Arthur Machen's translation of the 1894 London edition, with chapters found by Arthur Symons. Chapter Thirteen opens at ten in the morning, with Casanova calling on Madame d'Urfe in Paris. She receives him with open arms. He explains that her hoped-for operation, by which she was to become a man, must wait.

The delay, he tells her, lasts until Querilinto, a chief of the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross, leaves the Inquisition's dungeons at Lisbon. Casanova plans an Augsburg mission, under cover of Portuguese business, to free the adept. He asks for a letter of credit and presents of watches and snuff-boxes to win over the profane. Madame d'Urfe gladly supplies everything, doubting the congress will even meet. Readers watch Casanova's occult theater run on a rich believer's credit.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 280 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, October 27, 1827, devotes its thirteenth Shakespeare illustration to Elsinore, seen from Hamlet's garden. A delighted visitor's account leads the piece. The lapse of ages and the poet's fables, he says, vanished in the reality of Shakespeare's painting. He followed Hamlet everywhere on that consecrated ground: the platform's deep shadows, the royal Dane's grey ghost, Polonius killed in the queen's closet.

Modern Elsinore disappoints the same visitor as ill-built and red, without spire or palace. About a mile from town lies the place called Hamlet's garden, where tradition sets the Danish palace. From its hill the sketch shows Kronberg castle to the left, the Cattegat rolling at its feet, and the Swedish coast opposite. Four hundred merchant ships lay at anchor when the drawing was made.

Volume 19, No. 547, dated May 19, 1832, pictures Wilton Castle above the River Wye. The ivy-covered ruins stand opposite Ross, on the western bank. For several centuries the castle belonged to the Greys of the south, who took their first title from it and gained it in the time of Edward I.

Its position on the old border between England and Wales gives the history its frame. The district had once been held by the Silures, who resisted the Romans under Caractacus alongside their northern neighbours. Wilton's own ruin came much later. Royalist governors of Hereford ordered it burned to bare walls under Charles I, while its owner, Sir J. Brydges, was away.
the-practical-phrenologist-and-recorder-: O. S. Fowler's The Practical Phrenologist is a recorder and delineator of character and talents, built on a compendium of phreno-organic science. Fowler entered the copyright at Boston in 1869 and published the book himself on Tremont Street. The title page, though worn and hard to read in places, names him as a lecturer and former editor of the American Phrenological Journal. It also lists his earlier works on phrenology, physiology, memory, and matrimony. Nothing past the title page is shown here.
tob-0169:
Joseph Andrew Blackwell's translation presents the Elder Eddas, the old Norse poems associated with Saemund Sigfusson, alongside material from the Younger Edda of Snorri Sturluson. Gods and heroes speak in their own stark verse. Odin's gallows-wisdom in the Hávamál, the seeress's prophecy of Ragnarök, and the lays of Sigurd stand among the highlights.

These poems, preserved in Icelandic manuscripts, are the wellspring of Norse mythology: creation from a giant's body, the world tree, and the gods' foreknown doom at the twilight. Blackwell's version keeps their power in older English dress. Readers who know Norse myth only through retellings will find the originals stranger, funnier, and more fatalistic.
tob-10469:
Aquinas turns from God to human life in Part I-II of the Summa, the first half of its second part. The subject is how people act and why. Happiness, the will, good and evil in actions, and the passions all come under his question-and-answer method.

Habits receive close attention: how repeated acts become virtues or vices, and what roles law and grace play in making a life good. Aquinas maps the moral life with an engineer's care, defining terms before judging cases. Readers meet the framework behind centuries of Catholic ethics, including ideas about natural law that later reached far beyond the church.
tob-10969:
The complete Douay-Rheims Bible joins the Old Testament translated at Douai in 1609 with the New Testament translated at Rheims in 1582, in Bishop Richard Challoner's eighteenth-century revision. Challoner modernized spelling and softened the most Latin-heavy phrasing, producing the text most later readers know. For three hundred years this was the English Bible of Catholics worldwide.

From Genesis to Revelation, the translation stays formal and Latinate, close to the Vulgate that stood behind it. Psalms and Gospels alike carry the wording generations of Catholics prayed from memory. Traditionalists still favor it, and readers comparing English Bibles will find its differences from the King James Version instructive.
un-ga-res-34-169:
General Assembly Resolution 34/169, adopted on December 17, 1979, set out a Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials. The first number marks the Assembly's thirty-fourth session, which fixes the year; catalog entries dating it to 1966 are in error. Every member state received the code with a request to write it into national law and police training.

Eight short articles tell officers to serve the public, guard human rights, and use force only when strictly needed. Torture and cruel treatment are banned outright, and officers must shield the health of people in custody. The code also bars corruption and orders respect for the law even in hard cases. It remains a basic yardstick for police conduct worldwide.
un-ga-res-a-69-69:
A world pact to ban the use of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/69, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text holds that the use of such arms is the gravest threat to the life of mankind. It recalls the 1996 ruling of the International Court of Justice on the law of nuclear threat and use. Some cuts by Russia and the United States are noted with care.

A shared, binding pact that bars the use or threat of nuclear arms, the Assembly argues, would help clear the nuclear threat away. It would set the stage for talks toward the full end of such arms. The vote keeps alive a long push, led by states with no nuclear arms of their own.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/69, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, returns to the proposed Convention on the Prohibition of the Use of Nuclear Weapons. It repeats the Assembly's request that the Conference on Disarmament begin negotiations on an international convention. The convention would prohibit the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons under any circumstances. The demand is a standing one. It is meant to move the legal ban on use from declaration toward treaty.
un-sc-res-1269: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 1269 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1999. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-1369:
UNMEE's mandate was rolled forward on 14 September 2001. The Council had the Secretary-General's report of 5 September before it. The Algiers Agreements of June and December 2000 held, and the Temporary Security Zone was working. The Boundary and Claims Commissions had been formed. Three days after the attacks on the United States, the Council kept its focus on the Horn.

The Council extended UNMEE to 15 March 2002, at the troop and military observer levels set by resolution 1320 (2000). Both parties had to work fully and swiftly with the mission and honor the Algiers texts to the letter. The Temporary Security Zone had to stay fully demilitarized. The Council stressed that UNMEE's end was tied to the Boundary Commission finishing its ruling on the border. The parties were urged to settle open issues, free prisoners, and shift spending from weapons to rebuilding their war-torn lands.
un-sc-res-1469:
Western Sahara's referendum mission needed another brief extension in March 2003. On 25 March 2003 the Security Council renewed MINURSO until 31 May 2003. The Secretary-General had proposed the short term in a letter that month. He owed the Council a report by 19 May. The Council recalled its call the summer before for a political solution.

The two-month renewal was among the shortest the mission received. It kept observers watching the ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front. It also kept the referendum machinery formally alive. The Council stayed seized of the matter. Within months it would back a full peace plan instead of the old referendum track.
un-sc-res-1569: Sudan received the Council's formal attention in Resolution 1569, adopted unanimously on 26 October 2004. The Council rarely meets away from its New York home. Darfur's war and the long north-south conflict both demanded focus. The Council decides to hold its meetings in Nairobi on 18 and 19 November 2004. The agenda is the Secretary-General's reports on Sudan. Members will also talk with the African Union and the regional bloc IGAD about peace work nearby. The written record of the Nairobi meetings will issue later in New York.
un-sc-res-1669:
Congo's election year drew troops from a neighbor mission in 2006. Burundi's operation, ONUB, was winding down after a successful transition. On 10 April 2006 the Security Council let the Secretary-General move some of its strength west. Up to one infantry battalion could redeploy to MONUC in the Congo. A military hospital and fifty military observers went with the package. The loan ran until 1 July 2006.

The Council praised Burundi's people for their peaceful transfer of power. It restated Burundi's sovereignty and unity. The redeployment could be renewed with fresh approval. It showed how missions could share scarce troops across a region. The Congo's first elections in decades were the prize at stake.
un-sc-res-169:
Katanga's secession was met with forceful orders on 24 November 1961. The Congo's parliament had been restored, and a central government formed on 2 August 1961. Katanga's provincial rulers, backed by foreign money and mercenaries, kept up their armed defiance. United Nations staff had suffered fresh violence. The Council restated the aim of one Congo, whole and independent.

The Council strongly deprecated Katanga's illegal secessionist acts and the armed attacks on United Nations forces. Such acts had to stop at once. The Secretary-General was authorized to take vigorous action, with the needed measure of force if it came to that. His task was to seize, hold, and expel every foreign military and advisory figure outside United Nations command, and all mercenaries. States were asked to stop arms and war material from reaching Katanga. No state was to back the secession by act or by silence.
un-sc-res-1769:
Adopting Resolution 1769 on 31 July 2007, the Council acted on Darfur. The war there had killed hundreds of thousands since 2003. A small African Union force could not stop the attacks on civilians. Sudan had at last agreed to a joint force with a mostly African character.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, called UNAMID. It is authorized for an initial twelve months. Up to 19,555 troops and 3,772 police may deploy. The force takes over from the African Union mission by the end of 2007. It may use force to guard civilians, aid workers, and itself, and to back the peace deal.
un-sc-res-1869:
Bosnia and Herzegovina gained a new international overseer in March 2009. On 25 March 2009 the Security Council welcomed Valentin Inzko as High Representative. The Steering Board of the Peace Implementation Council had named him on 13 March. He succeeded Miroslav Lajčák in the post. The Council paid tribute to the outgoing holder's work. The job flows from the Dayton Peace Agreement of 1995.

The Council restated the weight it gives the High Representative's role. He guides the civilian side of the peace deal. He coordinates the agencies helping the parties carry it out. He also holds final authority on how the civilian annex is read on the ground. The appointment kept that structure in place.
un-sc-res-2669:
Action on Myanmar came with Resolution 2669, adopted on 21 December 2022. The military had seized power in February 2021 and still held the elected leaders in detention. Violence spread across the country, and activists had been executed that July. Displacement and poverty climbed fast, while aid workers faced tight limits.

The Council demands an immediate end to all forms of violence. It urges the military to free all prisoners held without cause, naming the detained president and state counsellor. Full aid access must open for everyone in need. The text backs the ASEAN peace plan and its special envoy. It also calls for conditions that let Rohingya refugees return home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-269:
South Africa would not leave Namibia, and the Council hardened its line in 1969. Pretoria had spurned resolution 264, which called its presence there illegal. On 12 August 1969 the Council condemned that refusal. It also condemned South Africa's defiance of the United Nations. A report on the Secretary-General's talks fed the vote. Four members held back, among them France and Britain.

Keeping troops in Namibia, the Council ruled, is an act of force. It strikes at the standing of the United Nations itself. It breaks the land's wholeness and denies its people a say in their rule. The Council backed the right of Namibia's people to fight for freedom. South Africa stayed for twenty more years all the same.
un-sc-res-369: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 369 is catalogued here as dating from 1975. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-69:
Israel's bid for United Nations membership came before the Council in March 1949. On 4 March 1949 the Council judged the application on the Charter's terms. It decided that Israel is a peace-loving state. It also found Israel able and willing to carry out the Charter's duties. Those findings are the legal heart of the text. Few admission resolutions spell them out so fully.

On that basis the Council recommended Israel's admission to the General Assembly. The vote was nine to one, with one abstention. Egypt cast the no vote. Britain abstained. The Assembly admitted Israel that May. The decision gave the new state its seat while the first Arab-Israeli war was ending.
un-sc-res-869: UNPROFOR's mandate was extended by one day on 30 September 1993. The Council restated resolution 743 (1992) and later texts on the force. It repeated its resolve to guard the force's safety and freedom of movement in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, acting under Chapter VII to that end. The extension ran only to 1 October 1993. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. The one-day term was a bridge, holding the force in place while the Council weighed a longer renewal, which followed in resolution 871 (1993).
un-sc-res-969: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 969 is catalogued here under 1995. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1269, adopted unanimously on 19 October 1999, is the Council's general resolution on international terrorism, not tied to a single attack. Alarmed by the increase in terrorist acts worldwide, it unequivocally condemns all acts, methods and practices of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable. That holds whatever their motivation, wherever and by whomever they are committed.

The Council calls on all states to carry out the anti-terrorist conventions they belong to and to join the rest as a priority. It sets out practical steps. States should cooperate to prevent attacks and bring perpetrators to justice. They should block the preparation and financing of terrorism at home. They should deny terrorists safe haven through arrest, prosecution or extradition. They should check that asylum seekers have not taken part in terrorist acts. They should share information to prevent attacks.

Resolution 1369, adopted unanimously on 14 September 2001, keeps the UN mission between Ethiopia and Eritrea for another six months. Both countries had signed the Algiers peace agreements in December 2000, ending their border war. The mission, UNMEE, patrolled a temporary security zone between them while a boundary commission prepared its ruling.

The Council renewed UNMEE's mandate into March 2002. It reaffirmed both parties' duty to meet their obligations under humanitarian, human rights, and refugee law, and to keep UN and Red Cross personnel safe. Support for the Secretary-General's good offices and for the African Union's role ran through the text. The border ruling itself arrived the following spring.

Two months of patience for the Sahara file came from this text of 2003. On 25 March, the Council adopted Resolution 1469 without dissent. The vote mission, MINURSO, was still waiting for a political opening. Morocco and the Polisario Front stayed locked in place. The Secretary-General had written to propose a report date in May.

The text extends MINURSO's mandate to 31 May 2003. The Secretary-General must report on the state of play by 19 May. That date was his own proposal. The short stretch was a holding move, nothing more. A bigger call came that summer. In Resolution 1495, the Council backed the envoy's peace plan for the territory.

In November 2004 the Security Council packed its bags for Africa. Resolution 1569, adopted unanimously on 26 October 2004, moved two days of meetings to Nairobi, Kenya. The sessions would run on 18 and 19 November. Their agenda was Sudan, then gripped by civil war and the Darfur crisis.

Members planned to discuss Sudan with the African Union. The regional bloc IGAD would also take part. Other peace efforts in the region were on the list. One rule was waived for the trip: meeting records could be issued later in New York. The move showed how seriously the Council took Sudan's wars.

Troops moved from one African mission to a twin in 2006. Burundi had just held sound polls. Its UN force, ONUB, had men to spare. Congo, next door, faced strain with polls of its own near. The chief wrote on 30 March 2006 with a plan to share the load. Resolution 1669 passed on 10 April 2006.

The chief could shift a set force for a short span. At most, one battalion of foot troops would go. A field hospital would move as well. Up to fifty men to watch and report could join them. The loan ran to 1 July 2006. It drew on a grant first made in December 2005. Fresh terms for both forces would let the Council judge if the loan should live on.

The Congo crisis and the breakaway province of Katanga are the subject of Resolution 169, adopted on 24 November 1961. Congo's parliament had been restored and a central government formed that August. Katanga's provincial leaders, backed by outside resources and foreign mercenaries, still claimed their province was a sovereign nation, a claim the Council flatly rejected. UN staff had faced violence in the fighting.

The Council insists that the secessionist activity in Katanga stop at once. It authorizes the Secretary-General to take vigorous action, including force if needed, to seize, detain, and deport foreign military staff, advisers, and mercenaries not under UN command. It asks states to block arms supplies that could serve warlike ends and to deny transport for them. It declares full support for the Central Government and urges all member states to back it.

Darfur's hybrid AU-UN mission is created in Resolution 1769, adopted on 31 July 2007. Sudan had accepted the hybrid operation at the June 2007 Addis Ababa consultations, the Darfur Peace Agreement remained unimplemented, and attacks on civilians and aid workers plus widespread sexual violence continued. The African Union's AMIS was to fold into the new force.

The Council authorizes the AU/UN Hybrid Operation in Darfur, UNAMID, for twelve months, at up to 19,555 military personnel and 3,772 police plus nineteen formed police units. UNAMID must take over authority from AMIS no later than 31 December 2007, with UN-provided command and backstopping and a predominantly African character. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes UNAMID to protect its personnel and humanitarian workers, support Darfur Peace Agreement implementation, prevent armed attacks, and protect civilians. UNAMID must also monitor whether arms are present in Darfur in violation of Resolution 1556 (2004).

Bosnia still had a foreign overseer in 2009. The war there had ended almost fourteen years before. The peace deal was signed at Dayton. Under Resolution 1869, passed on 25 March 2009, the Council backed a change at the top. Valentin Inzko of Austria would be the new High Representative. He took over from Miroslav Lajcak.

The Council praised the work Lajcak had done. It stressed that the High Representative has the last word on the peace deal's civil side. It also noted a list of goals Bosnia still had to meet. Five goals and two terms stood in the way. Once met, the overseer's office could close. A European Union envoy would take its place.

Myanmar's crisis reaches the Council's agenda in Resolution 2669, adopted on 21 December 2022. The military's state of emergency of 1 February 2021, violence against civilians and infrastructure, the July 2022 execution of activists, and mass arbitrary detention had deepened humanitarian need and displacement. ASEAN's Five Point Consensus of April 2021 had seen limited implementation.

The Council demands an immediate end to all forms of violence across the country. It urges the military to release arbitrarily detained prisoners, naming the detained State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi and President Win Myint. It calls for implementation of ASEAN's Five Point Consensus, with the Secretary-General or his Special Envoy to report orally by 15 March 2023. The Council backs coordination between the UN and ASEAN envoys. It also demands full, safe, unhindered humanitarian access and action on the root causes in Rakhine State so Rohingya refugees can return voluntarily and safely.

South Africa's hold on Namibia drew a sharp rebuke in Resolution 269, adopted on 12 August 1969 by eleven votes to none with four abstentions. Pretoria had refused to obey an earlier resolution demanding it end its administration of the territory, which the UN regarded as held illegally. The Council framed the defiance as a challenge to its authority under the Charter.

The resolution condemns South Africa and declares that keeping its administration in Namibia amounts to an aggressive encroachment on UN authority and a denial of the Namibian people's sovereignty. It backs the legitimacy of the Namibians' struggle against that presence. Above all, it orders South Africa to withdraw its administration right away, with 4 October 1969 set as the last possible day.

The observer force on the Golan Heights received a new term on 28 May 1975, under Resolution 369. The force, called UNDOF, watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. Two disengagement agreements had been signed after the October war of 1973. Tension in the area still ran high.

The Council repeated that the two disengagement agreements were only a step. The real goal was to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973, which demanded a cease-fire and peace talks. The parties were called on to put that resolution into effect at once. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another six months. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken toward Resolution 338.

Israel applied for UN membership less than a year after independence. War with its Arab neighbors had only just paused. Resolution 69 was adopted on 4 March 1949. Nine members voted in favor. Egypt voted against. Britain abstained. Few admission votes have carried such political charge.

The Council formally judged Israel a peace-loving state. It found Israel able and willing to honor the Charter. On that basis, it recommended admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly admitted Israel that May. Supporters saw the vote as completing the UN's own 1947 partition decision. Opponents saw disputed questions left unresolved. The short text remains a founding document of Israel's international status.

Resolution 869, passed on 30 September 1993, may hold the record for the shortest grant in the Council's life. It stretched the term of UNPROFOR, the guard force in Croatia and Bosnia, by one day. The new end date was 1 October 1993. The lines that back old texts are all but as long as the grant itself. Care for the force's safety, and its free range on all its tasks, is the cause the text gives for its act, under the Charter's hard chapter.

A one-day term was a bridge, not a plan. Talks on the force's fate were stuck mid-stream, as safe zones and air strikes split the hall. The Council kept its grip on the file, and a long grant came days later.

Thirty years after it was created, the Cyprus peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1994. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 12 December, recommended six more months. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond the end of the year. Patrols still met interference near the buffer zone, which worried the Council. Resolution 969 was adopted unanimously on 21 December 1994.

The Council extended the force's stationing until 30 June 1995. It pressed both sides to cut the number of foreign troops on the island and to reduce defense spending. An agreement of 1989, under which posts along the cease-fire lines were left unmanned, was to be extended. The leaders of both communities were also urged to promote tolerance between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. The text set a path of small, practical steps, while the island's division itself remained unresolved.
wagstaffe-question-of-witchcraft-debated:
John Wagstaffe published The Question of Witchcraft Debated in 1669, in the confident early years of the Royal Society. His discourse argues outright against the very opinion of witches. Wagstaffe does not hedge or qualify; he denies the whole business, which made his tract the boldest skeptical sortie of the Restoration.

He attacks the evidence, the confessions, and the theology that supports them. Glanvill's circle answered him hotly, since much turned on the outcome. A landmark of English unbelief, his book shows skepticism leaving private doubt for open print. Wagstaffe wrote before it was safe, and his daring still gives the tract its charge.
wallace-malay-archipelago-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace spent eight years in the islands of Malaysia and Indonesia collecting birds, insects, and mammals. His 1869 book The Malay Archipelago tells that journey in full. He supported himself by selling specimens to museums and collectors back home. He wrote it after he and Darwin had jointly announced natural selection.

Wallace describes volcanoes, jungles, rare birds of paradise, and the peoples who guided and fed him. He also notes a sharp line dividing the islands' animal life, still called Wallace's Line by scientists. The narrative mixes danger, illness, and wonder with calm, exact observation. The book remains a founding story of biogeography, the study of where species live and why.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-1-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace published Volume 1 of The Malay Archipelago in 1869, after eight years of travel in the islands between Asia and Australia. Wallace earned his living by collecting specimens for sale. At the same time he formed, on his own, the theory of natural selection that Charles Darwin also reached.

Volume 1 follows Wallace through Singapore, Malaya, and the great islands of the west, describing forests, volcanoes, and peoples. He logged birds, insects, and mammals, and noted sharp changes in species from island to island. Those changes led to the line now called the Wallace Line. The book mixes adventure, sharp observation, and science of the first rank.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-2-1869:
Volume 2 of Wallace's Malay Archipelago appeared in 1869, completing his account of eight years in the islands of Southeast Asia and New Guinea. Alfred Russel Wallace had collected more than a hundred thousand specimens on the trip. The second volume moves east, toward the lands of birds of paradise.

Wallace described the Aru Islands, New Guinea, and the Moluccas, with their rare birds and distinct peoples. He compared island species on each side of a deep divide now called the Wallace Line. His notes on the bird of paradise hunts remain famous. The volume closes a travel book that is also a founding work of the study of how species are spread across the earth.
